<meta>This is the title page for the third volume of the collected Latin works of Giordano Bruno (1548–1600), the Italian philosopher and cosmologist. This specific edition was part of a major 19th-century effort to preserve his manuscripts.</meta>

# GIORDANO BRUNO OF NOLA <note>original: "Iordani Brvni Nolani"</note>

## WORKS WRITTEN IN LATIN

### PUBLISHED AT PUBLIC EXPENSE.

->VOLUME III.<-

->CONTAINING WORKS NOW PUBLISHED FOR THE FIRST TIME.<-

1. Lamp of the thirty statues.
2. The books of Aristotle’s *Physics* explained.
3. On magic and Theses on magic.
4. On mathematical magic.
5. On the principles of things, elements, and causes.
6. Lullian medicine. <note>original: "Medicina Lulliana"; refers to the mnemonic and philosophical system of Ramon Llull, which Bruno heavily adapted.</note>
7. On bonds in general. <note>Bruno's "bonds" (vinculis) refer to the psychological and magical ways in which people are influenced or "bound" by others.</note>

->INCLUDING FIVE COPPERPLATE ENGRAVINGS.<-

->EDITED BY<-

### F. TOCCO AND H. VITELLI. <note>Felice Tocco and Girolamo Vitelli were prominent 19th-century scholars of Renaissance philosophy and classical philology.</note>

---

## FLORENCE

->FROM THE PRESS OF THE SUCCESSORS OF LE MONNIER<-

->1891.<-

# INDEX OF ABBREVIATIONS. <note>original: "INDICE DELLE SIGLE"</note>

---

*A* = Augsburg Codex. <note>original: "Codice di Augusta"; refers to a manuscript held in the library at Augsburg.</note>
*B* = Erlangen Codex 1215.
*C* = Erlangen Codex 1279.
*E* = *B* + *C*, in the *Aristotelian Commentaries*. <note>original: "Commentarii Aristotelici"</note>
*M* = Moscow Codex. For the abbreviations *M*^b and *M*^f, see page 508.
*Br* = folios 1-5^recto (= pages 637-652) and 162-168^recto, line 4 (= pages 571-597, 14) of the Moscow Codex (*M*). <term>recto: the front side of a leaf of parchment or paper</term>
*X* = folios 168^recto, line 5 to 180^recto (= pages 597, 15-633) of the Moscow Codex (*M*).
*A*^1, *B*^1 etc. = the reading <note>original: "lezione"; refers to the specific wording found in a manuscript</note> of manuscripts *A*, *B*, etc., before correction.

The symbols [ ] and ( ) indicate, respectively, text that is superfluous and text that is missing, either in all manuscripts or in the one upon which the edition <term>recensione: the process of critical revision and comparison of manuscripts to establish a text</term> is based.

<meta>This page continues from the list of abbreviations (sigla) and serves as the preface to the third volume of Giordano Bruno's Latin works. The editors, Felice Tocco and Girolamo Vitelli, are detailing the provenance of the manuscripts used to establish the text.</meta>

<meta>Handwritten shelfmarks at top: A3, 1879, v. 3</meta>

Until November of last year, the only manuscript known to us containing unpublished works by Bruno <note>Giordano Bruno (1548–1600), the Italian philosopher, mathematician, and occultist who was burned at the stake for heresy.</note> was the Noroff Codex (= *M*), a photographic copy of which had been sent to us by the Ministry of Public Instruction. However, before we began printing the volume we are now publishing, Professor Remigio Stölzle of the University of Würzburg informed us of a codex in the library of Augsburg (= *A*). Thanks to his efforts, this was generously sent to us by the librarian, Dr. Dobel. He also informed us of two codices from the library of Erlangen, 1215 (= *B*) and 1279 (= *C*), for which he himself kindly prepared a copy for our use. In our own name and that of all Bruno scholars, we express here our deepest gratitude to the learned professor, and we trust that we have not too unskillfully profited from his research and labors. 

Furthermore, for the *On the Principles of Things* <note>original: "De rerum principiis"</note>, the *On Bonds in General* <note>original: "De vinculis in genere"</note>, and many passages of the *Lullian Medicine* <note>original: "Medicina Lulliana"; refers to Bruno's works influenced by the logical and mnemonic systems of Ramon Llull</note>, which were often illegible in the photograph of the Noroff Codex, we appealed—not in vain—to the kindness of Professor Niccolò Grote of the University of Moscow. He first provided us with a copy of folios 89<sup>v</sup>—90<sup>r</sup> and 94<sup>v</sup>—95<sup>r</sup> <term>folio: a leaf of a manuscript; "v" (verso) is the back side, "r" (recto) is the front side</term> of the codex, executed by Mr. Al. Basistoff and collated <term>collated: the process of comparing a copy against the original to identify and correct errors</term> by Professors Zvétaeff and Korsch; he subsequently put us in contact with Mr. Giorgio Barténew, who had the courtesy

<meta>This page concludes the editors' acknowledgments and begins describing the editorial methodology for Giordano Bruno's unpublished Latin works. It highlights the collaboration with Cesare Paoli and discusses the challenges of working from photographic reproductions of manuscripts.</meta>

<page-num>IV</page-num>

to collate the parts of the codex <term>codex: a manuscript book, as opposed to a scroll</term> mentioned above. $^1$ To all these gentlemen we profess our deepest gratitude, and we shall be happy to be of service to them in our turn. Nor do we thank any less warmly our dearest colleague and friend Cesare Paoli, whose expertise and experience in paleography <term>paleography: the study and deciphering of ancient or historical handwriting</term> often succeeded in deciphering passages that were entirely undecipherable to us, especially in Bruno's own handwritten pages.

All four codices are described and illustrated with sufficient detail, and their respective value is determined in the pages following this preface. In those pages, the reader will also find what we have been able to establish regarding the chronology of Bruno’s works, which are now being published for the first time. Therefore, we shall speak here only of the method we followed in the review of individual works; however, we wish first to provide some additions to the edition of the *Aristotelian Commentaries* and the *Lullian Medicine* <note>original: "Commentarii Aristotelici" and "Medicina Lulliana"</note>.

In the edition of the *Commentaries*, we have generally ignored the marginal notes—almost all of which are of no importance—that appear in the codices (*B* and *C*); we have decided to transcribe them here, so that their absence will not be regretted.

->p. 301, 12 Substances are created simply; this becomes that. In an accidental way, a man becomes just. <note>original: "Substantiae simpliciter fiunt, hoc fit hoc; accidentaliter homo fit iustus." This is a reference to Aristotle's distinction between essential change (a thing coming into being) and accidental change (a thing changing its properties, like a man becoming "just").</note> *B*<-

$^1$ So that the reader may be able to appreciate how much we owe to these copies and collations <term>collation: the process of comparing different manuscripts to identify variations in the text</term>, we wish to note expressly that they were not only extremely useful for the pages that appeared illegible in the photograph, but they also gave us the means to avoid innumerable errors. Without them, we would have in good conscience accepted absurd readings as the actual text of the codex, caused by—we know not how—the photography itself. A few of the strangest examples may serve to explain: p. 666, 4 "is conquered" <note>original: "devincitur"</note>] "is tamed" <note>original: "domatur"</note> in the photograph of $M$ ($M^f$); 669, 2. 3 "is defined" <note>original: "definitur"</note>] "is named" <note>original: "denominatur"</note>, if anything, in $M^f$; 689, 13 "full of seed for Venus" <note>original: "ad Venerem semine plenus"; Venus here refers to physical love or procreation.</note>] "that appearance toward the Bond" <note>original: "ad Vinculum specien"</note> (sic!) in $M^f$; 14 "that" <note>original: "ille"</note>] "and" <note>original: "atque"</note> $M^f$; 19 "power from music" <note>original: "virtutem e musica"</note>] "a bond from Venus" <note>original: "vinculum e Veneri"</note> $M^f$ etc. We have indicated some other oddities in the notes (at p. 691, 23. 696, 1 etc.), but in general, we have silently accepted the readings guaranteed for us by Barténew or Basistoff, or by both together.

<meta>This page continues the editors' transcription of marginal notes found in the manuscripts of Giordano Bruno's Aristotelian commentaries, specifically from Codices B and C. It follows the discussion of how substances are formed.</meta>

<page-num>V</page-num>

**301, 14** The creation of all $^1$ things belongs to substances; likewise, in the Book of Moses <note>original: "Lib. Moises," referring to the Book of Genesis</note> he applies "becoming" only to substances. From this, it follows that light is not an accident <term>accident: a quality or property that exists only within a substance, like "redness" in an apple, rather than existing on its own</term>, since Moses says it was "made" $^2$, a term reserved for substances. That which is said to "become" or "be made" is always a subject, always a substance. *B* — To become is the property of substances; Moses also applies becoming only to substances. Thus, because light is said to have been made, one may argue that it is a substance. *C* — Cf. *On the Principles of Things* <note>original: "De rerum principiis"</note> p. 513, 3 ff.

**302, 5** Those things which exist simply <note>meaning, as primary qualities or accidents</note> are not said to "become": whiteness does not "become" [as a substance does], but is "in-made" or "made-with." *B*

**309, 3** Matter is nothing, because it has no form. In the same way, a letter is nothing because it lacks a word. Matter is, in a certain sense, nothing, because nothing derives its essential reason from matter; it has no form because it contains all forms; it has no single title because it holds them all. *B*

**310, 9** *following the word "connumeramus"*] Three things must be considered in matter: subjection—and the logic $^3$ of this subjection is one and the same; the appetite <term>appetite: a philosophical term for a natural inclination or "longing" of one thing for another</term> for receiving forms; and the power to receive something, which is $^4$ the lack of that which it wishes to receive. Appetite exists in matter because form does not long for itself, nor for its opposite; but matter, in a way, longs for what surrounds it. It does not long for things through itself, because all things are eventually dissolved back into it. To receive, to take, and to have belongs to matter; to be received, to be taken, and to be held belongs to form. That which longs is matter, just as the female longs for the male, or the ugly longs for the beautiful—not because matter is inherently ugly, for it is not, but it longs for beauty by happenstance. Form [gives] nothing... $^5$ to matter, nor does it take away, because matter is ungeneratable <term>ungeneratable: something that was not "brought into being" from something else, but exists fundamentally</term>; that which is ungeneratable is [not] incorruptible: such is matter. Matter does not long for this or that specific form, but for form in a general sense. *B*

**311, 17** How deprivation is a form of corruption. $^6$ *B*

**312, 2** The ancients were said to have argued with Light concerning primacy and rule; their dispute was finally settled by the reasoning $^7$ that Matter is the first and greatest of all things and contains the universe in potential, like a mother and a womb; light, however, is like a father and a sower. *B*

---

$^1$ Perhaps *omnis* (all) and later *Book of [Genesis]*?
$^2$ Read *dicat* (might say).
$^3$ Perhaps *ratione* (by the logic)?
$^4$ *illud et est* (that and is)] perhaps *id est* (that is)?
$^5$ Perhaps *Form gives nothing to matter nor takes anything away, because matter is ungeneratable.*
$^6$ For this and the two following notes, see the facsimile of manuscript *B* at the end of the volume. The second note (at line 312, 2) is taken from *The Torch of the Thirty Statues* <note>original: "Lampas trig. stat."</note> p. 37, 11-15.
$^7$ *ē rōe*] read *ea ratione [componitur]* (by that reason [it is settled]).

<meta>This page continues the transcription of marginal notes from Manuscripts B and C, further exploring Aristotelian physics and metaphysics, specifically the relationship between form, matter, and the nature of change in substances and living things.</meta>

<page-num>VI</page-num>

**312, 10** It is subjected without passion <term>passion: in this context, the state of being acted upon or undergoing a change from an external force</term>, which is characteristic of those things that are corrupted <note>original: "corrumpuntur," meaning to perish or break down</note>. *B.*

**312, 14.** For all material forms, which consist in a certain composition <gloss>1</gloss>, come as it were to a composite; their subject is not prime matter <term>prime matter: the most basic, formless reality that has the potential to become any physical thing</term> having pure potentiality, but already something existing in act <note>original: "actu existens," meaning it is already a specific, realized thing</note>. — **17** Transmigrating from species to species <gloss>2</gloss>, such as chyle <term>chyle: a milky fluid produced during digestion</term> into blood. — **25** When a corpse is made from a human, and consequently a transformation occurs from one species to another <gloss>3</gloss>, some think that a resolution into prime matter does not occur, but that while the body's form and quantity remain, the state of being a corpse succeeds upon the substance of the matter. The opposite is true: although it happens in an instant, it still resolves into the ultimate matter; for accidental forms follow the substantial one—dimensions, qualities, etc. Those things which are in the subject itself differ in species from those that were in the preceding one, even though they appear very similar. Accidents do not immediately succeed the form in relation to matter, but in relation to the substantial forms <note>substantial form: the essential nature that makes a thing what it is (e.g., "human-ness")</note> that mediate them. Regarding matter, it is not accidents that succeed, but substantial forms, just as in the reception of "humanity" there is a substantial form. *B*

**316, 3** Because Aristotle proposed at the beginning of Book I to discuss principles, causes, and elements, and in the previous book he completed the discussion of those things which have the nature of a principle and element. *B*

**317, 25** *See our note.* <note>original: "v. la nostra nota," referring to the modern editor's commentary</note>

**318, 4** What is natural is a composite of matter and form. *BC*

**320, 19** Abstraction is not from matter simply <note>the manuscript of Codex C transposes this to "simply from matter"</note>, but from particular matter. *BC*

**322, 19** Essence exists in two ways: by which something is physically or really, insofar as it is something; and logically or intentionally <term>intentionality: in medieval philosophy, this refers to the existence of an object in the mind or as an object of thought</term>. *BC*

**324, 23 sq.** *See our note.*

**325, 16** Regarding animals and beasts, one does not speak of fortune, but of chance <note>Aristotle distinguished between "fortune" (luck involving human choice) and "chance" (random events in nature)</note>. *B*

**327, 3** Things turned out (?) as well as if they had been made for that specific cause. *B*

**331, 24** Because for Aristotle this is ...... yet to treat the final [cause], therefore this is not the place here ....... regarding form. *B*

**343, 3** *See our note.*

<meta>This page continues the transcription and commentary of Giordano Bruno’s notes on Aristotelian physics, transitioning into the specific application of these principles to "Lullian Medicine"—a system based on the works of the medieval polymath Ramon Llull. The text moves from abstract definitions of action and matter to the practical classification of medicinal substances and humors.</meta>

<page-num>VII</page-num>

**347, 6** The word is not the agent, but the means through which action occurs; the word does not touch, but is touched by the word; it is not the *what* <note>the essence or thing itself</note>, but the *by which*; for actions belong to the subjects <note>original: "suppositorum," referring to the underlying individual substances that perform actions</note>. *B*

**348, 14** All action takes place in those things which share one common matter. *B*

**349, 7** Before anything is altered, it first undergoes a passion <term>passion: here meaning the state of being acted upon or receiving an impression from an external force</term>; alteration follows this passion, and corruption <note>original: "corruptio," the process of a thing ceasing to be what it was</note> follows alteration. — **13** Qualities are those things whose existence is not considered necessary. — **I.** They are said to be either generated or corrupted, because "to be generated" is to be composed of matter and form, and "to be corrupted" is to be broken down into matter and form; for the generation of a substance is a kind of birth, and the corruption of a substance is the emergence of some other substance. — **16** Digression. — **28** Likewise, it is clear <gloss>1: belongs to</gloss> that amber and rhubarb are used for yellow bile <note>original: "cholera"</note>, polypody <note>a type of fern</note> for yellow bile <note>original: "flava bilis"</note>, and scammony <note>a binding plant resin used as a purgative</note> for black bile <note>original: "atra bilis"</note>. In these treatments, one must be careful; if the simple medicine added is too weak, it may not draw out the humor, but instead be drawn in itself; it ought to comfort and strengthen the powers of the drawing agent. *B*

**367, 8** According to the four elements. *B*

**370, 3** It is called "straight" in the manner of Aristotle, since even this transformation seems to greatly imitate a circle, if it is considered rightly. *C* <gloss>2: Manuscript B is damaged on these pages.</gloss>

In that part of the "Lullian Medicine," for which we had the more extensive version in Besler’s hand <note>Jerome Besler was Bruno's assistant and scribe</note> (from page 571 to page 616, 8), we have inserted into the notes a few variations from the shorter original version. To provide a sufficiently exact idea of it, we transcribe here the first pages (written in Bruno’s hand).

## Artful Method of Medicine from Lullian Fragments.

<margin>162r</margin>
The proper subject of medicine is the human body, insofar as it is capable of being healthy or ill.

**§ I.** Our intention is not to provide a full treatise on medicine, but only to provide the method of applying medicine to the certain General Art of Lull, to which all sciences and faculties generally per— <note>the text cuts off, likely intended to be "pertain" or "apply"</note>

--- Page 12 ---
<meta>This page continues Giordano Bruno’s application of Aristotelian physics and Ramon Llull’s combinatorial logic to the field of medicine. Having previously discussed the nature of matter and action, the text now focuses on the definition of health as a specific proportion of elements and how a physician must analyze the unique "complexion" (temperament) of an individual patient.</meta>

<page-num>VIII</page-num>

...can be applied, through which method everyone will arrive at a true knowledge of the whole of medicine.

**§ II.** Health in the human body is considered insofar as it is that proportion consisting in the four elements <note>The classic four elements: Earth, Air, Fire, and Water</note> from which the matter of the human body is composed; health, therefore, is nothing other than the likeness of this proportion.

**§ III.** The elemental nature <term>elementativa: the power or principle of the elements</term> has a double mode of being: namely, objective and subjective. In its objective being, it is equally graded from the aforementioned four simple elements; and because from an equal proportion (as Aristotle says) neither action nor passion <term>passion: the state of being acted upon by an external force</term> follows, it is therefore ungeneratable and incorruptible (as the same Aristotle says); therefore, the physician can find that an "equal weight" exists.

**§ IIII.** In its subjective being, however, it exists in two ways: either in any given sphere, and thus the elements in it are unequally graded according to their qualities, because substance does not admit of "more" or "less" <note>In Aristotelian logic, an essence or substance cannot be "more" or "less" itself (a dog is not more or less "dog"), whereas qualities like heat can vary in intensity</note>; for each thing in its sphere has dominance by reason of the property of its place and the heavens—both in a diminished state in the concavity of the moon, where fire is dominant, and so with the others in their spheres—or in elemental things <term>elementata: complex bodies composed of the elements</term> which <insert>after "which," the word "by which" was deleted in the original manuscript</insert> are generated and corrupted in three of the aforementioned spheres; therefore the physician investigates such a mode in them, and especially in man.

**§ V.** However, because the physician does not heal "man" in general <note>original: "in comuni," a non-standard spelling of "communi" characteristic of Bruno's Latin</note>, but Socrates <note>A standard philosophical placeholder for a specific, individual person</note>, he therefore investigates such a mode of being in the individual person whom he intends to cure or whose health he intends to preserve.

**§ VI.** Through the Rule of G <note>In Ramon Llull’s system, the "Rule of G" refers to a specific combinatorial method for determining the proportions and qualities of a subject</note>, he must see of what quality and temperament <term>complexion: the specific balance of the four humors in an individual</term> a person is, properly and appropriately; for to be ignorant of the nature of the temperament is to be ignorant of curative or preservative medicine.

**§ VII.** Moreover, the temperament can be known in several ways: first, by investigating the internal birth of the person, which occurred at the instant of the introduction of the rational soul into the body—a body prepared by natural agents for the reception of the soul. At that instant, a spiritual <note>original: "spiritalis," abbreviated as "spalis" in the manuscript</note> influence reigned [gap in text], by grace of which fire has dominance, as in the choleric person; or air, as in the sanguine; or water, as in the phlegmatic; or earth, as in the melancholic. And he should not [merely] know the birth—

<summary>This page defines health as a specific proportional balance of the four elements and argues that a physician must move beyond general theories to treat the unique temperament (complexion) of an individual patient, determined by the moment the rational soul enters the body.</summary>
<keywords>health, four elements, Giordano Bruno, Lullian medicine, temperament, humors, rational soul, Rule of G, Aristotle</keywords>

--- Page 13 ---
<meta>This page continues Giordano Bruno’s exposition on medical theory, specifically focusing on how the timing of birth (nativitas) and the influence of celestial bodies dictate the "complexion" or temperament of a patient. He moves from the theoretical balance of elements to the practical difficulties physicians face in diagnosing these states.</meta>

<page-num>IX</page-num>

...[physic]al [birth] <note>The text is fragmented here, likely referring to the "terminal" or physical birth into the world</note> by which one comes into the light, except so that through it one can arrive at the knowledge of the first and true birth.

**§ VIII.** And because this seems impossible, since such a birth is irregular, it is no wonder if astrologers and physicians seem to err in their judgments. It can, however, be investigated in another way; <margin>**162v**</margin> for at conception, the woman's legs ache, menstruation ceases to flow, and there are many other signs in both the man and the woman—which I do not wish to recount—through which one can arrive at a true knowledge of the aforementioned birth.

**§ IX.** The complexion <term>complexion: in medieval medicine, this refers to the specific "temperament" or mixture of the four humors (blood, yellow bile, black bile, and phlegm) unique to an individual</term> is also read in the physiognomy <note>The practice of judging character or health from facial features</note> of men and in their actions; for instance, it is clear regarding the choleric, who are easily moved and wish <gloss>1</gloss> to dominate others just as fire does. The sanguine are lively, courtly, and playful, etc. The phlegmatic... are melancholic, etc.

**§ X.** However, the complexion is known in a truer way in those suffering from fever. For the evidence of this, it must be noted that the human body, being composed of the four elements, is governed by the celestial bodies; and thus the human body is ruled by them according to their various aspects <term>aspects: the specific angular positions of planets and stars relative to each other and the Earth, believed to influence terrestrial health</term>. Such aspects vary according to two motions: namely, that of the First Mover <term>First Mover: the outermost sphere of the universe in the Ptolemaic system, which rotates from east to west every 24 hours</term>, leading the other spheres with it, and that of the planets, which [move] from the west, etc. <gloss>2</gloss> Thus, from their different conjunctions and different aspects, various effects are generated in these lower realms <note>The "lower realms" refers to the sublunary world—Earth—where things are subject to change and decay</note>.

**§ XI.** Therefore, a physician must have knowledge of all the aforementioned things, unless he wishes to cure by mere chance; and because the four elements are in continuous motion, their operations and effects are diversified by different aspects. For this reason, the appetites of the healthy and the sick differ, and the circumstances of health and illness are varied, such as fever, pulse, urine, etc.

**§ XII.** Furthermore, it should be noted that according to this continuous motion in a natural day, each element has its own region <note>Meaning a specific "time-slot" or period of influence during the day</note>. For fire has three hours before noon and three after noon; earth has three before sunset and three after; water has three hours before midnight and three after; and air has three hours before dawn and three after. If a choleric person suffers from fever at noon and is healthy at midnight, and a melancholic person suffers from fever at sunset and is healthy at the dawn of day, a phlegmatic person suffers from fever at midnight...

...and he is healthy at noon; the sanguine person experiences fever at the dawn of the day and is healthy at the setting of the sun.

**§ XIII.** The complexion <term>complexion: in medieval medicine, the specific balance of the four humors (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile) that determines a person's health and personality</term> is also read in healthy urine. Although such urine is commonly said to be reddish-amber <note>original: *subrufa*</note>, it nevertheless varies in some way according to the different complexions. For instance, in a choleric person it is thin and clear; in a sanguine person it is a good golden color; in a phlegmatic person it leans toward whiteness; and in a melancholic person, it leans in some way toward blackness. All these things indicate the subject "I" <note>In the Lullian system used by Bruno, capital letters often represent specific variables or subjects in a logical diagram.</note>.

**§ XIV.** Once knowledge of any person's complexion and health has been obtained according to distributive justice <note>In this context, the proportional and proper balance of elements within the body</note>, infirmity must be investigated in those aforementioned <gloss>The word "aforementioned" was corrected or perhaps crossed out in the original manuscript</gloss> chambers. Specifically, this is done in the chamber of the fourth figure *DIK*, through which the physician must inquire into the primary principles in medicine and how they relate to lower things. There he will find that it consists of the four active and passive qualities, etc., and in the chambers *EIK*, *EFG*, *FGH*, and *GHI* <note>These "chambers" refer to the compartments in Ramon Llull’s combinatorial wheels, which Bruno adapted to organize medical knowledge</note>.

<margin>163r</margin>
**§ XV.** In the final chamber *GHI*, the investigation begins first through *H*, because the physician sees in a sick man that the vegetative power <term>vegetative power: the biological soul responsible for basic life functions like nutrition, growth, and reproduction</term> is weakened in its capacities. This is evident because he does not have a properly functioning appetite for judging what is sweet, bitter, etc. The digestive and expulsive powers also fail; but this could not happen unless the elementative power <note>original: *elementativa*; the power that regulates the four elements (fire, air, water, earth) within the body</note> itself were failing. 

Such a defect arises either by reason of "repletion" <note>an excess of bodily fluids or humors that causes a blockage</note> which hinders the movement of the elements, or by a wound through which the continuity of the passages <gloss>original: *meatuum*</gloss> is lost. This causes pain, and thus the subject suffers. On the contrary, both appetite and instinct cry out through pain, and the cause of that pain is the vegetative power *H*, which cannot perform its actions; its underlying cause is the elementative power, which cannot maintain its continuous motion. For, as has been said, the four elements in the human body each have a motion in their own region, and they complete that motion within twenty-four hours.

**§ XVI.** If the physician knows the aforementioned regions well, he will be able to find the cause of the disease and administer the appropriate medicine to the patient. To understand this, the following figure is provided <gloss>The original manuscript contains various incomplete sketches of this figure on different pages, with a note at the end of folio 163v stating "The figure follows"</gloss>.

# Second Treatise.

**§ I.** The physician must investigate the cause of this, even if he is not an expert in astrology <note>In the Renaissance, medicine and astrology were deeply linked; the "cause" refers to the celestial influences on the humors discussed on the previous page.</note>. And for this purpose, he should construct a figure made of two circles, one containing the other. The larger circle signifies the motion of the entire sphere <note>original: *universae sphaerae*</note>, while the smaller represents the motion of the seven planets; for the larger moves from east to west, but the smaller moves in the opposite direction.

**§ II.** And according to these two motions is the motion of the human body, naturally and elementally, etc. etc. ^1

Complying then with the wish of the Royal Ministry, from whom we hold the commission for this edition, we have added to the four facsimiles of Bruno’s manuscripts a reproduction of a page from the records of the **Company of Saint John the Beheaded** <note>Also known as the *Arciconfraternita di San Giovanni Decollato*, this was a lay brotherhood in Rome whose mission was to provide spiritual comfort to those condemned to death.</note> (volume XVI, page 87), where information has been preserved for us regarding the final hours of life of the man condemned to the stake. Here is the transcription: ^2

->Thursday, the 16th of the same month.<-

At 2 hours of the night <note>Historical Italian timekeeping began the day at sunset; "2 hours of the night" would be approximately 7:00 or 8:00 PM.</note>, notice was given to the Company that in the morning justice was to be carried out upon an impenitent <gloss>The original manuscript uses the abbreviation *InPente* for "impenitente," meaning someone who refused to renounce their beliefs</gloss> man; and therefore at 6 hours of the night, the comforters and the chaplain gathered in Saint Ursula; and having gone to the prison of the **Torre di Nona** <note>A notorious prison in Rome located near the Tiber.</note>, entered into our chapel and performed the usual prayers. The following person condemned to death was delivered to us, namely:

->To the Most Distinguished and Most Reverend Lord Prorector<-

Giordano Bruno the Nolan, excommunicated in public sermons by the primary pastor and superintendent of the church of Helmstedt—who made himself judge and executioner in his own action and in an unheard-of case—humbly requests, by the tenor of these presents, to be heard by the clarity of your Most Reverend Magnificence and by the dignity of the entire Distinguished Senate in public assembly <note>original: *concistorio*</note>, protesting against the public execution of that most unjust and private sentence; so that if anything should happen by right <note>original: *iure*</note> against his rank and worthy reputation, he may at least know it to have happened justly:² although according to the sentiment of Seneca:

> He who has decided anything while one side was unheard,
> though he may have decided what is right, has not been just himself. ³

Finally, regarding the critical edition <term>recensione: the scholarly process of comparing manuscript versions to establish the most accurate text</term> of each of the works published here by us for the first time, our task was very simple for those writings of which only a single codex <term>codex: a manuscript book</term> survived; in these cases, the edition is equivalent to a reproduction as faithful as possible of the manuscript that has preserved them for us. Such is the condition of the *Remarks on the Lullian Lamp* (vol. II, 2) reproduced from Codex *A*, of *On the Principles of Things*, of *On Mathematical Magic*, and of Bruno's own handwritten notes (pp. 637-652) reproduced from Codex *M*. Nor was the procedure much different for the two treatises *On Bonds in General* and *Lullian Medicine*, although in the former, the autograph notes were not to be overlooked wherever they could be used to correct the version written by Besler <note>Hieronymus Besler was Bruno's student and scribe, who recorded many of his lectures and dictations</note>, and in the latter, the original version (partially in Bruno's hand) had to be taken into account to correct and complete the imperfect final version, which was also written by Besler. <meta>This page continues the editors' explanation of their methodology for establishing the text of Giordano Bruno's works. They are describing the hierarchy of the manuscripts they used—specifically Codices A, B, M, and C—and justifying why they included or excluded certain variations in their scholarly notes.</meta>

...to be founded respectively on *B* and *M*, nor should any value be attributed to the variants found in *C* other than that of conjectures, except for those instances where they might be considered a more exact reading of the original in passages that were barely or not at all legible in the photograph provided to us. And naturally, when these variants seemed correct to us, we accepted them into the text with no more and no less confidence than that with which we accept our own conjectures. Thus also for the *Lamp of the Thirty Statues* <note>original: *Lampas triginta statuarum*; one of Bruno's works on memory and magic</note>, the foundation of the critical edition <term>recensione: the scholarly process of reconstructing a text by comparing different manuscript versions</term> is Codex *A*, from which the other manuscript (*M*) undoubtedly derives, and through which this work has been handed down to us. However, it was not possible to place all the variants of *M* before the reader's eyes without overloading the critical apparatus <term>apparato: the scholarly notes, usually at the bottom of the page, that track every difference between various manuscripts</term> with dull or useless readings; therefore, we have provided only a portion of them, and we have certainly given far more than was worth the effort. ¹ For not only will all those readings from *M* be found which may serve as more or less probable conjectural corrections, but even in places where the text of *A* is unsatisfactory and *M* offers variants—even if they are absurd—these were scrupulously recorded. Furthermore, wherever we were forced to amend the text ourselves through conjecture, we likewise noted the corruptions <term>corruttele: errors or distorted passages in a manuscript resulting from poor copying</term> found in *M*; thus, we reported in the apparatus a considerable series of gross errors and arbitrary modifications, for the sole purpose of sufficiently illustrating the character of the manuscript itself. Given this, it is easy to understand that when using our apparatus, one must decide case by case on the value of the variants from *M* to understand why they were included—a significant inconvenience, were our edition not primarily intended for those who already know how to critically handle historical texts.

¹ But we do not deny that some more or less useful variant might have been omitted; where a doubt later occurred to us, we mention it in the *Errata-corrige* <term>Errata-corrige: a list of corrections for errors discovered after printing</term>.

->XV<-

Others will certainly not hold this against us; rather, they will likely smile at the persistence with which we have preferred monstrous corruptions in the text over the arbitrary corrections found in manuscripts that lack authority.

Having thus reached the conclusion of our work—which was, for the most part, a most thankless task—we wish we could declare ourselves entirely satisfied with what we have accomplished. But unfortunately, it is only now that we perceive many of the difficulties presented by an edition of Bruno’s Latin works. For it must be confessed that we set about the task without an exact knowledge of Bruno’s specific vocabulary and grammar. From this stem many inconsistencies. Forms that seemed intolerable to us in the first volumes published, we were forced to resign ourselves to tolerating in the subsequent volumes; grammatical errors that we initially attributed to printers and copyists, we later became convinced were to be blamed on the author himself.

The orthography <term>orthography: the conventional spelling system of a language</term> itself, at least for a good part, could have been reduced to a more uniform system and one more in line with the author’s intentions with the help of the autographs <term>autografi: manuscripts written in the author's own hand</term>; however, these were unknown to us when we began printing the first volumes. For this reason, the spelling varies according to the different editions and the different manuscripts taken as the basis for the critical text <term>recensione: the scholarly process of reconstructing a text by comparing different manuscript versions</term> (*A* in the *Lamp of the Thirty Statues* <note>original: *Lampas trig. stat.*</note>, *B* in the *Commentaries*, *M* in the rest), and such orthographic variations are not rare even within the same line. To this must be added genuine errors of interpretation that we were unable to avoid, useless or false conjectures, here and there a few swapped sigla <term>sigla: abbreviations or symbols used in manuscripts to represent words or names</term>, and some inaccuracies in the numbers: in short, all those inconveniences which, in greater or lesser proportion, are never entirely avoided, and which every editor believes they would avoid if they were given the chance to start the work over from the beginning. But, on the whole, we would not be sincere if we did not express our conviction that scholars of the Nolano <note>the Nolano: a common nickname for Giordano Bruno, referring to his birthplace of Nola</note> must...

# THE MANUSCRIPTS OF THE LATIN WORKS OF BRUNO

## NOW PUBLISHED FOR THE FIRST TIME.

We are aware of only four codices <term>codices: plural of codex, a manuscript in book form rather than a scroll</term> of Bruno’s Latin works. Of these, the most important is undoubtedly *M* <note>The letter 'M' here designates the *Mosquensis* or Moscow manuscript.</note>, both because of the volume of works it contains and because it has preserved quite a few pages written in Bruno's own hand. It was described by Noroff in his catalog,¹ and with extreme accuracy by Lutoslawski in the *Archive for the History of Philosophy* <note>original: ‘Archiv für Gesch. der Philos.’, a major German academic journal</note> II (1889), pp. 526-571. We have used the photographs sent to us by the Ministry of Public Instruction, as we have never seen the original; we therefore refer to Lutoslawski's excellent description for everything that is either unnecessary to reproduce here or cannot be exactly described without inspecting the original.

The codex, "exported from Germany" (Noroff cited in Berti's *Documents* p. 112), was put up for sale in Paris in 1866 by the bookseller Tross; it was purchased shortly after by Mr. Abraham de Noroff (Berti, *Documents* p. 89 ff.), and is currently kept in Moscow in the Rumyantsev Museum <note>The Rumyantsev Museum was Moscow's first public museum; its manuscript collection is now part of the Russian State Library.</note>. It consists of 182 leaves (or rather 181, as number 180 was skipped by mistake; there are also two blank leaves after folio 160, see Lutoslawski pp. 527 and 559), all of which are paper except for folio 161. They contain:

*a*) 1-6: Autograph <term>autograph: a document written in the author's own handwriting</term> notes by Bruno.

Finally, the front side of folio 6 (the back side is blank) contains a figure identical to the one we find on page 358 of the *Aristotelian Commentaries*, with these differences alone: that *A East humid* and *C West dry* are respectively on the right and left instead of the left and right; therefore, the words of the internal quadrilateral are also swapped in position, so that between *South* and *East* there is *Air*, *Water* between *East* and *Midnight* <note>original: "Merinoc(tium)", a contraction for midnight or the middle of the night</note>, *Earth* between *Midnight* and *West*, and *Fire* between *West* and *South*. In the margin is written:

> Distillation in B <gloss>1</gloss> dissolution of freezing (?) D.
> Distillation in C dissolution of solidification D.
> Dissolution in A solidification <gloss>2</gloss> of vapors in B.
> Distillation in D solidification of vapors of stronger evaporation in B.
> Therefore, diurnal <note>daytime</note> distillations arise from causes contrary to nocturnal distillations.
> And these must be considered whether they arise from the side of the container or the side of the content: whether they proceed from both: likewise whether from a principal cause or through *antiperistasis* <note>original: "antiperistasin"; a philosophical term for the intensification of a quality when it is surrounded by its opposite, such as heat concentrating inside a body when the exterior is cold</note>.

b) 7-27: ('On Magic'); <gloss>3</gloss> p. 397-454.
c) 28-38: ('Theses on Magic'); p. 455-491.
d) 39-54: 'On the Principles, Elements, and Causes of Things', <gloss>4</gloss> p. 509-567.
e) 55-69: Incomplete draft of the 'Lullian Medicine' <note>Referring to the medical systems of Ramon Llull, which Bruno adapted</note>; see p. 570.

->XXI<-

*k*) 162-180 (marked 181): ‘Lullian Medicine’ <note>original: "Medicina Lulliana"; referring to the work of Ramon Llull, whose combinatorial methods deeply influenced Bruno's own systems of logic and memory</note>, complete original version; see p. 570.

*l*) 181 (marked 182): on the front side <note>original: "recto"</note> is an incomplete sketch of the figure that we have reproduced on p. 577 from folio 57r (cf. above p. x note 3). The back side <note>original: "verso"</note> is blank.

Folios 1-6, 162-168r (up to line 4), and 181 (perhaps also 161?) are in Bruno's own hand; folios 168v (from line 5) to 180 are by an unknown copyist; all the rest, namely 7-160, is in the hand of Girolamo Besler of Nuremberg <note>Besler was a student and amanuensis—a literary assistant—to Bruno during his time in Germany</note>. Cf. Sigwart p. 297 sq. That the first six folios and the last twenty were not originally part of the volume <note>original: "codice"</note> is clearly shown by a foliation <note>The numbering of the leaves in a manuscript</note> older than the one used for the current state of the manuscript. According to this older numbering, which Noroff refers to and Lutoslawski overlooks, the current folios 7-69, 70-86, and 87-98 were respectively 1-63, 66-82, and 84-95. This shows a difference of 6, 4, and 3 from the later numbering, as there were two blank leaves (we do not know if they were numbered) after 63 (now 69), and one after 82 (now 86); similarly, the current folios 162-181 were originally numbered 1-20. Furthermore, ‘The Torch of the Thirty Statues’ <note>original: "Lampas triginta statuarum"</note>, comprising folios 99-160r, also has its own numbering, and it is natural that this should be so; for although this work—like all that is contained in folios 7-98—is in Besler’s hand, it is written with much greater care than the preceding treatises. Unlike most of those, it was not written under dictation, but was certainly copied.

However, not even all of the current folios 7-98 formed a single homogeneous whole from the beginning. In fact, the paper of 87-98 (‘On Bonds in General’ <note>original: "De vinculis in genere"</note>) has a watermark <note>original: "marca di fabbrica"; a translucent design in paper used to identify the maker</note> identical to that of 99-160, but different from that of 7-10, as well as from the paper used for folio 6 and folios 11-86. Yet, despite the identity of the paper, 87-98 and 99-160 were originally two separate quires <note>original: "fascicoli"; sets of leaves nested together</note>. In the first, one can see the holes from an older binding at different distances from those of the common binding

Thus, to cite some examples that the reader can find in the facsimile, no paleography <note>the study and interpretation of historical handwriting</note> is sufficient to recognize *vocation* <note>original Latin: "vocatione"; referring to a calling or name</note> on page 254, line 19; *and choosing through it* <note>original Latin: "et per ipsam eligentes"</note> on 255, 2; *it matches* <note>original Latin: "congruit"</note> on 255, 16; *or by resolution* <note>original Latin: "seu resolutione"</note> (before *by a certain*) on 256, 11, etc. Certainly, after seeing that the Augsburg codex <note>the "codex of Augusta"</note> on page 255, line 12 has *the soul truly does not* <note>original Latin: "anima vero non"</note>, it is not difficult to perceive that Besler intended *no soul truly* <note>original Latin: "nulla vero anima"</note>; but would one have read it that way at first glance? And the same applies to *truly* <note>original Latin: "vero"</note> (it looks more like *word!* <note>original Latin: "verbo"</note>), *to be made* <note>original Latin: "fieri"</note>, and *of essence* <note>original Latin: "essentiae"</note> (which looks more like *absence* <note>original Latin: "adsentiae"</note>) on page 256, lines 6, 7, 15, etc. And as long as it is a matter of one or two words in each sentence, the context often helps to recognize what is needed; but especially *On the Principles of Things* <note>original Latin: "De rerum principiis"</note> and *On Bonds in General* <note>original Latin: "De vinculis in genere"</note> present, in the photographic copy we used, entire pages with many of the words more or less deformed in this way, even though that handwriting, viewed from a respectful distance, seems very clear and even elegant. In such cases, no conjecture <note>an educated guess used to fill in gaps in a damaged or illegible text</note> is sufficient, and one must prudently resign oneself to not reading. It seems, however, that in the original manuscript the difficulties of reading are fewer, and therefore (except for a few cases where we felt obliged to do otherwise) we have gladly followed the collations <note>the process of comparing different versions of a text to find the most accurate reading</note> of the kind gentlemen in Moscow, to whom we expressed our gratitude above. Nevertheless, there frequently appears in the text, and more often in the critical apparatus <note>the scholarly notes that record variations and doubts in the manuscript</note>, a confession of our ignorance: of many marginal notes, for example in *On Magic* <note>original Latin: "De magia"</note>, in the *Theses*,¹ and also in *Lullian Medicine* <note>original Latin: "Medicina Lulliana"</note>, we managed to read only single

**[Page XXV]**

<meta>BRUNI Latin Works, Vol. III.</meta>

On Palm Sunday (April 12, Old Style) of 1590,¹ 'The Lord Doctor <note>Referring to Giordano Bruno</note> will say farewell to the Academy, intending to depart perhaps three days later —— Regarding his studies, he certainly proceeds diligently; I have received from him a new treatise *On the Inventive Art* <note>original Latin: *De arte inventiva*</note> to be transcribed again; he is now dwelling on the *Medical Art* according to the *Art of Lull* <note>original Latin: *in Arte medica iam Lullii Arte*</note>. Regarding the images,² about which he had said many things, he will come to those once these are finished; indeed, he has often mentioned that he wants them written in my hand for himself'. And indeed, if by '*Medical Art according to Lull's art*' (which should probably be corrected to '*according to the Lullian art*' <note>original Latin: *iuxta Lullii artem*</note>) we mean the '*Lullian Medicine*' in the draft written by Besler’s hand, these dates find confirmation in the mutual citations of the two treatises. From '*On the Principles of Things*' <note>original Latin: *De rerum principiis*</note> (page 565, line 21), a note stating 'it will be discussed below in the following treatise' <note>original Latin: *dicetur inferius sequenti tractatu*</note> refers back to the '*Medicine*'. Conversely, the '*Medicine*' refers several times to '*On the Principles of Things*' as a work already written: page 574, 23 and following ('in the preceding treatise' <note>original Latin: *in praecedenti tractatu*</note>); 578, 10 ('in the above' <note>original Latin: *in superioribus*</note>); 581, 7 ('in the treatise *On Magic* near the end' <note>original Latin: *in tractatu De magia circa finem*</note>); and 592, 29 and following ('in the final treatise *On Magic*' <note>original Latin: *in ultimo tractatu De magia*</note>). Furthermore, '*On the Principles of Things*' in its turn assumes that the treatises we call '*On Magic*' <note>original Latin: *De magia*</note> were already written (page 517, 8: 'which were considered above' <note>original Latin: *quae superius considerabantur*</note> etc., that is—

¹ See V. Stölzle in '*Archiv*' etc. page 574 and following, note 2. We believe it is unnecessary to publish the entirety of Besler’s two letters here, of which Stölzle was kind enough to send us a copy: the information significant for Bruno’s biography has already been published by Stölzle himself. Of interest is the news that in the preceding week, Bruno had gone with Besler to Wolfenbüttel 'to receive the gift of 50 florins <note>A common gold or silver coin of the period</note> recently given by the prince visiting Helmstädt'. These fifty florins are to be added to the 'eighty scudi <note>Another type of currency; Bruno mentioned this amount during his trial</note> of those parts' (Berti² page 395 = Document page 21). In the second letter, dated April 22, it is stated that Bruno was forced to remain longer in Helmstädt 'due to the lack of carriages and the excessive and unfair demands of the one renting them'. Besler informs his uncle of this, 'lest his Uncle look for us in Magdeburg in vain', and adds that they are expecting a carriage for the following day, 'though it is very doubtful' etc. It is clear they do not expect to leave the next day, because Besler also says: 'I have given no money to the current courier; I will give some when he returns'.

And similarly, we do not now believe it necessary to refer page 505, line 25 to page 539 and following, rather than to page 501 and following. There do not seem to be other citations that are entirely certain; but if the reference from page 542, line 21 and following to page 499, line 8 and following is certain (and we could have also added the one from page 566, line 19 to page 500, line 22 and following), then page 525, line 7; 525, line 18; and 526, line 5 will also refer respectively to page 497, line 1 and following; 505, line 19 and following; and 504, line 24 and following, rather than to page 406, line 1 and following; 489, line 2 and following (compare note to page 433, line 2); and 433, line 26 and following. And however difficult it may be to imagine the composition of the entire *Magical Work* <note>original Latin: *Opus magicum*</note>—of which the *Lullian Medicine* <note>original Latin: *Medicina Lulliana*</note> in its second draft also forms a part in some way—it is clear that the magical chapters of *On the Principles of Things* are only its complement (page 512, line 12), and the words (page 567, line 15) "And these are the principal chapters" <note>original Latin: *Et haec sunt praecipua capita*</note> etc., have every appearance of a final conclusion to the entire work. Except that the final words of *On Mathematical Magic* have this appearance to an even greater degree (page 506, line 16: "These are the things that contain the entire reasoning of magic" <note>original Latin: *Haec sunt quae universam magiae rationem continent*</note> etc.), while we have now admitted that passages in *On the Principles of Things* recall passages in *On Mathematical Magic*. Probably this little treatise, which is after all a simple compilation and is found in the manuscript in a separate quire (Lutoslawski page 549), is to be considered as a "first part of magic," that is, superstitious magic (compare page 542, line 21 and 494, line 12 and following), to be placed, it seems, before the entire *Physical Work* <note>original Latin: *opus physicum*</note> (that is, pages 397-454 + 509-567). To us, at least, it would not be easy to understand pages 435-438 of *On Magic* if they did not presuppose pages 493-505 of *On Mathematical Magic*.

->XXVII<-

the paper used by Bruno in the letter (see above, page XII) to the Pro-Rector of the Julian Academy <note>The Academia Julia was the University of Helmstädt, where Bruno taught</note> dated October 6, 1589 (Sigwart page 301, Lutoslawski page 533); we must conclude that the entire part of the codex included between folios 5 and 87 was written in Helmstädt.¹ To be sure, someone might suppose that Bruno and Besler, upon leaving Helmstädt, took some blank paper with them, and that this was used later for the Beslerian copy of the *Lullian Medicine* <note>original Latin: *Medicina Lulliana*; this refers to Bruno’s work based on the systems of Ramon Llull</note>. But this seems to us an improbable hypothesis in itself, and it can furthermore be ruled out by other considerations. In fact, if that were the case, Besler’s very general words "he is lingering on the Medical Art" <note>original Latin: *immoratur in Arte medica*</note> etc., would have to refer to the first draft. Now, this first draft consists of a few pages in Bruno’s hand and the rest in the hand of an unknown copyist, but it is all on the same paper, which is different from that of folios 11–86. One would therefore have to admit that simultaneously (March 16, the date of the first page of *On the Principles of Things* <note>original Latin: *De rerum principiis*</note>; April 12, the date of Besler’s letter) Bruno was using two different qualities of paper and two different secretaries: things that are certainly not impossible, but not such that they should be believed without explicit proof. Furthermore, and this is an argument of some value, if it was the first draft of the *Lullian Medicine* that he was working on in April—when *On the Principles of Things* had already been written—why do the citations of this latter pamphlet occur only in the second draft and not in the first? Everything, therefore, leads us to conclude that the interruption of the Beslerian copy of the *Medicine* coincides with the departure from Helmstädt.

On the other hand, folios 87–98, which contain the treatise *On Bonds in General* <note>original Latin: *De vinculis in genere*; a work exploring the psychological and magical "bonds" that connect things or people</note>, also incomplete, were written later; there, on page 684, line 3, with the words "We have said in those things which... <note>original Latin: *Diximus in his quae*</note>"

->XXVIII<-

The last "Thesis" on page 491 (cf. p. 430, 7) refers back to *On Natural Magic* <note>original Latin: *De naturali magia*</note>. The fact that the paper is identical to the following work, *The Torch of the Thirty Statues* <note>original Latin: *Lampas triginta statuarum*</note>—a work copied in Padua from Sunday, September 1st to Tuesday, October 22nd, 1591 (New Style)¹—leads us to believe, along with the scholar Sigwart (p. 300), that *On Bonds in General* <note>original Latin: *De vinculis in genere*; this is one of Bruno's famous works on psychological and magical manipulation</note> was also written in Padua. Furthermore, it seems one can conclude without too much boldness that although Bruno may have already thought of composing this treatise while in Helmstedt, he had not yet set his hand to it; this is suggested by examining those few sheets of autograph notes <note>written in Bruno's own handwriting</note> which the codex itself has fortunately preserved for us. Since, in fact, in the first five sheets—all of the same paper—we find notes for *On Bonds* together with the draft of a letter written in Frankfurt no later than July 2, 1590, it must be concluded that the notes for *On Bonds* were also written in Frankfurt. Now, from the frequently cited letter of Besler <note>Hieronymus Besler, Bruno's assistant and scribe</note>, it appears that he intended to depart with Bruno from Helmstedt and accompany him to Magdeburg, where the meeting with Besler's uncle, the physician Wolfgang Zeileisen, would take place; nothing prevents us from admitting that this occurred. However, there is no evidence that Besler accompanied Bruno even further, to Frankfurt, and much less to Zurich; indeed, if there were any such evidence, we would find it hard to believe (cf. Sigwart p. 300 ff.). Therefore, if Bruno was preparing materials for *On Bonds* in Frankfurt, the redaction of this treatise in Besler’s hand cannot be earlier than their new meeting in Padua in the autumn of 1591.

->XXXIV<-

Regardless, if we are not mistaken in assuming a double stay for Bruno in Frankfurt, we might be able to determine with greater precision the time when folios 1–5 recto <note>The front side of the manuscript pages</note> of the Moscow codex were written. Indeed, between the two stays, we have no doubt that the first will be chosen, as it is the one closer to the date of July 2, 1590—the latest possible limit for the writing of folio 5 verso <note>The back side of the manuscript page</note>.

It remains for us to say something about the provenance of the Noroff codex <note>A manuscript collection formerly owned by the Russian statesman Abraham Noroff</note>. Lutosławski (p. 571) is inclined to believe that among the papers seized from Bruno by Mocenigo, and then transferred from the Venetian Inquisition to Rome, there were also the treatises and notes now collected in this codex; therefore, it would have to be considered as having been stealthily stolen from the archives of the Roman Inquisition. In truth, this hypothesis explains very well how papers from Helmstädt, Frankfurt, and Padua come to be found together, but on the other hand, it presents significant difficulties. In fact, when Bruno was asked whether all the writings indicated in the list he handed over to the Venetian Inquisitors were composed by him and were all his doctrine, he replied in the affirmative, excepting only the treatise *On the Seals of Hermes* <note>original: "De sigillis Hermetis"</note> etc.¹ Now, if that list included the short treatise which, for ease of citation, we have titled *On Mathematical Magic* <note>original: "De magia mathematica"</note>, it is unlikely that he would not have tried to lessen his responsibility for the compilation of this small work as well. For while the justification cited in *On the Monad* <note>original: "De monade"</note>² might hold for the other magical treatises, it certainly does not—

If it were permissible to weaken these objections with the example of other clear denials to which Bruno fearlessly exposed himself in his statements, it would perhaps be less easy to eliminate another difficulty faced by Lutosławski’s hypothesis. Indeed, at what time should we suppose these papers were removed from the Roman Archive? If a long time ago, it is not clear how they remained unknown for so long; if not long before Tross <note>An antiquarian book dealer</note> put them up for sale, one cannot imagine who could have written the marginal notes—which are not recent, but at least a century old—that occur there (for example, on p. 499, 32; 538, 4; 539, 15; 540, 1, etc.). ->XXXVI<-

Must we perhaps resort to the desperate hypothesis that some archivist of the Holy Inquisition had become a scholarly commentator on Bruno?

We would have therefore preferred to believe that our codex came from the legacy of Besler <note>Hieronymus Besler was a German student who served as Giordano Bruno’s secretary and scribe in Padua</note>, in whose possession—based on the information we have—no one today is able to prove that papers of Bruno's could not have remained. This supposition would be confirmed by the discovery of two incomplete treatises there, written in Besler’s own hand. One might imagine, in other words, that Bruno intended to have them completed by his secretary as soon as he had the opportunity to return to Padua. But for this to be a plausible hypothesis, one would also have to suppose that Besler was still residing in Padua when Bruno was arrested. Instead, in the aforementioned Venetian trial records <note>original: "costituti Veneti"</note> (Berti² p. 399 = Doc. p. 24 sq.), Bruno, speaking of his student “a German from Nuremberg, named Hieronymus Besler,” says that he “was in Padua a short time ago and served me as a scribe for perhaps two months.” Thus, at the very least, one must admit that Bruno believed him to have already departed from Padua, and this alone would be enough to cast doubt on our hypothesis. However, Sigwart <note>Christoph von Sigwart, a 19th-century philosopher and logic scholar</note> has provided us with more precise information, from which it appears that Besler was indeed no longer there, and that already before May 1592, he was enrolled as a student in Basel.¹

***

¹ Besler enrolled in Basel in the spring of 1592, before the appointment of the new Rector; therefore before May. His dissertation (*On Dropsy* <note>original: "De Hydrope"</note>) bears the date of August 5; the disputation took place on August 15, and the diploma, which is still preserved, is of the same date (? see Brunnhofer p. 324). Sigwart has furthermore shared with us a photograph of a letter from Besler “To the Magnificent and Most Illustrious Man Dr. Caspar Bauhin, now most worthy Rector of the Academy of Basel” <note>original: "Magnifico et Clarissimo Viro D. ->XXXVII<-

As things stand, it is prudent to refrain from all conjecture; only we do not see why, until proof to the contrary, one should not trust Tross <note>Ludwig Tross was a 19th-century German scholar and librarian who handled many rare manuscripts</note>, who attests to the codex’s origin from Germany (see above p. XVII). Do we perhaps know with certainty that all the papers seized by Mocenigo <note>Giovanni Mocenigo was the Venetian nobleman who denounced Bruno to the Inquisition in 1592</note> were delivered to the Venetian Inquisition, and that all those delivered to the Venetian Inquisition were transmitted to Rome? And is it not also possible that not even all of Bruno's papers could be seized by Mocenigo?

The two paper codices of Erlangen 1215 (= *B*) and 1279 (= *C*), described by Stölzle in ‘Archives for the History of Philosophy’ <note>original: ‘Archiv für Gesch. der Philos.’</note> III (1890), pp. 573-78, also possess no small importance, because they alone have preserved the *Aristotelian Commentaries* <note>original: ‘Commentarii Aristotelici’</note> for us. Codex *B* (20 $\times$ 15 centimeters), of which we also provide a photoengraved facsimile, contains only these *Commentaries*,¹ incomplete at the end (see p. 388, 16), and with two gaps after folio 68 (p. 369, 20) and after folio 70 (p. 379, 15). The handwriting, with many abbreviations from folio 29 verso (= p. 300, 18) onward, is from the 16th century, and the copyist is unknown, though certainly German. In contrast, Codex *C* (21 $\times$ 15 centimeters) is in the hand of the usual Besler² <note>Hieronymus Besler was Bruno's student and secretary</note>, which, besides the *Commentaries*—complete and without significant gaps—also contains the *On Magic* <note>original: ‘De magia’</note> and the *Theses*.³

But if one further considers that *C*, compared to *B*, is often incorrect and never possesses good readings, except in places ^1 where even the most ignorant copyist could have corrected by guesswork; ^2 that wherever *B* has corrections, the corrected reading appears in *C*, not the original one; ^3 that marginal notes from *B* appear in the main text of *C*, ^4 but not vice versa; that in short, *C* does not differ from *B* except for very common copying errors, ^5 or for equally common "slips of the pen" <note>original: *lapsus*</note> of any writer, or for the usual transposi—

->XXXIX<-

Since all the gaps currently found there are gaps of entire leaves, we do not know if other writings by Bruno were originally contained therein.

We anticipate an objection. The title of the *Commentaries* in *C* (see page 261, 1) is more detailed and, if you will, more exact than the one we find in *B*; furthermore, the epithet 'of Cambrai' <note>original: *Camaracensis*, referring to Bruno's lectures at the College of Cambrai in Paris</note>—an epithet unlikely to be the invention of common scribes—only appears in the title of *C*. But this objection loses all its weight, it seems to us, when dealing with a copyist like Besler, who was Bruno’s disciple and secretary. Furthermore, to remain consistent in our review, we have adopted (and we are glad we did not do otherwise) the simpler title from *B*, 'Books on Physics' <note>original: *Libri Physicorum*</note>, etc.; but one must not forget that *B* is a mutilated manuscript, and the hypothesis is not excluded that its current title might be a specific title for the first part of the *Commentaries* (pages 261-399), which paraphrases and summarizes books I-V of Aristotle’s *Physics*, and that a title page with a general title has been lost. ^1

->XLII<-

a notable error: "contrary assistance of the Doctors" <note>original Latin: *contraria Doctorum assistentia*; likely a misreading of "continuous assistance"</note>. Nor are we easily led to believe that the change to "a philosopher may freely hold an opinion" <note>original: *liceat Philosopho liberè opinari*</note> (p. 57, 27) in version *B*, compared to "one may freely hold an opinion philosophically within philosophy" <note>original: *liceat philosophicè in philosophia liberè opinari*</note> in versions *AH*, is an arbitrary alteration. And similarly, errors such as "than I can say" <note>original: *quam dicere possim*</note> instead of "than may be fitting" <note>original: *quam decere possit*</note>, "upon this" <note>original: *super hoc*</note> and "through this" <note>original: *per hoc*</note> instead of "upon these things" <note>original: *super haec*</note> and "through these things" <note>original: *per haec*</note>, and above all the aforementioned "contrary" <note>original: *contraria*</note> instead of "continuous" <note>original: *continua*</note>, seem to derive from a misreading of a manuscript rather than a printed edition. Finally, even the title of Master <note>original: *Magister*</note>, which Du Boulay gives to Hennequin <note>Jean Hennequin, a Parisian scholar who defended Bruno’s theses</note> (who, therefore, we should not imagine as being too young in 1586; see Berti² p. 364 onwards and Brunnhofer p. 322 onwards), derives from neither one nor the other printed edition. We have, therefore, some reason to believe that the phrase "of Giordano Bruno the Nolan of Cambrai" <note>original: *Iordani Bruni Nolani Cameracensis*</note> was also found by Du Boulay in the documents he had at hand and does not cite.¹ And so, reversing the hypothetical argument we made earlier, we will say instead that finding "of Giordano Bruno the Nolan of Cambrai" in a codex written by Bruno’s secretary clearly proves that in the title of the *Acrotismus* <note>Bruno's work *Articuli adversus Aristotelycos*, also known as the *Acrotismus*</note> as well, the term "of Cambrai" <note>original: *Camoeracensis*</note> is meant to be joined with "the Nolan."²

<meta>This page continues the philological investigation into the title "Cameracensis" (of Cambrai) used by Giordano Bruno. The author is challenging the chronological conclusions of the scholar Stölzle regarding when Bruno's Aristotelian Commentaries were written, based on when Bruno might have adopted this specific title in Paris.</meta>

->XLIII<-

Thus, we are not even persuaded by the reasoning offered by **Stölzle** (p. 575) to determine the time in which the *Aristotelian Commentaries* were composed. Since we know nothing, he says, of any public teaching by Bruno during his second stay in Paris, the epithet "Cameracensis" <note>original: *Camaracensis*; referring to the College of Cambrai</note> leads us to attribute the composition of the *Commentaries* to the time of his first stay (1581–83). But we would hesitate to base such reasoning upon an epithet that offers no guarantee of authenticity; because it is

<note>There is a large gap in the source text here, likely representing missing lines or a printing error.</note>

---

published; for it is also well to remember that only after the printing of *On Shadows* <note>original: *De umbris [idearum]*</note> was he appointed by King Henry III as an "extraordinary and provisioned lecturer" <note>original: *lettor straordinario et provisionato*</note> (Berti² p. 394 = Doc. p. 20). And as for the *Architecture* <note>original: *Architettura*</note>, it is indeed generally believed to have been printed after the *Song of Circe* <note>original: *Cantus Circaeus*</note>, which was in turn printed after *On Shadows* (see vol. II. 1 p. 182); but if the only argument for believing this is the citation of the *Song of Circe* on page 14, 2 of the *Architecture* (= p. 244 Gfr.), this, strictly speaking, only proves that the *Song of Circe* was already composed and known, not that it was already printed; since before its printing, this work was very well known and flawed copies were circulating, as the publisher Regnault expressly attests. Conversely, from the absence of "Cameracensis" <note>original: *Camoeracensis*</note> in the title of the *Song of Circe*, it is not permissible to deduce that Bruno could not be called such when this work was printed; since it concerns a publication made not by Bruno himself, but by Regnault. Therefore, for the time of the first stay in Paris, there is no trace of the title "Cameracensis." But what is more notable is that this epithet does not appear in the title of Hennequin’s theses, nor in that of the *Figuration of Physical Hearing* <note>original: *Figuratio physici auditus*</note> and the pamphlets on Mordente, all Parisian publications of 1586; while it is, on the other hand, evident that the "Cameracensis" of the Wittenberg publication must refer to something that occurred during Bruno's second stay in Paris. For, in the present state of our information, it would be pure conjecture to suppose that in printing the "arguments" <note>original: *rationes*</note> of the theses disputed in Paris in 1586 in Germany, Bruno thought to dig up a title that did not belong to him at the time of the dispute itself or had no connection to the dispute. New documents may teach us how, when, and in what sense Bruno could call himself "Cameracensis"; nor would we claim to hit the mark by conjecturing that the doctors of the College of Cambrai had promoted and favored the dispute against the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> of the Sorbonne, and perhaps on the occasion of the dispute had made Bruno "Cameracensis." It is enough for us to be able to later counter Stölzle by saying that even if one wanted to give importance to the epithet found in the Besler copy of the *Commentaries*, one should not necessarily refer its composition to a time prior to the years 1585–86.

->XLIV<-

a fact that, for now at least, the epithet does not appear in the original (*B*) of the manuscript <term>codex (C): a hand-written book</term> that provides it. Furthermore, the theses of **Hennequin** (cf. vol. II, 2 p. 221-24)—that is, the first draft of the *Acrotismus* <note>original: *Acrotismus*, a work containing Bruno's anti-Aristotelian articles</note>—were defended in May 1586, shortly before Bruno left Paris for the second time. Therefore, the title "Cameracensis" <note>original: *Camoeracensis*; referring to the College of Cambrai in Paris</note> which appears in the title of the *Acrotismus*, could just as easily appear in the title of the *Commentaries*, even if these had been composed, let us say, during his second stay.

But that the *Commentaries* are actually to be attributed to a time later than 1586 can already be inferred with probability from the fact that in this very year, Bruno published his *Representation of Aristotle's Physics* <note>original: *Figuratio physici auditus Aristotelis*</note> in Paris. This was a sort of preparation for the formal debate, mainly to demonstrate that he did not oppose **Aristotle** without knowing him well (see vol. I, 4 p. 133, 8 sqq.; cf. **Tocco**, *The Latin Works* <note>original: *Le opere latine*</note> etc. p. 102). Now, it is not likely either that he would have needed to prove himself an expert in Aristotle's natural philosophy if he had already commented on it publicly or privately in Paris, or that he already had a *Commentary* on the *Physics*, on *On Generation* <note>original: *De generatione*</note>, etc., by Aristotle composed at that time, and yet failed to make use of it for the Parisian publication. For although the purpose of the two works is different, and the treatment is also different, there are pages in the *Commentaries* on the first book of the *Physics* which, with slight modifications, could have been used for the *Representation*.$^1$

$^1$ It is not improbable, moreover, that the priority of the *Representation* <note>original: *Figuratio*</note> might also be proven by internal arguments; but this cannot be asserted without an accurate and laborious comparison, nor can all the errors and inaccuracies that occur in one or the other of the two works be used for a demonstration of this kind. To find, for example, in the *Commentaries* (p. 286, 25 sqq.) an exactly explained passage that, due to a slip of the pen <note>original: *lapsus calami*</note> (the swapping of the names of **Anaxagoras** and **Empedocles**), is corrupted in the *Representation* p. 148, 19 sq., naturally cannot have any value in claiming the former are later than the latter.

->XLV<-

And there are no lack of other signs. From what we have said above, it follows that the tradition of the **Commentaries** leads back to manuscript *B*, undoubtedly written by a German. Now, if the **Commentaries** are believed to have been composed during his first stay in Paris, we must also admit that **Bruno** himself carried a manuscript of them with him to Germany, at least as far as **Wittenberg** (where he matriculated on August 20, 1586). It would be quite improbable that during his brief and restless previous travels through German lands—in **Mainz**, **Wiesbaden**, and **Marburg**—he would have had the leisure and inclination to have it copied.<gloss>1</gloss> Well then, this manuscript—which was guarded so jealously for many years, which twice crossed the sea successfully and just as successfully accompanied **Bruno** "having escaped from the turmoils of France" <note>original: *e Galliae tumultibus elapsum*</note><gloss>2</gloss> during long and uncomfortable journeys—suddenly disappears in Germany, between **Wittenberg**, **Prague**, and **Helmstedt**, where **Bruno** lived and traveled far more peacefully. And when his secretary **Besler** wishes to make a copy, he finds nothing to copy except either the German manuscript *B* or a copy even more erroneous than *B*. It is much more probable that **Bruno** held lectures in Germany, publicly or privately, on **Aristotle’s** books on physics, not so much by choice as because that was the teaching in demand, likely without in-
