**Stölzle** <note>Remigius Stölzle, a 19th-century scholar of Bruno</note> also believes he can prove that the **Commentaries** are chronologically earlier than *On Magic* <note>original: *De magia*</note>; and we also consider them earlier, because after the end of 1589 or the beginning of 1590 we do not see how **Bruno** could have had the time or inclination for such Aristotelian paraphrases, as he was then occupied with many other heavy works of a completely different kind, most notably the works published shortly thereafter in **Frankfurt**. However, the citations on which **Stölzle** relies are deceptive; for there is no necessity to relate pages 466 and 472 of the magical treatises to page 345 and following of the **Commentaries** rather than to the text of **Aristotle** itself. Less uncertain seems the reference from *On the Immense and the Minimum* <note>original: *De minimo*</note> page 142, which **Stölzle** relates to page 340 of the **Commentaries**; but since the printing of *On the Minimum* was not finished before February 13, 1591, we do not gain much for the chronology of the **Commentaries**, which even without such clues we would certainly have placed in a period prior to 1591. More precise determinations are not possible except by simple conjecture.$^2$

<meta>This page continues the scholarly investigation into the timeline of Giordano Bruno’s writings. ->XLVII<-

Now, if one were to ask when, between 1586 and 1591, Bruno might have had the best opportunity to direct his teaching activities toward Aristotle, and to compose those *Commentaries* which—while remaining fairly objective—allowed the Commentator's own dissent to be glimpsed here and there, we would not hesitate to answer: during his residence in Wittenberg. It was at Wittenberg that he, while keeping his "philosophical freedom" untarnished, graciously complied with the polite requests of colleagues who did not look kindly upon new doctrines;¹ it was at Wittenberg that he read "a lecture on Aristotle’s *Organon* <note>The collection of Aristotle's logical works</note>... with other philosophy lectures for two years";² it was at Wittenberg that he published in 1587 the *Hunters' Torch of Logicians* <note>original: *Lampas venatoria logicorum*</note>, which was a reworking of Aristotle's *Topics*, and in the same year dictated his Commentary on the *Rhetoric to Alexander* <note>original: *Rhetorica ad Alexandrum*</note>.³ Certainly, if someone instead wished to attribute the composition of the *Commentaries* to his first year of residence in Helmstädt (1589), we would not claim to have decisive arguments to the contrary. We wish to remind readers, however, that it was undoubtedly the freedom of doctrine that attracted Bruno to Helmstädt, and that he would have taken great advantage of this freedom in his early days there for purposes quite other than paraphrasing Aristotle; nor, in any case, would Aristotelian paraphrases have so quickly brought him into conflict

Besides the *Commentaries*, codex *C* <note>A 'codex' is a manuscript book; here it refers to a specific volume in the Erlangen library.</note> contains, as we have said, *On Magic* <note>original Latin: 'De magia'</note> and the *Theses*; but even regarding the version of these short works, its authority is nil, because just as it derives from *B* for the *Commentaries*, so for the magical works it derives from *M*. This cannot be in doubt if we recall what we said generally about the majority of the works contained in *M*—namely, that they were written by Besler under Bruno’s dictation. It is useful, however, to add some further considerations.

Both codices, *C* and *M*, are in Besler’s hand. Now, *a priori* <note>A Latin term meaning 'from the start' or based on theoretical deduction rather than observation.</note>, given two of Bruno's manuscripts written by the same scribe, it is more than probable that one was copied from the other. And since, according to Stölzle’s <note>Remigius Stölzle was a 19th-century scholar who specialized in Bruno's manuscripts.</note> testimony, *C* shows very clear handwriting throughout, while *M* instead has many places written very carelessly or even completely illegible (at least in the photograph), it is to be supposed that *M* is the original and *C* is the copy. In fact, *M* has frequent erasures and corrections, while *C* is rarely corrected,¹ and constantly reproduces the corrected readings of *B*, never the original ones.

The very few exceptions² have no value: they are, as far as we can see, on page 422, line 25, a word easily erased in *M* and kept in *C*, and on page 441, line 16, the word *innumerable* <note>original Latin: 'innumerabiles'</note>

->LI<-

marginal additions by *M* appear in *C* within the text, placed differently than *M* intended (416, 24 sq. 457, 5).¹

For all these reasons, there is no doubt that 'On Magic' <note>original Latin: "De magia"</note> and the 'Theses' in codex *C* are copies of *M*, which has preserved for us the original text written under dictation. We therefore agree with Stölzle <note>Remigius Stölzle, a 19th-century scholar who specialized in Bruno's manuscripts.</note> (p. 577) that these two treatises are later than the *Commentaries*; but based on what was stated above regarding the chronology of codex *M*, it is truly not a case of thinking of the time of Bruno’s first stay in Paris, but rather it is certain that they were composed in Helmstädt between December 1589 and March 1590.

Finally, the Augsburg codex <note>original: "codice Augustano"</note> (= *A*), although—besides the fragmentary 'Observations on the Lullian Lamp' <note>original: "Animadversiones in Lampadem Lullianam"; referring to the mnemonic systems of Ramon Llull.</note> (published in vol. II, 2 p. 359-66)—it offers nothing unpublished except the 'Lamp of the Thirty Statues' <note>original: "Lampas triginta statuarum"</note> also preserved for us in *M*, it is nonetheless a truly precious manuscript, because without it, it would have been impossible to publish that important work of Bruno in a reasonably legible form. It is described with great diligence by Mr. Stölzle in the *Archive for the History of Philosophy* <note>original German: "Archiv für Gesch. der Philos."</note> III (1890), p. 389-93, nor will we repeat the entire description here. It contains 216 leaves (16 $\times$ 9 centimeters), of which folios 1, 2ᵛ-5, 62ᵛ-97, 104-105 (see p. 16, 3), and 206-216 are blank:

1) the Wittenberg printing of the ‘Combinatory Lamp’... <note>original: "Lampas Combinatoria"</note>

---

¹ It is well known how much Bruno favors participial genitives ending in *-tum*. Besler <note>Hieronymus Besler, Bruno's assistant and scribe.</note>, when writing under dictation, conforms to the taste of his master; when copying instead, he often substitutes the standard forms: 261, 9 *animantum* <note>An archaic Latin form for "of living things."</note> in *B*, *animantium* <note>The standard Latin form.</note> in *C*; 428, 3 *somniantum* <note>Latin: "of those dreaming."</note> in *M*, *somniantium* in *C*, etc. It is likewise known to anyone who has some familiarity with Bruno’s style that he despises all elegance. The only ‘elegance’ to which he seems to hold are the frequent word inversions—inversions that are at times truly intolerable. Now then, Besler, when writing under dictation, accepts them; when copying instead, he tries to re-establish a simpler order. Hundreds of examples can be gathered in the *Commentaries* (*C* compared to *B*), in ‘On Magic’ and in the ‘Theses’ (*C* compared to *M*), and in the ‘Lamp of the Thirty Statues’ (*M* compared to *A*).

<meta>This page continues the philological analysis of the manuscripts of Giordano Bruno’s works, specifically comparing Codex A and Codex M. It highlights specific textual corruptions, omissions, and errors made by copyists, particularly focusing on how Codex M often introduces "corrections" that further obscure Bruno's original meaning.</meta>

->LVI<-

A comparison with *Acrotismus*, page 60, lines 18 and following (Florence edition), would have been useful to establish the exact meaning and perhaps even to change the word *grace* <note>original Latin: "gratia (gra)"</note> into *kinds* <note>original: "genera"</note>; but who could have corrected the phrase *and by established rules* <note>original: "statutisque regulis"</note> in Manuscript *M* into *and in fixed ages* <note>original: "statisque saeculis"</note>? Even worse corruptions are found in the words on page 243, lines 15 and following: *On the part of no parent. The soul is without father and mother. If it has a cause, this is the efficient cause, but not the material; however, there is no way for it, inasmuch as* <note>original: "Ex parte nullius parentis. Anima est sine patre et matre. Qui si causam habet, hoc est efficiens, non autem materialis, eius autem nulla est via, utpote"</note> etc. Let us not even speak of the gaps of a few words (for example, 15, 12-14 *but—is nothing* <note>original: "sed-nihil est"</note> and 55, 15-17, which are omitted in *M*): suffice it to say that the entire 'Tree of Definitions' <note>original: "Arbor definitionum," a logical or mnemonic diagram common in Renaissance philosophy</note> at 228, 14–229, 27 (cf. 230, 1) is omitted in *M*, and naturally no one could have filled it in by conjecture. Moreover, already in the first pages we find readings in *M* that admirably falsify the meaning: we recall, for example, page 3, line 10, where it inappropriately adds *external* <note>original: "externis"</note> after *senses* <note>original: "sensibus"</note> (cf. 84, 18 and following; *On the Composition of Images* page 103, 26 and following), or 6, 5, where the word *more* <note>original: "plures"</note> (instead of *dust* <note>original: "pulveres"</note>) makes understanding impossible.

It will be more useful to stop and consider some other places where we can convince ourselves that *M* does not represent a different tradition from *A*. Thus, at 180, 4, we read in *A*: *They are* life <note>original Greek: ζῳή (zoē)</note> *life* <note>original Latin: "vita"</note>, and there is no doubt that it should be corrected to *They are* zoophytes <note>original Greek: ζῳόφυτα (zoophyta), meaning "plant-animals"</note> (or *zoophyta*, see the table on page 184).¹ Well, *M* writes *They are Motive [forces]* <note>original: "Sunt Motiva"</note>, evidently to extract some kind of meaning from what had no meaning, not because it had something different before it than what *A* offers. In another place (144, 3 and following), *A* gives *equally wicked ignorance* <note>original: "aeque ignorantia prava"</note> (*wicked* <note>original: "pravae"</note> is correctly corrected by *M*; cf., if there is a need, 490, 7. *Italian Works* 299, 36 Lagarde etc.), while *M* gives *and* <note>original: "atque"</note> instead of *equally* <note>original: "aeque"</note>, and we—

Elsewhere (75, 11), *M* "fixes" the grammar by changing *two wine-skins which* <note>original feminine form: "duas utres quas"</note> into the masculine *duos utres quos*, but we have demonstrated that in doing so, Besler <note>Hieronymus Besler, Bruno's assistant and scribe</note> was actually correcting Bruno himself. Likewise, there is no doubt that *they drank up* <note>original: "ebiberunt"</note> is a false correction of *they produced* <note>original: "ediderunt"</note> (69, 17), *to be* <note>original: "esse"</note> a false correction of *to that place* <note>original: "eo"</note> (46, 7), *on Mount Etna in them* <note>original: "in monte Aetna in e illis"</note> a false correction of *** *in his things* <note>original: "in e illius"</note> (86, 9),$^1$ and *at the most distant things* <note>so M, original: "ad distantissima"</note> a correction of *at the most immediate things* <note>original: "ad instantissima"</note>$^2$ (100, 13) etc.

From these and countless other instances, one must at least conclude that the source for *M* was a codex <note>a manuscript book</note> very similar to *A*. However, other passages force us to go beyond this conclusion.

In the 17th article of the *Statue of Vulcan* (86, 18) we read in *M* (where the article is numbered the 19th; see p. 85, 20): *He is said to have fashioned a wonderful work of art out of bronze, which he gave as a gift to Jove, by whom it was given* <note>masculine: "datus"</note> *to Europa, by whom to Erocrinus, by whom to Scenala* etc. Why this grammatical error? Because the word *whelp* or *puppy* <note>original: "catulum," which is masculine</note> is written unclearly in *A*, and whoever could not read it in *A* simply omitted it. Why is *I say* <note>original: "inquam"</note> (30, 4) replaced by *however* <note>original: "autem"</note> in *M*? Because the way *in|quam* was split in *A* was misread as *in which* <note>original: "in quam"</note>, which made no sense. Why do we find in *M* (41, 23 sq.): *so that there is nothing which is not bounded by itself* <note>original: "ab ipso finiatur"</note>? Because the word *itself* <note>original: "ipse"</note> in *A* is written in a way that makes it look like *by itself* <note>original: "ipso"</note>. From the first light proceeds the first good (that is, love), and the first truth (that is, the intellect): how could it occur to anyone to suppress the word *love* <note>original: "amor"</note> (34, 10)? Because in the handwriting of *A*, it was thought that *love* <note>original: "amor"</note> was a correction for *good* <note>original: "bonum"</note>. ->LVIII<-

I believe [the copyist of M] could not read what *A* had, just as we ourselves were unable to read it. Similarly, what we failed to read in *A* at page 42, line 27 etc.$^1$ is entirely omitted in *M*, and the same fate befell the word *resting* <note>original: "quiescens"</note> (19, 23), the reading of which initially presented difficulties even to us. But one of the most characteristic passages is at page 18, line 9 etc. There, the word after *deep* <note>original: "profundum"</note> was illegible to us; after repeated efforts, it seemed to us to read *gates* <note>original: "portae"</note>, and finding that *M* had also read *gates* there, we tried to restore the sense by conjecture as best we could. But both we and *M* were ridiculously mistaken: in *A*, it says *poets* <note>original: "poetae"</note>! <note>In many Renaissance scripts, the letters 'r' and 'e' can look remarkably similar, leading the scribe to see "portae" (gates) instead of the intended "poetae" (poets).</note> In another place (193, 23 etc.), it similarly seemed to us that *A* had *is reserved* <note>original: "reservatur"</note>, as is actually read in *M*, and we had restored it by conjecture as *are referred* <note>original: "referuntur"</note>; we realized in time that in *A* it is indeed written as *referuntur*.$^2$ In this codex, exchanges of the prefix *pre-* <note>original: "prae-"</note> with *re-* are frequent (*resuppose* and *presuppose*, *resume* and *presume*, etc.; see for example 146, 25), and thus at 248, 18 <gloss>re</gloss>p̅cipiendo is nothing other than *prescribing* <note>original: "praecipiendo"</note> corrected into *receiving* <note>original: "recipiendo"</note>; *M* turns it into *for receiving* <note>original: "pro recipiendo"</note>. Similarly, it is not rare in *A* to find the use of a single prolonged line to indicate both the abbreviation for contraction and the final *m*, so that rōe = *by reason* <note>original: "ratione"</note>, and roē = *reason* [as an object] <note>original: "rationem"</note>. From this comes the error of *M*, who read (211, 15) *species* <note>original: "specie"</note>, where *the species* [as an object] <note>original: "speciem"</note> (spe̅) was written. Then, the error committed by *M* at page 210, lines 23–24 is worthy of special mention.$^3$ The copyist of *A* had initially wanted to invert the words of these two lines (though in any case, he intended to invert both lines entirely, not just the first words of each line), and he later unclearly erased the transposition marks he had placed before *In the thing* <note>original: "In re"</note> and *In truth* <note>original: "In veritate"</note>; *M*, deceived by these marks, transposes them.

->LX<-

with *A*,^1 which has very clear handwriting in those places; nor can it be reasonably supposed that the frequent modifications regarding numbers, paragraph breaks, small tables, etc. (6, 15. 10, 9 and following; 12, 13 and following; 26, 6. 85, 20. 178, 8 and following; 181, 15 and following; 189, 5. 198, 12 and following; 203, 1. 206, 13 etc.) were made on the spot while the copy was being executed. It is far more natural that there was an intermediate copy, in which all or part of these external modifications (some certainly as Bruno himself would have desired them) had already taken place. And thus, even a portion of the corrections and errors that we now find in the Paduan copy was already present in its immediate original source.

Having thus established with more than sufficient certainty the derivation of *M* from *A*, it remains to determine the time in which the *The Torch of the Thirty Statues* <note>original: "Lampas triginta statuarum"</note> was composed. It is easy to demonstrate that it is neither one of Bruno's last works, nor one of those brought to completion during his stay in Padua—as, for example, Berti^2 supposed, led by the signature in *M* (see page 258, 16). Sigwart has already concluded, recalling the citation of the *On the Monad* <note>original: "De monade"</note>, that the date of the signature should be referred to the Beslerian copy, not to the composition of the work itself. In fact, if *The Torch of the Thirty Statues* is called a book *not published but written* <note>original: "non editus sed scriptus"</note> on page 128 (= page 456, 3 Fior.) of a 655-page volume that appeared at the Frankfurt autumn fair in 1591, it is evident that its composition could not have been finished on October 22, 1591, as Besler's signature states. But today we have a new testimony: that of Besler himself, who, in his letter (see above, page xxiv and following) of April 12, 1590 (see above), tells us: *I have received it from him to be copied once more* <note>original: "describendum denuo accepi ab eo"</note>.

->LXI<-

new treatise 'On the Inventive Art' <note>original: "De arte inventiva"</note>, which is undoubtedly our 'Torch' <note>original: "Lampas"</note>, elsewhere called 'The Inventive Art' <note>original: "Ars inventiva"</note> by Bruno himself. The 'Torch' was therefore already composed by the beginning of April 1590. But it is permissible to go back even further. Codex *B* of the *Aristotelian Commentaries* <note>original: "Commentarii Aristotelici"</note>, until proven otherwise, is to be considered prior to the time when Besler <note>Hieronymus Besler, Bruno’s student and scribe</note> entered into a relationship with Bruno. Now, in the margins of this codex, there appear—written in the same hand as the main text—certain propositions from the 'Torch' (see above p. v sq.); and it is enough to examine the corresponding passages in the two works to be convinced that those propositions passed from the 'Torch' into the margins of the *Commentaries*, and not the other way around. Therefore, codex *B* is subsequent to the 'Torch'. But observing the corruptions <note>textual errors or variations</note> that these propositions present in the margins of *B*, we can hardly bring ourselves to believe they are the result of a single transcription; we must instead believe that the marginal notes were already present, at the very least, in the codex from which *B* was copied. Since we are dealing with a work like the *Commentaries*, of which it is unlikely many copies were made, we thus arrive at a copy produced not long after the time of composition; and if we were right to believe the *Commentaries* were composed in 1587, we must assign the composition of the 'Torch' to approximately the same period.

Fortunately, there are even better reasons to support this thesis. The 'Observations on the Lullian Torch' <note>original: "Animadversiones in Lampadem Lullianam"</note> in codex *A* bear the date 'March 13, 1587', and the handwriting of the 'Observations' is perfectly identical to that of the following 'Torch of the Thirty Statues' <note>original: "Lampas triginta statuarum"</note>; nor is there any difference in ink or paper: in short, none of those variations that are easy to recognize in the handwriting of the same scribe across a span of years. And if there were a gap of years between the two writings, from where would this student-copyist in Wittenberg in 1587 have obtained an unpublished work by Bruno, written when the latter was no longer

Certainly, if there were solid arguments for attributing the composition of the *Torch* <note>original: "Lampas"</note> to a more recent period, we would have to renounce these deductions from paleographic clues—which, we do not wish to deny, are often fallacious. ->LXIII<-

Wittenberg, he had ready or nearly ready a *Cabalistic Torch* <note>original: "Lampas Cabalistica"</note>. And what could this scientific perfection of the inventive arts of Lullo <note>Ramon Llull, a 13th-century philosopher famous for his "art" of memory and logic</note> be, if not indeed the *Torch of the Thirty Statues* <note>original: "Lampas triginta statuarum"</note>, in which he restores to honor (p. 8, 15) "the use and form of ancient philosophy and of the early theologians, who were certainly accustomed to veiling the secrets of nature with symbols of this kind, not only" <note>original Latin: "usum atque formam antiquae philosophiae et priscorum theologorum, qui nimirum arcana naturae eiuscemodi typis velare consueverunt non tantum"</note> etc.?

Having thus approximately determined the time in which the *Torch of the Thirty Statues* was likely composed, we must mention a difficulty presented by its "tradition" <note>the history of how the manuscript was copied and handed down</note>. Besler’s copy <note>Hieronymus Besler, Bruno's student and scribe</note> was written in Padua in September-October 1591, whereas, as we admitted earlier, Besler had already received the manuscript from Bruno in Helmstädt in April 1590 to copy it. We must conclude that the copy in Helmstädt was not made; and it is quite natural it wasn't, because both Besler and Bruno were on the verge of departing for Magdeburg. What there had been no time to do in Helmstädt was resumed the following year in Padua, when master and pupil met again. But what is the meaning of the phrase "I received from him a new treatise to be copied anew" <note>original Latin: "describendum denuo accepi ab eo novum tractatum"</note> etc.? Does it mean he had already made another copy before? Or does it mean that just as the master had previously entrusted him with copying other works, he had now given him this one to copy as well? We favor the second interpretation. But this does not change the fact that between the manuscripts known as *A* and *M* there must be an intermediate copy, and this must be either the manuscript delivered by Bruno to Besler or perhaps a first copy in Besler’s own hand. Now this would be explained somehow if *A* were not itself a copy, and could be believed to have been written under dictation;¹ as, for example,

->LXIV<-

For the *On Magic* <note>original: "De magia"</note> and the *Theses*, Besler <note>Hieronymus Besler, Bruno's student and scribe</note> recopies into a more elegant, calligraphic script (codex *C*) the original draft that had been written under dictation (codex *M*). But how can we explain why Bruno did not possess the original draft himself, but instead provided for copying either codex *A*—which is itself a copy—or even a copy of a copy? One might argue that the case is not much different for the *Aristotelian Commentaries* <note>original: "Commentarii Aristotelici"</note>, since Bruno's secretary could not have copied these from the original draft either, but rather from codex *B*, or perhaps from a copy of *B*. 

However, for the *Commentaries* we have at least the advantage, if we may call it that, of not knowing where, when, or by whose commission they were copied by Besler; and in any case, we have been able to plausibly assume that Bruno did not have his own copy of them, because he originally had no intention of publishing them (see above, p. XLV onwards). But the *Torch* <note>original: "Lampas"</note> was copied in Padua "under Bruno's own eyes" (Sigwart p. 299), and it would be absurd to imagine that he had not already attributed importance to this work when he composed it. And did Bruno not see that the text provided for copying was full of blunders? For, as we mentioned, at least some of the errors that mar Besler’s Paduan copy must have already existed in the manuscript from which he was copying. It is understood that before sending the copy to be printed, he would have reviewed and corrected it (cf. *Documents* p. 23 = Berti, 2nd edition, p. 398), but would it not have been better to review the previous copy a little? Naturally, it would not be difficult for us to devise some solution to the problem by piling hypothesis upon hypothesis; but since these would appear purely arbitrary even to us, let it suffice for us to have pointed out the difficulty.

# PREFACE TO THE TORCH OF THE THIRTY STATUES.

...art and science follow [experience and expertise], while chance and fortune follow laziness and ignorance.

Since things are this way, we are aiming for that art through which we may be separated from the likeness of those who run about as if by chance or <margin>5</margin> fortune. Nor should we wander with those other <term>methodical thinkers</term> <note>original: "methodicis." In the 16th century, this referred to scholars who followed rigid, often simplified systems of logic or pedagogy, such as the followers of Peter Ramus, whom Bruno often criticized for being superficial</note>—whose arts we have elsewhere explained and expanded according to their capacity—along some slippery, harsh, inconsistent, and not entirely fruitful path and survey. We wish to avoid a situation where <margin>10</margin> one must snatch the sought-after fruits from a tangle of useless foliage and unwanted, undesirable briars.

Therefore, our purpose is to pave a way of discovery of such a kind <margin>and 98<sup>v</sup></margin> that we may proceed | most easily and appropriately of all. We shall do this by using principles that are closer and more specific to the subject, rather than those that are so remote they require great <margin>15</margin> condensation, labor, skill, and lengthy discourse.

# ON THE VARIOUS KINDS OF INVESTIGATION.

From the manifold methods of investigation:

One is through <term>resolution</term> <note>original: "resolutionem." In this context, it refers to the process of breaking a complex whole down into its simplest components—much like modern analysis.</note>, just as the invention of writing and grammar came about by <margin>5</margin> distinguishing spoken sounds and their signs.

Another is through <term>formation</term> <note>original: "formationem."</note>, like the making of a statue (or a likeness) out of wax that is pressed by various molds, so that from the same material we can shape now a man, now a horse, now a bird, <margin>10</margin> now a vessel, and so on.

Another is through the constant and ordered <term>addition</term> <note>original: "appositionem."</note> of divisible parts around an <term>indivisible unit</term> <note>original: "ἄτομον" (atomon). Bruno uses the Greek word for "atom" to signify the most basic, indivisible point of either spiritual or corporeal substance.</note> of spiritual or corporeal substance.

Another is through the varied <term>combination</term> <note>original: "combinationem."</note> of <margin>15</margin> different parts and elements, as happens in the construction of a house.

Another is through a certain ordered <term>subtraction</term> <note>original: "subtractionem."</note> from some unshaped whole, just as by removing material in various ways from an unshaped stone, we can bring forth <margin>20</margin> countless figures of plants, animals, and other organic forms.

Another is through various kinds of <term>mixture</term> <note>original: "commixtionum."</note>, a method that differs from composition. In composition, the parts retain their own form, either entirely or in some way; here, however, they do not at all, as is evident when liquids and powders <margin>5</margin> come together to form a single mass.

Another is through a certain <term>separation</term>, where it is understood that we are not so much the ones acting, as it is nature or <margin>99r</margin> intelligence acting <term>principally</term> <note>original: "principaliter."</note> through us or through something else.

Finally, another is through <term>presentation</term> <note>original: "obiectionem."</note> or, to speak more precisely, <margin>10</margin> <term>projection</term> <note>original: "obiectationem." Bruno is likely referring to how images are "thrown" onto the mind or a mirror.</note>. In the same way that we can project countless figures onto a mirror to be formed, and by turning that same mirror toward different regions, we can conceive all things in their various conditions through a single and equal power.

<margin>15</margin> The first species of <term>discovery</term> <note>original: "inventionis." In Renaissance philosophy, "invention" refers to the discovery of arguments or ideas.</note> seems more suited to the arts of discourse and disciplines of that kind, which proceed by certain simple principles produced and distinguished by human reason.

The second is likened more to working nature, or to chance <margin>20</margin> or fortune; to this is proportioned the kind of discovery which is explained in <gloss>appositive</gloss> verbal "places" <note>Bruno refers to "topoi" or "loci," the mental "places" used in classical rhetoric to find arguments.</note>.

The third emulates the operation of the <term>soul</term>, which works from the center of the seed—so intrinsic to matter—by taking up and attracting various parts; its craftsmanship is dissolved by <term>resolution</term> <note>The process of breaking down a whole into its parts, as defined on the previous page.</note> <margin>25</margin> proceeding in the opposite order.

# ON THE THREE UNFORMED AND UNFIGURABLE THINGS.

<margin>10</margin>Before we proceed to the ideal and formed statues, let mention first be made of the three "unfigurables" <note>original: "infigurabilibus." Concepts that cannot be represented by a specific shape or mental image because they lack form.</note> to complete the subjects worthy of consideration. These are Chaos, Orcus, and Nox <note>Night</note>. Of these, **Chaos** signifies the void <note>original: "vacuum."</note>, **Orcus** signifies the passive and receptive power, and **Nox** signifies matter.

<margin>15</margin>
## ON THE FIRST UNFIGURABLE THING: CHAOS.

Chaos, therefore, possesses no statue, no figure, no image, nor even the capacity to be imagined; rather, it possesses a "reason" <note>original: "rationem." A logical principle or ground.</note> insofar as it has a logical consistency <note>original: "ratiocinabilitatem."</note> not without truth. Of this subject, there are thirty articles:

<margin>20</margin>The first article is that the indicator of Chaos is the succession of bodies in the same place; for a part of air succeeds a part of air, and similarly a part of water succeeds a part of water. From this, it is understood that neither air nor water is the space itself, but rather they exist *within* space, which must surely be something different from both.

---

<margin>2 Aristotle, On the Heavens, p. 270^b 19. | 9 In some versions 'unformables' | 18 'Reasonability' | 22 'Neither air' corrected from 'neither part of air' in manuscript A.</margin>

<summary>Bruno introduces the "unfigurable" foundations of his system—Chaos (Void), Orcus (Potency), and Nox (Matter)—explaining that while they cannot be pictured, they are logically necessary. He begins the analysis of Chaos by defining space as a distinct entity that remains constant while different physical bodies move through it.</summary>

<keywords>Aristotle, Chaos, Orcus, Nox, The Void, Prime Matter, Space, Metaphysics, Thirty Statues, Philosophical Cycles</keywords>

--- Page 78 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of Chaos, the first of the three "unformable" principles introduced on the previous page. Having established that Chaos represents the void or space, Bruno now defines its relationship to matter and physical bodies, specifically addressing the philosophical problem of how two "dimensions" (the space and the body) can occupy the same place.</meta>

-># JORDAN BRUNO<-

II. Chaos is the first of all things, as Hesiod <note>original: "Hesiodus." Referring to *Theogony* 116: "Verily at the first Chaos came to be."</note> well sings; for although the universe may have existed from eternity, and nothing precedes [Chaos] in the order of matter or the order of time, yet in the order of nature nothing exists unless it were first able to be, and <margin>5</margin> nothing is received except by a pre-existing receptacle <note>Bruno argues that space (the receptacle) is logically prior to the objects that fill it.</note>.

III. It is unformed and unformable; for every shape or figure concerns a body and physical matter, while [Chaos] itself must be absolute <note>original: "absolutum." Independent or untied from.</note> from these, existing before every body and before every matter. Furthermore, it is more "one" <note>In the sense of being a singular, indivisible principle.</note> than matter; for matter is everywhere <margin>10</margin> terminable and definable, even if it is [currently] undefined and indeterminate, whereas [Chaos] is nowhere <note>original: "nusquam." Likely meaning it has no boundaries or specific location because it is the location itself.</note>.

IV. Furthermore, there is nothing in it; I say that it possesses nothing <margin>101</margin> <note>Folio 101.</note>; for bodies are not understood to be in it as if it were receiving a fullness <note>As if space were a container being filled up like a jar.</note>, <margin>15</margin> but rather they are "with" it, specifically where the dimensions of the void coincide in every way with the dimensions of the contained body, since the space of the void is the cause <term>caussa<gloss>the logical ground or necessary condition</gloss></term> for the body's dimension to exist. For a body does not exist unless it is able to be; and it cannot be <margin>20</margin> unless there is space; and this space is the void.

V. Its dimensions concur with the dimensions of the body in such a way that, although it [the void] exists and can exist absolute from the body, it is impossible for a body, through its own [dimensions], to be separated from the empty spaces, or from those things which belong to the void. Nor is it an obstacle that <margin>25</margin> those who consider things more crudely <note>Likely a critique of the Aristotelians who denied the existence of a vacuum.</note> object that the "penetration of dimensions" <note>original: "dimensionum penetrationem." ...[con-]taining space and is understood as a continuum, yet it fills nothing; it does not take on the character of a filler, but only the logic of something present.

XX. It cannot be understood as rare, nor dense, nor extremely rare, but is <margin>5</margin> conceived as being beyond all such distinctions.

XXI. It does not exist within a composition as if it were a component part, even though it is inherent and understood within composite things. Instead, it has the character of that which bounds parts and distinguishes the primary <term>individual bodies</term> <note>original: "corpora individuorum." Bruno is likely referring to atoms or the most basic units of matter which, though they may touch, remain distinct because of the intervening space.</note>; <margin>10</margin> it is necessary that it be placed between each of these as they meet in contact.

XXII. That which is inherent in bodies should be understood as not being moved at all by the movement of those bodies, contrary to what Aristotle thinks <note>Aristotle defined "place" (topos) as the inner surface of the containing body, meaning space moves with the container. Bruno argues space is an absolute, unmoving backdrop.</note>; instead, when those bodies move, a different vacuum—just as a different space—is occupied. For in no <margin>15</margin> other way than with a ring changing its location, the air which is within the ring's circumference does not move *with* the ring; rather, once the ring has moved, other air and another space enters it. We must judge the voids that seem enclosed within bodies in the same way. For **Chaos** <margin>20</margin> is one single continuum on all sides and everywhere; it is not divided by the diversity, distinction, proximity, or continuity of bodies, even though here it may be full and there it may be truly empty—though we also judge that there is nowhere a vacuum without at least some <term>ethereal body</term> <note>original: "corpore aethereo." For Bruno, space is never "nothing"; it is filled with a subtle, life-giving fluid (aether) even where solid matter is absent.</note>.

<meta>This page continues the technical definitions of space and the vacuum. On the previous page, Bruno explained that space acts as a stationary container that does not move even when the objects within it do. Here, he moves into the ontological status of space—arguing it fits neither the category of "substance" nor "accident"—and explores the various names given to it by ancient philosophers.</meta>

# LAMP OF THE THIRTY STATUES

...[as we understand space to] be), we understand it to be neither a **substance** nor an **accident**. It is certainly not a substance, because it is not the subject of any <term>substantial form</term> <note>In the philosophy of the time, a "substantial form" is what gives a thing its essential identity (e.g., what makes a tree a tree). Bruno argues space is too fundamental to have such a specific identity.</note> in the way that matter is, nor is it the subject of an accidental form as a composite thing is. Nor is it an accident, because it has no subject—nothing that "receives" it; rather, it is the very thing that receives all other things.

XXV. It is defined as that **in which all things exist**, because it is equal in extent to the infinite universe; as that **which is in all things**, because it is inherent in every composition and is the **receptacle** of every fullness; and it is that **through which all things exist**, because if space were removed, nothing would exist, or at least nothing could be imagined to exist.

XXVI. It is poorly defined as "that in which nothing is, but something can be," since an <term>atom</term> <note>original: "atomus." For Bruno, an atom is a fundamental unit of matter. He argues that while an atom contains nothing else, it is not "space" itself.</note> is also something in which nothing else is, and a "place" is simply where something can be. Rather, it was <margin>**103^v**</margin> well said that space is **that in which all things exist**, when considering all the other distinguishing features already mentioned.

XXVII. Its parts—in the sense that one might imagine it having parts—should be understood as having no inherent shape or figure. For the **vacuum** or space is not understood as being square or round in itself, except by "accident" or through some external reason; for instance, when a physical body, bounded by its own sides, is considered square, or when a hollow space is considered spherical.

XXVIII. This same reality is called **Chaos**, **vacuum**, **the void**, **the plenum**, **place**, and **receptacle**, depending on the different ways we look at it. It is called the **vacuum** <note>original: "vacuum." Meaning "empty."</note> because of its fitness for containing things; it is called **Chaos** because it cannot be shaped; it is called **the void** <note>original: "inane."</note> because it cannot be named or defined; it is called **the plenum** <note>original: "plenum." Meaning "fullness."</note> because of its actual containment of matter; it is called **place** because of the relationship to bodies...

<summary>Bruno defines space as a unique entity that is neither matter nor a property of matter, but the infinite, shapeless receptacle that allows all things to exist. He identifies space with historical terms like Chaos and the Vacuum, explaining that these names reflect different aspects of its nature.</summary>

# THE SECOND FORMLESS THING
<margin>5</margin> # ORCUS OR THE ABYSS.

The **Abyss** itself, or **Orcus**, follows <term>Chaos</term> <note>In Bruno’s philosophy, Chaos represents the primordial, infinite void or space.</note> just as a son follows his father. From the fact that space is empty and infinite, there follows a certain suitability, a lack, or an infinite desire. This is expressed in the proverb: "privation gives birth to appetite." <note>original: "privatio parit appetentiam." This is an Aristotelian concept: the absence (privation) of a form creates a natural "hunger" or drive in matter to acquire that form.</note>
<margin>10</margin> 

By the name **Orcus**, therefore, we understand something like a vast and infinite whirlpool. It adds a specific quality to the "empty": it is able, in some way, to conceive, desire, and attract all things. We shall describe it through thirty distinct conditions;
<margin>15</margin> for we cannot provide a specific visual idea or form for it.

I. First, it is called **Orcus** or the **Abyss** because of its vastness, which matches the vastness of its parent, Chaos. This is because an infinite appetite naturally follows an infinite
<margin>20</margin> vacancy and emptiness.

II. It is named **Acheron**, or "the joyless" <note>original: "illaetabile." Bruno is playing on a traditional but pseudo-etymology linking the river Acheron to the Greek *a-chairein*, meaning "without joy."</note>, by likeness to those who are never satisfied because of their poverty. It is the most joyless of all things, because it represents total **privation** and the contradictory opposition to existence itself.

<margin>25</margin> III. Anything that does not completely fill it is understood to be rejected. A finite thing placed against the infinite (or against an infinite desire) allows for no proportion or connection.

# THE TORCH OF THE THIRTY STATUES

...so great a good work of the immense universe was brought forth from Mother Night and Father Light <note>original: "a matre Nocte et patre Luce." Bruno often personifies metaphysical principles; here, the universe is the offspring of the interplay between darkness (potentiality) and light (actuality).</note>.

XII. It is called blind and confused because it has no form, no shape, and consequently no way of being known—this is so that the son <margin>5</margin> might not degenerate from his father, Chaos.

<margin>10</margin> XIV. It is understood to be the parent of every **vicissitude** <term>vicissitude: the constant change or "turning" of things from one state to another</term>, since all things—which are participants in its deprivation, its shadows, and its Chaos—are understood to be infected by a kind of maternal affection. For all things desire to be everything because of this principle. I mean to say that among individual things, there is nothing that does <margin>15</margin> not long to be the "whole," since the drive of **Orcus** <note>A name for the underworld or the god of the dead, used here by Bruno to represent the hungry void of matter.</note> and the daughters of Night <note>Usually a reference to the Fates or other dark deities who govern the limits of life.</note> reject every finite and determined light, lest they seem to degenerate from their first parent, Chaos.

XV. Just as the parent, Chaos, lacks everything on one hand, so his granddaughter, Night, seeks everything; in the middle is the son, **Orcus**, <margin>20</margin> who hungers for everything.

XVI. Just as Chaos neither moves nor consequently has a place in which it might find rest—knowing neither motion nor rest (for that which is immobile cannot truly be called "at rest")—so Orcus indicates rest. For by its desire, it does not <margin>25</margin> wish, nor is it able to wish, to be stripped of itself <margin>107^v</margin>. Night pursues rest and the "Good"; and because she always seizes it in a particular, finite form, she casts it away as if in indignation. That "whole," which cannot be held in all its parts at once, she seeks through all its parts successively...

<summary>Bruno explains the metaphysical genealogy of the void, describing Orcus (the Abyss) as the son of Chaos who embodies a primal hunger to be "the whole." This explains why all finite things in the universe are in a state of constant change, as they perpetually seek an infinite completion they can never fully grasp.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Bruno’s metaphysical exploration of Orcus (the Void or Underworld) and Night (Potentiality). # GIORDANO BRUNO

...requires. Just as Night searches for rest, so Orcus <note>In Roman mythology, Orcus was a god of the underworld, but Bruno uses the name to represent the metaphysical "Void" or the bottomless hunger of matter for form.</note> points the way.

XVII. Orcus does not cross over, nor can it desire to cross over into the heaven and the world of light <note>original: "mundum lucis"</note>, because in doing so it would cease to be itself, and the order of the universe would eventually be destroyed. Indeed, one cannot imagine—without a contradiction in terms—that "deprivation" could cease to be "deprivation," or that the desiring subject <term>appetitivum: the entity that feels a lack or hunger</term> could pass over into the object of desire <term>appetibile: the thing that is sought after</term>. For if the desiring subject is removed, no object of desire can exist, just as no desiring subject can exist if the object of desire is removed. Therefore, just as a universe of light, fullness, and spirit is necessary, so too is it necessary that there be a universe in which these things may shine, breathe, and fill. Such a desire exists, then, that it does not wish to *not* be a desire, just as every being cannot wish to be a non-being; and for this reason, the appetite of Orcus is called "indicative" <note>Meaning it points toward the light it lacks.</note>, while that of Night is called "pursuing."

XVIII. Within Orcus, the rivers **Acheron, Cocytus, Styx,** and **Phlegethon** <note>The four traditional rivers of the Greek underworld, representing grief, lamentation, hatred, and fire.</note> are said to exist, not because this deep essence <note>original: "abyssentia," a play on "abyss" and "essence."</note> is inherently sad, tearful, or grieving—since its own being is pleasant and peaceful to itself, and no less good and necessary in the nature of things. Hence, Pluto <note>The King of the Underworld.</note> does not envy Jove <note>Jupiter, the King of Heaven.</note>, nor can he. Rather, these names refer not to the emotions of Orcus itself, but to the effects Orcus has upon those beings who are a composition of light and darkness—those whose mother is Night and whose father is Heaven. If light excels within these composite beings, they lament when they find themselves in the valley of shadows;

# THE TORCH OF THE THIRTY STATUES

...but if in these same things the maternal portion prevails, they hate heaven and strive toward Orcus <note>In Bruno’s cosmology, the "maternal" refers to matter or potentiality, while the "paternal" refers to form or spirit. Those dominated by matter tend toward the void rather than the light.</note>.

XIX. Chaos is formless; Orcus is "unformable"; Night is that which is always being formed but is never fully formed. Thus, in the <margin>5</margin> midst of these, Orcus exists in such a way that, in its very unformability <insert>108r</insert>, it is not formed, yet it *desires* to be formed. On one side, the emptiness or Chaos is never formed, nor does it even desire to be formed; on the other side is Night, which is always being formed and always longs to be formed <note>Bruno is distinguishing between three states of "nothingness": pure Chaos (indifferent), Orcus (the hunger for form), and Night (matter actually receiving form).</note>.

<margin>10</margin> XX. Evil exists in such a way that it would not be well for evil not to exist; for it contributes to the necessity of the good. Indeed, if evil were removed, there would be no desire for the good; for how would the good be "desirable," "glorious," or "magnificent"? Therefore, it is necessary that Orcus exists, acting as the Amphitrite <note>original: "Amphitrites." In Greek mythology, Amphitrite is the goddess of the sea. Bruno uses her name here as a metaphor for a "vast ocean" that contains all the various forms of lack or evil.</note> of evils.

<margin>15</margin> XXI. Just as the highest good is neither created nor capable of being created, so too is Chaos—the opposite of that fullness—neither created nor capable of being created, nor are those things that follow from it. This remains true despite the saying that Chaos is the parent of Orcus, and Orcus the parent of darkness or Night; for in these matters, through this way of understanding, we recognize a certain dependency and order, rather than a cause or a sequential <margin>20</margin> derivation <note>Bruno is warning the reader not to think of these as literal biological parents, but as a logical hierarchy where one concept depends on the existence of the one above it.</note>.

XXII. Before its entrance <note>original: "vestibulum"</note>, grief, diseases, and avenging cares are said to dwell. This signifies the power of Orcus—its influence and influx—which is communicated to its daughter, Night, through a "seminal propagation." This encompasses <margin>25</margin> every alteration and change, which are the seeds of corruption and death.

# GIORDANO BRUNO

...to be procreated (for change and suffering are the door and gateway of death and corruption); at which the jaws of Orcus stand, because all these things are swallowed and snatched away by that very "Orcian abyssentia" <note>Bruno coins the term *abyssentia* by merging "abyss" and "essence" to describe the essential nature of the void as a bottomless pit.</note> of which we spoke.

<margin>5</margin> XXIII. There, the chains signify the unbreakable necessity of fate, by which all things are bound and held.

XXIV. Fire itself is the blazing and most active effect of activity, which proceeds from this desire. It is understood to transform everything into itself and draw it toward itself, just as <margin>10</margin> <margin>108v</margin> among the elements, the most active fire seems able to convert all things into itself in a similar way.

XXV. Within it, Ixion <note>In Greek myth, Ixion was punished by being bound to a forever-spinning wheel.</note> is imagined to be on the wheel, where "he both follows and flees himself" <note>original: "se sequiturque fugitque," a quote from Ovid's Metamorphoses, 4.460.</note>, to signify that the desire of Orcus yearns for everything in such a way that, since it cannot desire itself, it is understood to desire nothing. For otherwise, if it did not recklessly flee from itself, it would not be Orcus, but Heaven; and if it fully followed itself, there would be not only no infinite desire, but no desire at all. Thus, if it desired nothing, <margin>20</margin> Orcus would not exist.

XXVI. Within it, Sisyphus <note>The mythological figure condemned to roll a boulder up a hill for eternity.</note> is imagined to push a rock toward the summit of a mountain, only for it to fall back down immediately to the same plain. This signifies the drive of "deprivation" <note>term: deprivation <gloss>privatio</gloss>; a technical term in Renaissance philosophy referring to the state of matter lacking a specific form or shape.</note> toward light, form, and the realm of being; yet, because its nature is the void, it abandons the paternal <margin>25</margin> realm <note>Bruno uses "paternal" to represent the source of light, spirit, and existence, while the "maternal" represents matter and the void.</note>.

<summary>Bruno interprets the myths of Ixion and Sisyphus as allegories for the "void" (Orcus), arguing that matter's eternal struggle to attain form is a logical necessity of the universe. He explains that the void must "flee itself" to maintain the cycle of desire and creation.</summary>

# THE LAMP OF THE THIRTY STATUES

Within this, Tantalus is imagined to have his feast so present before him that he is yet perpetually deprived of it, to denote that desire is the perpetual companion of deprivation. <note>Tantalus was punished in the underworld by being placed in water beneath fruit trees, both of which receded whenever he tried to eat or drink.</note>

XXVIII. There the Erinyes—as Furies—those "weighty goddesses," are imagined to have their place, because Orcus, or deprivation, is the place and the cause of all anger, indignation, envy, and other such passions. <margin>5</margin>

XXX. Just as, on one hand, the more we judge the fullness of light to be incomprehensible, the more we reach it; so too do we know this region of deprivation and darkness more, the more we conceive of it as infinite <margin>15</margin> | and indeterminate. **109^r**

## CONCERNING THE THIRD UNFIGURABLE THING, NAMELY <margin>20</margin>
## NIGHT OR DARKNESS.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of "Night" (Nox) as a metaphysical concept representing First Matter. It transitions from the previous discussion of Orcus (the void or deprivation) to the characteristics of the underlying substance of the universe.</meta>

# GIORDANO BRUNO

...is considered the most ancient <note>Completing the word "antiquissima" from the previous page.</note> among the Gods; and for this reason, she can be represented. For **First Matter** <note>The fundamental "stuff" of the universe that exists before it takes on any specific shape or form.</note>, which is represented by **Night**, bears the image of the **daughter of Orcus** insofar as it is deprived of form and implies an inherent lack; but insofar as it is a subject <note>The underlying "support" or "stage" upon which all things exist.</note>, it reflects its own <margin>5</margin> nature. Thirty conditions of this "unfigured" thing are reported, of which:

**I.** The first is that by which the succession or order of light to light is understood; its approach and return indicate darkness and night. For just as we distinguish the nature of a **place** from the nature of the **thing placed** <margin>10</margin> within it—because different objects in the same space succeed one another—and just as we distinguish diverse qualities in the same subject (whose existence is distinguished from the existence of the subject for the same reason); so, when different natures are seen to succeed one another in a certain order within the same insensible matter, <margin>15</margin> we are compelled to distinguish that matter itself—as an immutable and permanent subject—from all the specific forms of nature.

**II.** It is conceived to exist by way of its difference from "place" and "the void," which are not parts of natural compounds; and it is distinguished from all artificial and accidental <margin>20</margin> forms, which require some physical, sensible matter to exist. For a **Shadow** is a certain insensible subject; it reflects no specific natural form itself, but is understood by reason to be the individual and immobile subject of all natural forms.

**III.** Following from the second point: just as we do not recognize a shadow except by its difference from light—whereas light is <margin>25</margin> <margin>109ᵛ</margin> knowable through itself—so it happens that we cannot know **Night** (or matter) except through the succession of forms—which are the **daughters of light**—occurring around that same subject.

<summary>Bruno defines "Night" as a metaphor for First Matter, arguing that while we cannot see matter directly, we know it exists as the permanent "stage" or "subject" that remains while various forms and lights pass over it.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of "Shadow" as a metaphor for First Matter. Having previously distinguished Matter from "Place" and the "Void," Bruno now defines Matter's role as the fundamental, unchanging "subject" or substrate that underlies all physical transformations in the universe.</meta>

### THE LAMP OF THE THIRTY STATUES

<margin>5</margin>
**IV.** This "Shadow" is called the "first subject" <note>The underlying substrate or "stage" that supports all physical existence.</note> because neither its parent—"Deprivation" (also called Orcus) <note>In Bruno’s mythology, Orcus represents the dark void or the absence of form.</note>—can be a subject, nor can the "Void" be a subject, for the Void is merely the container for subjects. Rather, the Shadow itself, which fills the entire primordial **Chaos** and matches the vastness of **Orcus**, is the first thing that is submitted to existence. It accepts the union of "act" <note>In philosophy, "act" or "actuality" is the realization of a possibility; here, Matter is the possibility that "marries" the light of form.</note> as if it were ready for marriage, for it is capable of being joined to light.

<margin>10</margin>
**V.** Following from this, the next point is that the Shadow must not be considered a mere fiction or something purely logical. Instead, it is a most constant reality—indeed, it is nature’s most stable foundation. In the world of nature, that which we see remaining perpetually is that insensible subject <note>A substance that cannot be perceived by the senses directly, but only through the forms it takes.</note> upon which the constant change of forms is carried out.

<margin>15</margin>
**VI.** This principle must be judged such that, in and of itself, it is the source of no action. It is not the nature of Matter to act; rather, its role is to be the recipient of action and to lie beneath the agent that acts upon it.

<margin>20</margin>
**VII.** By the same logic, we must conclude that Matter is **impassible** <note>Meaning it cannot be "hurt" or fundamentally changed by what happens to it; it is "immune" to the fluctuations of the things it carries.</note>. Although we see a varied fluctuation of things being born and dying upon its "back," any "passion" <note>In this context, the state of being acted upon or undergoing change.</note> or suffering belongs to the specific things that perish, and not to the Matter itself, which perpetually remains underneath. In this context, to "be acted upon" is one thing, but to "serve as a subject" is another. Thus, Matter serves as the subject without suffering any change to its own essence.

<margin>25</margin>
**VIII.** As for why some consider it to be "non-being," it should be understood in this way: they define "being" only as things that are composed of parts and specific forms. Just as at the other extreme, philosophers call the **First Cause** <note>God or the ultimate source of reality.</note> a "super-essence" or **beyond-being** <note>original: *hyperusian* / ὑπερουσίαν</note>—neither an essence nor a being because it towers above all things—so too should **First Matter** be understood as "non-being." However, it is "non-being" because it sits *below* being, serving as the foundation that sustains everything else.

**IX.** Of this [Matter], it is said there is no "Idea" <note>In Platonic philosophy, an "Idea" is the perfect, eternal blueprint of a thing. Since Matter is formless, it has no blueprint.</note>. <margin>5</margin> **XI.** <note>Section X is missing in the original manuscript.</note> It is the "first thing" from which something is made. <margin>10</margin> **XII.** It is that into which the final "resolution" <note>The process of breaking down or decomposing into basic elements.</note> of all corruptible things occurs. For whenever a "transmigration" from one form to another takes place—such as when **chyle** <note>A milky fluid produced during digestion.</note> becomes blood—the form of the chyle is cast off so that the Matter, stripped entirely of that form and all its conditions and circumstances, may take on the form of blood. And when the form and essence of blood are cast off, being completely naked, it takes on the form of an embryo. 

<margin>15</margin> We do not agree with those who philosophize more crudely, who claim that when a human becomes a **corpse**—and thus a transformation from one species to another occurs—there is no resolution into **First Matter** <note>The most basic, undifferentiated "stuff" of the universe.</note>. They believe that the same "body-form" and quantity remain, and that "being a corpse" simply settles on top of the substance of Matter. 

<margin>20</margin> We, however, understand that this change or corruption (though it happens in an instant) results in a return to the ultimate and "naked" Matter. We say that Matter is completely stripped of the preceding form and individual identity before it enters the subsequent form of a new individual. Therefore, this "resolution" does not require that Matter...

<margin>15</margin> For from this fact, when matter receives the substantial form of a man, it follows that it immediately and consequently receives the accidents of a man. <margin>20</margin> This serves to confirm the preceding point: that just as form differs in kind from form, so do accidents differ in kind from accidents; and consequently, they can be even less alike in number.

<meta>This page continues the technical definition of "The Shadow" (First Matter). # GIORDANO BRUNO

...[form], it follows that it takes on a specific quantity; for the quantity of a man follows the **form** of a man in matter, and the quantity of a sparrow follows the **form** of a sparrow. Therefore, just as no form belongs to the essence of matter, so too no determinate quantity belongs to it; and in this way it is understood as infinite. Thus, just as any form without matter is indefinite, so too is any matter without form; they are mutually defined when they come into a composition.

**XV.** In the **Shadow** <note>original: "umbra." Bruno uses "Shadow" as his primary term for First Matter—the dark, underlying "stuff" of the universe that has the potential to become anything but is nothing specific on its own.</note> there is multiplicity, and it is understood to be the passive principle of multiplicity—not because of itself, for it is one, but because of the **efficient cause** <note>The "efficient cause" is the agent or force that acts upon matter to create a specific object.</note> that forms it in diverse ways.

**XVI.** Matter itself has no cause, and all things that are entirely free from the Shadow do not know a cause, but are **beings in themselves** <term>beings in themselves: entities that exist by their own nature and are not dependent on another cause to exist</term>; for nothing is made or caused unless it was first able to be made or caused. Such a thing, therefore, exists through **potency** <note>original: "potentia." In philosophy, "potency" or "potentiality" is the capacity or "power" to become something else.</note>; thus, potency itself—which has no [higher] potency and whose potency does not belong [to another]—just like **actuality** <note>original: "actus." "Act" or "actuality" refers to the full realization or "finished" state of a thing.</note> itself, has no cause.

**XVII.** It has no name, nor does it give a name, because it is proper to nothing, nor does it possess any property. Therefore, it does not give a name, because a statue made from bronze is not said to *be* [bronze], but to be a statue; and in cases of this kind, it does not name, but **denominates** <note>original: "denominat." Bruno is making a grammatical and philosophical point: matter provides the material adjective (like "brazen" or "wooden") rather than the noun that defines what the object is (the "statue").</note> | <column-break/> <margin>111r</margin> (for a statue is said not to be [bronze], but to be *of bronze*); nor does it have a name, because it has no **species** <note>original: "speciem." Here meaning the specific "kind" or "type" that defines a thing's identity.</note>.

**XVIII.** It is indeed a part of the **composite** <note>A "composite" is any physical object made of both matter and form, such as a rock or a plant.</note>, but it is not the composite itself, nor is it a part of the essence; for it is a necessary constitutive principle of natural things, yet it is not included in their definition, because it is proper to no one thing,

...unless perhaps in the definition of natural things, insofar as they are natural and constitute a certain genus of beings.

**XIX.** It is said by Aristotle that the principle of its own transmutation is not from an intellectual nature, but from an <margin>5</margin> **intrinsic principle** <note>original: "principio intrinseco." Aristotle argued that nature is an internal source of movement or rest. Bruno is clarifying that this "internal" source in matter is passive (the ability to be changed) rather than active (the force doing the changing).</note>; he perhaps understands this, as he ought to understand it, as a passive principle, not an active one.

**XX.** It is not actually separable from the composition or from the **light** <note>In Bruno’s terminology, "light" often represents "form"—the defining characteristic that makes a thing what it is.</note>, but only by reason, just as it does not have its <margin>10</margin> own actual subsistence, but rather essence and being; for as was said above, the final resolution of every composite thing ends in matter, because in the composite that follows after the previous one is destroyed, nothing remains of the preceding **form** or species [in the subsequent one] except for the matter.

**XXI.** It is said to be neither a "what," nor "of what kind," nor <margin>15</margin> "how much," but all things in **potency** <note>original: "potentia." This is the classic Aristotelian definition of Prime Matter: it is not a specific substance (what), quality (kind), or quantity (much), but the raw potential to become any of them.</note>, because, as was said above, it is not a being, but below being, the base and foundation of being. It is not a "what," because **quiddity** <term>quiddity: from the Latin "quidditas," meaning the "whatness" or the defining essence of a thing.</term> refers to form or light. It is not quantity or quality, because it is the subject of these things only because of the substantial <margin>20</margin> form to which it is first subjected. If, therefore, it is permitted to call it neither quantity, nor quality, nor quiddity, and we cannot call it "non-entity," let us call it **iditas** <note>original: "iditatem." A term coined from the Latin "id" (it/that). While "quiddity" is "what-ness" (identity), Bruno uses "iditas" to mean "that-ness"—the raw, indeterminate existence of matter before it becomes a specific thing.</note>.

**XXII.** We can call it neither perfect nor imperfect, because nothing can or should be added to its essence or its being; it <margin>25</margin> is not "perfect" because it is not "made" [perfected], but it is said to be perfected **by accident** <note>original: "per accidens." Something happens "by accident" in philosophy when it is not part of the thing's essential nature. Matter isn't inherently perfect, but it "becomes" perfected when it happens to take on a form.</note>, because clearly something is perfected out of it when it encounters the light.

<margin>111v</margin> **XXIII.** It is said to be **one in number** <note>original: "una numero." This means that all matter in the universe is ultimately a single, continuous "stuff," rather than many different types of matter.</note>, not through a single form that it might have or a particular essence, because then it would have act...

<meta>This page continues Bruno's ontological definitions of matter (referred to here as "Night" or "Darkness") and its relationship with form (referred to as "Light"). Having previously established that matter is below the level of "being," Bruno now explains its unity and its role in the constant flux of the physical world.</meta>

-># JORDAN BRUNO<-

...anyone, but because it possesses no difference of forms; and therefore it is called "one" in a **privative** sense <note>original: "privative." In logic, privation is the absence of a quality that should be present. Here, matter is "one" because it lacks any distinct features that would make it "many."</note>, because in itself it has no formal unity, and not in a formal or restrictive sense; it is called "one," I say, through its **freedom from number** <note>original: "absolutionem a numero." Matter exists "before" the concept of counting things, because counting requires distinct individual forms. It is one because it is an undivided whole.</note>, not <margin>5</margin> through a concentration into a single unit.

**XXIV.** It possesses no nature of its own, nor is it said to have a nature, but it is nature itself, or a species of nature, indistinguishable from that other species or nature which is **Light**, from whose union <note>original: "coitu." Literally a "coming together" or "coupling." Bruno frequently uses biological or sexual metaphors to describe the metaphysical union of matter and form.</note> natural things are generated.

**XXV.** When Matter joins with light, they do not <margin>10</margin> bring about a mutual perfection, but from them something else is brought to perfection. They do not cause a mutual change (for Light persists in its essence and **Night** persists in its essence immutably), but that which arises from them is most inconstant and most changeable. <margin>15</margin> Thus, just as it is not possible to enter the same river twice—indeed, as they say, not even once—so it is not possible to name the same composite thing twice; indeed, while it is being named, it is already something else <note>Bruno is referencing the famous "flux" theory of Heraclitus. Because physical objects are constantly changing their matter and form, they are never truly "the same" from one moment to the next.</note>. Meanwhile, however, nothing is more invariable than Night (or darkness) and light.

**XXVI.** In this joining, motion and penetration do not <margin>20</margin> belong to the darkness, to which neither knowledge nor any motion can be attributed; rather, it is Light which approaches this immobile and utterly **brute** <note>original: "brutam." In this context, "brute" means dull, senseless, or inert, like raw unshaped material that cannot move itself.</note> thing, and recedes from it unmarred and unaltered.

**XXVII.** It may happen, perhaps, that light is <margin>25</margin> separated from darkness, if it is possible for one of these to be separated from the other; however, no reason allows us to understand Shadow, or Night, as being separated from darkness. For if any privilege and majesty...

<summary>Bruno defines matter as "Night"—a passive, inert, and immutable principle that, when joined with "Light" (Form), creates the ever-changing physical world. He uses the Heraclitean river analogy to show that while the underlying principles are eternal, the individual objects they create are in a state of constant flux.</summary>

In formal logic, sub-contraries are propositions that can both be true at the same time, unlike direct contraries. Bruno is suggesting that at the highest level of divinity, opposites do not negate one another.</note> by the Platonists, rather than "contrary." ->## ON THE STATUE OF NIGHT<-
<meta>112v</meta>

<margin>10</margin> **Night** possesses an idea or form in which one may complete thirty contemplations.

**I.** First, because she has a statue, she testifies that she is a Goddess (for she bears a resemblance to God). This is due to the fact that she is an uncaused cause <note>A philosophical term for a primary force that exists by itself and is not created by something else.</note> and, for many things—indeed all things beneath God—she holds the status of a primary principle. In those things where "being" <note>existence</note> is distinguished from "essence" <note>the nature or definition of a thing</note>, one may perceive **Night** as the Mother and **Light** as the Father.

**II.** She is titled the **Mother of gods and men**, since there is said to be a twofold shadow: the sensible and the insensible (that is, of material and immaterial things); for the matter of the sensible and the insensible is likewise twofold.

**III.** She is called an **Old Woman** because of her antiquity, by which she is judged to equal the vast age of time itself.

**IV.** She is **clothed in black robes**, because she is destitute, possessing nothing of her own <note>As "Prime Matter," Night is the empty vessel that can receive any form, but has no color or shape of its own.</note>.

<summary>Bruno introduces the "Statue of Night" as a metaphysical symbol for Prime Matter, describing her as a goddess and the "Mother" of all things who exists alongside Light. He defines Night as an uncaused principle that precedes the distinction between material and spiritual existence.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Statue of Night," a mnemonic and metaphysical exploration of Night as a symbol for primordial matter. In the previous section, Bruno established Night as a "Mother" and a primary principle equivalent to an "uncaused cause." Here, he details her specific physical attributes—her veil, wings, and chariot—to explain how matter interacts with form and light.</meta>

### THE LAMP OF THE THIRTY STATUES

**V.** She wears a black head-veil for this reason: because she originates from her parent, Orcus <note>original: "Orco." In Roman mythology, Orcus was a god of the underworld; here Bruno uses the name to represent the dark, bottomless depth of primordial matter.</note>.

**VI.** She has wings, because she brings about and accompanies variation and change.

<margin>5</margin> **VII.** She has black wings, because her "acquisition" <note>original: "adeptionem," referring to how matter takes on forms.</note> is stained by privation <note>original: "privatione." In philosophy, this refers to the absence or lack of a quality. Bruno suggests that when matter "takes" a form, it is still defined by the forms it lacks.</note>; for she possesses nothing and yet touches everything with her wings, so that she may be understood as clothed in privation and stripped of bereavement.

**VIII.** She has wings extended to an infinite degree, because she equals the privation of Orcus, the vastness of Chaos, and an immense emptiness.

<margin>10</margin> **IX.** She is carried in a two-horse chariot <note>original: "bigis."</note> because, as the Pythagoreans <note>Ancient followers of Pythagoras who believed the universe was structured by numbers; they associated the number two (the "dyad") with matter and division.</note> declare, matter is a kind of duality—the very principle of multiplicity—warring against the unity and simplicity of light.

<margin>15</margin> **X.** She is pulled by two black and winged horses, which signify her subjection and her power; they are black because they were led out from Orcus, for in her power she proclaims the bereavement of action, and in her subjection she proclaims the privation of limits.

**XI.** She is said to leap out from Erebus <note>original: "Erebo," a personification of darkness.</note> into the light, and to row back from the light to Erebus, because she is the single principle for both generation <note>coming into being</note> and corruption <note>passing away</note>.

**XII.** Orpheus says that she brings light to Orcus <margin>113r</margin> and also draws it down with her, because through the mediation of matter, privation and the void are filled and given form.

<margin>25</margin> **XIII.** The more she is raised toward the region of light, the more she seems to be thinned out; conversely, the more she retreats toward her paternal regions, the more she is perceptibly enlarged. This is because she casts off higher forms <note>celestial or spiritual ideas</note> with greater difficulty, as she has less power over them, while she discards lower forms with ease.

**XXVI.** It is said that Poverty <note>original: "Penia"</note> married Plenty <note>original: "Porus"</note>; for "Penia" signifies want, and "Porus" signifies fullness. <margin>5</margin> Yet their marriage is false, because she conceives nothing from him and retains nothing from him. **XXVII.** She is also said to be joined to Heaven <note>original: "Coelo"</note> as if through adultery, <margin>10</margin> yet from him she is never separated. By this, some wish to signify that matter is made perpetual under the form of heaven, as if that form fulfilled her desire. However, this is false; rather, what is perhaps signified is the immensity of matter, which, by constituting an infinite universe together with the void, <margin>15</margin> nowhere leaves the presence of the great Chaos <note>In Bruno’s philosophy, Chaos is not "disorder" but the primal state of matter containing all possibilities.</note> empty.

**XXVIII.** For that reason, she is said to cast away and despise the forms she receives, because she affects only naked and simple species. Therefore, natural forms—which arrive clothed in accidents <note>In philosophy, "accidents" are non-essential qualities like color or size that "clothe" the underlying essence.</note>—<margin>20</margin> are rejected and scorned by her because of her hatred for these accidents; for she detests the status of a stepmother. But if any lights or forms that are naked, proper, and consisting in a certain simplicity are offered to her, she retains them either forever or for an immeasurable age. For all <margin>25</margin> natural forms, which consist of a certain composition, arrive as something already composed; their subject is not "prime matter" <note>original: "prima materia," the most basic, formless stuff of the universe</note> possessing pure potential, but something already existing in "act." Thus, they are held in hatred by matter itself... <margin>27</margin>
