### ON THE FATHER, OR THE MIND, OR THE FULLNESS.

There is indeed no physical statue of the Father, yet his symbolic type is infinite light. In this light, three things coincide so that everywhere and in every place there is the sun, the ray, and the brightness. In this, there is no distinction, <margin>10</margin> but a total unity and identity of these three. It is as if a spring, a river, and a sea existed in the same subject, with the same quantity and the same form; for it is the spring into which the river flows, it is the river which is the same as the spring, and it is the river and the spring which are the same as the sea or lake. Thus, wherever you look <margin>15</margin> and whatever you see within it, it appears as and is the river, yet it is simultaneously the spring and the sea; what appears to be the sea is the same as the river and the spring; and what <margin>115r</margin> ap|pears to be the spring is the same as the sea and the river. We explain this symbolic type through thirty conditions or descriptions:

I. It is an infinite sphere, equal on all sides. It is not <margin>20</margin> called a "sphere" because it has outer edges equidistant from a center—which would imply it is finite, as Aristotle taught <note>Aristotle's physics required the universe to be finite and bounded; Bruno famously argued for an infinite universe with no fixed center or edge.</note>—but it is understood by way of analogy. For it is equally distant from every boundary because it is *infinitely* distant from them. And for that reason, it is called a sphere because of its equidistance from the <margin>25</margin> center; yet it is called an *infinite* sphere because it does not have just one cen-

# THE TORCH OF THE THIRTY STATUES.

...a simple middle outside of which a chosen point is not the middle; rather, it is a sphere in which whatever point is chosen is the middle, just as in infinite space we can say there is either no middle or that the whole is the middle. Therefore, it is called a sphere <margin>5</margin> whose center is everywhere, just as in the aforementioned <term>Amphitrite</term> <note>In mythology, a sea goddess; Bruno uses her name here as a metaphor for the "universal ocean" of matter or the World-Soul which flows through everything.</note> the river is everywhere and the source is everywhere. It is also called "equal on all sides" to distinguish it from a finite sphere, which possesses equality only in a single individual instance, not everywhere throughout the whole. One should not think it absurd that Parmenides <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who described reality as a single, unchanging, and spherical "Being."</note> <margin>10</margin> and others attributed the definition and name of "sphere" to the infinite. For just as we might define a sphere from its innermost nature as "a body in which length, breadth, and depth are the same," so we shall rightly define and consequently name the infinite, since otherwise it would lack a name. To distinguish it <margin>15</margin> from a finite sphere, we add "equal on all sides" and "whose center is everywhere." What more excellent definition could be imagined? If Aristotle had grasped this, he would have refrained from his criticism <note>Bruno frequently criticized Aristotle for arguing that the universe must be finite and that an infinite body cannot have a center or a shape.</note>.

II. "Being in act" <note>original: "ens actu"; a Scholastic term for something that is fully realized or existing in reality, as opposed to being merely possible.</note> signifies whatever is able to be, as is manifest in the <margin>20</margin> aforementioned source, which can be a river so that it is a river simultaneously and always; and in this same thing, potency and act are triple and threefold.

III. Consequently, it is an infinite sphere in which the center, the diameter, the circumference, and the fullness of dimensions are the same. <margin>25</margin> | For since the center can be a line, it already is **115v** a line; since a line can be a surface, through this transition it is a surface; since a surface can be a body, it is a body. Thus, the center, the body, and the line are the same.

IV. In this principle, being and essence are the same, inasmuch as it is both that which is and that by which it is—things which are indeed distinguished in all others besides itself... <margin>30</margin>

He argues that in this infinite state, potentiality and actuality, as well as being and essence, are one and the same.</summary>

### LAMP OF THE THIRTY STATUES

XII. He is more intrinsic to the substance of things, and more inward in each and every thing, than all things can be to themselves.

XIII. Whatever is in him, is himself, just as brightness is light itself, and a ray is the sun itself (for in him, different <term>rational concepts</term> <note>original: *rationes*. In Scholastic philosophy, these are the conceptual distinctions the human mind makes to understand a single, simple reality.</note> arise only from the way our intellect is formed); and just as all things which are in truth are truth, and whatever is in light is light, so he and what is in him are not different.

XIV. He is who he is; for besides him there is nothing; for other things are said to "exist" <note>original: *existere*</note>, as if standing *out of* another, or to "subsist," as if being *under* others, or to adhere and in-exist, like <term>accidents</term> <note>Qualities like "redness" or "height" that cannot exist on their own but must "happen" to a substance.</note>.

XV. He is whatever he possesses; for if he possesses wisdom, justice, magnitude, or goodness, he *is* goodness, magnitude, etc.

XVI. In him, being, power, and action are the same, whereas in all other things these are distinguished by the nature of the thing; therefore, he cannot do except what he does, nor will except what he wills. Yet with this there is such absolute necessity that it is also absolute freedom; for in him, necessity and will—just like all other things—are the same; for he cannot will except what he wills, nor can he will to be able <gloss>1</gloss> except what he is able <gloss>2</gloss> to do. <note>The glosses here refer to manuscript variations regarding the relationship between "willing" and "being able." A theological concept referring to the part of the divine essence that remains forever beyond human comprehension.</note>, infinite brightness and a profound abyss.

<meta>This page continues the numbered definitions of the "First Principle" (God or the One), specifically focusing on sections XXV through XXX. ### THE TORCH OF THE THIRTY STATUES

XXV. It is called the "greatest thing" itself, or rather **maximity** itself or **eminence**, because it surpasses every magnitude. Every finite magnitude is bounded at an infinite distance | <margin>117^r</margin> from it and toward it. However, "the greatest" is not <margin>5</margin> said in comparison to evils; for evils are in the category of defect, and they tend toward the minimum. <note>Bruno argues that God is the "Maximum" in an absolute sense, not a relative one. Evil, being a lack of being or a "defect," cannot be compared to the absolute fullness of the Maximum.</note>

XXVI. This nature is reachable by a finite intelligence—such as our own—only as if in a mirror. Since we are like those dwelling in **Plato’s cave**, we are not permitted to fix a direct gaze <margin>10</margin> upon it; instead, looking back from the opposite direction toward the bottom of the cave, we are allowed to perceive not the light itself but a trace of the light—not the species and ideas themselves, but the **shadows of species and ideas**. In this metaphor, the mirror consists of a transparent body in which no image could be discerned unless it were <margin>15</margin> bounded by the opacity of a shadow. Therefore, we cannot contemplate its face except in the traces and effects that exist around matter. <note>Bruno uses the famous "Allegory of the Cave" from Plato's *Republic*. He suggests that physical matter acts as the "shadow" or "opacity" that allows the divine light to become visible to human eyes as a reflection.</note>

XXVII. We are said to be **blessed** <note>original: *beatificari*</note> by the vision of it, because he who sees it, sees all things (though outside of the mirror and the <term>enigmatic likeness</term> <note>original: *aenigmaticam similitudinem*. This refers to the biblical concept from 1 Corinthians 13:12: "For now we see through a glass, darkly" (in a riddle/enigma).</note>). He who thus sees all things, <margin>20</margin> possesses all things and lacks nothing. Hence even **Aristotle** <note>Aristotle, *On the Heavens* (De Caelo) Book I. Bruno interprets Aristotle's "eternal life" as the ultimate realization of the intellect.</note> calls its activity and evidence "eternal life."

XXVIII. Its being is beyond all difference, all contrariety, and all agreement; for all these things come from it, both formally and fundamentally.

XXIX. It is the <term>tricausal principle</term> <note>original: *tricausale principium*. A philosophical term describing a single source that acts as three types of cause: the efficient cause (that which makes a thing), the formal cause (the design or essence), and the final cause (the ultimate purpose).</note> of all things; for <margin>25</margin> it is the **form of all**, the **efficient of all**, and the **end of all**; the form of forms, the efficient of efficients, and the infinite end. <note>In some manuscripts, the word "efficient" was recorded as "fashioning" or "shaping" (*effigiens*).</note>

XXX. It "reaches from end to end," so that it is above all things non-exclusively, beneath all things non-subjectively, and <margin>30</margin> within all things non-inclusively. <note>This is a classic paradoxical description of the omnipresence of God: He is everywhere, but not contained by any one place; He is above all, but not separated from them.</note>

<summary>Bruno defines the First Principle as the "Maximum" and the "Tricausal Principle" (Form, Efficient, and End), explaining that humans can only perceive the divine through its "shadows" or "traces" in the material world, similar to the prisoners in Plato's cave.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the definition of the First Principle as the absolute "Maximum" and the source of all causes (using Plato's cave allegory) to the specific nature of the First Intellect. JORDAN BRUNO

# ON THE FIRST INTELLECT.

Just as fullness is opposed to the void, and just as a lack follows the void, so a most active efficacy follows fullness: namely, the **first intellect**, the **first idea**, the fountain of all ideas. For after the most absolute unity <note>original: "unitatem absolutissimam." Bruno refers to the "One" or the Monad, the ultimate source in Neoplatonic thought.</note> follows <margin>5</margin> the principle of universality, like a **duality**, so that soon the emanation of the universe follows, like a **trinity**, succeeding the duality. It has no figure, because there is no particular thing that can represent everything—at least in a sensible and explicit way. However, if we can provide some type <note>In this context, "type" (typus) refers to a symbolic model or representative image.</note> of it, let it be understood as a **circle** that is soon <margin>10</margin> reflected around an **indivisible center**. For that indivisible point was itself fullness, whole everywhere and absolute from all things; let the circle also be a unity, whole everywhere, but communicating itself to all things. Ancient theologians <note>Bruno often uses "ancient theologians" to refer to a mix of Neoplatonists, Hermeticists, and early Church Fathers.</note> understand that center to be the **paternal mind**, which, while it contemplates itself, <margin>15</margin> produces a certain circle and generates the **first intellect**, which they call the **son**. When this conception is perfected in the image of its own essence, the mind, being well-pleased with itself, emits a radiance <note>original: "fulgorem."</note> which they call **love**, which proceeds from the father contemplating himself within the son. Here one may contemplate in the father the **essence of essences**, <margin>20</margin> in the son all beauty and the appetite for generating, and in the radiance the **spirit** itself pervading and vivifying all things. These things being so, let the first intellect be conceived by the mind according to thirty conditions:

->THE LAMP OF THE THIRTY STATUES.<-

I. Let there be a circle that is not only most bright, but is light itself around a center, around which a radiance <note>original: "fulgor"</note> spreads itself out to an infinite extent.

II. Let this same circle be conceived according to two movements <note>original: "progressus"; literally "progressions" or steps in a process.</note>:
<margin>5</margin> one by which it is reflected into itself, and the other by which | it looks <margin>**118^r**</margin> toward other things as if shooting out rays; this is to denote that it first understands itself most fully, and then all other things.

III. With that same circle expanding itself into a sphere, let the poured-out rays
<margin>10</margin> finally be understood as contained, to denote that it understands itself and all things in such a way that it understands itself in all things and all things in itself; and just as it is substantially one in the rays—at the beginning and at the boundary of the rays <note>The Latin "principio et radio terminorum" suggests the unity between the source of the ray and its furthest extent.</note>—so it comprehends all things not in a manifold act, but in a single, simple act of intelligence.
<margin>15</margin>

IV. Since this is the first **species** <note>original: "species"; here meaning the primary form, ideal image, or "Idea" in the Platonic sense.</note>, in which the **paternal eye** <note>The Divine Mind or the "Father" from which the Intellect emanates.</note> finds pleasure—as if in an image of fullness that represents all things fully—it must be believed that it is the **beauty of beauty**, namely the primary beauty, by whose
<margin>20</margin> participation and imitation all beautiful things are beautiful.

V. It is understood as **two-faced** <note>original: "Bifrons"; similar to the Roman god Janus, looking inward to the source and outward to the world.</note>, just as the Chaldeans <note>The manuscript has a gap "..... dai", which scholars reconstruct as "Chaldaej" (Chaldeans), ancient sages whom Bruno frequently cites.</note> used to imagine the universal Apollo (for by this name they designated the first intellect); for while it understands the Father, it does not understand in such a way as to somehow abandon itself, but rather so that it is then
<margin>25</margin> most fully in itself—indeed, it is then most fully itself. This also denotes that for it, the past is not past, and the future is not future, but the whole of eternity is for it a single, simultaneous, and perfect present.

<summary>Bruno uses the geometry of a circle and its rays to explain how the First Intellect simultaneously contemplates itself and the universe. He defines this Intellect as the "beauty of beauty" and an eternal, two-faced entity that perceives all of time as a single present moment.</summary>

# GIORDANO BRUNO

VI. Let a sphere be imagined entirely full of eyes, because, as Orpheus <note>Bruno frequently cites "Orpheus" as a legendary authority on ancient wisdom; here he refers to the concept of an all-seeing divine presence.</note> says, the eye is everywhere and sees everywhere, just as it acts everywhere. This is because every being is the work of intelligence, and <margin>118^v</margin> everything | that exists, exists for the reason that it is understood.
<margin>5</margin> VII. It is called a circle and a sphere most mobile of all, because it proceeds toward all things and is in all things; but it is so present everywhere—it spreads itself out in every direction—that it is always present everywhere and is never absent from anything. Whence its motion is understood to coincide with the greatest rest <note>This "coincidence of opposites" (motion and rest) is a central theme in Bruno’s philosophy, heavily influenced by Nicholas of Cusa.</note>, and for this reason it is called the most <margin>10</margin> mobile of all because it is the most stable, and the most stable because it is the most mobile. For that which is moved in a circle with infinite velocity has simultaneously departed from and arrived at every point; it moves everywhere at once and yet simultaneously remains everywhere. However, one must not for that reason understand it as "immobile" in the sense of being without motion, <margin>15</margin> lest we perhaps understand it to be detached from its own operation <note>original: "operatione"; meaning its active work or function in the world.</note>.
VIII. It is the light enfolding <note>original: "complicans"; a technical term meaning the unity that contains all diversity within itself.</note> all light; for whatever understands, understands by means of it, just as whatever shines, shines by light, and everything that shines is in the light; so whatever understands, understands within it, and therefore it is the true light of the universe.
<margin>20</margin> IX. It is the same fountain of life—or rather, the life of all things; for whatever exists, exists so that it may contribute to the order of the universe, but he causes the order of the universe who understands and dictates that order. This, however, is the First Intellect, which, since it grants and disposes order, distributes being and life, and is <margin>25</margin> essentially life itself.
X. Imagine for yourself a sphere or a globe that is a mirror on all sides, which is so placed in the midst of things that all the forms and figures of things are joined together in it from all around, so that these same... <note>The sentence continues on the following page.</note>

# GIORDANO BRUNO

...which is diffused and, like a spiritual nature, is whole everywhere, just as we perceive a single voice or a single spoken word <note>original: "unam vocem, unum verbum prolatum." Bruno uses the physical behavior of sound—heard by many ears at once—to explain how God can be "all in all."</note> to be whole everywhere; and, if an ear is present anywhere, it is heard everywhere; | <margin>119^v</margin> similarly, if a subject is present anywhere capable of <margin>5</margin> producing understanding, just as the spirit animates and gives life everywhere according to the nature of the nearest species; hence, the intellect and the soul should be understood to reach those things which participate in intellect and life, not by local motion <term>local motion: moving from one physical place to another</term>.

XII. Indeed, it is present in all things, not as a part nor <margin>10</margin> as a potential, but as an agent and shaper <note>original: "agens et formator." In Bruno’s philosophy, the Intellect is the "internal craftsman" that shapes matter from within.</note>, more present to things themselves than they are to themselves; hence it should be understood not as if it comes from the outside or moves through some progressive motion to perform its work, because it fills all things. But as for why it is called "separable" from things by philosophers—or rather, why it is called a <margin>15</margin> **separated intellect**—it should be believed that this was said because it does not belong to the substance of particular things and works within them in such a way that it does not exist as a part of them. It is also said to be "separable" from them, not because it begins to be absent from some place or ceases to be present, but because it stops its <margin>20</margin> operation through the dissolution of the thing. For just as a place is said to be the "place" of a body resting in it without any change in space, and when that body is dissolved, it is no longer its place—whereby the logic of "place" is separable from the body not only because the place ceases [to be its place], but because the thing located there ceases to be; so the <margin>25</margin> intellect is separable from things in which it was, not so much because the intellect itself is separated, but because the things are separated from it.

XIII. Thus let the analogy of the universal intellect be understood...

| <margin>120^r</margin> for our intellects and the participation of others, just as the vision which is in the eye relates to the vision which is in the sun; for in the eye is the principle of seeing, which is proportioned to the intellect they call **passive**, while in the sun is what they call the **active intellect** <note>original: "intellectui agenti." In Aristotelian philosophy, the "passive" intellect receives information, while the "active" intellect—often linked to God—enables the mind to process and understand truth.</note>. Just as one sun is sufficient for infinite eyes to actually see, so one active intellect is sufficient for infinite individual minds. Therefore, the action of the active intellect is represented by the symbol of the eye | directed toward the sun.

XIV. We must consider the difference between this first intellect compared to other illuminated intellects, and the sun compared to the senses which are to be illuminated and formed. For here, the intellect must be understood as a sun in the center and middle of the eyes, whereas there <note>referring to physical sight</note>, it is understood as a sun positioned opposite or across from the eyes. This is because both the active intellect and the **vivifying spirit** <term>vivifying spirit: the "spiritus vivificans," or the breath of life that animates all living things</term> produce, operate, and illuminate from within; for he is a craftsman who works not *around* matter, but *inside* all matter and nature.

XV. They say that nature is hidden, and lies concealed in the **darkness of light** <note>original: "caligine lucis." This is a paradoxical phrase meaning a light so bright it becomes blinding or "dark" to human senses, a common theme in mystical theology.</note>, in contrast to **Orcus** <term>Orcus: a Roman name for the underworld or the god of the dead, representing total darkness</term> who lies hidden in the darkness of shadows. Thus, it shines in all things; and because it does not shine in a way that matches other lights or is proportioned to the gaze of the eyes, but rather exceeds every gaze, it displays no appearance and no shape. There is neither throne nor chair for it, because it is infinite. And for this reason, it is said to blind the eyes while it illuminates them, and to illuminate the eyes while it blinds them; for he truly sees this light who sees it as invisible and incomprehensible; while he does not see it, who thinks that he sees and grasps it.

XVI. Of this there is no figuration, no formation, because he himself is the form, the figure, the former, the figurer, and the actor of all—

**XVII.** It was represented by a circle, which moved sometimes around its own center and sometimes entirely around another <margin>5 120^v</margin>, to indicate that two ways of understanding are attributed to it. As is quite well known among the Platonists <note>original: "Platonicis." Referring to the followers of Plato, who often used geometric metaphors for the soul's movement.</note>, one way is that by which it turns about itself, and the other is that by which it turns toward the Father <note>original: "patrem." In Bruno’s Neoplatonic framework, the "Father" represents the primal source or the One from which all things emanate.</note>.

**XVIII.** Just as all individual senses are referred and reduced to the **common sense** <term>common sense: the "sensus communis," a theoretical faculty in Renaissance psychology that unified different sensory inputs—like sight and sound—into a single perception</term> as to a single center, and emanate from it, so too are all individual intellects formed by one Intellect, and are reduced and referred back to that One.

**XIX.** Although the same light of intelligence diffuses itself to all things, it pours into each according to the capacity of its nature. Although it is poured out as a whole—I say it is present as a whole—it does not, however, shine forth totally everywhere; indeed, it shines forth totally nowhere. For no particular nature can reflect it fully, because it does not admit of equality <note>That is, the infinite light of the divine intellect cannot be fully contained by any finite, limited being; the container is always smaller than the source.</note>.

**XXV.** The Intellect is called the center of the second world; the first world is the ideal archetype, which is entirely whole throughout the entire sphere and is the center everywhere.

**XXVI.** In the act of understanding itself, one may distinguish a twofold action: one is, as it were, reflexive, and the other is direct. The first is that by which the Intellect acts immanently within itself; the second is that by which it is carried forth, as if by progression, into other things. We certainly find this same similarity in our own intellect and soul, in which we likewise distinguish between an immanent action <note>An action that stays within the agent, like thinking.</note> and a passing action <note>original: "transeuntem actionem." An action that produces an effect on an external object.</note>.

**XXVII.** The World-maker <note>original: "Mundi faber." Often referred to in philosophy as the Demiurge, the artisan-creator of the physical universe.</note> is understood as an agent acting and crafting from within, both ordering and completing the work of the architect.

**XXVIII.** He is understood to act without succession or "discourse" <note>original: "discursu." In this context, it refers to step-by-step logical reasoning. Bruno is saying the divine mind knows everything instantly rather than thinking through a sequence of ideas.</note>, because he makes all things and possesses all things simultaneously. He does not apprehend or engage himself by arguing or moving from one thought to another, even though he may awaken apprehension and discourse in certain other beings.

**XXIX.** This intellectual power is implanted in all things. From this, there is ready at hand in all things a most sufficient effective principle of knowledge, from whose light nothing can hide itself. # GIORDANO BRUNO

...apprehends the fullness, which is its own Word <note>original: "verbum suum." In Bruno’s Neoplatonic framework, the Word represents the first expression or "conception" of the divine principle.</note> declaring and reflecting the Principle; from this relationship and conception, the love of that beauty comes forth. Soon, for the constitution of the second universe, the first intellect conceives the idea of itself and—within that simple form—the ideas of all things. Delighted by this form, and stirred as if by a certain heat, it produces the Spirit, which proceeds from it like a brilliant flash <note>original: "fulgor." For this reason, it is called the **Soul of the World** and the **Spirit of All Things**. Let us denote this Spirit—which is otherwise impossible to represent in a physical shape—through thirty conditions:

<margin>12</margin> **I.** Imagine a base which proceeds from an individual point and stretches and expands itself into the widest possible space; yet it is not like a cloud, <margin>15</margin> which becomes more thin and vanishes the more it is expanded. Instead, it remains whole everywhere, persisting and subsisting according to its every power.

**II.** Just as the Father is like a center, and the Intellect is like a circle around that same center, so the Spirit and the Soul of the World <margin>20</margin> is like a triple circle. The first of these is called by the Platonists the circle of **Life**, the second the circle of **Sensation**, and the third the circle of the **Vegetation** <note>original: "vegetationis." This refers to the "vegetative soul," the basic biological power of growth and nutrition found in all living things.</note> <margin>122v</margin> of all things.

**III.** It must be believed that the Spirit does all things in all things without labor, because it is the Spirit of the universe and the mover of the whole. <margin>25</margin> No other mover can oppose it, because there is no mover outside of it; for those movers labor who have something outside themselves that can perish.

**IV.** Not by a progressive movement or by a movement through local space <note>original: "locali discursu." This refers to physical movement from one location to another; Bruno argues the World Soul doesn't "travel" because it is already present everywhere.</note>, but...

...it consists, from which it proceeds, just as the brilliance of rays is so entirely poured out into this hemisphere that it remains rooted in its whole substance within the sun from which it proceeds. <note>Bruno uses the sun and its rays as a classic metaphor for "emanation"—how divine power flows into the world without leaving its source.</note>

<margin>5</margin> **XI.** Understand that the soul is "in" the body only because its external work is perfected within the body. **XII.** Conceive of the soul’s descent and ascent much like a wheel: as some parts are seen to sink, others are necessarily raised. In the indivisible center of this wheel, we might imagine either perfect rest (if it is a truly singular point), or <margin>15</margin> a simultaneous rising and falling. Such is the nature of the soul: it simultaneously descends into lower things to give them life, and ascends to higher things to contemplate them. By this same logic, it is understood to be at once spread out through the multitude and vastness of the things it shares itself with, <margin>20</margin> and yet remains undivided and, in a more real sense, entirely whole within the source from which it proceeds.

**XIII.** In this way, the spirit and the soul of the world penetrate all things and exist in all things, yet they do not mix with anything. They do not pass into the substance of any other thing, <margin>25</margin> nor do they transform the substance of another into themselves. This is clearly seen in light: though its splendor is spread through the air, the light itself takes on no quality of the air.

**XIV.** This brilliance of divinity is incorruptible and un- <margin>123^v</margin> failing, just as its foundation is perpetually the same, and its center...

...of fullness, it remains perpetually the same; for while the indivisible essence <note>original: "essentia," the core reality of a thing</note> remains fixed, its "arm" stands firm, and its "hand" consists of that same essence.

**XV.** It acts within itself, producing all things; for outside of it, there is nothing. Within it is fullness <note>Bruno uses "plenitudo," often related to the concept of the *Pleroma* or divine totality</note> and it is itself within that fullness, though in different ways; just as a house is in its foundations in one way, and the foundation is in the house in another; or as splendor is in the sun in one sense, and the sun is in its splendor in another.

<margin>5</margin> **XVI.** Substance is both divisible and indivisible in all things. In the same way, we understand the soul in our body to be entirely whole everywhere according to its essence <margin>10</margin> (which is indivisible), but according to its acts and operations, it relates to one part in one way and to another part in another. Thus, the spirit is the same everywhere, but it does not work the same way in all places.

**XVII.** While we say the Soul of the World <note>original: "Animam universi," the vital principle that Bruno believed animated the entire cosmos</note> is indivisible in its substance, we grant that it is easily multiplied. This is like a single voice which is heard, <margin>15</margin> indivisible, in countless locations; it can be multiplied through the various listeners and the places where the air strikes and echoes, yet meanwhile it is heard as a whole everywhere, and is nowhere divided.
<margin>20</margin> **XVIII.** Thus, this radiance <note>original: "fulgor," a flash or brilliance</note> is something that passes through and is poured into every substance; it is not supported by the body, but rather it supports the entire universe everywhere.

**XIX.** Let the individual <note>original: "individuum," meaning that which cannot be divided further</note> be perceived in such a way that it is the same as the whole universe. For the universe is formal, essential, and an <margin>25</margin> intrinsic principle <term>intrinsic principle: a starting point or cause that works from within a thing rather than being applied from the outside</term> that is effective everywhere. It is as if a single indivisible voice, while being heard as a whole everywhere in the universe, does not lose its individuality for that reason, but rather confirms and witnesses to it. In the same way, the same visible "species" <note>original: "species visibilis," the form or image of an object that travels to the eye</note> is present in countless eyes; though it informs them all due to the <margin>30</margin> multiplication of the seeing subjects, it remains undivided.

...for they understand the "idea" <note>original: "idea," here referring to the archetypal pattern of reality</note> to be the soul of the world and the soul of others. For this reason, the Platonists do not believe that the souls of particular animals are parts of the soul of the universe, since that soul is indivisible; <margin>5</margin> for us, however, let this remains a matter of doubt for the present, although we incline more toward the latter view than the former.

<margin>124v</margin> **XXII.** Since matter is the cause of multiplicity and division, while form is the cause of unity, we say that the radiance of divinity is a spirit that is one in itself and produces oneness (for from the one, insofar as it is one, nothing proceeds except the one). <margin>10</margin> Nevertheless, because it exists, it operates within the extended and material universe. Because this universe receives division and distributes matter into a multiplication of parts, multiplicity occurs. Thus, that soul which appeared whole in the whole and one in the one now—since the body has been torn into many fragments, as it were, <margin>15</margin> and multiplied into diverse numerical hypostases <term>hypostases: distinct individual existences or substances</term>—becomes many souls, just as there are many subjects. Consequently, an equal number of living beings are produced, or at least bodies that are nonetheless animated, even though the soul does not exert its form <note>original: "speciem," referring to the formal essence or appearance</note> and powers everywhere. This is why some things are judged by certain people to be without a soul. 

<margin>20</margin> This is almost exactly like a situation where there is one sun and one continuous mirror: in that whole mirror, it would be possible to contemplate a single sun. But if it should happen that the mirror is shattered and multiplied into innumerable portions, we will see the whole and entire image of the sun represented in every single portion. <margin>25</margin> In certain fragments, however, either because of their smallness or because of an unsuitability in their shape <note>original: "infigurationis indispositionem," meaning the physical configuration is not fit to reflect the image clearly</note>, something confused or almost nothing of that universal form will appear, even though nothing...

<summary>Bruno explains that while the divine spirit is essentially one, it appears as many souls when reflected through the "multiplicity" of matter. He uses the famous metaphor of a shattered mirror to show how one sun (the World Soul) can be reflected in many fragments, though some fragments are too small or distorted to show the image clearly.</summary>

# OF GIORDANO BRUNO

...it is present nonetheless, though unmanifested <note>original: "inexplicata," suggesting the powers are folded or latent</note>. Thus, just as when a single mirror is shattered, the individual instances <term>supposita: the distinct subjects or reflections that exist under a general form</term> of the animals' souls are multiplied because the parts have been multiplied; yet if it should happen that all the parts merge back into one mass, there will be one mirror, one form, one soul—just as if all springs, rivers, lakes, and seas flow together into one ocean, there is one Amphitrite <note>Amphitrite: a Greek sea goddess, used here by Bruno as a personification of the single, unified ocean</note>.

**XXIII.** This universal spirit must be understood: just as it understands all things from their innermost depths as an intellect, so too it works from the innermost depths of all things. Thus, it holds within itself the forms <note>original: "species"</note> and orders of all things, and the movements and successions <margin>**125<sup>r</sup>**</margin> of the celestial spheres, as if they were written in its very self. It reads these all at once, yet it does not unfold them all at once, since the nature of matter cannot grasp an action that is free from the flow of change <note>original: "vicissitudine," referring to temporal succession or the "turn-taking" of events</note>.

**XXIV.** We must imagine this to be the first unmoved mover <term>unmoved mover: a philosophical concept of the primary cause of motion that remains stable and eternal while initiating all change in the universe</term>; for the intellect possesses reason, the mind possesses fecundity <note>the capacity to produce ideas</note>, but the spirit possesses operation <note>the capacity to act or work upon the world</note>. It is this spirit, therefore, which, remaining motionless in itself, grants that all things be moved. Hence that saying of the Pythagorean poet is correct: "the spirit nourishes from within" <note>original: "spiritus intus alit," a quote from Virgil's Aeneid (6.726) often cited by Bruno to describe the World Soul</note>.

**XXV.** It must be understood as the first and universal shaper of all things, or rather as the very "form of forms," distributing, ordering, and perfecting the actualization of every single thing.

**XXVI.** It is itself the preparer, disposer, and agitator of matter; for it does not merely assist matter by providing its shape, but it awakens a desire for the beautiful within matter itself.

**XXVII.** Everything it works upon, it directs toward itself, and it directs itself toward the celestial mind and intellect; from which it see—

--- Page 131 ---
<meta>This page transitions from the general metaphysical definitions of the previous page to the specific symbolic analysis of the "Thirty Statues." Here, Bruno begins with the first statue, Apollo, who represents the Monad or the principle of Unity. He uses the various components of Apollo’s traditional iconography (the chariot, the sun’s rays, the lion, the raven) to explain different philosophical aspects of how "the One" is understood in the universe.</meta>

### THE LAMP OF THE THIRTY STATUES. ###

I. Apollo’s chariot signifies unity through **containment**, by which the universe is one because it contains all things.

II. Apollo, not sitting upon the chariot but elevated above it, signifies unity through **absoluteness** <note>original: "absolutione," meaning being set free or detached from material constraints</note>, by which reason the mind is not only one, but is Unity itself.
<margin>5</margin> 

III. His nakedness denotes unity through **simplicity**, by which all things that are beyond composition <note>referring to things that are not made of parts, like the soul or God</note> are one.

IV. The constancy of his light designates unity through **invariability**, by which reason eternity is one.
<margin>10</margin> 

V. The solidity of the rays notes unity through **truth** or **purity**; by this reason we speak of "true gold" or "true wine" <note>original: "merum," meaning unmixed wine</note> because it is pure; on the contrary, we call a thing false because it is not one, but mixed with something else.

VI. The single body <note>original: "alveus," the hollow hull or frame of the chariot</note> of the chariot signifies unity through **entity** <term>Entity: the state of being or existing</term>, by which "being" and "one" are the same; for each thing exists precisely because it is one.
<margin>15</margin> 

VII. A single raven flying alone around his face signifies unity through the **negation of multitude**.

VIII. The lion, which precedes the pole <note>the "temo" is the central beam of the chariot to which the horses are attached</note>, signifies unity through **termination**, in the way that a center—at which all lines terminate—is a certain "one"; let the hub <note>original: "cardo," the pivot or axis</note> of the wheel's rays signify the same.
<margin>20</margin> 

IX. The fact that the wheel is golden, the pole is golden, the axle is golden, and all parts are golden, signifies unity through **matter**, just as water, snow, dew, and ice are materially one and the same.
<margin>25</margin> 

X. That all things receive a single naming—because they are the horses of Phoebus <note>Phoebus is a common epithet for Apollo as the sun-god</note>, or the horse of Phoebus—signifies unity through **name**.

XI. That Apollo presides over the chariot bodies, the bodies over the wheels, the wheels over the pole, and the pole over the horses, signifies unity through **analogy**.

***

<note>Critical notes on the Latin manuscript traditions (M and A):</note>
1 Manuscript M moves the number I to before the word "Apollo." 
11 Manuscript A reads "we shall say" (dicemus).
14 In manuscript A, the word "identity" is crossed out before "entity." 
16 Manuscript A spells "raven" as *corbus* instead of *corvus*. 
19 Manuscript M uses *quod* (that); Manuscript A uses *quem* (which). 
21 After "signify," Manuscript A crosses out "that the golden wheel, golden pole." 
25–26 Manuscript M reads: "because the Phoebean chariot, the Phoebean horses, the Phoebean lion [is] one." 
27 "Chariot-bodies" (*Alveis*) in Manuscript A; "chariot-body" (*alveo*) in Manuscript M. "Chariot-bodies" (alvei) is our correction; Manuscript A omitted it and Manuscript M has "chariot-body."

<summary>Giordano Bruno interprets the mythological figure of Apollo and his chariot as a multi-layered symbol for Unity (the Monad). Through eleven distinct points, he explains how unity is found in containment, simplicity, truth, and the underlying substance of all things.</summary>

## ON THE STATUE OF SATURN
## AND THE PRINCIPLE.

<margin>5</margin> Having completed our look at the previous figure, we shall now contemplate the first explanation of Saturn within the concept of the "principle." Saturn, therefore—the parent of the Gods who govern the threefold world <note>In the Hermetic and Neoplatonic traditions Bruno followed, the "triple world" usually refers to the archetypal (divine), celestial (stars/planets), and elemental (earthly) realms.</note>—reflects thirty conditions, representing as many modes of the "principle."

<margin>10</margin> A "principle" is spoken of in a general sense, insofar as it includes every kind of initiation, causation, and effectuation.

I. First, he is said to be born from Father Coelius <note>original: "Coelio." This refers to Caelus or Uranus, the personification of the Sky in Roman and Greek mythology. Saturn (Cronus) was his son.</note>, by which the principle of origin is signified. This is the source from which a thing is said to derive its lineage <margin>15</margin> and is understood as such, just as a natural "genus" is called the principle of generation.

II. Let him be understood as being produced from that same seed, to denote the *seminal principle*; for the seed is the material principle of propagation.

<margin>20</margin> III. Let him be understood as presiding over a council or a household, to signify what I might call the *authoritative principle*. This is because domestic or civil actions are governed by his authority and command; for this reason, he is named the "Prince of Princes."

<margin>25</margin> IV. From the fact that he precedes in order, he represents the *ordinal principle*. <note>An "ordinal" principle refers to the first item in a sequence or hierarchy, rather than the cause of the items that follow.</note>

### ON THE UTILITY OF THIS STATUE.

From this statue, one may not only derive the reasons and ways in which something is called a "principle," but also the order of inquiring about any thing whatsoever according to the conditions of acting as a principle, whether <margin>15</margin> actively or passively—insofar as all things either are a principle, or come from a principle, or possess a principle. Therefore, in all things, once the order is established, one must look to see from where something comes: originally, seminally, authoritatively (or principally), <margin>20</margin> ordinally <gloss>by way of order</gloss>, effectively, instrumentally, and so on. But if the thing itself is the principle *from which* or *out of which* something arises, one should seek in that same thing by what instrument, by what efficacy, by what order, by what authority, by what seeds, and in what genus it acts. Thus, let nothing | **130v** of this statue escape or pass by without yielding fruit <note>Bruno uses the word "fruit" (fruge) to mean practical application or intellectual benefit.</note>.

<meta>This page transitions from the general definition of a "principle" to a specific exploration of the "Statue of Prometheus." In Bruno’s system of thirty statues, Prometheus serves as the mnemonic and metaphysical symbol for the "Efficient Cause"—the active agent or craftsman that brings something into existence. Having previously discussed the cyclical nature of time and the "privative" starting point under the Statue of Saturn, Bruno now begins to categorize the thirty different ways an agent can act.</meta>

GIORDANO BRUNO

## ON THE STATUE OF PROMETHEUS.

We took the principle according to its most general definition, which encompasses and transcends all types of causes, insofar as its meaning extends to many things; now, consequently, certain primary members of the "principle" shall be subdivided. The first principle is the **efficient cause** <note>original: "caussa efficiens"; the agent or force that actually produces an effect.</note>, which is represented by Prometheus the craftsman. It possesses thirty modes of acting, by which an agent usually earns its definition and name.
<margin>10</margin> **I.** Therefore, let the **commander** and **author** be signified by the creative person of Prometheus himself.
**II.** The **architect**, **designer**, and **Daedalus** <note>Bruno uses Daedalus, the mythical master-builder of the Labyrinth, as a technical term for ingenious design.</note> are designated through Prometheus’s invention of the arts and his technical industry.
**III.** The **minister**, **servant**, and **attendant** are signified by the assistants standing by during his craftsmanship.
<margin>15</margin> **IV.** We denote the **patron** and **defender of the work** by Father Jupiter standing beside him.
**V.** We signify the **maker**, **executor**, and **shaper** through Prometheus modeling and forming humans from mud and bringing them into being.
<margin>20</margin> **VI.** We signify the **perfector** and the one who **joins the work to its end** through Prometheus illuminating the formed human with light, splendor, and the fiery power of the spirit.
**VII.** We signify the **enticing**, **provoking**, and **attractive principle** by the beauty of the human form placed before him.

## ON THE WORKSHOP OF VULCAN
### OR ON THE THIRTY PRINCIPLES OF FORM. <note>original: "rationibus"; in this context, it refers to the various ways "form" (the design or essence of a thing) can be understood.</note>

Since we have just indicated the principles and modes of the "efficient cause" <note>The "efficient cause" is the agent that brings something into being; the "formal cause" is the design or pattern it follows.</note>, it is consistent to consider the principle and cause nearest to it; for it is the role of the efficient agent to introduce **form** into **matter**, whether natural or artificial. Therefore, Vulcan <note>The Roman god of the forge, here symbolizing the craftsman who shapes raw material into specific forms.</note> is introduced as the artisan and shaper immediately following Prometheus.

XV. ...[per]petuity. Now, an **image** <note>original: "simulacrum"</note> differs from a **pattern** <note>original: "exemplo"</note>; for the former refers to the form of animate, perfect, eminent, and natural things—whence we speak of the "image of the world," the "image of Jove," or the "image of Caesar." A **pattern** or **model** <note>original: "exemplar"</note>, however, is more appropriately used for any kind of thing; thus we speak of a model for letters, for writing, for music, or for harmony, where we would not properly use the word "image."

XVI. The fact that Vulcan, in the manner of craftsmen, imprints a unique mark upon the lightning bolts signifies that **form** stands in for a mark or a sign. Just as we perceive the form of war in the sound of a drum or a trumpet—not as a likeness or a picture or a resemblance, but as a **sign**—so too is this aspect of form understood.

XVII. Let the **Book of Works** recall the logic of sensibility, intelligibility, and opinion, insofar as a book is visible, can be considered by reason, and is subject to error due to its difficulty; here a threefold logic of form is signified, insofar as a threefold judgment follows it.

XVIII. The fact that the same and an equal amount of time is prescribed for all works signifies the logic of form in respect to **identity**.

XIX. The same signifies the logic of form in respect to **uniformity** <note>original: "aequiditate"; likely implying equality or consistency of nature.</note>.

XXI. ## ON THE STATUE OF VULCAN.

In the workshop of **Vulcan** <note>In Bruno’s memory system, Vulcan represents the craftsman-like power that defines and distinguishes forms within the physical world</note>, we have a manifold concept and consideration of form, and an abundant discovery based on formal reasoning; but in his statue, let us hold the judgment, <margin>**134v**</margin>
<margin>10</margin> distinction, and definition of form according to its most proper principles.

I. Vulcan, therefore, is called and described as the **son of Juno** <note>Juno often represents the higher air or the dignity of the cosmos</note>, to signify the excellence and dignity of form over **matter**, and its lineage from **light**.

II. He was **brought forth in an instant**, to signify that **substantial form** <term>substantial form: the essential nature or "soul" of a thing that makes it what it is (e.g., "human-ness" in a person)</term> is introduced into matter without the passage of time.

III. He is said to be **born without a father**, to signify that form is drawn out from the **potentiality of matter**, especially the form which results from the mixing of light and darkness; for light—which is the **soul**, whether universal or particular—is from the father without a mother.

IV. He is called the **ugliest of the Gods** born, because those higher forms, which have an attraction and inclination toward **matter**—or toward night and shadow, which takes its lineage from **Orcus** <note>the Roman god of the underworld; here representing the "darkness" or "depths" of matter</note>—are understood to be affected by "ugliness" through that very attraction.

# JORDAN BRUNO

V. He is said to have been cast down into Lemnos <note>An island in the Aegean sea, traditionally the site of Vulcan's forge</note> by his mother on account of his ugliness, because material forms, having an affinity for night and darkness, are thrust down into the shadows; for the **Platonists** say that souls, constrained by a love for matter, are cast down from the higher realms.

VI. He was made **lame** by that fall, because forms that are constrained and bound to matter "limp"; they take on individuation, become particular, and are effectively deprived of immaterial operations. Hence, toward intelligible things <term>intelligible: things understood by the mind/intellect rather than perceived by the physical senses</term>, our soul behaves like an **owl toward the light of the sun** <note>A classic philosophical metaphor: just as an owl is blinded by the bright sun, the human mind is often blinded by the highest truths</note>.

VII. He was received and nurtured by **Tethys** <note>A sea goddess, daughter of Uranus and Gaia</note>, because forms in matter possess their consistency through **water**, which brings about the union of parts—either through seminal propagation (since all seeds are moist), or because every composition and joining together, which is the foundation of forms, is produced by water.

VIII. He is understood to have been cast down first in **heaven**, <margin>135r</margin> second in the **waters**, and third upon the **earth** (that is, in Lemnos). This is because there are three genera of forms:
1.  The **intelligible**, which is perceived by the intellect alone; 
2.  The **sensible**, which is perceived by the external senses; 
3.  The **intermediate** or **imaginable**, which is perceived by thought and the internal senses.

Just as the heaven is the most spiritual and the earth is the coarsest, water mediates between them. Forms of the first kind are **souls**; forms of the second kind are **colors, flavors**, etc.; forms of the third kind are **loves, hates**, etc.

IX. He is called the Overseer of Works in Lemnos, because **form gives being to the thing** <note>original: "forma dat esse rei"; a central tenet of Bruno’s philosophy—without form, matter is unrecognizable and lacks specific existence</note>.

X. He inhabits the island of **Trinacria** <note>The ancient Greek name for Sicily, meaning "three-cornered"</note>, because there is still a threefold genus of forms: first is the **physical**, which regards matter according to both how we think about it and how it exists; second is the **mathematical**, which abstracts from matter <margin>5</margin> in our consideration but not in its actual existence; and third is the **metaphysical**, which abstracts from matter in both consideration and existence.

XI. He is said to have fashioned a throne out of gold, being mindful of the injury done to him by his mother <note>Juno, who cast him out of heaven for his deformity</note>. He gave it to **Juno** as a gift so that she might remain bound by its hidden chains. This is to signify that the forms and species of lower things draw down higher forms through the power of a certain **linkage** <margin>10</margin> <term>linkage: Latin *concatenatio*. Bruno refers to the "Chain of Being," where the physical and spiritual worlds are interconnected</term> and mixing. Through certain rites, ceremonies, and "superstitions," material things are joined to kindred spirits, and through those spirits to the **particular soul**, and through the particular soul to the **World Soul** <note>original: *anima mundi*; the vital spirit that Bruno believed animated the entire universe</note>. <margin>15</margin> In this World Soul, and by its power, those who later perform wonders seem to have "bound" the deities to themselves.

XII. He is said to be married to **Aglaia**, one of the **Graces** <note>Aglaia represents "Splendor" or "Brightness"</note>, because physical form is never separated from matter, nor is it found outside of matter, but is brought forth from its very "womb."

<margin>20</margin> XII. <note>The original manuscript contains a numbering error here, repeating XII</note> He is also said to have **Venus** as a wife, by whom <margin>135v</margin> he is nevertheless despised. While he is intent on his labors, she allows **Mars** to perform his "duty" <note>Mars and Venus famously had an affair while she was married to Vulcan</note>, or perhaps he is hated because he is a bigamist. This is to signify that it is impossible for one single form to be found in two subjects at once, <margin>24</margin> and likewise, it is impossible for two **substantial forms** <term>substantial form: the essential nature that makes a thing what it is</term> <margin>25</margin> to be found within the same subject.

XIII. He is said to carry a torch at marriages or...

<margin>5</margin> **XIV.** He is said to have instituted the games called the **Lampadophoria** <note>original: *Lampadophoria*; ancient Greek torch-races held in honor of fire gods</note>, in which the rules of the game require that the runners reach the finish line with their lamps still lit. This signifies that neither form nor matter moves on its own; rather, it is the **composite** <term>composite: Latin *compositum*; the unified being created when form and matter are joined</term> that moves. <note>The "lit lamp" represents the form or soul that must remain present within the material body for it to have life and movement.</note>

**XVI.** He is said to have two islands in which he carries out his <margin>15</margin> blacksmithing work, **Lipari** and **Strongyle** <note>Modern-day Stromboli</note>. This is to note that matter is subject to a twofold type of form and action: the **intelligible** <note>Form as it exists in the mind or as a mathematical concept</note> and the **sensible** <note>Form as it is perceived by the physical senses</note>.

**XVII.** He is said to have fashioned a puppy out of bronze with marvelous craftsmanship. This denotes that physical form works through change and analogy within matter; in the natural world, form succeeds form in matter according to a certain fixed order. <note>The "passing of the bronze dog" symbolizes how one form is replaced by another in the continuous flow of nature.</note>

# LAMP OF THE THIRTY STATUES

<margin>5</margin> ...having been bound by an oath by the **Styx** <note>The river of the underworld; an oath sworn by its waters was considered unbreakable by the gods</note>, he demanded marriage to **Minerva** <note>The goddess of wisdom and craftsmanship</note>. Jupiter granted this to him in such a way that she herself might deny him. This is to note that corruptible form and incorruptible form—and, universally, the corruptible and the <margin>136<sup>r</sup></margin> incorruptible—cannot merge into the same **species** <term>species: here meaning a specific type or class of being</term>.

**XIX.** The fact that he shares an altar with **Prometheus** <note>The Titan who shaped humanity and gave them fire</note> signifies that in natural things, the **efficient cause** and the **formal cause** coincide. <term>efficient cause: the agent that brings something about; formal cause: the internal design or essence that makes a thing what it is</term>

<margin>10</margin> **XX.** The **Vase of Pandora** <note>Historically a large storage jar (*pithos*), though often called "Pandora's Box" in later tradition</note> was crafted by him; within it, the ideal forms of things were contained, and from it all evils later emerged for humanity. This notes that forms—which in the field of matter mutually oppose one another—actually harmonize and are in a certain way one when outside of matter. For example, the concept of good and <margin>15</margin> evil, the ugly and the beautiful, or the sweet and the bitter, is the same; one cannot be understood apart from the other outside of matter. Yet, within matter, these opposites cannot tolerate each other and stand wide apart; indeed, they are separated from each other by the greatest distance.

**XXI.** That he captured **Mars** and **Venus** with a certain invisible <margin>20</margin> net signifies that through the power of a specific form—such as the **soul**—opposites come together, live together, and are bound by the tightest of chains. For the "friendship" signified by Venus and the "strife" signified by Mars are the fundamental principles of all things; natural beings are constituted because opposites run together into one and <margin>25</margin> harmonize in a certain way through the power of the soul.

**XXII.** The fact that Mars could not cut those nets (however thin they were) with any iron signifies the **indivisibility of form**...

# THE LAMP OF THIRTY STATUES

...says; for every form, whether **accidental** <term>accidental form: a quality that can change without changing what a thing essentially is, like being "tan" or "sitting"</term> or **substantial** <term>substantial form: the essential nature that makes a thing what it is, like "humanity" or "gold"</term>, is in itself indivisible, yet it is divisible by reason of the subject <note>The "subject" here refers to the matter that the form inhabits</note>; that is, accidentally. This is just as the diamond, which is in itself unbreakable, is worked upon with goat's blood <note>original: "hircino sanguine." Bruno refers to an ancient and medieval belief, recorded by Pliny, that a diamond—the hardest substance—could only be softened or broken by the blood of a goat</note> or another connected substance.

<margin>5</margin> **XXIII.** The fact that Vulcan goes out and enters the workshop by walking signifies that all artificial and extrinsic forms are **accidental**, and none of these can be **substantial**. <note>Bruno suggests that forms added from the "outside" (like the shape of a statue) do not change the underlying essence of the material</note>

**XXIV.** Vulcan’s hammer, which he carries in his hand and in whose active power all things capable of being formed exist, signifies that just as in **primary matter** <term>primary matter: the raw, formless "stuff" of the universe</term> there are all indeterminate dimensions which can be bounded passively, so in universal form there are indeterminate dimensions which are bounded actively. <note>Matter is the "passive" receiver of shape, while Form is the "active" hammer that defines the boundaries of things</note>
<margin>136v</margin>

<margin>15</margin> **XXV.** The fact that Vulcan is refreshed by **nectar** signifies the incorruptibility of forms; for every form is said to consist of an invariable and simple essence. For that which is corrupted <note>Meaning "breaks down" or "decays"</note> is always a **composite** <term>composite: a thing made of both matter and form</term>; yet neither matter nor form, of whatever kind it may be, is corruptible.

**XXVI.** Vulcan’s unquenchable fire signifies that substantial form does not admit of intensification or weakening—for example, "more" or "less." <note>In Aristotelian logic, which Bruno is utilizing here, you cannot be "more" or "less" of a human; you either possess the form of humanity or you do not</note>

<margin>20</margin> **XXVII.** Vulcan working incessantly denotes that the continuity in things comes from **form**; for form makes the **ethereal region** <note>The heavens or the upper atmosphere</note> a single continuum, and makes all composite things into a unity.

**XXVIII.** The fact that Vulcan does not grow weary from continuous work signifies that every form, just like primary matter, is **impassible** <term>impassible: incapable of suffering, feeling pain, or being changed by an external force</term>; for all "suffering" or "undergoing" belongs only to composite things. <note>While a wooden chair can be broken, the "idea" or "form" of the chair remains unaffected</note>

<meta>This page continues Giordano Bruno’s "The Lamp of Thirty Statues," specifically focusing on the statue of Vulcan, who represents the philosophical concept of "Form." Following the discussion of Vulcan's hammer and movements, Bruno now explores the relationship between a thing’s essence, its power to act, and its actual operation, as well as the metaphysical "hunger" between Form and Matter.</meta>

# THE LAMP OF THIRTY STATUES

**XXIX.** The fact that the divine being works in a divine manner and administers divine works to Jove <note>Jove, or Jupiter, represents the supreme intellect or world-governing principle in Bruno’s cosmology</note> signifies that the principle of form and essence follows the principle of power <term>power: Latin 'virtus', referring to the inherent capacity or potential of a thing to act</term>, and this in turn follows the principle of operation; for everything that exists operates according to how it is able to act. For the form which is **substance** <term>substance: the essential nature of a thing that exists in itself</term> is followed by the form which is **power**, and this is followed by the form which is **action**.

**XXX.** Vulcan’s fire, always craving things that can be burned, signifies the application of natural form to matter, which it desires to absorb entirely. Just as fire would wish to change all things into itself, so too every form would wish to transform all things into its own species and likeness—just as, conversely, matter craves to be shaped by all forms.

<margin>137^r</margin>
In all these things, one may contemplate in an orderly fashion Vulcan’s lineage, nature, fortune, marriages, office, invention, art, place, works, affection, lifestyle or worship, abundance, vengeance, progress, instruments, nourishment, element, constant operation, unfailing power, and noble effects. From this, one may define **form** according to various principles; nor is the work of defining and distinguishing peculiar to this statue alone, but it also shares the work of discovery with his workshop. For there is an order to considering and weighing a thing, not only by examining the meanings of "form," but also according to the proposed method within these listed conditions.

<summary>Bruno uses the myth of Vulcan to explain that "Form" (the essence of a thing) naturally seeks to express itself through power and action, and has a reciprocal "hunger" to organize matter into its own likeness.</summary>

## ON THE STATUE OF THETIS
## OR ON THE SUBJECT. <note>The "Subject" here refers to the underlying material foundation or substance that "stands under" all physical things.</note>

Thetis represents for us the material cause:

<margin>5</margin>I. First, from the fact that she is called the daughter of heaven and earth, it is noted that the material cause is not "naked" matter or a mere shadow, but a composite of matter and light; for matter, in and of itself, does not have the character of a cause, but rather of a principle <note>In Renaissance philosophy, a "principle" is an internal source of a thing, while a "cause" is an external influence</note>.

II. She is called the mother of many Goddesses, because many species of things emanate from the <margin>10</margin>material cause.

III. She is called the most beautiful of all Goddesses, because she is perfected by every kind of beauty, specifically when the universal subject is given shape by all possible forms.

IV. She is called the Goddess of the sea, because all <term>subjection</term> <note>original: 'subiectio', here meaning the process of acting as the material foundation</note> and forma- <margin>15</margin>tion comes from water and through water; for this reason, Thales <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher who claimed water was the primary substance of the universe</note> called water the principle and element of all things. The Chaldeans <note>Ancient Babylonian sages often cited in Hermetic and Renaissance texts</note>, while they attributed the active principle to fire, the stars, or even the sun, attributed the passive and formable principle to water. Hence even our own [authorities] say that the spirit and the consuming fire generate and produce things by <margin>20</margin>warming the waters.

V. It is said to be within her power to give birth to a son who is better than his parent, as they say Prometheus <note>In mythology, Prometheus warned Zeus that if he moved to conceive a child with Thetis, the son would grow more powerful than the father</note> signaled to the Gods; this is because, many times, a more excellent form is awakened within the subject than was present in the lesser efficient cause <note>The "efficient cause" is the agent that brings something about</note>.

<margin>25</margin>VI. While Jove and Neptune were contending for her hand in marriage <margin>137<sup>v</sup></margin>

indeed, it takes on a form laboriously and rarely; and while this form is unique, those others are manifold. This is because perfect reasons, figures, and actions are rare, found in only a few singular instances; just as among the most perfect animals, one can count fewer than among others. <note>Bruno is arguing that while matter can take many "manifold" or lower shapes easily, achieving a state of "perfection" is a rare and difficult process.</note>

<margin>5</margin> **XVIII.** The general faculty, by which it is easily changed into all lower forms, is represented by the "Anaxagorean Chaos," <note>original: "Chaos Anaxagoricum." The philosopher Anaxagoras taught that the universe began as a mixture where all things were combined in a confused state before being ordered.</note> in which there is the beginning of all forms, as if in a confused and mixed state. This is perhaps "Thetis’s mirror," in which she contemplates herself not as uniform or explicit, | but as "omniform" (all-shaping) within a certain **138^v** <margin>10</margin> confusion and entanglement. <note>The "mirror" of matter reflects every possible shape it *could* become, but because it hasn't been shaped yet, those forms are all tangled together.</note>

**XIX.** Peleus is finally destined as her husband because, whatever may be said of her passive and formable potential, she must nevertheless be subjected to an efficient cause in order to emerge into "act" or reality. <note>Peleus represents the "efficient cause"—the craftsman or force of nature that forces the potential of matter to become a real, physical thing.</note>

**XX.** Their marriage is celebrated on Mount Pelion, because <margin>15</margin> the subject receives its dignity and renown from its most noble form—the one which is most closely related to the higher and celestial forms. It is primarily named after that highest form, just as it is customary for an Emperor—even if he is also a king, a prince, and a duke—to be addressed <margin>19</margin> absolutely by his most excellent title. So too with natural forms: even if many <margin>20</margin> concur into one (according to the logic of their various powers), the subject is celebrated under the title and name of the superior and higher one. Thus, although in plants there exists the form of a perfectly composed element as well as a vegetative form, it is nonetheless named "vegetative." In living creatures, beyond these powers, the name is taken <margin>25</margin> from the higher form (which is the "sensitive" or feeling part); and from the "intellectual soul" or "intellectual power," the being is named "Human." <note>Bruno explains that everything is a hierarchy. A human contains the properties of minerals and plants, but we don't call a human "a rock"; we name the being after its highest capacity: the intellect.</note>

<summary>Bruno uses the marriage of Peleus and Thetis to explain how "matter" (Thetis) requires an "agent" (Peleus) to become a specific thing, and how objects are defined and named by their highest or most "noble" quality.</summary>

<keywords>Thetis, Peleus, Anaxagorean Chaos, potentiality, efficient cause, hierarchy of forms, intellectual soul, Mount Pelion</keywords>

# GIORDANO BRUNO

**XXI.** It is said that all the Gods were present at this marriage because all superior causes <note>The "higher" forces or celestial influences in the universe.</note> flow into the subject of natural things—which resides in the realm of the elements—just as all the semi-diameters of the world extend from the universal circumference toward the center. This is similar to the belief that the Earth, situated in the middle of the universe, receives influence from all the stars and is therefore capable of being formed into all species. The Earth receives a greater influx of all things the further one progresses toward its middle and center, because it is there that all lines truly terminate and all the rays of the stars converge. Indeed, in locations outside the center, even if many lines meet, they are far from being able to join all the diameters together. From this, it followed that the ancients <margin>139r</margin> considered the center of the Earth to be the treasury of all riches, and for that reason, they imagined that Plutus <note>The god of wealth, often associated with the riches of the earth and the underworld.</note> held his royal palace there.

**XXII.** It is also said and imagined that Strife <note>original: "Lis." In the myth, Eris (Strife) was the only deity not invited to the wedding of Peleus and Thetis.</note> alone among all the Gods was absent, and that she threw a golden apple into the midst only as a gift. This signifies that all the causes that agree with one another come together for the constitution of a subject; however, Strife contributes through her gift, but not in person. This is because, in a physical subject, contraries are joined together rather than remaining in conflict; for where a composite thing is established and permanent, the "gifts" of Strife lie hidden under the cover of harmony or love. <note>Bruno is suggesting that while a physical object is made of opposing forces (like hot and cold), these forces must be in "concord" for the object to exist. Outright Strife would destroy the object.</note>

**XXIII.** It is said that all the Gods who were present at the wedding offered gifts, following an ancient custom that still persists among the Germans. Vulcan <note>The god of fire and smithing.</note> offered a knife, Mars a horse, and Juno a cloak <term>chlamydem</term> <note>A "chlamys" was a type of ancient Greek cloak or mantle worn by soldiers and travelers.</note>, and each of the others offered their own specific gift. This is because in every physical subject there is a virtue...

...the foundation of all powers converge, according to the capacity of all forms within the unity of form, just as in the unity of matter. Hence, Anaxagoras <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher who argued that "seeds" of all things exist in everything.</note> understood that **"all things are in all things"** <note>original: "omnia in omnibus."</note>.

**XXIV.** It is said that Thetis <note>In this allegory, the sea-goddess Thetis represents the "physical subject" or primordial matter.</note> gave birth to many sons, because within the physical subject, the realization of innumerable species <note>The distinct "types" or "forms" of things in the natural world.</note> is brought to completion.

**XXV.** Of these sons, she hid many under fire at night to test whether they were mortal—coming from a mortal father—and for this reason, almost all those sired by Peleus <note>Peleus represents the active force that shapes matter; being "mortal" here implies the transient nature of physical forms.</note> died. This is to signify that the species received by a physical subject—which consist of a composition of parts—are capable of being dissolved. This dissolution proceeds from the penetration of an external force between the component parts. It is well known that the breaking apart and "divorce" of parts happens in this way. Fire is the most dissolutive and transformative of all things because of its active power to penetrate. Among corruptible things, those that are more easily penetrated are consequently more easily dissolved, and thus they are most easily altered and destroyed.

**XXVI.** Of all those born, only Achilles survived. He was bathed in ambrosia <note>The legendary food of the Greek gods that granted immortality.</note> for a long time and placed under fire at night; he was able to endure through the power of that divine liquid. This is because, among all physical subjects, <margin>139v</margin> the **human subject** is unique. One part of the human is luminous—belonging to the category of light and a more divine nature—and is "bathed in ambrosia," meaning it is nourished and fulfilled by the "food of the Gods" <note>Referring to the human intellect or soul which seeks divine truth.</note>. Its other part resembles his mortal brothers. Thus, because the human leads a dual existence, it is not swallowed up by mortality, by virtue of its superior part.
