# JORDAN BRUNO

“You do not conquer without divine power” <note>original Latin: "non sine numine vincis." This phrase, likely referencing Ovid, implies that human achievement requires a connection to the divine or intellectual realm.</note>; because for the constitution of such a subject, a twofold nature—specifically, a lower and a higher—will be seen to concur.

**XXVIII.** Among her other children, Thetis is said to have given birth to **Clytie** <note>In mythology, a water nymph who loved the Sun-god Apollo.</note>, <margin>5</margin> whom Apollo loved deeply, and later abandoned because of his jealousy regarding her sister Leucothoe. This signifies a certain subject among living beings: the **rational soul**, which is shaped by the light of the **active intellect** <note>The "active intellect" (intellectus agens) is a philosophical term for the power that allows the human mind to turn raw sensory data into abstract knowledge.</note>. Just as physical compositions are subject to all natural forms, so too is the soul subject to all **intelligible species** <note>The mental forms or concepts that the mind "sees" when it understands something.</note>. <margin>10</margin> However, the soul is sometimes abandoned by its light because of its attachment to matter. For this reason, it is compared to the **moon**, which is observed and seen to be sometimes bright, sometimes dark, and sometimes **halved** <note>original Greek: διχότομος (dichotomos). This refers to the moon in its quarter phases.</note>, according to how it opposes and subjects itself, either in whole or in <margin>15</margin> part, to the light.

**XXIX.** It is said that although she is abandoned by Apollo, she does not for that reason fail in her love for that light, but is instead even more inflamed. Thus, perpetually following him with her eyes, tears, and sighs as he rises, progresses, and sets, <margin>20</margin> she was turned into a **heliotrope** <note>A flower, such as a turnsole, that turns to follow the sun’s path.</note> by the mercy of the Gods. This signifies that the light of the subject’s intelligence perpetually nourishes and fosters a desire for knowing, even if it is deprived of the "fire" of direct illumination. Because of this, the soul pursues knowledge with all its zeal, and incessantly and <margin>25</margin> indefatigably strives toward the truth of things. Hence, just as the heliotrope has an eternal turning toward the sun, so the human soul perpetually circles around the light of the intellect...

<summary>Bruno uses the myth of Clytie turning into a heliotrope to explain the human soul's natural and tireless drive toward intellectual truth, despite the distractions of the material world.</summary>

**XXX.** Thetis <note>In Bruno’s system, the sea goddess Thetis represents "matter" or the "universal subject" which receives all forms.</note> from the sea, in the sea, around the sea, and out of the sea signifies the manifold nature of the **subject** <term>subject (subiectum): in philosophy, this is the underlying "stuff" or foundation that supports qualities (like how "apple" is the subject of "redness").</term>. We may see the <margin>140^r</margin> subject, namely, as that **in which** something exists, just as snow is the subject of whiteness; **out of which** something is made, just as stone, wood, and cement are the subject of a house; **from which** something comes, just as stone is the subject of a statue through the cutting away of parts and a certain removal; **from which** something arises [by transformation], just as wax and meltable materials are the subject of diverse forms, such as a horse, a man, or a tree; and **around which** something revolves, just as nature is the subject of natural philosophy, and God is the subject of theology. 

Those things called "subjects of intention," around which speculation or contemplation is occupied, are also called **objects**; for a "subject" differs from an "object" in that the latter is said to be "subjected" only in respect to the powers of knowledge <note>The senses and the mind</note>, whereas the former is the basis for everything capable of receiving something. Thus, "objects" are spoken of only in respect to the external senses, the internal senses, reason, and the intellect—to which the "subject around which" [the subject of study] corresponds.

# THE WORKS OF GIORDANO BRUNO

<note>original: "causam et terminum"</note> ...the cause and the goal, for the sake of which all other things are done, are suited to be signified.

In the **Archer**, therefore, it must first be considered that we can assign a twofold seat to him: either here, after the other <margin>5</margin> principles, or else before the others. This is to denote that the **end** <term>end (finis): the goal or "final cause" in Aristotelian philosophy; the "why" something is done.</term> in one way precedes and in another way follows the other causes. This is because it is considered either as it exists in the **intention** <note>The goal as it exists in the mind before acting.</note> and moves the agent to act, or as it exists in the **execution** <note>The actual carrying out of the task.</note> as the completion <margin>10</margin> of the agent's work. In the first way, it has the nature of a cause in itself; in the second way, it is a cause only conditionally and through intermediate steps.

**II.** Because the "end" is distinguished into the **work** and the **tool** (as Aristotle says), there is an **intermediate end** and an **ultimate end**. An intermediate end is <margin>15</margin> like how digestion is the final cause of walking <note>meaning: one walks in order to aid digestion</note>; the ultimate end is like how health is the final cause of walking. An intermediate end <margin>140</margin> is like the stretching of iron is the end of striking it with a hammer; the ultimate end is the sword or the knife. This distinction is signified by the **shooting** of the Archer and the **hitting** of the target.

**III.** In the twofold consideration of the Archer's work—by which <margin>20</margin> he is understood to have progressed either by the shot itself and the act of shooting, or by referring the entire work of the art of archery to something external as a "good"—he notes that in some cases the end is the **action**, in others it is the **work** (which is the result of the action), and in still others it is something else entirely to which both the action and the work are directed. An example of the first: the end of a <margin>25</margin> glutton <note>original: "gulosi"</note> is not fullness, but the very acts of drinking and eating. An example of the second: the end of a shoemaker is not the sewing and the cutting, but

...clothing; an example of the third kind is that the goal of the tailor <term>tailor (vestiarius): one who makes or provides clothing.</term> is not the garment itself, but the state of being clothed. <note>Bruno is distinguishing here between the "product" (the clothes) and the "purpose" (the act of wearing them).</note>

**IV.** Furthermore, the **ultimate end** is distinguished into that which is "absolutely ultimate" and that which is "ultimate within a specific category." For example, in the **Archer**, the ultimate end within his own category is the capturing of the prey <margin>5</margin> or the game. This, however, is not the *absolute* ultimate end, but rather the specific goal toward which all the actions of the hunt are ordered and which is not itself ordered toward any other part of the hunt. For the capturing of the prey is further ordered toward the food and clothing of the master; <margin>10</margin> this is ordered toward the preservation of the human being; this toward the constitution of the human species; this toward the fulfillment of the genus; this toward the adornment of the world; this toward the constitution of the universe; and finally, this toward **God**, who is the **absolutely ultimate end**. <note>This "chain of being" shows how a small act, like hunting, connects upward to the divine purpose of the entire universe.</note>

**V.** In this absolutely ultimate end, one must consider the property by which the same thing is called both the "first" and the "absolute principle." <margin>15</margin> For these two coincide: the **ultimate end** and the **first principle**. For this reason, it is called the **alpha and omega** <note>original: "alpha et omega" — the first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, symbolizing the beginning and the end.</note>, the cause of causes insofar as it is the beginning, and the principle of principles insofar as it is the end.

<margin>20</margin> **VI.** Just as the art, the work, and the intention of the **Archer** are set aside if the hunt and the game are taken away, so too if the **final cause** <term>final cause: the "why" or purpose for which a thing exists or is made.</term> is removed, all other causes are simultaneously established or removed.

**VII.** Place the **Archer** between the **Fate** <note>original: "Parca" — referring to the Fates of mythology who govern necessity.</note> and the **Grace** <note>original: "Gratia" — referring to the Graces who symbolize beauty, favor, and utility.</note> to signify a twofold end: namely, the **necessary** <margin>25</margin> and the **useful**. The "necessary" refers to the preservation of the species; the "useful" refers to the specific occasion and the individual. <margin>**141^r**</margin>

**VIII.** Add the accidental qualities of the **end**, first by attributing a palm and a sword to the assistant <note>In Bruno's mnemonic system, "assistants" are secondary figures standing near a main statue to provide further meaning.</note>; this is to signify that the **end** is that which is fit, by its attainment, to be a reward, and by its deprivation, a punishment <note>original: "combinatio" (combination), but likely a scribal error for "comminutio" (threat or punishment), as indicated by the presence of the sword.</note>.

<margin>5</margin> **IX.** That toward which a purpose and intention strive is the **end**.
**X.** It is that which is pleasing and delightful.
**XI.** It is that which consists in either **use** or **enjoyment** <term>use (usus) vs. enjoyment (fruitio): a standard theological distinction where "use" is a means to an end, and "enjoyment" is the end itself.</term>, for which reason theologians establish a twofold end: that which we **use**, such as the execution of the laws and precepts, which is the end of the commandments; <margin>10</margin> (similarly, that by which we are fed and nourished, such as the **Victory of the Word** <note>original: "Verbi victoria" — likely referring to the triumph of Divine Reason or the Gospel</note> through which the church triumphs); and the end which we **enjoy**, which is the **ultimate end** that follows the retribution of the Great Day <note>A reference to the Day of Judgment or the final resolution of time.</note>.

**XII.** No one shoots an arrow at the stars or at things that are too close <note>original: "instantissima" — things pressing right against the archer.</note>; therefore, the **end** is defined as a purpose that is possible to attain.
<margin>15</margin> 

**XIII.** That which has the nature of a treasure or a "good"—which is indeed twofold, namely the **true good** and the **apparent good**—is the **end** itself; for one does not only intend what is actually good, but that which has the *appearance* of being good.

<margin>20</margin> **XIV.** The **end** is that which directs and regulates the one who is shooting. For the boundary of the intention is the "reason" for the action to be performed; he who intends a thing to be perfect and good strives to work in a perfect and good manner.

**XV.** The **end** possesses a likeness to something alluring and attracting, just as a **magnet** is said to draw iron, or as beauty is said to stir up love and entice the lover.
<margin>25</margin>

<meta>This page continues the exploration of the "Final Cause" (the "End") within Giordano Bruno’s philosophical and mnemonic system. It expands on how a goal or purpose (the "End") motivates human action, mitigates suffering, and serves as the ultimate standard for decision-making and creative work.</meta>

# LAMP OF THE THIRTY STATUES

**XVII.** Consider the **end** as the seasoning of labors; for because of it, we who labor find delight, or at the very least we temper the toil, <margin>141^v</margin> or lose the sense of hardship altogether. Hence Lawrence, in the midst of the burning coals, cheerfully insulted the prince <note>Saint Lawrence was a 3rd-century deacon in Rome famously martyred by being grilled on a gridiron; he is said to have joked with his executioners, "I am well done on this side. Turn me over!"</note>, <margin>5</margin> and Anaxarchus mocked the tyrant Nicocreon from the mortar in which he was being crushed <note>Anaxarchus of Abdera was a philosopher who, while being executed by a tyrant, reportedly cried out that his body was merely a "pouch" being pounded, but his soul remained untouched.</note>.

**XVIII.** The **end** is that toward which there is direction and elevation; and this mode differs from the preceding one, because the same end both directs and elevates, and is that toward which the direction and elevation are aimed.

<margin>10</margin> **XIX.** The **end** is the norm, the rule, and the cause of deliberation or choice; for every deliberation and piece of reasoning involved in consultation looks toward and intends an end.

**XX.** The **end** is defined as an elaborated operation and action. Hence the end is twofold: **intrinsic** to the action—just as the end of study is <margin>15</margin> contemplation, and the end of contemplation is truth; and **extrinsic**, which is situated in the result of the work, just as the end of agriculture is the harvest. Thus, the *productive arts* <term>factivae artes: arts focused on making a physical object (from Latin 'facere', to make)</term> are those which deal with external matter, as if toward an external end; whereas the *active arts* <term>activae artes: arts focused on internal conduct or moral action (from Latin 'agere', to act)</term> are those which deal with internal or intelligible matter, <margin>20</margin> using the terms "acting" and "making" in their proper sense.

**XXI.** The **end** is that which, once attained, we are said to have made a profit and a gain.

**XXII.** It is defined as the glorious fruit of good labors, the retribution, or the compensation.

<margin>25</margin> **XXIII.** The **end** is that which those who work rightly are accustomed to say they have attained by merit and by right.

**XXIV.** They define the **end** as that toward which intention tends and in which that same intention is terminated.

**XXVI.** They define the **end** as that for which one is asked without it being a mistake or a rash request, and which "hears" the one who asks <note>original: *rogantem exaudit*; in this context, it implies that the goal fulfills or answers the effort expended toward it</note>.

<margin>5</margin> **XXVII.** That which we seek out willingly.

<margin>142</margin> **XXVIII.** That which we find with joy.

**XXIX.** That in which we rest peacefully.

**XXX.** That in which all intention and the worker reach their conclusion.

<margin>10</margin> All these modes can be applied to various actions, passions, and circumstances to be fashioned in and around the **Archer** <note>original: *sagittarium*; Bruno refers here to the zodiacal sign or a specific mnemonic figure used as a mental "statue" or container for organizing these concepts</note>, as it seems best and most convenient to each person according to their own genius.

# ON MOUNT OLYMPUS

## FOR DESCRIBING ALL THE SIGNIFICATIONS OF THE "END."

<margin>15</margin> Just as there are various ways in which the **end of intention**—from which the name <term>final cause: the ultimate purpose or "that for the sake of which" something is done</term> is derived—[is distinguished], so too the **end**, according to its universal meaning, when divided into its various senses, provides an abundance of judgment for distinguishing and of invention for multiplying mental conceptions. <margin>20</margin> Therefore, let anyone be permitted to note, following the previous examples, the common circumstances and properties of **Mount Olympus** <note>Mount Olympus is used here as a "memory palace" or locus. Let the conditions suitable for representation be noted, and let others that are necessary be imagined.

...the significance of the end, which consists in the magnitude of a thing; thus the end of a line is a point, the end of a surface is a line, the end of a body is a surface, and so on.

II. From the shape and arrangement of the mountain, there occurs the <margin>5</margin> consideration of the **end** as the form and figure of a thing, by which every body is bounded and displays its own specific essence.

III. The location of the mountain brings to mind the **end** signifying place; hence the end of a place is the summit, the extremity, the bottom, the depth, etc.

<margin>10</margin> IV. Some transformation—as when considering that the mountain was once Atlas the astrologer <note>In mythology, the titan Atlas was turned into a mountain range; Bruno uses this metamorphosis to illustrate the transition between states</note>—to signify the **end** and the limit of change: the starting point <note>original: *terminus a quo*</note>, the ending point <note>original: *terminus ad quem*</note>, or that into which and out of which something moves.

<margin>142^v</margin> V. From the imagined ascent and descent to the peak and <margin>15</margin> to the base, there occurs the concept of the **end** regarding local motion, which is called **rest**.

VI. By similar reasoning, the following meanings may be applied, such as for the **end of time**: setting, rising, the bounds of night and day, or the present, which is the end of the past, and so forth.

<margin>20</margin> VII. For the **end of consistency**, such as emptying, exhaustion, uprooting, or cutting off.

VIII. For the **end of a speech** or narrative, such as the conclusion, the closing statement <term>peroration: the final part of a speech, intended to inspire or summarize</term>, or the epilogue.

IX. For the **end of extremities**, such as both terms outside the middle of an argument <note>In formal logic, the 'middle term' connects two ideas; the 'ends' or extremes are the subject and predicate that remain in the conclusion</note>.

<margin>25</margin> X. For the **end of a voluntary suspension** of work, such as a cessation, an intermission, or a delay.

XI. For the **end of an involuntary or violent suspension**, which is why it is called an obstacle, a hindrance, or a barrier.

XII. As the end of **distinction**, just as in material things there are hedges, walls, dry stone walls, and boundaries that divide fields; in logic, this is the link <note>original: *copula*; the word "is" that connects a subject and a predicate</note> and the disjunction.

XIII. As the end of **termination**, such as a definition and description, by <margin>5</margin> which things and intentions are delimited from other things and intentions.

XIV. As the end of **repression**, from which comes restraint <note>original: *effrenatio*; the editor notes this may be a corruption of *refrenatio* (bridling/restraint)</note>, checking, and withdrawal.

XV. As the end of **labor**, from which comes rest, relief, <margin>10</margin> assistance, refreshment, and breathing space.

XVI. As the end of **modality**, by which we understand that a thing has a limit and that a limit is prescribed for things; this is signified by the adverbs: **to the extent that**, **as far as**, **so much so**, **that**, **especially**, **above all**, etc.

<margin>15</margin> XVII. As the end of **judgment**, from which it follows that something has been <margin>143^r</margin> verified, formed, informed, or decreed; from which also comes what is gifted, condemned, or justified.

XVIII. As the end of **presence**, from which comes departing, leaving behind, the hidden, and the distant.

<margin>20</margin> XIX. As the end of **favor**, from which comes being destitute, abandoned, alienated, rebellious, failing, or despising.

XX. As the end of **success**, from which are named the outcome, the chance event, the result, the fruit, the offspring, a good or bad odor, and so forth.

XXI. As the end of **power** <note>original: *virtutis*; refers here to the strength or capacity of a thing</note>, from which something is said to be faint, <margin>25</margin> exhausted, weakened, obsolete, or enfeebled.

XXII. As the end of **operation**, such as gathering one's baggage, packing away tools, folding things up, or sounding the retreat.

XXIII. As the end of **the work**, from which something is said to be finished, consumed, perfected, or polished "to the very fingernail" <note>original: *ad extremum unguem*; an ancient idiom for a work so smooth and perfect that a fingernail cannot feel any seams or flaws</note>.

...is seen. The first [kind of goodness] is signified through Caelus <note>Caelus is the Roman personification of the sky. In Bruno's system, this "statue" or mental image serves as a container for thirty concepts related to the purity and perfection of the celestial realm.</note>, in which we denote thirty notions:

I. There is **Caelus naked**, signifying **purity**, because a thing <margin>144^r</margin> is called **good** when it is pure, uncontaminated by any outside or foreign addition, adjacency, or accident <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that a thing can lose without ceasing to be what it is (like the color of an object), as opposed to its "essence."</note>.

II. He is **alone and unaccompanied**, to signify **lack of mixture**; for we call wine or milk "good" when it is pure and unmixed. This unity differs from quantity, and it differs from nakedness: because nakedness denotes goodness through the exclusion of the "clothing" of accidents, while unity denotes goodness through the exclusion of mixture and altering companionship.

III. He is the substance of the **fifth essence** <note>original: *quintae essentiae*. In ancient and medieval science, the "fifth essence" (or ether) was the pure, incorruptible material that made up the heavens, distinct from the four earthly elements of earth, water, air, and fire.</note>, as they say, to denote goodness from the standpoint of **simplicity**. For no compound is truly and naturally good, because in every composition there is understood to be a certain logic of potentiality, matter, and defect, which indicates either malice or a privation of the good.

IV. **Caelus is immutable**, by which he indeed denotes goodness from the standpoint of **truth**; for something is good in its genus, species, or number if it is "true" to that genus or species. Hence we speak of a "good lion," a "good tyrant," or a "good serpent." <note>Bruno is using "good" in a functional or ontological sense rather than a moral one; a "good tyrant" is one who perfectly fulfills the definition of what a tyrant is, embodying the "truth" of that role.</note>

V. **Caelus is good** because he comes from a **good principle**; hence, in common speech, whatever is made by God is called good, and it is the same by reason of natural goodness. Conversely, the logic of malice, defect, or disorder—which is found in monsters and other defects or excesses of that kind—is referred to chance, fortune, or luck.

VIII. Whatever Heaven attempts is conducive to something and useful in some way; hence, **good** is noted as that which pertains to **well-being** <note>original: *bene esse*, a technical philosophical term referring to a state of flourishing or perfection beyond mere existence.</note>.

IX. All beings, therefore, of whatever kind they may be, are **good** if they are properly examined—and no less good for the sake of the greater ones if we consider the nature of a principle, where the goodness of the whole depends on the goodness of its parts.

X. <margin>25</margin> XVII. Because through Heaven all things are ordered toward a single **goal** <note>original: *scopum*. Literally a target or mark.</note>, we are led to consider **good** as whatever contributes to the order of the universe.

XXIX. Just as the Heavens <note>original: *Coelum*. In Bruno's philosophy, this refers to both the physical sky and the metaphysical realms of consciousness.</note> are threefold: 1. the intentional, which is abstracted from physical things and exists as an image in our mind—indeed, it is the very collection of intelligible forms; 2. the physical or natural, which is the object of our external senses; and 3. the metaphysical, which is archetypal and divine, into which divine men are carried away; so too is the Good threefold. Thus, we are drawn into the consideration of a threefold good: the intentional, the real, and the metaphysical; or, that which is a matter of opinion, that which is true, and that which is absolute.

<margin>10</margin> XXX. From the purpose <note>original: *finis*. The goal or "final cause" in Aristotelian philosophy.</note> of goodness—from the target of motion, order, and beauty—we arrive at the consideration of the Good, which is the same as the "End," the parts of which we explained above in its own proper "Statue."

<margin>15</margin> # OF THE FIELD OF VESTA
## AS CONCERNING FORMAL GOODNESS.

Astraea <note>The goddess of Justice, often associated with the constellation Virgo and the return of a Golden Age.</note> was born of Coelius <note>The personification of the Heavens (Uranus).</note> and Vesta <note>The goddess of the hearth, often representing the Earth or the central fire in Bruno's cosmology.</note>. She is called the Goddess of Justice. Let us imagine her holding the inscribed tablets of the moral law, in which one may read the circumstances and reasons of a person living morally. Their order is arranged so that:

First, something is judged good based on its character, nature, or lineage; for it is a common saying that "like generates like," which is why nobility is judged by blood. For it matters greatly among whom a person has been nurtured from childhood, because <margin>25</margin> "the new jar will long preserve the scent of what it first held," <note>original: *quem nova testa capit, diu servabit odorem*. A famous quote from the Roman poet Horace (*Epistles* 1.2.70), suggesting that early influences are permanent.</note> and the leaning of the growing tree follows the bend of the sapling.

# GIORDANO BRUNO

...the action and operation of human life is pursued by one who does not deviate to the left or the right; and consequently, to hold the middle ground between extremes, in which it is commonly accepted that all civil virtue consists <note>original: *in quo civilis omnis virtus consistere vulgatum est*. This refers to the Aristotelian "Golden Mean," the idea that virtue is the balance between the extremes of excess and deficiency.</note>.

XXVI. Not to despise that which they call **Synderesis** <term>Synderesis: a term in scholastic philosophy referring to the innate, habitual knowledge of the primary principles of moral action; the "spark of conscience" that remains even in the fallen state</term>, which acts as an internal remorse of conscience murmuring against perverse thoughts, crying out from the "stern" of our soul; and to be conformed to the image of the intelligible world and the architect of the sensible world according to its dictate.

XXVII. Not to cross the line—not, I say, in the manner of the **Stoics**, as if justice and moral goodness consist in some indivisible point <note>The Stoics famously argued that virtue was absolute; one was either perfectly virtuous or not at all. Bruno suggests a more flexible "line" that has "breadth," allowing for human degrees of goodness.</note>, but by understanding the "line" as having a certain width, so that it serves not as a strict boundary but as a guide for our actions.

<margin>147</margin>
XXVIII. To conform to **Nature** as it works and dictates (for Nature has engraved clearer precepts of morality within the inner chambers of divine reasoning, just as it has sown certain seeds of truth that are not yet fully opened); likewise, to expend all the faculties and powers which we have received from Nature for the sake of acting well, and to put them to use like one's own "talents" <note>original: *talentorum numerum*. A reference to the biblical Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14-30), implying a moral duty to develop and "invest" one's natural abilities.</note> to gain interest; for anyone is good insofar as they omit nothing within their own power and capacity, while concerning things that are impossible, there is neither justice nor injustice.

XXIX. **Goodness** must be considered according to the dictate of nature in those things which are capable of transgression, and which are inclined and impelled...

## ON THE FIELD OF THE OCEAN.

We depict the attributes of **magnitude** <term>Magnitude (*magnitudo*): in Bruno's system, this refers to "greatness" or "extension" in both a physical and metaphysical sense.</term> through the field of the Ocean. Therefore, we first consider a distinction in the Ocean, <margin>20</margin> which is followed by a distinction in the modes of magnitude. It possesses, then:
1. **Vastness**,
2. **Efficacy and power**,
3. **Excellence**,
4. **Location or containment**;
By these it signifies different modes of magnitude:
1. Of **bulk** <note>original: *molis*. Refers to physical mass or weight.</note>,
2. Of **power**,
3. Of **dignity**,
4. Of **containment or capacity**, <margin>147v</margin>
to which you may add a fifth, namely that of **number or multitude**. <margin>25</margin>

XV. Virile, mature, bearded.

XVI. Ready to act, difficult to be acted upon; or, acting with ease while suffering <note>original: *patiens*; here meaning "being the object of another's action" rather than just feeling pain</note> with difficulty.

XVII. Firm, immobile, stationary, unmoved, 
<margin>5</margin> yet capable of moving others.

XVIII. Prompt for action, agile, exquisite, prepared, equipped with sails, oars, and feathers <note>a metaphorical image for being fully prepared for swift movement</note>.

<margin>149<sup>v</sup></margin> XIX. Frequent, continuous, of uninterrupted action,
of unbroken constancy, with perpetual virtue <term>virtue: *virtus*, meaning inherent power or efficacy</term>, effectiveness, and 
<margin>10</margin> operation.

XX. Efficient by nature, willing, or out of habit—which is considered like a second nature; because just as it happens naturally for those things acting by nature, so too does no suffering <note>original: *passio*; the state of being passively acted upon by an external force</note> happen to those who are accustomed to their work.

XXI. Industrious, whose very activity is its rest, and for whom 
<margin>14</margin> resting would be, in a way, a state of violence <note>i.e., acting against its own nature</note>.

XXII. That which easily reaches its intended goal, which nothing opposes, nothing resists, or which nothing hinders.

XXIII. That which rises up eagerly and fearlessly against obstacles, if there be any.

<margin>20</margin> XXIV. That which is able to help and be present for the oppressed, helps and acts.

XXV. That which struggles, fights, and resists contrary forces.

XXVI. That which is not conquered, not overcome, does not flag, does not weaken—or does so barely.

<margin>25</margin> XXVII. That which attacks, conquers, overcomes, captures, and triumphs.

XXVIII. That which is formidable, dreadful, unattempted, inaccessible, avoided—from which adversaries turn away.

**XXIX.** Irrefutable, unconquerable.

**XXX.** That which possesses divine force or the likeness of divine power, as being either infinite, or the greatest of its kind, or simply great.

<margin>5</margin> Indeed, all these things, in the order they were surveyed, can be taken both passively and actively. For just as you considered virtue <term>virtue: *virtus*, meaning inherent power, efficacy, or excellence</term> from the perspective of aptitude, habit, study, attainment, help, and the other ways by which something is endowed with virtue and 
<margin>10</margin> efficacy in itself—whether by nature, art, or some gift of the Gods—so thereafter you should consider virtue from the perspective by which it actively makes other things apt, accustomed, studious, perfect, or helped. <margin>150</margin> In these cases, it rouses aptitude and habit, or promotes them toward power through study and action, or preserves them in that power; for the fulfillment of a perfect quality 
<margin>15</margin> and nature, once it is established in a subject, will—if found eminently within it—also be found to be communicative and diffusive <note>This reflects a Neoplatonic idea: a perfect thing naturally "overflows" its excellence into others</note>.

->THE FIELD OF EARTH<-
->OR ON POWER.<-

<margin>20</margin> We wish to signify potency or possibility <note>original: *potentiam seu possibilitatem*</note> through the Earth <note>original: *Tellurem*, referring to Tellus, the Roman goddess of the Earth</note> exposed to the Heavens. For just as virtue and active power belong to higher things, so possibility—or passive, receptive, and secondary active power—belongs to lower things.

Furthermore, one kind of power is for acting, another for suffering <note>original: *patiendum*; in this context, "to be acted upon" by an external force</note>, 
<margin>25</margin> another for impressing, for influencing, or for communicating.

<page-num>123</page-num>
<header>THE LAMP OF THE THIRTY STATUES</header>

...others are for receiving and complying. Likewise, there is a certain power for change according to substance, as in those things which are generated and corrupted; and a certain power according to dispositions, as in their accidents <term>accidents: non-essential qualities of a thing, like its color or temperature, that can change without the thing itself ceasing to exist</term> or those things which surround them. <margin>5</margin> There is also a power according to perfecting formation, such as that of the intellect and the senses, of power and the **intelligible species** <term>intelligible species: the mental forms or "blueprints" through which the mind recognizes and understands reality</term>, in which subjects the logic of contraries unites into one. Therefore, the power of contraries is one and the same; and in those things where the same physical subject is simultaneously wounded, affected, and informed <margin>10</margin>, it is necessarily affected and informed <note>original: "laedit, afficit et informat." Bruno is discussing how a single subject can undergo multiple types of change at once</note>. 

However, some things admit a potency that is not at all passive, not at all innovative, and not at all concerned with new dispositions, habits, or formations. Instead, in these cases, potency coincides with act, as in those things which belong to the **intelligible world** <note>In Neoplatonism, the "intelligible world" is the realm of pure thought and divine forms</note>, where all things <margin>15</margin> are in act whatever they are able to be <note>In the divine or spiritual realm, there is no "potential" that isn't already realized; everything is fully "actual" at all times</note>. Now, let us note in order the reasons and divisions by which something can be verified as being in potency or possessing power.

**I.** Therefore, there is an **effective** or **receptive force**, serving as a principle for doing or undergoing something.

<margin>20</margin> **II.** There is **impulse** <note>original: "appulsus"</note>, that is, an aptitude for motion, whether true or figurative, by which a subject or a power is drawn toward an object or a form.

<margin>150v</margin> **III.** There is **appetite** <term>appetite: *appetitus*, here meaning a natural striving or internal drive toward a specific goal or state of being</term> for such motion or for a likeness of motion, which must necessarily precede or accompany the <margin>25</margin> mobile or changeable thing in which this kind of potency resides.

**IV.** There is **impetus**, as a logic following from appetite, just as motion follows the faculty of moving or the capacity for mobility.

<page-num>124</page-num>
<header>GIORDANO BRUNO</header>

V. It is the **faculty** <term>faculty: the inherent ability or power to perform a specific action</term> of attaining the end toward which such a power is directed.

VI. It is the **ease** <note>original: "facilitas." Bruno distinguishes between simply having the power to do something and the ease with which it is actually accomplished</note> which follows or accompanies such a faculty; for in many things there is a faculty for those things which <margin>5</margin> are not performed without difficulty.

VII. It is the conviction and the hope <note>The editor notes that one manuscript uses the word "species" (appearance/form) here instead of "spes" (hope)</note> of attaining something easily or with difficulty, based on the fact that it has been done at some point.

VIII. It is the logical reason based on the fact that in the subject or the power there is something which precedes the act, or from which the act follows.

<margin>10</margin> IX. It is the relation and disposition <term>disposition: the state or "habitudo" of a thing that makes it ready to act or change in a certain way</term> toward something that subsequently follows or will exist in the future, by virtue of the fact that it is not currently present.

X. It arises from the fact that the subject is changeable and variable.

XI. Because from the subject, in the subject, of the subject, and concerning the subject, something can be made, or has been made, or is being made.

<margin>15</margin> XII. Because while remaining the same, it receives or can receive, or it imprints or can imprint some **habit** <term>habit: a stable quality or "habitus" (like a skill or a physical state) that a subject acquires</term> or disposition.

XIII. Because it is not always one and the same; it is not always "this," or always "not this," or "that."

<margin>20</margin> XIV. Because it looks toward some end which it has not yet attained.

XV. Because a readiness or preparation appears within it for acting or receiving.

XVI. Because it does not contradict the logic of **feasibility** or **actability** <note>original: "factibilitatis vel agibilitatis." Bruno uses these technical terms to describe the capacity for something to be made (factibility) or for an action to be performed (actability)</note>, nor is that logic inconsistent with it.

XVII. Because it is **indifferent** <note>In philosophy, "indifference" means a neutral state where a subject is equally capable of moving toward one outcome or its opposite</note> toward contrary or diverse ends, inasmuch as it can—no less or at least equally well—possess a being, disposition, <margin>151</margin> or operation that is other, diverse, or different from those it currently has.

XVIII. Because it is not necessary for one of two **contraries** <term>contraries: things that are most opposite within the same category, like black and white</term> or one of two **contradictories** <term>contradictories: a pair where one must be true and the other false, like "being" and "not-being"</term> to exist, nor is it impossible when it does not exist.

XIX. Because even if the **endpoint** <term>terminus: the final goal or limit of a process</term> of its motion is difficult, <margin>5</margin> it is not nevertheless insurmountable; likewise, although this power may regard some act with difficulty, or the subject may be influenced by some **disposition** <term>disposition: the state of being ready or inclined toward a certain change</term>, it can still happen that it is achieved.

XX. Because the **will**—whether rational, intellectual, or natural—ought not to be frustrated; however, we can <margin>10</margin> verify this in the subject either through power: **actively**, namely because the subject itself wishes to be changed; or **passively**, because it desires that another thing change it, provided this is not an inordinate appetite.

XXI. Because there is an exit (or outcome) of it, or a movement from itself toward something else.

XXII. Because there is a path for it toward something else.
<margin>15</margin> XXIII. Because it has an access or an entrance toward some endpoint.

XXIV. Because something is able to receive or contain it, or it itself is able to receive or hold something else.

XXV. Because the obstacles, which are able to remove or frustrate such a power, are taken away.
<margin>20</margin> XXVI. Because all obstacles are understood to have been removed.

XXVII. Because a fostering, acting, altering, and perfecting agent is present.

XXVIII. Because that same agent which is present wills it, and does not will it in vain but is able to act, both through its own force and through the subject's <margin>25</margin> disposition.

XXIX. Because the action is present, from which both active and passive power are necessarily presupposed.

XXX. Because it is already in **act** <term>act: the state of being fully realized or "actually" existing, as opposed to just being possible</term> and has been made; for everything that exists does so because it is able to exist <note>original: "quia esse potest." Bruno is arguing that if something exists in reality, it must have first possessed the logical potential to exist.</note>.

<page-num>126, 151</page-num>
<header>GIORDANO BRUNO'S</header>

## THE FIELD OF JUNO.

Juno is the archetype <note>original: *typus*</note> of the **medium** <term>medium: the "middle ground" or intervening space/mechanism that connects a cause to its effect</term>; for just as the air or the ethereal region mediates between the Sun (the father) and the Earth (the mother), so between the **active power** <term>potentia activa: the capacity to perform an action</term> <margin>5</margin> and the **passive power** <term>potentia passiva: the capacity to receive or be changed by an action</term> there is a certain necessary medium. This medium serves to disjoin, to distinguish, to join together, and to convey, among other functions.

Furthermore, no power is brought to its **act** <term>act: the reality or completion of a potential state</term> without some intervening medium; for this reason, the "medium" is numbered among the most general principles of **discovery and judgment** <note>These are the two main branches of logic: *inventio* (finding arguments) and *iudicium* (evaluating them)</note>. <margin>10</margin> Anyone can visualize this principle for themselves through the figure of Juno, following the likeness of the ethereal region over which Juno is understood to rule and hold command. The **statue** <note>In this work, Bruno describes thirty "statues" as mental images used for a memory system to organize all human knowledge</note> for this concept is very easy to construct—more easy than strictly necessary, because the progression of a thing is observed more worthily and no less conveniently through the actual order of the matter itself. Regarding the meanings of the "medium":

<margin>15</margin> **I.** The first meaning is that which is a **way**, a **path**, or a **line** between the extremes of a change.

**II.** That which occurs in the middle of a course to the agent, the one proceeding, the one promoting, or the thing being promoted.

**III.** That which **concurs** <note>original: *concurrit*; acting together with other forces</note>; for among all efficient causes, <margin>20</margin> everything except the **principal cause** <term>principal cause: the primary or most important source of an effect</term> holds the status of a medium, whereas the first and most chief cause does not.

**IV.** The **mode of acting and operating**; for the mode of acting is that through the mediation of which a thing is perfected and the agent completes its task. Indeed, the diversity of things to be done arises from the mode of acting, not only from the [principal cause...]

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the "Medium" (the intervening principle) from the previous page, specifically detailing the various ways or "modes" in which this mediation manifests in both logic and the natural world.</meta>

<page-num>127</page-num>
<header>THE TORCH OF THE THIRTY STATUES</header>

...proceeds from principles; for indeed, the same principles do not always produce the same effect.

**V. In terms of circumstances;** for the primary **agent** <term>agent: the entity that performs an action</term> and the **subject** <term>subject: the material or entity that receives the action</term> accomplish nothing without "accessories," the consideration of which coincides with the consideration of the effects themselves. Furthermore, since circumstances and necessarily concurring causes are everywhere infinite, it is certainly impossible to look to them all; however, it is both appropriate and possible to look to those which are closest and most related to the primary principles.

<margin>152r</margin>
**VI. In terms of the scale and its steps;** for any **form** <term>form: the essential nature or "blueprint" of a thing</term> is introduced into a subject by means of certain **accidents** <term>accidents: non-essential properties, like color or weight</term> and dispositions. These do not run together in a confused or haphazard way, but through certain and determined steps; hence it is rightly said that the **species** <term>species: the distinct types or categories of things</term> of things are like numbers. <note>original: *species rerum esse sicut numeros*. This refers to the Pythagorean and Aristotelian idea that essences are discrete; if you add or subtract even a tiny amount from a number, it becomes a different number entirely.</note>

**VII. In terms of the intermediate,** such as a messenger, a sign, an index, an envoy, or things proportional to these; just as in natural effects we see everywhere certain precursors going before both the cause and the effect.

**VIII. In terms of a pact,** a treaty, a law, an oath, or things proportional to these; for even in natural things one may conjecture that higher things exercise power and dominate over lower things as if by a law and a certain prescription, which is a necessary medium without which nothing is accomplished.

**IX. In terms of the bond,** or that which connects the active to the passive, the agent to the matter, or the celestial to the infernal—such as a knot, a chain, glue, and things proportional to these. Just as the **Platonists** <note>Followers of Plato and Neoplatonism, who heavily influenced Bruno's views on the soul</note> say that **spirit** <term>spirit: here meaning a subtle, vapor-like substance that acts as a bridge between the physical and the spiritual</term> is the medium by which the intellectual and immaterial—such as the **soul**—is joined to the body. Otherwise, since there is no likeness or "sympathy" between the soul and the body, a union would not be possible by any means.

<summary>Bruno defines five modes of the "Medium"—circumstances, gradations, intermediaries, laws, and bonds—which allow causes to interact with matter. He notably cites the Neoplatonic theory that a "spirit" must act as a physical-spiritual glue to bind the soul to the body.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the numbered list of definitions for the "Medium" (the middle or intermediate principle) from the previous page, shifting from logical and procedural categories to physical, spatial, and qualitative modes of mediation.</meta>

<page-num>128</page-num>
<header>GIORDANO BRUNO</header>

**X.** For that which brings extremes closer and binds them into one, just as water is the **medium** through which two types of powder can be united into a single mass.

**XI.** For a gap, an interval, an interstice, and everything
<margin>5</margin> that mediates between things touching each other—flowing between them insofar as they are contiguous; or even that which is cast between those things called "successive" (as Aristotle defines them), between which something of a different kind mediates. <note>Aristotle distinguishes between "contiguous" things (which touch) and "consecutive" things (which follow one another but may have a different substance in between).</note>

**XII.** For that which is inserted between, such as a wedge, glue,
<margin>10</margin> a nail, and similar things, or anything proportional to these.

**XIII.** For that which breaks apart, scatters, throws asunder, and <margin>152</margin> by its own interposed mass creates a discontinuity.

**XIV.** For a vehicle or a "carrier" <term>carrier: Latin *deferente*, a substance or space that conveys an influence</term>, just as the vacuum is called a medium, or space is called the medium through which light is poured from higher regions to lower ones; or as air is the medium which, when moved, brings scent and sound to the nostrils and ears.

**XV.** For the indifferent, or that which maintains itself indifferently, just as a judge is said to "mediate" between litigants and is called a neutral party; likewise, **Parian stone** <note>Parian marble, famous for its pure white color, was often used as a philosophical example of a "neutral" surface that doesn't bias the colors or materials placed upon it.</note> is said to have an indifference between true and apparent metal; and the color of the eyes (or the pupil) is said to be of no color, or of a "middle" color, so that it might be an unaffected judge of other colors.

**XVI.** For that which exists in a middle state or a **temperament** <term>temperament: the proportional mixing of qualities like hot, cold, moist, and dry</term>; since this is neither of the original components, but rather their qualities meet within it and are lessened—though not entirely removed—it is said to refer to the middle and to hold the character of a "medium" between the extremes or the components.

**XVII.** For a minister, or a servant, or for anyone...

<summary>This page lists several physical and metaphorical definitions of the "Medium," describing it as a binding agent, a spatial gap, a neutral judge, and a carrier for light and sound. Bruno emphasizes how the "middle" can both connect disparate things (like glue) and keep them distinct (like a neutral judge).</summary>

<meta>This page continues the definitions of the "Medium" (middle or means) from the previous page. It concludes definition XVII regarding subordinate agents and proceeds to define the medium as a tool, a process, a physical center, and a logical cause.</meta>

### THE TORCH OF THE THIRTY STATUES
#### WORKS OF BRUNO, LATIN VOL. III
#### 17

...that which concurs in a servant-like or ministerial manner to bring something to completion.

**XVIII.** For an instrument or organ, which likewise serves as a **medium** <note>original: *medium*</note> in an action.

<margin>5</margin> **XIX.** For every effect and process that occurs from the beginning of an operation and is distinct from the final result. These are called "intermediate works," which are directed toward the ultimate task and in which the actor does not yet rest.

**XX.** For all those things that contribute to an action besides the agent and the matter, whatever they may be. From this perspective, <margin>10</margin> **Plato** recognizes two primary causes: the subject <note>The underlying material or substance being acted upon.</note> and the **efficient cause** <term>efficient cause: Latin *efficiens*; the primary source of the change or rest; the "trigger" or "creator" of an action</term>.

**XXI.** For everything placed between extremes, which are said to be the most distant within any category.

<margin>15</margin> **XXII.** For whatever partakes of the extremes, and is therefore called either a neutral party between them or a combination of both. For example, we can say that the color **green** or **saffron** <note>Saffron was often treated as an intermediate color in ancient and Renaissance color theory, sitting between white/light and black/darkness.</note> is either partly white and partly black, or neither white nor black.

<margin>153r</margin>
<margin>20</margin> **XXIII.** For whatever is either equidistant from the extremes or is exactly neither of the extremes. From this, the "middle hours" between sunrise and sunset are so called—either properly, referring to the exact point of noon, or commonly, referring to all hours except the first and the last.

<margin>25</margin> **XXIV.** For the boundary in which the extremes meet and flow together, just as the center is called the **medium** of a circle or a sphere.

**XXV.** In **Logic**, for the "middle term" <note>The middle term is the crucial element in a syllogism that connects the two premises to reach a conclusion.</note> which is the cause and reason for those things verified affirmatively or negatively. To this, the words "for," "because," "namely," etc., are subservient.

--- Page 198 ---
<meta>This page continues the numbered definitions of the term "Medium" (Middle or Mean) within Bruno's philosophical system, specifically moving from logical and structural definitions to cosmological and anthropological ones.</meta>

# OF GIORDANO BRUNO

**XXVI.** In **Logic**, it stands for the **disjunctive middle** <note>original: *medio disiunctivo*</note>, which is served by words such as *either*, *or*, or *whether*; or it stands for the **copulative middle**, served by particles such as *and*, *also*, *furthermore*, and the like.

**XXVII.** For that which is the essence of every **order**; for this reason, where there is no middle, no order can exist. For the beginning does not create order, nor does the end create order by itself; rather, it is the **middle** that necessarily defines the beginning and the end, while it is not necessarily defined by them.
<margin>5</margin>

<margin>10</margin> **XXVIII.** For the **highest goal**; hence the **Pythagoreans** <note>Followers of Pythagoras who believed numbers and proportions were the essence of the universe.</note> and **Platonists** say that **God** is the "middle" around which the soul revolves. Likewise, the essence of any thing is called its center and its middle; and according to this reasoning, the **Mind** and **God** are called by the Pythagoreans the center of all spheres—that is, of all **substances**.
<margin>15</margin>

**XXIX.** For everything around which **motion** occurs; hence the axis, the center, and the poles are called the "middle," and the **equinoctial line** <note>The celestial equator.</note> is called the "girdle of the universe."

**XXX.** For that in which all or many natures converge; hence **man** is called the **middle of natures**, because every nature is realized within him. 
<margin>20</margin> He is also called the **horizon of the universe**; for just as the upper and lower hemispheres are joined in the middle horizon, so in man the **intelligible world** <term>intelligible world: the realm of thought, spirit, and divine ideas</term> and the **sensible world** <term>sensible world: the physical realm perceived by the senses</term> are coupled together. He bears the likeness of both worlds according to his **dual nature**, which consists of both soul and body.
<margin>25</margin>

# THE LAMP OF THE THIRTY STATUES

<margin>153v</margin>
## CONCERNING DEMOGORGON
## THAT IS, CONCERNING HABIT OR RELATION <note>original: *habitudo seu relatio*. In Bruno's philosophy, this refers to the way things are disposed or related to one another.</note>.

**Demogorgon** <note>A primordial deity in Renaissance mythology, often interpreted by philosophers like Bruno as the "soul of the world" or the dark, mysterious root from which nature emerges.</note> is the primary reason by which nature—absolute and sufficient unto itself—turns toward the universe that is to be constituted. 
<margin>5</margin> For by virtue of the relation or "habit" that he represents—which is a certain turning of attention toward establishing something external—all things that exist possess their being and existence. In his statue, both as it has been shaped and as it is yet to be shaped, one may, by examining its various parts, measure most sufficiently all things according to the universal relations they can receive. 
<margin>10</margin> There are, therefore, thirty differences of relative being and relations:

**I.** Between the **idea** and that of which it is the idea, which is said to be **similar** to it. In this relation, it must be noted that there is no **conversion** <note>original: *conversio*. A logical term meaning the relationship cannot be reversed: for example, while a portrait is like the person, we don't say the person is "like" the portrait in the same way.</note> from the similar thing back to the idea, even though there is a mutual habit and relation. 
<margin>15</margin> For man is said to be like **God** and made in the likeness of God; however, God is by no means said to be in the likeness of man, but rather the "idea" of man is said to reside within Him. The same must be judged regarding brute animals <note>original: *brutis*</note> in relation to man, because a "conversion" is only understood to exist between equals.

<margin>20</margin> **II.** Between **father** and **son**; this relation exists in those beings that are animate and possessing knowledge—at least rational beings—and where procreation comes from a similar substance, and the effect and the cause are **univocal** <term>univocum: having the same essential nature or name</term> and of the same nature. Hence, a human generating a human is a "father"; 
<margin>25</margin> however, the term is used improperly of a brute animal generating another brute animal, in which case we speak of a "cub," "chick," or "offspring."

<summary>Bruno introduces Demogorgon as the symbolic figure representing the relationship between the Absolute (God) and the created universe, listing the first two of thirty types of relations: that of Idea to Object and that of Father to Son.</summary>
<keywords>Demogorgon, Relation, Habitudo, Idea, Likeness, Father and Son, Univocal Cause, Rational Beings, Metaphysics</keywords>

<page-num>132</page-num>
<header>GIORDANO BRUNO</header>

**III.** Between the **progenitor** and the **offspring**, which also exists between causes and **equivocal effects** <note>original: *effectus aequivocos*. An "equivocal effect" is one where the cause and the result are of different natures, such as the sun (a celestial body) causing the growth of a plant (a biological organism).</note>; hence the **sun** and **man** are said to generate man <note>A reference to Aristotle's *Physics* (Book 2, Chapter 2), reflecting the Renaissance belief that human reproduction required both biological parents and the vital heat of the sun.</note>, and all things are said to be born from the heavens.
**IV.** Between the **agent** and the **object**, as between the **intellect** and the **intelligible species** <note>original: *speciem intelligibilem*. In medieval and Renaissance philosophy, this refers to the mental image or "form" of an object that allows the mind to perceive and understand it.</note>.
<margin>5</margin> **V.** Between the **efficient cause** and the **effect**, a relationship which extends to all artificial things as well.
**VI.** Between **cause** and the **caused**, which is a general relation common to the four types of causes enumerated above <note>The four Aristotelian causes: material, formal, efficient, and final.</note>.
<margin>10</margin> **VII.** Between the **principle** and that which **proceeds from the principle** <note>original: *principiatum*. A "principle" is a broader term than a "cause"; for instance, a point is the principle of a line, but it does not "cause" the line in a physical sense.</note>, which is a broader category than cause and the caused, as is clear from the definitions provided for "principle."
**VIII.** Between that which **is superior** and that which **is subordinate**, whether by dignity, | place, time, or other considerations. <margin>154</margin>
<margin>15</margin> **IX.** Between **master** and **servant**, or between **minister** and **teacher**.
**X.** Between the **master builder** and the **craftsman**, or the architect, the craftsman, and the **work produced**.
**XI.** Between **teacher** and **student**, which is mediated by another relation, namely between **fellow student** and fellow student, or **colleague** and colleague.
<margin>20</margin> **XII.** Between **action** and **passion** <note>original: *passio*. Here used in the classical sense of "undergoing" or being the recipient of an action, rather than an emotion.</note>, or between the **agent** and the **patient**.
**XIII.** Between the **adjunct**—that is, the thing which is added—and the **subject**, which is the thing to which it is added.
<margin>25</margin> **XIV.** Between the **large** and the **small**.
**XV.** Between the **excessive** and the **deficient**, which are mediated by another relation: that is, the **just** and the **equal**.

...it must be noted that here **disposition** <note>original: *habitus*. In this context, it refers to a "state" or "possession" of a quality, the opposite of "privation."</note> has a double meaning: namely, as it denotes the more perfect form of two contraries, to which the opposite is called **privation**. For this is how privation is customarily used in Aristotle's work—insofar as it is a specific principle of material things, and insofar as it is itself a kind of form, though it is the more imperfect or "less worthy" of the two contraries.
<margin>5</margin> Hence, **heat** is a form, while **cold** is a privation; **white**, **light**, **day**, **dense**, **beautiful**, and similar things are forms; **black**, **darkness**, **night**, **rare** <note>meaning thin or low density.</note>, **ugly**, and so on are privations.
<margin>10</margin> Therefore, since privation is understood in two ways: in one way as the **absence** and **withdrawal** of a preceding form (without which the presence of a subsequent form is impossible, because two substantial forms <note>A "substantial form" is the essential nature of a thing; according to the physics of the time, a single piece of matter cannot be two different essential things at the exact same time.</note> cannot exist together in the same subject); and in this way, privation is a "principle of things by accident" <note>original: *principium per accidens*. An indirect cause; the "clearing of the stage" so a new thing can appear.</note>
<margin>15</margin> (though not purely accidental, because without it nothing happens). In this way and for this reason, it is related to the **disposition**, which is the establishing of the subsequent form.
In another way, it is taken as the **inferior form** of two contraries—just as we call cold a "privation" and heat a "form." In this way and manner, it is a **principle in itself** <note>original: *principium per se*. A direct, fundamental cause.</note> of natural things,
<margin>20</margin> and its meaning runs along with the name of "form." Hence, when one speaks of a double essential principle—namely, **matter** and **form**—there "form" signifies in two ways. And according to this meaning of privation, we say that privation is related in one way to the form (as one
<margin>25</margin> contrary to another), and in another way to the subject (as a form is related to that which it gives form).

# EXPLANATION OF THE HORN OF ACHELOUS
## OR, CONCERNING "POSSESSION." <note>original: *de Habere*. Bruno uses the verb "to have" as a noun to describe the philosophical state of possessing attributes or qualities.</note>

<margin>20</margin> Among universal principles, "possession" itself is numbered; for in all subjects, of whatever <term>genus</term> they may be, we inquire into and examine the logic of "having," although in the First and Supreme Being <note>The ultimate source of existence, or God, where essence and existence are one.</note>, to possess is the same as to be. However, it is of a threefold difference, according to which it is verified throughout the universe <margin>25</margin> in composite things—either with respect to higher things or from higher things...

He argues that while ordinary things "have" qualities, in the supreme being, "having" and "being" are identical.</summary>

<header>GIORDANO BRUNO</header>

[re]spect of inferiors or from inferiors, in respect of equals, of similar things, of coordinated things, or of things distinguished together; just as it is to have [something] from the Gods and with the Gods, from humans and with humans, from elements, stones, plants, and beasts, and with the same.
<margin>5</margin> And this "state of having" <note>original: *habere*. Bruno treats the verb "to have" as a philosophical noun representing the concept of possession.</note> is subdivided into intrinsic and extrinsic: the intrinsic follows the animal and intellectual powers, as well as the natural powers; the extrinsic follows circumstances, assistance, inherence, and states <term>states</term> <note>original: *habitus*. In this context, it refers to a "disposition" or a lasting quality a person possesses, like a skill or a moral virtue.</note>. Moreover, for those who categorize more specifically, thirty modes <note>original: *rationes*</note> of having occur:

I. It arises from a universal and common nature—namely, with those things which share the same denomination, name, similarity, analogy, or coordination.

II. From the nature of a genus <note>In logic, a "genus" is a broad category, such as "Animal."</note> held in common with those things which fall under the division of the same unambiguous <note>original: *univoci*, referring to a term that has one constant meaning.</note> genus.

III. <margin>155</margin> From the nature of the difference <note>original: *differentiae*. This is the specific characteristic that distinguishes one species from another within the same genus—for example, "rationality" is the difference that distinguishes humans from other animals.</note> and the species held in common with those that have the same essential, proximate, and specific definition.

IV. From the nature of a property <note>original: *proprietatis*. In Aristotelian logic, a "property" is a characteristic that is not part of a thing's essence but is unique to it and always follows from that essence, such as a human’s ability to laugh.</note>, which follows the essential difference and is always manifold.

V. It is a mode of having from things appropriated and joined to oneself—specifically, from all those things that fall short of <note>original: *citra*</note> the essential property and difference.

VI. From divine grace particularly, as in cases where something is possessed not by natural principles or by art, but from a source above and beyond natural reason.

VII. Generally from gift and grant, where we have something in our capacity by permission—namely, those things which are distributed to us by law and right.

# LAMP OF THE THIRTY STATUES.

...yet not most certainly and most clearly; not through entreaty or petition, because He possesses absolutely; not by being supplied, as if someone were suggesting or furnishing something to Him; not because He might receive profit from it; not for the sake of reward, nor so that He might find something He had searched for (for He has all things present and <margin>5</margin> **prompt** <note>original: *promta*</note>); not to profit or acquire (for all things are His own); | not so that something might be returned or bestowed upon Him, <margin>156v</margin> as if He had given a loan (for everything is His everywhere and for Himself); not so that He might find something without labor, or through plunder, fraud, deceit, or <margin>10</margin> usurpation, but from the merit of rule, governance, favor, protection, custody, and preservation. 

Hence, He wishes us to be, as it were, merchants and traders—laborers toward the attainment of those things which, nevertheless, we are only able to merit, pursue, obtain, and have by His gift. Thus, He seems to have <margin>15</margin> entrusted to us our natural and free faculties; and in place of works that are most unworthy or even non-existent, He titles Himself the "rewarder" and "compensator" of those works He accepts as worthy. For example, regarding a cup of cold water <note>A reference to the Gospel of Matthew 10:42, where even the smallest act of charity is promised a reward.</note>, He says and promises that we shall have a hundredfold and eternal life. 

Likewise, for our service, He <margin>20</margin> causes us to have "talents of grace" <term>talenta gratiarum: spiritual gifts or abilities bestowed by God</term>, which are said to be hidden or buried in the earth <note>original: *effossa*, literally "dug out" or "buried"</note> by those who are idle or who misuse them for earthly things. Similarly, regarding other modes, we cannot say that God "has" things in a servant-like way <note>original: *ministerialiter*</note>, or by loan, by law, by liberty, or by reason of imputation, <margin>25</margin> or as a "handle" <note>original: *ansae*, a logical term for an occasion or starting point</note>, or as a general gift, concession, or grace; nor by appropriation, property, species, genus, or analogy. Yet nothing forbids—on the contrary, all reason dictates—that this very "having" belongs to Him effectively, imperatively, and authoritatively; because, to be sure, to "have"...

<summary>Bruno argues that God's possession of the universe is absolute and self-contained, yet God allows humans to "earn" divine rewards through the use of natural faculties and spiritual "talents" as if they were earned wages.</summary>

## THE FIELD OF MINERVA
### OR, ON KNOWLEDGE.

<margin>5</margin> Nor should we omit, among other things, the universal method of considering things from the perspective of notice or knowledge. For everything that enters into contemplation and discourse must be examined according to the conditions of its knowability and verifiability (upon which <margin>10</margin> consequently every other thing depends). For the principle of truth, which follows from affirmation and negation—which are themselves preceded by comprehensive mental forms <term>species: the mental images or "forms" that represent external objects in the mind</term> and reasons—takes its beginning from these sorts of components.

<margin>157</margin> First, then, the principle of cognition depends on the principle | <margin>15</margin> of the **natural constitution** <note>original: *naturalis complexionis*</note>, which is attributed to a natural and "ordered" Saturnine melancholy <note>Bruno refers to the Renaissance belief that a "balanced" melancholy temperament—associated with the planet Saturn—was the mark of deep thinkers, philosophers, and prophets.</note>.

Second, character and innate talent follow this; for their principle is the natural temperament and the arrangement of the bodily organs.

III. There is instinct or inclination, which follows character and talent; and from this, we speak as if of a **guiding spirit** <term>genium: often translated as "genius," referring here to a person's inherent nature or a protective spirit that governs one's fate</term>, <margin>20</margin> because the events of fortune and one's pursuits follow this. Hence, it is a common saying among the Platonists that "he who changes his pursuits, changes his spirit and his fortune" <note>original: *qui studia mutat, genium mutat atque fortunam*</note>.

IV. There is the sense of hearing, by which we are first built up and <margin>25</margin> informed.

V. Sight is the sense that confirms and strengthens the disposition of the listeners; it reinforces new ideas and expands them through <term>species: the mental images or "forms" that represent external objects in the mind</term>.

VI. Imagination <note>original: *phantasia*</note> is an internal sense that serves as a receptacle and storehouse for the <term>species</term> perceived from the outside.

<margin>5</margin> VII. The cogitative faculty is the sense for "spiritual" things <note>In this context, "spiritual" refers to non-material intentions or qualities that are not directly sensible, such as utility or danger.</note>. It receives what is not directly sensed from a sensible or sensitive apprehension—for example, a sheep perceives enmity and the dread of death from the mere visual form of a wolf.

VIII. Reason follows the senses (in the general sense of the term); it compares <margin>10</margin> preceding, prior, and known <term>species</term> with subsequent ones that are unknown in themselves, making them knowable through those that came before.

IX. Intellect is either the established habit of truths acquired through discursive reasoning <note>the process of step-by-step logical movement from one premise to another</note>, or it is a simple apprehension—a clear and concentrated vision—of those things which <margin>15</margin> reason gathers together in a scattered or fragmented way.

X. Mind <note>original: *mens*</note> refers to a certain light and radiance within us that proceeds from both the senses and the intellect.

XI. Memory is the power of retaining <term>species</term> that have been received and processed. This is twofold: **sensitive memory** <margin>20</margin> for sensible forms (which the <term>Peripatetics: the followers of Aristotle</term> also call imagination), and **intellective memory**, which retains forms perceived by reason and intellect; in a sense, this latter form is the mind itself.

XII. Recollection <note>original: *reminiscentia*</note> differs from memory because <margin>157v</margin> <margin>25</margin> memory retains what is naturally memorable without effort or industry, <unclear>...</unclear> <note>The original manuscript has a gap here; the sense suggests that memory is spontaneous while recollection is active.</note> whereas that which is somewhat hidden and does not occur to memory on its own is brought to mind through recollection via effort and a specific process of comparison.

-># GIORDANO BRUNO<-

XIII. **Discernment** <note>original: *discretio*</note> is the faculty that distinguishes between diverse, different, and contrary <term>species: the mental images or "forms" that represent objects in the mind</term>.

XIV. **Ecstasy** <note>original: *ecstasis*</note> is the faculty for withdrawing from the senses and from present things; it is an approach to higher realms and a <margin>5</margin> certain continuation of human reason into divine or demonic intelligence, whether that intelligence be good or evil.

XV. **Inspiration** <note>original: *enthusiasmus*</note>, which is attributed to prophets, seers, and poets—at least those who are truly poets and seers.

XVI. There is a certain **irradiation**, or a glow or spiritual heat, <margin>10</margin> that impels and excites the genius toward operations far above the ordinary. In the wise—who become poets and philosophers not only by natural gift, but also through a certain industry and study—this state follows after ecstasy. This was seen in Plato and Socrates, who, for many hours of the day, <margin>15</margin> were lifted outside their senses and applied themselves entirely to the power of the intellect. Among such men, the better they are as philosophers, the better they are as seers.

XVII. Next follows **suspicion** or questioning <note>original: *suspicatio*</note>, which is the power by which someone, trusting himself less, always doubts his own propositions and even those things evident to others. From this, the sect of the **Academics** <note>The Academic Skeptics, a school of Greek philosophy that advocated for the suspension of judgment</note> <margin>20</margin> decides nothing, but examines <note>original: *digerit*</note> everything. In some people, this power creates and prepares a disposition for attaining the truth; for in others, the path to wisdom is blocked <note>The original Latin *concluditur* suggests the path is "shut up" or finished prematurely</note> by false presuppositions that are accepted as if they were self-evident, conceded, or proven. <margin>25</margin> However, in all doubtful matters that are subjects of controversy, especially among the wise, it is better to lean upon this power; for those who flee from it and remain distant are unfit to know anything beyond the commonplace.

# THE TORCH OF THE THIRTY STATUES.

XVII. There is **faith**, which is a propensity for giving assent; and this is twofold: theological and philosophical. The first concerns things unknown and hidden, yet nevertheless most certain, because it is about things known by a higher light—namely, things revealed by the Gods, who are not <margin>5</margin> envious. The other is philosophical, | <margin>158r</margin> which concerns things that are most manifest and self-evident by the power of our own light; hence, faith is spoken of concerning the <term>disposition of first principles: the foundational, self-evident truths (habitus principiorum) from which all reasoning begins</term>, just as science is spoken of concerning the conclusions that are logically <margin>10</margin> deduced from those principles. This twofold power of assenting is sometimes regulated, and then it retains the name of faith simply; at other times it is perverted (as when, on one hand, human and diabolical things are thrust upon us as divine by false prophets and apostles, or on the other hand, we are circumvented either by a false imagination or by a disturbance of the senses; <margin>15</margin> or where, when the sense is wavering, it is fixed to one side), and then it is not faith, but **credulity** and **imagination**.

XVIII. There is **judgment**, which is the power of examining that which has been apprehended, proposed, or indicated through the senses or reason; it reflects upon discourse and other things, so that, <margin>20</margin> after one has perceived, argued, and understood, one may consider and make, as it were, a second comparison, seeing whether one has perceived or argued correctly; just as is customary among arithmeticians, who, having made a calculation, reckon it again and again.

<margin>25</margin> XIX. There is **sagacity**, which is a distinctive and apprehensive faculty regarding errors that may be introduced by fabled deceivers and impostors; it consists in a power partly judicial and partly investigative, by which—just as we perceive a scent with our nostrils—so we perceive a sophist and a deceiver with our natural wit <note>original: *ingenio*</note>. XX.
