Prudence is spoken of in regard to good things directed toward the good, while <margin>10</margin> craftiness is used in evil things directed toward the evil.

XXI. There is **shrewdness** <note>original: *argutia*</note>, and it is a power consisting in the virtue of a disposition that resists craftiness. For the crafty person looks to <margin>158</margin> deceive, but the shrewd person is the one who is not deceived by him, or who even overcomes and confounds the crafty one. This is done most effectively <margin>15</margin> when one pretends not to perceive the craftiness and suddenly catches the adversary while he remains confident in his own deception. It is also a power regarding the category of virtue. The "little wits" are the apes of these men.

XXII. There is **ingenuity** <note>original: *solertia*, sometimes translated as resourcefulness or quick-wittedness</note>, which is the power by which someone <margin>20</margin> judges a proposed matter promptly and almost without any intervening consideration.

XXIII. There is **consideration**, whose end and goal is the same as that of ingenuity, but it operates through discourse and comparison. ## ON THE LADDER OF MINERVA

<margin>5</margin> Since a habit <term>habitus: a stable disposition or state of mind, such as a skill or a settled way of thinking</term> or disposition follows a power or faculty, we should consequently define the habits of knowledge, now that the cognitive powers themselves have been defined. We call this the "Ladder of Minerva" <note>Minerva is the Roman goddess of wisdom; Bruno uses this metaphor to describe the step-by-step ascent of the human mind toward divine understanding.</note> because we ascend from the first to the <margin>10</margin> last through certain steps, as it were; for habit follows habit, and disposition follows disposition, in a specific order.

I. Therefore, there is the habit of first principles or common notions <note>original: *communes notiones*; these are fundamental truths recognized by everyone, such as "the whole is greater than the part."</note> implanted in us along with the natural power of reasoning; and from this, they are called believed and self-evident <margin>15</margin> propositions.

II. There is a habit or collection of sensible forms <term>species: in Renaissance psychology, these are the mental "images" or impressions that external objects leave upon our senses</term>, which are gathered from the external senses into the storehouse of the internal sense; from this, we possess present forms and likenesses <note>original: *simulacra*</note> of sensible things that are actually absent.

<margin>20</margin> III. There is a system of pre-cognitions, which is a habit following closely upon the one just mentioned—just as thought follows imagination <note>original: *phantasia*</note>, and the apprehension of enmity, danger, loss, and death follows the apprehension of a wolf, a lion, or a snake; and this is called the habit of thoughts.

<margin>25</margin> IV. There is a habit of presuppositions, regarding those things which, although they have not been presented to the senses nor placed before the internal eyes, [are believed...]

XIII. There is **demonstration** <term>original: *apodixia*; a Greek term for a logical proof that provides absolute certainty</term>, which is opposed by the **sophistical** state of mind. For this reason, just as the sophist builds a house that is decorated on the outside to look as if it were made of stone, yet beneath the paint it is merely mud (for appearances are sufficient for him), the demonstrator strives for the true reality of the thing.

XIV. There is **recognition**, which is the state by which someone both possesses a certain faculty and acknowledges the weight of their own ability. This is hindered by the state of **arrogance**, belonging to those who presume beyond their own weight and strength; hence it is also called **presumption**, insofar as someone "takes before" <note>original: *prae se sumit*; Bruno is playing on the etymology of *praesumptio*, meaning to take something up before it is granted or before one is ready.</note> themselves.

XV. It is called **orthodoxy** <term>original: *orthodoxia*; literally "right opinion" or "straight thinking"</term>, being the state of mind aligned with the rectitude of reason, intention, and purpose.

XVI. **Divination** or **prognostication**: for one is said to "divine" when predicting something without the use of reason, whereas "prognosticating" is to know something as if from a great distance—not from immediate causes, but from remote ones.

XVII. There is **counsel**, which is the state of having the faculty to inform and regulate others, combined with the right reason for choosing and giving assent.

XVIII. There is **judgment** <term>original: *sententia*; here meaning a formal conclusion or a "verdict" of the mind</term>, which is the effect of counsel and a certain state of reaching definitions, which follows after the deliberations that came before.

<margin>16</margin> XIX. There is **experience**, which is a collection of many particular instances and exercises; from this, the reasoning of inductions and examples can be drawn.

XX. **Faith** <note>Bruno distinguishes "faith" here as a logical conclusion of the mind's journey, rather than just religious dogma.</note>, which is certainly not taken here as a power, but as a state of mind <term>original: *habitus*; a settled disposition or mental "clothing"</term>, which is a firm assent following after experience, judgment, counsel, and the other things mentioned above.

Hence, two things come together to constitute this kind of habit: the "mode of knowing" as the form, and "science" or "understanding" as the matter.

This is "meta-knowledge"—the awareness of one's own certainty.</note>. This is opposed by **perfidy** and **obstinacy**, which are a firm assent toward false things, whereby one does not know yet firmly believes he knows, and <margin>25</margin> would neither deign to hear the contrary nor endure it.

the reasoning of the just and the true as it has been apprehended; this is hindered by **dissolution** <term>original: *dissolutio*; here meaning a loosening of moral or intellectual rigor</term>, which is a certain contempt for justice and goodness that usually creeps in from a habit of doing evil. Likewise, it is hindered by a **lack of self-control** <term>original: *impotentia*</term> in errors, which is found in those who have always been accustomed to erring, concerning whom it is said: <margin>5</margin> "When the wicked man has come into the depth of sins, he shows contempt." <note>original: *Impius, cum in profundum peccatorum venerit, contemnit*; a reference to Proverbs 18:3</note>

**XXVII.** There is **Seriousness** <term>original: *gravitas*; a steady intellectual weight or sobriety</term>, which is a habit by which one feels certain about certain things and doubtful about doubtful things. This is hindered by **levity** <note>lightness or fickleness of mind</note> and **perversity** <term>original: *dyscolia*; a Greek-derived term for a difficult or ill-tempered disposition</term>—namely, a bad habit by which someone defines any matter whatsoever as if <margin>10</margin> it were certain. Concerning such people, Aristotle says that they are those who grasp very little and who, looking at only a few factors, pronounce judgment easily—just as <note>original: *Aristoteles*; referring to the *Posterior Analytics* or *Ethics* regarding rash generalizations</note> inexperienced soldiers are sometimes accustomed to being bolder due to their ignorance of the dangers.

**XXVIII.** **Theory** <term>original: *Theoria*</term> is a kind of **architecture** <margin>15</margin> that orders intellectual operations, just as an architect presides over mechanical operations.

**XXIX.** **Practice** <term>original: *Praxis*</term> is the right execution according to a theoretical definition.

**XXX.** **Wisdom** <term>original: *Sapientia*</term> is a complete and perfect <margin>20</margin> habit, encompassing the perfections of all other universal habits. For the **Peripatetics** <note>the followers of Aristotle, who walked while teaching</note>, it is considered the final end and the highest happiness that a human being can attain insofar as they are human—that is, in this current state of life. For if there is any other state for a human being according to the **subsistence of the soul** <margin>25</margin> outside the body, they do not attribute that state to a human "insofar as he is human," since they do not call the soul "the human being," but rather a part of the human being.

<header>THE TORCH OF THE THIRTY STATUES.</header>

# ON THE FIELD OF VENUS
## THAT IS, ON CONCORD.

It is a general rule in every investigation to look to the genus, to commonalities, and to those things in which the subject agrees with the rest, in order <margin>5</margin> to obtain the first part of a definition; then, one must look to those things in which it differs from others to capture the "difference." For we shall have rightly defined any specific thing only when we have looked to these two aspects <note>This refers to the Aristotelian method of defining something by its "genus" (general class) and "specific difference" (what makes it unique within that class)</note>. Now, however, concord is threefold: the first is in the thing itself, the second is in the will, and the third is in action. We denote the first, therefore, <margin>10</margin> by the **Field of Venus**, the second by the **Statue of Venus**, and the third by the **Knots of Cupid**.

I. First, therefore, agreement according to the thing is observed <margin>161^r</margin> in regard to the same genus, the same species, or the same individual number.

II. In regard to the same subject, in which all categories <margin>15</margin> <term>original: *praedicamenta*; the ten fundamental ways of being or being described, such as substance, quality, or quantity</term>, transcendental principles <term>original: *transcendentalia*; concepts like 'Being' or 'Good' that apply to everything</term>, logical intentions <note>concepts formed by the mind to understand objects</note>, and mathematical reasonings constitutively converge or can converge; for we can contemplate all these things in a single human being.

III. Accordant is that which is implanted and bestowed by nature.
<margin>20</margin> IV. Congenital, such as twins or full brothers.

V. Generation, such as offspring, blood relation, and lineage.

VI. Imitation, emulation, pursuit <note>original: *consectatio*; the manuscript shows signs of correction, possibly to *concertatio*, meaning competition or contention</note>, image, figure, something sketched, or something transcribed.

VII. Familiar, such as the domestic, fellow citizens, those of the same <margin>25</margin> race, and whatever pertains to the same place.

VIII. Fellowship <term>original: *sodalitium*</term>, such as a guild <term>original: *collegium*</term>, a private assembly <term>original: *conclave*</term>, a gathering, and similar things.

<summary>Bruno introduces the "Field of Venus" as a symbol for Concord (agreement), detailing the various ways things can be in accord, ranging from biological kinship to shared logical categories.</summary>
<keywords>Concordia, Field of Venus, genus, definition, categories, kinship, imitation, fellowship</keywords>

**XXVI.** Every participant, partner, and possessor.

**XXVII.** Every symphony, harmony, consonance, and congruence.

<margin>5</margin> **XXVIII.** Every correspondence, sequence, and consequence.

**XXIX.** Every charm, beauty, shapeliness, and fairness <note>original: *speciosum*; refers to beauty derived from 'species' or form</note>.

**XXX.** Everything that exists insofar as it is itself, to the extent that it is itself, and belongs to something according to its kind,
<margin>10</margin> or in its own right and properly.

The application of this manifold meaning regards all things equally and can be exercised in all things alike. Although on the surface of meaning certain terms are adapted to specific types of things being signified, they are nevertheless used here in such a way that they are adapted to all things according to their own logic, as they are adaptable to all. Therefore, regarding those things to which these terms are applied literally, let them remain and be understood according to their proper meaning; but regarding those things to which they are applied by likeness—in such a way that the
<margin>20</margin> thing compared does not have its own specific name assigned to it—the terms are taken metaphorically or with a mark of similarity. For example, when we say that justice, temperance, and prudence are in the same category of virtue, just as certain men are in the same college, room, and "tent-companionship" <note>original: *contubernio*; a military term for sharing a tent, used here to describe the close proximity of virtues in the soul</note>; so they possess, as it were, the same
<margin>25</margin> intention, "conspiracy" <note>original: *conspirationem*; literally a "breathing together" or acting in concert, not necessarily a plot</note>, and approach, and they stand in the same end, just like those things that act and understand according to an intention; for in this way the virtues correspond to one another just as virtuous people do.

<meta>This page continues from the discussion of "Concord" (Agreement) in the Field of Venus. On the previous page, Bruno defined types of harmony, beauty, and physical mixtures. Here, he shifts from "natural agreement" (the way things fit together physically) to "agreement of the will," arguing that every level of existence, from raw matter to the Divine, possesses a form of desire or purpose.</meta>

<page-num>154</page-num>
<header>GIORDANO BRUNO</header>

# ON THE STATUE OF VENUS.

Following the consideration of the modes of agreement according to the physical thing, there follows the mode of agreement according to the will. Just as agreement according to the physical thing is a general principle in all matters of <margin>5</margin> probable inquiry, so too is concord according to the will. <margin>16</margin> For in all things, whatever they may be and of whatever kind they are, there is a will. Indeed, what can be "less" than that which is imagined to be matter, which philosophers call "nearly nothing"? <note>Bruno refers to the Aristotelian concept of "prime matter," which is pure potentiality without form, and thus almost non-existent.</note> Yet in matter itself there is a <margin>10</margin> will—indeed, an insatiable and unquenchable will <note>original: *insatiabilis et inexplebilis voluntas*; Bruno describes matter’s eternal "hunger" to take on new forms.</note>. Immediately, all things that follow, just as they have a form, so they also have a will, by which all things in their own way desire to exist and to be preserved. This can be inferred even in the smallest particles of earth and water, which flee from their opposites and unite within themselves, contracting; just as <margin>15</margin> straws, stalks, and membranes flee from the presence of fire, contract, and recoil. There is, therefore, a manifold will: **natural**, such as is found in matter and in imperfectly mixed substances; **spiritual**, as if from a hidden form, such as in the magnet drawing iron, or in the onyx-stone stirring up phantasms <note>original: *phantasmata*; in Renaissance magic, certain stones like onyx were believed to provoke visions or nightmares</note>; **sensi-<margin>20</margin>tive**, such as is in those endowed with sense and in man according to the appetitive and irascible powers <note>original: *concupiscibilem et irascibilem*; the "appetitive" soul desires pleasure, while the "irascible" soul drives one to overcome obstacles or fight</note>; **rational**, such as is in man insofar as he is man; **intellectual**, such as is in the higher intelligences or the Gods; and **mental**, such as is in God, which is the same as His very substance.
<margin>25</margin> Therefore, the reasons for concord (or agreement) and will, which belong to this category, should be understood through these distinctions and applied to each individual kind of being.

<meta>This page continues the "Statue of Venus," which explores the concept of Concord (Agreement). Having previously discussed physical harmony, Bruno now begins a systematic list of thirty "notions" or concepts that define how "Agreement of the Will" functions across all levels of existence.</meta>

<page-num>155</page-num>
<header>THE LAMP OF THE THIRTY STATUES.</header>

Now, therefore, let agreement according to the **will**—following the previously mentioned reasons which are verifiable in their own way in all things—be explained, as is the custom, through thirty concepts.

<margin>5</margin> I. First, then, is agreement in the **aptitude** of the will, insofar as something inclines toward that which it wants, or toward that with which it agrees, fits, or suits.

II. There is **facility**, by which such an inclination passes into action.

III. There is the **compliance** of the passive principle toward the active, or of the terms of agreement toward a mutual respect. <note>In Bruno’s philosophy, every relationship involves an "active" giver of form and a "passive" receiver of form; "compliance" is the harmony between them.</note>

<margin>10</margin> IV. There is **complacency** <note>or "satisfaction"</note>, which follows like an act of the aforementioned compliance.

V. There is **delight**, which is the endpoint of satisfaction.

VI. There is **adoption**, or what is proportional to adoption; namely, a certain sanction or decree concerning the object of delight.

<margin>15</margin> VII. There is **consensus** or reciprocity between things that can be connected and brought into harmony, insofar as they correspond to one another, just as in love they constitute a certain reciprocity: *Love* and *Love-Returned*. <note>original: "ἔρως, ἀντέρως" (Eros, Anteros). In Renaissance thought, Anteros was the god of requited love, ensuring that affection was mutual.</note>

<margin>162v</margin> VIII. There is, and there follows, **excitement** or the panting of one thing for another, which consists in a certain impulse <margin>20</margin> by which things resist whatever opposes them or hinders their union.

IX. There is **approval**, whether natural, rational, or of another kind (as mentioned above), by which parts and matters of agreement or harmony are situated as they ought to be.

X. There is **observance**, specifically a regard and relation, <margin>25</margin> like the casting of an eye toward what is suitable in order to follow it, to avoid its opposite, to turn away an impediment, to admit what is favorable, and to bring back what is useful into the center.

XI. There is **attention**, by which anyone [grasps] the present occasion...

<summary>Bruno begins a thirty-point definition of how "Agreement of the Will" operates, detailing the psychological and natural stages of desire, from initial inclination and mutual compliance to delight and active excitement.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the list of concepts related to the "Statue of Venus" (Concord/Agreement). It picks up at the end of a discussion comparing how "natural" processes (governed by necessity) differ from "voluntary" processes (governed by choice).</meta>

<page-num>156</page-num>
<header>GIORDANO BRUNO</header>

...embraces it without delay; for everywhere in nature, the gathering and execution according to the present occasion is most prompt. For nature always does everything it is capable of doing; it acts while it can, where it can, and how it can. It is different, however, in those beings who act by sensitive and rational will. <note>Bruno is distinguishing between the "promptness" of natural laws—which act instantly and necessarily—and the deliberate, often delayed choices made by animals (sensitive will) and humans (rational will).</note>

XII. There is **assiduity** <note>original: *sedulitas*</note>, which is like an arousal to promptly seize that which is desired, fitting, or suitable.

XIII. There is **concupiscence** <note>In the 16th century, *concupiscentia* referred to any intense longing or appetite, not just sexual desire.</note>, which is also proven to exist in its own way in all things. Specifically, in the nature of all composite things, there is not only a desire and a suitability based on likeness, but also a certain "lust" for transforming disagreeing and contrary things into something agreeable and similar, and for building a single identity out of diverse parts. This is why contraries rush toward one another: both hope to convert the other into itself. It is like two enemies rushing to seize the same field—that is, to occupy the same matter. For fire wants to occupy the matter of water as if it were a foreign province, and water wants the matter of fire no less. Therefore, concupiscence is like a "concordant striving" <note>original: *appiscentia*, a term likely coined by Bruno to describe a shared reaching or grasping for a goal.</note> by which contraries strive in a common way. Perhaps it is through this hope that the combinations of contraries in nature are formed. For we see that harmony is made from strife, a meeting from contraries, stability from things that resist each other, and dissolution <margin>163</margin> caused by the victory of one contrary over another. Therefore, concupiscence—which is harmony in the will and the appetite for the same thing—is the cause of all war. <note>This is one of Bruno's famous paradoxes: war and conflict arise not from total difference, but because two things "agree" in wanting the same thing (the same matter or the same space).</note>

XIV. There is **striving** <note>original: *adnixus*</note>, which follows concupiscence; it is a certain diligent impulse, or something similar, toward union <note>original: *concubitum*; while literally meaning "lying together," Bruno uses it here to describe the physical or metaphysical joining of elements.</note>.

# THE LAMP OF THE THIRTY STATUES

XV. **Accommodation** is the attainment of a certain and fitting order, position, and stability within that with which something agrees, or desires to agree.

XVI. **Sympathy** is a certain mutual acceptance <margin>5</margin> and embrace.

XVII. **Pleasure** <note>original: *complacentia*. In Bruno’s time, this meant a state of being "well-pleased" or finding satisfaction in something, rather than modern "self-satisfaction."</note> is a deliberate will, through which that which is loved is sought after; it is that state where, because a fittingness exists, one loves and joins with another freely.

XVIII. **Binding** and **Sanction** are a stable and <margin>10</margin> firm consistency or subsistence <note>This refers to the "standing" or "firmness" of a thing—the state where an agreement becomes a permanent part of one's existence.</note>.

Following are the modes proper to rational and intellectual beings:

XIX. **Forgiveness**, remission, sparing, and the like.

XX. **Communion of use** <note>The shared use of property or resources.</note>.
<margin>15</margin> XXI. **Council**, coherence, and a shared life.

XXII. **Courtesy**, affability, or the ease of social interaction.

XXIII. **Service** and **obedience**, such as occurs in the relationship of inferiors toward superiors, or <insert>of</insert> those bound to those who have served them well.
<margin>20</margin> XXIV. **Compliance** <note>original: *obsecundatio*. A cooperative spirit or deference.</note> or **deference**, which exists between equals and those who are similar; it is not a matter of obligation, but of providing mutual assistance equally.

XXV. **Repose**, that is, a peaceful, settled, tranquil, and safe concord; the achievement or possession of harmony.
<margin>25</margin> XXVI. A **pact** or **treaty**, or a law, which arises from common consent and will.

XXVII. **Obligation**, an oath, or a binding constraint, which is a duty based on law and a pact that must not be violated.

# GIORDANO BRUNO

XXVIII. It is **patronage** and **clientage**, namely the relationship of the protector to the protected, and of the protected to the protector.

XXIX. It is **hospitality** and the **guest-gift** <note>original: *xenium*, a gift or token of hospitality given to a guest</note>, <margin>163</margin> namely a common concord and love that overflows even toward strangers.

<margin>5</margin> XXX. It is **charity** <note>original: *caritas*, the highest form of love</note>, as the most perfect and consummate concord, by which each person has a soul so harmonious within itself that it is directed equally toward God and toward all people—not only friends, but also enemies. <margin>10</margin> We are drawn, impelled, and invited toward this perfection by the son of almighty God, so that he may raise us into the likeness of the Father, "who makes his sun to rise on the good and the bad, and sends rain on the just and the unjust" <note>Matthew 5:45</note>. This releases us from the barbaric condition (shared with beasts and the inhuman) <margin>15</margin> of those who love only friends and neighbors, but hold strangers and enemies in hatred.

II. **Calling**, appealing, and invitation.
III. **Requesting**, prayer, and imploration.
IV. **Pursuit** and chasing.
V. [It is] **A favorable hearing** <note>original: *exauditio*, specifically the act of a superior hearing and granting a petition</note>.
<margin>25</margin> VI. **Conversion**.

## ON THE STATUE AND MEMBERS OF CUPID, OR ON THE DIFFERENT TYPES OF WILL.

We represent the various types and attributes of the **will** through the figure of **Cupid** <note>original: *Cupidinem*; the god of desire, used here as a personification of the soul's driving force</note>. Furthermore, just as the will is manifold <note>having many forms or parts</note>, so too is Cupid manifold. Likewise, just as the will arises from a manifold principle, so the origin of Cupid is imagined and described in many ways; for to some he is without father or mother, while some attribute one set of parents to him, and others attribute another.

Just as one type of will is natural, primary, and material, while another belongs to composite things <note>beings made of multiple elements</note>, another is spiritual, and another is of a different nature; so Cupid is said by some to be born without a father. This is because the will and **appetite** <term>appetite: in this context, the natural "inclination" or "hunger" of a substance to realize its potential</term> which exists in **prime matter** <note>the most basic, formless substance of the universe</note> and the **first efficient cause** <note>the primary source of all action or change</note> have no prior cause or principle; rather, one of these is the principle itself, and the other is the cause.

Accordingly, it is said by **Hesiod** <note>original: *Hesiodo*; an ancient Greek poet</note> that he comes from **Chaos**; <margin>164</margin> and this represents the appetite of **secondary matter** <note>matter that has already taken some form but remains in a state of flux</note>, found in subjects that are imperfect, confused, mixed, and conflicting, which desire peace, rest, and tranquility.

He is said by the poetess **Sappho** to be born of **Heaven and Earth**, which refers to the will and appetite by which the superior bodies <note>the celestial spheres or stars</note> protect, influence, and preserve the inferior bodies through a kind of love, while these inferior things in turn obey and comply with them.

He is said by **Plato** in the *Symposium* to be born of **Porus** <note>original: *Poro*; meaning "Resource" or "Plenty"</note> and **Penia** <note>meaning "Poverty" or "Want"</note>, to signify common or animal love, which arises from both abundance and lack. He is said to have been born at the time when the Gods... <note>the text breaks off here as it prepares to describe the birth of Love at the feast of the gods</note>

Just as we distinguish Cupid here, so the statues of others should be distinguished in a similar proportion.

<margin>25</margin> XVI. It is **delay** <note>original: *mora*</note>, as it were the reason by which the entrapped person is detained, as if suspending judgment and lingering in the act of giving their consent.

<margin>165<sup>v</sup></margin> **XVIII.** There is what is generally called **incantation**, which follows from contemplation <note>original: *commentatio*; in Bruno’s psychological system, this refers to the deep, focused mental processing of the beloved's image</note>. <meta>This page continues Bruno's systematic categorization of the stages of Love's influence on the soul. Having previously described how the lover is "ensnared" or captured by the beauty of an object, Bruno now details the subsequent emotional states—ranging from the heights of joy and physical exultation to the inevitable anxieties of suspicion, jealousy, and grief that arise when one loves something subject to change.</meta>

<header>GIORDANO BRUNO</header>

**XXIV.** There are **delights**, namely the pleasure found in the use of that which is held dear.

**XXV.** There is **joy**, namely a certain fruition that follows that use, or a sense of festivity arising in the soul from attainment and use—whether in reality or in expectation, and whether in the present or the future.

**XXVI.** There is **exultation** <note>original: *gestio*; the physical expression of internal joy</note>, namely a certain explicit indication and proclamation of joy manifesting itself externally. Hence, those who cannot hide their joy are said to "exult," <margin>10</margin> for they reveal it through outward gestures and actions.

**XXVII.** There is **suspicion**, which follows and accompanies love; for regarding those things we love and possess as dear—if we truly love them—since they are changeable or movable, we live in fear for them.

<margin>15</margin> **XXVIII.** **Fear** and **jealousy** follow <note>original: *zelotypia*; in Bruno's time, this meant both a "zeal" for the object and the painful "jealousy" regarding its potential loss</margin>, namely a certain dread and heavy | affliction toward those things or persons by whom we <margin>166</margin> might be cheated, deprived, or frustrated.

**XXIX.** **Grief** and **sadness** follow, which are the effects of jealousy and love. From this it happens that we can never truly <margin>20</margin> and purely rejoice in changing things; consequently, it happens that one wavers in love, because jealousy involves an inclination toward indignation regarding the things for which we have such zeal.

**XXX.** There is **hope** and **faith**; for we easily hope for what we love, and easily believe in things present and future. Hence the saying, <margin>25</margin> "What do we lovers not hope for?" <note>original: *quid non speramus amantes?*; a reference to Virgil's *Eclogues* 8.26</note> and that other, "What they love, they fashion for themselves in dreams" <note>original: *quod amant, per somnia fingunt sibi*; a reference to Virgil's *Eclogues* 8.108</note>.

<meta>This page transitions from the emotional psychology of love into a metaphysical cataloging of "Difference" or "Diversity." While the previous page examined how love wavers due to the changeability of objects, Bruno now introduces the "Skin of the Goat Amalthea"—a mythological symbol for the "Aegis" of Jupiter—as a metaphor for the vast container of all universal distinctions. He draws heavily on the "Art" of the medieval mystic Ramon Llull to categorize how things differ from one another.</meta>

->LAMP OF THE THIRTY STATUES.<-

# ON THE SKIN OF THE GOAT AMALTHEA.

Jupiter’s aegis <note>the protective shield or breastplate of Zeus/Jupiter</note>, made from the skin of the goat Amalthea <note>the mythological goat that nursed the infant Jupiter</note>, contains all things inscribed within it; in it, one may read everything. Therefore, it is suited for us to signify the principles of diversity <margin>5</margin> and multiplicity in things. Just as we tend toward unity and the concept of a universal whole through concord and love, so through these [statues/categories] we tend toward the concept of that part of a definition which limits, distinguishes, and truly defines the thing to be defined. Difference, as well as concordance and the other most universal principles signified above, <margin>10</margin> illuminate all things and run through all things, just as has been suggested in the Art of Llull <note>original: *Arte Lullii*; referring to Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316), whose system of combinatory logic deeply influenced Bruno</note>.
Now, at this point, let only thirty differences and meanings of diversity be enumerated in order.
<margin>15</margin> I. First, there is the name of **difference** for every reason by which individual things differ from themselves or from others.
II. There is **otherness** <note>original: *alietas*</note>, by which someone differs from another or from himself by an accidental difference; hence that saying: "Stranger, for you seem <margin>20</margin> different to me now than you did before." <note>original: *hospes, namque alius mihi nunc atque ante videris*; a reference to the Odyssey when Odysseus is transformed by Athena</note>
III. There is **something else** <note>original: *aliud*</note>, by which one thing is separated from another by an essential difference; hence it is said "a man is one thing, a beast is another."
IV. There is **the other** <note>original: *alterum*</note>, which grammatically suggests a difference between two or both.
V. There is **the altered** <note>original: *alteratum*</note>, namely something <margin>25</margin> varied in disposition or habit, while remaining the same according to its substance.

<meta>This page continues the catalog of the "Thirty Statues" or categories of difference, which Bruno uses to map how objects in the universe are distinct from one another. On the previous page, the author introduced the concept of "Difference" and "Otherness." Here, he moves through more specific logical and metaphysical classifications, drawing on Aristotelian logic and his own unique, often colorful, examples to define the ways things can be "not the same."</meta>

GIORDANO BRUNO

VI. **Diversity** <note>original: *diversum*</note> is what is inferred in those things which also properly differ by genus. <margin>160</margin> For "differences" are properly said to be those which exist within the same genus <note>a "genus" is a general class, like "animal"</note>; hence, according to Aristotle, things of different genera that are not subalternately placed <note>original: *non subalternatim positorum*; referring to classes that do not fall one under the other, like "knowledge" and "color"</note> [have different sets of specific differences].
<margin>5</margin> VII. **Disparity** <note>original: *disparatio*</note> is that which is considered in those things which are so "other" from one another that it cannot be understood how they might agree or be subdivided by genus or any other common reason. Regarding the genera of **substance** <term>Substance: that which exists in itself (like a tree or a person)</term> and **quantity** <term>Quantity: the measurement or extent of a thing</term>, we say they are "diverse," as if they share the same meaning or name of "being"; <margin>10</margin> but between the **breeches of St. Francis** <note>original: *femoralia S. Francisci*; a humorous example of a physical relic</note> and the **Lord's Prayer**, we perceive such a diversity and otherness that we can grasp no agreement either in name or in reality.
VIII. **Distinction** is that by which, according to various modes, something is said not to differ from itself or from another, but to be distinguished, according to the <margin>15</margin> reasons to be presented below.
IX. **Subordination** <note>original: *subalternatio*</note> or **coordination**; for these always presuppose a difference in number, dignity, and so on.
X. **Variety**; hence what the poet says concerning a certain person's head: "One part combed, one part shaved, one part twisted—who <margin>20</margin> would have believed it to be a single head?"
XI. **Aversion** <note>original: *aversum*</note>, which denotes a difference emanating from a different respect <note>a different "respect" means looking at a thing from a different perspective or relation</note>, because one thing is referred to this, and another to that.
XII. **Repulsion** <note>original: *taedium*</note>, which adds an "act" beyond mere relation; it not only looks elsewhere, but also tends elsewhere.
<margin>25</margin> XIII. **Multiplicity** <note>original: *multiplex*</note>, the opposite of simplicity; hence we speak of the "double" or "triple."
XIV. **The Deficient**, **the Rebellious**, or **the Deviating**; namely, that which is in motion (or at its limit after motion) away from a state of concord toward a state of difference, with an aptitude for contrariety <note>the potential to become an opposite</note>.

<meta>This page continues the catalog of "The Thirty Statues," a mnemonic and philosophical system where Giordano Bruno classifies the various ways things in the universe can be distinct, separated, or different from one another. On the previous page, he defined Diversity, Disparity, and Distinction. Here, he continues with types of separation, transition, and lack of proportion.</meta>

# THE LAMP OF THE THIRTY STATUES

XV. **Interwoven** or **interjected**, which refers to something that differs in any way from the thing into which it is placed or inserted.
XVI. **Distinction**, **distance**, or **interval**, which is the gap between items differing by number, but is not the differing thing itself.
<margin>5</margin> XVII. **Separation**, like a partition, fence, or hedge, which represents either the difference itself or the circumstances surrounding that difference.
XVIII. The **abstracted**, **separated**, or **torn away**.
XIX. The **distant**, **lengthened**, **removed**, **sequestered**, or **set aside**.
<margin>10</margin> XX. The **foreign**, **extraneous**, or **barbaric**. <margin>167^r</margin>
XXI. The **distributed** or **ordered**; this signifies difference with regard to number or various subjects, because "to distribute" is the same as "to give to different things." This is the origin of what are called distributive signs: *all*, *none*, and *some*. <note>In logic, these terms "distribute" a property across a group of subjects.</note>
<margin>15</margin> XXII. **Departure** or **withdrawal**, acting as the starting point of difference based on location or shared participation.
XXIII. **Transition**, serving as the middle ground between the boundary of agreement (or form) and the boundary of difference (or the contrary or privation <term>Privation: the absence of a quality that should normally be present, like blindness being the privation of sight</term>). In this state, there is neither true agreement nor true difference, but rather a <margin>20</margin> midpoint between the two that could take on the name of either.
XXIV. The **inconstant**, such as anything changeable, whether in its accidental qualities <term>Accident: a property that can change without changing the essence of the thing, like hair color</term> or in its very substance; thus, difference exists both in external and internal principles.
<margin>25</margin> XXV. **Dissimilarity**, which is a difference based on outward appearance or form.
XXVI. **Antipathy** <note>original: *asympathia*</note> and **apathy**, through which diverse things do not mutually affect or "feel with" one another.

XXX. There is the **principle that constitutes** a species under a genus, or an <margin>10</margin> individual under a species, by which the difference is called **constitutive** of the species. For these two functions are not the same; we divide genera through more differences than we use to constitute species.

The second to last mode is called the **division of the genus**, and the last is the **constitution of the particular**. To these modes, add the <margin>15</margin> principles and themes of **difference** which can be drawn from the opposites of "agreement"; for to each of the aforementioned members <margin>16^r</margin> signified, the differences of **contrariety** are opposed.

<note>original: *DE CAMPO LITIS*. Bruno uses "Strife" (or conflict) in the Heraclitean sense: the struggle between opposites that allows the world to function.</note>

...in the same category; hence it is characteristic of opposites to be as far removed from one another as possible. Some of these are **mediated**, while others are **immediate**. "Immediate" opposites are like health and sickness <note>meaning there is no middle state between them</note>, while "mediated" opposites are like white and black <note>which have intermediate colors like gray between them</note>. In every category <note>original: *genere*</note>, this logic <margin>5</margin> of **contrariety** is found, whether it be in a <term>substance</term> <note>a thing that exists in itself, like a tree or a person</note> or an <term>accident</term> <note>a quality that exists only in something else, like "greenness" or "height"</note>; otherwise, it is said to be a property of **quality** to admit its contrary.

II. An **opposite** is that which is perceived as unpleasant, joyless, or disagreeable, because it is felt to be either truly or apparently evil. <margin>10</margin>

III. It is an opposite if it strikes dread or fear into any subject.

IV. It is that which is refuted or rejected—that which is "refutable" or "rejectable."

<margin>15</margin> V. It is that which is avoidable or to be avoided, insofar as it flees from its opposite or is crushed by its opposite.

VI. That which is excluded and loathed, cast out, or repelled.

VIII. That which besieges, constricts, and causes one to shrink.

XI. That which causes torment or twists in pain.

XIII. That which kicks back, resists, and strives against.

XIV. That which weighs down, exerts pressure, or crushes.

XV. That which drags, leads, or moves one against their will.

XVI. That which hinders, holds back, and binds as if with <margin>30</margin> shackles <note>original: *compedibus*</note>.

# THE LAMP OF THE THIRTY STATUES
<note>original: *LAMPAS TRIGINTA STATUARUM*</note>

XVII. That which diverts from the goal in the opposite direction, twists back, or repels.
XVIII. That which weakens one’s strength, blunts, or wounds.
XIX. That which subdues or mutilates.
<margin>5</margin> XX. That which brings about damage, harm, and loss.
XXI. That which impresses a non-perfective <term>passion</term> <note>original: *passio*; here meaning an effect or state of being acted upon by an external force</note>. For some passions are **perfective** <note>improving or completing the thing</note>, such as the formation of the senses by sensible things, the intellect by intelligible things, and matter by form; others are **corruptive** <note>destructive or decaying</note>, such as the effect of heat on cold, <margin>10</margin> moisture on dryness, or fire on water.
XXII. That which defiles, adulterates, or alters; for this follows from a corruptive passion, which is **alteration**; hence those things that are not capable of being acted upon <note>original: *passibilia*</note> are least subject to alteration and adulteration.
<margin>15</margin> XXIII. That by which something is frustrated—for example, when it is cheated of its intended and perfect act or action. To this belongs every obstacle that creates and brings about difficulty.
XXIV. Everything dangerous, perilous, or ruinous, just as <term>Charybdis and Scylla</term> <note>mythological sea monsters representing two opposing dangers</note> are said to be the opposites of ships.
<margin>20</margin> XXV. Everything that expels and casts something out from its own place or its own subject; hence the famous definition of contraries: those things which mutually repel one another.
XXVI. Things that cannot exist at the same time in the same subject; hence they never stand together, but as much as <margin>25</margin> ⟨one⟩ enters, the other departs.
XXVII. Whatever things exterminate one another—that is, those where one is always outside the boundaries of the other, and thus the boundaries of one are extended in such a way that they are contracted to the same measure, quantity, and power as the boundaries of the other.
<margin>30</margin> XXVIII. Things that are naturally suited to occupy the same subject;

# ON THE AEON
## OR ON ETERNITY.
<margin>15</margin>

Beyond those things which consist in harmony and composition, and those which battle in contrariety, there remains and stands above them the invariable and immutable: namely, eternity or the eternal. Its thirty modes <note>original: *rationes*; here referring to the logical definitions or characteristics of the "statue" of Eternity</note> can be described in as many types.

<margin>20</margin> I. The first mode of eternity, therefore, is that it either does not need a sustainer to preserve it, or it possesses a sustainer perpetually.

II. Because it is immutable <note>unchanging</note>.

III. Because it has nothing into which it may pass; for everything that ceases to be, ceases into something else or ceases from being something.

<margin>25</margin> IV. Because it needs no nourishment; since it loses nothing of its own substance, it requires nothing from the outside to be restored. It is that from which all things flow, and into which nothing else flows.

**XXX.** That which is being itself; for "being" is that which *is*. For that which is variable and subject to decay is, in a way, "non-being," insofar as it participates in non-being; because where there is decay, there is also possibility or potential; where there is (passive) potential, there is <margin>20</margin> in some way matter, and in the same way, non-being. Therefore, that which truly *is*, is eternal.

From the conditions listed above, one may derive the principles of eternity, as well as those of decay, change, immutability, truth, and <term>being-in-itself</term> <note>original: "per se entis."</note>. # ON THE APPLICATION
## OF THE THIRTY STATUES.

### AND FIRST, ON THE APPLICATION OF THE SIX UNFIGURABLE THINGS.

<note>original: "infigurabilium." In Bruno's system, these are the highest, most abstract principles that cannot be represented by physical shapes or finite images.</note>

It remains, now that we have, as it were, set the warp of the loom, 
<margin>5</margin>to now weave upon it, to apply it, and to describe and define the work of defining, judging, and discovering. Since, therefore, all things consist within the <term>scale of nature</term> <note>original: "scala naturae." A traditional philosophical concept of a "ladder" or hierarchy where all beings are ranked from the lowest form of matter to the highest spiritual reality.</note>, and these either belong to the primary triad—being at the lowest step of nature—or they belong to the supreme or secondary triad—being at the second 
<margin>10</margin>step of nature—or they are in the middle, being closer to one or the other of the extremes or equidistant from both; it is certain that if we have attentively considered the principles of the extremes, we will easily be able to deduce the principles of the middle things. We must, therefore, look toward the properties of the supreme and the properties of the lowest: the 
<margin>15</margin>nature and order of each, and their participations on this side or that. And then, just as all intermediate colors are composed of white and black, so from the principle of the supreme (as light) and the lowest (as darkness), there follows the principle of all colors and all visible things—as a participation in 
<margin>20</margin>light and darkness, matter and form, <term>act and potency</term> <note>original: "actus et potentiae." A core philosophical distinction: "act" is a thing's fully realized state, while "potency" is its capacity or potential to become something.</note>, according to their specific kinds.

In the supreme region or degree, therefore, there is fullness, fertility, and <term>accomplishment</term> <note>original: "patratio." This refers to the bringing of something to completion or the full execution of an action.</note>; in the lowest region or degree, there is capacity, lack, and longing. In the first or supreme degree 
<margin>25</margin>there is the highest possession, riches, dignity, and a triple power (active, communicative, and formative); in the lowest degree there is

immaterial, simple, immortal, and divine. For although they are 
participants in darkness in reality or in likeness, they are named such 
<margin>25</margin>because everything is named after that which predominates in it. 
The opposite is true for those things which, from the middle step and 
the same horizon, are closer to the lowest. Thus, setting aside the 
highest and lowest steps—which have entirely <term>incommunicable</term> 
<note>original: "incommunicabiles." Meaning their natures are so pure or so base that they cannot be shared or blended with other levels of existence.</note> 
characteristics—all higher things take on the character of the low...

...of higher beings, insofar as they are below the highest and seem to tend toward the lowest; whereas lower things take on the character of the higher, insofar as they are distanced from the bottom and recede from it and approach toward the highest. And the more they approach the <margin>5</margin> boundaries or are distanced from the boundaries, the more intensely or more weakly they receive the character of those extremes. But that which consists in the horizon <note>Bruno uses "horizon" here to mean the mathematical or metaphysical midpoint—the boundary line where the spiritual and material worlds meet.</note>, or in the middle step, is like a certain individual with a dual nature: according to one of these, it is continuous with the lowest of the superior things; according to the other, however, with the <margin>10</margin> highest of the inferior things.

# ON THE CHARACTER OF THE COMMUNICABLE PREDICATES <margin>171^r</margin>
# IN THE VARIOUS STEPS OF THE SCALE.

There are certain predicates <note>original: "praedicata." Attributes or qualities that can be "predicated" (affirmed) of a subject.</note> common to the lowest and the highest step, such as being simple, uncomposed, unmixed, without <margin>15</margin> form, and incapable of suffering <note>original: "impassibile." In philosophical terms, this means "incapable of being acted upon" or "unaffected by external influence."</note>. These things are indeed said of the void, matter, and shadow, but in a privative sense <note>original: "privative." Describing a quality by the absence of its opposite; for example, "darkness" is the privation of light. Here, matter is "simple" only because it lacks any parts yet.</note>, because they are simple and unmixed in such a way that they either enter into composition or exist around composition and are, by some logic, related to composite things. Regarding the mind <gloss>and</gloss> the intellect, however, they are said truly and <margin>20</margin> negatively <note>original: "negative." This refers to "Negative Theology," where the highest divine principles are defined by what they are *not* (e.g., God is "infinite" because He is "not finite").</note>. In the former, I say, that "un-" <note>Referring to the Latin prefix *in-* used in words like *incompositum* (uncomposed) or *immixtum* (unmixed).</note> signifies a negation, but in the latter, a privation; for they have a certain aptitude or congruence for composition or with composition. <margin>22</margin> Therefore, that which is near the first step is so incorruptible and incapable of suffering that it admits such characters neither through itself nor by accident, neither in <margin>25</margin> reality nor by circumstance; whereas that which is in the lowest step receives these characters only by accident and by circumstance.

<summary>Bruno explains that while the highest (Mind) and lowest (Matter) levels of existence share descriptions like "simplicity," for the Mind it is a perfect negation of parts, whereas for Matter it is merely a lack (privation) of form. He defines the "horizon" as the midpoint where the spiritual and material realms are linked.</summary>

In these matters, therefore, the void <note>original: "vacuum." In Bruno’s physics, this is the infinite, empty space that acts as the container for all matter.</note> is simple and uncompoundable in a privative sense <note>original: "privative." This means it is "simple" only because it lacks parts or internal structure.</note>; fullness <note>original: "plenitudo." Likely referring to the divine plenum or the totality of being.</note> is simple and uncompoundable in a negative sense <note>original: "negative." This means it is simple because it transcends the very possibility of being divided or composed.</note>; matter is simple in a privative sense, yet it is capable of being compounded. Similarly, material form is a composite subject; the form—or the soul—is the "act" <note>original: "actus." In philosophy, "act" is the realization or expression of a thing's potential; the soul is what makes the body a living thing.</note> <margin>5</margin> of the composite being. The Gods are forms in act existing outside of material composition, yet they are still considered "composites of the first act" <note>This suggests that while they aren't made of matter, they are still "composed" of existence and the potentiality they receive from a higher source.</note> because of their potentiality, insofar as they have a way of being that is received from and dependent upon another.

## THE SCALE OF NATURE.

<margin>10</margin> It is established for us—according to a truly physical and ancient philosophy that is most consistent with the nature of things—that the scale of nature consists of thirty steps. Concerning these, beginning from the lowest and proceeding to the highest, we first propose the four lowest simple things.

<margin>15</margin> ### ON THE FOUR LOWEST SIMPLE THINGS.

These are: the void, which is the receptacle of bodies;
the shadow <margin>17:</margin>|, which is the potential to be formed and to be illuminated; matter, which is the primary receptive subject; the atom <note>original: "atomus." Bruno’s atom is the "physical minimum," the smallest possible point of matter that cannot be divided any further.</note>, which is the physically <margin>20</margin> indivisible substance into which the final material and real dissolution of bodies occurs, as if by a practical geometric division.

<margin>25</margin> ought to exist here; though there is an agreement according to their limbs and [physical structure]...

## ON PERFECTE COMPOSITED BEINGS
### NEAR THE LIGHT.

<margin>172</margin>
Perfectly composed beings, however, as intellectual and divine substances established in a more constant body in which the <margin>5</margin> fourfold element <term>fourfold element: the traditional four elements of earth, water, air, and fire, which Bruno believes combine to form all physical matter</term> concurs, are the stars in general. Among these, in some water predominates, as they shine with a borrowed light; these are "earths" <note>original: "tellures." Bruno uses this term to describe non-luminous planets that, like our Earth, reflect the light of a sun.</note>, of the kind commonly called "Planets," whose light does not twinkle. Of these, only those near us are visible; the more <margin>10</margin> distant ones are less visible due to the smallness of their bodies and the weakness of their light, and thus very few of them are perceptible to our senses. Others are those in which fire predominates; these are larger bodies and shine by their own light, and all of these twinkle <note>original: "scintillant." Bruno correctly identifies that stars (suns) twinkle due to their own intense light, while planets generally provide a steady reflected light.</note>. These bodies are called by the name of Gods and are the principal <margin>15</margin> members of the world; the fiery ones are entitled with the names of Gods, while the watery ones are called Goddesses. Thus, as their kind is twofold, so their general name is twofold: for they call the Sun or Apollo "Liber" <note>Liber was an Italian deity of fertility and wine, often identified with Bacchus/Dionysus; Bruno uses him here as a masculine archetype for self-luminous suns.</note>, and they call the Moon "Trivia" or "Diana" or <margin>20</margin> "Ceres" <note>Ceres is the goddess of agriculture; Bruno uses her as a feminine archetype for reflected-light bodies like planets and moons.</note>. Hence the Pythagorean <note>Bruno likely refers to the poet Virgil, whom he considers a vessel of Pythagorean wisdom, specifically citing the beginning of the *Georgics*: "Liber et alma Ceres."</note> says "Liber and nurturing Ceres," understanding all Gods under the name of Liber and all Goddesses under the name of Ceres.

## ON THOSE WHICH ARE NEARLY SIMPLE.

Those which are nearly simple are of two kinds. For there is the nearly simple universal spirit, which is the air <margin>25</margin> filling the universal vacuum, and which they think is Amphitrite <note>Amphitrite: A Greek sea goddess. Bruno uses her name to personify the vast, fluid "ether" or "spirit" that fills the space between celestial bodies.</note>...

<summary>Bruno classifies celestial bodies into two categories: self-luminous "suns" (dominated by fire) and reflecting "earths" or planets (dominated by water), associating them with masculine and feminine divine archetypes. He also introduces the concept of a universal spirit or "air" that fills the perceived vacuum of space.</summary>

## ON PURELY SIMPLE SUBSTANCE.

<margin>173r</margin>
Truly, the most simple substance—which is neither composed of parts nor capable of being combined with others, and which deviates from simplicity neither by its own nature nor by accident—is threefold. First is the **Operating** or **active** substance; this is the spirit or love, which they call the **Soul of the Universe**. This substance does not enter into the composition of particular things any more than light does, which is present in the air in such a way that it is not <insert>not</insert> <note>The word "non" (not) was missing in some manuscript versions but is essential for the sense that light remains distinct from the air it illuminates.</note> composed with the air, nor can it be a part of it. Therefore, it differs from the spirit which is the air, or the "Amphitrite of souls" <term>Amphitrite of souls: In mythology, Amphitrite is a sea goddess; here, Bruno uses her name to describe the vast, fluid medium of air or aether that "bathes" or contains all individual souls.</term>; for it has the character of an agent and a worker entirely, and in no way the character of a part or an element.

Next is the **primary respective substance**, which is turned toward the patterns of things to be established; this is the **primary Intellect** and the source of ideas, or the **ideal world**. Some call this the "Son," while others call it the "Word" <note>original: "Verbum," referring to the Logos.</note>, containing all things within itself.

Above all things, however, is the **Mind** <note>original: "Mens." In Bruno's Neoplatonic framework, the Mind is the highest, most transcendent level of reality.</note>, the absolute first, the fullness itself, or the **Father**.

#### More Material

<note>"Formal" here refers to the "Form" or soul-like quality that gives a thing its identity.</note>

- **Universal**
    - Imperceptible { Spirit or air

<note>Substances made of multiple elements or parts.</note>

#### More Material or Shadowy

- From water { The Spring, The River

    - Stone and gem, in which earth abounds
    - Metal, in which water abounds
- **Animate**

<meta>This page continues the logical structuring of the "Tree of Substance" introduced on the previous page. Having established the broad categories of simple and composed substances, Bruno now explains the specific methodology for defining any particular thing by tracing its lineage from the "roots" of universal being down to the specific "joints" of its individual identity.</meta>

# THE TORCH OF THE THIRTY STATUES

<margin>175^v</margin>
The method for deriving a definition for any particular substance from the order of the provided tree is as follows: first, we consider its **root**, which is the first term—that is, substance itself. This is the first <note>original: "genus"</note> and the highest, most universal category. Second, we consider the **trunk**, which is always double, signifying the first division. Third, the **branch**, which is only double, signifying the third division. Fourth, the **bough** <note>original: "brachium," literally "arm"</note>, which is at least double, representing the fourth division. Fifth, the **hands**, at least two, representing the fifth. Sixth, the **fingers**, at least two, representing the sixth. Seventh, the **joints**, at least two from each finger, which signify the seventh division. For the eighth, ninth, and tenth, one may add others if necessary, which you might call the second, third, or fourth joints, and so on, until you reach the final term, which is the **most specific species** <term>Most specific species: In logic, this is the "species specialissima," the lowest level of classification that can still be defined, just above the individual person or thing.</term> or particular.

Therefore, when we define something, we proceed from the universal genus—either the most remote one found in the root, or a closer one resulting from the differences found in the branches or boughs—moving through the intermediate differences from the assumed genus down to the very last.

Thus, if we wish to define the **Father** or the **Mind**, we say it is a substance that is perfectly simple, **negatively uncomposed** <note>Negatively uncomposed: Being so simple and unified that the very concept of "parts" cannot even be applied to it.</note>, and the first absolute. If we wish to define **matter**, we say it is a substance that is perfectly simple, **privatively uncomposed** <note>Privatively uncomposed: Lacking parts currently, but possessing the potential or "hunger" to be composed into something else.</note>, and primarily receptive. These terms were declared previously in the explained scale of the nature of substance. The pattern of this progression is:

\* \* \*
<note>The following diagram elements are indicated: Root, Trunk, Branch, Bough, Hand, Fingers, Joints</note>

And so, the designation of the particular species is completed—or, as I should better say, the members or the steps of the scale.

# 170. ON THE EXPLAINED SCALE OF PREDICATES <note>original: "praedicatorm," referring to things that can be "predicated" or stated about a subject.</note>

## OR THE ATTRIBUTES OF SUBSTANCE AND NATURE SPOKEN OF UNIVERSALLY.

<margin>5</margin> Consequently, now that the meanings and species of substances have been arranged, we must proceed to arrange their universal attributes. First, we consider those that are commonly <margin>10</margin> stated about all things. Some of these are absolute predicates, others are relative <note>original: "respectiva"</note>, and others are intermediate (being, in a way, partly absolute and partly relative). Others are, as it were, origins and effects—which are common predicates—while others are their surrounding circumstances. In <margin>15</margin> total, there are thirty.

## ON THE ABSOLUTE PREDICATES.

Absolute predicates are:
First, **Being** <note>original: "Ens"</note>, or that which is in act; it signifies a subsisting nature, of which it is true to say "it is," and false <margin>20</margin> to say "it is not."
II. **Entity** <note>original: "Entitas"</note>, as the very actuality of being; or **Actuality**, as the entity of that which is in act. However, "being" <note>original: "ens"</note> and "that which is in act" differ from "entity" and "actuality" in the same way that "light" <note>original: "lumen"</note> and "that which shines" differ from "brightness" <note>original: "lux"</note> and the quality by which a thing shines.

<summary>Bruno begins a new section of his mnemonic system, shifting from the classification of substances to the thirty "predicates" or attributes. He defines the first two absolute predicates: Being (the thing that exists) and Entity (the quality of existing), using the analogy of light to distinguish between them.</summary>

<keywords>Giordano Bruno, metaphysics, predicates, Being, Entity, Actuality, logic, attributes of substance</keywords>

--- Page 255 ---
<meta>This page continues the systematic classification of the "Thirty Statues" or universal predicates of substance. Having previously defined "Being" (Ens) and "Entity" (Entitas), Bruno now moves on to distinguish the nuances between essence, the act of being, subsistence, and nature.</meta>

# THE LAMP OF THE THIRTY STATUES.

III. There is **Essence** <note>original: "essentia"</note>, insofar as it is the nature or that which is like the form which gives being to a thing, just as the soul gives being to an animal; and that which is signified by a definition is called "essence" in a definite sense.

<margin>5</margin> IV. There is the **Act of Being** <note>original: "esse"</note>, insofar as it is that which results from the constitutive principles; it is not only what is signified by the definition, but also everything that concurs to completely constitute the nature of the thing. For in a definition, certain material principles do not enter into the primary components, <margin>10</margin> such as flesh, bones, nerves, humors, heat, etc. Although these say nothing about the "essence" of the thing (in respect to which they are called **accidents** <note>technical term for non-essential properties, like the color of one's hair</note>),|<margin>176v</margin> they nevertheless constitute the "act of being" of the thing through themselves, insofar as the thing cannot exist without them.

V. There is **Subsistence** <note>original: "subsistentia"</note>, insofar as it is the effect of the thing itself and the actuality of those things which lead to the being of the thing, along with the circumstances and accidents by which a natural thing exists as a particular individual. Therefore, **Being** <note>original: "ens"</note> is like "man"; **Entity** <note>original: "entitas"</note> is like "humanity"; **Essence** <note>original: "essentia"</note> is like "rational animal," and so on; the **Act of Being** <note>original: "esse"</note> is that which constitutes the composite of the rational soul and the body; <margin>20</margin> **Subsistence** is the complete internal logic by which Socrates or Plato is truly and sensibly Socrates himself, precisely what he is.

VI. There is **Nature** <note>original: "natura"</note>, insofar as it is the essence or entity according to that logic by which it is the principle of motion in a movable thing, or the principle of operation in any thing whatsoever, so that <margin>25</margin> it may act according to what it is—that is, according to its own self. Thus, nature and essence are the same thing, but it is called "nature" according to the definition just stated: namely, as the principle of acting or being acted upon in that which acts or suffers.

...according to what corresponds to its essence, because everything acts in accordance with how it is; and so we have the definition of **Nature** <note>original: "natura"</note> spoken of universally, and not only as it is the "principle of motion in movable things" <note>Bruno is referencing the classic Aristotelian definition of nature as the internal source of movement or change</note>; for the principle of acting and being acted upon—and more broadly of acting alone or being acted upon alone—embraces

VII. There is **Unity**, or **Truth**, or **Goodness**, which
<margin>10</margin> are the same, because that which is simple and one is true. For that which is twofold or manifold is not true or pure; likewise, that which is one and true—namely, the one and the pure itself—is good. Thus, what is "one water" is "true water," "pure water," and "good water"; similarly "true gold," "good gold," and "one gold."
<margin>15</margin> Therefore, "Truth" here is not the kind that consists in the logical arrangement of affirmation and negation <note>meaning this is "ontological truth" (the reality of being) rather than "propositional truth" (whether a statement is correct)</note>; similarly, this is not moral goodness, but truth is the very **reality** and **simplicity** <note>the state of being uncompounded or not made of parts</note> of the thing, and consequently its unity; likewise, goodness is the nature of the thing. In the same way, "**The One**" is not taken as the start of a number or a part of a sum,
<margin>17^r</margin> <margin>20</margin> but absolutely | for **being** in itself; not, I say, numerically or as something reducible to the category of quantity, but essentially and fundamentally. Therefore, these three are the same and signify primarily; for before these, nothing is, nor does anything come to be.

# ON PREDICATES

## PARTLY ABSOLUTE, PARTLY RELATIVE, OR INTERMEDIATE BETWEEN BOTH.

The intermediate predicates <note>attributes or qualities we say about a subject</note> are those that follow. The
<margin>5</margin> first of these is **insofar as** <note>original: "secundum quod"</note>, and it is that which mediates between a thing’s nature and its essence, etc., and those qualities that supervene <note>occur as an addition or change</note> and follow from them; thus, the logic of those later qualities arises from the former. For instance, **divinity** insofar as it is divinity receives certain definitions; **unity** and **goodness** insofar as they are
<margin>10</margin> unity and goodness, and each thing insofar as it is what it is.

II. <note>This is Statue IX in the broader sequence</note> There is **Necessity** <note>original: "necessitas"</note>, to which is opposed **Contingency** <note>original: "contingentia"</note>. These two are taken in a simple way: either absolutely, as they are the forms of the thing according to itself; or in another way, as they relate to
<margin>15</margin> effects or subjects. For example, divinity is absolute necessity in itself, but it is also necessary in relation to other things. For necessity according to its absolute definition is infallible and immutable truth, existence, and unity. There is a similar judgment regarding the contingency of those things of which it is spoken.

<margin>20</margin> III. <note>This is Statue X in the broader sequence</note> There is **Perfection** <note>original: "perfectio"</note>, and **Imperfection** is its opposite. Perfection is something absolute, as it signifies the unity and totality <note>the state of being a complete whole</note> of a thing; it is also relative, insofar as it is spoken of and referred to that which is "perfectible" <note>capable of being made perfect</note>. Similarly, imperfection is either referred to that of which it is spoken, or is considered according to itself, although an absolute logic for imperfection does not exist, so...

<summary>Bruno defines "intermediate predicates," specifically focusing on the concepts of "insofar as," necessity, and perfection, distinguishing between their absolute existence in a thing and their relative existence in relation to others.</summary>

<margin>15</margin> it is relative insofar as it is the same as other things, diverse from other things, or same by identity and diverse by diversity.

<meta>This page continues the list of "Unequally Relative Predicates" from the bottom of page 191. Bruno is systematically defining the ways in which things relate to one another when they are not of equal status or rank.</meta>

First is **origination** <note>original: "principiatio"; the process by which a "principle" or source relates to that which flows from it</note>, by which a principle is referred to that which is originated. Indeed, sometimes this principle can originate as much as can be originated, but it does not always originate as much as it is capable of originating. (Furthermore) a principle, according to its many meanings, does not possess proportion or equality with that which is originated, as is evident in the cases of **unity** [relative to] **number**, or a **point** [relative to] a **line**. <note>In Bruno’s geometry and metaphysics, a point is the "principle" of a line but is not "equal" to it because a point has no dimension while a line does.</note>

II. There is **mediation**, by which a middle term is referred to the extremes or to those things of which it is the middle; among these, there is no equality, as is apparent.

III. There is **termination**, which, although it is sometimes made equal to "origination" in certain boundaries—such as at the endpoints of a line or at the same point on a circumference (which serves as the same subject or boundary for the ending of one thing and the beginning of another)—is nonetheless not always understood in this way.

IV. **Causation**, as it is the principle naming a subject insofar as something exists because of it. It is opposed to "causability" <note>the capacity to be caused</note> and the "cause" itself. By its very nature as a cause, it always stands above the effect and that which comes from it.

<margin>178</margin>
V. **Inclination**, which is a propensity toward being or becoming, toward acting or undergoing <note>original: "pati"; the state of being acted upon by an external force</note>, or toward giving or receiving.

VI. There is **number**, spoken of universally, as the principle concurring in the constitution of a subject; hence, beyond simple essence and unity, all things are a certain kind of number. <note>This reflects Pythagorean influence, suggesting that the structure of all complex things is essentially numerical.</note>

VII. There is **measure**, spoken of universally, as the "weight" or "importance" <note>original: "momentum"</note> of every thing that has a limit. Hence, except for that which is simply infinite, just as the species and nature of all things are determined and distinct, so too is their specific weight or "momentum."

VIII. There is **similarity**, or a relation between a like thing and that to which it is likened, which is found in all things; however, it is structured so that inferior things are said to be similar to superior things, but not vice versa. Those superior things are instead called the models to which the inferior ones are likened. <note>In Bruno’s philosophy, a reflection is "like" the person in the mirror, but the person is the "original" rather than being "like" the reflection. This maintains a cosmic hierarchy from the divine down to the material.</note>

<margin>5</margin> IX. There is **life**, which is the first act of nature; for just as nature is the principle of every operation by which each thing acts according to what it is, so life is the very formality <note>In scholastic philosophy, "formality" refers to the specific essential character of a thing.</note> and efficacy of nature. Through this, those things that are perfect possess the principle of acting perfectly and hold the perfect act of nature. <margin>10</margin> Consequently, not everything that possesses a nature is said to possess life, but only those things that possess a more perfect nature.

### DEFINITION OF THESE TERMS.

These are indeed applied consequently to each and every member of the previously established scale of substance <note>original: "scalae substantiae"—referring to the hierarchical ladder of existence described on page 184.</note>; for all these signify either substance, or that which is within substance, or that which adheres to substance, or that which surrounds substance.

## ON THE ROOT OF THE TREE.

Therefore, that which stands for the **root** is the category, or the predicament <note>term: "predicament" (original: praedicamentum); in Aristotelian logic, this refers to one of the ten highest kinds or categories of being.</note>, or the reason, or the intention <note>term: "intention" (original: intentio); in medieval logic, an "intention" is a mental concept or the way the mind "tends toward" an object.</note>, or the word, or the sign; <margin>5</margin> because it happens that these terms can be understood either as predicates that actually belong to substances, or as signifying those predicates—namely as the intentions of them—or as the words or names by which they are signified. Therefore, when any of these terms is to be defined, it is taken either as a thing, namely **metaphysically**; or as the primary concept of the thing, namely **intentionally** or **logically**; <margin>10</margin> or as a word, namely **grammatically** or by a logic that stands midway between grammar and logic. If they are grasped in the first way, they are called "beings surrounding a substance"; <margin>179<sup>v</sup></margin> if in the second way, they are called reasons or intentions; if in the third way, they are called words or meaningful expressions. <margin>15</margin> And so, at the root, for the genus <note>term: "genus"; the broad class or category to which a specific thing belongs.</note> of these things, you may at your pleasure first place either **being**, or **reason** or **intention**, or the **word** or **expression**.

# ON THE STATUES OF DISTINCTIONS

Since we have examined the subjects and the most universal predicates, we must now see how and in what manner those predicates are connected to the subjects. For this reason, <margin>5</margin> let certain "figures" <note>original: "personae." Here Bruno refers to symbolic statues or characters used in his memory system.</note> be arranged for these distinctions and accounts; in their twin limbs, one may observe the twin members of a distinction.

Let the first statue, then, be that of Atlas, divided or distributed into fifteen twin parts, so that it is distinguished by thirty members. Of these, the right shall be the member of light, and the left the member of darkness—one, I say, of a more perfect account, the other of an imperfect one. They are: I. Right and left eye, II. Two ears, III. Two temples, IV. Two nostrils, V. Cheeks, VI. Jaws, VII. Shoulders, VIII. Arms, IX. Breasts, X. Hands, XI. Thighs, XII. Hips, XIII. Knees, XIV. Shins, XV. Feet.
