# THE TORCH OF THE THIRTY STATUES

...[of the abso]lute and in comparison; in the IV, of the perfect and the imperfect; in the V, of the mobile and the stable (or rather, the movable and the fixed, or the inconstant and the permanent); in the VI, of the solitary and the accompanied; in the VII, according to itself (properly and according to the reality) and according to another (improperly and according to the mode); in the VIII, simply and within a genus; in the IX, infinitely and finitely; in the X, from itself and from another; in the XI, primarily and secondarily; in the XII, essentially and by participation <note>original: "participative." In Neoplatonic philosophy, this refers to a lower thing sharing in the qualities of a higher source.</note>; in the XIII, simultaneously and successively; in the XIV, by itself and by accident <note>original: "per se, per accidens." A core Aristotelian distinction between what belongs to a thing's essence versus what happens to it by chance or external circumstances.</note>; and in the XV, according to the whole and according to the part.

<margin>10</margin>Regarding the first member—the absolute and the respective—it is said that a thing can be considered "absolutely" in three ways, as manifested in this proposal. First, as it is distinguished against the **respective**; here it is the distinction of anything considered either without a relationship to others, or with a relationship to them. Second, "absolutely" as it is distinguished against the **contracted** <note>original: "contracte." Bruno uses "contraction" to describe how a universal, infinite idea is limited or "squeezed" into a specific, finite physical form.</note>. According to this reasoning, something considered absolutely is taken more generally, more universally, and more extensively, as it is not limited by a specific difference or any other kind of application. (For example, "animal" spoken of absolutely refers generally to everything that possesses the nature of an animal; but "contracted," as it receives the limitation of a specific difference, it is said of certain groups and finally of a specific individual. Thus, matter considered absolutely and form considered absolutely are one and infinite; but "contracted," they are many and finite. <margin>181v</margin> For matter is limited by form, and form by matter).

<margin>25</margin>Third, "absolutely" as it is distinguished against the **comparative**. This is where a "likeness of contradiction" sometimes occurs, because the distinction is not considered within the thing itself. For instance, the world, man, and so on are good **absolutely**; yet they are bad **comparatively**, if, for example, they are compared to the "Best" <note>original: "optimo," referring to the ultimate Good or God.</note>.

Regarding the distinction according to itself and not according to...

other; "successive" things are those that have an order according to before and

Therefore, while this statue does not have a middle ground, it does have that which denies both [extremes]; just as between "absolutely" and "relatively" there is that which is in neither way. ## ON THE STATUE OF TYPHON.

<margin>5</margin> In the statue of **Atlas**, we were considering the right and left sides, for he has no front parts <note>In Bruno’s memory system, Atlas represents a simpler model where things are only "either/or."</note>; but in **Typhoeus** <note>Also known as Typhon, a monstrous giant. Therefore, just as those fifteen <margin>15</margin> [distinctions] were noted in the latitudes <note>This refers to a previous grid or "map" in Bruno's system of logic.</note>, so let these | <margin>18</margin> distinctions be noted in the same order. For example, the substance <margin>20</margin> of a human being receives one definition regarding the soul or internal nature, but another regarding external things; this logic is different from those that follow, as will be seen.

middle effects are the instruments of the first cause, as are all middle effects in respect to those above them; for universally, secondary causes <note>original: *secundae caussae*; in Aristotelian philosophy, these are the natural causes we observe, which are set in motion by a 'First Cause' or God.</note> are instrumental in respect to primary causes.

<margin>15</margin> and meaning <note>original: *significare*; the capacity to signify or point to a higher truth.</note>.

<margin>20</margin> the back part of the statue are the non-beings.

Concerning the ninth distinction, the same judgment applies.

Concerning the tenth latitude, that which is act <term>act: in Scholastic philosophy, 'act' (actus) refers to the full realization or perfection of a thing's potential.</term> receives predicates intensively; that which is pure act receives them most intensively; that which is matter, or like matter, receives them extensively <note>meaning across a physical space or quantity rather than in quality or "intensity."</note>; that which 
<margin>25</margin> partakes of both light and darkness receives them partly intensively and partly extensively; and that which is not a being receives them in neither way.

...that which is immobile; within motion is that which is moved; within rest is that which is capable of being moved. <gloss>that</gloss>

Concerning the twelfth distinction, between the "definitive" and the "circumscriptive" <note>original: *definitive et circumscriptive*; Scholastic terms describing how things occupy space. A soul is "definitively" in a body (present throughout without taking up volume), while a physical object like a book is "circumscriptively" in a place (occupying a specific volume defined by its boundaries).</note>, there is that which is in neither way—or rather, that which is in both ways in the most eminent
<margin>5</margin> degree—such as that which is everywhere, but not as if in a physical place. <unclear>...</unclear> <note>The Latin manuscript is missing punctuation and potentially some text here. A secondary manuscript adds: "Definitively, like the soul in the body, where there is no corner where it does not act; Circumscriptively, like a tablet, a table, or a book in a place."</note>

Concerning the thirteenth, something is said to be "subjectively" <note>original: *subiective*; referring to the underlying subject or matter that possesses a quality.</note> in this manner for our purposes when it is so by reason of the nature assigned to the subject, but "formally" <note>original: *formaliter*; according to the essential "form" or definition of the thing.</note> when it is by its own proper nature. Hence, regarding the same person we can say "the musician runs"
<margin>10</margin> and "the musician does not run"; for the musician formally, insofar as he is a musician, sings or makes music, yet the musician—as the underlying subject who possesses the music—is able to run. <note>original: *Omnes operationes sunt suppositorum*; a philosophical principle meaning "all actions belong to the individual person/subject," not just to their abstract qualities.</note>

In the fourteenth latitude, between the evident and the hidden is the "confused," or that which is partly evident and partly hidden, or
<margin>15</margin> neither; and for this reason, in this state, the preceding part and the following part coincide.

In the fifteenth latitude, everything except that which is at the highest level—which is the end <note>original: *finis*; the ultimate goal or purpose.</note> alone—is either purely for the sake of the end (as are those at the lowest level), or they are partly
<margin>20</margin> an end with respect to those below them, and partly for the sake of an end with respect to those above them. In the things that follow, they are non-beings.

<meta>This page continues the transition from the "Thirty Statues" binary opposites to more complex tripartite structures. Having discussed distinctions that lack a middle ground, Bruno now introduces the "Three Hypostases of the Giants," which allow for a "middle" or intermediate state between two extremes. This marks a shift from simple dualities to the three-fold way things exist: in the mind of the creator, in the object itself, and in the mind of the observer.</meta>

->JORDAN BRUNO<-

# ON THE THREE HYPOSTASES OF THE GIANTS <note>original: *hypostasis*; here meaning a fundamental state of being or an underlying reality.</note>

### IN WHICH THE FOLLOWING TRIPLE GENUS OF DISTINCTIONS IS NOTED.

Consequently, after those most general distinctions—which either lack a middle ground or have an unnamed one (not famous by its own name but described by the negation or composition of both extremes)—we must now bring forward those that admit a certain and named middle ground. These are of three types: some are according to the natures of things as they are **beings**; the second as they are **conceivable** or **knowable**; the third as they are **speakable** or **signifying**.

The first type is represented in the person of the Giant Enceladus <note>Enceladus was one of the Giants of Greek mythology who rebelled against the gods. Bruno uses him here as a mnemonic figure to represent the ontological "latitude" or range of physical existence.</note>. In him, there is a distinction that has *before the thing* on the right, *after the thing* on the left, and *in the thing* in the middle. Beings of the first kind are "ideas," which Plato called "before the many" <note>original: *ante multa*; the abstract blueprint of a thing existing before the physical objects themselves.</note>; those of the second kind are physical and conjoined forms, or the composite things themselves, which are called "in the many" or "the many" <note>original: *in multis* or *multa*; the form as it exists within matter.</note>; those of the third kind are intentions or concepts derived from things, which are commonly called "after the things" or "after the many" <note>original: *post multa*; the mental concept formed after observing the physical objects.</note>.

---

| To the Right | In the Middle | To the Left |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| I. Before the thing | In the thing | After the thing |
| II. Subjectively | Virtually | Objectively |
| III. Really | Intentionally in the first degree | Intentionally in the second degree |

*and so on, until*

| | | |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| XV. Most of all | Especially | Scarcely |

Concerning point I, it should be noted that Beings of this Genus are Ideas, which Plato called "before the many," etc.

# THE TORCH OF THE THIRTY STATUES <note>original: *Lampas Triginta Statuarum*. This is one of Bruno's major works on the art of memory and metaphysics, where he uses "statues" as mental images to organize all human knowledge.</note>

In the second mode, [a thing] exists subjectively, virtually, and objectively: so that the **subject** is the substance of the thing, in which and around which the subject is found; **power** <note>original: *virtus*; in this context, it refers to the innate "virtue" or efficacy and potential of a thing to act.</note> is the effectiveness of the thing; the **object** is that which is presented to a specific faculty.

<margin>5</margin> III. It exists really, according to a first intention, and according to a second intention. **Real** things are those which exist outside the mind. Things of **first intention** are the images, forms, and all mental concepts <note>original: *intentiones*; a technical term in Scholastic philosophy referring to the way the mind "stretches toward" an object.</note> which exist in the mind in such a way that something outside the mind corresponds to them immediately. **Second
<margin>10</margin> intentions** are concepts founded upon those first ones, such as the concepts of logic. Of the first kind is "man" in nature and in act; of the second, "man" in voice, in concept, and in mental focus; of the third, the concept of a "species," which is founded upon the concept of "man." <note>Bruno is explaining that while "a man" is a real being, the mental idea of a man is a "first intention," and the logical category of "species" is a "second intention" because it is a concept about a concept.</note>

<margin>15</margin> IV. Naturally, violently, voluntarily: the first is that which comes from the internal principles of a thing; the second is that which comes from necessity or some other reason against nature; the third (which is the middle ground) comes from the **will**, which mediates between that which is according to nature and that which is against it. <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "violent" movement (original: *violenter*) refers to any motion or state forced upon an object by an external force, contrary to its natural inclination.</note>

<margin>20</margin> V. It is 1. without order, 2. unordered, or 3. ordered. The first is said of all **simples** <note>original: *simplicibus*; fundamental elements or units that cannot be divided.</note>, in which, since there is no multiplicity, there certainly can be no order (for order does not exist where there is no plurality); "unordered" is said of that which either tends toward order, or falls away from order, or is capable [of order].

---

<summary>Bruno continues his metaphysical classification, distinguishing between physical substance, mental concepts (intentions), and the origins of action (nature, force, or will). He also defines "order" as a property that requires multiplicity, noting that simple, indivisible units are beyond the concept of order.</summary>

<header>GIORDANO BRUNO</header>

...ordered towards both; it is that which constitutes many things in a certain ratio and dignity according to **before** and **after**. <margin>189</margin>

VI. It exists as a **starting point**, an **endpoint**, and a **middle**: the first is that from which movement, decline, or change begins; the second is the way or the medium through which movement occurs; the third is that toward which or to which it tends. <margin>5</margin> <note>original: *terminus a quo* (point from which), *terminus ad quem* (point to which), and *medium*. These are standard Aristotelian terms for describing change.</note>

VII. It exists **most eminently**, **sufficiently**, **equally** (or evenly), and **with defect** (or deficiently): things of the first kind are expressed in the superlative degree; the second, in the comparative or positive; the third, in the diminished. <margin>10</margin>

VIII. It exists **superfluously**, **justly**, and **wantingly**; this distinction differs from the previous one because "superfluously" is not the same as "most eminently" or "eminently." Eminence signifies excellence and dignity perpetually, whereas the superfluous signifies unworthiness, monstrosity, and injury. <margin>15</margin> Similarly, the opposites of these will differ by opposite reasons—those which are at the other extremes, such as "deficiently" and "diminutively." Furthermore, "equally" or "evenly" differs from "justly," because two superfluous or wanting things can be **equally** so, yet they are not **justly** so. <margin>20</margin> <note>Bruno is making a moral and ontological point: being "superior" (eminent) is a virtue, but having "too much" (superfluous) is a vice or a deformity.</note>

IX. It exists **well**, **better**, and **less well**; these parts are the form of all predicates, just as "the good" is said of every being according to certain degrees.

X. It exists according to **being**, according to **power**, and according to **operation**; because in all things, the first is by reason... <margin>24</margin> <note>original: *secundum esse, secundum posse et secundum operari*. This triad represents the core of Bruno's philosophy: a thing's essence (to be), its capacity (to be able), and its actual activity (to act).</note>

XI. **Fully**, **emptily**, and **half-fully**; because some things <margin>5</margin> receive a certain predication <term>predication: the logical act of attributing a property or quality to a subject</term> entirely, some not at all, and some in a certain manner.

XII. **Before** (antecedently), **with** (concomitantly), and **after** (consequently): in the first class are all things that are causes, principles, and elements, and <column-break/> which take precedence; in the second are those which consist <margin>185r</margin> [together]; <margin>10</margin> in the third are those which follow.

XIV. **Principally**, **reductively**, and **accessorily**: <margin>15</margin> of the first class are those which properly exist, act, have power, and are spoken of, such as **substance** and **quantity**. Of the third class are things like **accidents** <term>accidents: properties that are not essential to a thing's nature, such as a person's hair color</term> in relation to substance, and **universals** <term>universals: general concepts or qualities shared by many individuals</term> in relation to the primary substance. <margin>25</margin> For all things are reductively present in these, as was shown in the **second tree** <note>original: *secunda arbore*. <margin>5</margin>XV. **Most** (or Greatest), **Especially** (or Chiefly), and **Scarcely**: The first, **Most**, is beyond all limits and is more general and common than that which is "most eminent" or "superfluous," appearing on the right side of the seventh and eighth distinctions <note>Bruno is referring to his earlier lists of categorization in this same work</note>. The second, **Especially**, refers to that which is exactly as much as it ought to be or can be. The third, **Scarcely**, is counted even among non-beings; for example, **matter** is said to be "scarcely non-being" or "scarcely being" <note>Bruno follows the Aristotelian idea that raw matter, without form, barely exists because it is only the "potential" for a thing, not the thing itself</note>. <margin>10</margin>here by "Scarcely"; however, as a particle of negation not depending on a noun, it has another meaning which cannot be applied to or understood within the limbs of this Giant <note>The "Giant" refers to Alcyoneus, one of the thirty mnemonic statues Bruno uses to organize human knowledge</note>.

XIII. According to the first two ways, there is regular predication <margin>20</margin> or speech.

# THE LAMP OF THIRTY STATUES

...because it occurs through the fixed determination of authors. For example, the word "to create" <note>original: "creare"</note> has been applied and adopted to mean "making simply out of nothing," even though from the beginning it was not understood in that way. Similarly, "predestined" <note>original: "praedestinatus"</note> is applied to one destined for glory, while "foreknown" <note>original: "praescitus"</note> is applied to one destined for destruction. Therefore, among 
<margin>5</margin> philosophers and contemplative theologians, one must be careful not to think that they can reach a demonstrative conclusion based solely on the force of a word or its etymology. This is because, for the most part, names do not signify based on their first imposition <note>The original, literal act of naming a thing</note>, but are destined to signify in another way according to the necessity of the subject matter. 

We see this also among 
<margin>10</margin> philosophers: the word "rational" signifies the essential difference of a human being <note>In Aristotelian logic, the "essential difference" is the specific quality that distinguishes one species from others in the same genus; for humans, that difference is reason</note>. Yet, by the literal force of the word itself, nothing is signified except a certain accident <note>An "accident" is a property that is not part of the core essence of a thing. Here, Bruno argues that "having the ability to reason" is technically a property or an act, not the essence itself</note>. For being able to reason, possessing reason, or being capable of reasoning—and everything else that can be said in this vein—is an accident. 

Aristotle says, therefore, that the substantial and essential differences of a 
<margin>15</margin> thing are unnamable. However, he does not contradict himself when he offers certain terms to stand for these essential differences. For names are not used strictly for what they signify [their literal definition], but as they are used to point toward or "con-signify" <note>original: "adsignificant," a logical term for words that carry additional meaning alongside their primary reference</note> the truth. For "rational," as rational, con-signifies the subject of 
<margin>20</margin> reason; this subject could be signified no less effectively by the term "risible" <note>original: "risibile," meaning "capable of laughter." Medieval logicians often used "the ability to laugh" as a property unique to humans, though it is not our "essence"</note>. Nevertheless, the former name [rational] is judged more prudent and is the one commonly adopted.

<summary>Bruno argues that the names we give to things (like "rational" for humans) are often linguistic conventions or "accidents" rather than the true, unnamable essence of the thing itself. He warns scholars not to rely too heavily on the literal etymology of words when trying to understand the fundamental nature of reality.</summary>

<keywords>Aristotle, essence, accident, rationality, semantics, creation, predestination, naming, logical difference</keywords>

# ON THE APPLICATION
# OF THE INVENTIVE AND JUDICATIVE ART

## EXPLAINED IN THE VOLUME OF THE THIRTY STATUES
## FOR THE APPLICATION OF THE PRESENT METHOD.

5 I. The reason for the title must be considered; for it is called a Lamp <note>original: "Lampas"</note>, because it is a light by which we acquire and perfect the clarity and judgment of all subjects, just as one does for all colors.

It is then called [the lamp] of thirty statues, not because <margin>18r</margin>
10 we have brought or ought to bring statues for everything, but because all things can be conveniently fashioned into statues <note>The original Latin "statuificabilia" is a Bruno neologism, suggesting that any concept can be given a mental "form" or "image" to aid memory</note>, since the principles of all of them can be explained in an orderly way within certain hypostases <term>hypostases: the underlying substances, foundations, or fundamental realities of a thing</term>, members, and surrounding pictures. Therefore, just as it is done in the statues of Night, Saturn, Prometheus, Thetis, and
15 Juno, so it can be done in its own way for other things. Among these, there are some that do not require a statue or any other method of portrayal <gloss>or "shaping"</gloss>, but by the very order of the thing which they present, they are very easy to remember and provide a path for the most extensive mental discourse. These are what you might conveniently label under the title of "Atria" <note>Halls or courtyards; Bruno uses these as mnemonic "rooms" to organize categories of knowledge</note>, 
20 such as those of Ocean, Mars, Tellus <note>The Roman goddess of the Earth</note>, Minerva, Venus, Cupid, the Ladder of Minerva, and the Arrows of Cupid; others, however, for which the name "Campi" <note>Fields or open plains; these represent less structured areas of knowledge</note> is more suitable—which represent (and can represent) the reasons and causes of things in no particular order—will be handled correctly if one wishes to fashion them into statues.

<summary>Bruno introduces his mnemonic system, explaining the metaphorical titles of his work: the "Lamp" provides intellectual light, while "Statues," "Atria" (Halls), and "Campi" (Fields) serve as visual tools for organizing and recalling complex ideas.</summary>

# LAMP OF THE THIRTY STATUES.
<sig>28</sig>

## THE UTILITY OF THIS LAMP COMPARED TO OTHERS.

This Lamp perfects the Lamp of the Logicians <note>original: "Lampadem logicorum"; Bruno refers here to formal Aristotelian logic</note>: I. because it supplies the matter for the forms of that logic, and it serves the intentions <margin>5</margin> of genus, property, definition, and accident by showing the subjects in their proper order. It does this by revealing the series of nature in a scale of subjects, and consequently the series of genera, differences, and formable definitions. It proceeds from the root to the trunks, from the trunks to the branches, all the way to the final terms—the fruits, so to speak. Furthermore, the properties and other circumstances, both of real things and of every kind of being, are most easily defined from this source. This occurs whenever it happens that subjects are examined <note>The translator follows the suggested reading "discurrere" (to run through/examine) rather than the OCR's "peregrinari" (to wander)</note> through the members <margin>188v</margin> of those hypostases <term>hypostases: the fundamental underlying substances or foundations of a thing</term>, that is, the personages of the Giants <note>Bruno uses "Giants" as a metaphor for his primary mnemonic categories or "statues" that hold vast amounts of information</note>, according to each of the thirty statues. From here, one may also take the demonstrative means <margin>15</margin> to prove anything about individual subjects and their parts, whether negatively or affirmatively, universally or particularly.

II. It perfects the Lamp of Lull <note>original: "Lampadem Lullii"; referring to the "Great Art" of the 13th-century philosopher Ramon Llull</note> for the same reason: because it provides subjects and predicates that are defined, formed, and distinct, whereas Lull’s system provided them as undefined. And therefore, for all parts of that invention—which we highly recommend—there is a method of combination <term>artificium combinandi: the Lullian technique of rotating concentric circles to generate all possible logical propositions</term>. Not only is a series of absolute and relative <margin>20</margin> predicates contained here, but also the same...

# ON THE DISTINCTION
# OF THE FUNCTIONS PERTAINING
## TO THE VARIOUS MEMBERS OF THE THIRTY STATUES.

Of the thirty statues we have explained, the first three are statues of Fullness <note>original: "plenitudinis"; representing the divine source or the totality of being</note>, <margin>10</margin> which are opposed by an equal number of statues of Emptiness <note>original: "inanitatis"; representing the void or the lowest potential of matter</note>. These represent the highest and lowest steps of the Ladder of Nature <term>Ladder of Nature: the "Scala Naturae," a traditional philosophical hierarchy stretching from God down to inanimate matter</term>. They are suited for introducing the principles of predicates <note>attributes or qualities asserted about a subject</note> which apply, or can apply, to any subjects whatsoever, according to their arranged orders, such as their distance from the highest and <margin>15</margin> lowest points, and the analogy they hold to the middle.

<margin>18</margin>
# ON THE APPLICATION
# OF THE REMAINING STATUES.

Of the statues previously enumerated, fourteen remain. By running through their members <note>the specific parts or attributes of each mnemonic figure</note>, the path to general discovery <note>original: "inventionis"; the rhetorical "ars inveniendi" or the method of finding arguments</note> <margin>20</margin> is opened, since their various modes are brought forward. Consequently, there are those first six and four others: namely, the statue of Thetis, representing the Subject; the Field of Cupid, representing Will; the statue of Vulcan, representing Form; and Mount Olympus, representing the End <note>original: "finis"; in Aristotelian terms, the final cause or purpose of a thing</note>...

# ON THE LOGIC
## OF THE ORDER OF THE MODAL STATUES.

The present order of discourse proceeds conveniently from the logic of the One to the logic of the Principle; for first is the One,
<margin>5</margin> as it is the absolute logic of a thing, which is followed by the logic of beginning <note>original: "principiandi"; the act of functioning as a starting point or source</note>, which is relative. This is followed by the relation <note>original: "habitudo"; the way one thing is positioned or related to another</note> of the principle to that which is originated. This is followed by the disposition <note>original: "habitus"; a stable state, quality, or "clothing" of a thing</note> or something similar to a disposition, which exists according to that relation. This is followed by knowledge, generally so-called. Knowledge is followed by being an agent; for
<margin>10</margin> everything acts as it knows, namely from the logic of the agent or from an ideal conception. Form follows the agent, because the goal of an action is the introduction of that form. The magnitude and momentum <note>original: "momentum"; here implying the weight, importance, or active force of a thing</note> of a thing are derived from the logic of its form. To have or to possess follows the
<margin>15</margin> magnitude of the form and the action. Will follows the logic of having or lacking. The medium <note>original: "medium"; the middle ground or instrument</note>, through which the will is carried toward its object, follows the act of that will. Concord is the contact of the will of those things in agreement through the medium. The differences between things arise from a manifold logic of concord or concurrence;
<margin>20</margin> for the manifold union <note>original: "coitus"; literally a coming together or joining</note> of matter with form introduces number and the variety of things. Finally, it is fitting for the end—whether of consumption <note>The Latin text here is debated; it may mean "completion" (consummatio) or "conception," referring to the final realization of an idea</note> or of perfection and intention—to conclude the discourse.

<margin>190r</margin>
When proceeding to <term>practice</term> <note>original: "praxis"; the application of theoretical knowledge</note>, we must first examine what the proposed subject is, that it is, and of what quality it is: namely, whether it is a
<margin>5</margin>
substance, or rather belongs to a substance; whether it is a <term>being</term> <note>original: "ens"; a thing that exists</note>, or something belonging to a being. If it is a substance, we must ask if it is so truly and properly, or only by way of resemblance. For there are certain things, such as those at the lowest level of the **ladder of nature**, which are certainly not <term>accidents</term> <note>original: "accidentia"; in traditional logic, an accident is a quality (like color or size) that can change without the object itself disappearing</note>, because they do not come upon a thing that already exists in actuality, which is the primary definition
<margin>10</margin>
of an accident; indeed, it is called an "accident" as if it were "approaching" <note>original: "accedens"</note> and "supervening." **Chaos**, therefore, the **void** <note>original: "vacuum"</note>, and **privation** <note>original: "privatio"; the absence of a form or quality that should be present</note>—which in nature even precedes the logic of **matter**—are so far from being accidents of things that they are the very foundations to which substances are added, joined, or arrive. And although these may be nothing, yet since
<margin>15</margin>
all things are able to exist within them, the **intellect** seems entirely unable to escape the conception of the empty, the vacuum, or space. This is evident from arguments against those who posit that the physical world is merely corporeal, dimensioned, and finite. Therefore, although they do not
<margin>20</margin>
strictly take on the definition of accidents or substances, if we wish to distinguish everything that is and truly is into only two categories, we must certainly refer these to the order of substances; and so we have done.

Secondly, we must see, if they are substances, in what order they are understood—for instance, which step of the ladder they occupy: whether
<margin>25</margin>
**light** or **darkness**, the luminous or the dark, and at what distance. For in this way we will first consider the disposition...

...and drawn out from principles; and then the **tree of substance** <note>The "Tree of Porphyry" or "Tree of Substance" was a traditional logical diagram used to classify beings from the most general category (Substance) down to the specific individual</note> or of subjects must be approached, and it must be seen how it flows forth from the root, through which trunk, through which branch, all the way to the final <term>difference</term> <note>original: "differentiam"; the specific quality that distinguishes one species from another within the same genus</note>. <margin>5</margin>according to its constitutive principles and according to the constituted being itself, which is signified by its complete definition.
Then, once it has been so defined, it must be led through the **thirty forms**, which are explained in the <term>predicamental catalog</term> <note>original: "catalogo praedicamentali"; Bruno's specific list of thirty categories or "statues" used to organize all knowledge</note>, namely those things that belong to substance and essence—such as being itself, existence, etc.—
<margin>10</margin>all the way to the last, which is **life**. Moreover, it must be seen according to which modes and which reasons these predicates apply to those subjects:
First, indeed, by taking two-part distinctions for which there is no middle ground.
II. Those for which the middle ground is unnamed, being a <margin>15</margin>combination of the extremes.
III. Those which concern the being of the thing, having a named and determined middle ground.
IV. Those concerning the knowledge of the thing. <margin>20</margin>
V. If the matter so requires, concerning the signification of the thing.
Then, when the thing itself has been thus sorted out—namely, having seen the preparation of the subject according to the contemplation of the extremity of the steps—
II. From the existence of the subject and its "birth," so to speak, <margin>25</margin>through its derivation from the root of the tree.
III. The perfection and expansion of the subject through universal predicates.

# THE PRACTICE EXPLAINED
# FOR DEFINING ANYTHING
### WHATEVER MAY BE THE NATURE OF THE DEFINABLE THING.

With these preliminaries thus arranged, we must now arrive <margin>15</margin> at the final goal of the entire apparatus, which is threefold: defining all things under general yet <term>proximate reasons</term> <note>original: "proximis rationibus"; the most immediate logical categories that explain what a thing is</note>, verifying all things, and demonstrating all things by those same reasons.

## ON THE METHOD OF DEFINING UNIVERSALS.

<margin>20</margin> It is well-known enough that every definition consists of a <term>genus</term> <note>A broad category, like "animal"</note> and a <term>difference</term> <note>The specific quality that distinguishes a species, like "rational" for humans</note>. Moreover, the genus is threefold: supreme, intermediate, and proximate. The first is the root of the tree; the second is the trunk of the tree or around the trunk; the third is that which is proximate to the <term>most specific species</term> <note>original: "speciei specialissimae"; the final, most individual category that cannot be divided into further sub-types</note> or the final species.
<margin>25</margin> Therefore, just as the genus of the tree is manifold, so also must the genus of the trunk be manifold. Thus, the first tree is

<meta>This page continues the logical classifications begun on the previous page, moving from the definition of signs and intentions to the specific categorization of powers, habits, acts, and objects within Giordano Bruno's philosophical system. # THE LAMP OF THE THIRTY STATUES

Concerning the third part, there are various types of <term>powers</term> <note>original: "potentiarum"; the capacities or abilities of a thing to do or receive something</note>: some are active (and of these, some are divine, some natural, and others added or acquired), while others are passive. The first kind are those by which a thing is able to make, act, form, or complete; the second kind are those by which a thing is able to be made, received, formed, or completed.

Concerning the fifth part, some <term>habits</term> <note>original: "habitus"; here meaning settled dispositions or states of being, rather than repetitive actions</note> are physical, and others are spiritual—that is, some pertain to matter and the body, while others pertain to the spirit or the soul; | <margin>193r</margin> some are internal, and others are external.

Concerning the sixth part, acts are distinguished in the same way as habits.

Concerning the seventh part, some objects are perceived according to the senses (and this is twofold: external, such as colors, tastes, visible things, and all other things <note>The original Latin "universalia" here is likely a transcription error for "universa alia" (all other things), as universals are typically objects of the mind, not the physical senses</note>; and internal, such as mental images and things that can be imagined), while others are perceived according to the intellect, which are generally called <term>intelligibles</term> <note>original: "intelligibilia"; concepts that can only be understood by the mind, like "justice" or "mathematics"</note>.

Concerning the eighth part, some art and operation belongs to the body, such as walking; another concerns the body, such as clothing or dressing it; another looks to the cultivation of the mind, which we generally call the * * * liberal [arts] <note>The manuscript has a gap here, likely intended to read "the arts which we are accustomed to call liberal," referring to the traditional academic subjects like grammar and logic</note>; another relates to the necessities of life and the composite of both body and soul, such as agriculture in general and the medicine of perfection.

Likewise, some operations are immanent <note>original: "immanentes"; actions that remain within the person, like thinking or feeling</note>, while others are transient <note>original: "transeuntes"; actions that produce an effect on something else, like building a house</note>; and of these, some concern higher things, like the contemplation of God; others concern equals, such as justice and distribution; others concern lower things, like favor, help, and governance.

Concerning the tenth part, some terms <note>original: "terminorum"; refers to limits, boundaries, or the basic components of a logical proposition</note> are physical, others concern bodies (such as a geometric point), and others concern incorporeal things, such as numbers.

It reflects Bruno's effort to create a systematic "map" of all possible human knowledge and experience.</summary>

# GIORDANO BRUNO

Concerning the eleventh [part], some <term>second intentions</term> <note>original: "intentionum secundarum"; in logic, these are concepts that refer to other concepts, such as "species" or "genus," rather than to physical objects</note> are moral, others are rational, and others are mathematical; from these, practical applications follow.

Concerning the twelfth [part], effects are distinguished in the same way as <margin>5</margin> operations: some are divine, some are natural, and others are artificial; and of these, some are conceptual, while others are practical.

Concerning the thirteenth [part], some attributes are relative, and others are absolute.

Concerning the fourteenth [part], some parts are primary, others <margin>10</margin> are proximate, and others are ultimate; some are large, others are small, mediated, and so on.

Concerning the fifteenth [part], some signs are divine, others are natural, others are technical <note>original: "technica"; referring here to signs created through human skill or artifice</note>, and so on. These are further divided in the same way as effects. <meta>13</meta>

### Definitions:

<margin>15</margin> 1. Entities or substances are defined by the terms explained in the <unclear>***</unclear> <note>The original manuscript has a gap here; scholars suggest the word "arboris" (of the tree) was intended</note> root, the trunk, and so on.

2. Categories, which signify substance, are defined by the terms of the first active trunk; the remaining <term>accidents</term> <note>original: "accidentia"; non-essential qualities of a thing, like its color or size, which can change without the thing itself ceasing to exist</note> are defined by the remaining trunks.

<margin>20</margin> 3. <term>Powers</term> <note>original: "potentiae"; the capacities or abilities of a thing</note> are defined by their operations, such as "the sensory is that which is able to sense."

4. <term>Habits</term> <note>original: "habitus"; here meaning a stable disposition or state of being</note> are defined by acts, such as "the art of building is that by which the builder builds."

5. Acts are defined by their objects, such as "to see is to <margin>25</margin> perceive colors," or by their subjects, such as "to sculpt is to form an image out of stone."

# THE LAMP OF THE THIRTY STATUES

-> **[Definitions Continued]** <-

6. **Objects** [are defined] by the powers [that perceive them], such as: "color is a quality apprehensible through sight or the visual faculty."

7. **Art, action, and operation** [are defined] by their limits: the agent, the <margin>5</margin> subject, and the end <note>original: "finem"; here meaning the purpose or goal</note>, or by two of these, provided the agent is not omitted.

8. **An instrument** [is defined] by the agent and the end, such as: "a hammer is a tool <term>organon</term> <note>original: "organon"; the Greek word for tool or instrument, often used in logic to refer to the "tools" of reasoning</note> which a smith uses for expanding, crushing, etc.; a pen is an instrument used by a writer for writing."

9. **Terms** <note>original: "termini"; in this context, it refers to the boundaries or limits of a thing</note> [are defined] by those things to which they belong, such as a point by the line of which it is the end, matter by the substance, and numbers by <margin>10</margin> number.

10. **First intentions** [are defined] by the real beings they represent; **second intentions** <note>In Scholastic logic, a "first intention" is a concept of a real thing (like "a horse"), while a "second intention" is a concept of a concept (like "species" or "genus")</note> are defined by their proper genera and differences, which are: I. moral, II. rational, III. mathematical, IV. grammatical.

<margin>15</margin> 11. **Effects** [are defined] in two ways: I. as the ends and limits of actions, such <margin>194^r</margin> as "a garment is the final work of a tailor"; II. as directed toward a purpose, "as a garment is the work of a cobbler <note>The manuscript shows the author may have initially started writing "weaver" before settling on "cobbler"</note> or an instrument for covering the body."

12. **Attributes, forms, or predicates** [are defined] through the "according to which" and "by which," such as "goodness is that **by which** a good person does good deeds, and virtue is that **according to which** <margin>20</margin> we are called virtuous."

13. **Parts** [are defined] by taking them in relation to their whole <note>The Latin "suas" (its) is used here, though editors suggest the original meaning was "defined by their wholes"</note>, such as "a stalk is a particle of straw, a finger is a part of the hand."

14. **Signs and indications** [are defined] by those things of which they are signs, such as "nouns and verbs are signs of simple intentions <note>original: "intentionum"; mental concepts</note>, while <margin>25</margin> sentences are signs of complex intentions."

15. The terms of **distinctions** are not defined except by numbers, such as "first, secondarily, simply," and the like.

# THE LAMP OF THE THIRTY STATUES.

[The case] should match. I say that a case [matches] a case either formally—that is, under the same figure of speech—or equivalently—that is, only under the same mode of signifying. For example, to one asking “what is a sensitive [being]?” the response should be “the apprehension of sensible species” <note>In Renaissance psychology, "species" are not biological categories, but the mental images or "likenesses" of objects perceived by the senses.</note> <margin>5</margin> (this is to respond through the same case); or “what is an intelligent [being]?” ℞ <note>original: "℞"; a common abbreviation for "Response"</note> “that which apprehends immaterial species”; for then the response is given through the same case equivalently. Formally, however, you will respond through the same case and termination by saying, “it is an apprehending [entity] of immaterial species.” <margin>10</margin> But if you were to say “apprehensive,” you would not define it properly, because the one asking for a definition accepts the term in act <term>in actu</term> <note>Referring to something currently performing its function</note>, whereas the one providing the definition accepts the term in potentiality <term>in potentia</term> <note>Referring to the underlying capacity to perform a function</note>.

# ON THE METHOD
# OF VERIFYING OR ENUNCIATING.

As for what concerns the second work of reason, which <margin>10</margin> is composition or verification, it will be necessary to see how predicates are joined to subjects and how true enunciations <note>An "enunciation" is a statement that affirms or denies something, which can be judged as true or false.</note> are made, in order to recognize by what logic and in what manner anything is said of another thing.

After we have distinctly perceived and held the <margin>15</margin> definition of the subject or the thing under consideration, it will be easy to judge how all predicates are said of them. Furthermore, he who knows the logic and conditions of the proposed and enumerated predicates will be able to easily infer the logic of all others that can be imagined, because <margin>20</margin> all predicates are either these, or parts and species of these, or modes of these, or their contraries, or similar to them, or proportional. Since, therefore, we have exemplified and introduced these matters, we shall judge that we have exemplified and introduced all things in their own way. The logic for completing <margin>25</margin> this teaching requires that we see how the predicates—namely, the terms of the thirty statues <note>These "statues" are the foundational mnemonic and logical concepts in Bruno's system, acting as universal categories.</note>—are said of the enumerated subjects...

This process will be carried out in such a way that the subject under consideration passes toward the predicate through the limbs of Atlas and Typhon—that is, the first two Giants; for it is within the limbs of the Giant that the subject is formed, modified, interpreted, <margin>5</margin> and distinguished. Therefore, some subjects are themselves light and fullness, others are emptiness and darkness; others are participants in both. Among these, some are closer to the light, some closer to the darkness, and some are indeed equidistant: some are simple, while others are composite.

Thus, bright things, <margin>10</margin> insofar as they are bright, are generally formed through the right side of each Giant; opaque things are formed through the left; and mixed things are led out through one side by one reasoning, and through the other side by a different distinction.

<margin>19v</margin> | Regarding subjects, those which are light itself—such as fullness, intellect, and love—run through the thirty statues <margin>15</margin> in a formed state. # THE TORCH OF THE THIRTY STATUES

...in no way materially and, as it were, subjectively, because it is <term>pure act <note>original: "actus purus"; in Scholastic philosophy, this refers to a being with no unfulfilled potential—entirely realized and complete, often identifying the divine principle.</note></term>, most clearly evident in its existence, yet hidden in its essence <note>original: "quoad quid esse," literally "according to what it is."</note>, as the end of all things and that which is never directed toward an end. Therefore, from the limbs and parts of the second <term>Giant <note>Bruno uses the figures of Giants as mnemonic and philosophical frameworks to map out the structure of reality and logic.</note></term>, it sometimes receives <margin>5</margin> both [sets of predicates], insofar as both distinctions signify perfection. Having seen, then, how all predicates are modified in the light, it is clear enough how they are verified according to the opposite reasoning regarding the darkness—that is, concerning the void, matter, <term>passive potential <note>The capacity to be acted upon or changed, as opposed to the power to act.</note></term>, and similar things. Therefore, all these are spoken of <margin>10</margin> negatively regarding those things at the lowest level of nature; some are spoken of <term>privatively <note>A "privative" description notes the absence of a quality that ought to be present (like "blindness" is a privation of sight), whereas a "negative" description is a simple denial.</note></term>, but all things will be spoken of simply negatively regarding non-being. Regarding those things in the middle, through a greater or lesser participation in one or the other extreme—that is, light or darkness—these predicates <margin>15</margin> are attributed according to a greater or lesser degree.

<margin>197<sup>r</sup></margin> As for what pertains to operations and instruments, acts and powers, signs, and the rest enumerated, it is clear enough that these follow the condition of the subjects in which they exist, to whom they belong, from whom they come, and the end for which <margin>20</margin> they exist. If these subjects are indeed infinite, simple, eternal, and universally participate in the "right side" <note>In Bruno’s system, the "right side" represents the positive, light-filled, and active principles of the universe.</note> in whole or in part, then the things following them will be the same. For the condition of the subject is followed by the condition of power, virtue, and wisdom; the condition of the end is followed by the condition of matter and <margin>25</margin> instrument. Thus, when the subjects, principles, means, and ends are most perfectly placed, all things are at their best.

<summary>Bruno explains how philosophical predicates are applied to beings based on their proximity to 'light' (pure act) or 'darkness' (non-being), establishing that the quality of an action or instrument depends entirely on the nature of the subject it belongs to.</summary>

# ON THE MODES OF DISTINCTION
## AND OF DERIVING DIFFERENCES
### FROM THE ARTICLES OF THE THREE FINAL GIANTS.

Although all the modes by which <term>predicates <note>In logic, a predicate is a property or characteristic attributed to a subject (for example, in the phrase "the soul is immortal," "immortal" is the predicate).</note></term> are present in subjects—
<margin>5</margin> whether they be metaphysical, physical, or artificial—have been explained in the first two <term>Giants <note>Bruno uses the metaphorical figures of "Giants" as mnemonic and philosophical frameworks to organize the entire structure of reality and logic.</note></term>, there is still a further consideration. This is because all things are considered in a twofold way: in one way according to their **mode of being**, and in another way according to their **mode of conceiving** (which is followed by a third, the **mode of signifying**). Therefore, the third Giant 
<margin>10</margin> indicates all predicates according to the first mode <note>The mode of being (how things exist).</note>, the fourth according to the second <note>The mode of conceiving (how we think about things).</note>, and the last according to the third <note>The mode of signifying (how we name or speak about things).</note>. Through the third Giant, therefore, all beings are conceived either as **before the thing** <note>original: "ante rem"; referring to the cause or the idea of a thing before it physically exists.</note> or as in the **effective principle**; or as **in the thing** <note>original: "in re"; the thing as it exists in reality.</note> or as in the **effect and act**; or **after the thing** <note>original: "post rem"; the existence of a thing in our minds or language after the physical object is gone.</note>, and this in a twofold way: in the **concept** (<term>intention <note>original: "intentione"; in Renaissance philosophy, an "intention" is the mental image or representation of an object.</note></term>) 
<margin>15</margin> and in the **sign** (the spoken word).

This distinction is followed in the disposition—or according to the disposition—of the **process of becoming**, and the **finished state**; this distinction is then followed by the others noted and declared in order in the members of the aforementioned third Giant.

<margin>20</margin> Furthermore, as things themselves come into consideration, their distinctions must be investigated from the members of the fourth Giant. For where <margin>117</margin> we have explained the conditions of a thing insofar as it **is** and insofar as it **is conceived to be**, we must likewise look to the members of the fourth Giant, from which we must first distinguish whether...

<summary>Bruno explains how his system of "Giants" categorizes reality into three modes: how things exist (being), how we understand them (conception), and how we describe them (signification). He further breaks down existence into states before, during, and after a thing's physical presence.</summary>

## ON THE FINAL AND THIRD PRACTICE.

Once the definition of the <term>essence <note>original: "essentiae." The fundamental nature or "what-ness" of a thing.</note></term> of a thing is known, along with the essence itself and the reason by which all predicates are spoken of them, it will be easy thereafter to prove anything about anything. This is done by applying all principles, or certain ones, according to those conditions which preserve and 
<margin>15</margin> respect the integral logic of the thing; if this logic is destroyed, one will necessarily fall into error everywhere. If, therefore, we wish to prove anything about anything, we can take <term>middle terms <note>original: "media." In a syllogism, the middle term is the link that connects the subject and the predicate in the conclusion.</note></term> from anywhere, provided they are suited to the logic or definition and the property of the subject. This will be easy for one who knows the 
<margin>20</margin> definition and the mode or form and the specific difference of distinction by which such a predicate is said (or can be said) of such a subject. For example: **Man** is a substance composed of the intellectual and the material, a middle point between the higher and lower nature, and a bond between both; therefore, **unity** 
<margin>25</margin> does not belong to him according to the logic of something **absolutely simple**, but rather as something **contracted** and **composite**, coordinated, of parts breathing together, and...

**V.** Everything to which the definition and essence of <term>substance <note>In philosophy, a "substance" is something that exists in itself, while an "accident" is a quality that can only exist within something else (like the color of a leaf).</note></term> belongs is truly a substance; but it belongs to the soul to be a being existing through itself and to be the subject of powers; therefore it is not an accident.

...for its own existence; but the soul exists <unclear>exi[st]et</unclear> and subsists through itself; it is also the subject of accidents and operations; therefore <note>Therefore, the soul is a substance, not a quality of something else.</note>.

**X.** Every <term>accident <note>In traditional philosophy, an "accident" is a property that can change without changing the essence of a thing, such as the color of a shirt.</note></term> names its subject accidentally, just as from "whiteness" a thing is called "white," or from "knowledge" a person is called "knowing"; but the soul names its subject substantially, in that the subject is called "animated" <note>original: *animatum*, meaning "endowed with a soul."</note>; therefore —. **XI.** The soul exists within the order and coordination of the <term>ladder of substances <note>The "Great Chain of Being," a hierarchy ranking all existences from base matter to the Divine.</note></term>, because it is said to be at the boundary between intellectual substance and physical or material substance; therefore, it is not an accident. This <term>analogy <note>Bruno refers to "analogy" here as a structural relationship where things occupy similar relative positions on different levels of reality.</note></term> is not merely a matter of words, but relates to the degrees and positioning on said ladder; it has an aptitude for both higher and lower substances, but it is never placed in the order of accidents. For a thing is "analogous" when it is described according to "prior" and "posterior" <note>This refers to the logical or ontological order—which comes first and which follows.</note> among things spoken of, and holds the logic of prior and posterior among things that exist.

->From the Workshop of Vulcan.<-
<note>Vulcan represents the internal fire or the craftsman of nature who works within matter to give it form.</note>

First, from the reason of the <term>idea <note>In the Platonic sense, an "idea" is the perfect, eternal archetype or blueprint of a thing.</note></term>. Because there is no "idea" of an accident; but of the soul, there is said to be a primary idea, and then the ideas of all other things.

2. From the perspective of the instrument. Because every accident, in respect <margin>20</margin> to its subject, is like its instrument; but the soul is not an instrument of the body (as if it were something through which the body acts), but rather it is the soul that performs all these works by means of the body.

3. From the perspective of arrival or approach. Every accident comes to a composition or a subject that is already essentially established; <margin>25</margin> the soul, however, receives a subject that is yet to be essentially established. <note>Meaning the soul is what makes the body a "human body" or "living thing" in the first place, rather than just being a passenger in a pre-existing machine.</note>

->From the Statue of Vulcan<-
<note>In Bruno’s mnemonic system, Vulcan represents the "internal craftsman" or the formative fire that shapes matter from within.</note>

1. **From the reason that he is the son of Juno.** <note>Juno often represents the air or the vital spirit in this context.</note> No <term>accidental form <note>A quality that exists only because it is attached to something else, like the "redness" of an apple.</note></term> is elevated above the <term>subject <note>The underlying material or thing that possesses qualities; here, the body.</note></term> of which it is an accident; but the soul, according to its nobility, dignity, and being, excels the <margin>200^r</margin> matter which it rules and from which it can be <term>released <note>original: "absolvi"; meaning the soul can exist independently of the physical body.</note></term>; therefore, it is not an accident.

10 2. **From the aspect of instantaneous production.** Every accident is said to come to a subject through <term>alteration <note>A gradual change in quality, like water slowly heating up.</note></term> and preparation over time and through motion, but the soul arrives in an instant; therefore, it has the nature of a <term>substantial form <note>The essential nature that makes a thing what it is; for Bruno, the soul is what makes a human "human."</note></term>, through which <term>generation <note>The sudden emergence of a new being.</note></term> occurs, rather than mere alteration.

15 3. **From the aspect of a single parent.** The soul comes from the father without a mother, because if it has a cause, that cause is <term>efficient <note>The agent that brings something about (like a builder).</note></term>, not <term>material <note>The "stuff" something is made of.</note></term>; for there is no matter for the soul, since it is an individual substance; however, every accident arises from the "womb" of matter or the subject.

20 ->From the Field of Thetis<-
<note>Thetis, a sea goddess, here represents the vast, "moist" expanse of matter or the physical world which requires the light of the soul to be visible or organized.</note>

1. Every accident relates to its subject as color does, and all matter is like darkness; but the soul belongs to the sphere of light; therefore, it is neither accident nor matter, but an immaterial substance. The <term>major premise <note>The first statement in a logical argument.</note></term> is clear from what was said before, because the soul presides over, rules, governs, and gives life to matter.

<summary>Giordano Bruno uses the mythological figures of Vulcan and Thetis to argue that the soul is an independent, immaterial substance. Therefore, if it possesses such an object, it has such a power and such | a nature; it is necessarily a substance.

### From the Field of Coelius.
<note>original: "Ex campo Coelii." In Bruno's memory system, Coelius (the Heavens) represents a higher, more abstract level of contemplation.</note>

1. **From nakedness.** Every <term>accidental form <note>A property that is not essential to a thing’s nature, such as its color, weight, or temperature.</note></term> is like a garment for matter, and the corporeal <term>substantial form <note>The essential "blueprint" or nature that makes a physical object what it is.</note></term> is necessarily clothed in these accidents. But the soul is neither a 
<margin>5</margin> garment for the body's substance, nor is it, by its own nature, clothed in the body's accidents; rather, it is a kind of "naked" substance and nature.

2. **From the perspective of solitude.** Every accident exists within the composition or mixture of the body, as it arises from the 
<margin>10</margin> union of matter and substantial form; the soul, however, is said to be a form that exists without matter, and it must necessarily be so, because it rules over matter.

3. **From the reasoning of the fifth essence.** Every material form is bound to matter; but the soul relates to mate-
<margin>15</margin> rial things as a builder relates to a house, or a sailor to a ship. <note>original: "nauta ad navem"; a traditional Aristotelian analogy Bruno uses to illustrate that the soul is the pilot of the body, not a part of its physical structure.</note>

### From the Field of Vesta.
<note>original: "Ex campo Vestae." Vesta, the goddess of the hearth, represents the inner core or the essential fire of being.</note>

1. **From character.** The soul is said to be "in the image and likeness of God" by theologians, and by philosophers, a "simulacrum of divinity" or the "daughter of the Mind"; as such, it should not be an accident 
<margin>20</margin> nor a material form.

2. Material form itself is light bound to darkness; a material accident is like a blackness or a color resulting from darkness; the substance of the soul, however, neither results from matter, nor is it bound to matter.

<summary>Bruno uses the symbolic "Fields" of Coelius and Vesta to argue that the soul is a "naked" and independent substance, distinct from the material "garments" of the body. He emphasizes that the soul acts as the pilot of the body and reflects a divine origin, existing beyond the reach of material composition.</summary>

3. **From will.** The soul breathes toward its own region and the first light, because it loves truth and is nourished by truth and strives toward divine things; therefore it is not an <term>accidental property <note>In Aristotelian logic, an "accident" is a quality that can change without the thing itself ceasing to exist, like the color of a shirt.</note></term>, nor is it the "form" of the body in a way that would reflect the body's own limited nature.

<margin>5</margin> ### From the Field of Oceanus.
<note>original: "Ex campo Oceani." In Bruno's system, Oceanus symbolizes the vastness of the soul's reach compared to the physical limits of matter.</note>

<margin>201^v</margin> 1. **From breadth.** The soul, in its being, power, and operation, exists and acts independently; it is capable of reaching beyond the boundaries and limits of the physical world, and it desires things beyond matter and the body. Every accidental and physical form, however, ends where the body ends.
<margin>10</margin> 2. Every natural and material form, if it is a <term>substantial form <note>The essential nature that makes a thing what it is.</note></term>, arrives at <term>prime matter <note>The most basic, formless "stuff" of the universe.</note></term>; if it is an accidental form, it is added to a pre-existing compound. But the soul does not join the body in this way; rather, all matter joins and is taken up by the soul, out of which the soul has fashioned a body for itself. Therefore, the soul is neither something that simply "joins" a body, nor is it an accident of the body. <margin>15</margin> This is made even more evident by the fact that the "form" of a tree comes to a small grain of mustard seed as if to a soul already existing in the center of that seed; the soul does not arrive at a tree that is already fully formed.

3. **From the perspective of youth.** Every power and efficacy of a <margin>20</margin> material form grows and is perfected, gradually reaching its own limit; the soul, however, is that which causes the body to grow, while the soul itself does not grow, but remains perpetually the same.

->From the Field of Juno.<-
<note>In Bruno's memory system, the "Field of Juno" serves as a mental location for categorized arguments regarding how forms and spirits interact with matter.</note>

1. **From the perspective of the path or medium.** The soul is not the medium or the path through which the body acts, but the body is the medium and the path through which the soul completes its functions; therefore, the soul itself is not the "act" of the body or a form inherent to it, but the body is the soul's organ and instrument.

2. **From the perspective of encounter.** Because the soul encounters the body rather than being "drawn out" from the body—just as light does not emerge from the darkness, but is poured into the darkness. 3. **From the perspective of concurrence.** The soul and the body concur in the constitution of the living animal not as an accident and its subject, but as two subjects capable of being united through the <term>spirit <note>original: "spiritus." In Renaissance thought, the spirit is a subtle, vapor-like substance that acts as the "glue" or bridge between the immaterial soul and the physical flesh.</note></term>, of which the soul is the more primary member, <margin>202^v</margin> acting as the ruler, the governor, and the former.

# JORDANUS BRUNO

[it is directed toward what is] arranged, but adopts the matter which it might arrange for itself; therefore, it is an agent acting upon matter, not an <term>accident <note>original: "accidens." A philosophical term for a quality that cannot exist on its own, like the color of an apple, which requires the apple to exist.</note></term> or a form inherent in matter.

3. **From the perspective of the intended goal.** That which intends or "aims" within a living being, as the primary subject of appetite and cognition, is the soul; such a thing cannot be a mere accident, but must be the foundation of noble powers and acts.

---

->From the Horn of Achelous.<-
<note>In Bruno’s mnemonic system, "The Horn of Achelous" (the Cornucopia) represents a category of arguments concerning the abundance and origin of life. Achelous was a Greek river god whose broken horn became the symbol of plenty.</note>

1. **From what is possessed naturally.** The soul does not naturally possess a body or matter. Instead, the <term>Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras who believed in the transmigration of souls.</note></term>, <term>Platonists</term>, <term>Chaldeans <note>Ancient Babylonian sages often associated with mystical and astrological wisdom.</note></term>, and the core insights of all wise men testify that this union with the body happens to the soul as if by chance. It is so far from being "naturally" the form of the body, or a <term>harmony <note>original: "harmonia." The theory that the soul is just the "tuning" or balance of physical parts.</note></term> resulting from the body, or even specifically a certain "perfection" of the body.

<margin>15</margin>2. **From the perspective of its own properties.** The soul possesses virtues which in no way recognize matter; for it possesses intellect and an intelligible will, which are both subjectively and objectively detached from matter. If this is so, why should the soul's essence—which is the foundation of these powers—not be detached from matter with even greater reason? Therefore, although the soul may not exercise certain acts, nor can it exercise them without the body, it is not for that reason understood to be bound to the body. Indeed, just as a **lyre-player** <note>original: "citharoedus." A traditional metaphor used to explain that while the musician (the soul) needs the instrument (the body) to produce music (physical action), the musician's existence and talent do not depend on the instrument.</note> is not detached from the lyre during the act of playing, yet the lyre contributes nothing to his most essential acts, in which he exists as an independent nature.

3. **Concerning appropriation.** Because it is not the body that appropriates the soul to itself, but rather it is the soul that [appropriates] the body; nor— <margin>25</margin>

<summary>This page argues that the soul is an independent agent that organizes the body, citing ancient traditions (Pythagoreans, Platonists) to claim the soul's union with matter is incidental rather than essential. ->From the Hall of Demogorgon.<-
<note>In Bruno’s system, "Demogorgon" represents the primordial ancestor or the dark, mysterious source of the gods and the universe. His "Hall" contains arguments about the most ancient and fundamental origins of the soul.</note>

1. **From the ideal relationship to the Idea.** The soul is related by its own primary and principal relationship not to the body, but to God. <margin>10</margin> For it has a relationship to the body only so that it might use it, move within it, and drive itself; but it looks toward the abyss of light as the place where it may find rest. Therefore, its fellowship with the body and matter is a pilgrimage and a kind of wandering; consequently, the soul does not acknowledge matter as its proper <term>subject <note>original: "subiectum." The underlying material or foundation that supports qualities.</note></term>, <margin>15</margin> whether substantially or accidentally.

2. **From the relationship of father and son.** Because the soul is called the daughter of God and man is called the true son of God. An effect that shares the same nature as its cause, such as a human producing a human.</note></term> effect, <margin>20</margin> and in a certain way a father to that which is kindred and similar to himself.

3. **From the relationship between the begotten and the way it is begotten.** Every material physical form, if it is accidental, proceeds from the alteration of the subject. If it is essential, it proceeds from matter in a certain way through the path of <term>generation <note>The process of coming into being or being born.</note></term>, <margin>25</margin> or by the logic of generation, which is defined as the progress toward a new <term>act <note>original: "actum." Because of the soul, a thing is said to "become this specific thing," rather than merely being "of such a quality." Therefore, the soul does not fit the definition of an accidental form.

The soul, however, since it is a spiritual substance, persists in the truth of its essence no less than elementary and physical matter does. 
<margin>15</margin> Hence it is well said, even in the sacred writings, that the body is dissolved into dust—that is, into <term>atoms</term> <note>original: "atomos"; Bruno was a pioneer of "atomism," believing that the universe is made of indivisible, eternal particles, and that death is merely the rearranging of these particles.</note>—while the spirit truly returns to its source. This is not the condition of an accidental form, nor of something vanishing into nothingness like a sound, a color, or any sort of symmetry.

<meta>This page continues the logical proof of the soul's immortality and independence from the body. Having established that the soul is not a byproduct of physical matter, Bruno now examines why the soul cannot "leak away" or "dissolve" like physical properties do.</meta>

# THE TORCH OF THE THIRTY STATUES

...consisting of that which binds and retains them together, it is not merely a shaped thing, but an indivisible substance, thus preserving itself, as it is unable to depart from itself.

**2. From the perspective of dissipation.** <note>original: "effluxus"; literally an "outflow," referring to the way physical qualities leak away or diminish over time.</note> Because every <term>accident</term> <note>A property that depends on something else to exist, like the color of an apple.</note> flows into nothingness through corruption, so too does the form that results from a composition of parts when those parts are dissolved and separated. The substance of the soul, however, because it is indivisible, does not suffer this dissipation.
<margin>5</margin>

**3. From the perspective of transformation.** <note>original: "transmutationis"</note> Everything that is corrupted either vanishes—as accidents and material forms are said to be corrupted—or it passes into something else, as matter is said to be corrupted into a new thing. The soul, however, neither vanishes (because it does not have the nature of those material forms) nor does it pass into another thing (because it is a simple and "naked" substance). Rather, it perhaps moves elsewhere to operate, or moves toward different actions in terms of number, but it does not move into a different way of being as a subject.
<margin>10</margin>
| <margin>**205<sup>v</sup>**</margin> This is just as if a sailor were to move from one ship to another, or from the steering of a ship to the building of a house. Therefore, it must be placed entirely within the category of substances and <term>efficient causes</term> <note>original: "efficientum"; the active agents that produce effects in the world.</note> acting upon bodies, and not in the category of bodies, composites, or forms enslaved to bodies.
<margin>15</margin>
<margin>20</margin>

Thus, we have run through the arguments proving that the soul is a subsisting nature—not an accidental form, not an <term>entelechy</term> <note>original: "entelechia"; a term from Aristotle meaning the "actualization" or "functioning" of a body. Bruno argues the soul is an independent entity, not just the body's "function."</note>, not a "harmony," nor any other such thing. Many more means can be taken to prove the same point (and any other) by following the remaining parts of the "statues," of which we have selected only the first three. However, those that follow will seem more convenient and weightier everywhere, because we have made it our custom to keep this order: to proceed from the better <note>The manuscript suggests a transition from "lighter" or "more accessible" arguments to "weightier" ones.</note> means to the weightier and most powerful ones.
<margin>25</margin>

<summary>Bruno argues that the soul is an indivisible substance that does not dissolve when the body dies, comparing its transition to a sailor moving between ships. He concludes this section by distinguishing the soul from Aristotle's "entelechy," asserting its status as an independent agent.</summary>

<meta>This page serves as the concluding exhortation of Giordano Bruno's work on the "Thirty Statues." # GIORDANO BRUNO

...as we proceeded, so much so that everywhere the last part seems to include the perfection of all the others.

Therefore, giving thanks to God, we have completed the <term>Inventive Art</term> <note>original: "Artem inventivam"; Bruno’s method for discovering new ideas and organizing knowledge through memory.</note> through the <term>thirty statues</term> <note>original: "triginta statuas"; a complex system of thirty mental images used as "memory palaces" to store and retrieve information.</note>. It remains for each person,
<margin>5</margin> according to how much they believe they can obtain good, better, or the best fruit from the light of this teaching, to accustom themselves well, better, or best to these practices. For it counts for much not only to have encountered good discipline and to be guided by a good spirit, but this seems most essential: that one believes in what they possess, and cultivates their field according to that faith. 
<margin>10</margin> Through constant meditation—as if watering the seeds cast into the **field of the intellect**—one should make them grow, take increase, and wait for the fruit in its proper season. But the unfaithful and the despairing, whom even the gods testify they cannot heal, bury their **talent** <note>A reference to the biblical Parable of the Talents, where a servant is punished for burying his money rather than investing it.</note> 
<margin>15</margin> in idleness, torpor, and innate laziness; they abandon the harvest to be gnawed by mice.
