# THE BOOKS OF ARISTOTLE’S PHYSICS
## EXPLAINED BY THE MOST ILLUSTRIOUS LORD DOCTOR
### GIORDANO BRUNO OF NOLA.

---

Our intention, Aristotle says, is to investigate, inquire into, and discover the knowledge of nature to the best of our abilities. For we understand that the universal happiness of man, insofar as he is human, consists in this; 
<margin>5</margin> for the highest excellence <note>original: "summum specimen"</note>, according to the condition of his form <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "form" refers to the essential nature or "soul" of a thing that makes it what it is.</note>, consists in this: that he be perfected through the <term>speculative sciences</term> <note>The "speculative" or theoretical sciences (like physics and metaphysics) were considered the highest form of knowledge because they seek truth for its own sake rather than for practical use.</note>, 
<margin>10</margin> since in the entire realm of living creatures, man has obtained the first place precisely because he appears to excel in mind and intelligence. Therefore, since the human species, in its various parts and individuals, embraces the condition, quality, and likeness of all other species (namely, among various humans, some are likened to certain animals and others to others; 
<margin>15</margin> indeed, some may be compared to oxen, others to lions, and others to donkeys, so that in the very <term>complexion</term> <note>A term from ancient medicine referring to the balance of bodily humors and physical temperament.</note> of their bodies and every inclination they seem so affected as to be types of this pattern; and this extends even to that reason which is granted by nature), in true

<header>GIORDANO BRUNO</header>

...however, the true standing <note>original: "consistentia"</note> of man—by which he is truly and simply a man, far beyond the likeness of the condition of animal imperfection—is granted by nature to very few, if indeed it is granted to any at all. 
<margin>3</margin> But by a certain divine ordinance, through study, contemplation, and care—which proceeds from a certain wonder <note>Aristotle famously claimed that philosophy begins in wonder (thaumazein). Bruno here links this wonder to the "care" and "study" required to transcend animal instincts.</note>—some among men turn the eyes of 
<margin>5</margin> reason more intensely toward the light of intelligence. From this, after universals <note>General concepts or categories that apply to many individual things.</note> have been collected—partly through their own discovery and experience, and partly through teaching and discipline—they may acquire that most desired <term>habit</term> <note>From the Latin "habitus" (Greek: hexis); a stable internal disposition or state of mind, such as the possession of a branch of knowledge.</note>
<margin>10</margin> which we say is appropriate to man insofar as he is human. We say this because, if there is any happiness belonging to the soul when it is set free from the body, that happiness pertains only to a part of him, not to the whole man. 
And the reason for this is that if there are any other virtues, 
<margin>15</margin> faculties, perfections, or acts in which the human species displays a certain divinity, they all, without controversy, depend upon human intelligence as their indicator, light, and guide. All remaining virtues are referred to the habits and acts of the will, which certainly follow 
<margin>20</margin> the habits and acts of reason. Just as that power [reason] has been reformed, perfected, and illumined, so too must that which follows it [the will] follow accordingly.

<margin>4^r^b</margin> <margin>2^v</margin> ->The goal of contemplative philosophy is the knowledge of nature.<-

Knowledge is distributed into various categories, according to the different ways in which it is received. For there is external sense regarding external sensible things, which is properly called "sense." 
<margin>25</margin> Likewise, there is internal sense regarding the appearances <note>original: "species"</note> of sensible things in the <term>imagination</term> <note>original: "phantasia"; in Renaissance psychology, the faculty that stores and combines images received from the senses.</note>...

# ARISTOTLE’S BOOKS ON PHYSICS EXPLAINED

...contained and received by the <term>common sense</term> <note>Latin: *sensus communis*. In Aristotelian psychology, this is the internal faculty that integrates the data from the five individual senses into a single coherent perception.</note>; which are then succeeded by thought, imagination, and memory. Immediately following this is the type of cognition called **reason**, in which the species <note>Latin: *species*. These are the mental images or representations of objects that the mind works with.</note> that have been remembered and thought out are compared with one another, so that certain unknown things may be inferred
<margin>5</margin> from those already known. Reason is followed by the **intellect**, which does not move step-by-step <note>original: *non discurrit*. This refers to "discursive" reasoning, or the process of moving from one premise to a conclusion.</note>, but knows by a certain immediate longing and application, just as a sense knows through a present object of perception. And this power is for that reason more divine than the others, because it is assimilated to divine cognition. However, because it happens that the intellect is deduced and emanates from
<margin>10</margin> sense and reason, it testifies to its own lowliness <note>original: *ignobilitatem*. Bruno suggests that because human intellect relies on lower sensory inputs, it is "lowly" compared to the pure, unmediated intellect of God.</note> by its very origin. Therefore, that most eminent mode of knowing, which [operates] without step-by-step reasoning, logic, or the comparison of species <unclear>***</unclear>, is the **mind**.

<margin>4v B</margin>
These modes of knowing being established, since the 
<margin>15</margin> purpose of our present contemplation is to bring forward an account <note>original: *rationem*</note> that pertains to nature, and we hear all philosophers agreeing in this: that they call the knowledge of it **science**, and not opinion, not sense, not imagination, not history, and not mind; the reason for this distinction must be brought forward for the 
<margin>20</margin> understanding of our subject matter and discoveries. In our proposal, therefore, regarding natural, physical, and individual things—at least regarding those external forms <note>original: *species*</note> by which they thrust themselves upon the external senses, the common sense, the phantasy, and the cogitative faculty—there is a certain **sense**. But concerning things that can be thought and the comparisons 
<margin>25</margin> of those sensible forms, there is a certain **imagination**. 

To proceed from these sensible things, according to a certain argumentative act, toward things that can be understood <note>original: *intelligibilia*</note> is, without doubt, **reason**. From many such comparisons, relationships, and apprehensions...

# JORDANO BRUNO

Things that are kept within the fold of this lower cognitive power are, in a simple sense, **memory**, but in a rational sense, **experience**. <margin>30</margin> Memory is a certain retention of these things, while experience is a certain skill <note>original: *peritia*. Here, Bruno refers to the practical expertise or "know-how" gained by repeatedly observing the same thing.</note> derived from them.
<margin>5</margin> Following a <term>habit</term> <note>Latin: *habitus*. A stable disposition or state of mind that allows one to perform an action or reach a conclusion reliably.</note> of this kind—which he [Aristotle] attributes even to the **brutes** <note>Referring to non-human animals, which Aristotle and Bruno believed possessed memory and a rudimentary form of experience, but not the higher faculty of universal reasoning.</note>—there follows that reasoning which we believe to be proper to man, namely **art**. Art is considered a certain universal habit that deals with particulars and action. To this habit succeeds another habit, forged from several universals, which
<margin>10</margin> is ordered toward contemplation and knowledge and is sought for its own sake. And this is properly called **science**, which is defined by us in the book *Posterior Analytics* <note>One of Aristotle's primary works on logic, specifically focusing on how scientific knowledge is demonstrated through syllogisms.</note> as "a habit of reaching a conclusion sought through demonstration." To know is indeed said to be "to recognize through demonstration," <margin>5 B</margin> as when some unknown universal is obtained through a necessary deduction from certain known universal principles; this deduction encompasses both the necessity of the form and logical consequence, as well as the necessity of the matter and the result.

->On the method of proceeding in the science of nature.<-

<margin>20</margin> Since the method and order are manifold: namely, **compositive**, when moving from parts to the whole; **divisive**, when from the whole to parts; **inventive**, when from particulars to universals; **judicative**, when from universals to particulars; and **resolutive**, when we proceed from a universal and
<margin>25</margin> whole concept to a distinct concept—as when we resolve a demonstration into propositions, and the knowledge of propositions into the knowledge of simple terms—

# EXPLANATIONS OF ARISTOTLE'S BOOKS ON PHYSICS

Likewise, whenever we resolve a name and the thing named into their defining parts, it happens that—out of all these modes, according to the diverse subjects or objects of consideration, and also according to the diverse ends or purposes—now one and now another is put to use.
<margin>5</margin> For the geometer and the grammarian necessarily proceed from parts or elements—such as lines, angles, and points, or letters and syllables—toward figures and words; however, nature proceeded in these matters in the opposite order. For bodies and figures existed before their parts were conceived or distinguished;
<margin>10</margin> <margin>5$^v$ B</margin> likewise, names and verbs existed | before syllables and letters. For the inventors of these things first set these composites before their own eyes, and by dividing them into their own immediate and primary parts, they arrived at a certain and defined number of principles, so that thereafter, when judging and
<margin>15</margin> teaching, they might proceed in the opposite order. <margin>3$^v$ C</margin> | Similarly, for those attempting another method and mode of knowing, from the repeated and multiplied apprehension of sensible and particular things, there arises memory, experience, and a universal <term>habit</term> <note>original: *habitus*. A stable mental state or acquired capacity that allows for consistent action or understanding.</note>.
First, indeed, this is a specific habit, collecting infinite individuals into one; thereafter, it becomes a generic habit, connecting several species into one,
<margin>20</margin> so that at last, in judging and teaching, a progression might be made from universal generic knowledge to specific knowledge, through the distinction of the <term>genus</term> <note>A broad category (like "animal") that is divided into species (like "human" or "horse") by identifying specific differences.</note> according to its proper differences. Now, therefore, for those not inquiring for the first time, but
<margin>25</margin> pursuing a discipline after an inquiry has already been made according to doctrine, one must proceed from universals to particulars, just as one moves from generalities to specialties; for concerning particulars, which are individuals, there is no science <note>original: *de particularibus... non est scientia*. A foundational rule in Aristotelian logic: science deals with universal laws and definitions, not the unique, accidental features of a single individual object.</note>.

<margin>6^r 3</margin>
### Explanation of the Text

Since, therefore, one must proceed from the knowledge of elements, principles, and causes—specifically anyone who follows a <term>judicial and doctrinal method</term> <note>original: *iudicativam et doctrinalem methodum*. A systematic approach to making judgments and providing instruction.</note> regarding those things that consist of principles, causes, and elements (seeing as this is the progression of <term>demonstration</term> <note>original: *demonstrationis*. In Aristotelian logic, a proof that leads to certain knowledge by showing why something must be the case.</note>, by which we clearly resolve the whole and the universe into those things from which it is composed and fused: let it not be thought that by "principles," "causes," and "elements" we are using mere synonyms, since these should be distinct in <term>demonstrative or speculative science</term> <note>original: *scientia demonstrativa seu speculativa*. Knowledge gained through logical proof or theoretical contemplation of nature.</note> according to nature; for a **principle** refers to more things than a **cause** and an **element**, given that the rising or the birth of the sun is called the **principle** of the day, but not its **cause**; a **cause** likewise signifies more things than an **element**, given that the <term>efficient</term> <note>The source of change or the "maker" of a thing.</note> and the <term>final</term> <note>The purpose or goal for which a thing exists.</note> are **causes**, but not **elements**, since elements are the constitutive parts of a thing, out of which it is composed and into
<margin>6^v 3</margin> which it is resolved: | therefore, one must proceed from principles, causes, and elements to the knowledge of those things which possess principles, causes, and elements), since all these are discovered in the contemplation that concerns nature, they are established first as things to be acquired in a contemplation of this kind. Whether it be the thing itself or the knowledge of things, if they possess these three, they must be investigated through them.

<margin>4^r 4</margin>
#### Nature's causes, principles, and elements are not the same as its essence.

<margin>25</margin> Nature presents itself to be contemplated either regarding its essence and being, and in this way there is no path and order toward it from causes,

I. For, **effectively**, the causes of this kind of knowledge are things that are <term>originated, caused, and composed of elements</term> <note>original: *principiata, causata et elementata*. Bruno refers to the physical objects in the world that result from these principles.</note>;

...[I have been] accustomed to calling it the contemplative [intellect], sometimes in potential habit, sometimes in actual practice), which relates to <term>intelligible species</term> <note>original: *species intelligibiles*. These are the mental forms or "concepts" of things that the mind can grasp, as opposed to the physical "sensible species" that the eyes see.</note> as an internal eye, just as the external eye relates to perceiving sensible species;
<margin>4^{v)}</margin> VI. **Subjectively** or materially, these are the | things themselves through their forms, which exist on the surface of the beings of nature or natural substances;
VII. **Objectively**, they are the species or forms that emanate from things themselves toward the senses, thought, and reason (some of which are called <term>first intentions</term>, and others <term>second intentions</term> or conceptions <note>A "first intention" is the direct mental concept of a real object, like "this horse." A "second intention" is a higher-level concept of that concept, such as the category of "species" or "genus."</note>);
VIII. **Instrumentally**, first, there are three operations of the intellect regulated by the habit of logic: namely, **conception**, **verification**, and **discourse**;
IX. **Instrumentally**, in the next degree, there are three types of demonstration: from the **sign**, from the **cause**, and **simply** <note>Bruno is distinguishing types of logical proof: moving from effect to cause (sign), cause to effect (cause), or absolute logical necessity (simply).</note>, the first of which is specific to physics, the second to metaphysics, and the third to mathematics (the first proceeding from the causes of knowing, the second from the causes of being, and the third from the causes of both being and knowing);
<margin>8^{r3}</margin> X. **Methodically**, it is the | path and way of proceeding to generate a scientific habit within itself; for there are certain principles of the science of nature from which we pursue natural science, thus following the order of judgment, teaching, and discipline:

First, let us consider the **universals of nature**, namely those things found in the universal genus of natural things: first, the **principles** (such as nature itself, <term>privation</term> <note>original: *privatio*. In this context, it refers to the absence of a form that is naturally expected to be there, a key concept for understanding change.</note>, the instant and time, the boundary and place or vacuum, the finite or infinite); then the **causes** (namely efficient causes, some of which are *per se* [essential], such as nature and the motor <note>The "mover" or active force.</note>, and others *per accidens* [incidental], such as fortune and chance); and finally the **elements**, which are found in things constituted by nature as their primary and internal parts—namely, **matter** and **form**.

Bruno is laying out how the study of nature is organized, moving from universal principles to the specific details of the physical world following the traditional Aristotelian sequence of books.</meta>

# EXPLANATION OF THE BOOKS OF ARISTOTLE'S PHYSICS

<margin>5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 8<sup>v</sup> B, 5<sup>r</sup> C</margin>
Secondly, we will proceed consequently to the specific details of nature. First, in the books *On the Heavens and the World*, we will contemplate nature in things that are movable according to the first and primary type of motion—that is, the heavens and the elements—insofar as they are driven by primary and secondary <term>local motion</term> <note>original: *latione*. In this context, it refers specifically to movement from one place to another, which Aristotle considered the most fundamental type of change.</note>. Second, in the books *On Generation*, we will study nature according to the second and immediately following type of motion, namely origin and destruction <note>original: *ortu et interitu*. Often translated as "coming-to-be and passing-away," referring to the birth and death of things.</note>; and subsequently according to the other <column-break/> types that follow: alteration, increase, and decrease. (And thus far will be the first part of the contemplation of nature, which is rigorous <term>science</term> <note>original: *scientia*. To Bruno and his contemporaries, "science" meant certain knowledge derived from first principles and logical demonstration, rather than just any investigation.</note> and follows the method of science). Third, in the books *On the Soul*, *On Sense and the Sensible*, *On Memory and Reminiscence*, and the others belonging to this category, we will proceed according to the principle of vital and rational motions, just as we followed the principle of natural motions in the sections above. (And this is the second part of the science of nature, which has the character of a <term>history</term> <note>original: *historiae*. In the Renaissance, a "history" was a descriptive account or a collection of observed facts, considered less rigorous than "science" because it deals with specific examples rather than universal laws.</note> rather than rigorous science). Fourth, in the books on *Meteorology*, we deal with "mixed" compounds that are imperfect, which appear in the upper and lower regions of the universe; and successively we deal with "mixed" compounds that are perfect and more perfect in the books *On Minerals*, *On Plants*, and *On Animals*. These we call entirely "historical," because they are occupied with the particular species of things that can be born and perish, and with other types of motion that affect them—things which are very close to individual cases. Regarding these, rigorous science is not possible, nor is a mere description suitable for one who is contemplating the proper method of teaching.

<margin>30, 9<sup>r</sup> B</margin>
Applying this, therefore, to the tenth reason mentioned above—namely, the methodical reason, by which we must proceed from certain principles of this science—we say that the path of this teaching is from universals to the specific types of nature. This method...

-> # GIORDANO BRUNO <-

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, likely completing the word *methodus* (method).</note> [The metho]d takes on a twofold reasoning: one is innate in us, by which we proceed from <term>universals</term> <note>original: *universalibus*. In Aristotelian logic, these are general concepts like "animal" or "body" that apply to many things.</note> perceived confusedly and indistinctly, and from a whole conceived confusedly and indistinctly; the other, by which we proceed from universals clearly accepted and from the whole clearly perceived toward the contemplation of species and parts.

That the first mode is innate to us is evident from several factors: first, from external sense itself, namely sight <margin>5</margin> (for from a distance we first see that something is a body; second, when it moves, we recognize it as a living body or animal; third, when we distinguish the limbs, we perceive it to be a man; finally, we say it is <term>Socrates</term> <note>Socrates was the standard example used by medieval and Renaissance philosophers to represent a specific, individual person.</note>); secondly, the same is clear <margin>5^v</margin> in a painting, which first puts forward a certain confused | outline and shading, in which it describes the whole animal or story, so that it may then proceed to delineate the particulars <margin>15</margin> exactly and clearly; <margin>9^v3</margin> | third, it is manifest in the way of conceiving, which is first according to the name, then according to the definition (for in the name we know confusedly, but in the definition, distinctly); fourth, it is proportional to what is said regarding the cognition of children, which <margin>20</margin> is from the indistinct and confused, when they first call all men fathers and all women mothers, before they reach the point of recognizing this specific father and this specific mother as defined for themselves.

In this way, progress has occurred in the knowledge of these principles, moving from the confused to the distinct, from the <margin>25</margin> unorganized to the organized, from the incipient to the perfect, and from the shaded to the excellently explained. This progression indeed may be contemplated in two objects: I. by comparing philosophers to philosophers, namely the ancients to us; II. by comparing philosophy to philosophy, as—

A grammatical term used here to mean nature as the primary subject or essence—the internal principle of the thing.</note>, as the internal essence of natural things (which is the principle of motion or the acting force, like the first and proximate mover), or matter itself and form, are not movable, except by accident <note>meaning they move only because the object they inhabit is moving, not because they move in themselves.</note>. The fifth reason is that a specialist in a particular science should only dispute with those with whom there is a common ground in principles, leaving aside those who either do not hold these principles or hold contrary ones. **7v C** I do not say that we absolutely deny them a disputation, since principles especially ought to be certain and corroborated—for from trust in them, the trust and the very habit of science proceeds—but I say that one treating a particular science and proposing particular conclusions must not dwell upon the proof of the principles. Rather, one must dispute with him who, from principles held in common by both you and himself, deduces something against your conclusions from those same principles.

<margin>13</margin>
### The reason why one should, after all, dispute against them.

Therefore, a dispute with Parmenides, Melissus, and other philosophers of that same opinion proceeds not out of merit or duty, but from a certain appropriateness. For although <margin>5</margin> their reasons are not "physical" or "natural" <note>Bruno means they do not follow the rules of natural science because they deny change and multiplicity.</note>, they nevertheless concern physics and nature. For this reason, we do not think we should deal with them with the greatest intensity, but they should only be touched upon lightly.

### Aristotle's arguments against those who speak about nature in a non-natural way.

<margin>10</margin> The first common argument against the aforementioned thinkers proceeds by asking them how they understand "the one" and how they understand "being." For we argue first from a consideration of the subject, and second from a consideration of the predicate in this question: "being is one." <note>This refers to the logical structure of the sentence "Being is one." Is "being" the thing we are talking about (the subject), and what does it mean to say it is "one" (the predicate)?</note> If, <margin>15</margin> therefore, you say being is one—even though "being" itself takes on ten different meanings according to Archytas <note>Archytas of Tarentum was a Pythagorean philosopher. Aristotle credited the Pythagoreans with the origins of the ten Categories (substance, quantity, quality, etc.).</note>—it must be asked <margin>1.</margin> whether it is one substance, or one quantity, or one underlying thing, or one quantified thing. If it is one underlying thing, is it one complete substance, such as a single horse, or a part of a substance, <margin>20</margin> like a single soul? If it is a quality, is it like "one white thing" or "one hot thing" or something similar? These things surely differ greatly among one another, and it is not possible to call them "one." <margin>ε C</margin> But if they understand "the one" to be a substance, a quantity, and a quality all at once—or a substance that possesses quality and quantity—then regardless of <margin>24</margin> whether they take these things to be separate and distinct from one another or not, it is absolutely necessary for them to be many and diverse.

He uses Aristotle’s logic to show that "being" cannot be "one" in a simple sense, because being is categorized into many different types like substance, quality, and quantity.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the logical refutation of the Eleatic philosophers (Parmenides and Melissus), who argued that all of reality is a single, unchanging "One." Having previously discussed the definition of "being," the author now moves to the specific logical contradictions in their arguments regarding "substance" and "the one."</meta>

<page-num>277</page-num>
<header>EXPLANATION OF ARISTOTLE'S BOOKS ON PHYSICS</header>

**The second argument.** Therefore, if they understand this "one" to be something existing apart from <term>substance</term> <note>In this context, "substance" refers to the fundamental "stuff" or essence of a thing that exists on its own, such as a person or a tree.</note> (whether they intend for substance to exist alongside it or not), they will surely fall into a great inconsistency and absurdity <margin>5</margin> (if, however, one may call the impossible "inconsistent and absurd"). This is because none of the other categories of being can exist without substance, for they are either located *in* a substance or are *predicated of* a substance.

**The third argument** is taken from the words of Melissus <note>Melissus of Samos (5th century BCE) was a follower of Parmenides who argued that the universe is one, motionless, and infinite.</note>, who, by denying plurality, actually ends up assuming it. Since he says that "the one" <margin>10</margin> is infinite, he assumes a substance when he says "the one" (the subject), but he assumes a <term>quantity</term> <margin>14^v B</margin> when he says "infinite." This is because "infinite" and "finite" are characteristics of quantity, not of substance or quality. Thus, if a substance has a specific size (is "quantified"), there are already two things present, not one. If, however, it is <margin>15</margin> only a substance, then it cannot be infinite, nor can it possess magnitude or number.

->Arguments taken from the perspective of the "one."<-

**The fourth argument.** Since the word "one" is used in many ways, just as the word "being" is, we must ask them <margin>20</margin> in what way they understand being to be "one." Do they mean it as a **continuum**, where all the parts are joined at a single common boundary? Or as an **indivisible** "one," <margin>89.</margin> which lacks any parts at all? Or thirdly, as **one in definition** (one in "reason" or "essence")? Or as a **single name** <margin>25</margin> used for the same thing—just as synonyms are used to explain a single reality with different names, such as "pure wine" and "wine"? <note>original: "merum et vinum". In Latin, "merum" refers specifically to undiluted wine; Aristotle uses this as a classic example of two different words that point to the exact same substance.</note>

<summary>This page refutes the philosopher Melissus by showing that describing the "One" as "infinite" creates a logical contradiction, as it implies both substance and quantity. It also breaks down the different ways "one" can be defined, challenging the Eleatic school to clarify their terminology.</summary>

When later thinkers were moved by these or similar difficulties, and because they did not trust themselves to resolve those inconsistencies, they fled to a double safeguard. Some removed the mark of the <term>copula</term> <note>The "copula" is the linking verb "is" which connects a subject to a predicate.</note> from their speech, so that they would not be forced by it to admit a "multitude" <note>original: "esse fateri"</note>, which is testified to by the fact that the predicate is different from the subject it is spoken of... they even removed the verb itself from
<margin>20</margin> speech. Lycophron <note>A 4th-century BC sophist who argued that we should not use the word "is" because it implies that one thing is actually two (the thing and its property).</note> did this by mutilating the sentence; others did it by varying the words. Lycophron would not say "the man is white," but "the man white"; others would say "the whited man" or "the man whites," as if they were setting up an excellent shield against these inconsistencies. But
<margin>25</margin> truly, "being" is not spoken of in only one way and as a single thing because of this; furthermore, we prove that things are diverse both by definition and in reality, both from the multitude of their parts and from their contrariety, as has been said. Others...

They did not consider it absurd for the same thing to be both one and many; they only considered it an inconsistency for opposites <margin>16</margin> and contraries to be one. From this, they understood that those things in which an opposition of contrariety is found truly and properly constitute a <margin>5</margin> multitude. However, we consider it sufficient for a multitude that "being in potentiality" is one thing, and "being in act" is another; for there is a "one" in <term>potentiality</term> <note>The capacity or possibility for something to exist or happen.</note> and a "one" in <term>act</term> <note>The state of actually being or currently existing; reality as opposed to possibility.</note>, and likewise a "being" in potentiality and a "being" in act. Thus, we conclude that it is not difficult to dissolve the principles from which they argue; for as we said from the start, they proceed <term>sophistically</term> <note>Using clever but false arguments, especially with the intention of deceiving.</note>, <margin>10</margin> deceiving both in the matter and the form of their argument.

<margin>90</margin>->*He descends more specifically to the opinion of Melissus and Parmenides.*<-

What we said regarding the <term>paralogism</term> <note>A piece of illogical or fallacious reasoning, specifically a "formal" error in the structure of a syllogism.</note> of both Melissus and Parmenides <margin>15</margin> must now be demonstrated. For they <note>original: "Melyssi... Parmenidis"</note> argued as follows: "Everything that has been made has a beginning; the universe was not made; therefore, it has no beginning." First, then, he errs in the form of the logic, because he takes the middle term affirmatively with the major premise, but negatively as a predicate with the minor. <margin>1^Pr</margin> Second, he errs because he does not treat the <margin>20</margin> middle term as one simple thing, but as something with multiple meanings. In the proposition "that which is made has a beginning," "beginning" <note>original: "principium"</note> is used for that which comes before duration (a beginning in time). Yet, when he concludes from the fact that it has no beginning or end that the universe is immobile—because it <margin>25</margin> has nothing outside itself by which it might be moved—he takes "beginning" and "end" to mean that which concerns magnitude or bulk (physical boundaries). Third, even if the "one" were infinite according to this second mode...

Sixthly, because it is impossible (even if generation, corruption, alteration, duration, or time are removed) to make it so that the things which exist are "one" in <margin>10^r C</margin> species, unless someone takes this "one" as a single <term>matter</term> <note>The underlying "stuff" of the universe.</note> from which all things are made, as do those who say all things are "one water."

And yet, in the very face and heart of nature, a multitude is necessarily introduced, since it is necessary that what *is* be distinguished from that *from which* it comes; and among the things that exist, there is a distinction between one and another, such as a human being from a horse. Likewise, one contrary is not its own opposite, just as heat is not cold.

->Concerning the specific ways in which he argues against Parmenides.<-

Since the opinion of Parmenides and his arguments in some way agree with the arguments and opinion of Melissus, it happens that he <note>Aristotle.</note> must deal with him partly with the same and partly with other arguments. He <note>Parmenides.</note> has this further in common: that he both assumes false premises and <margin>5</margin> commits logical fallacies <note>original: "paralogizat"</note>. He accepts false things indeed when he considers "being" <note>original: "ens"</note>, which is spoken of in many ways, as if it were spoken of in only one way <margin>1</margin>; his conclusion does not follow, because even if "white" were that "one" which signifies being, he still could not defend his thesis. This is because "white" does not eliminate multiplicity—neither by <margin>10</margin> way of continuity, nor as a single continuous thing, nor as a unity of reason <note>Meaning that even if everything were "white," you would still have the "thing that is white" and the "whiteness" itself.</note>. For the definition <note>original: "ratio"</note> of a white thing is different from that of "whiteness"—namely, the difference between a <term>subject</term> <note>The underlying thing that possesses a property.</note> and a <term>quality</term> <note>The attribute or characteristic of that thing.</note>—even though the quality is not separated from the subject. Furthermore, in the time of Par-<margin>15</margin>menides, they did not see this distinction between subject and <term>form</term> <note>The essential nature or "shape" of a thing's being.</note>.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Text 26. It is necessary for those who say that "being" is one to accept this term according to its most powerful and primary meaning, unless they wish to distinguish that which is <term>predicated</term> <note>Something stated or asserted about a subject.</note> from that of which it is predicated. For if "being" signifies only an <margin>20</margin> <term>accident</term> <note>A non-essential property, like color, that can change without the thing itself ceasing to exist.</note>, then that to which it "happens" <note>The word "accident" comes from the Latin for "falling upon" or happening to something.</note> will be "non-being," and thus "being" itself, which truly is, would exist within that which truly is not.

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;27. Since that which truly is should not be an "accident" to anything, it must signify <term>substance</term> <note>The underlying reality or essence of a thing that exists in its own right.</note> rather than an accident; therefore, if an accident is taken to mean "being," then that which truly is will <margin>25</margin> not be an accident of being.

<margin>10^v C</margin>
->That true being cannot be a substance.<-

text 28. It is established, therefore, that "true being" <note>original: "vere ens"</note> does not signify an accident. That it does not signify substance in this way is manifest from the fact that it would possess neither any magnitude nor any <margin>5</margin> multitude; it would not have magnitude as a finite or infinite quantity, nor multitude whereby one part is distinct | from another <margin>18^v B</margin> or at least different from it. And since the whole itself is not divisible, it would not be divided into that which truly is; for if it is divided into that which truly is, then surely there must be a difference <margin>10</margin> between the whole and the part, and likewise between one part and another part, and the definition <note>original: "ratio," referring to the essential logic or formula of a thing.</note> of one must be different from the definition of the other. Similarly, if that which truly is, is one in its essence <note>original: "ratione"</note> or one by definition—for instance, if "human" is true being or a unity—then it is necessary that both "animal" and "two-legged" are also true being; <margin>15</margin> for if "animal" and "two-legged" are not true being—namely, substance—then they must surely be accidents. If this were so, they would either be accidents of the "human" or of some other subject. But it is impossible for them to be accidents in any way, since they would have to be either a <term>proper passion</term> <note>A property that belongs exclusively to a specific subject, such as "the ability to laugh" belongs to humans.</note> or a <term>common passion</term> <note>A property shared by many different types of things.</note>: <margin>20</margin> if it were a proper passion, then it would be necessary for the subject to be included in its definition, just as "nose" is in the definition of "snub-nosed," "tongue" in the definition of "stammering," or "shin" in the definition of "lame"; or it will be a certain common passion, which is not placed in the definition of the subject. In whichever way it might be, it will be absolutely necessary that <margin>25</margin> that which is an accident and that to which it happens <note>The subject in which the accident exists.</note> are always diverse, both in definition and in reality.

29. Furthermore, proper accidents, in whose definition the subject is included, cannot be resolved according to the definition...

This is because "infinite" is not a number, but rather the "innumerable"; <note>Bruno highlights a distinction here: "infinite" suggests a lack of limit, while "innumerable" suggests something that cannot be counted, yet can still coincide with a single substance.</note> therefore, it does not imply a multitude, but coincides with the "one," which is the substance of the whole, of which it is not permitted to produce a distinct species.

### He argues specifically against Anaxagoras.

Therefore, in dealing with Anaxagoras, let us first <margin>10</margin>bring forward his reasoning, and second, explain the inconsistency of that opinion. As for the first point, the reason why Anaxagoras judged there to be infinite principles is because he accepted that most true notion common among all philosophers, that
> "nothing comes from nothing" <note>original: *ex nihilo nihil fit*</note>,
and consequently
<margin>15</margin>> "whatever is made, is made from what exists" <note>original: *quicquid fit, ex ente fit*</note>.
Hence, whatever is in composite things must be the same before it is in them. Therefore, before things and species were distinguished by the mind—so that the appearance <note>original: *vultus*</note> of individual species might appear—they were together; thus the whole production or generation of things consists in a certain segregation or <margin>20</margin>separation. | The second reason is because he saw that <margin>**21^v B**</margin> contraries are made from contraries, as air, vapor, and then finally water are made from fire; likewise, he saw fire separated from earth and flint. Since, indeed, it is not fitting for a contrary to be made from a contrary, he thought it worth considering that a contrary instead <margin>25</margin>comes out of its contrary as if through a certain dissociation and tearing apart, rather than through alteration or another mode of production. | For how is it possible to think that fire is made from... <margin>**12^v C**</margin>

Therefore, since production of this kind appears perpetually, one must <margin>5</margin> judge that opposites are within opposites—those things, evidently, from which they can be separated. Third, he argued as if solving and diluting the difficulty which the senses themselves introduce (since the senses do not perceive opposites within opposites or "all things in all things"). He claimed that those <term>similar parts (homoeomeries)</term> are found in everything according to <margin>10</margin> a certain imperceptible size. He argued that just because the external appearance of things varies, we should not say that one thing is not present in another. Indeed, he attributed the difference between things not to specific parts that might exist in some but not in others, but rather to a certain excess and deficiency. Where <margin>2r</margin> <margin>15</margin> the parts of wood superabounded, there was wood; where the parts of iron superabounded, there was iron; and similarly for the rest. This was the reason that things took on their specific names and characters in their outward appearance and surface; but in truth, nothing is purely and simply what it seems, such as "white," "sweet," "flesh," or "bone"; for the <margin>20</margin> nature of any thing is not a single one, but because of the superabounding part, it appears to be one thing.

### Against Anaxagoras.

We see that this opinion is crippled by many reasons and their causes. First, because it removes the knowledge or science of principles; <margin>25</margin> for in this way, there is no limit to their number. There would be as many principles as there are things—if indeed those can be called "principles" which do not establish other things, but merely expose themselves and bring themselves into the open. Thus, corresponding to the number and the indefinite multitude of species, there would be their principles,

->**WORKS OF BRUNO, Latin Vol. III, 37**<-

...and alongside infinite individuals and infinite particulars, there would also be infinite <margin>13r C</margin> principles, both according to the multitude of particular forms and according to the multitude of parts and <term>atoms (minima)</term>. Thus, it would not be permitted to recognize either the matter or the form of things, and consequently not even the <term>composite (the whole object)</term>, the knowledge of which depends on those things from which it is made <note>original: *quibus est*; refers to the constituent parts that define a whole</note>. 

Second, just as in natural things every species is determined by a maximum and a minimum size—since a wild olive tree <note>original: *oleaster*</note> never rises to the mass <margin>22v B</margin> of a cultivated olive, nor a rabbit to the mass of an ox, nor an elephant to the size of a mountain—so each of these has a certain boundary below which it cannot be thinned out, and a certain limit beyond which it cannot be increased. If this is so in the whole bodies, then it must necessarily be the same way in the parts; for instance, if the head of an animal cannot be just any size, then neither can its brain. If the nose and the eye cannot be just any size, then the vein, artery, bone, and similar parts will not be of just any size. Therefore, it is necessary to conclude that it is not possible for "anything to be in anything," since anything <note>meaning any specific substance like bone or water</note> cannot be of just any size or any quality.

Third, if it is the case that all things do not "become" <note>in the sense of new creation</note> but are "separated" (because things do not change so as to cease being themselves and become others, but instead exist one inside another); if, likewise, the name of a thing comes from the majority of its parts; and if, furthermore, anything is made from anything or separated from anything—such as water from flesh—I add this: every finite body is consumed by the subtraction of a finite part. From all these points, the opposite of Anaxagoras's view follows: namely, that anything is *not* in anything. For if a separation of the parts of flesh from water occurs once, there will no longer be as many parts of flesh in the remaining water, but...

...fewer: through the repeated and repeated subtraction of these parts, it is necessary to arrive at a limit where no further parts of flesh can be found within the water. For this reason, that <margin>2</margin> water will no longer contain all things within itself. It follows, therefore, that all things are not in all things perpetually. 

However, if he <note>Anaxagoras, the ancient Greek philosopher being critiqued here</note> should claim that this segregation does not stop—that is, that it never reaches a final limit because every part is always separable from every other part—the consequence would be that within a finite size, there would be an infinite number of things of equal size. For instance, in ten pounds of flesh, there would be ten pounds of flesh an infinite number of times, or finite things would be equal to infinite things <note>This is a classic critique of infinite divisibility: if you can pull an infinite number of parts out of a small object, that small object must logically be as "large" as the universe</note>. 

Likewise, it would follow that since all things are in all things, all things would also be present in each of its <margin>170</margin> individual parts. Since these parts are infinite, just as there are infinite things in the whole, there would also be infinite things in the individual parts, and even in the parts of those parts. Thus, the most absurd conclusion follows: that there would be an infinite number of things within an infinite number of things, an infinite number of times.

Fourth, since every body necessarily becomes smaller when a part is removed, and since (as stated above) natural species are defined by their smallness and greatness—and therefore the quantity of flesh is limited in both its maximum and its minimum size—it must be that there is a "maximum flesh" at a certain level and a "minimum flesh" <note>original: *minimam carnem*; refers to the "natural minimum," the smallest possible unit of a substance that still functions as that substance</note> at another. Now, if all things are in all things, there would still be more flesh within that "minimum" flesh; likewise, there would be something smaller than the minimum <note>which contradicts the very definition of a "minimum" limit</note>.

A fifth reason follows: if infinite things are found within infinite bodies (such as in flesh, blood, or brain), then <margin>23</margin> surely those things which do not exist—for instance, things existing below the threshold of dimension | and magnitude—would be no less "real" than those which possess dimension and magnitude. Furthermore, those things separated or set apart according to Anaxagoras’s logic <note>original: *ratione Anaxagorica*</note> would be just as much "beings," and just as true and existing, [as the things we see]. <meta>This page transitions from a specific critique of Anaxagoras’s "Mind" to a broader historical survey of how ancient philosophers—including Parmenides and Democritus—all converged on the idea that "contrariety" (the tension between opposites) is the fundamental driver of creation.</meta>

# THE WORKS OF GIORDANO BRUNO
**WORKS OF BRUNO, Latin Vol. III, 292**

When considering those who have posited either one or many <term>principles</term> <note>original: "principia"; in this context, the fundamental "starting points" or "first causes" from which all matter and life arise</note>, whether they speak according to the laws of nature or otherwise, they all agree in this: they propose that a certain **contrariety** <note>The state of being opposite or in conflict, such as hot vs. cold</note> is the primary factor in the production of things. Indeed, even 
<margin>5</margin> **Parmenides**, after he named "being" <note>original: "ens"</note> as one and immobile, soon—when he began to speculate more closely upon the nature of things—posited the contrary principles of **hot** and **cold**, treating them as the substances 
**fire** and **earth**. Likewise, among those who said there were many principles, some speak of the **rare** and the **dense** revolving around a single subject, 
<margin>10</margin> as well as the **void** and the **solid**, following the way of speaking used by **Democritus**. Of these, Democritus accepted one as "being" and the other as "non-being." Others, however, considered a certain contrariety based on local differences, insofar as according to such <unclear>differences</unclear> <note>The original Latin has a gap here, likely intended to be "differences" or "positions"</note> **atoms** 
<margin>241</margin> and the first elements are the producers of various forms, 
<margin>15</margin> such as up and down, or front and back; from which follow the angular and the non-angular, the straight and the round.

We approve of this position held by all of them, as it is brought forward not without reason; for there are three conditions for principles, which, if they stand, make it 
<margin>20</margin> necessary for there to be a contrariety between them. The **first** condition is that they are not made from one another; the **second** is that they are not made from other things; the **third** is that all things are made from them. These are precisely the conditions of the first contraries: because they are not 
<margin>14</margin> from other things, they are "first"; likewise, because they are not from each other, | one is not prior to the others; thirdly, since they are not from each other, they 
<margin>25</margin> do not possess the nature of identity, nor of similarity, nor of simple diversity, but rather of **contrariety**. However, since this is not immediately obvious, it must be gathered by the following reasoning, by which we introduce the proposal as if from our own perspective.

### ARISTOTLE’S BOOKS ON PHYSICS EXPLAINED

Everything that comes to be, arises from its contrary; whatever is destroyed, is destroyed into its contrary. For indeed, like is not destroyed into like—water does not turn into water—nor is like generated from like, such as water from water (since in <term>generation</term> <note>The process of something coming into existence or being born</note> it is required that something 
<margin>5</margin> new has emerged). Nor does a thing arise from just any random 
different thing; for instance, a musician does not come from a sailor or from a geometer, and a white thing does not come from a philosopher. Rather, whatever | comes to be, comes from a <margin>**25$^r$ B**</margin> 
**non-being** of that specific kind—and not just any non-being. For example, a musician comes from a **non-musician**, not in the sense of a "non-musician" who happens to be white, but 
<margin>10</margin> rather from one who is "unmusical" <note>original: "immusico"</note>, in whom the state of being a musician can succeed the lack of it; that is, someone with a certain aptitude for the skill, combined with the current absence of it. In our school of thought, this is called <term>privation</term> <note>original: "privationem"; a technical term meaning the absence of a quality that a thing should naturally possess, like "blindness" is the privation of sight</note>, which signifies a certain participation in the contrary 
form. For indeed, "white" comes from "non-white"—not 
<margin>15</margin> from just any non-white thing, but from black or some intermediate color. Similarly, when a white thing is destroyed, it ceases to be; it is not destroyed into "unmusical" or "musical," but is understood to be destroyed into "non-white"—not just any "non-white" 
in an infinite sense, but into black or an intermediate, 
<margin>20</margin> into a contrary or a "sub-contrary" <note>An intermediate state that isn't the absolute opposite, but is still on the opposing spectrum</note>.

Because there is a twofold process of coming-to-be and destruction—namely, that of **simple** things and that of **composite** things—it is easy to find the name and the logic of the contrary in simple things, as when 
<margin>25</margin> black comes from white. In composite things, however, it is not so. For when a **human** comes to be, he comes from a "non-human," and specifically from a defined kind of "non-human"—namely, from that **subject** <note>The underlying material or "stuff" that takes on a form</note> which embraced a previous form, which then had to give way immediately upon the arrival of the human form. <margin>10</margin> Finally, we must observe that in a certain way they teach the same things, and in another way, different things. They teach the same things according to the rule of analogy, because they take their contraries from the same arrangement—namely, from the same **ladder of nature** <note>original: "scala naturae"; the hierarchical order of reality from the simplest elements to the most complex beings</note>. In this ladder, by certain steps and a defined order, there is a descent from the first contraries to the lowest, and from the lowest back to the first; there is likewise a defined ascent and descent from the intermediate states to the extremes. Thus, all these thinkers will meet at a single point, because they philosophize and contemplate within a single order. 

<margin>15</margin> In another way, however, they say different things—that is, according to their own specific reasoning, by which some have occupied and chosen different steps on that same ladder. As has been said, some depart further from the senses by ascending toward things **more known to nature**, while others depart further from reason and intellect by descending toward things **more known to us** <note>Bruno uses the Aristotelian distinction: "more known to us" refers to specific, sensory objects, while "more known to nature" refers to the universal, abstract causes behind them</note>.

### That beyond two contraries there must be a third: the subject.

<margin>20</margin> After this, we must consider whether the principles of reality are two, or three, or more, since it has been seen that there is neither just one principle nor an infinite number. 

There cannot be just **one**, because there must be contraries <note>For change to happen, there must be two opposing states, like hot and cold</note>. 

There cannot be **infinite** principles, because things must be capable of being known. Furthermore, it is better—following Empedocles—to establish and assign all things from a finite number of principles, than—following Anaxagoras—to do so from an infinite number. 

<margin>25</margin> For it is in vain and reckless to seek from many what we can nonetheless obtain from fewer—if indeed we can appropriately say "nonetheless" where there is no comparison between what we attain with a few principles and what we pursue with an infinite number. 

<margin>30</margin> Moreover, if there were an infinity of contraries, one could not imagine the **essential character of a principle** <note>original: "ratio principii"</note>, because among contraries some are prior and others posterior (for instance, white and black follow from the rare and the dense...

<meta>This page continues the logical investigation into the number of "principles"—the fundamental building blocks of the universe—as discussed in Aristotle’s Physics. While the previous page categorized the views of earlier philosophers, this page begins a formal critique, arguing that nature cannot be explained by just one or two opposing forces alone; there must be a third underlying "subject" that undergoes change.</meta>

# ARISTOTLE’S BOOKS ON PHYSICS EXPLAINED

...and the **dense**, the **sweet** and the **bitter** follow from the <margin>27v B</margin> **hot** and the **cold**, and the **moist** and the **dry**), but the **principles** <note>original: "principia"; the fundamental starting points or primary causes of reality</note> must be constant and not derived from others, as has been said. Thus it is clear that the principles are neither infinite in number, nor is there only one.

**Text 51.** Someone might easily conclude by doubting that there are only two principles; for, given two contraries, one might ask: "How will **density** produce **rarity**, or the **hot** produce the **cold**? Likewise, how will **friendship** gather **strife** <note>This refers to the theory of Empedocles, who argued that "Love" (Friendship) and "Strife" were the two forces that moved the elements</note> and make something out of it, or conversely, will **strife** pull **friendship** apart and make some third thing?"

**52.** Furthermore, since principles are contraries, it seems necessary that something must be placed beneath them, which would be the **substance** <note>original: "substantia"; the underlying reality or "stuff" that exists in its own right</note> or the **subject** <note>original: "subiectum"; the substrate that remains the same while its qualities change (for example, the wax that stays wax even when it melts from hard to soft)</note> of that contrariety. This is because the very name of a "principle" refers to some subject that acts as the principle; from this it appears that there is a principle behind the principle. It would then follow that, just as a subject is prior to its predicate or attribute, so there will be a principle of the principle.

Furthermore, nothing is contrary to **substance**. That is to say, an **accident** <note>A non-essential quality, like being "hot" or "bitter," which can change without destroying the object itself</note> is not opposed to substance, nor is one substance opposed to another substance. Instead, all contrariety exists *around* substance and *in* substance, but not *as* substance itself. For addition happens within it and around it, but does not constitute the substance itself. Likewise, if these contrary principles are taken in such a way that they are not a specific substance, then this question arises: <margin>16v C</margin> "How will **substance** be originated from things that are not substances? Or how can something else, which is not a substance, exist before substance does?"

# GIORDANO BRUNO

<margin>2</margin> **Text 53. Therefore, to preserve both the earlier reasoning** regarding the opposition of the first principles, and also to ensure we do not make "opposition" the principle itself—as if an **accident** <note>original: "accidens"; a quality or property that can change without destroying the thing itself (like hair color)</note> or quality could exist before **substance** <note>original: "substantia"; the primary "stuff" that has qualities; the underlying reality</note>—we are forced to place beneath these two opposites a certain third thing, or a single nature. This is what the ancients called the "universe" or "that which is," such as water or fire or some middle-ground between them.

->A comparison between those who posit a third thing as the underlying subject for opposites.<-

51. Among those, however, who introduce a third thing as the **subject** <note>original: "subiectum"; the substrate or "canvas" upon which change occurs</note> for the opposites, those are judged to speak more rationally who choose a subject that, by its own nature, does not admit opposition. That is, the subject itself should not be one of the opposites, but rather indifferent to all opposites and capable of receiving all of them, since it must be found in every natural species and individual. For this reason, those who introduced a subject that is less **sensible** <note>original: "sensibile"; meaning something that can be perceived by the physical senses</note> seem to have done better and "caught the scent" of the nature of the thing more closely. Since fire, earth, air, and water are all entangled in their own oppositions, those who introduced a subject different or distinct from these elements did not act irrationally. Among all of them, however, those who chose **air** as the subject seem to have spoken best, because air has differences that are less perceptible—or even least perceptible—to the senses than fire or water. Following them, those who made **water** the subject did better than those who chose **fire**, for fire is the most active of the elements and possesses the most powerful opposition. | Therefore, they shape that one <margin>2</margin> subject, whatever it may be, with opposites, such as **density** and **rarity**, or **excess** and **defect**; hence the ancient opinion that there are three principles: one [the subject], and [the two opposites] superabundance...

<summary>Bruno argues that change requires three principles: two opposing forces and a third, neutral "subject" that undergoes the change. He evaluates which elements (air, water, or fire) the ancients best chose as this neutral foundation, favoring air for its subtle, less-perceptible qualities.</summary>

...and deficiency. But other later thinkers want that **one** thing to be the agent that acts, and those **two** things to be the subjects that are acted upon <note>original: "patiantur"; to be the passive recipient of an action</note>, just as **Plato** did; others, however, want those **two** to be the agents that act, and that **one** thing to be the subject that undergoes change or receives it, such as **Empedocles**, **Anaxagoras**, and ourselves. <margin>17r C</margin>

<margin>5</margin> ->The conclusion that there are no more than three principles.<-

Therefore, to those who examine the matter both from what has been said and from other points that can be weighed, it will appear that there is a specific logic by which the **principles** <note>original: "principia"; the fundamental origins or starting points of all things</note> are no more than three. For although there are many types of **opposites** <note>original: "contraria"</note>, there will certainly be only one primary type; thus, there will be two first opposites, for which a single underlying thing will suffice to undergo or receive change. 

<margin>10</margin> If indeed there were more principles—suppose, for instance, there were two sets of opposites—it would then be necessary for there to be a certain middle nature, separate from both, through which they could unite and come together. But if they generated all other things from one another in this way, one of the sets of opposites would be useless. 

<margin>15</margin> Furthermore, it is impossible for there to be multiple primary sets of opposites, because that would result in several different and distinct categories of things; yet among all categories, there is one that is first, which is **substance** <note>original: "substantia"; the primary "stuff" or essence that exists in itself</note>. Therefore, among the sets of opposites, there is one primary set, which exists within substance or according to substance— <margin>29r B</margin> 

<margin>20</margin> such as the force that causes **generation** <note>coming into being</note> and **corruption** <note>passing away</note>. From this primary set follow those that create hot and cold, large and small, rare and dense, right and left, up and down, and all other things that belong to quality, quantity, relation, position, and so on. 

<margin>25</margin> Since there is one first category and consequently one first set of opposites, by that same reasoning through which in every category there is a certain opposition...

<summary>The author argues that nature requires exactly three principles: two opposing forces and one underlying subject. He maintains that because all things belong to the primary category of "substance," there must be one primary pair of opposites (creation and destruction) that governs all other physical qualities.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the reduction of principles. Having established that principles must be few in number, Bruno now transitions into a detailed analysis of the mechanics of change (transmutation), focusing on how a subject persists through the acquisition of new forms and the loss of old ones.</meta>

# GIORDANO BRUNO

...opposition and the first one; clearly all **oppositions** <note>original: "contrarietates"</note> will seem to be reduced to one, just as every **genus** <note>a general category in logic</note> is first divided by one difference, which is thereafter subdivided by others.

---

->In every change, something must serve as the underlying subject.<-

<margin>5</margin> One thing is said to "become" another in two ways: namely, **simply** or as a **composite**. <margin>170</margin> For example, "the musical" comes from "the unmusical," or "a human" from "a non-human"—this is the simple way. It also happens as a composite from a composite, such as when "a musical man" comes from "an unmusical man." Likewise, "becoming" is expressed in two ways: **substantively**, as when we say "this becomes that" <margin>10</margin> (for instance, "water becomes vapor" or "air becomes fire"); and partly substantively, partly **adjectivally**. When we say "air comes from water," the "becoming" is substantive; when we say "a musical person comes from an unmusical one," the "becoming" is adjectival. For if it were substantive, "unmusicality" itself would have to turn into "musicality," which does not happen. However, when it is said <margin>15</margin> "the unmusical becomes musical," the proposition is true if both are taken substantively—that is, "unmusical" signifies the **subject** <note>original: "subiectum"; the underlying matter or person that remains the same</note> possessing such a **privation** <note>original: "privatione"; the lack or absence of a quality</note>, and "musical" signifies the subject with its **form** <note>original: "forma"; the specific quality or essence being acquired</note>. Thus, while the composite comes from the composite, <margin>291</margin> we use two ways of speaking: "the musical comes from the unmusical" and "a musical man comes from an unmusical man."

**Text 59.** But where something is said to "become" in a simple sense, we must consider what in this **generation** <note>original: "generatione"; the process of a thing coming into being</note> is permanent and what is not permanent. The permanent part is the **subject** itself; the non-permanent part is the **opposite** <note>original: "contrarium"</note> itself, whether taken simply or as a composite. For when a man becomes musical, the subject "man" remains, while the opposite—namely "unmusicality"—ceases to be; likewise, the opposite "unmusical man" ceases to be.

---

<summary>Bruno explains the Aristotelian logic of change, distinguishing between the permanent subject (like a man) and the changing qualities (like musicality) that are gained or lost.</summary>

60. Given these circumstances, we must consider that beyond the two contraries, there must be a certain **subject** <note>original: "subiectum"; the underlying matter or substrate that remains throughout a change</note> which is underlying both contraries; this subject is indeed one in number and serves as the foundation for those things which are two <margin>5</margin> in number.

61. In that context, although it is sometimes permissible to say of a subject that "this comes from this"—for example, "air comes from water," just as from a contrary "hot comes from cold"—nevertheless, it is more proper to say that the **subject** <margin>18<sup>r</sup> fol. C</margin> *becomes* this thing, while the **contrary** is said to *become* this thing *from* that thing. This is universally true for things that do not persist <margin>10</margin>. * * * <note>The asterisks and the critical apparatus below indicate a gap (lacuna) in the original manuscript or a distinction between "becoming simply" and "becoming compositely."</note> Even in these cases, it is sometimes said that "this comes from this," such as "a statue from bronze," but we do not say the bronze *is made* this; for "the bronze does not become the statue" <note>Bruno is distinguishing here between the material (bronze) and the finished form (statue); the bronze exists before and after, but the "statue-ness" is a new configuration.</note>. Likewise, we say "from an unmusical man, a musical man is made" and "the unmusical man becomes a musical man." Therefore, since "becoming" is expressed in many ways <margin>15</margin>—both simply and compositely, of things that persist and things that do not, and in both direct and indirect forms—one must conclude from all this that a single subject underlies the two contraries.

63. However, regarding **generation** <note>original: "generatione"; the process of coming into being</note> and **substantial change** <margin>30<sup>r</sup> fol. B</margin> <margin>20</margin>—the topic we are currently dealing with and for whose principles we search—we observe that things do not come to be as a sort of composite or from a composite. Indeed, we are not considering accidental change, but substantial change. Regarding this, we must note in our proposal that among things that come to be **simply** <note>original: "simpliciter"; change involving the very substance of a thing rather than just its traits</note>, some come to be by **transfiguration** <margin>25</margin>, such as a statue from bronze (insofar as it does not take on a new quantity or substance, but only a shape); others by **addition**, such as a tree from a seed; others by **subtraction**, such as a statue from stone; others by **composi-** <note>The text breaks off here; likely "compositione" or "composition."</note>

...[composi]tion, as a house is made from stones and wood; others by transformation, as water is made from snow.

64. From all of these examples, it is right to observe that what is produced is always a certain **composite** <note>original: "compositum"; something made of multiple parts, specifically matter and form</note>; for form is neither produced nor destroyed, and likewise matter is neither produced nor destroyed. If it were otherwise, these would not be **principles** <note>original: "principia"; the fundamental starting points that cannot be broken down further</note> at all, but would instead be **derived products** <note>original: "principiata"; things that come from principles</note>. Furthermore, "becoming" is spoken of in two ways: in one way, it is meant **absolutely** <note>meaning something begins to exist as a substance, like a human being born</note>, and in this sense we mean what we have just said; in the other way, it is meant according to a certain mode or <margin>18</margin> with an addition—namely, when we say "this becomes | *this*." In this latter way, "becoming" seems to apply to the principles themselves; for the **subject** <note>the underlying material</note> does not "become," but rather it becomes *this* specific thing. The same is true for the opposite.

### 65. That the three principles are, in a certain sense, two.

Defining the number of principles, we can say that in one sense there are two, and in another sense there are three. There are indeed two **intrinsic principles** <note>internal to the thing itself</note> existing "in themselves"—whether in the finished thing or in the process—which have the character of an **element**. However, there are three if we include the principle that has the character of a **cause** or a **primordial mover** <note>original: "principiantis"</note> rather than an element. This is the **contrary** which we call **privation** <note>original: "privatio"; the absence of a form, such as "unshaped" before a statue is made</note>. We say this belongs more to the process of **generation** <note>the act of coming into being</note> than to the things already generated, because such a principle is of the kind that is not seen within the finished product; therefore, it is considered a principle **by accident** <note>original: "secundum accidens"; it is necessary for the change to start, but it doesn't stay as a physical ingredient in the final result</note>.

Since all things come to be from principles, one of these is that which always maintains the same character, namely the **subject**; the other...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Aristotle's principles of nature from the previous page. # EXPLANATION OF ARISTOTELIS'S BOOKS ON PHYSICS.

...[in the same way, the things] which change around the subject—namely, what approaches and what departs—are **contraries**. That which departs, or the contrary that is cast away, is called by the name of the 'contrary' or **privation** <note>original: "privatio"; the absence of a form or quality that should naturally be there</note>; while the contrary that approaches and remains in the composition is called the **form**.

67. From these points, it is clear that one is free to say there are two or three principles, depending on different perspectives; likewise, one may say the principles are contraries or not contraries. There are **two** principles if we look at the elements from which the resulting thing is composed. In this view, there is no place for "privation," because when we define the **subject**—that is, when we give its essential definition—we are satisfied with **matter** and **form**. But there are **three** principles if we look not at the finished product, but at the process of **production** <note>original: "productionem"; the act of coming into being or "becoming"</note>. In this process, it is impossible for a new form to arrive unless the previous one departs. This is because it is impossible for two **substantial forms** <note>original: "formas substantiales"; the fundamental essence that makes a thing what it is, such as "human-ness" or "oak-tree-ness"</note> <margin>19r C</margin> to exist in the same subject at once; a single matter cannot belong to two different essences or two different species simultaneously. Furthermore, we say the principles are **not contraries** if we consider those things which exist in themselves <note>original: "per se"; things that exist in their own right rather than as a property of something else</note>; for form is not a contrary to matter, nor is it the opposite of matter. | <margin>31r B</margin> Moreover, it is permissible to call the principles **contraries** if we look at those two things which have the nature of form [the form being lost and the form being gained]. These cannot coexist in the same subject. Because of this, as was said above, nothing is made except from that which is its opposite and, in some sense, its contrary.

->On Matter.<-

Then, **generations** <note>original: "generationes"; the process of things being born or coming into existence</note> arise from contraries, under which a single subject is always understood to reside. The contraries themselves—that is, the forms—have a distinct name and definition; but the subject itself has neither its own specific name nor a definition...

<summary>Bruno explains that there are two principles (matter and form) when considering a finished object, but three (matter, form, and privation) when considering the process of change. He emphasizes that two fundamental essences cannot occupy the same matter at the same time.</summary>

(For every definition and name is derived from the **form**); therefore, in and of itself and absolutely, [matter] is indefinable, unnamable, and unknowable. It is, however, known, named, and defined—as first the Pythagoreans <note>Followers of Pythagoras who believed numbers were the ultimate reality</note>, and later Timaeus and <Plato> taught—
<margin>5</margin> through a certain **analogy** <note>original: "analogiam"; a comparison between two things to show their similarity</note>, that is, a likeness and proportion to the subjects of artificial [man-made] things. For just as the wood remains a single **matter** <note>original: "materia"; the raw "stuff" that makes up an object</note> under the craft of a carpenter, being the same and one in all the things that are made through that craft, and every change occurs around that one and the same thing; so also in the multitude of
<margin>10</margin> forms which nature produces into the open, one must understand there to be only one **subject** <note>original: "subiectum"; the underlying thing that stays the same while its appearance changes</note>. This subject, moreover, is known through its analogy to the various forms that are seen to occur successively around it; for what was food, later becomes **chyle** <note>original: "chylus"; a milky fluid produced during digestion, once thought to be a distinct stage of transformation</note>, then blood, then sperm, then an
<margin>15</margin> embryo, and so on. In these forms, which follow one another such that one does not arrive unless the other departs, it is manifest that one **substantial form** <note>original: "forma substantialis"; the essential nature of a thing</note> does not "receive" or turn into another,
<margin>19v</margin> but | there is a third thing which, while it was previously under one form, is immediately after under another, and then, in order and succession, will be under all of them: that thing is **matter**.

<margin>31v</margin> 70. And so, we have spoken of the **principles** <note>original: "principiis"; the fundamental starting points or elements of nature</note>: how they are two, how they are more, how two are contraries, and how a third thing must be placed under them as a subject. Furthermore, how these principles relate to one another and what the subject actually is, is not yet
<margin>25</margin> manifest.

71.
