Contrary to the simple way of being is that which arises from heat as well as that which arises from cold. In its complete form, this is putrefaction <note>The process of organic decay or rotting.</note>; in its incomplete form, it is a kind of path or state, such as old age and dryness, the ultimate end of all which is a withered decay <note>original: "marcedo"</note>. <margin>5</margin> Putrefaction is also not strictly said to be the end of those things which are destroyed by violence. For if flesh and bone were to be burned (whereas their natural end is putrefaction), they instead belong to the general <margin>49</margin> category of "corruption" <note>original: "corruptio." In this context, it refers to the breakdown of a complex substance into its basic elements.</note>. Indeed, both moist and dry things are subject to rotting. Corruption occurs when a thing is <margin>10</margin> broken down according to its parts, which are then separated from one another, because that which limits and contains dominates over that which is limited and contained. And for this reason, since fire is the limit-giver <note>original: "terminativus." Fire was considered the most active element, defining the boundaries of others.</note> of all elements, it alone is said not to rot. For earth rots into the water that <margin>15</margin> contains it, water into the air that contains it, and air into fire. Furthermore, putrefaction is the destruction of that natural heat which resides within every moist thing. Therefore, putrefaction seems to be defined by a lack of its own heat, since cold and heat meet in <margin>20</margin> the process of rotting in such a way that putrefaction is defined as a shared suffering <note>original: "passio." In the philosophical sense, this means a state of being acted upon by an external force.</note> caused by an external coldness. Putrefaction is followed by a permanent dryness; for all things that rot eventually become drier. As the internal heat departs, that natural moisture also evaporates, which <margin>25</margin> was maintained by the operation of the heat. Consequently, once the active principle is removed, its specific effect must also necessarily be removed. In winter, and when cold weather is most dominant, less rotting occurs, because external heat (which usually [interacts with] internal heat...)

...is an imperfection caused by a lack of its own internal heat in the passive opposites. Concoction <term>Concoction: From the Latin *concoctio*, meaning "cooking together." In Aristotelian physics, this refers to any process where internal heat brings a substance to maturity or perfection, including digestion and ripening.</term> is primarily a species closely related to generation, taking the name "generation" in a broad sense; for, as has been said, it is rather a certain perfection of the thing generated. Of this, in turn, there are three species: **ripening**, **boiling**, and **roasting**; while of "inconcoction" <note>original: *inconcoctionis*; the failure of the cooking/ripening process.</note> there are just as many opposites: **rawness**, **contamination**, and **scorching**. <margin>69v B</margin> Indeed, we do not provide these names of the species as strict technical terms, but as well-fitted analogies, since better ones cannot be devised. 

Item, it should be noted that in the definition, it is said to be "perfected by its own internal heat"; this does not, however, exclude external aids from contributing to perfect concoction and ripening, such as: food, baths, the local climate, and similar things. Item, one must consider how the principles of concoction and ripeness apply in their own way across all the various kinds of subjects that undergo them. For we do not only speak of apples on trees as being "ripe," but similarly a **fetus in the womb** is called mature, as is **concocted food** in the stomach, **must** <note>Young, unfermented wine.</note> in the wine-vat or in the cask, and even a **swelling** or an **abscess** when it has turned to pus. For this reason, nearly all such things are signs of health, just as they are judged in urine, excretions, and waste products— <margin>51r C</margin> which are called "concocted" for this | reason: because they indicate that the **internal heat** is dominating the moisture. Item, the "concoctible" matter—that is, matter subject to this process—is always thicker, more astringent <note>original: *stypticior*; meaning contracting or bitter.</note>, and harder, just as the matter of a thing already concocted is more broken down, manageable, and soft.

### On the types of concoction and inconcoction.

-><-

Among those things that are called "ripened" and "concocted," some are spoken of <margin>70</margin> | properly, and others metaphorically. Those things are called concocted and ripened—and thus perfected—in the **proper** sense when the seeds <margin>5</margin> within them are able to produce another thing of the same kind as themselves. These are called "mature" by a specific name and the term refers to fruits and other things that emit seed; for example, fruits are mature when their seed can produce something similar. Other things, however, are called "mature" metaphorically or by **transference**, <margin>10</margin> seeing as we cannot use another name for these other things because no better name has been assigned or could easily be assigned, as was said above. Therefore, in one way it is called "mature" in the most proper sense; subsequently, it is used properly for all things that are brought to their limit by natural heat or cold. <margin>15</margin> Hence, **swellings** and **phlegm** <note>original: *pituitae*; in the medical theory of the time, "phlegm" was one of the four humors that needed to be "cooked" by the body's heat to be expelled.</note> are said to be "ripened" by natural heat concocting the moisture existing within them. In these cases, when the spirituous substances <note>original: *spirituosa*; the subtle, gaseous fluids believed to circulate in the body.</note> are matured, they become watery; when thin substances are matured, they become thicker. Just as maturation is a certain perfection of <margin>20</margin> natural heat, so **rawness** <note>original: *cruditas*; the state of being "undigested" or "unripened."</note> is its imperfection. Rawness, like maturation, is spoken of in many ways; for **urine**, **excretions**, and **distillations** are called "raw" because they have not been overcome by natural heat. Furthermore, in a more common sense, **pottery** is called raw <note>i.e., un胜fired earthenware.</note>, and **milk** and many other things are called raw <margin>25</margin> which have not been acted upon by heat in a suitable manner. | **Boiling** <margin>70</margin> <term>Boiling: original *elixatio*; the process of "cooking" or "perfecting" something using moist heat.</term> is concoction by a moist heat existing throughout the whole of the thing being boiled, within a limiting liquid. In these cases, then, the concoction is performed by the fire that is within the moisture, where the excretion is driven out by the external moisture through heat. However, things that are **roasted** in pans <margin>30</margin> are acted upon by an external heat, but not a moist one.

A **boilable** <note>original: *elixabile*; referring to the process of boiling or seething, known in Greek as *hepsesis*.</note> body is one in which there is a moisture capable of being overcome or affected by fire, or by the heat existing within the moisture. For the "boilable" is not distinct from these things, unlike a stone, in which <note>The original text contains a gap here. Based on Aristotle, this likely means "there is no moisture" or "no moisture can escape."</note> although moisture may be present, it cannot be overcome due to its thickness, whereas in wood it is overcome. | <margin>51ᵛ C</margin> Wood, gold, and many other things are said to be "boiled" **metaphorically**; for no other name has been assigned to the way they undergo this species of <term>concoction</term> <note>Concoction (*pepsis*) is the general Aristotelian term for any process where natural heat matures or transforms a substance.</note>. Milk, must <note>unfermented grape juice</note>, and similar things are also said to be boiled when the flavor within their moisture is transmuted into some new form by external fire or heating air. Just as there are different methods of boiling and concocting, so too are there different ends; some are directed toward **eating**, some toward **sipping**, and others toward some other use; indeed, we even say that medicines are boiled.

Therefore, "boilable" things are all those that can become thicker, smaller, heavier, thinner, or more refined, such as whey, curds, etc. **Oil**, however, is not boiled in and of itself—at least when pure—because it undergoes none of these changes. It makes no difference whether boiling occurs through artificial instruments or natural ones, nor does the medium or the efficient cause change the nature of the process.

### On soddenness.

**Soddenness** <note>original: *inquinatio*; translating Aristotle’s *molypsis*, referring to an imperfect or failed boiling where the heat is insufficient.</note> is the <term>inconcoction</term> of that which is indeterminate within a body, occurring due to a deficiency of heat. This happens when the concocting heat surrounding the moisture is driven out by cold; for this reason, sodden things are harder than those that have been properly boiled.

### On Roasting.

**Roasting** <note>original: *assatio*</note> is a <term>concoction</term> <note>Concoction (*pepsis*) refers to the "ripening" or processing of matter by heat.</note> produced by a dry and external heat. Roasting differs from **boiling** because boiling transforms and ripens through the heat of moisture, whereas roasting does so through the heat of **fire**. Thus, roasting comes from dry heat, and for this reason, in roasting, the outer parts are drier than the inner parts; however, in boiling, the inner parts are drier than the outer. In man-made things <note>referring to culinary or chemical preparations</note>, there is a greater need to roast than to boil, because it is difficult to heat the exterior and interior parts equally, since <margin>10</margin> the internal and external are not at an equal distance from the heat of the fire. Nor can they be affected equally, since the parts closer to the fire are dried out more quickly; as the outer passages <note>or pores</note> close up, the moisture existing inside cannot be expelled, but remains trapped within. It is otherwise in boiling; for after <margin>15</margin> the moisture has penetrated along with the heat impressed upon it, it acts more easily through all the parts.

->That an animal is not formed during concoction, as some believe,<-
->but in a certain excretion or waste, which putrefies in the lower belly.<-

For the **Peripatetics** <note>The followers of Aristotle, named for their habit of walking while teaching.</note> propose three locations of digestion and three <margin>20</margin> operations of digestion: the first is in the **stomach**, where the digestion occurs that distinguishes the <term>chyle</term> <note>The milky fluid of digested food.</note> from the thicker waste products; subsequently, this chyle is ripened in the parts near the **liver**, where the second digestion occurs. From here, the thicker waste is moved into the urine, which is expelled through the bladder, while the more refined part becomes the <margin>25</margin> **four humors**: blood, yellow bile <note>original: *cholera*</note>, phlegm, and black bile <note>original: *melancholia*</note>. According to their opinion, the blood especially is carried to the heart along with a certain influence from the others...

of the humors, which are then spread by the power of the heart throughout the entire body, using the **vital spirit** <note>original: *spiritu vitali*; in Renaissance physiology, a subtle substance that carries life and heat from the heart.</note> as a kind of vehicle. There is also another kind of excretion <note>original: *egestionis*</note> that occurs through all parts of the body; for something always flows out and is expelled from the entire skin, <margin>5</margin> and from the matter of this final excretion, things like nails and hair are generated. Thus, the living being <note>original: *animal*</note> is formed in that excretion which is second in order, namely in the lower belly, since the seed and the humors closest [to the being] in form are born so that they may be converted into the substance of the nourished body from the finer parts <margin>10</margin> which are separated from that **concoction** <note>original: *concoctione*; the process of "ripening" or "cooking" matter into a usable state.</note>. For concoction or digestion is nothing other than the separation of the finer parts from the coarser ones, of which the finest serve the work of nature. This is the order by which a living being is formed after concoction; however, according to the opinion of the physicians <note>referring to followers of Galen</note>, there is a different <margin>15</margin> judgment. They are content with a "proper" double digestion: speaking more broadly, they hold that the first occurs in the palate and in that grinding <note>original: *contritione*</note> which takes place in the mouth. These same people, unlike others, do not later accept that secretion of spirits which occurs in the heart, but instead fix the seat [of digestion] in the **liver** <note>original: *hepate*</note>, which they claim to be the <margin>20</margin> source of the blood. The philosophers <note>The Peripatetics/Aristotelians</note> think otherwise, for they claim the source of blood <insert>is the heart</insert>; <margin>52v C</margin> the liver, however, is like an ocean, while the veins are like rivers. They view the nerves of the sensory and motor spirits as a certain very fine body diffused through the nerves, which is necessarily spread from the heat and life of the heart. <margin>25</margin> Regarding universal digestion, by which something flows out from the whole body, they seem to have neglected to treat it rashly—though the omission of the digestion that occurs in the heart is excusable, since it is not so perceptible to the senses.

<summary>This page contrasts the anatomical theories of 'physicians' (Galenists) and 'philosophers' (Aristotelians) regarding the heart and liver's roles in digestion and blood production. It describes how the finest parts of matter are refined into vital spirits and bodily structures like hair and nails.</summary>

### On moisture, dryness, hardness, and softness.

Moisture is easily limited <note>original: *terminabile*; meaning it easily takes the shape of its container or boundary.</note>, and the moister a thing is, the more easily it is limited—namely, by a boundary belonging to something else. Dryness is limited with difficulty. Furthermore, moisture is the reason that dryness is bounded, and dryness is the reason for moisture, not only in the elements—where water is limited <margin>5</margin> by the earth below and above, and air is limited by fire—but also in compounds, as in mixtures where water defines the flour, and the flour defines the water <note>A classic Aristotelian example: water holds the flour together into dough, while the flour gives the water a stable shape.</note>. Since earth is the most properly "dry" of the elements, and water is the "moist," the whole logic of bounding and defining is directed toward water in compounds; hence, nothing is defined <margin>10</margin> without these two, and these are the very matter of bodies. For this reason, living beings are never generated anywhere except in earth and water. Following moisture and dryness, two qualities naturally succeed them: namely, hardness and softness. The hard is that which does not give way into itself <margin>15</margin> along its surface; the soft is that which gives way into its own depth when the surface is compressed. Something is called more or less hard or soft according to whether it gives way more or less in this manner. Thus, water is not "soft," because it does not give way by the compression of its surface, but is instead penetrated <note>Bruno distinguishes between "softness" (like wax) and "fluidity" (like water), which allows objects to pass through it rather than just deforming.</note>.

<margin>20</margin>Chapter II. Therefore, it is necessary for the hard and the soft to be limited by their own boundary; for they are defined by the compression or the resistance of their own surface. Drying and hardening, and moistening and softening, are related actively to active qualities, and passively to passive qualities; as it has been said, the <margin>25</margin> "patient" <note>original: *patiens*; the thing being acted upon or receiving the change.</note> exists because of moisture or dryness, while the "agent" <note>the thing causing the change.</note> exists because of heat and cold. All drying is either the drying of water or of something watery, while all moistening is of earth or something earthy. Therefore, of the elements, <margin>30</margin> earth and water seem to be the most passive. <sig>53</sig>

Consequently, heating and cooling, or moistening and drying, occur either essentially <note>original: *per se*</note> or accidentally <note>original: *per accidens*</note>. Essentially, water moistens; however, fire and the sun also moisten accidentally by breaking down thickened and solid matter into water, moisture, and air. Likewise, they moisten by driving moisture or cold from the external parts to the internal, or from the lower parts to the 5 upper (for in this way the middle region of the air and the middle part of the earth are moistened and cooled). This latter process occurs through **antiperistasis**, which is to say, through the juxtaposition of opposites <note>A theory in ancient physics where a quality is intensified or displaced when surrounded by its opposite, such as cold concentrating in a cellar during a hot summer.</note>. Drying happens in two ways: either from moisture added to a surface or from moisture that is innate; 10 in the first way, soaked wool is dried, and in the second, milk, water, and so on. Drying occurs either by the action of heat or cold, and this happens either internally or externally. Internally, it occurs by heat causing the moisture to evaporate—as when a moderately damp garment is dried by the internal heat causing the 15 moisture to evaporate—and externally, as by the sun or by fire. In both cases, drying is achieved by the removal of moisture or by its solidification <note>original: *concreto*</note>; removed, indeed, by heat, or solidified by cold.

...of **earth**, as in milk and blood. Likewise, there are certain moist substances in which there is a greater amount of earth, such as niter <note>likely saltpeter or natron</note>, salt, and certain stones, which seem to be classified in this category and solidify in a similar manner. If the whey is not removed from milk, it is easily boiled down <margin>5</margin> by fire (for it burns and evaporates just like water); but once the whey—which is the watery part—is separated, and rennet <note>original: *coagulum*; a substance used to curdle milk</note> is added to strengthen its density, it thickens significantly more, evaporates very little or not at all, and provides more nourishment. Diseased blood does not clot, or clots less; it is a sign of unhealthy blood when it fails to clot.

Those things which solidify by means of cold and dryness are dissolved by heat and moisture, and therefore by fire and water. However, for those things which solidify from two causes, it happens that they become insoluble, such as bricks; for in that case, <margin>15</margin> when the heat has "sweated out," the majority of the moisture is compressed by the cold, and for that reason they are not dissolved back into their original form by either heat or cold. For it is common for those things to be dissolved which solidify from cold alone, such as mud thickened by cold, or snow. Iron, having been liquefied by heat and <margin>20</margin> solidifying again by cold, is insoluble. Wood contains both **earth** and **air**, and therefore it cannot be melted or softened, but is combustible; and because it has a greater amount of air, it floats on water. Of all the various types of wood, ebony alone does not float, because there is more earth in it than air, <margin>25</margin> much or all of which has evaporated. Pottery <margin>54</margin> <note>This marginal number likely refers to a leaf number (folio 54) in the original manuscript</note>, moreover, once it has been hardened by fire, consists of earth alone, and is not afterwards dissolved by water; for once it has solidified, the water has no entry through the pores through which the more subtle spirit <note>original: *spiritus*; referring here to fine vapors or air trapped within the clay</note> departed, nor is it dissolved by fire, because the fire itself was what bound it together.

<margin>25</margin> is a burning with the simultaneous discharge of the dry and the moist by the power of heat; but when the discharge is of the moist alone, it is instead called **evaporation**.

## How bodies are recognized to consist more of the moist or the dry.

Of bodies, some are **similar**, others are **dissimilar**: similar bodies are, first, the elements; second, metallic things such as gold, copper, silver, etc.; third, other minerals, stones, and gems;
<margin>5</margin>and fourth, those found in animals and plants, such as flesh, bones, nerves, skin, etc. <note>In Aristotelian terms, "similar" (homogeneous) parts are those where any small piece is the same substance as the whole, whereas "dissimilar" (heterogeneous) parts are complex organs.</note> Others are **dissimilar**, such as plants—which consist of wood, bark, leaf, root, etc.—and the parts of animals, like the face, hand, and foot. Among similar things that are types of earth, such as stones and wood, it is easy to recognize that the
<margin>10</margin>**dry** predominates if more of the substance remains as sediment than is lost through the evaporation of fire and heat. Truly, some things, even if nothing or very little evaporates or exhales, are seen to consist mostly of the **moist** because they are liquefiable, and they are of a watery nature <note>original: *aqueae naturae*. Ancient science classified metals as "watery" because they could be melted into liquid.</note> (although all things that evaporate from moist bodies are water, not all things that are
<margin>15</margin>water evaporate, on account of the metals). Some things are common to earth and water, such as milk; some to earth and air, such as honey; some to water and air, such as oil. When wine is new, it belongs more to the earth; when it is old, it is more airy. New wine evaporates more and is thickened greatly by
<margin>20</margin>heat and is solidified less by cold; likewise, it has more earth because it has not been purified. <note>original: *defecatum*. This refers to the settling of dregs or sediment.</note> From this, it happens that it is more capable of being thickened, as is clear from the fact that the Arcadians <note>A reference to a people in ancient Greece noted in classical texts for this practice.</note> dry wine in skins by hanging them in smoke, so that it may then be scraped off and drunk. <margin>| In 56</margin> Among those things that are solidified by cold, water dominates in some,
<margin>25</margin>such as hail, snow, frost, etc.; in others, however, earth dominates. Those things which are solidified by heat include cheese, nitre <note>A term for naturally occurring saltpeter or sodium carbonate.</note>, and pottery. In pottery, because all the moisture has sweated out, earth clearly dominates; however, in those things where the moist remains on account of its own viscosity...

<margin>10</margin> heat. <margin>15</margin> ->The activity of bodies is more evident than their substance.<-

There are some things which, when they are transformed, show the change of nature clearly through many signs, just as when ash is made from wood, or smoke from fat; but in some things it is not so, such as in the limbs of a living man and a dead one. Someone 
<margin>20</margin> might think that the flesh of the living and the dead is the same, and the eye the same; however, these are spoken of no less equivocally <note>original: "aequivoce." This refers to the idea that a "dead eye" is an eye in name only, as it cannot see.</note> than a painted eye, a stone eye, and a living eye; likewise a lyre or a stone tortoise-shell <note>original: "fides seu testudo." Ancient lyres were often made from tortoise shells; Bruno is contrasting a decorative stone version with a functional musical instrument.</note>, and a true one which has its own activity and purpose. 
<margin>25</margin> The nature of a substance, therefore, is indicated by its acts or operations, just as any form is observed through its powers, since actions follow from potential, and potential from essence. Therefore, those things are of one and the same species which perform one and the same activity;

In the same way, an eye that does not see, a tongue that does not taste, or flesh that does not feel, are spoken of **equivocally** <note>original: "aequivoce." In Aristotelian logic, things are "equivocal" when they share the same name but have different definitions. For example, a "real" eye and a "stone" eye are both called "eyes," but only one performs the function of seeing.</note> with that which senses, tastes, and sees. Some people only perceive a difference when the flesh has significantly wasted away, as in the bodies of those long dead; however, the wiser perceive it as soon as sensation and life are gone. 
<margin>5</margin> For this <insert>dead</insert> flesh no more belongs to the species <note>original: "speciei." Here meaning the true nature or essential form of a thing.</note> of true flesh than it does when it has become ash. In the category of inanimate bodies, one is the same as the other; thus, one differs no less than the other in terms of their substance, <note>original: "secundum substantiam." Substance refers to the essential reality of a thing, rather than its appearance.</note> regardless of any accidental similarity. <note>original: "accidentali similitudine." An "accident" is a property that can change without changing the thing's essence. A dead body has the "accidental" appearance of a person, but its "substance" has changed.</note> Just as in these cases there is a change in substance that is sometimes difficult to recognize, the same happens in other things—in plants, air, silver, blood, and the like—where obtaining certain knowledge is even more difficult.

# (ON MAGIC.)

Before discussing Magic—just as before discussing any subject—the name must be divided into its various meanings. There are as many meanings of "magic" as there are types of "magicians."

<margin>5 1)</margin> First, "magician" is used to mean a wise person. Examples of this kind include the followers of Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Trimegisti"; Hermes Trismegistus was a legendary Egyptian figure believed to be the author of the Hermetic Corpus, a series of sacred texts on philosophy, magic, and religion</note> among the Egyptians, the Druids among the Gauls, the Gymnosophists <note>original: "Gymnosophistae"; a term meaning "naked philosophers," used by the Greeks to describe Indian yogis or ascetics who lived in the forest</note> among the Indians, the Cabalists among the Hebrews, the Magi among the Persians (who descend from Zoroaster), the *Sophi* <note>original: "Sophi"; from the Greek *sophos*, meaning "wise"</note> among the Greeks, and the <margin>10 2)</margin> Sages among the Latins. Second, "magician" is used for one who performs wonders solely through the application of active and passive forces <note>in Renaissance science, "active" qualities were typically heat and cold, while "passive" qualities were moisture and dryness</note>, as is the case in medicine and chemistry in their general sense; this is what is commonly called <term>natural magic</term> <note>natural magic was considered a legitimate science that used the hidden, but natural, properties of herbs, stones, and metals</note>. <margin>3)</margin> Third, magic occurs when circumstances are added to these natural acts so that the works of nature or of a higher intelligence seem to be manipulated to provoke <margin>15</margin> wonder through appearances; this is the species called <term>prestigiatory</term> <note>original: "praestigiatoria"; from the Latin for "juggling" or "illusion," referring to magic that deceives the senses or uses "glamour"</note>. <margin>4)</margin> Fourth, magic arises from the power of <term>antipathy and sympathy</term> <note>the belief that all things in the universe have natural attractions (sympathies) or repulsions (antipathies) toward each other</note> between things—for example, through those things that repel, transform, or attract, such as types of magnets and similar objects. These works are not reducible to mere active and passive qualities,

<meta>This page continues the list of definitions for magic from the previous page. It concludes the tenth category (prophecy vs. sorcery) and begins a deeper philosophical analysis of the term "magician," contrasting the scholarly definition with the common religious superstitions of the time.</meta>

-># GIORDANO BRUNO<-

<margin>10)</margin> Our people do not label these with the name of "magicians," for among them the word "magician" carries a bad reputation due to its unworthy misuse; instead, it is called not magic, but **prophecy**. Finally, "magician" and "magic" are taken in an unworthy sense, so that they are not numbered among the previous types, nor should they be. In this sense, a magician is an evildoer <term>maleficus</term> <note>original Latin: *maleficus*; one who uses magic to cause harm</note>, however 5 foolish, who, through commerce with an evil spirit <term>cacodaemon</term> <note>original: *cacodaemone*; from the Greek *kakodaimōn*, meaning an evil spirit or demon</note> and a certain pact, has been instructed <note>original: *informatus*; shaped or equipped</note> with the power to harm or help. According to this reasoning, the word is not used by wise men or even by grammarians themselves, but by certain 10 **hooded ones** <note>original: *bardocucullis*; literally "cloaked in a heavy hood," a derogatory reference to monks</note>, such as the one who wrote the book *The Hammer of Witches* <note>original: *De malleo maleficarum*; a famous 15th-century treatise on the prosecution of witches</note>. This is how the word is used today <margin>8r1</margin> by all writers of this sort, as can be read in the commentaries, catechisms, and dreams of ignorant priests. 

15 <margin>59</margin> Therefore, when the name "magician" is used, it must either be understood with a clear distinction before it is defined, or, if it is taken in an absolute sense, then according to the precept of logicians—and especially **Aristotle** in Book V of the *Topics* <note>original: *V. Topicorum*</note>—it must be understood in its most powerful and noble 20 sense. As it is used by philosophers among philosophers, a **magician** means a **wise man with the power to act**. Nevertheless, it happens that when the word is uttered simply, it is taken for what it signifies in common speech. And yet, there is one common speech among one type of priest and another among those who philosophize much about a certain evil spirit 25 who is called the **Devil** <note>original: *Diabolus*</note>, and quite another according to the common customs and beliefs of various nations.

With this distinction having been established, we generally accept a threefold magic: **divine, physical, and mathematical**. Magic of the first and second kind is necessarily of the genus...

<summary>Giordano Bruno clarifies the definition of "magician," distinguishing between the "wise man" of philosophy and the "evil sorcerer" feared by the Church, specifically critiquing the Malleus Maleficarum. He introduces a three-part classification of magic: divine, physical, and mathematical.</summary>

...the monad <term>monas</term> <note>The "Monad" refers to the ultimate, indivisible unit of reality—the source of all being, often identified with God or the One</note>, who are the cultivators and inhabitants of the stars (one of which is the earth), descends into daemons <term>daemones</term> <note>In Bruno’s Neoplatonic philosophy, "daemons" are not "demons" in the modern sense, but intermediary spirits or intelligences that inhabit the elements and the celestial spheres</note>, then daemons into elements, elements into mixtures <term>mixta</term> <note>Physical bodies composed of a combination of the four elements</note>, mixtures

Soon, the living being ascends through the mind to the senses, through the senses into mixtures, through mixtures into elements, through these into daemons, through these into
<margin>59v</margin> the stars, through these into the incorporeal Gods | (whether of ethereal substance or of corporeality), through these into the soul of the world <term>anima mundi</term> or the spirit of the universe, and through this into the contemplation of the One—the most simple, best, greatest, incorporeal, absolute, and self-sufficient being. Thus, from God there is a descent through the world to the living being; conversely, there is an ascent for the living being through the world to God. He <note>God</note> is at the peak of the ladder—pure act and active power, the purest light. At the root of the ladder, however, is matter: darkness, pure passive power <term>potentia passiva</term>, which is just as capable of becoming all things from the bottom as He is capable of making all things from the top. Between the lowest and highest steps are the intermediate species; the higher ones participate more in light, act, and active virtue, while the lower ones participate more in darkness, potency, and passive virtue.

Whence all light found in the lower things, since it reaches them through the higher, exists more eminently in the higher things. Likewise, all darkness found in the higher things exists more strongly in the lower. However, the proportion and efficacy of darkness and light are not equal; for light diffuses and penetrates even to the lowest depths of darkness, but darkness does not reach the purest orb of light in the same way. Therefore, light comprehends darkness, and conquers and overcomes it by an infinite margin.

<summary>Bruno describes the "Scale of Nature," a metaphysical ladder connecting God (the Monad and Pure Act) to Matter (Darkness and Pure Potency), detailing how the soul can ascend through various stages of being to reach divine contemplation.</summary>

...lest the wicked race of men turn [this knowledge] toward the destruction rather than the benefit of their fellow kind. <note>Bruno often prefaces his magical writings with warnings that these secrets should not fall into the hands of those who would use them for harm, a common trope in Hermetic literature.</note>

<margin>9r M</margin>
**(Thesis VI.)** Generally, there are two types of efficient cause <term>efficiens</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, the "efficient cause" is the agent or force that brings something into being or initiates change.</note>: nature and will. Will, in turn, is threefold: human, demonic <note>original: "daemonis." Bruno refers to "daemons" in the classical Greek sense—spirits that act as intermediaries between the divine and the mortal—rather than exclusively evil entities.</note>, and divine. Nature, for our current purpose, is twofold: intrinsic and extrinsic. Intrinsic nature is further divided into two: matter or the subject, and form with its natural power. Extrinsic nature is also twofold: that which is rather called the "image" <term>effigies</term> of nature—a trace and a shadow or light—and that which remains in the thing and on the surface of the subject, such as light and heat in the sun and in other hot things; and finally, that which emanates and flows out from the subject, such as the light which is shed by the sun and found in illuminated things, and the heat which [is found] with light in the sun and found in heated things. <note>Bruno is distinguishing between the internal essence of a thing and its external "radiation" or influence on the world around it.</note>

<margin>60r</margin>
From the contemplation of the number of these causes, we can descend to the diffusion of power or the production of effects, moving from the first cause through the intermediate ones down to the nearest and lowest. This is done by limiting the universal cause—which does not regard this subject more than that—toward a particular effect, by disposing a specific subject more than it was previously disposed. <margin>According to the 2nd book of Aristotle's *Physics*</margin> Since the cause and its power remain immutable, contrary effects (not just different ones) are produced according to the diverse reception <term>subiectio</term> and management of the matter. <margin>One cause acts in different respects—not because of changes in itself, but because of how other things relate to it. This refers to an immutable cause, such as the Sun and the Heavens; the Sun does not become more hot or cold, and yet it produces contrary effects. Likewise, there are "separate substances" (spiritual beings) which, though immobile themselves, move other things.</margin> Wherefore, on the part of the efficient principle, that one and simple thing suffices—just as one sun, one heat, and one light—which, through turning toward or away, and through proximity or distance, produces winter and summer both mediately and immediately.

<summary>Bruno defines the types of efficient causes—nature and will—and explains how a single, unchanging source of power (like the sun or God) can produce diverse or even opposite effects depending on how the recipient is "disposed" or positioned.</summary>

Yet, within the order of the universe—which is filled with a single spirit diffused everywhere—there is a sense that exists everywhere and in all directions. Depending on the capacity of each thing, it feels such effects and passions, as can be observed in all objects.

...if it has a connection with the **World Soul**, that impossibility often cited regarding physical bodies—which cannot occupy the same space at the same time—does not follow. For in spiritual substances, the logic of this matter is different. It is just as if countless lamps were lit, <margin>5</margin> which combine into the power of a single light; it does not happen that one lamp's light hinders, blunts, or excludes another's. A similar thing occurs with many voices diffused through the same air at once, or likewise with many visual rays (to use common phrasing), because they are deployed to perceive the same visible object as a whole. Here, <margin>10</margin> all rays penetrate through the same medium—some obliquely and others directly—and they do not for that reason dull one another. In the same way, innumerable spirits and souls diffused through the same space do not hinder one another, such that the diffusion of one would block the diffusion of infinite others.

<margin>15</margin> Since such power belongs not only to the soul, but even to certain **accidents** <term>accidents</term> <note>original: "accidentium." In the philosophy of Bruno's time, an 'accident' is a property or quality (like color, sound, or heat) that exists in a thing but is not the thing itself.</note>—such as <margin>Folio 11v, Manuscript M</margin> | voice, light, and sight—by that same logic the soul is entirely in the whole and in any part of the body. And because it captures distant and diverse **forms** <term>species</term> <note>original: "species." Here meaning the sensory images or "blueprints" of objects that travel through the air to be perceived by the mind.</note> all around itself far beyond its own body, it is a sign that <margin>20</margin> according to its primary act and substance, it is not enclosed within the body. That is to say, it is not in the body **circumscriptively** <note>original: "circumscriptive." This is a technical term meaning to be contained within physical boundaries, like water in a cup.</note>, but only **definitively** <note>original: "definitive." This means the soul is "defined" by where it acts; it is present wherever its power is felt, rather than being stuck in one physical spot.</note> in terms of the secondary acts to be unfolded within and through the body. Behold the principle by which the cause of countless effects—which cause such wonder—is brought forward; its reason and power are sought. This divine substance and soul should not be in a worse condition than the **accidents** which proceed <margin>25</margin> from it as its effects, traces, and shadows. If, I say, a voice operates outside the body where it is born, and is present as a whole in countless ears all around...

Why should that substance which produces the voice not be entirely in various places and parts, and bound to certain members?
   To these points, it must also be observed that **hidden intelligences** <term>hidden intelligences</term> <note>original: "intelligentiae occultae." From this, certain signs | <margin>**62^r C**</margin> leaning toward one another, looking at one another, and embracing one another are arranged for **love**; conversely, those turning away and scattered are for **hatred and divorce**; those cut short, mangled, or disrupted lead to **destruction**; knots lead to <margin>15</margin> **binding**, while unfolded characters lead to **dissolution**. And these are not fixed in a certain and defined form, but anyone—according to the dictate of their own **inspired passion** <note>original: "furoris." Such were the more suitably defined letters among the **Egyptians**, which are called **hieroglyphics** or sacred characters, in which there were certain images for designating individual things.

->Concerning the regard for the communion or fellowship of things.<-

From this, one may believe and consider the cause by which action is directed not only toward nearby things, but also toward distant things according to the senses; for in reality, as was stated above, this occurs through the **communion of the universal spirit** <note>original: "spiritus universalis." Also known as the *Anima Mundi* or World Soul, this is the invisible "breath" or life-force that Bruno believes permeates every inch of the universe, linking all things together regardless of distance.</note>, which is entirely in the whole and in every part of the world. Thus it happens that, just as different lights meet together in the same space, so too various **souls**—whether in potential or in act, and whether finite or infinite in number—are associated together in the universe. 

**Bodies** are not like this, for their being is defined circumscriptively <note>meaning they have strict boundaries or "circumferences."</note> by their own surface or periphery, and they consist of various and innumerable parts in various and innumerable places (where by "place" we understand "space"). Thus, in no way can a body act upon another body, nor matter upon matter, nor can parts of the same matter and body act upon other parts of a body; rather, all action comes from **quality**, from **form** <note>In the philosophical tradition Bruno follows, "form" is the internal blueprint or soul of a thing that gives it its specific identity and power.</note>, and ultimately from the **soul**. 

This [the soul] first changes the **dispositions** <note>Internal states or arrangements of a thing's nature.</note>, so that the dispositions may then change the bodies. In this way, a body acts on a distant body and on a nearby one, and on its own parts, through a certain **consensus**, bond, and union which comes from the form. And because every body is therefore ruled by a soul or by a certain spirit connecting parts to parts—just as it happens that one soul acts upon another everywhere and from every side as if it were near—so it also necessarily happens that it acts upon the body, wherever it may be...

...that which serves and underlies that soul. Therefore, whoever understands this indissoluble continuity of the soul and how it is bound to the body by a certain necessity will possess a significant principle, both for practical action <note>meaning the practice of magic or "operating" on the world</note> and for a truer contemplation of the nature of things. 

<margin>13r</margin>
From this, the reason why a **vacuum**—meaning a space without any body—does not exist will be readily apparent; for one body does not withdraw from a place unless another immediately follows it. While the soul leaves its own specific body at the end of life, it cannot truly leave the **universal body** <note>original: "universum vero corpus." Bruno suggests that while we lose our individual physical form, our essence remains within the physical fabric of the entire cosmos.</note>; or, if you prefer, it cannot be abandoned by the universal body. For in leaving one simple or composite thing, it is carried into another, whether composite or simple; or, having left one body, it is caught or supported by another. 

Thus, the soul has an indissoluble bond to **universal matter**; and because the soul's nature is whole and continuous everywhere, it recognizes corporeal <note>physical</note> matter as something that exists everywhere. From this follows the conclusion that a vacuum does not exist if we define it as "space without a body." Rather, a vacuum is simply a space in which different bodies follow one another and move. 

<margin>63v</margin>
From this also comes the continuous motion of the parts of one body toward the parts of another—specifically, through continuous and uninterrupted space. It is not as if an empty void sits as a gap between one full thing and another, unless we choose to call "vacuum" a space in which there is no **sensible body** <note>original: "corpus sensibile." A body that can be perceived by the five senses, like a stone or a tree, as opposed to "insensible" bodies like thin air or light.</note>.

(Thesis XVIII) A truly continuous body is an **insensible body**—specifically, an airy or ethereal spirit—and this is the most active and effective of all, because it is most closely joined to the soul. 
<margin>We call "spirit" the subtle, insensible body, but "soul" the governing substance that is entirely present everywhere.</margin>

...and the presentation of ideas. From this it follows that, since forms are diverse and contrary—differing also in the logic and distinctions by which some coincide with others—so too the points of contact and impulse are contrary. Some things flee from others, and some pursue others; all of this proceeds from the condition of their composition.

And just as all things desire to be preserved in their own being, so they are pulled away unwillingly from the place of their own preservation and stability, resisting with a strength that is not easily overcome. 
<margin>5</margin> This resistance is so powerful that the sun or fire cannot draw water toward itself through the space of the air until it has first assimilated that water to the air—that is, converted it into the consistency of vapor. <margin>15</margin> consent. Thus, by gradually approaching closer and closer to the likeness of fire, it finally becomes fire itself.

...indissoluble bodies, most solid, having no continuity or divisibility in themselves, and therefore they are not convertible into another body; for the substance of water, or spirit, or air—which is one and the same—will never migrate into the <margin>5</margin> substance of atoms or the "dry" principle, nor vice versa.

<margin>15</margin> ->On the twofold motion of things and attraction.<-

The motion of things is twofold: natural and preternatural <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "preternatural" refers to things happening outside the usual course of nature, often due to external forces, whereas "natural" movements come from within the object itself.</note>. Natural motion is that which comes from an intrinsic <term>principle</term> <note>An internal source or cause.</note>; preternatural is that which comes from an extrinsic principle. Likewise, natural motion is that which is <margin>20</margin> suited to the nature, stability, or generation of a thing; preternatural is that which is not. And this latter is twofold: violent, which is against nature; and ordered (or coordinable), which is not repugnant to nature. Commonly speaking, natural motion is held to occur according to all classes or categories, by those who do not <margin>25</margin> distinguish between motion and change. <meta>This page continues Bruno's classification of the types of motion. He began to define motion as either natural (things in their proper place) or preternatural (things out of their place).</meta>

<page-num>418</page-num>

# JORDANUS BRUNO

...twofold: one belongs to things naturally established and dwelling in their own proper place—and this motion is either circular, or imitates circular motion; the other is of natural things not naturally established <note>i.e., things that have been displaced from where they "belong" in the cosmic order</note>, and this motion is straight.

<margin>5</margin> For air moves in a straight line to fill a **vacuum** <term>vacuum: an empty space. Bruno lived in an era where the possibility of a "void" was a major scientific debate</term>; in a straight line <margin>14<sup>v</sup></margin> a stone is carried through the air, and heavier bodies are carried by penetrating through water, so that they may reach a place in which they might either rest naturally or be moved. In a straight line, as much as possible, <margin>10</margin> an opposite flees from its opposite—as smoke, vapor, and water flee from fire (for along that line they are led more quickly to a greater distance).

<margin>✓</margin> In a straight line also, like tends toward like and what is suitable to itself—as **chaff** <term>palea: light straw or husks</term> moves toward **amber** <term>ambram: Bruno is referring to static electricity, where rubbed amber attracts light objects</term>, and iron toward a magnet, so that they may better and more effectively find rest or move together.

<margin>15</margin> There is a third species of motion, <margin>64</margin> which is the **flux and influx** <term>fluxus et influxus: the constant flow of particles or "effluvia" moving in and out of all matter</term> of all parts from all natural bodies, which from every side eject something from themselves according to a manifold reason; and this motion for the time being shall be called **spherical**. For it is <margin>20</margin> not according to a single straight line—either as if moving from a center, or toward a center, or around a center—but according to infinite lines as if from the same center. This is because all bodies cast out and emit something from their internal depths from the entire curved perimeter or surface; and conversely, they also receive and take things into themselves.

Things grow and are strengthened when <margin>25</margin> the influx of suitable materials exceeds the efflux; but on the contrary, they grow old, decrease <note>original: "decrescunt." One manuscript version says "crescunt" (grow), but the context of aging suggests "decrease."</note>, and become sluggish when the influx of foreign materials and the efflux of natural materials becomes greater. Finally, from this cause, corruption and change exist in things—all of which change is either alteration or dissolution * * * <note>The original text contains a gap or "lacuna" here; the early editors noted they could not determine what words were missing.</note>. Regarding the two motions of the first kind...

***

<summary>Bruno defines three types of motion: circular (natural state), straight (returning to a natural state or fleeing opposites), and spherical (the constant exchange of matter/energy between bodies). He explains that growth and decay are the results of the balance between the "influx" and "efflux" of these particles.</summary>

<keywords>circular motion, straight motion, spherical motion, vacuum, magnetism, static electricity, flux and influx, growth and decay, Giordano Bruno, physics</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Bruno’s discussion of the "flux and influx" of particles. Having just mentioned that all things are in a state of constant emission and reception, he now distinguishes between the types of influences that travel from one body to another—ranging from the physical (heat, sound, smell) to the spiritual (emotions and magical fascinations).</meta>

<page-num>419</page-num>

->### ON MAGIC<-

...there is no controversy regarding the senses, as the consideration and listing of them is common knowledge; however, to one who considers more deeply, a third kind <note>Bruno is likely referring to a third category of "effluvia" or influence—beyond the purely physical and the purely sensory</note> will be found to be not only true and fitting, but even necessary. That which is perceptible to the senses is most evident in those things that have the most sensible qualities, as in fire, 
<margin>5</margin> which does not heat in just one direction or part, but all around; wherever it is suddenly kindled, it inflames and illuminates in every direction. So also voice and sound, when the medium <note>the air or environment through which sound travels</note> is equally disposed in all directions, penetrate equally in every direction. 
<margin>10</margin> Likewise, regarding the sense of smell, it is clear from <insert>**15^r M**</insert> fragrant things that certain particles continuously flow out; for that **accident** <term>accident: in philosophy, a property (like a scent) that cannot exist on its own but must belong to a substance</term> does not travel around unless it is composed of specific parts or a specific substance flowing out. Similarly, along with the **species** <term>species: the "form" or image of an object that travels through the air to the eye</term>, the **simulacrum** <note>a mental or physical representation of an object</note>, and other such sensible accidents, 
<margin>15</margin> countless other properties are poured out with certain specific parts. These parts are remarkably distant from those smallest sensible things, as is evident even in some things which, no matter how small their quantity, remain fragrant for many years. Beyond these kinds of sensible qualities 
<margin>20</margin> or powers, which are transmitted **spherically** <note>moving outward in all directions like an expanding ball</note> from bodies, there are others—more spiritual and subtle—which act not only on the body and the senses, but also on the inner spirit, and reach the deeper faculties of the soul by instilling certain emotions and passions, as is 
<margin>25</margin> commonly known regarding the power of many stones, roots, and minerals. This is also evident in fascinations <note>magical charms or "the evil eye"</note> and in those things which are accomplished actively and passively through a glance of the eye—just as the **basilisk** <note>original Latin: *regulus*; Greek: *basiliskos*. A mythical serpent said to kill with its gaze</note> kills with the sharpness of its sight, even when seeing a person from a great distance.

<summary>Bruno explains how physical properties like heat, sound, and smell radiate in all directions via tiny particles, then argues that spiritual and magical influences—such as the power of gems or a basilisk's gaze—operate through similar, though more subtle, spherical emissions.</summary>
<keywords>effluvia, sensation, fire, sound, smell, species, spiritual power, fascination, basilisk, spherical radiation</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Bruno’s exploration of the hidden forces of the world. Having established that all things emit "effluvia" or particles, he now categorizes the types of "attraction" that exist in nature—ranging from the magnetic pull of iron to the physical suction of a vacuum—to explain how objects influence one another at a distance.</meta>

<page-num>420, 64</page-num>
<header>GIORDANO BRUNO</header>

->How the magnet draws iron, coral draws blood, etc.<-

(XXII.) From these points follows the reasoning by which the **magnet** <term>magnet: Latin *magnes*, believed in the Renaissance to possess a "soul" or a specific vital force that sought out iron</term> attracts according to its kind. Furthermore, attraction is of two types: one is **by consent** <term>by consent: Latin *ex consensu*, referring to a natural harmony or agreement where things move toward what is like themselves or toward their natural home</term>, as when parts are moved toward their whole, or things to their proper place, where like things are snatched up by like things, and compatible things by compatible things; the other is **without consent**, as when a contrary is drawn by its contrary because of the victory of that which the other cannot escape. An example is when moisture is snatched away by fire, as is evident in a heated basin placed over a basin containing water, which is swallowed up by the power of the heat so that it ascends rapidly. The same is manifest in the **vortices and whirlwinds** <note>original: *vorticibus et turbinibus*</note> that occur in the sea, such that sometimes even ships themselves, along with the waves, are snatched up into the heights to a great distance.

In fact, such snatching happens in three ways. One way is through **sensible reasons** <margin>15^v</margin> <note>causes that can be perceived by the senses, such as heat or visible motion</note>, as in the cases just listed, and also where, through the attraction and absorption of air, those things which are in the air are also drawn in. This is also evident in the pipes through which water is swallowed, ascending in every direction of space by following the stated principle; because, once the air contained in the pipe is drawn out, and since other air cannot move in to take its place, water or earth or something else must succeed it to fill the space. But if nothing is able to succeed it, the air itself is called back and held by the very force of the space, as is sometimes evident to those who are sucking or drinking with the opening obstructed, whose tongue or lips <note>The text ends mid-sentence, describing the physical sensation of a vacuum pulling on the mouth</note>...

<summary>Giordano Bruno distinguishes between "attraction by consent" (natural harmony between similar things) and "attraction without consent" (violent or physical forces like heat and vacuums). He uses practical examples like magnetic pull, whirlpools, and the suction of water through pipes to illustrate how matter is moved by these invisible forces.</summary>

<keywords>magnetism, attraction, vacuum, natural philosophy, suction, elements, harmony, Giordano Bruno</keywords>

<meta>This page continues Bruno’s classification of physical and hidden forces. He transitions from explaining mechanical suction (like a vacuum or pump) to "insensible" attraction, specifically magnetism and the behavior of fire, which he attributes to the movement of atoms and a natural "appetite" between similar things.</meta>

<page-num>421</page-num>
<header>### ON MAGIC</header>

By the power of the mediating and compressed air, they are most tenaciously glued to the orifice and, conversely, sucked out, so that the **spirit** <term>spirit: Latin *spiritus*, referring here to a subtle, vaporous substance or air-like matter within the pores of a body</term> is drawn out from their pores to restore or refresh what had been taken away from that place or space.

There is also another species of insensible attraction by which the **magnet** draws iron. We cannot attribute the reason for this to a vacuum or anything of that sort, but only to the **efflux** <note>the flowing out of tiny, invisible particles</note> of parts from all bodies, or of **atoms**. For it happens that when atoms of one kind reach atoms of a similar or related nature, or of a generative species, and they encounter one another, then an **appetite** <note>a natural "desire" or inclination of matter to move toward what is compatible with it</note> and an impulse of one body toward the other is kindled. Consequently, the whole that has been overcome moves toward the more powerful whole; for toward that which all parts have an impulse, the whole must also move. 

This is visibly clear in lit lamps: if a nearby lower lamp is extinguished, the flame will descend—as if snatched downward—through its smoke or those flowing **spirits** (which are in a state ready to become flame or fuel for fire) to relight the lower torch. This is also seen in the small flames of a torch which, lest they perish once the **moisture** <margin>**65ʳ C**</margin> <note>original: *humore*; Renaissance science believed moisture or "oily" humidity acted as the fuel for fire</note> in their own substance is consumed, manifestly strive toward matter arranged nearby—namely, to the place of a larger flame—traveling or advancing <margin>**16ʳ M**</margin> in a straight line or across. 

So it happens with the "overcome" parts of iron, which run toward the magnet in every direction through another kind of virtue or attracted quality. For not every operation in natural things and such mixtures is to be referred solely to **active and passive qualities** <note>Aristotelian qualities like hot, cold, moist, and dry</note>, although sometimes...

<summary>Bruno argues that magnetism is not caused by a vacuum but by the "appetite" of atoms seeking their own kind, comparing the way a magnet draws iron to how a flame can travel through smoke to relight a wick.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Bruno’s discussion of "insensible attraction," specifically focusing on magnetism and electricity (static attraction) as explained through his theory of atomic "efflux." He moves from general principles to specific examples like amber and medicinal rhubarb to distinguish these forces from standard elemental qualities like heat or cold.</meta>

<header>### GIORDANO BRUNO</header>

they must also necessarily concur, though not primarily. That this attraction arises through the **efflux of parts** <note>the streaming out of invisible, subtle particles or atoms</note>, which occurs from such subjects, is indicated by the fact that a **magnet** <note>lodestone</note> that has been rubbed, and **amber** <note>original: *ambra*; referring here to yellow amber which exhibits static electricity when rubbed</note> when drawing straw, and iron are all greatly 
<margin>5</margin> strengthened; for that heat induces a greater efflux of parts, the power of which is to open the pores and rarefy the body.

It is also clear from this how, in its own way, **rhubarb** <note>original: *rhabarbarum*; used in Renaissance medicine as a purgative</note> draws **bile** <term>bile: or *cholera*, one of the four bodily humors believed to cause illness if out of balance</term> from the extremities or 
<margin>10</margin> peripheral parts of a living creature toward the intestines. This happens when it is of sufficient strength—not so strong, I say, that it is expelled by nature before it can work, nor so 
weakly that it merely moves the humor and does not attract it. That the attractive power and efficacy in the magnet and similar things 
<margin>15</margin> does not come from a passive or active quality—according to the common understanding of action or passion, such as is found in the forms of the **four elements** <note>earth, water, air, and fire</note>—is signaled by the fact that the iron itself, once it has been touched by a magnet, is imbued with the same power of drawing 
other iron. If this power came from an elemental quality, 
<margin>20</margin> this would not happen; for heat and cold, which come to subjects accidentally, vanish once the heating agent is absent. It is necessary, therefore, to refer this to the efflux of parts: those parts which, flowing out from the magnet, have flowed into the iron as a **spiritual substance** <term>spiritual substance: *spiritalis substantia*, referring to a subtle, vaporous matter that carries force, rather than something "supernatural" in the modern sense</term>.

It is difficult to devise another reason or even a likely one 
<margin>25</margin> for these effects. Once this reason is perceived—which is consistent with itself in every respect—it is easy to examine the various chimeras and dreams with which others have fabricated the causes of this attraction.

The same judgment and cause apply to the claim that a **diamond** <margin>16<sup>v</sup> M</margin> is said to hinder this attraction; similarly, various other things, which are born with their own particular **efflux** <note>the streaming out of invisible, subtle particles or atoms</note> of power, are able to dull the power of another, just as others strengthen and sharpen it—as it is said that the diamond imprints **high-mindedness** <note>original: *magnanimitatem*; the belief that certain gemstones could instill moral virtues in the wearer</note> upon the soul of the one wearing it.

(XXIII.) Regarding the attraction of the **magnet** <note>lodestone</note> by the pole, it is not easy to provide a cause, unless that which they say is true: that in 그 region very many and great mountains of a similar species are found—though this is difficult to believe. For suppose that were true: the question remains why such attraction occurs at every distance. For we are not speaking here of the passive rather than active attraction of the magnet; whether one magnet truly attracts another magnet, I have not yet tested this. 

Furthermore, if such mountains exist and possess power at such a great distance, <margin>65<sup>v</sup> C</margin> surely if they attract a needle from the **torrid zone** <note>the tropics, the hottest part of the earth</note> or the tropics, they ought to attract armed men from our own regions; but this seems altogether ridiculous. Consider also that the magnet attracts iron when nothing lies between them but air, and it does so in a straight line; yet, from our regions to those parts where the mountains and cliffs of lodestone are, beyond the **Northern Sea** <note>the Arctic</note>, the great **bulge of the earth** <note>the curvature of the globe</note> stands in the way.

Therefore, the magnet would attract iron or (if it attracted by reason of likeness) another magnet, if, while our magnet was at point A, the mountains were at point D; but they are necessarily found at B or C, so that a great distance clearly intervenes...

<summary>Giordano Bruno critiques the contemporary theory that compasses point North due to giant magnetic mountains, arguing that such a force would be strong enough to pull armored men and would be blocked by the Earth's curvature.</summary>

...whether marked by the straight line AB or AC, then also the immense **swelling of the earth** <note>original: *tumor terrae*; refers to the curvature of the globe which, in Bruno's argument, would physically block a "straight line" of magnetic pull from distant mountains</note> marked by the arcs AB and AC. Therefore, that commonly held and famous reasoning <note>the theory that mountains at the pole pull the needle</note> appears [absurd] <note>The transcription says *absoluta* (absolute/finished), but the editor suggests *absurda* (absurd), which fits the context of Bruno's critique</note> in many ways. And to these stated reasons we also add this: that those magnetic mountains <margin>5</margin> do not possess the power of attracting a magnet by reason of **similarity** <note>the idea that "like attracts like"</note>; for if that were the case, we would see a large magnet attracting a small piece of another magnet. Therefore, we do not provide some "attraction" as the cause of this effect—because, as has been said, it would be more reasonable for iron to be attracted from that source—but rather a **flight born of antipathy** <note>original: *fugam ex antipathia*; Bruno suggests the needle isn't being pulled by something it loves, but is turning away from something it "dislikes" or is fundamentally different from</note>; <margin>10</margin> for the nature of that mineral <margin>17</margin> <note>referring to the lodestone/magnet</note> and of iron is indeed contrary, as they are **offspring of the earth** <note>original: *foetus terrae*; products or "children" of the terrestrial element</note> and of a cold, earthy consistency. Thus, the opposite happens to them as happens to almost all **flowers**, which turn toward the sun and follow it by looking toward the sun's path; [the magnet] not only...

<summary>Bruno uses geometry to argue that the Earth's curvature would prevent polar mountains from attracting magnets in a straight line. He proposes that magnetic orientation is caused by "antipathy" (repulsion from a contrary force) rather than "sympathy" (attraction to a similar one).</summary>

->**Epilogue of the movers by which things are moved.**<-

We find that **local motion** <term>movement from one place to another</term> occurs for several reasons:

1.  **First**, for the consistency and preservation of life, which is achieved through motion. By the power of the soul and the **innate spirit** <note>original: *spiritus nativi*; the vital "breath" or force that Bruno believed animated all matter</note>, things move circularly within their own place, as was said above.
2.  **Second**, through flight from a **contrary** <term>an opposing or harmful force</term>.
3.  **Third**, through the pursuit of what is suitable or good.
4.  **Fourth**, through expulsion or being thrust out by a driving contrary force.
5.  **Fifth**, through a violent attraction, even of a contrary, caused by the needs or appetite of the mover for matter that can be converted into itself.
<margin>66r C</margin>
6.  **Sixth**, through **animal choice** <note>movement driven by the senses or the will of a living being</note> coinciding with the consent of a natural power.
7.  **Lastly**, through **violence** <note>in the Aristotelian sense: motion forced upon an object against its natural inclination</note>, which by art or by some effort of nature hinders natural forces and twists them elsewhere. Or even by nature itself, which while strong in one part to move something, hinders and blunts the nature of another movable object of lesser power, as happens almost everywhere; for the natural flow of one body of water is hindered by the meeting of the flow of another, as occurs in...

<margin>
That the magnet flees heat and the sun is also evidenced by the fact that it is damaged and destroyed by heat, which dissolves its parts, as is evident in the greater outflow of substance that proceeds from such bodies when they have been heated...
</margin>

<summary>Bruno classifies the seven types of local motion, ranging from internal biological drives to external "violent" forces. He uses the way plants and magnets react to heat to argue that movement is often a survival mechanism—either seeking what is good or fleeing what is harmful.</summary>

->**On the bonds of spirits.**<-

<margin>5</margin> <note>original: *Nihil est sine anima, plantæ sunt animata...* "Nothing is without a soul; plants are animated... and others."</note> It was stated above that some spirits inhabit **denser** matter and others **subtler** matter; some reside in composite bodies and others in simpler ones; some are in **sensible** <term>perceivable by the senses</term> things, others in **insensible** things. For this reason, the operations of the soul are readier for some, more difficult for others, blunted for some, adapted for others, and taken away from others. <margin>10</margin> Likewise, some operate more powerfully according to one genus, and others according to another; hence, certain operations, acts, and pleasures are given to humans which are denied to **demons** <note>In Bruno’s philosophy, *daemones* are not necessarily "evil" but are intermediary spirits or "intelligences" that occupy different levels of the cosmos</note>, and vice-versa. For the demons, however, there is a readier penetration regarding bodies and the insertion of thoughts, since <margin>15</margin> they thrust certain impressions into the **internal senses** <term>the faculty of imagination or "phantasy" where the mind processes sensory data</term> to such an extent that we sometimes seem to think for ourselves the very things that they suggest. Indeed, their communication seems to hold itself proportionally—and there is a certain analogy—to the way someone might wish to rouse a specific sense. <margin>20</margin> From a greater distance, there is need for a shout, so that through the sense of hearing, concepts may be led to someone’s internal sense. When nearby, a shout is not needed, but rather a lowering of the voice; when closest of all, it is enough to whisper into the ears. For a demon, however, there is no need for ears themselves, nor for a voice, nor a whisper; instead, <margin>25</margin> it penetrates the internal sense itself directly, as has been said. In this way, they not only send dreams and cause voices to be heard, but also whatever...

...that hears and understands voices, yet does not distinguish between the possible and the impossible, the suitable and the unsuitable, in the manner of dreaming men and those whose **imagination** <term>phantasia: the mental faculty that processes sensory images</term> is disturbed; and this kind is usually driven from bodies by the very threats of death, imprisonment, fire, and the like.

They are skilled in languages and sciences, but they assert nothing with constancy, as they are an envious kind who instill confusion and doubts into the minds and senses of men.

Truly the **ethereal** kind, pure and bright, all agree is entirely good and a friend to upright men, but an enemy to none; just as among the aerial ones, some are friends to certain people while others are enemies and hostile.

But the **watery** and **terrestrial** ones are either enemies or not friends, as they are less rational and therefore more fearful, and according to that saying: 
> "whom they fear, they hate" <note>original: *quem metuunt, oderunt*. This is a famous line by the Roman poet Ennius, quoted in Cicero’s *On Duties* (De Officiis) 2.7.13.</note> 
and they gladly cause harm.

But the **fiery** ones, who are more properly called Gods and heroes, are said to be the ministers of God, whom the Kabbalists <note>Followers of Jewish mysticism</note> call **Ishim** <note>original: *Fissim*. This likely refers to the *Ishim*, the lowest rank in the Kabbalistic hierarchy of angels, often associated with human-like forms or "man-like" souls.</note>, **Seraphim**, and **Cherubim**, of whom the Prophet of the Psalms said: 
> "who makes his angels spirits, and his ministers a flame of fire"; <note>original: *qui facit angelos eius spiritus, et ministros eius flammam ignis*. See Psalm 104:4, also quoted in Hebrews 1:7.</note> 
from which **Basil** and **Origen** <note>Early Christian theologians (Church Fathers) known for their philosophical approach to scripture.</note> correctly gather that angels are not entirely incorporeal, but **spiritual substances**—that is, animals of a most subtle body—whom divine revelation signifies through fires and flames of fire.

In every order of spirits there are presiding officers and princes, shepherds, leaders, rulers, and ranks, by which the wiser and more powerful rule and command the weaker and more unrefined; and these empires are not eternal, nor are they of such <margin>5</margin> short duration as human ones, since their lives are in many ways incomparable to our lives, | just as it is easier for a soul to unite with a **simple body** <term>simplex: a body consisting of a single element, like pure air or fire, rather than a complex mixture</term> <margin>67^r C</margin> than | one **composed** of opposites, such as ours. <margin>18^v M</margin> They easily maintain that their bodies are very easily **penetrable** <term>passibilia: capable of being acted upon or permeated by external forces</term>, <margin>10</margin> just as air is penetrable, or water, more so than certain composite bodies. Furthermore, they are restored with that same ease, just as divided air is very easily made whole again, and parts of water flow back together after they have been pierced. It is not a playful or poetic fiction when **Virgil** <note>referencing *Aeneid* 6.260 and 290–291</note> asserts that **Aeneas**, passing through the places of the shadows with a drawn sword, terrified them. <margin>note: ...history from the fable... etc. M</margin>

Other spirits inhabit human bodies, others the bodies of other animals, others plants, others stones and minerals; and absolutely nothing is devoid of spirit and intellect. Nowhere has a spirit obtained an eternal seat destined for itself, but <margin>20</margin> matter fluctuates from one spirit to another, and from one nature or composition to another; likewise, the spirit fluctuates from one matter to another. This is **alteration**, **change**, **passion** <term>passio: the state of being acted upon by an external agent</term>, and finally **corruption**—namely, the separation of certain parts from other parts and their composition with new ones; for death is nothing other than **dissolution**. And yet, neither any spirit nor any body...

<summary>Bruno describes the hierarchical social structure of spirits and explains their physical nature as being composed of single elements, allowing them to be easily divided and instantly healed like air or water. He concludes by arguing that all matter is infused with spirit and that death is merely a process of material and spiritual reorganization.</summary>
