nothing perishes, but there is only a continuous change of **compositions** <term>complexionum: the specific combination of qualities or elements that make up a body</term> and **activities** <term>actuum: the active operations or "ways of being" of a substance</term>.

According to the various activities that proceed from various compositions, there are various loves and hatreds, since <margin>5</margin> all things (as has been said) desire to consist in their present state of being; for they either understand nothing of another state or a new way of being, or they are in doubt of it. Therefore, there is a certain general bond of reciprocal love of the soul toward its own body and (in its own way) of the body toward the soul. From this depends <margin>10</margin> the diversity—arising from the variety of natures and the attachments of the bonds by which both spirits and bodies are bound—about which we must soon deliberate, after we have defined the **analogy** <term>analogia: the proportions or hierarchical relationship</term> of spirits and composite beings.

### On the analogy of spirits.

<margin>15</margin> **Porphyry**, **Plotinus**, and other **Platonists** <note>Porphyry and Plotinus were foundational 3rd-century philosophers of Neoplatonism, a school of thought that heavily influenced Bruno’s ideas on the soul and the hierarchy of the universe</note> distribute bodies to spirits in such a way that the purest and best, who are even designated by the name of **Gods**, are of a fiery substance as far as their body is concerned, and they claim this substance is the most simple and pure. Those, <margin>20</margin> however, who consist of other thicker elements, do not exist without the participation of a subtler element, <margin>19^r</margin>| so that those of the **air** <margin>67</margin>| possess air mixed with fire; those of the **water** possess air with fire; and those of the **earth** possess air and water with fire. They are invisible substances because of the thinness of their bodies. Furthermore, the terrestrial and aqueous ones are sometimes made visible at will by **condensed and thickened vapor** <note>original: "concreto et inspissato vapore"</note>, and they even appear in purer regions where the air is more serene and tranquil. I have happened to see them at the mountains of Liber and Laurus <note>original: "montes Liberi et Lauri"; likely referring to peaks in the Campanian region near Bruno's home in Italy</note>, and not I alone; they frequently appear to the inhabitants of that place. To them, they are sometimes (though only moderately) troublesome, leading away and hiding livestock, only <margin>5</margin> to bring them back to their own stalls after a few days. That there are subterranean demons is confirmed not only by the senses, experience, and reason, but also by a certain divine authority <margin>25</margin> in the book of Job—the work of a most wise man of great and profound philosophy. Origen <note>An early Christian theologian (c. 184–253 AD) known for his theory of the pre-existence of souls</note>, Pythagoras, | <margin>19v</margin> and the Platonists even number human beings among the <term>daemons</term> <note>original: "daemones"; in the Neoplatonic sense, these are not necessarily "demons" but intermediary spirits or rational souls</note>. For this reason, both Christian theologians and the better schools of <margin>15</margin> philosophers call this life a certain path and passage, a pilgrimage and a military service <note>original: "militiam"; referring to the concept of *militia est vita hominis super terram* (the life of man on earth is a warfare)</note>. And this is what we were saying from the beginning: <margin>20</margin> that every spiritual substance is reduced to one, and every material substance to three <note>Bruno refers here to his metaphysical system where the "One" is the formal/soul principle, while matter is often categorized by three primordial qualities or elements</note>; the soul is one—its own God—and the first mind is one above all things, and the soul of the universe is one.

In addition to these things, it is very likely that all diseases are evil spirits, which is why they are driven away by song, prayer, contemplation, and <margin>25</margin> the ecstasy of the soul, and are provoked by their opposites. <margin>If indeed in stones and plants and their parts and roots there are certain powers that penetrate even to the soul, by instilling fear, joy, or magnanimity—as with the onyx—then all the more so can there be certain powers in certain men according to certain orders and numbers.</margin>...illuminators, through whose power certain types of diseases are dissipated, as they say of Cyrus and other kings of the Persians, who cured those with spleen ailments by the touch of a thumb. For it was by these spirits that sacrifices and the slaughter of animals were invented; they have declared themselves to be greatly delighted by the preparation and the smoke of these offerings. These beings must possess a <term>complexion</term> <note>A term from medieval medicine referring to the physical constitution or balance of humors in a body</note> very similar to our own; among them, some are partial to certain races and nations while detesting and loathing all others. 

Some of these spirits are famous, well-known, and more powerful, while others are more plebeian, whom the Romans called "gods of the plate" <note>original: "patellares Deos"; minor household deities to whom small food offerings were made on a special dish (patella)</note>, specifically those for whom there were no fixed sacrifices or offerings. It is not credible that such dishes are as necessary to them as they are pleasurable (for they are able to acquire what is necessary for themselves by their own means); nevertheless, these things are sought out for their luxury, which they could <margin>20r M</margin> | least of all provide for themselves without human assistance. For even if they know many things better than we do, they cannot move or alter many things as effectively as we can, because they are of a more spiritual, noble, and refined constitution. But corporeal substance differs from this kind of substance of the mind, the soul, and the sublime spirit, in that the entire body is a whole within the whole and the universe, while the spirit itself is entirely present in any part, clearly constituting a certain whole everywhere and reflecting an image of the whole—in some places more clearly, in others more

into a thousand pieces, it nevertheless reflects the image as a whole from all the parts. So also the various parts and underlying essences <term>hypostases|The individual expressions or 'subsistences' of a single underlying reality</term> of water, when torn from the whole Amphitrite <note>original: "Amphitrite"; a Greek sea goddess, here personifying the sea as a single entity</note> or the universal Ocean, receive different names and properties; yet all of these, subsequently flowing together into one Ocean, have one name and property. Thus, if all the parts of spirit and air were to flow together into one Ocean, they would produce one soul—though they are otherwise many and innumerable. Hence, according to their primordial consistency, philosophers say there is one matter, one spirit, one light, one soul, and one intellect.

<page-num>436</page-num>
<header>GIORDANO BRUNO</header>

...metaphysics. In the first part is the foundation, in the second the steps, in the third the summit of the ladder: the first concerns the nature of active and passive principles according to their kind; the second concerns times, places, and numbers; the third concerns universal principles and causes. This is the "threefold cord, which is not easily broken." <note>A reference to Ecclesiastes 4:12, suggesting that these three levels of knowledge combined provide a strength that cannot be easily undone.</note>

(§ V) The second bond <term>vinculum|a magical link or "binding" that connects the practitioner, the ritual, and the object of the magic</term> is threefold, being required in the practitioner, in the act itself, and in the subject upon whom the operation is performed. It consists of faith or belief, as well as invocation, and finally love and ardent affection, combined with the application of active forces to passive subjects; for it is the nature of the soul to effectively change bodies or composite things, while it is the nature of the body to materially change the soul. <margin>The second bond consists in the works of the will</margin> Unless these elements are present—especially when healing, moving, or agitating—nothing will be achieved. Hence, the most successful <note>original: "fortunatissimus"</note> mage is the one in whom many believe, and who possesses great power of persuasion.

(§ XI) III. The third bond, which is considered the efficient cause, is the number of "princes" <note>Bruno refers to high-ranking spiritual entities or planetary intelligences as "princes."</note> who are distributed according to the four cardinal points of the universe for those works sought from the heavens and from nature. <margin>The remaining bonds are derived from external relations, operations, means, circumstances, and subjects</margin> Besides these, there are princes who do not have a fixed location, responsible for voluntary and supernatural effects.

<margin>21<sup>r</sup></margin>
(§ XII) IV. The fourth bond is the soul of the world <term>anima mundi|the vital spirit or "breath" that animates all of nature as a single living organism</term> or the universal spirit, which couples all things and unites everything to everything; thus, an entrance is provided from all things to all things, as was stated in the preceding sections.

(§ XIII) V. The fifth bond consists of the souls of the stars and the rulers of places, winds, and elements.

(§ XIII) VI. The souls or spirits <note>original: "daemones"; here used in the ancient Greek sense of intermediary spirits that mediate between the divine and the earthly, rather than "demons" in the modern sense.</note> presiding over seasons, days, weather, and the elements themselves.

He categorizes these links from the internal psychological state of the mage to the external hierarchy of celestial and elemental spirits.</summary>

(XXIV) To this end, so that actions may be completed in things, three things are required: **active power** in the agent <note>the 'agent' is the person or force performing the action</note>, **passive power** in the subject or "patient" <note>the 'patient' or 'subject' is the entity receiving the action; 'passive power' refers to its capacity to be changed</note>—or a disposition, which is a certain aptitude or a lack of resistance or an impotence of resisting (all of which are reduced to one term, namely the **power of matter**) <margin>15</margin>—and **due application**, which occurs through the circumstances of time, place, and other concurrent factors. To say it all in one word: they depend on the agent, the matter, and the application. From a defect in any of these three, every action is perpetually hindered, simply speaking <note>original: "simpliciter loquendo"</note>. <margin>20</margin> For even if the flute-player <note>original: "tibicen"</note> is perfect, he is hindered by an imperfection in the flute, and the application of one to the other is in vain. Therefore, the impotence of the matter imposes an impotence upon the efficient cause and an inappropriateness in the application. This is what we mean when we say that by a defect of these <margin>24</margin> three, action is perpetually hindered, speaking absolutely; but looking at it properly, the defect can arise again from...

...by only two or by just one, not however by one in a definite sense, but by understanding them individually across all cases; as when the flute player is perfect and the application is present, but the flute itself is lacking, or when the player and the flute are both present, but the application is hindered. Where the <margin>5</margin> whole reason for the effect’s success consists in the application, then the first reason (the agent) concurs with the third; for the agent is sometimes nothing other than the applicator, and to act is nothing other than to apply.

(25. 26) Not every thing is born to be acted upon by every other thing, nor <margin>10</margin> to act upon everything; but, as was said in the *Physics* <note>Referring to Aristotle’s *Physics*, a foundational text for Renaissance natural philosophy</note>, all passivity <note>the capacity to be changed</note> comes from a contrary and all action is upon a contrary—and not always, but only when the subject is disposed to it. Hence the well-known saying: "the actions of active things take place in a well-disposed recipient" <note>original: *actiones activorum in patiente bene disposito*</note>. | From this, the reason is clear why <margin>70^r C</margin> water is mixed with water and water is tempered by water because of similarity, affinity, or a shared symbol <term>symbolum|in Renaissance natural philosophy, a "symbol" is a shared quality or "token" between two things—such as moisture or coldness—that allows them to link together</term>. <margin>15</margin> Thus, once the union has been made, they cannot be separated from one another by any artifice. Truly pure wine is easily received by water and receives water so that a mixture occurs; but because the parts of wine contain within themselves something of heat, air, and spirit, they do not possess a symbol in every way <note>meaning they are not identical in their elemental makeup</note>. <margin>20</margin> Therefore, they are not mixed at the level of their smallest parts, but are kept distinct within a heterogeneous compound in a large enough mass that they can be separated again by a certain art. This also happens with <margin>22^v M</margin> seawater which, when distilled <term>sublimata|the process of heating a substance to separate its components; here referring to the distillation of salt from water</term> in a certain way, yields fresh water; or likewise when filtered through wax vessels. If the mixture were <margin>25</margin> perfect, this would not occur. Oil, however, never mixes with water, because the parts of the oil cohere and stick together as if they were in love with each other <note>original: *quasi amatae*; Bruno often uses the language of "love" or "attraction" to describe the physical cohesion of matter</note>; hence they neither | penetrate nor are penetrated...

<meta>This page continues Bruno's exploration of the physical requirements for interaction between an agent and a subject. Having established that "well-disposed recipients" are necessary for an effect to occur, Bruno now moves into the specifics of how the internal structure, grain, and orientation of a substance (like wood or flesh) determine whether an influence—be it physical or magical—can penetrate it.</meta>

<page-num>440</page-num>
<header>GIORDANO BRUNO</header>

...from the parts of water. Therefore, one who attempts the mixing of bodies with other bodies must pay great attention to the condition of the parts; for indeed, not all things are miscible with all other things. 

(27) One must therefore attend to the position, composition, and difference of the parts, since a whole is penetrable by another whole through one side, but not through the other. For this is true in all things, as is evident in stones and wood and even in <margin>5</margin> flesh itself, which are penetrable—or more penetrable—through one part or side than through another. This is clear in the flow of humors <note>vital bodily fluids</note> pushed along the length of fibers, because wood is split more easily along its length; however, wood is penetrated <margin>10</margin> more easily by moisture through its width than its length, since the pores placed between the fibers allow for tubes or channels in that specific arrangement.

(28) One should not, therefore, only inspect the quality and position of the parts, but also the condition of the form of the whole. For there are certain "passions" <note>external influences or physical effects</note> <margin>15</margin> naturally suited to be received by one subject which are not received by another. For example, numbness is caused by a crampfish <term>torpedo|an electric ray known since antiquity for its ability to deliver a numbing shock</term> in the hand of the fisherman, but not in his nets; and, as a certain comic poet used to joke, the fires of love scorch the midriff and <margin>20</margin> burn the heart, while the breast itself remains raw and cold.

(29) Likewise, it happens in thunderstorms <note>original: *tonitruis*, referring here to the specific effects of lightning</note> that they sometimes melt a sword or steel while the scabbard remains entirely unchanged; thus also a wonder occurred in Naples to a certain noble and very beautiful girl, whose hair around her private parts <margin>25</margin> was scorched <note>original: *pilos circa vulvam combussit*</note> while she was otherwise unharmed. They even report that when the wood of a wine barrel is burned away, the wine remains standing firm or frozen in place. And many things of this kind...

# ON MAGIC.

...occur because of a hidden, ultimate reason found in the **atoms** <note>original: "atomis"; in Bruno's philosophy, these are the fundamental, indivisible building blocks of matter</note> of that kind of fire, which is so active | <margin>70^v C</margin> in one case that it remains inactive in another. They also report that for this reason, the **laurel** and the **eagle** are the emblems of emperors and poets: because they are never struck by lightning, as if they were as dear to Apollo and Jove as are leaders and poets.

As for human beings—to whom the same things do not happen as occurred to that girl <note>Bruno likely previously mentioned a specific case of a person with unusual physical properties</note>—the reason lies in the fact that not everyone is of the same **complexion** <term>complexionis|the unique balance of the four "humors" or bodily fluids that determines a person's physical and mental nature</term> and temperament, nor do they all admit the same quality of **spirit**. Indeed, in some people, such a spirit exists that they can even hinder rains and command the winds and other storms. Thus, the wonders that occur in bodies must be attributed to a certain complexion; some of these exist by the privilege of the whole species, while others exist by the specific prerogative of certain individuals, due to the innumerable differences found within them.

Therefore, **magicians** <margin>23^r M</margin> observe both such species and individuals so that they might "borrow" the effects of these powers <note>original: "virtutum"; refers to the inherent magical or physical properties of a substance</note>. Similarly, prudent commanders do not place nobles, friends, or those recommended to them in charge of armies or appoint them as ministers of war; instead, they choose the **more fortunate**—those who have a habit of escaping such dangers more luckily. Likewise, they believe that through the suspension <note>wearing an object around the neck</note>, carrying, or other types of application of certain plants and minerals, certain prerogatives of these powers are acquired for oneself...

442 GIORDANO BRUNO

...as if by a certain mediating contact, such that emperors armed with a laurel crown do not fear lightning.

(xxx) To this point belongs the fact that certain things are poisons to specific animals, just as **hemlock** <note>original: "cicuta"</note> is generally poisonous to man, yet for others it is a most pleasant food, so that they easily grow fat from it. Similarly, one must contemplate the differences in nutrients, poisons, and antidotes according to various species. From this arises a significant principle of both **magic** and **medicine**: the ability to distinguish between different **complexions** <term>complexionum|the specific physiological and spiritual makeup of a living being, determined by the balance of its internal qualities</term> and the underlying causes of sickness and health, as well as the principles for changing habits or dispositions—or preserving them—through the application of external substances. 

The **chemist** <note>original: "chymicus"; in this context, an alchemist or early scientist studying the properties of matter</note> also knows how **nitric acid** <term>aqua fortis|literally "strong water," a potent acid used by early scientists to separate and purify metals</term> acts upon hard substances like iron, silver, and bronze, but not at all upon gold or lead. Conversely, he knows how **quicksilver** <note>original: "vivum argentum"; mercury</note> very rapidly absorbs oil, which is entirely rejected and cast away by gold. Furthermore, there is an immediate power in the seed or juice of **vervain** <note>original: "verbenae"</note> to break a stone in the bladder, yet this same substance seems not at all violent toward the flesh, bone, membrane, or other parts of the body.

(xxxii) There are those who attribute the reasons for these things to the looseness or narrowness of the **pores** <note>original: "foraminum"; the tiny gaps or channels within the structure of matter</note>. I might easily concede this in some cases, but in the most important and numerous instances, it is by no means true—as with all the examples just listed. For there is no logical reason why nitric acid should penetrate one substance rather than <margin>71</margin> another simply because of a greater looseness of its pores. Similarly, that "spirit" of vervain, which acts against a stone but not against bones and flesh, does so even though the latter have more open pores. And what will they say regarding the **diamond** <note>original: "adamante"</note>, which indeed by a most subtle body...

<summary>Bruno argues that the specific effects of medicines, poisons, and acids are due to the internal "spirit" and temperament of substances rather than just the physical size of their pores. He uses examples from alchemy (nitric acid and mercury) and herbal medicine (hemlock and vervain) to demonstrate these unique natural sympathies.</summary>

# JORDANUS BRUNO

...we understand this in a rather rare sense, since the most powerful incantations or songs (as some have experienced) seem to possess more **dissonance** than **consonance**. Indeed, the soul of a semi-wild man was of such a nature that the rhythms of a **horse’s whinnying** <note>original: "hinnitus equini"; Bruno suggests that crude or animalistic souls respond better to sounds that mimic their own nature rather than refined human music</note> could have more easily swayed it. Therefore, as in the proverb of the **ass at the lyre** <note>original: "asino ad lyram"; a classical Greek and Latin proverb referring to someone attempting something for which they have no natural aptitude or appreciation</note>, not all songs are suited to all listeners. And just as different harmonies suit different souls, so do different magicians bind different spirits.

(xxxiv) These bonds are tenacious not only because they are perceived through hearing or gain an entrance into the soul—just as the voice of the **Marsi and Psylli** <note>ancient tribes from Italy and North Africa, respectively, who were legendary in antiquity for their power to charm snakes with chants and their immunity to venom</note> is a most powerful voice over the serpent—<margin>71</margin> but also because the effect of the bonds is perfected through the **analogy of spirit to spirit** (from the binder to the bound), even when a hidden whisper does not actually reach the object to be bound. For those who are enchanted do not always hear the voices of the enchanters, nor, if they are heard, are they always immediately or perceptibly affected.

(xxxv) To this topic belongs the fact that the "numbers" of one voice or sight can confound and blunt the "numbers" of another voice. This is why some people, upon seeing a **wolf**—which is commonly called a **lynx** <note>original: "lupo, quem cervarium vulgo appellant"; Bruno refers to the "lupus cervarius," often identified as a lynx, and the ancient folklore (mentioned by Virgil and Pliny) that if a wolf sees a man before the man sees the wolf, the man is struck dumb</note>—lose their voice, being bound by that spirit, and cannot easily form words. And they tell of an instrument made from **lambskin** with a drum... <note>Bruno is likely leading into the sympathetic/antipathetic properties of materials, such as the legend that a drumhead of wolf skin will ruin the sound of one made of sheepskin</note>

...we are drawn toward those things which, struck by fear, flee from us and hate us.

(XL) To this category belong prayers and petitions, with which certain equals or princes are solicited <margin>5</margin> where the reasons or pretexts of honor and justice alleged therein have no effect; to these men, the proposals of a single fool or jester are sometimes more powerful. Thus, wiser men are sometimes accustomed to ensnare the minds of princes through such words as if they were more suitable **bonds** <term>vincula|The central concept of this treatise: the "bonds" or "fetters" used to capture the attention, will, and soul of another.</term>, as was found in the case of **Pope Julius III** <note>Julius III (reigned 1550–1555) was known for his love of entertainment and his patronage of the arts, often preferring the company of wits and jesters to solemn diplomats.</note>, <margin>10</margin> who would dismiss and cast aside those praying, pleading, and weeping; <margin>72r</margin> but if someone had approached him after the kissing of the feet with a single **joke** <note>original: "scomma"; a biting jest or witty taunt.</note> or some other witty remark, he was able to obtain from him whatever he desired.

Therefore, whatever orators handle for the purpose of persuading and dissuading or for moving the passions belongs to the art of **incantation** <margin>15</margin> <term>incantatio|In Bruno's sense, this is not just "spells," but the psychological "enchantment" performed through speech and rhythm.</term> and to that species of the bond of the spirit which is through songs or verses; one part of which art they have indeed passed over, allowing it to remain hidden in the bosom of magicians, philosophers, or the more cunning politicians, <margin>20</margin> which **Aristotle**, however, largely encompassed in the ***Rhetoric to Alexander*** <note>A treatise once attributed to Aristotle (now usually attributed to Anaximenes of Lampsacus), which focuses on practical persuasion and political strategy.</note>. This art is reduced to two points of consideration: one being that the **incantator** <note>The one attempting to "bind" or influence another through speech.</note> should consider what is fitting for himself and what suits him; the other, what might please or delight the one being incanted or bound, <margin>25</margin> having considered his character, status, **temperament** <term>complexio|The specific balance of "humors" (blood, bile, etc.) in an individual, which determined their personality in Renaissance medicine.</term>, and habits. It is not the place at present to weave and bring forward all these things.

### The Third Kind of Bonds: From Sight

<margin>24^v M</margin>
(XLI) The spirit is also bound through sight, as has been touched upon in various places above, when forms pass before the eyes in one way or another. From this, active and passive **fascinations** <term>fascinatio|In the Renaissance context, this refers to a physical-spiritual process where one person's gaze "infects" or "binds" another's spirit, often associated with the 'evil eye' or the first spark of romantic love.</term> proceed from the eyes and enter through the eyes; <margin>5</margin> hence that saying: "I know not what eye fascinates my tender lambs." <note>original: "Nescio quis oculis teneros mihi fascinat agnos"; a quote from Virgil’s *Eclogues* (3.103), referring to the belief that an envious gaze could wither livestock.</note>
The appearance of beauty also strikes the affect of love; its opposite produces abomination and hatred. Furthermore, through the affections of the soul and spirit, something is poured into the body itself, which <margin>10</margin> exists under the steering of the soul and the tempering of the spirit. There are also other kinds of affections which are received through the eyes and immediately affect the body in some way; for we are moved to sadness and compassion or grief by certain sorrowful faces, as <margin>15</margin> if from obvious causes.

There are others which instill even worse impressions upon the mind and body through the eyes, but not in a way that we can evidently judge; nevertheless, they move us most effectively through things that are within us—namely, through the manifold **spirit** <margin>20</margin> and the **soul**. For even though a single soul thrives in the whole body, and all the members <margin>72^v C</margin> | primarily serve that one soul, yet because the whole is vivified by a certain "total spirit" and the whole soul and all its parts, the reason for many spiritual affections must be referred to **something else that knows and lives within us** <margin>25</margin>, which is affected and disturbed by those things by which we ourselves are least disturbed or affected. Sometimes we are more harmfully touched and wounded by those things...

<summary>Giordano Bruno explains how the sense of sight acts as a "bond" that can enchant or "fascinate" the spirit, noting that visual impressions can physically affect the body and influence the subconscious "spirit" even without our conscious awareness.</summary>

<margin>25<sup>r</sup></margin>
...[even though] we do not feel some blows as much as others we do feel; so also many things seen and images <gloss>species</gloss> brought in through the eye do not cause a sense of disturbance in the open and external sensory powers. Yet, when these are more deeply immersed, they affect us even lethally; the immediate perception of these things is referred to the internal spirit, as if to another sense and living being <note>original: "animal." Bruno often uses "animal" in the classical sense of a "living thing" possessed of "anima" (soul).</note>. Therefore, we will not so lightly disagree with certain Platonists and all the Pythagoreans, who establish that one human being is composed of many living beings living as if by themselves, of which sometimes, when one is destroyed—even the primary one—the others survive for a long time.

(XLII) Therefore, it is manifest stupidity to judge that we are only harmed or affected by those visible images <gloss>species</gloss> which induce an obvious disturbance of the sense and the mind. It is no different than if someone were to think they are only harmed—or harmed more—by those blows which are felt, or felt more strongly. Yet we have experienced that the prick of a needle or a thorn plucking at the skin causes more annoyance and torment than a sword driven from one side to the other; the sword's graver effect is eventually felt, though without the sensation of the injury at the very moment it penetrates the parts of the body. In the same way, many things stealthily captivate and impress themselves upon the spirits through the eye, even to the destruction of the soul, although they do not induce that [obvious] disturbance caused by lighter objects. Just as when we see certain gestures, emotions, or movements, we are compelled to tears; so too, some people, when they see another's blood shed or the dissection of a corpse <note>original: "cadaveris incisionem," referring to an autopsy or surgical cut.</note>, are driven even to the fainting of the soul. There is no other cause for this than the affection <term>affectio|In Bruno's psychology, an 'affection' is a state where the soul is 'acted upon' by an external image, changing its internal disposition.</term> binding us through the eyes.

->The fourth bond comes from the imagination.<-

(XLVII. XLVIII) The function of the imagination <note>original: "phantasia." In Bruno's time, "phantasia" and "imaginatio" were specific faculties of the mind responsible for storing and processing sensory data.</note> is to receive the images <gloss>species</gloss> brought in from the senses, to retain them, and to combine or divide them. This happens in two ways. The first is by the will or choice of the person imagining—this is the work of poets and painters, those who compose fables, and generally anyone who combines images <gloss>species</gloss> using their reason. The second way occurs outside of one's will or choice. This second way is also twofold: it is either caused by a voluntary, choosing agent, or by something moving from the outside. These external movements are further divided: they can be mediated, as when a person induces disturbances through voices or visions <gloss>spectra</gloss>, using sight or hearing; or they can be immediate, such as by a spirit <note>original: "spirituali"</note>, a rational being, or a demon <term>demon: in Renaissance philosophy, "daemons" were intermediary spirits—not necessarily evil—that could bridge the gap between the physical and spiritual worlds</term> who acts upon the imagination through dreams or even while awake. Such an agent stirs up internal images <gloss>species</gloss> so powerfully that something seems to be perceived by the external senses. 

<margin>25ᵛ M
73ʳ C</margin>For this reason, those who are possessed <term>energumens: individuals believed to be influenced or inhabited by external spirits</term> seem to see certain spectacles and hear certain voices or pronouncements which they believe are truly being suggested by external objects. Consequently, they assert most stubbornly and constantly that they have seen and heard real things. In these cases, it is not their senses that are being deceived, but their reason. For what they hear, they truly hear; what they see, they truly see. However, because an object is presented to them through the internal sense via an imaginary image <gloss>speciem phantasiabilem</gloss>, they mistakenly believe they are seeing it through external sound, through the ears, or as a physical form brought in through the eyes. They claim that the "intentions" <note>In medieval psychology, an "intention" is the mental representation of a thing as it exists in the mind.</note> of their internal senses are the actual objects themselves. Thus, it happens that they do not even wish to be brought back to a more sober perception by those standing around them, whom they instead [consider...]

<summary>Bruno defines the imagination as the fourth "bond" of magic, explaining how it can be manipulated by external spirits to cause hallucinations. He argues that in these states, the senses are functioning correctly, but the reason fails by mistaking internal mental images for external physical reality.</summary>

<margin>5</margin> (XLIX) Furthermore, in this bond <term>bond: Latin "vinculum." In Bruno's philosophy, "bonds" are the various ways things are linked, influenced, or captured by physical and spiritual forces</term>, the material principle is not pure—contrary to what is believed by the very coarse and most troublesome persistence of certain common doctors—nor is the efficient cause <note>efficient cause: the primary agent that produces an effect</note> purely of a demonic or diabolical nature, as some theologians argue for their part. Instead, both factors concur: <margin>10</margin> on the material side, there is the melancholic humor <term>melancholic humor: in Renaissance medicine, "black bile," associated with the planet Saturn and believed to cause both madness and profound genius</term>, which we call the tavern or the bathhouse of Saturnine demons; but as a moving and efficient cause, there is also the demonic spirit itself. Since this spirit is not an entirely incorporeal substance—given that <margin>15</margin> demons seem endowed with many animal-like emotions <note>original: "affectibus animalibus"</note>, even very serious ones—it is nonetheless a spiritual substance, to which nature has granted a body that is finer and less accessible to the senses. In this class of beings, it is said that no fewer species are found than there are of living, composite, and sensible creatures. Just as a specific soul <margin>20</margin> runs, as it were, to a specific seed suitably placed in a specific location—or emerging from it, produces a certain form of an animal or living thing and makes it emerge, so that from this seed an olive tree is born, from that one a dog, and from that one a human—likewise, in this body, constituted in this or that way, these things are born more easily, while **26** <margin>25</margin> those are born more easily in another. Hence the poet says: *"Here crops grow more successfully, there grapes flourish more happily"* <note>original: "Hic segetes, illic veniunt felicius uvae." A quote from Virgil’s Georgics (1.54), used here as an analogy for how different physical temperaments are "fertile ground" for different types of spirits.</note>. In the same way, from a certain balance and constitution of the heart, the brain, or the animal spirit <term>animal spirit: "spiritus animalis," a subtle, vapor-like substance that was thought to bridge the gap between the physical body and the soul</term>—or from its imbalance or disturbance—as if in its own field and from its own seed...

<summary>Bruno argues that psychological disturbances like mania and melancholia are caused by a combination of physical factors (the "melancholic humor") and external spiritual influences (demons). He uses the analogy of seeds in soil to explain how certain physical temperaments are more naturally suited to host specific types of spirits or mental states.</summary>

good or evil spirits and the principles of intentions arise. 
From this, there is a certain mutual consequence: that such bodies produce such souls, and such souls produce such bodies into a state of consistency <note>original: "consistentiam." This refers to the stable, functional union of soul and body.</note>, according to what they call the substantial and specific difference and subsistence. This can certainly be removed <margin>73v C</margin> from the person, partly through incantation—namely, through that rhetorical, friendly, and medicinal persuasion that restores the besieged spirit—and partly through the evacuation or expulsion of harmful matter by means of purgative drugs <note>original: "pharmaca." Therefore, to establish these things—whether for good or ill, whether according to the nature of the species or outside of it—a material principle is required, as well as a formal or efficient genus. ...are expelled and driven out by such wondrous, free, and ordered intentions, he <note>Bruno is likely critiquing a specific materialist or medical contemporary here.</note> concludes that they are nothing other than humors <term>humors: the four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) believed to determine health and temperament</term>. Since the senses happen to be bound and tied in all these ways, the physician or the magician must focus especially on the work of the **imagination** <note>original: "phantasia." In this period, the imagination was seen as the bridge between the physical senses and the higher mind.</note>; for this is the gate and the chief entrance to all the actions, passions, and affects that exist in a living creature. From this binding follows the binding of a deeper power, <margin>15</margin>which is the **cogitative faculty** <term>cogitativa: the mental power that evaluates and judges the images provided by the imagination</term>.

->On the fifth bond, which comes from the cogitative faculty.<-

(L. LI) The bond of the imagination is weak in itself, if the bond of the <margin>740</margin>cogitative faculty does not double its strength. For those phantoms <margin>20</margin>which bind and tie the mind of an ignorant, foolish, gullible, and superstitious character, are mocked, despised, and treated as empty shadows by a sober, well-born, and disciplined mind. Hence all practitioners—whether magicians, physicians, or prophets—achieve nothing without **prior faith**, and they operate <margin>25</margin>according to the degrees of that prior faith. — Here we understand "faith" <note>original: "fides." Bruno uses this in a psychological sense: the subject's belief or expectancy that the treatment or spell will work.</note> in a more universal sense than is usually understood by any one of them individually or by all of them together. —

<summary>Bruno argues that psychological "bonds" (influences) require the cooperation of the victim's own mind; specifically, a magician or doctor cannot influence someone unless that person's "cogitative faculty" accepts the influence through faith or belief.</summary>

# ON MAGIC

(LII) In some cases, this <note>The "binding" or influence mentioned on the previous page.</note> is stirred up through powers that are well-ordered and prepared beforehand, while in others, it is stirred through powers that are disturbed. Much is achieved by the "bonds" <term>bonds: Latin *ligamenta*; Bruno's term for the psychological ties that connect one person's influence to another's mind</term> produced by the words of a skilled orator, or from an appearance that creates and nurtures a specific disposition in the **imagination**—which is the only gate to all internal feelings and is the **bond of bonds** <note>original: "vinculum vinculorum." Bruno views the imagination as the essential bridge between the physical world and the inner spirit.</note>. Hence the famous saying of **Hippocrates** <note>An ancient Greek physician often called the "father of medicine."</note> is well known: 

> "The most effective of physicians is the one in whom most people believe," 

and this is because he overcomes the majority through his eloquence, his presence, or his reputation. This applies not only to a physician, but to any type of magic <margin>**27<sup>r</sup> M**</margin> or any other form of authority; if the one performing the "binding" cannot overcome or penetrate the imagination of the subject, they will hardly be able to accomplish anything by other means.

(LIII) Even theologians believe, concede, and preach concerning him who can do all things by himself <note>Bruno is referring here to Jesus Christ, specifically the Gospel accounts (e.g., Matthew 13:58) where Jesus is described as being unable to perform many miracles in his hometown due to the people's lack of faith.</note>, that he was unable to heal those who did not believe in him. The entire reason for this inability is attributed to the imagination, which he could not "bind." For his fellow townspeople, who knew his humble origin and upbringing, despised and mocked the physician and the divine figure; hence the common saying: 

> "No prophet is accepted in his own homeland." 

Therefore, it is easier for some to "bind" those among whom they are less known. This is because of reputation and the "preparation of faith," a power through which the soul disposes itself, opens up, and unfolds—as if opening windows to receive the sun. If these windows were otherwise kept shut, no entry would be granted to those impressions sought by the "binder’s" art, which works by striking the subsequent bonds: hope, compassion, fear, love, hatred, and indignation.

# GIORDANO BRUNO ON MAGIC

...anger, joy, patience, and the contempt for life, death, and fortune—indeed, all those things whose powers pass from the soul into the body to bring about a change.

<margin>74<sup>v</sup></margin>
It does not require very deep contemplation to understand how these other types of bonds I have listed—which follow after faith and opinion—bring about such a change. As for the soul’s more spiritual powers that follow—namely memory, reason, experience, intellect, and the mind—it is not my purpose here to examine them. This is because the actions of these powers do not overflow into the body or change its physical state. Instead, every transformation begins in the faculties that precede the **cogitative faculty** <note>In Renaissance psychology, the "cogitative faculty" (cogitativa) was the part of the brain that processed and "thought about" sensory images.</note>, though it is effectively and primarily driven by the cogitative faculty itself. 

Consequently, every active and passive magical force, as well as the various types of magical bonds, are restricted to this level. As **Plotinus** <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonic philosopher whose works on the soul were essential to Bruno’s magic.</note> asserts, both the wise and the foolish can be bound through the natural principles inherent in these faculties—unless there is some principle within the subject strong enough to repel or cast off these magical "ejaculations" <term>ejaculations: the outward casting of spiritual force or influence from one person to another</term>. For as I noted earlier, not everything can penetrate <margin>27<sup>r</sup></margin> everything else, nor can all things be mixed together—just as oil does not mix with water. **Plotinus** himself testifies to this, and his student **Porphyry** confirms it in his *Life of Plotinus*: the sorceries of a certain Egyptian, who sought to bind and harm Plotinus, were actually turned back upon the one who cast them <note>The story appears in chapter 10 of Porphyry's biography of Plotinus; Plotinus's superior soul was said to be "un-bindable."</note>. Let this conclude our discussion **on bonds in general** <note>original: "De vinculis in genere"</note>.

<meta>This page transitions from the psychological mechanisms of "bonds"—how one mind influences another through emotion and belief—to a formal, taxonomic definition of Magic itself. Bruno begins here to categorize the term "Magic" from its broadest possible meaning (general wisdom) to its most specific and technical applications.</meta>

# (THESES ON MAGIC)

### I.

<margin>28<sup>r</sup> M  
76<sup>r</sup> C</margin>
The term "Magic" is understood in many ways: most generally, generally, properly, and most properly. In the **first way**, it refers to every kind of science and wisdom. In the **second way**, it refers to natural science, or the science of natural things in general. In the **third way**, it refers to that wisdom which encompasses a threefold genus of "real" sciences <note>In the Scholastic tradition, "real sciences" (*scientiae reales*) dealt with things as they exist in reality, such as physics or metaphysics, rather than just mental constructs.</note> along with a threefold genus of moral sciences and a threefold genus of rational sciences <gloss>Logic, Metaphysics, and Mathematics</gloss>. In the **fourth way**, it refers to a skill aggregated from all of these, or many of them, combined with the power of knowing or acting in a wondrous manner. 

This fourth type is itself twofold: either acting through one’s own power, or through another. This is further divided in a threefold manner: acting through things that are higher <note>Such as planetary spirits or divine intelligences.</note>, equal, or lower <note>Such as elemental forces or minerals.</note>. This corresponds to the various circumstances noted and included in the ten definitions by which one is called a **mage** <note>In his related work *De Magia*, Bruno provides ten distinct definitions of a magician, ranging from a wise man/prophet to a malicious sorcerer.</note>. At present, we are understanding "Magic" according to the definition by which it is most properly named.

### II.

Magic is threefold: divine, physical, and mathematical. It is thus considered in two ways: either from the perspective of the subject—that is, the science—

---

<note>original: "triplice rationalium... logica, Metaph. Mathem." The editor notes that in manuscript M, a gloss identifies these rational sciences as Logic, Metaphysics, and Mathematics.</note>

<summary>Bruno begins his formal theses by defining magic as a spectrum of knowledge, moving from general wisdom and natural science to a specific, multifaceted power of action and insight. He categorizes magic into three primary branches: divine, physical, and mathematical.</summary>

## IV.
<margin>Manuscript M, folio 28v</margin>

The principle of magic is to consider the order of **influx** <note>original: *influxus*. In Renaissance philosophy, this refers to a "flowing in" of power or spiritual energy from the heavens down to the Earth.</note> or the **ladder of beings**, through which we discover that God transmits something into the Gods, the Gods into the stars, the stars into demons, the demons into the elements, the elements into <margin>5</margin> **mixed bodies**, and so on.

Distinguish between types of influx. Influx is twofold: **essential** and **accidental**; and the latter is further divided into **intrinsic** and **extrinsic**. The first type of influx bestows existence [being], while the second bestows the *mode* of being or the perfection of being. And here it must be noted that in this order, higher things are bound to lower <margin>10</margin> things as those that favor, protect, and move them; meanwhile, lower things are bound to higher things as those that comply and obey. Likewise, one must distinguish between the **ascent** and **descent** of this ladder. This is also twofold: **contemplative**, by which things are known, and **active**, by which things are made. This "making" is also twofold: **principal**, by which they truly exist, and <margin>15</margin> **accidental**, by which they are adapted or applied to our use.

Distinguish also regarding the progression of **light** and **darkness**, which are found on the ladder. For light and darkness are understood in two ways: in one sense, they signify **substance**—in which case light signifies act and **form**, while darkness signifies potential and **matter**; or they signify **accidents**, and <margin>20</margin> then light signifies the active and perfecting power of the **species** <note>original: *specierum*. Here referring to the formal qualities or "blueprints" of things.</note>, whereas darkness signifies the passive and perfectible power of the underlying subjects.

## V.

According to the three aforementioned levels of magic, three **worlds** are understood, etc.

<margin>25</margin> Here a distinction must be made regarding "world" according to its | **common**, **proper**, and **most proper** <margin>Manuscript C, folio 77r</margin> meanings. In the first sense [common], "world" is the same as the **universe**, and in this sense there is only one, as the totality...

---

<summary>Bruno describes the "Ladder of Being," a hierarchy through which divine power flows down from God to material objects, and explains how a magician can use this ladder through contemplation or action. He also redefines light and darkness as philosophical symbols for form and matter.</summary>
<keywords>Ladder of Being, Influx, Hierarchy of Nature, Light and Darkness, Metaphysics, Form and Matter, Giordano Bruno</keywords>

--- Page 526 ---
<meta>Continuity: Following the discussion on the "ladder of being" and the flow of influence (influx) from higher to lower realities, Bruno here defines the different ways the term "world" is understood. This categorization is essential for understanding how the magician interacts with different layers of reality—from the divine archetype to the physical earth and the human mind.</meta>

<page-num>458</page-num>
<header>GIORDANO BRUNO</header>

[The world] is one absolutely, according to the meaning intended by Parmenides and Xenophanes <note>Pre-Socratic philosophers who argued that reality is a single, unchanging, and unified "Being."</note> when they said that **being is one**. In a second way, the world is distinguished—as has just been said—according to three types of being, which cannot be reduced to a single category; for the **intelligible**, the **natural**, and the **rational** <note>These represent the realm of Ideas/God, the realm of physical Nature, and the realm of the human mind/Logic.</note> differ by more than just their class; that is, they do not merely differ within a single category, but are <margin>5</margin> entirely different categories of existence. In a third way, "world" is understood as it was by Democritus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher who proposed that the universe is made of atoms.</note>, who understood worlds to be innumerable and infinite; he took the Earth to be one world, the moon another, and each of the stars another, <margin>10</margin> of which there is no set number.

The term "world" is also used improperly, proportionally, or by way of likeness, as when **man is called a "world"** <note>original: *homo dicitur mundus*. This refers to the concept of the "microcosm," where the human being is a miniature version of the entire universe (the macrocosm).</note>, because his parts represent the parts of the universe, just as individual animals and plants do in their own way.

<margin>Folio 29r</margin> This distinction of the world according to the three aforementioned meanings <margin>15</margin> is confirmed by the truth of nature, by reason, and by divine revelation: first, because nothing exists in the **sensible world** <note>The physical world we perceive with our senses.</note> that does not depend on the **archetype** <note>The original divine "blueprint" or idea of a thing in the mind of God.</note>; second, because nothing exists in the mind’s **intention** <note>A technical term in logic for a concept or mental representation.</note> that is not fundamentally rooted in actual things;

<margin>20</margin> Distinguish between "fundamentally" and "really"; **second intentions** <note>Concepts about concepts (like "species" or "definition").</note> exist fundamentally, while **first intentions** <note>Direct concepts of objects (like "tree" or "stone").</note> exist really. Second intentions are founded upon first ones; logic deals with second intentions joined to first ones. See Avicenna in the book *On Sufficiency*. <note>Avicenna (Ibn Sina) was a Persian polymath; his *De Sufficientia* is part of his massive philosophical encyclopedia, *The Book of Healing*.</note>

third, because truth does not contradict truth, and this distinction is found many times in the **divine books** <note>Referring to the Bible or sacred scriptures.</note>.

<summary>Bruno defines the "world" in three ways: as a single unified existence, as a hierarchy of three realms (Divine, Physical, and Mental), and as an infinite plurality of stars and planets. He also introduces the concept of man as a microcosm and explains that the mind's concepts are rooted in physical reality.</summary>

### VI.

In general, the **efficient cause** <note>The "efficient cause" is the agent or force that brings something into being or produces a change, such as a carpenter building a chair.</note> is twofold.

At this point, one must distinguish the efficient cause—or the agent—according to the main categories of distinction. Likewise, distinguish the cause according to the same criteria. <note>Manuscript "C" clarifies this twofold nature as "Nature and Will." This suggests that things are brought about either by natural necessity or by the conscious intent of an agent, such as a magician or a deity.</note>

<margin>5</margin>
### VII.

The element of all things is, in truth and properly, **one**; in the next sense, **two**; and in the following sense, **four**. These are: one matter; two contraries; and the four primary and simple bodies established by **Empedocles** <note>A pre-Socratic philosopher who famously proposed that all matter is composed of four roots: Earth, Water, Air, and Fire.</note>.

<margin>10</margin>
**The Reasoning.** Because the material principle <note>original: *principium materiale*; the underlying "stuff" of the universe.</note> is only one, insofar as it underlies the two contraries as well as the four primary bodies. Since these bodies are transmutable into one another, it is necessary that they meet in a certain common matter; for things that are transformed into one another must share a common subject. Therefore, there is first **one subject**;
<margin>15</margin> <margin>77<sup>v</sup> C</margin>
secondly, this is distinguished into **two contraries** acting as subjects, such as fire and water, or the sun and the earth; thirdly, it is distinguished into **four**, of which two are active and two are passive.

When we posit two elements, we should not call "hot" and "cold" mere accidents <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a non-essential property, like the color of a shirt. Bruno argues here that these qualities are fundamental to the very "substance" or essence of the elements.</note>, but rather substances, and complete substances at that. In this way, we say the **sun and the earth** are the principles of all particular substances or species, just as **Hesiod, Virgil, and Parmenides** do.

### VIII.

It is foolish to refer all operations and effects of natural things solely to active and passive qualities; <note>Bruno is critiquing a purely physicalist or Aristotelian view of nature that only looks at "hot, cold, moist, and dry." He implies that magic involves deeper, hidden (occult) powers beyond these basic physical traits.</note>

---

<note>Translator's note on variants: Line 2: Manuscript C specifies the twofold efficient cause is "Nature and Will." Line 7: Manuscript M reads "three" instead of "two" for the second level of elements. Line 18-21: The passage regarding the sun and earth as principles is noted in the margins of both the C and M manuscripts.</note>

<summary>Bruno outlines the hierarchy of physical principles, arguing that all matter stems from a single underlying substance that manifests as pairs of opposites (like the Sun and Earth) and the four traditional elements. He argues that these are not just physical properties, but fundamental substances, and hints that nature cannot be explained by simple physical qualities alone.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: Following the previous page's discussion on the fundamental elements (the "one" matter and the "four" bodies), Bruno now transitions into how these elements are acted upon by higher forces. ...for these are the effects of the soul and the spirit, which acknowledge none of these [physical] qualities.

The distinction is found in Section VIII. For among those **powers** <note>original: *virtutum*; in this context, "virtues" or "powers" refer to the inherent capacities or forces through which a thing acts upon another.</note> which are carried from one subject to another, some are sensible—that is, acting through active and passive qualities—which are accessible to the external senses. Others are more hidden, being understood through the action of thought and imagination, such as those which affect the **concupiscible** <note>The "concupiscible" faculty refers to the soul's natural appetite or desire for what it perceives as good or pleasurable.</note> and **irascible** <note>The "irascible" faculty refers to the soul's power to resist obstacles or "fight" for what is desired.</note> faculties. Qualities of the first kind are stirred up by a certain physical contact of their own; but those of the second kind are stirred up neither by contact nor always. Both kinds of qualities proceed from composite bodies and flow into the same, owing to the communion of spirit and soul. However, they do not both proceed from corporeal qualities—namely, those which primarily come from the elements—but rather from qualities which exist in the substance of the soul and the spirit (which, if they are bodies at all, must be of a different kind from those others). This is because such qualities do not perpetually require the physical approximation of one subject to another, but are stirred up in a subject by the **imagination** alone. Hence, both the internal and external soul, when it has risen into some meditation or thought, alters its own body; yet no one says the soul does this through physical contact, since its substance is indivisible <margin>29v</margin> | and its powers are not bodies, nor are they present in the whole and in the parts after the manner of bodies.

### IX.

Whatever exists immaterially in a place is there as a whole. This is true not only of an **immaterial substance**, such as the soul—which is "all in the whole and all in any part"—but also of **immaterial qualities**, such as the voice and the **species** <note>original: *species*; in Renaissance philosophy, "species" are the "likenesses" or "images" of objects that travel through the air to reach our senses without carrying the physical weight of the object itself.</note> of sensible things that are carried [through a medium].

<summary>Bruno distinguishes between physical forces that require contact and spiritual/mental forces (like imagination) that can alter the body and environment without physical touch. He argues that the soul and its qualities exist "immaterially," meaning they are present in their entirety throughout a space rather than being divided like matter.</summary>

...into the eyes, and images in mirrors and parts of mirrors. Therefore, the spirit and spiritual things are not bound to a [specific] place or subject.

<margin>78r C</margin>
Distinction: The soul is whole in the whole [body]—that is, according to its **essence** <note>The "essence" refers to what the soul is in itself, its core identity.</note> and its **power** <note>original: *potentia*; here meaning the soul's inherent capacity to act.</note>—but it is not "totally" in the whole—that is, according to its **operation** <note>original: *operationem*; referring to the specific work the soul does, like seeing or hearing.</note> and its **act**. This is because the soul does not see from every part of the body, nor does it hear from every part, because the organs for seeing and hearing are not everywhere; thus, it is not "totally" [present] through all parts.

Likewise, a distinction must be made concerning power, between **primary power** and **proximate power** <note>Bruno uses these terms to distinguish between the soul's general ability to give life (primary) and its specific ability to use a physical tool like an eye (proximate).</note>. Primary power exists where the soul’s essence is; proximate power exists where the organs and media are. The primary power is whole in the whole and in every single part, but the second [proximate power] exists only in certain and defined parts.

## X.

No production and no **generation** <note>The process of bringing a new living thing into existence.</note> occurs without an **idea** <note>original: *idea*; in Bruno’s thought, this is the divine "blueprint" or archetype that guides the formation of a living thing.</note> and without **knowledge**—specifically by an **efficient cause** <note>term: *efficient cause* (Latin: *efficiens*); the agent or force that actually produces an effect or brings a thing into being.</note> who produces something according to the standard of a proposed idea. 

The idea, however, by which a human begets a human and a lion begets a lion, is not separate, but joined to the lion itself and the human itself. The efficient cause, truly, is partly separate and partly joined; the **matter** <note>The physical substance out of which something is made.</note> is neither separate nor joined.

<gloss>Regarding Knowledge: A distinction. There is the sensitive knowledge of **sensible** things <note>Things that can be perceived by the physical senses.</note>, and the intellectual knowledge of **intelligible** things <note>Things that can only be understood by the mind or intellect.</note>.</gloss>

<gloss>Also concerning the **efficient cause**: that which is joined is the soul and its own nature; that which is separate is the sun, the star, and the air <note>In the worldview of the time, the sun and stars were considered "efficient causes" of life on Earth, providing the necessary heat and celestial influence for generation.</note>.</gloss>

<summary>Bruno defines how the soul resides within a body, distinguishing between its essential presence and its localized functions. He also introduces the "Idea" as the necessary blueprint for all biological generation, driven by both internal (soul) and external (celestial) efficient causes.</summary>

<keywords>soul, essence, power, primary power, proximate power, generation, Idea, efficient cause, sensible vs intelligible knowledge, cosmology</keywords>

--- Page 530 ---
<meta>Continuity: Following the discussion on page 461 regarding the soul's presence in the body and its distinction between essence and operation, Bruno now moves to define the fundamental nature of Matter and the classification of Ideas.</meta>

<page-num>462</page-num>
<header>OF GIORDANO BRUNO</header>

<margin>78v</margin>
**Matter**] That which was one thing later becomes another; however, it is not that what was in one is later in another. Because matter itself is that to which forms are joined—rather than being something joined to forms—it is not the thing that comes and goes. Instead, it is that to which something arrives and from which something departs, whether **accidentally or substantially** <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "accidental" change is a change in property (like getting a tan), while "substantial" change is a change in what the thing is (like wood burning into ash).</note>, mediately or immediately. Matter itself is an individual substance prior to quantity, and prior to the logic of part and whole.
For this reason, regarding the nature of matter—which is primary and the subject of **substantial form** <note>The "substantial form" is the essential nature or "blueprint" that makes a thing what it is (e.g., the "dog-ness" of a dog).</note>—one cannot identify "this or that part" within the composite whole in the same way one identifies "this or that hand," "this or that part of the head," or "this arm joined to this shoulder."

**Distinction regarding the Idea.** The Idea is understood in three ways: **before the thing**, **in the thing**, and **after the thing**. The first way is the most proper, the second is proper, and the third is the common way of speaking.
The **Idea before the thing** is that which is the cause of the thing to be produced and the principle existing before it; just as the "form of a dog" is the immediate principle by which this bread is converted into canine seed, and the "form of a man" is the cause by which the same bread is there converted into human seed to produce a man.
And this "form before the thing" is twofold: **universal**, which exists by the power of universal producing nature, by which man simply generates man, and animal generally generates animal; and **particular**, which exists by the power of this or that individual natural subject, by which this specific man generates this specific man, or this specific dog generates this specific dog.
The **Idea in the thing** is that which is found within the produced things themselves, and is considered a part of the composite.
The **Idea after the thing** is that which is found in the senses, the intention, the reason, or the intellect, which abstract the species <note>original: *species*; here meaning the mental "image" or "form" of an object stripped of its physical matter.</note> from the things.

### XI.

Generally speaking, **Ideas** are **metaphysical beings** <note>Beings that exist as divine archetypes beyond the physical world.</note>; the **vestiges of Ideas** are **physical beings** <note>Physical objects, which Bruno views as "tracks" or "footprints" left by the Ideas.</note>; and the **shadows of Ideas** are **beings of reason** <note>original: *entia rationis*; mental concepts or thoughts that exist only in the mind.</note>. The first are proportioned to the seals that leave an impression.

<summary>Bruno defines matter as the unchanging substrate beneath all physical change and categorizes "Ideas" into three states: the creative cause (before the thing), the internal structure (in the thing), and the mental concept (after the thing).</summary>

<keywords>Matter, Idea, Substantial Form, Metaphysical Beings, Beings of Reason, Generation, Universal Nature, Shadows of Ideas</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: Following the previous page’s introduction of the Idea as existing in three states—before the thing, in the thing, and after the thing—Bruno continues to refine these definitions and explains the relationship between the soul, the body, and the universal spirit.</meta>

### THESES ON MAGIC

...the second through impressed forms, the third through those perceived by the eye or **30^r M** <note>The "M" refers to the specific manuscript source (the Noroff Manuscript) being transcribed.</note> sense.

An Idea, in a universal sense according to a universal principle, exists where there is no place, motion, or time (for it is a form existing outside of a subject). <margin>5</margin> However, insofar as this form serves as an exemplar joined to matter, it creates or produces a physical form; but insofar as it is an abstract **species** <term>species: here meaning a mental image or representation</term> separated from matter through the act of sensory or rational cognition, the third kind of Idea is completed—the kind which is caused by natural things and depends on them, just as a <margin>10</margin> secondary class depends on the primary.

From the experience of things, it is manifest that every soul and spirit maintains a continuity with the spirit and soul of the universe. The soul is not contained by the body; rather, the body is contained by the soul, just as—universally speaking—matter does not embrace <margin>15</margin> form, but form embraces matter.

Form limits and contains matter, because it is the nature of form to define matter, seeing as it grants and describes both shape and size to it; hence, just as the shape of an ant is different from that of a dog, so too is its size. <margin>20</margin>

**Reasoning.** The soul is not "somewhere" as if in a place, but rather as if in a subject. It is not present as an **integral part** <gloss>quantitative</gloss>—in the way a physical part of the body exists within the body—but as an **essential part** <gloss>substantial</gloss>, just as the soul and the body together constitute the existence of a living being. Likewise, it is not present in any location (such as the body it brings to life) as something bounded, but rather as the force that sets the bounds.

<margin>79r</margin> <note>original: "hoc est quia terminat, non terminatur; 3. item non est circumscriptive, sed definitive; 4. item non inhaerenter, sed adsistenter."</note>...this is because it limits and is not limited; 3. likewise, it is not present by circumscription <term>circumscription: occupying a space that matches the object's boundaries</term>, but by definition; 4. likewise, not by inherence <term>inherence: existing as a property of a subject</term>, but by assistance <term>assistance: acting as a governing or guiding presence from "outside" the material constraints</term>.

### XII.

The soul is not bound to the body by itself and immediately,
<margin>10</margin> but by the mediation of the **spirit** <term>spirit: in Renaissance philosophy, a subtle "vapor" or fluid that acts as a bridge between the immaterial soul and the heavy material body</term>—that is, by a certain extremely subtle corporeal substance which is, in a way, an intermediate between the substance of the soul and that of the elements; the reason for this connection is that the soul itself is not an entirely immaterial substance.

**Distinction.** "Material" is taken in one common way for every-
<margin>15</margin> thing that is sensible, as people commonly call things material that are exposed to the senses themselves. Secondly, more commonly, it refers both to the elements themselves and to the nature within those elements, as well as to those things compounded from the elements. Strictly, in the third way, everything is called material which has matter as a part of itself. <margin>20</margin> Fourthly, by reduction (since it is primarily used in the three ways mentioned above), everything is called material which has dealings with matter; for indeed all corporeal **accidents** <term>accidents: properties like color or weight that are not essential to a thing's identity</term>, which exist around bodies, are something material and corporeal—not because they are bodies and matter, but because they concern the body and matter. In this way, all physical substantial forms are also material,
<margin>25</margin> and the soul is necessarily a corporeal and material form, as even the **Peripatetics** <term>Peripatetics: followers of Aristotle's philosophy</term> will not deny. However, regarding the matter which pertains to its intrinsic substance, we are not disputing that for the time being.

Everything that possesses form and matter within itself is material; all physical things, whether they are simple or composite, are material.

## XIII.

<margin>5</margin> Not only this substance which is the soul, but also most accidents <term>accidents: properties or qualities of a thing (like color, heat, or thought) that are not essential to its being a "thing," but depend on a substance to exist</term>, wherever they are, they are present in their entirety; they are not restricted to any place by their own nature. This is because it is only the nature of a body to be entirely contained by circumscription <term>circumscription: a physical state where an object's boundaries exactly match the boundaries of the space it occupies</term> in a single space or location, and to be found in countless spaces and locations according to its countless parts.

<margin>10</margin> **Reason.** For these are the conditions of a continuous, stable quantity, consisting of parts that have position, and of their boundaries—namely, the line, the surface, the body, and the point. Every boundary of a line is somewhere; a point is somewhere.

<margin>15 30^v M 79^v C</margin> 
## XIV.

Immaterial substances, just as they are present in their entirety wherever they are, so too are they present in one and the same space—in the way they are able to be—whole in the whole and whole in any part of it <note>original: "totae in toto et totae in qualibet parte illius"</note>. Just like accidents, which are not inherently the boundary of bodies, <margin>20</margin> countless whole entities can exist in the same space without mutual penetration <term>mutual penetration: the physical impossibility of two solid bodies occupying the exact same space simultaneously</term>, which would otherwise require one to give way to the other. Furthermore, all [these immaterial things] inhabit the whole as a whole, and all parts of the whole as a whole.

### XV.

For this reason, every soul is in the whole <term>horizon: in Bruno’s thought, the "horizon" represents the boundary or meeting point between the spiritual and material worlds, or the full range of a soul's influence</term>, and it receives influence from the whole horizon, and imprints itself upon the whole horizon; hence there is a place for **magical operations**—which are nonetheless **physical** <note>Bruno often argued that magic was simply "advanced physics" or the use of natural laws that are not yet understood by the common person</note>—by which a subject at a great distance is able, through a certain spiritual power, to imprint certain affects and passions onto a remote subject.

Against this, it seems to be the case that "every action occurs through contact." <note>A standard Aristotelian principle: *nulla actio in distans* (no action at a distance)</note> Here, one must distinguish between types of **contact**, as is found in the chapter *On Touch* in the book *On Generation* <note>original: "De tactu in libro De generatione"; referring to Aristotle's *On Generation and Corruption*</note>; and touch is distinguished into **real**, **natural**, or **physical** (as it is commonly called), and **virtual** or **potential**. By this latter type, even certain words—such as insults, which are nothing but sounds reaching the ear—reach the powers of the soul through a certain meaningful and representative power, namely the cognitive and the appetitive <term>appetitive: relating to desires or the "appetite" of the soul for certain things</term>, from which follow anger, contempt, and other emotions. Similarly, a certain image of beauty is carried from the eye to the innermost powers of the soul, from which arise love, pleasure, and joy; these do not proceed through the contact which the common people call "physical," yet they are not without contact.

### XVI.

Hence, it is not unbelievable or against reason, but very much in harmony with the nature of things, that a Physician can cure the wounds of someone who is far **absent**, not only by applying specific parts <margin>80r</margin>

## XVII.
<margin>31^r M</margin>

The most active bodies are those that are imperceptible to the senses, which Lucretius calls <term>hidden bodies: "corpora caeca"; in the Lucretian tradition, these are the invisible atoms or particles that make up the world and cause physical changes without being seen</term>; and the more perceptible a body is to the senses, the less active and more passive it is. <margin>10</margin> Of this kind is the **spirit**, which we call the same as air, and which many of the philosophers have called the **soul**; from this spirit, fire—as it is defined by Aristotle—seems to differ only by a certain <term>accident: a non-essential property or quality (like heat or color) that does not change the core essence of a substance</term>. Therefore, it seems better to name **three elements**, adding **light** in the place of fire, <margin>15</margin> just as Moses, the Chaldeans, Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurius Trimegista"; Bruno refers to the legendary Egyptian sage and purported author of the Hermetic texts</note>, and Orpheus did.

Beyond those things in article 18, it should be noted that Aristotle said fire is nothing other than "rubbed air," and he said it was generated from the rubbing of air, which results from the speed of celestial motion; <margin>20</margin> therefore, fire does not differ from air in its path any more than vapor differs from water—namely, only in the fact that it is more rarefied. Furthermore, just as vapor <unclear>does not produce</unclear> a new species of element with respect to water, so too that fire should not produce [a new species] with respect to air.

Hence, the cause of fire seems to be **light**, which <margin>25</margin> suddenly, without a continuous succession of motion, awakens heat from an immense space and brings forth the fire we speak of; and light seems to be an element and—
