the principle of fire, and not, on the contrary, some <term>accident: a non-essential property or quality (like heat or color) that does not change the core essence of a substance</term> proceeding from fire. And this is manifest in mirrors that receive the rays of the sun; by casting those rays into a deep and dark opposite cavity and imprinting a hot power by means of illumination, they <margin>5</margin> heat and burn bodies. In this case, it is not a likely impression of light through heat, but of heat through light; nor is it heat *with* light, but heat *from* light. For the nature of elemental heat is not to thrust itself suddenly into a body, but to do so with time and succession. Therefore, heat has light as its precursor, but heat itself is not the precursor to light; <margin>10</margin> as is also manifest in itself, because bodies are illuminated before they become hot, and the primary participation of fire is light rather than heat.

### XVIII.

Natural motion is twofold: straight and circular. The first <margin>15</margin> belongs to natural things not naturally situated <note>This refers to objects that have been moved out of their proper place in the universe, such as a stone lifted into the air</note>; the second belongs to natural things naturally situated. The first also belongs to natural things desiring to be in a better state; the second to those already in a good state. The first belongs to parts fleeing or pursuing <note>original: "fugientium et persequentium"; parts moving away from harm or toward a place of preservation</note>; the second belongs only to the whole and to the parts within their whole.

<margin>20</margin> **Reasoning.** Because all natural things in their own place either rest or move circularly; and a whole body, such as the **Earth** <note>original: "tellus"</note> or the **Moon**, does not move with straight motion. <margin>31^v</margin> Rather, only the parts of those bodies move in that way | when they <margin>25</margin> are outside their proper seat, or whenever they strive toward a better place of preservation. That parts move circularly within the whole itself is manifest in rivers and the succession or transmutation of places—as when mountains migrate into plains and valleys, and these into mountains; likewise the sea into the continent and the continent into the sea.

All falls of parts are arc-like, and water ascends and descends in an arc from the bowels [of the earth] and to the bowels.

### XIX.

That circle as well—the one defined as a rotation from a single point back to that same point, and where every radius from the center to the circumference is equal—is not natural. It is not found <margin>5</margin> in any natural subject, whether you consider the size and mass of bodies or their motion and change; for no sense-perception or experience has ever confirmed, nor can it confirm, a circle of that kind. Therefore, a "circle" in nature should be understood as a sequence of things with a regular cycle <note>original: "vicissitudine"</note>, in which there is a return to *similar* <margin>10</margin> states, but not to the *exact same* state.

We must distinguish between two types of circuit: the physical and the geometric—or the natural versus the rational and artificial. The first exists in natural things; the second is merely a work of mental contemplation. For the sun never has, and never will, <margin>v</margin> <note>This margin note likely refers to a "verso" or specific manuscript correction</note> <margin>15</margin> return to the exact same point in its daily or yearly motion—nor will any of the stars that appear to move.

<margin>81^r C</margin> <note>Manuscript folio 81, recto, from codex C</note>

### XX.

Beyond these two types of motion commonly recognized by the <term>Peripatetics: the followers of Aristotle, who dominated medieval and Renaissance science</term>, there is a third type. This is a motion that is neither "at the center" nor "around the center," <margin>20</margin> but rather *from* the center—that is, the way something flows out from all natural bodies—and *toward* the center—that is, the way something flows into all natural bodies. And this <term>efflux: an outward flow of influence or substance</term> consists not only of physical matter, but also of certain <term>accidents: non-essential qualities or properties, such as heat, light, or spiritual influence</term> which exist in bodies, come from bodies, and move toward bodies. This motion we call neither "straight" nor <margin>25</margin> "circular" according to the types mentioned before.

## XXIII.

Regarding the attraction of a magnet toward the pole, there are various opinions. However, setting all of these aside, we approve of that explanation which is not based on attraction to a similar <margin>5</margin> species—namely, the idea that there are "magnetic mountains" located there (for that cause does not actually produce this effect). Instead, we assert that the entire and firm reason for this movement arises from a flight from its contrary and a certain <term>antipathy: a natural repulsion or "dislike" between opposing forces</term> which the magnet has toward opposite places.

->The reasons are found in the 23rd article.<-

<margin>10</margin> ## XXIV.

In every action, whether it be magical, physical, or of whatever kind it may be, three things are required: an active power, a passive power, and the proper application of the one to the other. From a defect in any of these, an impediment arises—either in <margin>15</margin> whole or in part, absolutely <note>original: "simpliciter"</note> or in a certain respect <note>original: "secundum quid," meaning a limitation or qualification of a statement</note>—in all productions.

A distinction must be made here between power and action; for one kind of action is <term>immanent: an action that stays within the agent, like thinking</term>, while another is <term>transient: an action that passes from the agent to an external object</term>, and so on. Likewise, a distinction must be made regarding a defect in all three requirements, considering them either absolutely or in a certain respect. <margin>20</margin> For, in an absolute sense, if there is an impediment to one of those three factors in things that require all three, | an impediment to all of them follows. In a certain respect, <margin>32ᵛ M</margin> however—that is, on the part of its own specific principle—an impediment can exist without necessarily involving a failure of one or two of the other factors.

## XXV.

->Every action and every change is from one contrary to its contrary; for there is no change from like to like, nor from the same thing to itself.<-

<margin>5</margin>It must be observed that transformation <note>original: "transmutation"</note> belongs to those things which share the same matter, or those which have a common <margin>82r</margin> <term>subject: the underlying substance or "stage" where physical changes take place</term>; hence that common proposition: <note>original: "contraria apta nata sunt fieri circa idem"</note> "contraries are naturally suited to occur within the same subject." For this is the function of <term>contraries: opposing qualities like hot and cold</term>, that they mutually expel one another from the same place or subject, and in turn succeed one another in that same subject or place; <margin>10</margin>thus heat and cold exist around the same compound, just as sweet and bitter concern the sense of taste, light and darkness concern the sense of sight, and so on. This relates to the doctrine found in Book I of the *Physics* <note>Referring to Aristotle’s Physics, a foundational text for Bruno’s natural philosophy</note>, which concerns generation from contraries.

## XXVI.

<margin>15</margin>It is no obstacle to this rule that certain "affections"—or "passions," if you prefer to call them that—exist between likes and likes, or likes with likes and dislikes with dislikes, or even contraries with contraries, such as in mixtures, compositions, and perceptions <note>original: "apprehensiones"</note>.

<margin>20</margin>For the judgment regarding these things is different than the judgment regarding actions and passions <note>In this context, "passions" refers to the experience of being acted upon by an outside force</note>. Water mixes with water better than it does with wine, and wine mixes with water better than it does with oil or something fatty, because it is more similar; likewise, in the composition of mud, water and dust combine, and in <margin>24</margin><term>oxymel: a traditional medicinal drink made of honey and vinegar</term>, honey and vinegar combine. Furthermore, sensory and <margin>25</margin>intellectual perception occurs through the <term>similitudes: the mental likenesses or "species" that represent an object to the mind</term> of forms abstracted from objects.

<summary>Bruno explains that fundamental change only occurs between opposing forces (contraries) within the same substance, while mixtures and perceptions rely on similarity and the gathering of different elements.</summary>
<keywords>contraries, transformation, Aristotelian physics, mixtures, oxymel, perception, similitude, subject and matter</keywords>

...with those things which are on their surface. We must also note the distinction between different types of similarity. For there is a similarity of **equality** (parity), one of **analogy**, one of **proportion**, and one that is **properly so-called**: 

1.  The first is how one human is similar to another human. 
2.  The second is how a human is similar to God. 
3.  The third is a ratio, such as how the sense relates to the thing felt, just as the intellect relates to the thing understood. 
4.  The fourth is how the <term>species: the mental "form" or image</term> of Socrates in the imagination is similar to the form that exists in the actual, physical person himself.

### XXVII.

For the proper application of the <term>agent: the active force or "doer"</term> and the <term>patient: the passive recipient of an action</term>—as well as things meant to be mixed, composed, or perceived—it is especially necessary to respect how their parts relate to one another. Specifically, the practitioner <note>original: "operante"</note> must consider through which spatial differences bodies are permeable or able to be penetrated.

The reasoning for this is found in the examples in Article 27.

### XXVIII.

<margin>33r M 82v C</margin>
Beyond the quality and position of the parts, the practitioner must furthermore understand what is required to "capture" those influences or <term>accidents: non-essential qualities, like color or temperature, that can change without destroying the object</term> by which things must be transformed. These must be naturally suited to be received by such <term>subjects: the physical matter being worked upon</term>. Indeed, this is the most important part of every operation conducted according to a prescribed goal: to see which things are acted upon by which others, and according to which specific types of transformation they are changed.

The reasoning for these points is drawn from the examples in Article 28.

### XXIX.

To this is related the explanation for the miracles that occur from the fire of lightning bolts; however, the differences between those active <term>accidents: non-essential qualities, like heat or color, that can change without destroying the object itself</term>, to which certain dispositions in the active forces correspond, <margin>5</margin> can be defined by no human judgment or art.

This is sufficiently proven because no opponent can encounter any premise or reasoning by which they could reveal the cause of these things; for it would be necessary for such a person to be capable of producing effects of this kind by that same reasoning. It is proven, moreover, by the authority of both Aristotle and the common body of <margin>10</margin> philosophers <note>scholastic thinkers of the Middle Ages and Renaissance</note>, who say that the "ultimate differences" of things are hidden and unnamable—meaning we can provide neither a name nor a definition for them. It is likewise defended by listing the effects found in Article 29, for which no explanation can be brought forward.

### XXX.

<margin>15</margin> What is said becomes manifest also in the case of nutrients, poisons, and antidotes, where different things suit different individuals, and certain things are poisons to some while they are nourishment to others; for which no one can provide any reason other than the contrariety or diver-<margin>20</margin>sity of "temperament" and "complexion" <note>the unique balance of the four bodily humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to determine health</note>. Yet, in what exactly that contrariety and diversity consists will not be easily declared.

If a debater can provide that explanation, we will gladly be taught by him.

### XXXI.

<margin>33r M</margin>
<margin>82v C</margin>
<margin>25</margin> These differences, without a doubt, do not arise from the internal and specific differences of things, but from certain "transcending" <term>accidents: properties that are not part of a thing's essential definition but affect how it interacts with others</term>.

<summary>Bruno argues that the specific causes of "miraculous" natural phenomena, such as lightning or the varying effects of poison, are hidden from human reason and defy naming. He suggests these effects stem from external "accidents" and individual temperaments rather than the core essence of a substance.</summary>

And in the preface to his book on *Physics*, Averrhoës says that habit is the greatest cause <margin>20</margin> by which poisons are not only turned into antidotes, but even into nourishment.

## XL.

Not only do physical and mathematical types of incantation <note>original: "incantationis"</note> possess the power to bind the body—not just the spirit—but logical types do as well.

This is evident in the kind of incantation performed through the art of rhetoric. Rhetoric conquers minds directly and immediately, but it also conquers bodies indirectly as a consequence. This occurs through emotions <note>original: "affectibus"</note> such as wrath, indignation, fear, and other similar feelings. These states are characteristic of living beings because of the soul, and they can grow so powerful that they lead to the very destruction of the body. By "bonds of the body," we mean every condition in which the body is so tied down by a specific passion of the emotions that some of its actions are damaged or hindered; this is what it means to be "bound" <note>original: "devinctum"</note>. Thus, to induce a sickness is to "bind," while to effect a cure is to "release" <note>original: "solvere"</note>. For this reason, it has become a common habit of speech to say that those who are cured are "released" or "freed from infirmity," which signifies being outside the bonds by which they were held.

## XLI.

We do not doubt—nor should any wise person doubt—that sight <note>original: "visum"</note> can also bind, or that through sight the spirit can be tied, impressed upon, and altered, and that consequently notable changes are generated in the body and the whole composite being.

This is proven by the examples brought forward in Article 41, and it is well enough established that certain visible forms <term>species visibiles: in medieval and Renaissance philosophy, these are the "images" or "likenesses" of objects that travel through the air to the eye</term> can stir up horror, loathing, hatred, love, joy, sadness, and indignation, accompanied by a total alteration of the person seeing them. Therefore, this alteration [passes] into the body...

## XLIII.

Everything that affects the faculty of knowing <note>original: "potentiam cognoscitivam," the mind's ability to perceive and process information</note> must slip into the soul through the gateway of the imagination <note>original: "phantasiae," here referring to the mental faculty that bridges the gap between the senses and the intellect</note>; for there is nothing in the reason which has not, in some way, been in the senses; and nothing passes from the sense into the reason that is not carried through the imagination. From this comes that famous maxim: "nothing is in the intellect which was not previously in the sense." <note>original: "nihil est in intellectu quod prius non fuerit in sensu," a fundamental principle of Aristotelian and Scholastic philosophy</note>

This is understood in terms of its origin, its occasion, and its foundation; for in reality—or specifically—the forms <note>original: "species," the mental representations or "images" of things</note> in the sense are entirely different from those in the intellect. For sensory forms, such as colors, tastes, and sounds, are not present in the intellect or reason either by themselves or by accident; and therefore, the reason (or opinion) is not primarily conquered by these. Thus, Epicurus and Heraclitus correctly said that the sense neither fails nor is it deceived; <margin>35<sup>v</sup> M</margin> for all falsity lies beneath the act of affirmation and negation. The sense, however, neither affirms nor denies, but only receives the forms presented to it. To see brass <note>original: "aurichalcum," or orichalcum, a golden-colored alloy often mistaken for gold</note> is, for the eyes, a real occurrence (that is, according to the external form); likewise, it is real for the imagination according to the internal form (if we understand "imagination" as the power that apprehends and retains forms; otherwise, strictly speaking, it is not the role of the imagination to define, but rather <margin>85<sup>v</sup> C</margin> to form mental images <note>original: "imaginationis," here emphasizing the specific act of "imaging" as opposed to "phantasia" which collects the data</note>). However, to judge that brass is gold, or even to judge that it is brass itself through the act of affirmation, is the work of a more inward power. Naturally enough, the sense is true and the imagination is true, provided it truly senses and truly apprehends and holds the form of the object.

## XLIV.

Neither the external sense, nor the internal "common sense," <note>original: "sensus communis," the faculty believed to unite the data from the five individual senses into a coherent whole</note> nor the imagination is deceived or deceives.

<summary>Bruno outlines the pathway of human knowledge, asserting that all information must enter the intellect through the senses and the imagination. But from the disturbance of these [sensory images], it follows that one is both deceived and deceives; for the cogitative faculty <note>original: "cogitativa," the mental power that processes, compares, and judges sensory data</note> is, in itself, immediately and properly the one that is misled, and it is according to this faculty that an opinion is called true or false.

## XLV.

<margin>5</margin> No particular sense <note>such as sight, hearing, or touch</note> knows that it is sensing, nor does it recognize the difference between itself and another sense, nor does it in any other way possess a reflexive act <note>original: "actum reflexum," the self-aware ability of a faculty to observe and analyze its own operations</note> regarding its own action.

For the function of sight is to see, but it is not its function to know whether it sees truly or falsely; rather, this belongs to an internal power, <margin>10</margin> namely the common sense <note>original: "sensum communem," the internal faculty that unifies and interprets the various inputs from the five external senses</note>. Therefore, the reflexive act of the cognitive power begins with cogitation (the thinking faculty), and it is this faculty that is primarily and properly "bound" <note>original: "vinciri," to be tied or fettered. In Bruno’s magic, "binding" refers to how the mind is captured or influenced by ideas or illusions</note> by errors of opinion. The bonds and knots <note>original: "vincula et nodi"</note> arise from the nature of the sensory forms and from the disturbed actions of the senses, whether external or even internal; yet it has been said that the imagination <margin>15</margin> and the sense are "bound" in their own way, so that the difference between the bonds of that kind and this kind is easily apparent.

Under the name of imagination <note>original: "phantasiae"</note>, we generally understand every internal sensitive power that exists before the cogitative faculty, which includes the common sense.

<margin>20</margin> ## XLVI.

There is a certain analogy <note>a structural correspondence or "ladder"</note> that leads from the body to the spirit, from the spirit to the sense, from the external sense to the internal, from sense in general to reason, from reason to the intellect, and from the intellect to the mind; hence, from the obligation and impediment <margin>25</margin> of the preceding faculties, the impediments and | bonds <margin>860</margin> <note>original: "ligamenta," ties or ligatures that restrict the soul's function</note> of the subsequent ones follow.

### XLVII.

Theologians quite reasonably introduce two kinds of foolishness (which even philosophers ought to acknowledge), if we define a "fool" as someone who does not perceive <note>original: "sapit," which carries the double meaning of "to taste/savor" and "to be wise."</note> in the common way or <margin>15</margin> like the masses. This happens in two ways: in one way, by thinking and feeling *below* common opinion and in a worse manner—namely, with sense and thought more deeply immersed in darkness; and in another way, *above* the common sense, with one's outlook emerging higher through refined character and the mind’s insight.

The first kind are fools simply and relatively; the <margin>20</margin> second are fools only relatively <note>meaning they appear foolish only in comparison to the average person because their wisdom is beyond common understanding.</note>. The first arises from disturbance, mixture, and confusion; the second from the processing, distinction, and order of the principles of knowledge. The first kind is usually caused by the dominance of some "furious" spirit—irrational, headlong, and clinging to matter—whereby the individual's own spirit of the universe, within their particular <margin>25</margin> microcosm <note>the human being viewed as a miniature reflection of the entire universe.</note>, grows sluggish or, so to speak, stunned, while some foreign and external influence rages more or less throughout. Just as an excess of wine leads to fury and various disordered excitements, so too through the proper tempering and "drinking" [of spiritual influences] the mind is refined and...

Just as a living being is driven by hunger into sorrow, sadness, resentment, anger, negligence of affairs, and other similar so-called "Saturnine" <note>Influenced by the planet Saturn, which in Renaissance astrology was associated with melancholy, gloom, and heaviness.</note> emotional states, so too from certain specific nutrients and <margin>86v</margin> medicines, various emotional states arise from the various "principles" of these states. These principles are the various <term>spirits: subtle, vaporous substances that Renaissance thinkers believed acted as the bridge between the physical body and the immaterial soul</term>, of which there are as many kinds as there can be types of <term>complexions: the specific balance of bodily fluids or "humors" that determined a person’s temperament.</term> There are as many modes as there can be degrees within each type. Hence, some of those principles are rational, others are irrational in their action; some follow a nature related to one planet, while others follow a nature related to <margin>36v</margin> another. To define these, the underlying physical complexion does much; this is why the same wine drives some entirely into a stupor and robs them of their senses, while it makes others possess a more subtle and vigorous wit and a certain "Jovian" <note>original: "Ioviae." Influenced by Jupiter, associated with a joyful, noble, and expansive disposition.</note> disposition. Still others it makes sad, others lustful, others energetic and "Martial" <note>original: "mavortios." Influenced by Mars, the god of war; associated with aggression and strength.</note>, and others pious, holy, sighing toward heaven and deploring the state of this present age. All of this occurs because of a certain external spirit that enters the body. Thus we see that through certain material things from the outside, one's disposition and character are changed by the indwelling spirit which clings to the ingested matter; when that matter is digested, the spirit is digested; when it is expelled, the spirit is expelled; while it clings, the spirit clings, and by binding, it conquers and fetters the person. To this class of "bindings"—specifically those arising from indwelling and inherent spirits—belong mania, folly, and other states which many physicians (who talk more than they reason) rashly attribute entirely to "black bile" <note>original: "atram bilem." One of the four humors, traditionally linked to melancholy and madness.</note>. All such people possess less wisdom than the common opinion suggests and are truly fools.

There is another kind of person whose spirit or soul, although touched by certain bodily conditions, is nevertheless not penetrated or conquered by them. Instead, through a vigorous virtue of the mind, such a person possesses a higher wisdom, so that they are not only immune to the disturbances of fools, but even to the trembling of the common people. They do not believe what the masses believe, they do not fear what the masses dread, and they despise those things for which the masses gape. The common people, standing in the middle and establishing the limits and orders of wisdom according to their own measure, consider everyone positioned outside their boundaries and lines to be...

### XLVIII.

In this second mode, individuals are disposed so that even if they possess—by the order of nature—the work of thought following after the work of the <term>phantasia: the faculty of the soul that produces mental images or "phantasms"</term> (since thinkable <term>species: mental forms or concepts</term> are abstracted from imagined forms—just as the forms of fear and love arise from imagined forms that are disordered, monstrous, and alienated from harmony with this power; for example, the image of a snake or a lion does not favorably affect the present sense—whether it is conceived by the external senses or fabricated by the work of the imagination—which is called **cogitative** in humans and **estimative** in beasts), they nevertheless act upon the imagined forms more than they are affected by them.

For the **soul, being more vigorous** and less drowsy within the body, possesses a powerful reflection of judgment and operation over those images, distinguishing truths from appearances and a doubtful sense from one that is defined and certain. Thus, with the sense itself acting as judge and witness, the soul concludes—contrary to the opinion of the multitude—that not everything that seems to move is actually moving, and that not everything seen is necessarily good, just, or true. [XLVIII.] Likewise, it does not only distinguish those things that arise from an ordered...

### XLIX.

<margin>10 15 87^v</margin>
Regarding those who are **possessed** <note>original: "energumenos"</note> or **daemoniacs**, who speak in various languages beyond their own natural ability and demonstrate a mastery of various sciences: physicians err with a certain thick-headed persistence when they deny that there are <term>daemones: spirits or intermediary beings</term> and alien intellects; likewise, certain <term>sacristans: clerics or those in charge of sacred rites</term> err when they deny that this state arises from the qualities of the **humors** <note>The four bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, black bile, yellow bile) believed to determine temperament</note>, instead attributing the whole matter to the work of a demon. However, every line of reasoning from all sides proves that this effect arises from a certain new **living being** <note>original: "animal." In Bruno's philosophy, an "animal" is any "animated" entity formed by the union of a soul/spirit and matter</note> produced and conceived within, whose body is composed of the "matter" of the physicians and whose soul is from the "spirit" of the sacristans—though the condition of that [new] living being is different from the condition of the one to whom the body originally belonged.

<margin>20 37M 25</margin>
This is evident from what is said in Article 49, to which we add that we do not call this an "internal living being" or an "internal species of living being" [except] according to its true species and the customary meaning of "living being," but rather according to a certain proportional or analogical sense. In this same way, the stars, the spheres, and the world itself are sometimes called "living beings" <note>original: "animalia"</note>—sometimes because of an **attendant soul**, sometimes only because of a **moving soul**, but not necessarily because of an **inherent soul** that acts upon and animates them in the same way as in plants and those things commonly called "animals."

### L.

From the <term>cogitativa: the cogitative faculty; the "highest" internal sense that organizes images into concepts</term>—namely, the sense that follows the <term>phantasia: imagination</term>—arises the principle of all emotions, knowledge, and will, whether in theoretical or moral matters, and whether they be virtuous or wicked.

<margin>5</margin> For just as the regulation of the cogitativa follows the rule of the preceding senses, so too the disposition of the intellect and the will follows the regulation of the cogitativa.

### LI.

Faith <note>original: "fides"; in this context, it refers to "belief," "conviction," or "assent" as well as religious faith</note> is twofold, just as knowledge and emotion are twofold; <margin>10</margin> namely, sensory and rational. The first is founded upon the faculties that come before the cogitativa and rests within it; the second is founded upon the powers and virtues that follow it and takes its beginning from it. These two forms of faith are mutually regulated and regulating.

<margin>15</margin> The reason is that sensory faith is better or worse mostly <gloss>rather</gloss> on the side of matter, whereas rational faith is so more on the side of form. The principle of sensory perfection is, of itself, a well-disposed body or organ; but the principle of rational perfection is a well-harmonized and tempered spirit, and a soul that is well-freed and <margin>20</margin> purified. 

Therefore, just as the affections of the body follow those of the soul (for a soul that is joyful, free, and in harmony with itself preserves a well-disposed body, as Zoroaster <note>Zoroaster was a legendary ancient Persian prophet to whom many "Chaldean Oracles" were attributed in the Renaissance</note> said: "If you accustom the soul to dwell upon divine objects, you will free the body itself from corruption" <note>original: "si anima consueveris divinis incumbere obiectis, et corpus ipsum a corruptione liberabis"</note>), so also, conversely, <margin>25</margin> from a body that is well-strengthened and tempered, there follows a more regulated sense and a mind <note>original: "animus"</note> that is more peaceful, tranquil, and vigorous.

<summary>Bruno explains that the "cogitativa" (the faculty of thought) is the bridge between our physical senses and our higher intellect, influencing both our moral character and our physical health. He argues that a purified soul can preserve the body, while a healthy body supports a tranquil and sharp mind.</summary>

### LII.

->Of those things which alter or move the cogitative faculty, some principles are purely physical, while others are positive <note>original: "positiva"; here meaning established by human will, convention, or ritual practice</note>; and these latter are of no less efficacy than the former.<-

For <term>species: mental images or impressions</term> are renewed in the soul or arrive anew—some regularly from external objects, others from a disturbance of the <term>phantasia: the imagination</term> without any art; and the principal [causes] <note>original: "praecipua"; the text has a gap here, likely "causes" or "sources"</note> of these are the seeds of thoughts or emotions formally, but materially they are certain types of nourishment. From this, it is easy to conclude the universal reason or art for inciting specific dreams <margin>38r</margin> and of disposing the cogitative faculty at will in a certain artificial way, and finally of healing or bewitching the soul (by "soul," I mean the whole person, for the sake of the soul or its faculties). This method is practiced by certain contemplatives, <term>apocalyptics: those who seek or claim divine revelations</term>, professors of the <term>Ars Notoria: a medieval "notory art" aimed at gaining rapid knowledge through prayers and mystic figures</term> and prophecy, and <term>theurgists: those who perform rituals to invoke the presence of deities or spirits</term>. These people, through a certain dietary regimen and specific preliminary meditations, dispose, promote, and habituate the mind toward a certain kind of piety, so that finally—being most foolish—they believe they enjoy the conversation of certain "tragic deities," and they see and report marvelous things; such things, however, must be categorized as folly and the worst kind of <term>mania: madness or frenzy</term>. 

And we know from constant experience that specific types of dreams are brought about by specific foods, thoughts, and emotions: some toward <term>Venus: signifying lust or romantic love</term>, some toward tragic and mournful things, some toward the sight of beautiful spectacles—namely fields, gardens, and orchards—some toward seas and rivers, some toward fires, stars, and suns, some toward winds and storms, some toward quarrels, brawls, and rages, some toward terrors, prisons, captivities, horrors, and terrible phantasms, to which much is contributed by that which...

Therefore, the mind becomes accustomed to being ill or being well—that is, to being wise or being foolish—according to the types of <term>species: mental images or impressions</term> upon which it is nourished; to which nourishment, baths, and ointments contribute materially, while those things captured through the external senses contribute efficiently.

If someone should grow accustomed to hearing the voices of cattle, the talk of peasants, of the ignoble, the ignorant, and the semi-wild; likewise to seeing such countenances, <margin>88v C</margin> such miserable, tragic, wretched, and unfortunate sights; | likewise the angry, the proud, and the furious—thus the soul is entirely infected. Thus, the greatest care and caution must be taken regarding where and with whom one is raised and educated: under what pedagogy, what religion, what worship, and what books or authors one becomes accustomed to. All of which will generate character—not by accident, but truly by their own nature—producing the worst or even worse results if they are bad, and the best or even better if they are good; and along with this, they generate one's <term>genius: a person's guiding spirit or innate temperament</term> and fortune.

## LVI.

All affects and bonds of the will are reduced to two and relate back to them, namely to the <term>irascible: the faculty of the soul associated with anger, courage, and vigor</term> and the <term>concupiscible: the faculty of the soul associated with desire, longing, and pleasure</term>, or hatred and love; ultimately, hatred is reduced to love; therefore, the single bond of the will is love.

It is proven because all other affects that anyone could mention or devise are nothing else—formally, fundamentally, and originally—than love. For **envy** is a certain love of oneself by which one cannot tolerate a superior or an equal; **emulation** is similar.
<margin>10</margin> **Indignation** is a love of virtue, by which one takes it badly that the unworthy should fare well, while the worthy do not; **shame** and **fear** are nothing other than a love of honor and of that thing for whose sake one fears. The same is true of all other affects. Finally, the **hatred** of one thing is nothing other than the love of its contrary or opposite. Therefore, **anger** is also
<margin>15</margin> ultimately a form of love. He who has mastered that philosophy or magic which knows how to handle the supreme, principal, and most general bond—love—will have achieved enough; for this reason, perhaps, love was called the "great daemon" <note>original: "daemon magnus"; in the Platonic tradition, a 'daemon' is a powerful intermediary spirit connecting the human and the divine, rather than an evil entity.</note> by the **Platonists**.

Folios 70-86^v of the Moscow Codex (referred to as **M**) contain another untitled magic treatise,¹ which for the most part consists of <term>excerpts: selected passages taken from a larger work</term> from **Trithemius**, **Agrippa**, and **Pseudo-Albertus Magnus**. We would have gladly overlooked this compiled section entirely, limiting ourselves to reproducing only the first paragraphs and whatever else possessed Bruno’s personal character (and that he is indeed the compiler is demonstrated by the citation of *On the Shadows of Ideas* <note>original: "De umbris idearum"</note> at page 502, 23 and following, and the correspondence of page 495, 17 and following with *On Magic* <note>original: "De Magia"</note> page 453, 14 and following). 

However, we felt it necessary to provide extensive information about the rest of the text to enable the reader to judge the relationship the entire treatise has with that chapter of *On Magic* which refers to it (compare above to page 435, 23; 438, 6 and following; and Lutoslawski, cited work, pages 537 and 550). We therefore provide a kind of <term>collation: a critical comparison of different manuscripts or texts to identify variations</term> with the works from which Bruno draws. But since he does not reproduce them literally, and only extracts what seems to him to be of fundamental importance (see 506, 17 and following), our collation serves only to give a general idea of how the material is treated and distributed. 

In general, we can say that the more or less extensive considerations found in the source texts are omitted; instead, Bruno simply extracts the names, qualities, and attributes of the spirits and similar details. For Trithemius’s *Steganography* <note>original: "Steganographia"</note>, we are using the 1606 edition (Frankfurt, from the printing house of Mat—

# (ON MATHEMATICAL MAGIC.)

<margin>70r</margin> I. God flows into the angels, the angels into the celestial bodies, the celestial bodies into the elements, the elements into <term>mixtures: compounds formed by the four elements, such as minerals, plants, or living tissues</term>, mixtures into the senses, the senses into the soul, and the soul into the living being. <margin>5</margin> Conversely, the living being ascends through the soul to the senses, through the senses into the mixtures, through the mixtures into the elements, through the elements into the heavens, through these into <term>daemons: in the Renaissance sense, these are intermediary spirits or guiding intelligences, not necessarily "demons" in the modern sense</term> or angels, and through those into God or into divine operations.

II. Thus, there is a descent from God, or of God, through the world to the living being; but there is an ascent of the living being through the world to God. <margin>10</margin> God is at the summit of the ladder; the <term>cabalistic: referring to the Kabbalah, a tradition of Jewish mysticism influential in the Renaissance</term> Jacob is at its root and foundation. The degrees of the intermediary creatures, according to their numbers, constitute the height of the ladder, through which the superior operating powers descend to lower things and the lower things climb to the higher. <margin>15</margin> For this ascent and descent is designated by the exit and entry of the two gates—<note>original: "Cancri et Capricorni"</note> Cancer and Capricorn (one of which is called the gate of the Gods, the other the gate of men)—as described by the ancient authors of profound philosophy. <note>Bruno refers to the Neoplatonic belief that souls enter the physical world through the sign of Cancer and return to the divine realm through Capricorn.</note>

Three-headed wisdom <note>original: *Sapientia triceps*</note>—from which Cerberus, barking from his three heads, is assigned to guard the three-headed Hecate <note>A goddess of the moon, crossroads, and magic, often depicted with three faces or bodies</note>—repels those who are obscure and affected by the blindness of ignorance; it admits into the **Elysian fields** <note>The final resting place of the virtuous in Greek mythology</note> only those who, through metaphysics, descend from the summit of the ladder through the mathematical steps to the physical foundation... <note>The text here indicates a missing portion or lacuna in the original manuscript.</note>

IV. The **physical foundation** consists of two active elements, earth and fire, which, being placed on opposite sides, form the steps of the **ladder of nature** <note>original: *scala naturae*; the hierarchical structure of all existence from base matter to the Divine</note> for the constitution of natural things and stabilize them by their combination; their virtues, powers, operations, and acts have been explained to us in their proper place through the physical elements.

V. For the present, therefore, this discipline proposes the following as a completion of the first part, which rests on supernatural power: contemplation, faith, worship, ritual, and a purity directed toward pure things. As a completion of the second part, it proposes time and the seasons, order, the attainment of concord for the sake of harmony, and strife for the sake of conflict, the evasion of impediments, and execution at the proper moment. As a completion of the third part, it proposes the application of active things to passive things, skillfully prepared for one another. We shall clarify the reason for all these things in the following discourse through three treatises. The first of these concerns worship or the path toward worship; the second concerns observance and the distribution of time, as well as the logic of figures, numbers, seals, characters, and rings; the third concerns the quality, logic, application, property, and order of things.

<margin>70v</margin>
VI. Since there exists a triple nerve <note>Or "triple strength"</note> of this faculty—which, when complete and perfect, is most powerful for all bindings and most effective for confirming every solution—it is understood that the wisest among the **Hebrew Cabalists** <note>Bruno is referring to King Solomon, the traditional author of the biblical book of Ecclesiastes</note> said: "**a threefold cord is not easily broken**" <note>original: *funiculus triplex difficile rumpitur*; a quote from Ecclesiastes 4:12</note>. We call the first cord **invocation** and the direction of the soul toward the higher virtues; for we are powerless in ourselves, like craftsmen who can do nothing unless they have borrowed material from...

<summary>Bruno outlines the structure of his magical system, dividing it into supernatural, temporal, and physical components. He uses the biblical metaphor of the "threefold cord" to emphasize that successful magic requires the combined strength of spiritual invocation, mathematical timing, and physical application.</summary>

VIII. Therefore, **faith and belief** should flourish in the operator, together with the hope of obtaining the thing and accomplishing the business; and he ought to take care to excite the same in the one upon whom he has decided to confer good things; but he should procure fear,

### XII. Concerning the soul of the world and of worldly things according to the magic of the ancients.

<margin>73r</margin> It has been granted by the most noble poets and the wisest philosophers that the heaven and the world are animate—that is, possessed of a soul—as are the celestial bodies that we see. They agree that a single universal spirit is implanted in the entire machine of the world, and that a single mind, infused through its limbs, agitates the whole mass, as Pythagoras <note>Pythagoras (c. 570–495 BC) taught that the universe was a living being governed by numerical harmony.</note> says. If indeed these lower, mixed, and partial things possess a soul and life, why not the universe itself, from which these are produced as if from a certain fertile [source]? <note>The Latin here is damaged, possibly reading *foeto* (pregnant/fertile).</note> Why should it not be considered a more noble and principal body than a plant or a tree? For why should we deny that earth and water live, which from themselves generate, vivify, nourish, and increase innumerable plants and living beings? How could life come from non-living things? How could a non-living thing produce a living soul? 

And Theophrastus <note>Theophrastus (c. 371–287 BC) was Aristotle's successor; Bruno likely encounters this via Pico della Mirandola, who argued that it is "impious" to suggest the heavens are inanimate.</note> says that one should not be considered a philosopher who doubts that the celestial bodies live and are animate—animated, I say, by a rational soul, so that they might conspire among themselves toward a perpetual order and produce their works through certain rational principles. Therefore, let there be a "reason" or governing principle of earthly things in the earth, of lunar things in the moon, and of solar things in the sun. This soul is not like the soul of a lowly body, but is intelligent, and with its body it creates one of the Gods. This soul possesses far better reasons for its actions than we have for our own bodies; and it is fitting that a more perfect body be formed by a more perfect soul. 

From this comes that most perfect, most regular, and most ordered movement—not wandering or straying back and forth, but holding the most select path toward the best end, where the perfect mind does not change its counsel. Together with other bodies, it constitutes as if a single monochord <term>monochord: an ancient musical instrument with one string used to demonstrate mathematical ratios of sound; here it symbolizes the unity of the cosmos</term> and the universal harmony sung by the lyre of Apollo.

Indeed, the names they devise for the celestial souls—some of which are "knowing" and others "vivifying" <note>original: *vivificantes*; giving life</note>—are of the following sort according to Orphic and ancient theology: thus, in the ninth sphere, the cognitive power is Bacchus Cribronius <note>Bacchus "of the Sieve," a mystical title for Dionysus representing the intellectual power that sifts or separates the pure from the impure.</note>, and the power of vivification is the Muse Calliope—

<summary>Bruno argues for the "Anima Mundi" or World Soul, asserting that the universe and celestial bodies must be living, rational entities because life cannot emerge from what is dead. He uses the metaphor of the "monochord" and Apollo's lyre to describe the harmonious, intelligent movement of the heavens.</summary>

## SECOND TREATISE.

XXV. Beyond those things which have been said, it must be observed that everything must be examined according to a certain number and measure of times, places, and the things to be handled. For time rules over temporal 
<margin>5</margin> things and contains them, just as the lower bodies are contained by the higher celestial bodies; for this reason, the ancients believed that time resides in the first heaven <note>In the Ptolemaic cosmology of the period, the "first heaven" or *Primum Mobile* was the outermost sphere that initiated all movement and time.</note>. Therefore, it should be noted generally that effects associated with Jupiter (Jovial), Saturn (Saturnine), and Mars (Martial) are to be 
<margin>10</margin> attempted when those specific planets are well-disposed and fortunately situated in the heavens. Without observing these conditions, no other preparations, no voices <note>In this context, "voices" refers to incantations or spoken formulas.</note>, and no rituals can have any power; for it would be just as if someone were to scatter seed at an improper time, failing to notice that different times are required for different seeds—and as it is in one matter, so it is in all. Why is this so? Do we not also 
<margin>15</margin> see certain religions designate <unclear>diverse</unclear> <note>original: "cultus .....es". The manuscript is partially corrected here; it likely refers to specific or fixed rituals.</note> ceremonies and various rites to specific and diverse times? For the diversity of times is manifold. Each of the planets has its own ages, its own years, its own stages of life, its own lunar cycles, days, and hours; so that for matters that are perpetual and meant to endure for a long time, the rules of the "great revolutions" <note>Major astrological cycles, such as the conjunctions of outer planets.</note> must be observed; for things not so long-lasting, 
<margin>20</margin> the rules of the minor cycles; for less distinguished matters, the rules of daily cycles; and for common matters pertaining to individual persons, the rules of the hourly domains must be observed, which can occur three times in a natural day. We must take account of these hours for our present purposes, since those effects which pertain to changes in laws, 
<margin>25</margin> governments, and those things which arise from general causes would be attempted by us rashly and in vain <note>The author argues that a practitioner should focus on the "hours" for personal magic, as attempting to change the fate of nations without aligning with grander astrological cycles is futile.</note>.

## THIRD TREATISE.

XXVI. In the application of active and passive <note>Active and passive principles refer to the Aristotelian idea that some things act (like fire) while others are acted upon (like wood being burned).</note> agents, one must first consider the properties and natures of the elements. We must consider them as pure or as composite; as more or less subject to decay; as the forces that accomplish all things in all matters; as things that are purified and reduced to simplicity through art <note>In this context, "art" refers to alchemy or laboratory techniques used to refine substances.</note>; and as things that are combined to create diverse species. We must also understand how pure elements can achieve great things, while impure composites—arranged through countless degrees—can perform innumerable feats. Indeed, specific species are produced through certain orders, and through these elements come all bindings, loosenings, transformations, predictions, the drawing-in of good things, and the driving-out of evils. Knowledge and shrewdness regarding these elements is the foundation of all magic.

### On the power of fire, as well as earth, water, and air.

I. Fire, the most active of all things, penetrates everything, etc. <note>original: "Ignis activissimus..." Bruno is here summarizing the work of Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa, a famous 16th-century occultist whose book *On Occult Philosophy* is referenced by page numbers in the text.</note> II. The kinds of composite things must be considered, and how they are distributed among the four underlying elements, etc. III. It must be considered in a certain order how these elements are related to the heavens, just as... <insert>[80v]</insert> IV. One must consider the powers that depend upon the most immediate elements. V. One must consider, as far as possible, those virtues <note>In Renaissance science, a "virtue" is a specific power or property inherent in a substance.</note> which can hardly be traced back to any of the elements—such as the power to repel poison, to attract iron <note>A reference to magnetism.</note>, or to purge yellow bile <insert>[81r]</insert>—and those virtues which can achieve a great deal with very little matter, and which thereby manifest themselves. It is not our purpose here to consider from where or how those hidden virtues <note>original: "virtutes occultae." These are "occult" not because they are evil, but because they are "hidden" from the senses and only known by their effects.</note> are infused. For we do not approve of the tales many people tell about the rays of the stars, nor do we join in the talk about the "Ideas" <note>Platonic Ideas or Forms.</note> and the reasons of the World Soul <note>original: "anima mundi." This is the concept that the universe itself is a living being with a soul that connects all things.</note>. It is enough to know how different species, and different individuals of the same species, receive different influences through different preparations and arrangements. VI. One must consider how the virtues of things are to be investigated and tested...

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;These are the points which contain the entire logic of magic; they alone suffice for a wise and perceptive man. I did not wish to provide specific examples and other details in which others occupy themselves, since such things can be of no
<margin>20</margin> use to one who lacks the logic of these matters, and they are attempted in vain. Furthermore, to one who understands these principles and meditates deeply upon them, not only such examples, but similar, greater, and even the greatest things are accessible. If anyone, therefore, thinks that we have not provided a complete art, and have not gathered everything from the studies of others for the perfection of this science—only
<margin>25</margin> omitting the superfluous—let him know that this is a defect of his own judgment and a frailty of his intellect, because he has been made less fit by the heavens to perceive these and other matters. If some authors seem to have written larger books, it is because they have mixed in much that is extraneous and irrelevant to the matter,
<margin>30</margin> perhaps to make the art less accessible—which we also could have done.

# ON THE PRINCIPLES, ELEMENTS, AND CAUSES OF THINGS.

->Year 1590<-
->March 16, Monday <note>original: "☽," the symbol for the Moon, traditionally used to denote Monday.</note><-

<margin>5</margin> The <term>efficient causes [causae efficientes] <note>In the philosophical tradition Bruno follows, the "efficient cause" is the agent or force that brings something into being or initiates change.</note></term> and moving causes of things are the intellect and the soul. Above these is one absolute principle: the mind, or truth. Their essence and power are infinite both <term>intensively and extensively [intensive et extensive]</term>. They are infinite "extensively" because they are within the infinite whole, or everywhere; they are infinite "intensively" because they are entirely present within the whole and entirely present everywhere.

<margin>10</margin> But the mind exists in a more <term>eminent [eminentius] <note>To exist "eminently" means to possess a quality in its highest, most perfect, and causal form, surpassing the way that quality exists in the physical world.</note></term> way. It is "whole in the whole" in such a way that it is also entirely outside the whole and above the whole, since it is an absolute being, sufficient in and for itself. The intellect and the soul, however, are not outside the whole nor above the whole—unless you confuse the meanings of "mind" and "intellect" by taking

<margin>15</margin> both under one definition. Yet, the intellect exists within and alongside <term>intelligible things [intelligibilia] <note>Objects of thought that are understood by the mind rather than perceived by the physical senses.</note></term>; the soul exists with and within living things—whole in all of them, and whole in each individual. The intellect, too, is entirely in all and entirely in each. The mind, however, exists within itself, or as its very self, or by itself.

<margin>20</margin> Beneath these is one infinite space, capable of containing infinite substance, in which something can exist. For just as these visible things, which reach our senses, fill this space which matches their magnitude, so there are things that can or do fill another space,

<meta>Continuity: This page continues from the discussion of the infinite nature of the Mind and Intellect, transitioning here into a defense of the physical infinity of space and the material principles (earth and water) that occupy it. # OF GIORDANO BRUNO

---

outside of this very [world] and into the infinite, there is a space that is certainly of no less <term>receptive power [potentia receptiva] <note>The capacity of space to contain or "receive" matter. Bruno argues that if space exists here, it exists everywhere with the same properties.</note></term> than this one; indeed, no one unless they are out of their mind would call into doubt whether this space exists. 
Whether, indeed, just as it possesses the same power [to receive], it also possesses the same 
<margin>5</margin> <term>actuality [actus] <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "actuality" is the realization of a possibility. Bruno is arguing that if space *can* be filled with worlds, it *must* be filled with them, otherwise the "power" of the universe would be wasted.</note></term>, no philosopher except one of very weak intelligence would doubt. For that power which established this filled space can also continually fill a space of the same and similar power, provided that passive and active power are everywhere the same. And we have shown this with many arguments 
<margin>10</margin> in the dialogues *On the Infinite, the Universe, and the Worlds* <note>original: "De infinito et universo et mundis." This is a Latin reference to Bruno's 1584 Italian work "De l'infinito, universo e mondi."</note>.
Within space, there are then two material things: namely, earth and water. We sometimes call the earth "the dry," and sometimes "atoms"; water is sometimes vapor, and sometimes it is more thinned out as air.
<margin>15</margin> Two stable immaterial things are the spirit and the soul, as they are commonly called.
In the two material principles—namely water and earth—darkness resides; and they are referred to by the name of "darkness," especially water, which is sometimes called the <term>Abyss [Abyssus]</term> and sometimes the <term>Styx [Styx]</term> <note>In Greek mythology, the Styx is the river of the underworld; Bruno uses it here to represent the cold, dark, primordial state of matter.</note>.
<margin>20</margin> It is understood as the procreative source of all things, as understood by Thales <note>Thales of Miletus (c. 620–546 BCE), the Greek philosopher who proposed that water is the fundamental substance of all matter.</note> and Moses, who introduced the "Spirit of God brooding over the waters" <note>A reference to Genesis 1:2.</note>, as if giving them a procreative power, just as when a hen broods over eggs. And because all the seeds of things are moist, he therefore calls the seed 
<margin>25</margin> of all things "water"; hence, in dividing the world into the lower and the higher, he uses a way of speaking by which the lower forms are called the "waters beneath the firmament" and the higher forms the "waters above [the firmament]."

<summary>Bruno argues for an infinite universe filled with worlds, asserting that space's capacity to hold matter is realized everywhere. <margin>39v</margin> ...firmament. From this point, all the divine philosophers, mages, and poets understand the Styx—which they view as the womb <note>original: "matricem," though the manuscript is slightly unclear and could potentially be read as "creatricem" (creatress)</note> of waters—to be the mother of the Gods or of the distinct forms of things. This is what Orpheus, Linus, Hesiod, and all the poets signify when they say 
<margin>5</margin> that the Styx is the "inviolable oath of the Gods" <note>In Greek mythology, the gods swore their most binding oaths by the River Styx. Bruno interprets this "inviolability" as the fundamental, unchanging nature of matter.</note>. A proof that this is the matter of all things is that dry things—or atoms—have no foundation or consistency without water binding, uniting, and sustaining them. Therefore, <term>Thales <note>Thales of Miletus (c. 624 – c. 546 BCE), often called the first Western philosopher, who famously proposed that water is the fundamental substance of the universe.</note></term> rightly said that water is the foundation of the earth. Our contemporaries do not understand this, but it was understood by 
<margin>10</margin> the <term>Psalmist <note>original: "Psaltes," referring to King David or the author of the Psalms.</note></term> when he said that God "founded the earth upon the waters" <note>A reference to Psalm 24:2.</note>. Moses also introduces the dry land as if it were appearing out of the waters and exerting itself from them. Indeed, water must be at the center, just as there must be a glue at the middle around which the things to be bonded are gathered; 
<margin>15</margin> for the earth, or the dry land, being very light and unstable, cannot be the foundation for water.

In the two immaterial principles—namely, spirit and soul (I call them "immaterial" because they are not matter, even though they exist *within* matter, for spirit and soul do not "receive" 
<margin>20</margin> water and earth, but are themselves received)—there is **light**. This is because light is certainly rooted within all things, just like the spirit and the soul; and sometimes people use the name "light" to mean the soul and the spirit. From light combined with water, or with a moist nature, **fire** proceeds; for all light, which we commonly call light, and all fire-light, 
<margin>25</margin> consists in the moist. Therefore, where there is no moisture, there is no fire, neither in <term>actuality [actum] <note>The state of being currently active or manifested.</note></term> nor in <term>potentiality [potentiam] <note>The inherent capacity to become something or produce an effect.</note></term>. <meta>Continuity: This page continues Bruno’s interpretation of the Genesis creation narrative through the lens of his own "deeper philosophy." <page-num>512</page-num>
-> IORDANO BRUNO <-

Moses <note>The "he" refers to Moses, whom Bruno treats as a master of natural philosophy encoding secrets in the Book of Genesis.</note> does not name fire, but it was sufficient for him to have spoken of light and of the waters or the abyss. He understands fire to be a composite substance rather than a fundamental principle. Thus, light was the first thing produced after the establishing of the abyss and the spirit, and this refers to the 
<margin>5</margin> work of the first day. However, fire—which is the sun <note>original: "sol," though the manuscript uses the astrological symbol ☉</note>, namely visible light within a luminous body—is the work of the fourth day. Moses does not distinguish such fire from the waters (as has been stated), but rather calls the stars "waters above the heavens" or the firmament. He does this because, as has just been noted, fire is substantially water; where there is 
<margin>10</margin> no moisture, there is no fire.

With this distinction of primordial things established, and for the completion of this deeper philosophy (so far as it pertains to the contemplation and operation of nature), we shall set aside the metaphysical consideration of the mind 
<margin>15</margin> and the intellect. We also defer the contemplation of the spirit and the soul to another specific treatise. For now, we only bring together the universal principles: first, concerning light and fire generally, using the common way of speaking; second, concerning the spirit, wind, or air, also in its 
<margin>20</margin> common meaning; third, concerning water, vapor, or darkness; and finally, concerning the earth or the dry land.

...of species or images, likewise of active qualities, in which there is an alterative and transformative principle.

I. It is called a substance because, firstly, by the authority of Hermes <note>original: "Mercurius," referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage</note>, the Chaldeans, and Moses—who all testify that created things are not
<margin>5</margin> "concreated" <note>Meaning they are primary entities, not just properties added to an existing object.</note>, as has been said, referring to the work of the first day in their parables. Secondly, by reason: because it is bound to no subject but is free from every subject, and it produces heat—conditions which are foreign to the nature of those things called "accidents" <note><term>accidents</term>: In traditional philosophy, these are properties like color or shape that cannot exist on their own without a physical body to "inhabit." Bruno argues light is a substance because it exists independently.</note>.

<margin>10</margin> II. It is of itself imperceptible to the senses, since "light" <note>original: "lux"</note> is not what is sensed, but rather the "shining thing" <note>original: "lucidum"</note>. That is, in its pure simplicity, light is not an object of the senses, but only when it is in a composite state. For this reason, Moses rightly places the creation of the "luminaries" <note>the sun and moon</note> on the fourth day, distinguishing "shining radiance" <note>original: "lumen"</note> from "primordial light" <note>original: "lux"</note>.

<margin>15</margin> III. It is said to become sensible through a moist substance, because light does not shine until it has moved into the substance of fire; this occurs when it enters a luminous body, either of its own nature or through another. A body that is luminous of its own nature is a moist substance which light kindles by penetrating it deeply—such is the nature of every flame
<margin>20</margin> and every ignited thing. Light acts "through another" when it strikes a transparent body bounded by something opaque with a smooth surface. Hence we see water, glass, crystal, and all other such things shine, which do not exist without water. Therefore, we conclude that every luminous body is aqueous <note>watery</note>, while light itself is a certain substance
<margin>25</margin> within water, or with water, or around water.

<meta>Continuity: On the previous page, Giordano Bruno distinguished between "lux" (the internal, primordial source of light) and "lumen" (the visible radiation). He argued that light and fire are present even in dry, cold substances like lime and ash in a "seminal" or potential state. Here, he provides an experimental proof involving ash and water to show how these principles interact and how light can be concentrated into fire.</meta>

<page-num>515</page-num>
# ON THE PRINCIPLES OF THINGS, ETC.

A vessel full of ash can receive as much water as the same vessel can when empty. The reason for this, as we understand it, is that the water is condensed, narrowed, or diminished by the ash; likewise, the body of the ash 
<margin>5</margin> is thickened by the water. Thus, the water occupies a smaller dimension of space because of the ash, and the ash a smaller dimension because of the water. Therefore, as much as the two could occupy in two separate places, they now occupy in half of that space. This is not due to what they <note>Bruno is likely referring to the Peripatetics, or followers of Aristotle.</note> call "sympathy" <note>original: *sympathia*; a term used in ancient physics to describe a natural attraction between substances.</note>—that is, of the dry for the moist and the moist for the
<margin>10</margin> dry—since those two qualities are called "passive" by these same thinkers, not active. Rather, it comes primarily from a hot nature existing in the ash and a cold nature existing in the water; from this, there follows an alteration in the dryness of the ash and the moisture of the water. Therefore, fire is in the ash originally, primordially, and
<margin>15</margin> causatively; whereas in the water, it is present really, effectively, and finally in a way that can be sensed. Thus, Democritus <note>An ancient Greek philosopher (c. 460–370 BCE) famous for his atomic theory; Bruno often invokes him to support his own ideas on the physical nature of light.</note> spoke well when he called light a "dry substance," which produces heat in a moist environment and shines forth from that heat. When this light is communicated and diffused from a luminous body, it 
<margin>20</margin> produces heat, as is evident in mirrors <note>original: *speculis*</note> which, from a concave surface, reflect light and stir up heat in the bodies opposite them; and in jars full of water, which, from a convex surface, transmit light and fire into the object placed beneath them. 

Just as God—not without a great hidden mystery <note>original: *arcano*</note>—is said by Moses to have produced light, and after light all things that exist 
<margin>25</margin> after the spirit and the water (or the abyss and the heaven), so too anyone who wishes to perform wonders in nature will contemplate and observe the powers of light according to his capacity, and thus his works...

<margin>20</margin> Magicians say that if a vine produces a grape in oil, it infuses such spirits and virtue into this moist substance that light poured through it will represent the image of the grapes in the dark. Wonderful are the things they report.

<margin>5</margin>Regarding other contemplations about fire, discussing its motion at length belongs to the physicist; however, this point can pertain to the present speculation: that one should consider beyond what was considered above regarding the circular motion of elements or bodies in their own place, or what follows from circular motion.

<margin>10</margin>Light or fire, as it is implanted in all composite things, possesses the motion of the mover rather than the moved; for that which is moved does not seem to be fire itself, but rather something ignited. This is seen in wood, lamps, candles, and in all matter that is consumed: there flies out a smoke or vapor which, being close to the kindling power, appears ignited, shines, and is sensible to the touch.

<margin>15</margin>And it is this [the vapor] which, as if fleeing its opposite <note>The "opposite" here likely refers to the cold or the density of the surrounding air.</note>, is dispersed through space or the void; the common people call this "fire" and say it "ascends upward," whereas the ignited vapor is actually driven no more upward than in all directions, in a spherical expansion.

<margin>20</margin>But we, looking more deeply into the nature of the thing, say that the fire which keeps the candle lit and whose substantial seeds remain, is not the flame itself, but that which inflames the vapor, or that which produces the flame and casts out that light. This remains in the candle as long as

<margin>25</margin>it is lit and provides it with fuel <term>pabulum</term> <note>literally "fodder" or "food"; the material that sustains a fire.</note>. Hence, that torch which we see burning, we should understand as being numerically the same for scarcely a single instant; <margin>5</margin> although it appears immutable and constant, we must nevertheless judge it to be continually different, because the smoke flying above is always different, and it is into this smoke that a changing flame is necessarily and always being converted. We admit that this same fire also ascends upward by corroding the substance, and likewise moves to the right and left in pursuit of the nourishment and food <note>original: *pabulum*. A common term in ancient physics for the material that "feeds" a flame.</note> that it is able to reach.

Furthermore, in the examples listed—such as the candle, etc.—the motion is entirely downward, <margin>20</margin> and an upward motion would be contrary and destructive to it. From these points, an opportunity for no small contemplation opens up, if we distinguish true fire from common fire, and vital fire from luminous fire, and that fire which is the life of living things and animals from destructive, corrosive, and <margin>25</margin> violent fire; likewise, fire according to one species and quality, and fire according to other species.

<meta>Continuity: Following the discussion on page 518, Bruno continues his exploration of the "spirit-like substance" of fire. ### ON THE PRINCIPLES OF THINGS, ETC.

...we call fire; motion, life, and sensation in all these things which move, live, and feel by their own power, come from this fire or heat. When this heat is intrinsic to things, it is called **native** <note>original: *nativus*. In Renaissance philosophy, this refers to the "innate heat" believed to be the source of life in living beings.</note>; when it comes from the outside, it is called **extraneous** and **foreign**. And these two species of fire are usually contrary to one another and mutually expel each other from substances.

From this, observe the error of the common people and especially of the physicians <note>Bruno is likely targeting the followers of Galen, the ancient Greek physician whose system of "degrees" dominated medieval and Renaissance medicine.</note> who speak in common terms. As if there were only one species of heat or fire, they establish "degrees," by which they say this thing is in the *first* degree, that in the *second*, this in the *third*, and so on up to the *seventh* or even further. From this follows a wondrous composition and a multiplication of words without sense or meaning. For who would relate the heat of fire—which is perceived by touch—to the same species as the heat of ignited things? For ignited things receive degrees of intensity and lessening through touch, and are said to be "more cooked" or "less cooked" by the fire, just as they are called more or less raw, undigested or digested. 

Then there are other things that are "hot" according to the sense of taste, and these follow innumerable species. For the heat of an onion <note>original: *caepae*</note> and of garlic <note>original: *allii*</note> is of one species, while the heat of watercress, thistle <note>original: *cardellae*</note>, and cloves <note>original: *garyophyllorum*</note> are altogether other species of heat. They are vastly diverse <margin>42ʳ</margin> according to their specific kind, and they do not belong to the same scale that would encompass all their degrees. 

Hence, heat of one species added to the heat of another species does not intensify it, nor does it help or promote it, any more than light helps sound, or sound helps or promotes sight. For these things, although they may run together under the general labels of "hot," "cold," "moist," and "dry," are nevertheless not the same according to...

the assertion that "contraries concern the same thing" <note>original: *contraria sunt circa idem*. A principle in Aristotelian logic meaning that opposite qualities can only exist within the same category or subject.</note>. <margin>10</margin> mobile, swift, and furious, following a temperament reflecting the disposition of fire—it does not, however, possess heat and dryness according to a **univocal** reason <note>In philosophy, "univocal" means using a term in exactly the same sense. Those fragrant and comforting substances best suppress and temper that condition, while the existing spirits of the brain
<margin>15</margin> comfort and strengthen it, so that they are more powerful in driving out that contrary and unnatural **Erinyean** plague <note>original: *erynnicam illam pestem*. <margin>20</margin> in all medical cures: that nothing be introduced that weakens nature, and nothing be omitted that restores it.

You cannot say these are merely vapors, humors, or similar things that push against bodies in this way—for what, then, pushes the humors and vapors? You might say, perhaps, "moved air."
