<page-num>523</page-num>

# ON THE PRINCIPLES OF THINGS, ETC.

I will inquire into what exactly moves the air or spirit, until one arrives at that first motor and impeller, which some call "spirit"—which moves other things by moving itself—but Plato calls the "soul," which he defined as a <margin>43r</margin> **self-moving number** <note>original: *numerum se ipsum moventem*. A Pythagorean-Platonic concept suggesting the soul is a mathematical principle of order that possesses its own inherent motion.</note> moving in a circle; and <margin>5</margin> truly this must be so, if the search is to rest in a first principle and not proceed into infinity. Neither sense nor reason leads me to the heavens by claiming that the motions of air and water are caused by the moon, and so on; for how is it that from a single or double motion of the moon, and from the one motion of the heavens—<margin>10</margin> which is imagined to sweep all things along—there does not follow one single spirit or one single wind? Instead, we see countless differences in locations and even more differences in these sorts of currents and spirits appearing everywhere. And in individual animals and living things, that same principle is found—yet it is diverse according to its own specific <margin>15</margin> and numerical differences. To these individual differences, that imaginary celestial motion seems to contribute or pertain not at all; for if that motion exists, it is universal and one; and thus the breathing <note>original: *spiratio*. Referring to the flow of "spirit" or life-force.</note> that would come from such a motion would be of that same uniform condition. We, however, are speaking of and inquiring into the **spirit** <note>original: *spiritu*. The active, subtle substance that bridges the gap between the material body and the immaterial soul.</note> that exists within and acts upon individual things, <margin>20</margin> and we finally define it as a **substance mobile in itself**, which by its own motion communicates life, growth, and consistency to animated things. It is itself living through itself, and other things live through it; it is the vehicle of all things.

---

<margin>15-23</margin> <margin>It must not be overlooked here that there are innumerable motors in a single individual, or at least several principal ones; for there is one motor that moves the blood through the veins, another that moves the spirit from and to the heart, and another which is voluntary, by which animals move their limbs and progress freely as they please. Even the **Peripatetics** <note>Followers of Aristotle’s school of philosophy.</note> themselves recognize two motors: nature and the will (or choice). And certainly those two motors are very different, as is evident in their effect; for we command the one, but we are subject to the other even against our will. The motivating principles of these particular movements are either the spirit itself—where the soul moves itself—or they occur by means of the spirit, where the spirit moves itself first.</margin>

<summary>Bruno argues that motion in the universe and in living bodies cannot be explained by a single celestial force like the moon, but instead comes from an internal "spirit" or "soul" that is inherently self-moving. He distinguishes between different types of internal motors, such as those governing involuntary biological functions (blood flow) and those governing voluntary actions (will).</summary>

<meta>Continuity: Following the discussion of spirits as aerial and physical intermediaries on the previous page, Bruno now transitions into the nature of "water" and "vapor," arguing that all subtle, evaporating, or purifying substances are essentially forms of the same element in different states of density.</meta>

<page-num>527</page-num>

# ON THE PRINCIPLES OF THINGS, ETC.

That which evaporates from bodies is water; and vapor itself is thought to differ from water only in its rarity <note>In the physics of the time, "rarity" referred to the degree of thinness or expansion of a substance, as opposed to "density."</note>, which is a matter of a certain accident <term>accident</term> <note>original: *accidente*. In philosophical terms, an "accident" is a property that can change (like temperature or density) without changing the essential nature or "substance" of the thing itself.</note>. Just as there are various spirits, so there are various differences among waters; for the mixtures of species are varied, <margin>5</margin> and from these, waters proceed according to their various virtues. And indeed, water—insofar as it is considered a simple element—is not sufficient for the unique and special arts of magic or medicine. This is because not every water, regardless of its type, can accomplish everything. While elemental water <note>The idealized, pure element of Water, one of the four building blocks of the universe.</note> does everything fundamentally and through its **primary power**, it does not do so through its <margin>10</margin> **proximate power** <note>original: *potentiam proximam*. "Primary power" refers to the general capability of an element, while "proximate power" refers to its immediate, specific ability to produce a particular effect in a practical operation.</note>. It is this proximate power that constitutes the particular art and science which we need and which we seek.

From this, just as we recognize the principle and matter of things, we also recognize the principle of regenerations, restorations, and <margin>15</margin> purifications. This is the source of those ritual cleansings, those baptisms, and what is usually referred to as the triple purification (namely, of water, sulfur, and fire). We do not understand this as being triple according to its substance, but rather according to its accidental state. For that which evaporates, is drawn out, and breathes forth <margin>20</margin> from sulfur—in which the cleansing power consists—is vapor and consequently water. A flame, as it is called a "burning vapor," is also water according to its substance. Thus, every cleansing established through magic or divine rite is referred back to water. Therefore, the keepers of sacred rites <note>original: *sacristae*. Here, Bruno refers to those who manage religious or magical ceremonies.</note>, from both the literal text <margin>25</margin> and the broader context, recognize this one element of generation and regeneration and bear witness to it in their ceremonies.

Indeed, if water had a single degree, manner, and constitution in all things, then all things would have the same mixture, life, and character. However, water in the sea is of one kind; in springs and rivers, it is another; in plants, <margin>29</margin> it is yet another...

<summary>Bruno argues that all vapors and spirits—including fire and sulfurous fumes—are essentially "water" in different states of density. He claims this "element of regeneration" is the true basis for all magical, medicinal, and religious purifications.</summary>

<page-num>528</page-num>
<header>GIORDANO BRUNO</header>

...according to different kinds, it is one thing or another: in metals it is something else entirely; in trees it is moisture, pitch, resin, and other such things; in herbs it is sap; in the bones of animals it is marrow; in the veins it is blood; and through the adjacent parts of the arteries, the fibers <margin>5</margin> of the flesh, and the passages of the pores, it is a subtle spirit—namely, vapor—appearing where there is snow, where there are clouds, and everywhere according to specific differences.

Its first, greatest, and most powerful function is to unite and bind things together; <margin>10</margin> and, according to the differences of these combinations or bindings and unions, to produce diverse and distinct things. It folds together a union that is more intense or more rare—yielding parts that are easier or harder to dissolve <term>dissolve</term> <note>original: *resolutionis*. This refers to the breaking down of a compound into its constituent parts.</note>—following various degrees. Whence water, for one reason, is in the sun, in which it shines when ignited by light, <margin>15</margin> grows hot, and emits fiery rays; for another reason it is in the region of darkness, or the abyss, or the ocean, or the realm of Amphitrite <note>Amphitrite is the Greek goddess of the sea; Bruno uses her name here as a poetic term for the ocean.</note>, where it reflects light only from its surface like a mirror; for another reason, water is burning oil or a juice that neither receives nor nourishes a flame. From this substance comes solidity, thickness, and the weight of bodies; for it <margin>20</margin> contracts and thickens itself so that it may compress many of its own parts into small dimensions or a narrow space. It allows these parts to be held together by the power of "the dry" or of atoms <note>Bruno often blends the classical theory of the four qualities (Hot, Cold, Moist, Dry) with atomism, suggesting that "dry" atoms provide the structure that water holds together.</note>—just as was said above concerning ashes, which are themselves contracted by water, and through which water itself is drawn into a narrow space. From this follows the form <margin>25</margin> of hard stone; or a harder form still, if there be a different arrangement of ash, powder, or a dry subject, from which metals, stones, gems, and the whole genus of things come forth—all of which unfold the diverse <margin>< 4</margin> differences of soul and spirit.

Through this moisture, bodies are fully inserted into other bodies, mixed, joined, held together, clung to, and added; and within its seeds resides the power by which one body is bent toward another, and the male is universally drawn to the female, and the female to the <margin>5</margin> male, and like to like. As soon as this is emitted, that fire and force is extinguished and <margin>10</margin> does not rise again until a new humor is restored or added. From these mixtures of seed with seed, waste with waste, part with part, and various combinations of diverse substances, those most powerful <margin>45r</margin> medicines <term>pharmaca</term> <note>original: *pharmaca*. In the Renaissance context, this refers to potent chemical or herbal preparations that could be either healing or poisonous.</note>, | beneficial and highly effective, are produced; from these, the whole of practical medicine and the greatest part of magic are forged as if from their own proper elements.

### On the Earth.

Earth is the most solid and simplest element, from which bodies are commonly thought to derive their solidity. <margin>20</margin> Here we do not take "earth" to mean this living globe <note>Bruno refers to the planet Earth as a "living globe" or "animal globe," reflecting his belief that the Earth itself is a sentient, living being.</note> from which we have obtained life, nourishment, and our physical bodies—which we understand to be one of the stars and a planet consisting of parts proportional to the parts of all living beings. By participation and union with this earth, all things live, and into its parts all things are <margin>25</margin> dissolved; hence it is rightly called the Mother of things. For no less a reason does the Earth itself live than do the other things that live through it and in it; therefore, it is called the Mother of the Gods, Cybele <note>A Phrygian mother goddess associated with the earth and fertility.</note>, Ceres <note>The Roman goddess of agriculture and grain.</note>, and many other names.

<summary>Bruno describes moisture (humor) as the primary force behind physical attraction and the "binding" of matter, which serves as the basis for medicine and magic. He then defines "Earth" not as the planet, but as the fundamental element of solidity and the "Mother" of all living things.</summary>

->by other names, such as **Isis**, most wise antiquity inscribed and worshiped her; and so she is called by both a common and a proper name, **Earth** <note>original: *tellus*. Bruno uses the word *tellus* to refer to the Earth as a goddess or a global entity, whereas *terra* refers to the physical element of "dryness."</note>.<-

Here, however, we are not discussing the goddess or the planet, but that which is properly called **earth** <note>original: *terra*</note>, an element distinct from the others. That is to say, if we set aside fire, set aside air, and set aside spirit and water in all their forms, this element is a body that is, in its own nature, the most rare <note>original: *rarissimum*. In Bruno’s physics, "rare" means the opposite of dense; he argues that pure earth without water is an incredibly thin, non-dense substance.</note> and the lightest. For just as was said in the opinions concerning water, all density, gravity, and weight comes from the number of parts coming together—whether many or few, more tightly or more loosely—into a single mass. 

Moreover, every coming together, union, mixing, and adhesion occurs through the "gluing" and binding power of **moisture** <note>original: *humidum*</note>. Therefore, earth—or "the dry" <term>arida</term> <note>original: *arida*. Bruno often uses "the dry" as a synonym for the element of earth, representing the principle of stability without the binding force of liquid.</note>—is, by itself, a most rare and subtle body. Its parts are so separated from one another that they could hardly stick together at all without water. 

Because of this, it is an imperceptible body, being **indivisible** <note>original: *individuum*. This is the literal meaning of "atom": something that cannot be divided further.</note>. For everything that can be perceived by the senses is a certain quantity endowed with a sensible quality; and this sensible quality is founded only upon dimensions or a certain mass. However, every mass comes from the composition and the coming together of many primary parts. Consequently, everything that can be sensed—whether visible or tangible—is divisible into innumerable (though not infinite) parts. 

And so, to one considering the matter more deeply, it is manifest that earth, or "the dry" in itself, is nothing other than **atoms** <note>original: *atomos*. Bruno was a key figure in reviving the ancient Greek idea that the universe is made of tiny, indivisible "seeds" or particles.</note>, or those indivisible bodies which cannot be divided by any natural virtue or any other power. For what **active power** <term>potentia activa</term> <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "active power" is the force that acts upon something, while "passive power" is the capacity of a thing to be changed.</note> could divide that which has no parts, and to which, evidently, no **passive power** <term>potentia passiva</term> responds? If primary bodies of this kind come together and hold fast to one another, they certainly do not have this quality from themselves but from water; and for that reason, it is not enough for us to cite atoms as the material principles [of the world]...

<summary>Bruno argues that the element of earth, when separated from moisture, is actually a collection of weightless, invisible, and indivisible atoms. He explains that density and physical mass only exist when moisture acts as a "glue" to bind these dry atoms together.</summary>

<meta>Continuity: Following the discussion of the Earth as a global entity (Tellus) versus earth as a physical element (terra), Bruno now defines the roles of the specific elements—water, spirit, and light—in the formation and life of matter, leading into his description of atoms.</meta>

<header>GIORDANO BRUNO</header>

But for the composition or binding of things, we add **water**; for the gift of life, for order, and for governance, we bring in **spirit**; and for sensation, motion, beauty, digestion, love, and strife, we bring in **light** or **fire**, the first element. 
Nor, because of this, do we reject the way others think about these principles—those who, in order to arrive at a single element, refer spirit, water, and light back to **atoms**; in their view, a distinction would have to be made between these atoms and the **dry** <note>original: *arida*. Bruno uses this term as a synonym for the element of earth in its purest, most unmixed state.</note>. 
However, we set aside that way of philosophizing as being more for contemplation and less for action. For we find that such a breakdown, while perhaps more agreeable to pure logic, is less suited to nature and practical application, and is also very far removed from what our senses tell us. 
<margin>45v</margin>
Therefore, by the **dry** and the **atoms**—or the **element of earth**—we mean that substance which remains when the spirit, vapor, and moisture have been separated from a compound. It is finally broken down not into a continuous substance (like moisture, vapor, spirit, or light), but into a **discrete** one. It stands in proportion to the other elements just as ash and dust stand to water and smoke. Yet, it is not literally dust and ash, because those are visible to our senses due to the underlying substance <term>hypostasis</term> <note>original: *hypostasin*. A Greek-derived term referring to the substantial foundation or "standing-under" that gives a thing its consistency.</note> and the thickness of their parts, from which moisture has not been entirely removed. 
In fact, those tiny bodies <note>original: *corpuscula*. Bruno is invoking a famous image from the Roman poet Lucretius: dust motes dancing in a sunbeam as a visual metaphor for the invisible movement of atoms.</note> come closer to the likeness of atoms—those which do not settle or lie still, but are seen in sunbeams entering through a window, especially when the air is calm. They move up and down and in every direction with a steady pulse; they seem to do this from an internal drive, since among thousands of them, you will hardly see two moving with the same speed or direction. Thus, you cannot believe they are simply being carried along by the movement of the air itself. 
Whatever this may be, this much for the present—

<summary>Bruno defines the roles of the elements (water as a binder, spirit as a governor, light as a source of sensation) and describes "the dry" (earth) as a discrete, atomic substance. He illustrates the independent motion of atoms using the classical metaphor of dust motes dancing in a sunbeam.</summary>

...we conclude that the element of earth, when entirely freed from moisture, is nothing other than these types of **corpuscles** <note>original: *corpuscula*. Bruno uses this to describe the smallest physical particles, though he distinguishes these visible motes from true, indivisible atoms.</note>. Indeed, these are the ones visible in the sunlight, which are actually composites—not true atoms—and consequently not without some water. However, they imitate the motion of simple things because they have so few joined parts, and thus they do not participate in much contrariety <note>In Renaissance physics, "contrariety" refers to the struggle between opposing qualities like hot/cold or wet/dry. Simpler things have less internal conflict.</note>. Therefore, let no one call the element of earth "heavy" by looking at composite things, such as actual stones or the mixtures that appear on the globe; for such a notion is a fiction resulting from very little reflection.

The role of earth, or of atoms of this kind, in the nature of things is (as we have said) to grant **solidity** and a **boundary** to bodies. It does this not by itself, but in conjunction with **water**. For water grants consistency to these particles so that—mediated by the water—those things which are otherwise fluid, fleeting, and discontinuous or scattered may constitute a single body. In turn, the earth or atoms provide the **boundary** <term>termination</term> <note>original: *terminationem*. The specific limit or edge that defines a physical object's shape.</note>. 

On this point, **Aristotle** spoke well (behaving, as he himself says of others, like an unskilled fencer who occasionally lands an excellent blow, though not through skill). He said that the nature of the "boundary" comes from the earth or the **dry** <note>Aristotle, *On Generation and Corruption* II.2 and *Meteorology* IV.4.</note>; for in a composition, the dry is bounded by its own limit, whereas the **moist** is bounded by something else <note>original: *alieno terminatur*. This refers to the idea that a liquid has no shape of its own and must be contained by something external.</note>. And although he spoke well here, he did not understand it quite so well. For water—whether the sea, rivers, or springs—takes its shape from its "vessel," the earth that contains it. Similarly, air is contained within channels <note>original: *meatibus*. The pores or passages within matter.</note>, taking the shape of "lakes" <note>original: *lacorum*. While some manuscripts read *locorum* (places), Bruno likely means pockets or "pools" of air.</note> or pipes. He should have understood the same thing regarding **fire**, which is subtler than air, and all the more so because...

<summary>Bruno defines the element of earth as a collection of dry corpuscles that provide solid shape and boundaries to objects when bound together by water. He critiques Aristotle for correctly identifying that "the dry" provides boundaries while failing to realize that all fluid elements (water, air, fire) are shaped by the "vessels" of the solid element.</summary>

...has the nature of moisture <note>original: *humiditatis*. In Renaissance physics, this refers to the quality of being fluid or wet.</note>, because that which is more subtle is less able to be bounded by its own limit. For instance, water—being denser than air—is more capable of being bounded than air itself. However, if we look at the primary elements in their simple state, none will appear without its own proper boundary, just like the first and smallest bodies and individuals <note>original: *individua*. Bruno uses this synonymously with atoms, meaning "things that cannot be divided."</note>. This is true whether you reduce all composite things to these atoms in the manner of **Democritus** and **Epicurus** <note>Ancient Greek philosophers who founded the school of atomism, suggesting the universe is made of tiny, indivisible particles moving in a void.</note>, or whether you distinguish them as we have distinguished them. 

But in those things which **Aristotle** considered—namely, composite things that we can perceive with our senses—it is clear that they bound one another. <margin>46</margin> For in the globe <note>original: *tellure*. Referring to the Earth as a physical sphere.</note>, there is no earth without water; the earth certainly does not possess its shape, solidity, consistency, or hardness without water, as is clear from what we have already said. For the vessel that contains water is not made of pure earth, nor does it contain more earth than water. This is because no atom adheres to other atoms unless it is surrounded on all sides by water, which allows it to be glued together. 

Even the atom itself is a minimal and indivisible thing; for if it were divisible, it would consist of even more parts, which (following the same logic) could not be joined together without water. Behold how in these bodies, which seem to be the driest and hardest of all, a wonderful <unclear>mass</unclear> <note>The original text is unclear here; the editor suggests *moles* (mass or bulk).</note> of water predominates. 

Therefore, to our senses—or for the consistency of the forms we perceive—the boundary and shape do not come from the earth any more than they come from the water in actual practice. This is true even though we primarily attribute the "ability to be bounded" to water (when it is shaped by earth in a mixture), just as we attribute the "ability to be united" (or the coming together of scattered parts) to the earth through the medium of water.

<margin>Plato and Timaeus support this opinion, saying that even the stars do not have solidity and shape without earth...</margin> <note>original: *Huic sententiae adstipulatur Plato et Timaeus...* Reference to Plato's dialogue *Timaeus*, which discusses the composition of the universe from the four elements.</note>

<summary>Bruno argues that solid objects require a mixture of earth and water, as earth atoms cannot stick together to form shapes without the "glue" of moisture. Even the hardest substances contain water, which allows the dry particles to form boundaries and consistency.</summary>

# ON TIME.

->First, concerning the dominion of the elements.<- <note>original: *Primo de dominio elementorum*. This sub-heading was noted in the original manuscript as being in a different hand, likely Bruno’s own, added during a later review.</note>

To complete this discussion, the greatest and most important task—and, as it seems, the very form of the entire matter—is <margin>5</margin> to take account of time; for both natural actions and those of the will occur with a certain alternation and order. This is manifest to the senses themselves in the four seasons of the year, which exist according to the dominion of the four qualities <note>The primary qualities of Hot, Cold, Moist, and Dry, which were believed to govern all physical transformations.</note> accepted by the common people, or the four temperaments. <margin>10</margin> These are subsequently distributed at certain equal intervals into twelve differences; hence they are called the twelve months, acting as parts of this measurement. By these months, the four aforementioned differences [the seasons] are multiplied, while for each season, one considers its beginning and youth, its middle and consistency, <margin>15</margin> and its decline and end. For the beginning of any season is in one zodiac sign, its middle in another, and its end in another. In this way, the year—or the cycle of the sun or the earth—is distributed. Above this is the celestial year, which is proportionally subdivided into four and then into twelve equal parts; below it is the lunar year, <margin>20</margin> which is also subdivided under those same signs: first into four, second into twelve similar parts, and thirdly subdivided into 48. Hence, the observation of the 48 mansions <note>Refers to the ancient division of the sky into "stations" or constellations used to track the movement of the stars and planets.</note> and figures was introduced with great learning and importance, first by the wise Chaldeans <note>Ancient Mesopotamian astronomers and astrologers whom Renaissance thinkers regarded as the original masters of celestial wisdom.</note> and then followed by all others according to the sufficiency of their capacity...

<summary>Bruno introduces the study of Time as the essential framework for all natural and human actions, explaining how the year is divided by the four seasons and the twelve signs of the zodiac. He aligns these cycles with the movements of the sun, earth, and moon, tracing the origins of this astronomical knowledge back to the ancient Chaldeans.</summary>

...so that from the **pre-lunch period** <note>original: *anteprandio*; the late morning hours</note> to the **pre-dinner period** <note>original: *antecenium*; the late afternoon hours</note> it is summer; from the pre-dinner period to the **silence of night** <note>original: *conticinium*; the first part of the night when everything falls still</note> it is autumn; and from the silence of night to **dawn** it is winter. Therefore, all years or cycles should be distributed in such a way that this division applies first to the **Year of Heaven**—which they call the proper motion of the **eighth sphere** <note>The sphere of the fixed stars; ancient astronomers calculated its slow rotation (precession) to take roughly 36,000 years</note>, which some extend to 36,000 years and others to approximately that amount. Next, it applies to the year or circle of the **earth** or the **sun**; for it makes no difference whether the earth revolves around the sun, or the sun around the earth, as they cover the same spaces. Finally, it applies to the "year" of the earth's circumference around its own center, or the **daily motion** <note>The 24-hour rotation of the earth on its axis</note>, by which people imagine the universe is carried around the earth with the swiftest speed.

To us, the consideration of the **first year** [the Great Year] seems more relevant to the change of seasons and of fortunes, by which these lower things are changed and arranged not by annual, but by **secular** <note>In the sense of "ages" or very long periods of time</note> successions. The **second year**, which is commonly called "the year," concerns the transformation of the **elements** in general, and the changes that occur in those things that are generated and decay within the cycle of the earth. The **third year**, which is commonly called "the day," concerns the proportional change that occurs through individual nights and days—the time of darkness and light, | <margin>**47**</margin> of cold and heat—which change in individual days just as they do in years. <margin>This distinction also pertains to the stages of life of animals, divided into 4 and 12, beginning from spring and ending in winter; likewise, for those who look deeper, it pertains to the timing of fortunes, illnesses, and other dispositions and habits.</margin> To think that the proportional division differs between full days, quarters of days, or twelfths is vain and false. Hence, if the distinction of the **faces of the signs** <note>original: *facierum signorum*; in astrology, these are the "decans," or 10-degree subdivisions of the zodiac signs</note> made by astronomers is for any purpose, it certainly is not for this one, nor for those things that proceed from it and follow the same order, concerning...

<summary>Bruno defines three types of "years": the 36,000-year cycle of the stars, the solar year, and the daily rotation of the earth. He argues that the same fourfold seasonal logic (Spring, Summer, Autumn, Winter) applies proportionally to all three cycles, influencing everything from the elements to human fortune and health.</summary>

### On time and the dominion of the seven planets or the seven princes.

Regarding the order and succession of the dominion of the **four elements** or the four qualities, which are commonly called "active" and "passive" <note>In Aristotelian physics, Hot and Cold were active, while Moist and Dry were passive</note>, this has been discussed according to universal and common principles. However, as for the dominion of **occult qualities** <margin>We call "occult qualities" those which do not pertain to the body but to the soul <note>original: *animae*; or "animal spirit"</note>, or to the accidents, revolutions, and sequences of fortune. They also contribute to the "fortunes" of the changes that occur in bodies, such as death, life, brevity, and longevity, because souls, when changed, change the bodies, just as conversely, changed bodies change the souls.</margin> and of more profound impressions...

<summary>Bruno argues against the infinite mathematical subdivision of time periods into beginning, middle, and end, while defining the 28-day lunar cycle as a single "day." He introduces the concept of "occult qualities"—deeper forces governed by the planets that influence the soul and the fate of the physical body.</summary>

->On finding the arc of the day and of the night.<-

The arc of the day <note>original: *arcus diei*; the path of the sun above the horizon</note> is taken from the point of the East to the point of the West, and from the instant in which the center of the sun's body is on the line of the horizon, ascending, to when it is on that same line, descending.
<margin>5</margin>That arc, whatever its size may be, will distinguish six regions of the sky if it is distributed into six equal parts, and it defines the boundary of the six true, authentic houses <note>original: *domorum*; the twelve divisions of the celestial sphere in astrology, though Bruno argues for a specific way of calculating them</note>. In this way, indeed, the houses follow the measure of the signs and the course of the planets, as well as the distinction of the parts of the sky according to the perpetual order of the signs and the alternation of light and darkness, heat and cold, <margin>10</margin>and other subsequent qualities and virtues. Nor is there any reason for you to be deceived along with the common crowd, but leave them in their blindness and keep this secret; for God and nature do not allow this confusion: that there should be the same prerogatives <margin>15</margin>and the same degree of light for the good and the bad <note>likely referring to the distinction between "benefic" and "malefic" astrological influences</note>. Thus, regarding the arc of the night, one takes the remainder and the complement, adding or subtracting that difference by which the sun approaches one or the other tropic, or recedes from one or the other. How the arc itself is to be divided into <margin>20</margin>six equal parts has been defined by us in our *Geometry* <note>Bruno likely refers to his work *De Minimo* or *Articuli adversus mathematicos*</note>. Therefore, the distinction of the houses is not to be understood according to some other uncertain, inconsistent distribution founded on no higher reason, but such should be taught to the common people; for it is a sacrilege <note>original: *nefas*</note> for just anyone to know just anything.

->On the distinction of aspects.<-

With this doctrine established, no reason follows for the difference of conjunction, opposition, and other aspects <note>original: *aspectus*; in astrology, the specific angular distances between planets that were thought to influence earthly events</note> between the planets, since their order is forever one and immobile; for this reason, one planet will never fall under the same line with many others, or even with one other. <margin>49⁻</margin> And yet, they perpetually maintain their closeness and distance from one another at those certain, defined intervals which were designated in the preceding circle.

Moreover, it must be noted here that the doctrine concerning aspects, according to this path, is not only not vain <gloss>not vain</gloss>, but is indeed necessary and most fitting, provided however that it is applied to this practice in its own way—which is easy for even a person of average talent to discover. For the elucidation and completion of the knowledge of this practice, one principle must be observed for the theory of measuring the cosmos <note>original: *cosmimetricum*</note> and another for astrological judgment, namely for the distinction of the houses and their parts. First, with the two arcs divided by the aforementioned method, the ratio of the aspects of trines <note>an aspect of 120 degrees</note>, squares <note>an aspect of 90 degrees</note>, and others that are below and around these, should not be taken from an equal division of the circle—as the common house-makers <note>original: *domifactores*; astrologers who calculate the twelve "houses" or divisions of the sky</note> do—but by a proportional division. In this way, the beginning of <term>Aries</term> <note>the first sign of the zodiac</note> is linked to the beginning of <term>Gemini</term> <note>the third sign of the zodiac</note>, the middle to the middle, and what is at the beginning of the one to what is at the beginning of the other, and so on. Thus, individual degrees are linked to individual degrees, and the remaining to the remaining; just as the judgment is in the trine aspect, so it is in the square aspect, and just as it is in those, so it is in all parts, as is evident in the present figure.

<summary>Bruno argues that while planets maintain fixed positions in his system, the traditional astrological "aspects" (geometric relationships) are still vital if calculated through proportional division rather than equal segments. He critiques "common" astrologers, proposing a more mathematically rigorous way to link signs like Aries and Gemini.</summary>
<keywords>astrology, planetary aspects, house-making, Aries, Gemini, trine, square, cosmic measurement, proportional division</keywords>

Secondly, it must be observed how the signs <note>the twelve signs of the Zodiac</note>, the other celestial images <note>original: *imagines caelestes*; the constellations</note>, the mansions of the moon <note>the 28 divisions of the sky the moon passes through in a month</note>, and all other surrounding conditions—just as with all categories of things—are distinguished by their parts and members in such a way that some reflect the <margin>5</margin> nature of one planet, while others reflect the nature of another planet.

Therefore, I pass over certain things that express the nature of several planets at once, such as the image of Hercules <note>the constellation Hercules</note>, which expresses the nature of Jupiter because of his lordship, victory, and triumph, but also the nature of Mars <note>original: ♂</note> because of force, violence, impulse, and devastation. The head <margin>10</margin> of the Gorgon <note>original: *caput Gorgonis*; refers to the star Algol in the constellation Perseus, traditionally considered one of the most "unlucky" stars</note> [reflects] the nature of Mars <note>original: ♂</note> because of violence, death, and the shedding of blood; but because of the power of poison, destruction, accusation, and envy, it reflects the nature of Saturn <note>original: ♄^ni</note>. The Lyre <note>original: *Cythara*; the constellation Lyra</note> reflects the nature of Venus <note>original: ♀</note> and Mercury <note>original: ☿^ii</note>; the Raven <note>the constellation Corvus</note> the nature of Mercury <note>original: ☿^ii</note> and the Sun <note>original: ☉^is</note>. This is easy to gather from the collected myths or histories, in which the deeds <margin>15</margin> of certain noble men and heroes, along with their names, are related to kindred stars. From this, Jupiter <note>original: ♃</note>, the mortal king of Crete, is said to have been translated into heaven, because on account of his deeds <note>The text ends mid-sentence; Bruno is likely arguing that planetary names and influences are derived from the character of the historical or mythical figures for whom they were named.</note>

...the name of that star and those constellations through which [a planet] is believed to receive its influence. <margin>5</margin> A similar judgment is applied to the other stars noted according to the ancient custom, which has for the most part been preserved untainted—as has been stated regarding the powers <note>original: *virtutes*</note> of these various distinctions. Likewise, whenever a judgment must be made concerning any matter—such as life and death, health and sickness, marriage, wealth, or poverty—
<margin>10</margin> one must consider that these things are also referred to the nature of specific planets. For instance, wealth is attributed to the Sun <note>original symbol: ☉</note>, while poverty, death, and sickness in general are attributed to Saturn. More specifically, some conditions belong to Mars, such as those that are hot and dry; others to Saturn, such as those that are cold and dry; others to the Moon <note>original symbol: ☽</note>, being cold and moist.
<margin>15</margin> Likewise, certain spiritual <note>or psychological</note> ailments pertain to Mars, such as anger and rage; to Jupiter <note>original symbol: ♃</note>, "black bile" <note>original: *atra bilis*; melancholy</note>; to Venus <note>original symbol: ♀</note>, jealousy and all things arising from love. Thus, by considering subjects that are governed by time, motion, and the alignment of the heavens and seasons, it is easy to perceive where there is favor or opposition. One can see how things stand in their youth or their decline, just as there are diverse starting points <note>original: *principia*</note> for the actions and arrangements
<margin>20</margin> from which various sequences and outcomes follow. For example, grain that is sown while the Sun occupies Gemini <note>original symbol: ♊</note> or Cancer <note>original symbol: ♋</note> does not reach maturity. In this way, all things have fixed conditions and beginnings; through these origins, they proceed toward their growth, their end, or their perfection.
<margin>25</margin> The same judgment applies to all other accidents and events, such as the beginning of becoming wealthy, the onset of illness, or the start of pleasing or displeasing the public. Not just any beginning leads to its intended end; but to speak more precisely of these matters and...

...this is not the place to consider [every detail], where we ought only to indicate the universal principle <term>original: *rationem*; here meaning the underlying logic or governing rule</term> of things. From this, anyone of even modest talent can easily collect for themselves the fragments of truth that are scattered amidst the many vanities filling the books of astrologers and practitioners of judicial astrology <note>Judicial astrology refers to the practice of predicting specific human events and fates, which Bruno often critiqued for its superstitions while seeking the "true" natural philosophy behind it</note>. One can then test, correct, and find completion. We are showing the way for this—a way we have come to know through the favor of the "sun of superior intelligence" <note>A Neoplatonic metaphor for divine or intellectual illumination that reveals the truth behind physical appearances</note>. Up to this point, it has not been granted to us to perform trials and experiments regarding particular details, on account of the more urgent occupations and the many obstacles by which we are bound. These [principles] are more than half the work, as anyone can see for themselves; through frequent and continuous experience, the logic of even particular things will easily suggest itself to those walking this path, without the need to study other books.

## ON THE VIRTUE AND VICES OF THE INDIVIDUAL SIGNS AND PLANETS, NAMELY THE LIGHT AND DARKNESS OVER WHICH EACH DOMINATES.

It belongs to this teaching to consider how, everywhere in the corporeal <note>physical</note> world and in those things surrounding bodies, good is mixed with evil and evil with good. This is just as in physics, where there is nowhere matter without form, nor form without matter, nor "act" without "potency," or "potency" without "act" <note>Bruno uses the Aristotelian terms *actus* and *potentia*—the distinction between something being fully realized and its potential to become something else</note>, nor light without darkness and darkness without light. For the Good is only one, absolute above all things and separate from all things; therefore, there is no evil without good nor good without evil, whether in the planets, in the zodiac signs, or in all the various species of things. <margin>5</margin>

<margin>15</margin>

<margin>20</margin>
poverties, and poverty once again leads back to study. Thus, from all things there is an entrance to all things; the same things are respectively good and evil, the beginning of goods and evils, and the end of goods and evils. ## ON THE POWER OF PLACE.

It is manifest from many reasons and examples that place is a significant principle in the performance of all things; for various powers are impressed upon different locations by the <term>celestial assembly<note>original: caelesti synodo; the collective influence of the stars and planets, acting like a governing council over earthly affairs</note></term>. There are <margin>5</margin> indeed certain things of such a nature that they are produced in all places, though not everywhere in the same way, equally, or according to the same dispositions and qualities; hence, different homelands reflect the different customs of men. For the <term>spirits<note>original: spiritus; the subtle, vital substance that connects the human soul to the body and environment</note></term> of men are entirely governed by their regions and their own sky, as can be <margin>10</margin> seen where a harsh sky produces harsh men—though they may be able to moderate this through accidental and external education, the goodness of princes, laws, institutions, and religions; nevertheless, that root of nature is always implanted in the deepest parts. It follows naturally from this, and is confirmed by custom everywhere, that although all are lovers of their <margin>15</margin> homelands (drawn by their native soil), many are nevertheless ashamed of "bad" homelands and conceal the lowliness of their origin when among foreigners. Hence, where Calabrians, and likewise the wicked Vandals, Goths, Lombards, Getae, and Tartars are considered as such...

---

<note>
It should also be noted in magical and even sacred acts how turnings toward this or that region and relations are strictly observed. Ancient Christian temples—although today they do not consider this because they do not hold those magical or divine reasons at this time—all have the orientation of the altar toward the <note>original: orientem; the East</note>. Some are oriented toward the south, but these are later than the former; toward the west and north, however, there are none. In sacred rites they also observe what is to be performed in the middle of the altar, what at the right <term>horn<note>original: cornu; the side or corner of the altar</note></term>, and what at the left; what the priest does facing the people, and what with his back turned to the people. The entire ceremonial law of Moses is filled with this.
</note>

<summary>Bruno argues that geographical location and celestial alignment determine the character and customs of people, as the "spirit" of a person is shaped by their environment. He extends this principle to the ritual orientation of temples and religious ceremonies, noting that even Christian and Mosaic traditions rely on these "magical" laws of placement.</summary>

...further to the East, according to the different conditions of places, some of these people are indeed more and others less similar to Germans or Spaniards. It does not follow from this that, whatever the character of a nation might be in general, a few men cannot emerge as most extraordinary where it is least expected, owing to other 
<margin>5</margin> circumstances (since place is not the entire weight or cause of a thing, nor does it create it entirely). Thus, in effect, that which is not common to the whole nation can be a unique property of certain specific individuals. For Germany, in those regions 
<margin>10</margin> located in Switzerland and <term>Swabia<note>A cultural and linguistic region in southwestern Germany. In Bruno’s time, this area was a significant center for humanist learning and the Reformation.</note></term>, has produced such human <term>talents<note>original: ingenia; refers to innate ability, genius, or natural disposition.</note></term> that for many ages the talents of specific foreigners have not been comparable to them. This level of variation is harder to 
<margin>15</margin> achieve in other species of animals and plants; for human talent can vary much more than the ordinary course of nature. There are, moreover, certain things that are born in one region or several, but are denied to others; just as it is said of balsam and cedar, that they grow only on Mount Lebanon and in Palestine; in 
<margin>20</margin> other places, they claim only something else known by a common name can be found. There is no trace of olives in Germany or in the colder parts, while in <term>Libya<note>The Latin term "Libya" was often used by Renaissance authors to refer to the northern coast of Africa or the continent of Africa in general.</note></term> there is a wonderful abundance and fertility. The same is true of pepper, cinnamon, and many other things which Asia brings forth but are denied to Europe and Africa. 
What we say generally about these species according to the 
<margin>25</margin> distinction of regions should also be understood regarding the parts of each region—namely, in specific places, and most specifically down to individuals. Just as no one man can be found who is entirely similar to another, so too a <term>virtue<note>original: virtus; in this context, it refers to an inherent power, quality, or essential property of a place or thing.</note></term> in one place is unique and not shared by another, according to its own specific disposition.

What we are saying here regarding these common and sensible qualities must also be understood regarding <term>occult qualities<note>In Renaissance philosophy, these were hidden properties of matter—such as magnetism or medicinal effects—that could not be explained by the four basic elements (earth, air, fire, water) but were felt through their effects.</note></term>; this is why different <term>spirits<note>original: genii; refers to the protective or guiding spirit of a specific place.</note></term>, different <term>household gods<note>original: lares; Roman deities traditionally protecting a home or specific locality.</note></term>, and different presiding or particular <term>divinities<note>original: numina; the spiritual power or presence inhabiting a place or object.</note></term> are assigned to various places. <margin>5</margin> For it is not without reason and truth that it has been said that "all is one," and that the One is above all and is the Whole. Subject to this One, first, are a few principles and heads; subject to each of these are multitudes and armies of those who, individually, are still the <margin>52ʳ</margin> governors and princes of many others. Thus, from the <term>Monad<note>The ultimate, indivisible unit or "One" from which all multiplicity in the universe originates.</note></term> there is a descent to <margin>10</margin> infinite multiplicity through things that are finite and indeterminate; and conversely, there is an ascent from infinite things back to the Monad by gathering the many into one. In this way, the universe is one: an infinite space in which there are innumerable stars or worlds. In each of these worlds, there are innumerable princes, corresponding to the <margin>15</margin> innumerable particular places found both on the surface of each globe—such as this earth—and in its depths. Anyone who is ignorant of this can understand nothing; whoever does not practice according to these principles can achieve nothing except by chance.

The success and outcome of affairs proves this; indeed, in <margin>20</margin> medicine, magic, fortune, and life itself, a change of location sometimes contributes a great deal—it even seems to be everything. In one place, men are unfortunate, unappreciated, or weak in mind and body; in another, they flourish in one or several of these aspects. This is caused by the diversity of the presiding powers. <margin>25</margin> Homer celebrated Mount Parnassus, where he says that while sleeping he was suddenly transformed into a poet by a <term>divine breath<note>original: numine afflante; the idea of being "breathed into" by a god, the root of the word "inspiration."</note></term>; nor is this a mere fable, even though everyone who writes verses today makes the same claim about Parnassus and the <term>Spring of the Horse<note>original: fonte Caballino seu Pegaseo; referring to the Hippocrene fountain on Mt. Helicon, which was said to have been struck open by the hoof of the winged horse Pegasus and offered poetic inspiration to those who drank from it.</note></term>. Hesiod testified to the same thing regarding himself. Moses in

There the bones of his wife Sarah rested, and there Isaac and Jacob were buried. <margin>20</margin> When Joseph was dying in Egypt, he bound his kin with a strict command that his bones should be moved, after a long time, to that same place. This clearly signifies that they did not hold to that "Diogenic indifference"—referring to the philosopher Diogenes the Cynic, who was satisfied with the sky as his roof, the whole of space as his grave, and the <margin>25</margin> stars of heaven for his funeral ceremony. This religious devotion to specific places was observed most strictly not only by the Hebrews, but also by the Romans, Greeks, and Egyptians. It was not without taking the omens of the location that Romulus laid the first foundations [of Rome], and he established different temples on different hills within the same walls. ### ON THE POWER OF NAMES.

In addition to these principles, it is relevant to consider that a great power is inherent in names. It is believed that the fortune and status of a named thing follow the specific power of its name. Furthermore, many affirm that a change in names corresponds to a change in <margin>5</margin> fortune or of one’s <term>genius<note>original: genii; in this context, the "genius" refers to a person's guiding spirit or their innate divine nature.</note></term>. That the Hebrews, Greeks, and other nations believed this is made very manifest through their published writings. First, those who are most devoted to religion and faith—and who hold it as a primary principle and axiom that God does nothing in vain—preach that it was not without cause <margin>10</margin> that the names of many patriarchs were changed.

For the name of Abraham was changed, and the <term>Kabbalists<note>original: Cabalistae; followers of a tradition of Jewish mysticism that seeks hidden meanings in the Hebrew language and scriptures.</note></term> say that by the power of a single letter, the *He* [ה] <note>The original manuscript M incorrectly used the letter *Chet* [ח]. The addition of the letter *He* transformed the name "Abram" into "Abraham," symbolizing his new status.</note>, he acquired the faculty of procreating. They say the same thing regarding Jacob: that when he was destined to rule over his brother and the nations through the blessing and the birthright, his name <margin>15</margin> was changed to Israel <note>Genesis 32:28.</note>. The same is said of Isaac, and of the change from Sarai to Sarah. 

Likewise, in the book of the Christians, we find that Christ called Simon the Galilean "Peter," and also "Cephas" <note>original: Cepham; from the Aramaic word for "rock," mirroring the Greek "Petros."</note>. | <margin>53</margin> Also Saul, when [God] wished to promote him into a "vessel of election" <note>original: vas electionis; a biblical term for a person chosen by God for a specific divine purpose.</note>, was called Paul after his name was <margin>20</margin> changed. Many Christian sects observe this practice even now; when people are received from the laity into the number of the "hooded ones" <note>original: cucullatorum; referring to monks or friars who wear a cowl.</note>, or from the clergy into the number of Popes, they change their names—though some do so pointlessly, merely following custom.

<summary>Bruno explores the esoteric "principle of names," citing Biblical and Kabbalistic examples to argue that name changes signify and effect a profound transformation in a person's destiny or spiritual status.</summary>

...of the name, not of the principle. The Roman pontiffs <note>The Popes of the Catholic Church.</note>, by casting a kind of lot, as they say, must choose names for themselves by decree; it is forbidden for anyone to be titled with the name of Peter, for they fear destruction under that name. Not only do the <term>Kabbalists<note>Followers of Jewish mystical traditions who believe words and letters hold divine power.</note></term> <margin>5</margin> and the sacristans of that sort confirm this, but even the astronomers do. The Platonists observed this through their art, and among them their leader Plotinus; in his *Life*, his disciple Porphyry reports that Plotinus changed the names of many of his disciples, as he was also deeply imbued with <margin>10</margin> Chaldean and Persian disciplines. Porphyry reports of himself that his own name was changed by his friends; for he was first called Malchus <note>The name "Malchus" is Semitic for "king"; "Porphyry" is the Greek equivalent, referring to the "purple" robes worn by kings.</note>.

Among their experiments, they report that from the **parity** and **imparity** <note>The "even" or "odd" count of letters in a name.</note> of the letters which make up the joined names of a husband and wife, it is possible to know beforehand which of them will die first. Likewise, from the <margin>15</margin> parity and imparity of this kind, for two who enter into <term>single combat<note>original: monomachiam; a duel or one-on-one fight.</note></term>, they claim it can be predicted which of them must fall. They provide examples in many cases: Achilles and Hector, Aeneas and Turnus, Antoninus and Faustina, Cleopatra and Antony. And I myself have observed this in many cases, and found it otherwise in <margin>20</margin> very few. 

And from this arises a difficulty due to the difference of names translated from Greek into Latin, from Latin into Italian, and for Italian names which are pronounced differently in different dialects. For example, some write the name **John** as *Gioanni*, others *Giovani*, others *Ioanni*, others *Zuanni*, others *Zanni*, others *Zani*, others <margin>25</margin> *Ioan*, others *Iohannes*; the power of all of these seems to me to be...

<margin>12</margin> <note>original: "Haec non scribimus..." I do not write these things because I hold these disciplines in high or even moderate regard, but so that I may conclude my proposition, which is part of this consideration: namely, that there is a certain hidden power in names and in that which follows their change. Therefore, for those wishing to provide forewarnings or perform other physical works, it would not be a vain method to inquire into that which is deduced from this true principle.</note>

...in the number of his name, which follows the form in which it was given to him. Bede <note>The Venerable Bede (c. 673–735 AD), an English monk and scholar famous for his chronological and historical writings.</note>, considered among the most famous and mature authors, also wrote on this subject, defining the number corresponding to the days of the months, lunar stations, Latin letters, and business affairs; through these, he is said to have prophesied and predicted marvels.

And in our own time, I know a man personally <note>original: "ex facie," literally "by face." The marginal notes identify this man as Brocardus of Nuremberg.</note> <margin>Brocardus of Nuremberg</margin> who, in a very specific manner using the Hebrew alphabet, predicted the manner of death of many princes and the changes of certain states, although he is sometimes mistaken in certain cases, and he himself admits this is because he does not entirely grasp the understanding <margin>53v</margin> of it. 

The <term>Kabbalists<note>Followers of Jewish mystical traditions who believe that letters and numbers are the building blocks of the universe.</note></term> hold great mysteries regarding the number of letters and the secrets surrounding them, so that they understand the sum of all operations and intelligences to be situated in the power of names and the knowledge of them—as they say regarding the Messiah, concerning the name given to him above every name—but they add certain occult reasons, which are intellectually joined to that written name. 

In the prophecies of Daniel also, the reasons for many successes are referred to numbers and names. In the prophecy of the book of the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation (13:17-18), which discusses the "number of the beast."</note>, mention is made of that devastating beast, along with the power of the number of its name.

## ON THE POWER OF GESTURE.

In gesture also there is much and the greatest reason, and a principle of no small importance for predicting <term>prognosticandi<note>The art of foretelling the course of a disease or a future event based on current signs.</note></term> or foreknowing, based on that principle that we can derive such principles from all surrounding and 
<margin>5</margin> accompanying circumstances. This is because things correspond to other things; all natural objects, both those held in the womb of nature <note>original: "in gremio naturae."</note> and those on the surface of sensible things, are so coordinated that they also possess a certain correspondence and joint 
significance. It is true that we cannot know all things exactly from all signs
<margin>10</margin> because of our mediocre experience, and because so few people turn their minds to it, observe, and take note. Because of this, I saw a little book compiled by a certain doctor in which that prudent man, relying on this principle, had applied to his own art the title of this inquiry, **On the power of gesture** <note>original: "De virtute gestus."</note>.
<margin>15</margin> Specifically, he considered the physical appearance <term>habitum<note>Could refer to a person's general physical constitution, their clothing, or their habitual disposition.</note></term>, posture, the ground, the location, the spoken word, and other circumstances when he first encountered a sick person. 
Immediately following this, he would note the outcome and success of the case; as these initial differences varied among different people, the outcomes of the illnesses were also different—some being favorable, others fitting their specific signs. 
<margin>20</margin> Thus, from continuous use and application, he collected certain universal rules <note>original: "universalia."</note>, verified in most or even all cases, so that through this single aspect of physical appearance he became a supreme physician.

Hunters also have certain universal rules based on encounters, by which they proceed so far as to return home and...

...they should abstain from their purpose <note>This continues the thought from the previous page: if the signs are bad, the practitioner should stop.</note>. It is a common saying that it is a bad omen to encounter a monk, but a good omen to encounter a beautiful girl, or a pregnant woman carrying a water-jar—from which rain <note>original: "unde pluvia"</note> comes. Conversely, meeting a person who limps, a beggar, a lack of necessary things, or an obstacle, or a wild beast with its young, foretells a sterility of business <note>Meaning the enterprise will be unproductive or unsuccessful.</note>. These same things can all be observed in their own order, since it is foolish and vain to believe that there is no power of significance in all things, as has been said, because of a certain correspondence and coordination of the affections <term>affectuum<note>In Bruno’s philosophy, this refers to the internal dispositions, moods, or "tunings" of things that connect them to one another.</note></term>. Even though the will 
<margin>54r</margin> 
of individual beings is not coerced, and not absolutely defined toward one of two | opposites, nevertheless, liberty and choice run and define themselves according to a certain order. And indeed, nothing is absolutely fortuitous; furthermore, "fortune" and "chance" are merely names for events whose causes are uncertain to us. When compared to our limited knowledge, they seem random; but to one who understands all particulars as they are arranged under universal causes, he possesses a most exact account of every singular and individual thing. And for us, regarding those things which are necessary for our state of life, this knowledge is not difficult to attain through inquiry, discovery, and observation, although for a mind that is dull, sluggish, and filled with vanities... <note>The text cuts off here, likely continuing the critique of those who fail to observe nature's signs.</note>

<margin>
Regarding this teaching, one should consider what has been discovered through full experience: that the leaves of the hellebore <note>A plant used in ancient and Renaissance medicine, often associated with treating madness or "melancholy."</note>, if plucked with an upward motion, cause evacuation through vomiting, but if plucked with a downward motion, they cause evacuation through the bowels. I have experienced the same thing myself with the herb that takes its name from Mount Olibanus near Salerno <note>Likely referring to Rosemary (Rosmarinus officinalis), though "Olibanum" usually refers to frankincense; Salerno was the site of the most famous medical school in the Middle Ages.</note>, where it grows in great abundance; everyone in that neighborhood uses it to purge any harmful humor <term>humorem<note>In ancient medicine, "humors" were the bodily fluids (blood, phlegm, yellow bile, black bile) that determined health and temperament.</note></term> without injury and with clear benefit. This serves to prove the doctrine of different gestures. Furthermore, there is a difference if one plucks an herb with or without the root, or if it is dead or alive; just as in the pruning of vines and in the order of cutting plants, one observes not only the time, but also the gesture, along with the disposition of the subject.
</margin>

<summary>Bruno argues that seemingly random encounters (omens) are actually meaningful signs based on the interconnectedness of all things, and that "chance" is simply a name for causes we do not yet understand. He uses the example of medicinal herbs—where the direction in which a leaf is plucked changes its medical effect—to demonstrate the hidden power of physical gestures.</summary>

...for those more attentive to their studies. # ON NUMBER AND MEASURE.

Beyond the reckoning of time, by which all things are distributed and bestowed—which Solomon also reduced to seven heads when he said, "all things have their time, and all things under the sun pass through their own spaces"—he added seven pairs of opposites with fourteen parts: a time to rejoice, a time to be sad, a time to gather, a time to scatter, etc. <note>Ecclesiastes 3:1–8. Bruno refers to the famous "To everything there is a season" passage.</note> And Christ said that he had come in the "fullness of time" <note>original: "plenitudine temporis"; Galatians 4:4.</note>; when he was pressed by his adversaries, he said, "this is your hour and the power of darkness" <note>Luke 22:53.</note>; when he had fled from those wishing to stone him and wished to return to them not long after | <margin>54ᵛ</margin>, and his disciples objected, saying, "They were just now seeking to stone you, and you wish to go back there?", he responded, "Are there not twelve hours in the day?" — where nothing is more evident than the fact that not every hour gives all things or the same things, but different things at different times.

I pass over how, in the ceremonies of two or three of the most famous laws <note>Bruno likely refers to the Jewish, Christian, and perhaps Islamic or Ancient Egyptian/Roman religious legal systems.</note>, festivals and worship are prescribed for certain times: new moons <note>original: "neomeniae"</note>, sabbaths, the feast of tabernacles <note>original: "scenopegiae"</note>, and passovers. *Two versions of 'Lullian Medicine' <note>This work applies the combinatorial logic of the 13th-century philosopher Ramon Llull to medical theory.</note> exist in the Moscow codex <note>The Moscow Codex is a vital collection of Bruno's manuscripts that remained unknown to western scholars until the late 19th century.</note>: one shorter and complete on folios 162–180 (erroneously marked 181 in the codex), and another more extensive but incomplete on folios 55–69. The first is in Bruno's own hand (= Br) up until the end of Chapter IV, 'On Quotidian Fever' <note>original: "De Febre quottidiana"; a fever that recurs every day.</note> (folio 167v), and for the remainder is in the hand of an unknown copyist (= X); the second version is in the hand of Besler <note>Hieronymus Besler was Bruno's student and dedicated scribe during his final years in Germany.</note>. See Lutoslawski in 'Archives for the History of Philosophy' <note>original: "Archiv. f. Gesch. d. Philos."</note> II (1889) p. 560 and following. We reproduce the second version (= M) and supplement it with the first (= Br + X). It should be noted, however, that for Br + X we provide the full collation <term>collation: the line-by-line comparison of different manuscript versions to identify variations and errors</term> only in the second part (that is, from the point where M ends), while for the part where we have M, the Br or X variants serve as evidence only for the specifically cited passages. Furthermore, we provide a sample of the first version in the preface to this volume. Here it suffices to mention that the first version is shorter: for example, it lacks everything that the second version contains in the marginal notes. Some passages of M were kindly collated by Mr. Barténew (= Mb). Of the marginal annotations, we reproduce only those which we were able to read with some certainty from the photograph of M (= Mf).*

§ I. Our intention is not so much to present the principles of medicine in the common manner—those which are most immediate to clinical practice—as it is to limit and modify that general art of *Llull* <note>Ramon Llull (c. 1232–1316) was a philosopher and mystic who developed a "General Art" using logical diagrams to synthesize all branches of knowledge. Bruno frequently adapted Llull's work into his own systems of memory and science.</note> for all sciences and <margin>5</margin> faculties according to his intentions, so that anyone may easily arrive at a knowledge of the whole of true medicine.

<margin>10</margin> § II. The proper subject of medicine is the human body, insofar as it is capable of being healed or falling ill. Health in the human body, however, <margin>15</margin> is a certain proportion consisting in the active and passive qualities of the four elements <note>The four elements are Fire (hot/dry), Air (hot/wet), Water (cold/wet), and Earth (cold/dry). In this period, health was viewed as a balance (crasis) of these qualities.</note>, or at least a proportion similar to that proportion.

§ III. An element or "elementative" <term>elementativa: a technical term in Lullian philosophy referring to the fundamental power or essence of the elements that precedes their physical manifestation</term> has a twofold <margin>20</margin> mode of being: objective and subjective. The elementative in its objective being is equally graded from the four aforementioned elements; but because action does not follow from an equal proportion (as *Aristotle* <note>Aristotle argued that for change or movement to occur, there must be an inequality or a "higher" and "lower" state; a perfect balance of forces results in stasis.</note> says, and as reason itself dictates) nor does...

passion <note>original: *passio*; in this context, the capacity to be acted upon, the necessary counterpart to action</note>, and for that reason the elementative <term>elementativa: a term from the philosophy of Ramon Llull referring to the fundamental essence or power of the elements that precedes their physical form</term> in this mode of being is ungenerable and incorruptible; and in this way, equal weight, measure, symmetry, and so forth can be established.

§ IV. In its subjective being, however, it likewise has a two-fold mode of being: one in any given sphere or in its own region, and thus the elements in it are unequally graded according to their qualities, because substance does not admit of "more" or "less" (for each thing has predominance in its own sphere by reason of the property of that place, while the other elements are in that same common place—just as fire dominates in the concavity of the lunar sphere <note>In the traditional cosmology of Bruno's time, the "sphere of fire" was located just below the moon. The physician investigates the movement of the elements in these alone, and of these, especially and properly in man.

§ V. Yet, because the physician does not heal "man" in general, but rather Socrates <note>Socrates is used here as a standard philosophical placeholder for any specific, individual person, much like "John Doe."</note>, he must therefore investigate this subjective mode of being—following the general principles of the art—in the individual human being whose health he intends to restore or preserve.

§ VI. ### § VII. In how many ways the complexion can be known.
There is a manifold method by which we can distinguish the complexion <term>complexio: in medieval and Renaissance medicine, this refers to the specific balance of the four humors and four qualities (hot, cold, moist, dry) that determine an individual's temperament and health.</term>, of which some ways are more remote, some are closer, and others are most proximate. To begin with the more remote ones, the complexion is known first by investigating the **interior birth** <note>original: *nativitas interior*</note>, which occurred at the instant of the introduction of the **rational soul** into the body, which was prepared by natural agents for the reception of the soul. In that instant (for the action of nature differs in nothing, but is immediately and necessarily instilled into the well-disposed recipient), a **spiritual influence** prevailed. By grace of this influence, fire predominates in the choleric person, air in the sanguine, water in the phlegmatic, and earth in the melancholic. The inquiry into the birth outside the womb, by which the fetus is brought into the light, is of no value, except so that through it we may be able to arrive at the knowledge of the first and true birth.

### § VIII.
Furthermore, since a birth of this kind <note>i.e., conception and animation</note> is irregular, being of an indefinite time, it seems impossible to investigate its nature with success; and therefore it is no wonder if both astrologers and doctors are for the most part mistaken in their judgments. <margin>56r</margin> Therefore, it must be sought by another way, since in conception, or at the instant of conception, there are certain accidents by which a woman can surely recognize that this kind of birth coincides with them. I do not wish to recount the signs which are in the woman and in the man—though general ones are widely known; for in conception, the woman’s legs ache and the menses cease to flow.

### § IX. The second method of investigating the complexion.
Next, the complexion is read in the **physiognomy** <term>physiognomy: the practice of assessing a person's character or health from their outer appearance, especially the face.</term> of man...

<summary>Bruno discusses the methods for determining a person's "complexion" or temperament, arguing that the moment of "interior birth" (conception/animation) is the true diagnostic key, rather than the moment of physical birth. He notes that because this moment is hard to track, doctors and astrologers often err, suggesting instead that physical signs in the mother can provide better evidence.</summary>

<margin>5</margin> ### § X. **Third reason.** 
However, the complexion <term>complexion: in medieval medicine, the "complexio" is the specific balance of the four humors—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that determines a person's health and personality.</term> is known in a truer way in those suffering from fevers. In this matter, it must be observed—as is commonly known—that the human body is constituted of the four elements. It is ruled and governed by the celestial bodies according to their various aspects <term>aspects: the specific angular positions of planets and stars relative to one another, believed to exert influence on Earth.</term>. These aspects <margin>See the properties of the planets.</margin> are indeed <margin>10</margin> varied according to two motions: namely, the daily motion of the first heaven <note>The *primum mobile*, the outermost sphere of the universe in the Ptolemaic system, which rotates the entire sky once every 24 hours.</note>, and the proper motion of the planets themselves. From the varying opposition and encounter of these two motions—sometimes in a general sense and sometimes specifically regarding the other diverse bodies—different aspects are generated here in these lower regions <note>The "sublunary" world, or the Earthly realm subject to change and decay.</note>. Therefore, a physician <margin>15</margin> (unless he wishes to heal by mere chance) must have knowledge of the principle by which this continuous motion is continuously diversified, producing different operations and effects. For from different aspects above and dispositions below, there arise different appetites, movements, and passions in the sick and infirm, as well as in their circumstances <margin>20</margin>.

<margin>5</margin> § XIV. In the final chamber **GHI**, the investigation begins first through **H**, because the physician first observes in the sick person that the vegetative power <note>The "vegetative power" (virtus vegetativa) refers to the most basic level of biological life responsible for growth and nutrition, shared by plants, animals, and humans.</note> is weakened in its capacities. <margin>10</margin> Such a defect arises either by reason of repletion <note>A state of being overfilled with humors or food, causing a blockage.</note>, which hinders the movement of the elements and that rule by which the humors in our body have their own rhythm (when they are well-disposed) much like the fixed rhythm found in the motion of the heavens; 
<margin>15</margin> or it arises by reason of a wound or emptiness, through which the continuity of the pathways <note>original: *meatuum*</note> is lost and the flow is cut short. From this, pain is caused; the subject suffers and cries out against their own instincts and appetite through pain. The cause of that pain is the subjective **H** <note>representing the vegetative power</note>, which cannot 
<margin>20</margin> perform its actions; and the cause of this is the substance **I** <note>representing the elemental power</note>, because it lacks its continuous motion.
