# CHAPTER II.

§ I. Even if a physician is not skilled in astrology, he will derive from this figure a reasoned investigation of the causes, means, and effects of the matter at hand. The figure, therefore, is composed of two circles; 
<margin>5</margin>the larger signifies the diurnal motion <note>The daily rotation of the heavens from East to West.</note> or the "world" motion, while the smaller signifies the proper motion <note>original: *motum proprium*; the individual movement of planets along the zodiac, which moves West to East.</note> of the seven planets. The larger moves from east to west, the smaller in the opposite direction.

This proper motion of the planets is not to be sought in any way other than what we have shown 
<margin>10</margin>previously <note>original: *in superioribus*; Bruno refers to his earlier discussion on page 538 regarding the calculation of planetary positions.</note>; and according to it, the causes of fortune, of motions and alterations, and of life and death must be investigated.

§ II. According to these two motions—whether naturally and elementally, or voluntarily and by chance, namely from 
<margin>15</margin>material or bodily principles as well as from principles less material and which are not considered bodily—there is the motion of the human body and the dispositions of the soul within it; since lower things are naturally and elementally constituted 
<margin>20</margin>under the influence of higher things, or, to speak more accurately, the law of particular and composite things is subordinated to the law of universals, principles, elements, and causes.

Here, the circle of the zodiac—the signs of life and death—can be applied starting from the head of the man, at whose crown [the figure] establishes Spring, passing 
<margin>25</margin>down through the feet, through which they establish Winter. For this zodiac is

<margin>5</margin> Lull must understand this outermost circle to be the primary one in this business, since—as we noted in the treatise *On Magic* toward the end—the day or year of the diurnal revolution is proportioned to the year of the solar revolution. Next, it should be observed that he most appropriately prescribes the day to take its beginning <margin>10</margin> from noon, since the line of the horizon is, for a thousand reasons, hidden or extremely difficult and perpetually uncertain, due to the inequality of the earth's surface <note>i.e., mountains and valleys make it hard to see the exact moment the sun "touches" the horizon</note>. Also, because the instant when the center of a celestial body touches that line is not easily definable, whereas the shadow <margin>15</margin> at noon, as it is commonly taken, from the point preceding noon and the point succeeding it, is more exact and certain. We have established a most exact method of finding the meridian line <unclear>...</unclear> not just by physical or geometric precision, but accepted in a practical <note>original: *crasso modo* (in a "thick" or rough manner)</note> way, with eyes turned away from the south <note>original: *meridie*</note> and turned toward the pole in its proper place; <margin>20</margin> namely, by dividing the circle of any perpetually visible star <note>a circumpolar star that never sets</note> into four parts, marking the highest and lowest points, and dropping a perpendicular line onto the plane of the horizon.

# GIORDANO BRUNO

F and so on, which cause the seven circulations of the seven days of the week, and are said to be caused by the seven planets.

§ II. **The First Circulation.** — The first circulation occurs by ascending from E of the smaller circle to the house of A itself on the <margin>5</margin> larger circle, and from there from B to F, thus from B to E, F to B, C to F, G to C, D to G, H to D, and A to H.

These subsequent circulations are said by <term>Lull (Ramon Llull, the 13th-century philosopher whose "Art" Bruno is adapting)</term> in some places to constitute healthy houses, in other places houses that are partly healthy and partly infirm, and in others houses that are entirely infirm. Regarding this, it must be noted that a region is judged <margin>10</margin> "healthy" because, from the meaning of the two letters—one from the larger circle and the other from the smaller circle—there follows a constitution that conforms to the region of the sky. For instance, toward the east there should be air and an aerial constitution; toward the south, fire and a fiery constitution; toward the west, <margin>15</margin> likewise, earth; and toward the point of midnight <note>the North</note>, water with its constitutions. In such a case, the natural motion is ordered because it conforms to the norm of the universe as a whole. 

A house is "partly healthy and partly not" (though for the most part healthy) when the meaning of the letter on the lower circle coincides with the meaning of the upper circle in one part, <margin>20</margin> but not in the other. In this case, one virtue comes out doubled, confirmed, and predominant, while the other virtue is weakened because of this dominance. 

A house is more "infirm" when the opposite occurs—namely, according to the other quality which serves. A house is entirely "infirm" when both qualities of the letter <margin>25</margin> on the lower circle are contrary to the qualities of the letter on the upper circle.

Applying this doctrine to our purpose, we say that the lower circle signifies the constitution of the <term>microcosm (the "little world," referring to the human body and the individual subject)</term>, while the upper circle signifies the constitution of the <term>macrocosm (the "great world," or "megacosmos")</term> or the diurnal circle. The diurnal circle <margin>30</margin> signifies the constitution of the four elements in their simple, subjective being; the circle of the microcosm, however, signifies the constitution within the "elemented" or composite body, which was described above <note>original: *p. 572, 15 sqq.*</note> as "subjective being in the second manner."

### LULLIAN MEDICINE

§ III. **On the houses of the first circulation and first on the four of the first region.** — The houses AE, BF, CG, and DH are healthy, and the region composed of these houses is healthy. This is indicated by the letters within them, which correspond according to the qualities signified in the alphabet. For E, which is moist and hot, corresponds with A, which is <term>Air (the element associated with moisture and heat)</term>; F, which is hot and dry, corresponds with B, which is <term>Fire</term>; G, which is cold and dry, corresponds with C, which is <term>Earth</term>; H, which is cold and moist, corresponds with D, which is <term>Water</term>.

§ IV. **On the four houses of the second region.** — The houses of the second region, which are also four—namely BE, CF, DG, and AH—are partly healthy and partly infirm; they are healthy insofar as the letters agree, but infirm insofar as they disagree.

§ V. **The Kingdom of Fire.** — In house BE, the letters B and E agree through heat, because both B and E are hot, but they disagree through moisture and dryness <note>B (Fire) is dry, while E (Air) is moist</note>. Because two instances of heat acting in agreement are more powerful than the opposition of moisture and dryness, the house BE is therefore more healthy than infirm. Furthermore, because fire is hot by its very nature <note>original: *per se*</note>, while air is hot only by association <note>original: *per accidens*; in medieval physics, fire was the primary source of heat</note>, it follows that fire dominates in this kind of place, while air is <margin>59^r</margin> subjected. And because fire, which is the ruler, is dry (for dryness accompanies heat, which is its own quality), dryness is the mistress in this house, and moisture the handmaid.

§ VI. **The Kingdom of Earth.** — House CF is also partly healthy and partly infirm; it is healthy due to the two instances of dryness agreeing, and infirm due to heat and cold disagreeing. Thus, Earth is queen through dryness; and because—

§ II. **The Kingdom of Dryness.** — In House EF, F is the master and E is the subject. In this house, there are two instances of heat: one is inherent <note>original: *propria*</note> through F and the other is acquired <note>original: *propriata*</note> through E. Because that which is inherent carries more weight than that which is acquired, heat is the queen. Dryness (which is the inherent quality of <term>Fire</term>) is the mistress, while moisture (which belongs to the acquired quality) is the handmaid. Thus, in this house, the mistress and the handmaid, being in disagreement, cause infirmity; however, the heat of fire and the heat of air cause health through the concord between the inherent and the acquired qualities.

<margin>Folio 59^v</margin>
§ III. **The Kingdom of Dryness.** — In House BC, C is the master and B is the subject. Because C causes dryness in B, while B causes nothing in C, dryness is the queen. Since coldness causes itself in C and C overcomes B, coldness is the mistress and heat is the handmaid. This is assuming, however, that C is in its own region, because at noon <note>original: *meridie*; likely referring to the peak of the sun’s influence</note>, B is the queen.

§ IV. **The Kingdom of Dryness.** — In House FG, G overcomes F through two instances of dryness, one inherent and the other acquired. From this, it follows that dryness is the queen, coldness is the mistress, and heat is the handmaid.

§ V. **The Kingdom of Coldness.** — In House CD, D overcomes C because D is cold of itself <note>original: *per se*; essentially</note> and C is cold by accident <note>original: *per accidens*; incidentally</note>. Therefore, since there are two instances of coldness, the Kingdom of Coldness follows, where moisture is the mistress and dryness is the handmaid.

§ VI. **The Kingdom of Coldness.** — In House GH, H overcomes G because H is cold of itself, whereas G is cold by accident. Thus, H is the master through two instances of coldness; moisture is the mistress and dryness is the handmaid.

§ VII. **The Kingdom of Moisture.** — In House AD, A is the master through its inherent <note>original: *propriam*</note> moisture, while D is the subject through its acquired <note>original: *appropriatam*</note> moisture; therefore, moisture is the **queen**, heat is the **mistress**, and coldness is the **handmaid**. <note>In Bruno’s medical system, these roles represent the hierarchy of influence a quality has on the body’s temperament.</note>

<margin>5</margin> It should be noted here that each of the four qualities belongs to two elements: to one primarily <note>original: *proprie*</note>, namely that which it fits first, and to the other by acquisition <note>original: *appropriate*</note>, which it fits secondarily and in a diminished degree. Now, Fire is primarily **hot**; Air is primarily **moist**; Water is primarily **cold**; Earth is primarily **dry**. Therefore, according to these primary associations, the qualities reign as **queens**; <margin>10</margin> according to the others, they either act as mistresses or serve as handmaids.

§ VIII. **The Kingdom of Moisture.** — In House HE, moisture is the **queen** following the same sequence, heat is the **mistress**, and coldness is the **handmaid**.

### CHAPTER V.

<margin>15</margin> § I. **The Third Circulation.** — The houses of the third circulation are AF, EC, BG, FD, CH, GA, DE, HB.

**The Region of Air itself.** — In House AF, F is the master and A is the subject because of the heat which belongs to F inherently <note>original: *per se*</note> and to A accidentally <note>original: *per accidens*</note>. From this, it follows that **dryness** <margin>20</margin> is the mistress, because it agrees with coldness, which is an active form of heat; <note>Bruno often employed paradoxical physics where qualities could transform into their opposites or act through them.</note> here, moisture is the handmaid because it agrees with A. However, A is not entirely a subject because it is in its own region, whereas F is not in its own region; therefore, its mastery is weakened.

<margin>25</margin> § II. **The Region of Heat.** — In House EC, there are equal opposites; but because E is in its own region and C is in a foreign region, E is the master and C is the subject.

§ III. **The Region of fire itself.** — In House BG, B is the master and G is the subject, because B is in its own home and G is a traveler <note>original: *peregrinus*; in Lullian logic, a "traveler" or "pilgrim" is a quality operating outside its natural element</note>.

§ IV. **The Region of the hot and the dry.** — In House DF, there is <margin>60r</margin>
<margin>5</margin> an equality of opposition between heat and cold, and moisture and dryness; nevertheless, because F is in its own region, while D is in a foreign one, F is therefore the master and D is the subject. Coldness is not quite the mistress, nor is moisture quite the handmaid.

<margin>10</margin> § V. **The Region of Earth.** — In House CH, C is the master and H is the subject, because C is dry by its very nature <note>original: *per se ipsum*</note> and is in its own region; and H is a traveler. Coldness is the mistress and moisture is the handmaid.

§ VI. **The Region of the cold and the dry.** — In House AG,
<margin>15</margin> there is an equal opposition between the moist and the dry, and the hot and the cold, but G dominates because it is in its own region, whereas A is a traveler; hence, coldness does not dominate much, nor does heat act as a handmaid.

§ VII. **The Region of the hot and the moist.** — In House DE,
<margin>20</margin> E is the master by nature, but not by fortune <note>In this context, "fortune" refers to the accidental or situational strength of a quality</note>, insofar as it is a traveler; there, E possesses its own inherent moisture, while D possesses moisture by accident or by acquisition.

§ VIII. In House BH, there is an equal opposition between
<margin>25</margin> the cold, the hot, the moist, and the dry; but because H is in its own region and B is not, H dominates and B serves. Neither does moisture dominate much, nor does dryness act much as a handmaid; and this is because its mastery is not sufficiently effective, since it arises merely from the property of the region.

Regarding rotations of this kind, it must be noted that the middle circle—although designated as "mobile" by Llull <note>Ramon Llull (1232–1316), the philosopher whose combinatorial system Bruno is adapting</note> as we find in the manuscript copies—is actually immobile in practice. Therefore, let only the small circle be rotated (as is also clear in actual practice). However, lest there be any doubt as to how it should be fixed in position, one must look to the parts of the daily circle. As shown in previous sections, some parts refer to Air (the parts near the East, which are spring-like); others to Fire (the parts near the South, which are summer-like); others to Earth (the parts near the West, which are autumnal); and others to Water (the parts near the point of midnight, which are winter-like). 

Thus, the parts of this second circle should be arranged so that the airy signs—Aries, Taurus, and Gemini <note>original symbols: ♈ ♉ ♊</note>—are positioned equally before the eastern point and equally after it. This follows the rule that Air and Blood <note>the humor associated with the element of Air</note> dominate for three hours before sunrise <note>original: ☉$^{lis}$ (Solis)</note> and three hours after. 

Similarly, the same must be done for the other three following summer signs: let the 15th point of Leo <note>original symbol: ♌</note> be the end of the designated three hours before noon, and let the 16th degree be the beginning of the three remaining hours after noon until the end of Virgo <note>original symbol: ♍</note>, since fifteen minutes <note>In the context of the 360-degree celestial circle, 15 degrees correspond to one hour of time; Bruno likely refers to these units of measurement here</note> are assigned to each hour. 

In this way, following our order, the other parts of the Earthly and Watery signs reflecting the constitution of autumn and winter are to be distributed. But one must remember, according to our doctrine, that <insert>**Folio 61, verso**</insert> these hours are not equal [in length], but exist in a double order of equality. This occurs when the arc of the day is divided equally into smaller parts, and the arc of the night is divided equally into larger parts—specifically outside the time of the equinox, when night is longer than day; or conversely, when the day is longer than the night, namely when the Sun <note>original: ☉$^e$ (Sole)</note> approaches the Tropic of Cancer <note>original symbol: ♋</note>. 

Therefore, we must proceed not by a blind and logical order, but by a clear, evident, and physical order. We advance this Art of Llull toward its intended goal, from whom we have received and recognized no small amount, once the universal principles are grasped...

### LULLIAN MEDICINE

According to standard rules, the astrological aspects <note>the angular distances between planets</note>, the stars relative to the signs of the zodiac, and those things which are surrounding them in their latitude toward either pole—once those six distinguishing circles have been drawn—you will then be able to judge most exactly and, without error, weigh every detail down to the smallest point. 
<margin>5</margin> Indeed, from the very outcome of events, it will be possible to judge, correct, and restore whether a birth chart <note>original: "nativitas"</note> was correctly established. Furthermore, from the deviation of the patient themselves, you will be able to distinguish exactly, according to the forms of their alteration, the specific parts, quantity, and quality of the **humors** <note>the four bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—thought to determine health</note> and **temperaments** <note>the physical and mental character resulting from the balance of humors</note>; how they increase or decrease, how they intensify or 
<margin>10</margin> relax, and how they may tend toward corruption and death, or be repaired and restored. For universal principles, it was enough for Llull <note>Ramon Llull, the 13th-century philosopher whose "Art" Bruno is refining</note> to look at things in a general way <note>original: "crasso modo," literally "in a thick or coarse manner"</note>, such as the differences between regions, the qualities within those regions, and things that are mobile or stable, or 
<margin>15</margin> residing in their own or another's "house" <note>an astrological division of the sky</note>. From this follows the logic of planetary dominion and servitude, and of exaltation and depression <note>technical terms for when a planet is at its strongest or weakest influence</note>. However, it happens that those who look at too few factors are not able to judge many or specific things. It is enough, therefore, for him to have shown the way; it is for us to have paved, distinguished, and cleared it. 
<margin>20</margin> As for what is required in the final place regarding the definition of each specific detail: if it is not granted to us to spend time on astronomical instruction here, let it be sought from those works published by the most proven authors. Ultimately, however, it will be the task of practitioners to apply this doctrine to individual cases.
   Regarding the completion of this art, it will suffice for our present 
<margin>25</margin> Lullian instruction to collect the properties and virtues of the houses, aspects, planets, signs, images, the mansions of the moon, and the various conjunctions <note>original: "synodorum"</note> where various powers usually converge. If time is given, we shall bring all these things forward most aptly and clearly in the form of images—numbering fewer than 
<margin>30</margin> one hundred—according to the rules explained in ***The Thirty Seals*** <note>original: "Triginta sigillis"; referring to Bruno's 1583 book on memory and logic, "Explicatio triginta sigillorum"</note>.

## ON FEVERS.

After we have completed the treatise on the **regions** <term>regiones: conceptual "spaces" or categories in the Lullian system where elemental and planetary forces interact</term> of health and illness, within whose scope <note>original: "latitudine"</note> all health and infirmity are established; for the celestial or universal bodies of nature do not induce health or infirmity beyond or outside of these regions; 
<margin>5</margin> therefore, if a sick person is to be treated, they must be treated within these bounds. Consequently, the hours of the daily cycle admit no movement outside of these. And just as a transparent body <note>original: "corpus diaphanon"</note> is colored in different ways by the presence of different colors, or as the 
<margin>10</margin> same mirror is shaped by various straight and oblique figures, or as the air is similarly activated by light and darkness; so these same aforementioned regions are disposed in various ways according to the different influences of external bodies, and they indicate, designate, and define the disposition of the human body. Therefore, a physician 
<margin>15</margin> ought to keep them before his eyes like a mirror, and according to their indication, investigate the causes, principles, and elements of diseases.

Four general species of fever are cited, according to the fact that there are four qualities in man: namely, **continuous**, **quotidian**, **tertian**, and **quartan** <note>These classifications describe the cycle of the fever: "quotidian" peaks daily, "tertian" every other day (3rd day by inclusive counting), and "quartan" every third day (4th day by inclusive counting)</note>. Each of 
<margin>20</margin> these has its own region, just as the tertian is treated through house <note>the "houses" here refer to specific combinations of concepts on the Lullian wheels</note> BF, the continuous through house AE, and the quotidian through house DH,

### LULLIAN MEDICINE.

...quartan fever <term>quartana: a malarial-type fever that peaks every four days, associated in this system with the "house" or combination CG</term> through house CG. And we say it is possible for a continuous and acute fever to be of house BF.

->Concerning tertian fever.<-

<margin>**63**^**r**</margin>
The region of the tertian fever <term>tertiana: a fever that peaks every three days</term> extends from BF to AE and CG, and it possesses one triangle, whose two lines agree and one is in opposition; for they agree from B to A through heat, and from B to C through dryness, and from A to C through opposition <note>In Lullian medicine, these letters represent elements or qualities: B is usually Fire (Hot and Dry), A is Air (Hot and Moist), and C is Earth (Cold and Dry). Thus, Fire (B) shares heat with Air (A) and dryness with Earth (C), but Air and Earth are opposites.</note>. And in this triangle, B is the master and causes the tertian fever, if B flows too much heat into A and receives too little dryness from C itself, because the line from A to C cannot bear that excessive imbalance <note>original: "intemperiem"</note>, and it is changed according to its substance, and altered into infirmity and corruption. Therefore, B is the cause of the tertian fever. And it is called "tertian" because on one day the infirmity is intense, while on the following it is extended or more relaxed. And if B abounds too much in A through heat, the intense tertian has its power from heat, and the extended or relaxed state from dryness.

But if the tertian fever is multiplied through house BF, a **double tertian** follows; for the multiplication can be so great that house BF gains dominion over all other houses and regions; for on the third day it changes into CG, and on the fifth day it returns to house BF; and therefore on the fifth day it afflicts the patient more strongly than on the third, and on the ninth than on the seventh, and on the thirteenth than on the eleventh, and so with the others; and the tertian fever is multiplied so much through house BF that the double tertian is altered into a continuous fever.

Bruno further describes the "double tertian" fever, where a repeating pattern of elemental shifts leads to increasingly severe symptoms that can eventually become a continuous illness.</summary>

1 If a tertian fever <term>tertiana: a fever recurring every three days, associated here with house BF</term> is perceptible on the first day in house BF, it is a bad sign, because B is less strong against D and C than H is. Thus, from what we have said about the tertian fever, the 
5 doctrine concerning the fevers of all other regions is inferred. For if these [fevers] proceed in the same order according to their numbers, and are increased and strengthened, they tend toward an intensification leading to the corruption of the subject <note>i.e., the destruction of the patient's body</note>; on the other hand, if they proceed otherwise, it is different. 
Although judgment can be made about the others from what has been said 10 concerning the progress of tertian fever, we will nevertheless say something about the remaining ones in their proper order. 
Just as in the quotidian fever <term>quotidiana: a fever that recurs daily, associated here with house DH</term>, which is in house DH, entirely opposite to house BF itself, and which has the opposing triangle DAC with two concordant lines—namely DA through humidity and 15 DC through coldness—and one contrary line CA, as has been said, because CG and AE are contraries; so it is with the others.

### Concerning continuous slow and very acute fever.

A continuous and slow fever differs from a very acute one, because the latter triumphs in all regions and appears equal in them by trampling upon <note>original: "inculcando"</note> natural operation, while the slow 20 continuous fever is greater in some regions and lesser in others; the very acute fever, by its strength, frequently harasses nature and conquers everywhere, so that the dominion of the soul is hindered, as it were, and it cannot even move the body as its own instrument. From this it happens that a patient suffering from such a fever 25 speaks indistinctly. Therefore, when someone suffering from a tertian or quotidian fever speaks rashly and without cause, it is a sign of the transformation of the tertian or quotidian fever into a continuous one; for nature seems to succumb to the disease <note>The variant in the Brussels manuscript reads: "so that it might be more vigorous against nature."</note>.

### Concerning the quotidian fever.

The quotidian fever <term>quotidiana: a fever that recurs every single day</term> is treated through house DH; it attacks the patient daily, differing from a double tertian fever. For the quotidian itself is caused by phlegm <note>original: "phlegmate"; the humor associated with cold and moisture</note>, from which a
<margin>5</margin>double tertian cannot be caused. Likewise, this quotidian fever dissolves matter more forcefully and, due to its persistent continuation, is more contrary to nature (since, as it does not allow for a pause in the struggle between nature and the disease, this same continuity weakens <margin>63v</margin>
<margin>10</margin>and eventually suppresses the power of the restorative forces or natural virtues, unless some favorable factor intervenes). Hence, through the pulse, the urine, and the variation between day and night—which are divided into four parts as was said above—it can be seen how the fever runs through each and all of the aforementioned regions and houses.

Note then that, according to this art, there are four principal terms or points, both in the daily revolution of the macrocosm <note>The "greater world" or the universe at large</note> and in the revolution of the elements or qualities in the microcosm <note>The "lesser world," meaning the human body</note>, just as there are four elements and four tri-
<margin>5</margin>angles pertaining to the species of the fever itself, which are signified by the letters ABCD and EFGH. <note>In Llull's system, letters are used as variables to represent different concepts; here, ABCD likely represents the four primary elements or humors, while EFGH represents their specific combinations or pathological states.</note> Similarly, in fevers there are four points: the onset of the attack, the peak of the heat, the beginning of the decline, and the point of exhaustion; and one must consider how this internal order runs in agreement or disagreement with the external order, from which you may take your method of prognosis
<margin>10</margin>and of healing.

Llull therefore says to investigate the principles and causes of any disease through the "angle of the beginning," which he does specifically regarding the degrees of the elements. For if the fourth degree <note>Medieval medicine categorized the intensity of an elemental quality (like heat or moisture) from one to four; the fourth degree was the most intense and often dangerous.</note>, which
acts through appetite <note>original: "appetitum"; referring to the natural inclination or "drive" of a physical substance to reach its goal or state</note>, is corrupted and taken away by the fever, <margin>**64r**</margin>
<margin>15</margin>the other degrees subordinated to that fourth degree and tending toward a single end will not hold together. Each of the elements desires an end suitable to itself, and one is not ruled or ordered by the other; for each has its own nature, distinct from others or contrary to another. Therefore, where one form is
<margin>20</margin>destroyed, there follows a formless disorder of the other elements which—as we have shown in the book *On Generation* <note>original: "De generatione"; likely referring to Bruno's own work or the Aristotelian tradition regarding how matter is formed and decayed</note>—are coordinated, chained together, and united simultaneously, so that a certain circle can exist among them. For earth migrates into water, water into air, and air into fire; so that earth, which is
<margin>25</margin>cold and dry, is united to air, which is hot and moist, by means of water, which agrees with earth in its coldness and with air in its moisture. Similarly, water migrates into fire through the medium of air; for air acts as a mediator to bind them both, agreeing with water in moisture and with fire in heat.

<meta>This page continues Bruno's exploration of "Lullian Medicine," applying the combinatorial logic of Ramon Llull to the four qualities—heat, cold, moisture, and dryness. <page-num>600</page-num>
<header>GIORDANO BRUNO <note>original: "IORDANI BRVNI"</note></header>

To dissolve or eliminate [a disease], the removal or destruction of one primary quality is sufficient. Since that quality is proper to one element, it cannot be restored by the remaining elements; for it is never truly appropriated by any of them <margin>5</margin> unless that element to which it belongs remains and holds dominion. Therefore, the elements will be mixed together without any order. The cause of this mixture and disorder is the destruction of the <term>fourth degree<note>In medieval medicine, the intensity of a quality (like heat or cold) was measured on a scale of one to four. The fourth degree was the most extreme and often considered life-threatening or foundational to the element's identity.</note></term>, which held the other degrees under its control. Thus, the end of that fourth degree brings about the end of the others as well.

<margin>10</margin> **Regarding the fourth degree.** Just as the fourth degree of coldness itself is D or H, the third degree is C or G, and between that and the fourth degree sits GD; the second degree is AE, and between that and the fourth HA mediates; the first degree is B or F, because the heat of B is not entirely intense or infinite, but finite, and [its limit] is reached through <margin>15</margin> the participation of its opposite; and therefore the first degree of the opposite quality is said to exist within it. In this way, one must judge the fourth degree: what is A, what is B, and therefore what is C. Thus it is understood how, when the fourth degree is removed, the remaining degrees are taken away; for if coldness is not present at the peak of <margin>20</margin> midnight <note>Bruno uses the cycle of the day as a metaphor for elemental cycles; midnight represents the absolute peak of "Cold."</note>, it will never be present again.

Since CG (cold and dry) <gloss>original: "frig. et sic."</gloss> cause death and AE (hot and moist) <gloss>original: "cal. et hu."</gloss> cause life, death and fever may coincide when C and G consist in the predominance of <term>melancholy<note>One of the four humors of ancient medicine, associated with the element of Earth; it is characterized as being cold and dry.</note></term>. For this resides in the west, in the "house of the earth"; and the fever pertaining to this house is more dangerous than all others. Such is the <term>quartan fever<note>A type of fever, often associated with malaria, where paroxysms (chills and heat) recur every fourth day (every 72 hours).</note></term>, <margin>25</margin> which attacks the patient from the fourth day unto the fourth day.
[In the house of CG, the natural simple fourth degree of C itself is thrown into disorder because of an overflow of three points...]

# ON URINES.

To gain a clearer understanding of fevers and diseases, the physician examines the urine. Just as there are four elements, so too there are four [primary] colors. And just as
<margin>5</margin> various <term>complexions</term><note>In medieval medicine, a "complexion" is the specific balance of the four qualities—Hot, Cold, Moist, and Dry—that determines a person’s health or temperament.</note> of things arise from the four elements being combined and graded in different ways, so too all other colors are contained within the power of the four primary colors. Their differences are judged by the predominance of one element or another, depending on whether there is more or less access to certain colors
<margin>10</margin> through the greater or lesser involvement of one or another element.

All differences in color are caused by one primary distinction: that between white and black, dark and light, or light and shadow.

<margin>15</margin> The principal and fundamental differences are: clear and dark; white and black; thick and thin; watery and dense.

Furthermore, differences arise based on transparency, clarity, and subtleness on one hand, and darkness, thickness, and confusion on the other. Thus, there are many
<margin>20</margin> specific variations in the colors of urine, just as there are variations in the <term>humors</term>.<note>Humors: The four vital fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—believed to regulate health.</note> Whoever approaches these with a more specific and proper consideration will judge and treat patients more precisely.

---

For just as one element in its active state contains others in potentiality, so does its color contain all of their colors. There are many other colors that appear specifically from the dissolution of the humors to signify particular illnesses; and because through universal principles one can descend to particular cases (*page 606, line 1*) etc. X; *compare Lull, page 36a*. *Line 4:* "are | and are" in manuscript M1. *Lines 15 and 16:* recorded in the margin of manuscript M.

He maps the four primary colors of urine—transparency, light, blackness, and whiteness—onto the four Lullian "houses" or elemental categories (A, B, C, and D).</meta>

<page-num>606</page-num>
<header>GIORDANO BRUNO</header>

Furthermore, since the path to particulars <note>Specific cases or symptoms.</note> opens through universals, we must now speak of the four primary differences in urines, which are found in the four houses or regions. <note>In the system of Ramon Lull, "houses" or "regions" refer to specific compartments in his mnemonic and logical diagrams used to categorize information.</note>

<margin>5</margin> The proper color of **A** is **transparency**, <note>original: "diaphanitas"</note> as is evident in illuminated air, which, when combined with light, represents nothing in itself besides whiteness.

It should be noted that the <term>diaphanous</term> <note>From the Greek *diaphanēs*, meaning translucent or transparent.</note> is not a color, but the translucent matter of a body (for "diaphanous" and "transparent" are the same thing). This quality is indeed shared by water, air, crystal, and all those bodies which, when placed in between, do not block the image set beyond them from being perceived by sight. However, by Lull, it is more commonly understood that "diaphanous" signifies a confused and indistinct white. Nor is this done rashly, because just as whiteness is the receptacle for all other colors, so too is the diaphanous.

The color of **B** is **light**, and the reason is because it illuminates <margin>66</margin> the air with light; which it could not do unless light were its proper color.

The color [of **C**], however, is **blackness**, as is evident in shadow; for due to the absence of light, the air receives color, specifically because of the presence of earthy vapors.

He calls light a color according to the more common understanding of color, insofar as it is the proper <term>subject</term> <note>The specific object or range that a sense is designed to perceive.</note> of the visual power, just as flavor is the proper subject of taste. He likewise calls blackness a color; for the visible thing in which one cannot see any shadow is pure light, which is not properly a color, but the **indicator of colors**.

The color of **D**, however, is **whiteness**, and it is evident through the lily and snow—that is, through thickened water, congealed in a <term>compound</term> <note>A "compound" is a physical substance made of multiple elements, like a plant or a body fluid.</note> in which it dominates, whether that compound be perfect or imperfect.

In composite bodies, it possesses degrees according to the ranking of qualities shown by the **Figure of Medicine**. <note>The "Figure of Medicine" is a specific combinatorial diagram from the works of Ramon Lull, used to calculate the degrees of heat, cold, moisture, and dryness in a patient.</note> Specifically, by moving through and rotating around the diagram, it becomes clear first through the first rotation; for the **House of AE** [is healthy and] <note>The brackets [est sana] indicate a reconstruction of the text likely missing in some copies.</note> produces healthy urine, as can be read in its color. For the color of urine represents its origin and cause, just as every effect reveals its cause and location. Its color is clear and golden, derived from the colors of **Fire** and **Air**, in which neither the colors of **Water** nor **Earth** appear, due to the distance between the **House of AE** and the **House of CG**, which is its opposite.

<margin>10</margin> But if that "house" is altered by illness through a predominance of blood, it will be recognized by a blood-like color. The urine is then red and thick in its substance. Because **A** is opposite to **C**, **C** cannot serve as the subject that reflects the brightness of **B**, nor can **B** manifest the blackness of **C**. <note>In Bruno’s elemental mapping, A, B, C, and D represent the four elements or their primary qualities. Here, he is explaining why certain colors cancel each other out or dominate based on their positions in the Lullian wheel.</note> Therefore, in this redness, **A** is demonstrated in both color and matter, while **B** is demonstrated only in matter.

<margin>18</margin> <margin>Note in margin: because in matter and color, Air is the king and Fire is the lord; because [it is shown] only in matter, therefore A reigns and B dominates.</margin> Hence, if this is correctly perceived, **A** will be found to have **B** subordinate to it, insofar as in the urine, **A** is demonstrated through both color and matter, whereas **B** is demonstrated only through matter... <note>The dots indicate a gap or "lacuna" in the original manuscript's text.</note> caused by the dominance of **B**, **B** is manifested in matter and <term>virtue</term>, <note>original: "virtus". In this context, it refers to the active power or functional strength of an element rather than moral virtue.</note> while **D** is demonstrated only in matter—which is thick and serves as the subject for **A**. Therefore, such urine is red and thick. From this, one understands how the elements are diversified by both matter and virtue. The redder and thicker the urine is, the more it contains of the matter of each element.

Therefore, the matter should be reduced through <term>phlebotomy</term> <note>the medical practice of bloodletting</note>, so that the motion through which A and B operate does not cease, so that the active power of CD may remain.

<margin>10</margin> Do not be troubled by the fact that we sometimes use "region" for "house" and "house" for "region"; likewise, sometimes A is put for E, B for F, C for G, and D for H; for in this discussion we do not make distinctions between the specific qualities and their proper subjects or elements. <note>Bruno is simplifying his combinatorial system here, treating the abstract qualities and the physical elements as interchangeable for the sake of the medical diagnosis.</note>

<margin>15</margin> Returning to the proposal, we say that the **House of BE** signifies clear, golden urine that is intense and shaded in part, by reason of the Earth infusing its dryness into B, with which Fire colors the transparency of the sick person's urine; for transparency is the handmaid, blackness the mistress, and clarity the queen.

<margin>20</margin> If you see clear, golden urine, know that it belongs to the **House of BE** and is of the nature of Fire and Air.

In the **House of BF**, the urine is unhealthy due to an abundance of dryness and heat, and the clarity is very intense because the transparency receives the shadow of Earth instead of blackness, [the...]

...[we say] however, that it is healthy throughout the region in itself; but if it is altered by excessive yellow bile <note>original: *cholera*</note>, healthy urine produces a clear color, as if one were mixing a saffron color with white.

In **House CF**, there is illness, as was stated in the first circulation <note>A "circulation" refers to a full turn or movement through the Lullian combinatorial wheel</note>; and just as the House is infirm, so also the urine appears, because water overcomes earth with its coldness and earth overcomes fire with its dryness. But by accident, due to the illness, an alteration in the opposite direction follows because of the excessive abundance present in that house, expelling coldness with heat and moisture with dryness; and thus the urine remains not very clear nor golden, but black against the whiteness and thick, lacking transparency <note>original: *diaphanitatem*</note>.

<margin>67<sup>v</sup></margin>
In **House CG**, the urine is black because of earth, but clear because of whiteness; but because earth is the queen <note>i.e., the dominant element in this combination</note>, the blackness fights against the whiteness as its opposite. But if this whiteness has a great agreement with transparency, a brown color reigns in that house, which is composed of whiteness and blackness.

By **transparency** <note>original: *diaphanitatem*</note>, understand fineness or rarity and clarity, which is the opposite of thickness, density, viscosity, and so on.

In **House DG**, the urine is white because of water and black because of earth; from which follows a very intense brown color. But because transparency accords with whiteness and light, whiteness overcomes blackness—though not entirely—since blackness accords with brightness through dryness.

In **House DH**, urine is white and clear through the influence of water and air; but if it is altered by illness, blackness prevails against whiteness with brightness and dryness against moisture, turning the transparency <note>original: *diaphanitatem*; a key concept in uroscopy referring to how much light passes through the sample</note> white.

<margin>5</margin> In **House AH**, Air <note>represented by the letter A</note> reigns through moisture and Water <note>represented by the letter H</note> suffers through coldness; and because Air acts upon Water and not the other way around, the House is altered by illness. The colors of House CF enter the House through coloring, whereby the urine is confused, as it is something which coalesces from opposites; and these opposites are recognized by "good" colors <margin>10</margin> placed between "bad" ones, and generally by the variety of consistency and its heterogeneous form.

->On Urines in Particular<-

Just as we have spoken about urines through the first circulation <note>A "circulation" refers to a full cycle of combinations on the Lullian combinatorial wheel</note>, so it can be said for the others in their own way; however, for their <margin>15</margin> greater clarity, they must be discussed further in detail.

It was said above concerning urine signifying the dominance of blood <note>The "sanguine" humor</note>: now we must look at urine signifying the dominance of yellow bile <note>original: *cholerae*</note>. For just as two humors are demonstrated and recognized through the touch of the pulse by the two different strikes <margin>20</margin> which the pulse makes against the fingers, so in <margin>68</margin> a **simple tertian fever** <note>A malaria-like fever where the paroxysm occurs every third day, traditionally attributed to an excess of yellow bile</note> fire and earth demonstrate their colors in the urine. For in the fact that the urine is clear and red, it is demonstrated that fire has a great brightness, which is perceptible within the blackness of earth, just as is evident in the [spark] that is drawn from a stone, which is not <margin>25</margin> perceptible except in the dark. Therefore, fire demonstrates its brightness better in the dark than elsewhere; hence it is revealed...

# LULLIAN MEDICINE

...the mixture of the color of fire with earth, because its brightness is more brilliant when contrasted with the blackness of earth.

Red color appearing in the urine indicates blood, which corresponds with Air; for Air is revealed in the color <margin>5</margin> of blood. Water, however, is revealed in the substance <note>original: *materie*; referring to the physical consistency or "body" of the fluid</note>, as occurs in wine, in which there is much water; because of this abundance, the color of wine leans toward white. And just as the four elements are revealed in their own operations, so too are their operations shown in the urine through the aforementioned <margin>10</margin> colors. The more the red color increases in the urine, the less clarity there is in it. The reason for this is that its subject is more heavily filled with the matter of **C** <note>In Bruno’s medical system, the letter C represents the element of Fire and the quality of Heat</note>; therefore, fire does not have a medium in which to manifest its brightness so strongly, nor does earth manifest its blackness except within a fiery brightness. For this reason, <margin>15</margin> thick and red urine signifies matter that is more corrupted than simple and clear red urine; for the demonstration of the four elements themselves is obtained through their works, which is manifested through the **green triangle** <note>A mnemonic tool in Lullian logic used to map relationships—specifically "Difference, Concordance, and Contrariety"</note>—namely the first one—in which their operations <margin>20</margin> are diversified, harmonized, and opposed. Thus, in the urine, the significance of the dominant **phlegm** <note>One of the four bodily humors, associated with Water and Cold</note> is shown through color.

Where, however, the color in the urine is caused by the dominance of **DA** <note>The combination of the elements Water (D) and Air (A)</note>, the color of **BC** <note>The combination of Fire (B) and Earth (C)</note> will be hidden; thus, it will be white and thick with some part <margin>25</margin> of redness, resembling the **washings of raw meat** <note>original: *loturae carnis crudae*; a traditional medical term for a pale, pinkish, cloudy sediment in urine</note>. If, however, it is white and thick without the participation of any other color, then it demonstrates that the dominance of **D** <note>Water/Phlegm</note> is not moderate, but extreme; if however it be...

BY GIORDANO BRUNO

# ON PULSES.

The types of pulses are generally four in number, primarily to demonstrate the operation of the four elements. This operation begins in the heart, which sends these four elements <margin>5</margin> through all parts of the body, giving to those parts primarily **B** <note>Water</note>, so that it may strengthen the natural heat within them, and preserving and retaining **D** <note>Earth</note> for itself, lest the greatest abundance of **A** <note>Air</note> existing there should be able to destroy the heart itself.

->Concerning the pulse signifying the dominance of yellow bile.<-

# ON THE REGIONS OF DIGESTIONS.

## Treatise 7. Sole Chapter.

Digestion <note>original: *Digestiva*; refers here to the digestive power or the process of "cooking" the humors</note> occurs in a healthy house, whereas indigestion occurs in one that is infirm. In a healthy house, such as house AE <note>In the Lullian system, these letters represent specific combinations of elements; AE typically refers to the Sanguine "house," governed by Heat and Moisture</note>, <margin>5</margin> it occurs through the moist and the hot reigning against house CG <note>CG typically represents the contrary qualities, such as Cold and Moisture (Phlegmatic)</note>. But if house CG enters house AE, C alters A and G [alters] E; and the digestive power of **AE** is made a servant in its own house, and consequently indigestion is brought about by the house of CG, just as the house of DH <note>Representing the Melancholic or Cold/Dry qualities</note> is made hot by the house of BF <note>Representing the Sanguine or Hot/Moist qualities</note>. <margin>10</margin> And so the physician must preserve digestions by preventing one house from entering another house by way of <term>contrariety</term> <note>original: *contrarietatis*; the opposition of elements, such as Heat vs. Cold, which causes disease</note>, but rather by way of <term>concordance</term> <note>original: *concordantiae*; the harmonious agreement of elemental qualities that maintains health</note>.

# ON APPETITE

## Ninth Treatise. Chapter I.

<margin>5</margin>§ I. **Appetite** <note>original: *appetitus*; in this context, it refers to a general "inclination" or "desire" of any faculty to seek what it lacks</note> is a general power having many species under it, much like an appetite extended through the regions of various **houses** <term>houses: in the mnemonic and philosophical system of Ramon Llull, which Bruno adapted, "houses" represent specific logical or astrological compartments used to organize knowledge and physical properties</term>. And because these houses are diverse, they cause different appetites; for instance, the house of **AE** causes one appetite and the house of **BE** another, and so on with the others, because **E** under **A** is in its own region, while **B** under **E** is not. From this it follows that one appetite exists in one house, and another in a different one. Thus, a certain appetite exists through 
<margin>10</margin> **delight**, and the reason for this is that it is in its own house; and another exists by way of **sadness and passion**, as in the house of **BD**, in which **D** grieves because it is in the region of **B**, and it desires to be in the house of **H**, which is its own proper region.

§ II. Of appetites, one is for drink, another for 
<margin>15</margin> food, another for sleep, another for fullness, another for evacuation, and another for rest or <margin>170</margin> a stable state. This is apparent in the conditions of the "houses," as was indicated in the **third house of the fourth circulation** <note>This refers to a specific position in Bruno’s complex Lullian combinatorial wheels, used to map the relationship between elements and physical states</note>, in which the **handmaid**—namely, **moisture**—perpetually desires water, and the 
<margin>20</margin> **lady** <note>original: *domicella*; a young noblewoman or maiden</note>—namely, **dryness**—desires wine, and so it goes for food and other things in their own way; but in the house **BD**, the opposite occurs. Appetite participates with the **sensitive form** <term>sensitive form: the faculty of the soul that processes sensory information</term> and the **imaginative form**, because these powers are joined together; and thus appetite arranges the "species" <note>original: *species*; the mental images or representations of external objects</note> of the sensitive power, and the sensitive power arranges those of the imaginative.

# ON THE HUMORS

## Tenth Treatise. Chapter I.

For the sake of greater clarity regarding the matters discussed above, we must consider the four **complexions** <term>complexiones; the specific balance or "mixture" of the four primary humors in an individual, which determined their physical and mental health</term> in human beings, from which various **appetites** <note>natural inclinations or desires</note> are produced.
<margin>5</margin>

## On the Choleric Humor. Chapter 2.

There is the **choleric** complexion, in which **fire** is the predominant element and consequently **earth** is present as well. Thus, the choleric person, by the nature of fire, is proud and wishes to dominate others, just as fire dominates the other elements. For this reason, the choleric naturally seeks to overcome others and not be overcome. Because dryness follows from this <note>both fire and earth are "dry" qualities in Aristotelian physics</note>, the choleric is also somewhat **melancholic** <note>original: *melancholicus*; here Bruno suggests a overlap between the dry humors</note>; thus he is quickly moved to anger, is very subtle <note>original: *subtilis*; meaning sharp-witted or possessing refined perception</note>, and quickly forgets, owing to the emptying out of the earth element.

<margin>15</margin> <margin>170</margin>
## On the Sanguine Humor. Chapter 3.

The **sanguine** humor consists of **air** and **fire**, which are the more noble elements; consequently, the humor derived from them is more noble. Because air is subtle and expansive—leaving no empty space—and possesses the most excellent form (that is, a fiery form), it has a great and balanced appetite. Therefore, the sanguine man is gluttonous because of this great appetite, and consequently prone to lust <note>original: *fornicator*; used here as a medical observation of the "airy" and "moist" temperament's physical urges</note> due to the lack of the earth element, and he is very cheerful.

---

<header>LULLIAN MEDICINE.</header>

### On the Phlegmatic Humor. Chapter 4.

The **phlegmatic** humor consists of the **coldness** of water, which is highly restrictive <note>original: *restrictiva*; meaning it causes contraction or tightening</note>, as is evident in crystal <note>original: *crystallo*; in medieval science, rock crystal was often thought to be water permanently frozen into stone</note> and ice, and from the **moisture** of air, which is filling <note>original: *repletivus*; refers to the air's ability to occupy space and permeate</note>. Therefore, the **phlegmatic** man is 
<margin>5</margin>greedy, gluttonous, wandering, and lazy; and because women retain much coldness, they are naturally tenacious (or greedy) and idle.

### On the Melancholic Humor. Chapter 5.

The **melancholic** humor consists of the **dryness** of earth—which 
<margin>10</margin>possesses a small amount of **form** <term>form; in Lullian and Aristotelian philosophy, "form" is the active, organizing principle that gives matter its identity. Bruno argues that the "heaviness" of earth limits this vital activity.</term> by reason of its heaviness—and also from the **coldness** of water. Therefore, the melancholic man is very changeable <note>original: *mobilis*; here implying mental instability or being easily swayed by dark thoughts</note>, thinking of the lowest things, of shameful things, and of evil. 
He is quickly moved to anger, by reason of the smallness of his form, and is slow to find pleasure. By reason of his coldness, he is 
<margin>15</margin>greedy and lazy, because he does not participate in heat <note>heat was associated with vitality and action</note>.

<header>GIORDANO BRUNO</header>

# ON THE DEGREES OF ILLNESSES.

## Eleventh Treatise. Chapter 1.

§ I. Before a physician <note>original: *medicus*</note> approaches to treat any patient, he needs not only to know their **temperament** <term>temperament (complexio); in medieval and Renaissance medicine, this refers to the specific balance of the four humors—blood, yellow bile, black bile, and phlegm—that defines an individual's health.</term>
<margin>5</margin> and the cause of the disease—which can be gathered from the preceding sections—but also the **degree of the illness**; for sometimes medicines are given that are contrary to the disposition or temperament of a person in such a high degree of heat or cold, etc., that they lead the person into physical decay <note>original: *corruptionem*; here meaning death or the total breakdown of the body's systems</note>. Therefore, the aforementioned things must be
<margin>10</margin> observed and noted with the greatest diligence.

### On the Knowledge of the Degree of Illnesses. Chapter 2.

<margin>17</margin> <§ I.> To obtain knowledge of the degree of illness or the patient's decline <note>original: *lapsus*; the "fall" or sinking into a diseased state</note>, one must consider what was said
<margin>15</margin> previously concerning the temperament; for we said that in a natural day there are 24 hours divided into four parts, and each part is assigned to that **element** which belongs to its temperament—just as the triangle <note>original: *triangulus*; likely a reference to the triangular diagrams used in Lullian art to show relationships between elements and qualities</note> in its own region from morning until midday, which most belongs to the temperament of **air**;

§ II. And that triangle which is from midday until
<margin>20</margin> night, belongs to the temperament of **fire**;

§ III. And that which is from sunset until midnight, belongs to the temperament of **earth**;

§ IV. And that which is from midnight until the rising of the sun, belongs to the temperament of **water**.

<summary>Giordano Bruno explains that a doctor must accurately measure the "degree" of an illness to avoid prescribing medicines that might fatally clash with a patient's temperament. He begins to categorize these degrees by dividing the 24-hour day into four segments, each corresponding to one of the four classical elements.</summary>

<header>LULLIAN MEDICINE.</header>

### On the degrees of tertian fever. Chapter 3.

The illness therefore governs according to the previously mentioned **triangles** <note>original: *triangulos*; referring to the geometric diagrams used in Lullian art to represent the relationships between the four elements and their qualities</note>. According to how the illness begins or ends in those four regions, the physician <margin>5</margin> can determine the degree of the illness. For example, if a fever begins in the first hour of the day, it is in the first degree of humidity; if in the second hour of the day, it is in the second degree; if in the third hour, it is in the third degree; and if in the fourth hour, it is in the fourth degree. This applies to the **tertian fever** <term>tertian fever: a fever where the paroxysms return every third day; in this system, it is categorized by the qualities of heat and moisture</term>, which is situated between the hot and the humid.

<margin>10</margin> ### On the degrees of other fevers. Chapter 4.

§ 1. And if the fever is of a contrary nature specifically through **cholera** <term>cholera: yellow bile, one of the four bodily humors, traditionally considered hot and dry</term>, it follows the order from midday until sunset, according to the same order we described from morning until midday. If the tertian fever is double <note>original: *duplex*; a condition where two cycles of tertian fever overlap, causing daily symptoms</note>, it follows the aforementioned double order; <margin>15</margin> and if it is a **quotidian** <term>quotidian: a fever that recurs every single day</term>, it follows the aforementioned order in a triple fashion; and thus it continues steadily through the predicted order through the entire circle. The same is true for the **quartan** <term>quartan: a fever that recurs every four days, typically associated with black bile and the "cold and dry" quadrant</term>, according to when it begins in its own region of the circle. If only the physician were able | <margin>177^v</margin> to recognize the degrees of <margin>20</margin> illnesses and harmonize them with the degrees of **electuaries** <term>electuary: a medicinal paste or conserve made by mixing botanical powders with honey or syrup</term>. The ancient physicians did not establish such an order.

### On the second way of investigating the degrees of illnesses. Chapter 5.

§ 1. There is also another way of investigating the aforementioned degrees of illnesses, namely according to the order and manner <margin>25</margin> of **generation and corruption** <note>original: *generationis et corruptionis*; the Aristotelian concept of the natural cycle of things coming into being and passing away</note> of any given thing.

<header>GIORDANO BRUNO</header>

§ 2. On the **choleric** <term>choleric: one of the four temperaments, dominated by "yellow bile" and characterized as being hot and dry</term> man. For the sake of clarity, it must be noted that in a choleric man, **B** <note>In this system, B represents the element of Fire or the quality of Heat</note> exceeds **C** <note>C represents Earth or Dryness</note> by one degree, and exceeds **A** <note>A represents Air or Moisture</note> by two degrees, and exceeds **D** <note>D represents Water or Coldness</note> by three degrees. Therefore, in a choleric man, B is divided into four parts: the first, being the highest, is in the fourth degree; the second is equal in quantity to C; the third part is equal in quantity to A, while the fire heats the subject matter of D in the second degree.

For the first part of B is simple; it is an active force and not a passive one, and it possesses a natural appetite for preserving the **species** <note>original: *speciem*; the essential form or nature</note> of that choleric man. Indeed, at the beginning of generation, the fourth degree of B generated a single, simple **point** <note>Bruno uses geometric progression—point to line to surface to body—to explain how life forms</note>, which indeed descended (so to speak) toward the earth for the purpose of receiving one point from C itself. Therefore, B more readily receives dryness from C than it gives heat to the air, and it does so before it acts against D. For according to natural reason, fire exists more within itself than in another, and the same follows for the other elements. Thus, because fire first desires for itself rather than for another, at the beginning of the generation of the choleric man, fire itself exists in a single simple point.

Afterward, however, it approaches the earth, receiving dryness from it, as has been said; once received, there are two points which form a **line**. After this, it approaches the air, to which it offers heat, and then there is a line with width <note>i.e., a two-dimensional plane</note>. Consequently, a fourth point is generated from D, and then the **body** <margin>17<sup>r</sup></margin> of that choleric man is generated and completed, possessing length, width, and depth.

Since this is the case, the **seventh point** <note>original: *punctus septimus*; a governing center or "soul" point in Lullian geometry that coordinates the other elements</note> is revealed through this, which is a powerful lord and ruler in the fourth degree. It is this point which, through the influence of the **seven planets**, moves the other degrees; it exists in the person so conceived at the beginning for generation, and at the end...

<header>LULLIAN MEDICINE</header>

...moreover, the whole proceeds toward **corruption** <term>corruption: in Aristotelian and Lullian physics, this is the process of decay or the breaking down of a substance into its parts</term>, as is evident through the **red triangle** <note>In Lullian diagrams, the "red triangle" typically represents the relationships between the "hot" qualities: Fire, Air, and the Choleric humor</note>; for in the "angle of the beginning," it appears how, through **rule K** <note>Rule K is a logical rule in the Lullian Art used to distinguish between different categories or to show how one thing acts as a principle for another</note>, **B** <note>B represents Heat or the element Fire</note> is the principle for **C** <note>Dryness or Earth</note> and **A** <note>Moisture or Air</note> themselves, by way of operation—receiving this from C and giving it to A.

Indeed, the principle of **D** <note>Coldness or Water</note> itself, as it exists in the choleric person, is found in **C** and **A**, and this is by way of both operation and sustenance. Through operation, insofar as A is given to D and receives C from D; through sustenance, because C and A themselves assist D against B.

And because B agrees in majority with the choleric temperament (insofar as it is in the fourth degree), it must therefore be the principle for C (which is only in the third degree) and for A (which is in the second). Nevertheless, it is not fitting for it to be the principle for D; for B is the contrary of D. For C and A are the principle for this D; but if D were the principle for C in the choleric person, then a greater thing would have been initiated by a lesser thing within a "greater" <note>the dominant element</note> (which is B), which is contrary to the "lesser" (which is D). But this is impossible, therefore etc.

§ III. On **corruption**. Just as was said concerning **generation** <term>generation: the process of coming-into-being or physical creation</term>, so is corruption signified; for just as in the natural appetite of fire, it first agrees with one "point" <note>Bruno uses "points" as the basic units or building blocks of elemental quality</note> rather than another, so in the process of corruption, it first begins to corrupt the point of that element with which it has the least agreement, and so on by degrees.

**On the other humors.** § IV. And just as this was exemplified in the choleric man, so in its own way can it be exemplified in the other [temperaments]; and all the aforementioned things can be drawn from the **figure of medicine** <note>original: *figura medicinae*; the central diagram of Ramon Llull’s medical system which uses rotating circles to calculate health and disease</note>.

It concludes by noting that the same geometric rules of "points" and "degrees" apply to the decay (corruption) of the body and the other three temperaments.</summary>

# ON THE CARE OF THE SICK.

->Twelfth Treatise. Chapter I.<-

---

§ I. Just as we have indicated the general nature of illnesses and health within the regions of the aforementioned figure <note>This "figure" refers to a Lullian combinatorial wheel used to map the relationships between elements and humors</note>, so the physician
<margin>5</margin>can perform cures generally in three ways: namely, through **similarity**, through **contrariety**, and through **composition**.

§ II. **By similarity.** By similarity, for instance: if the illness is in the "house" <term>house: a specific compartment or combination on the Lullian wheel</term> of AC in the first circulation <note>original: "primae circulationis"; referring to the first or outermost rotating circle of the Lullian diagram</note>, and the patient is of the CG complexion, the physician ought to give
<margin>10</margin>medicines of AE against the region of CG, so that the house of AE may have the suitability <note>original: "convenientiam"</note> of its own region.

§ III. **By contrariety.** If, however, the cure is performed through contrariety, it should be done in this manner: namely, that if the illness is due to excessive abundance—for example, if AE were to have an excessive abundance in the region where they are—the physician must
<margin>15</margin>increase <note>original: "multiplicare"; in this context, it means to strengthen or reinforce a specific quality</note> CG with foods or electuaries <term>electuary: a medicinal paste made by mixing powders with honey or syrup</term> from their region, so that in that region AE cannot have the power to pass over into other contrary houses.

§ IV. **By composition.** The third way, through composition, involves both suitable and contrary things. For example, if it is supposed that
<margin>20</margin>the illness occurs through the house of BE in the first circulation, and this because of an excessive abundance of dryness, the physician should administer [treatment] through AE and through AH against the house of EF, and the house of CH should be increased against house BF.

# ON THE SIXTEEN GENERAL ELECTUARIES.

## Thirteenth Treatise. Chapter I.

<margin>5</margin>§ I. There are four elements, namely ABCD, and four qualities, namely EFGH, as is clear in the figure of medicine <note>The "figure of medicine" refers to a Lullian combinatorial diagram where letters represent elements (Air, Fire, Earth, Water) and qualities (Heat, Moisture, Cold, Dryness)</note>; therefore, sixteen electuaries <term>electuary: a medicinal paste or conserve made by mixing powdered drugs with syrup, honey, or sugar</term> can generally be made in this way.

### Chapter II. On the degrees under the dominion of fire.

Under the dominion of Fire, there are four types of graduation. The first is like pepper <note>original: "piper"</note>, which is hot in the fourth degree | and **179<sup>r</sup>**
<margin>10</margin>dry in the third, moist in the second, and cold in the first.
§ II. In cinnamon <note>original: "cinamomo"</note>, Fire is in the third degree of heat, Earth is in the second degree of dryness, Air is in the first degree of moisture, and Water is ungraduated <term>ungraduated: having no full degree of intensity, being present only in fractional parts</term>, specifically in three parts.
§ III. There is another type, such as fennel <note>original: "faeniculus"</note>, in which Fire is
<margin>15</margin>in the second degree of heat, Earth is in the first degree of dryness, Air is in three small parts <note>original: "minutis"; refers to subdivisions or fractions of a degree</note>, and Water is in two.
§ IV. There is a fourth type, such as anise <note>original: "anisum"</note>, in which Fire is in the first degree of heat, Earth is in three small parts, Air is in two parts of moisture, and Water is in one small part of one
<margin>20</margin>degree.
§ V. Through these four types or plants mentioned above, and through others similar to them, the region of Fire is extended, in which Fire itself is the master; and just as we have spoken regarding region B <note>Region B represents Fire in this system</note>, so you should understand the regions of A, C, and D in their own way.

# ON BONDS IN GENERAL.

<meta>This page serves as an editorial introduction to Giordano Bruno’s treatise "On Bonds in General," establishing the relationship between the manuscript sources in the Moscow codex and previous scholarly transcriptions by Lutoslawski and Sigwart.</meta>

In the treatise *On Bonds in General* <note>original Latin title: "De vinculis in genere"</note>, which in the Moscow codex (designated as *M*; for the specific sigla *M^l*, *M^b*, *M^f* see above, page 508) occupies *folios 87 to 98r*, the editors have incorporated most of those notes written in Bruno's own hand <term>autograph: a manuscript written in the author's own handwriting</term> (designated as *Br*) found on *folios 1 to 5r* (for *folio 5v* see the preface, page XVIII) of the same codex. Compare Lutoslawski in the *Archive for the History of Philosophy* <note>original German: "Archiv für Gesch. d. Philos."</note>, Volume *II* (1889), pages 529 and following, and 553 and following.

We therefore believe it is appropriate to place before the treatise *On Bonds* all of the autograph notes by Bruno that we were able to decipher from the photograph. We have, however, omitted the frequent marginal titles that appear there, such as *Types of Bonds, The Loosening of Bonds, The Binder, The Bindable, etc.* <note>original Latin marginalia: "Vinculi species, Vinculorum relaxatio, Vinciens, Vincibile"</note> Most of *folio 4r* (specifically page 648, lines 15–31 and page 649, lines 11–28) and several other propositions (page 637, lines 1–16; page 640, lines 5–9; page 641, lines 3–10) had already been deciphered by Sigwart and Lutoslawski. See also Noroff in Berti’s *Documents*, etc., page 93 and following, or in Frith’s *Life of Giordano Bruno*, page 346 and following. 

In these specific passages, we have carefully noted the discrepancies between our own reading and those of the aforementioned scholars,^1 so that the reader does not assume the variations in our text are due to errors in transcription or printing. Furthermore, we do not doubt that much more could be corrected in the sections that were read only by us.

---

^1 We provide only the name of Lutoslawski, however, who notes on page 530, note 6: "I am indebted to Professor Sigwart for a transcript of folios 1r, 4r, and 5r, which he prepared from a facsimile and a photograph; this transcript greatly facilitated my reading of the very indistinct handwriting, so that I was able to decipher a large part of the other pages." <note>This note explains the collaborative paleographic effort required to read Bruno's difficult script.</note>

### On the bond of the spirit { natural, animate, divine.

Without these [bonds], one is not a physician, not a diviner, not a practitioner <term>operator: in this context, one who performs "works" of magic or alchemy</term> <margin>5</margin>, not a lover, not a philosopher, and so on. Through these things, all people are all things.

Nothing is absolutely beautiful so as to bind [the observer], but rather it is beautiful in relation to something; otherwise, donkeys would love beautiful women, and monkeys would neglect <note>original: "abolerent"; Bruno uses this to argue that if absolute beauty existed, animals would be attracted to beautiful humans instead of their own kind.</note> their own offspring. Similarly, nothing is absolutely good so as to attract, but since all things <margin>10</margin> or the universe and being itself are composed of contraries, so too is the good composed of contraries; for there are some things that consist of fire, others of water, and so forth.

->If the entrance could be closed to you,<-
->so much more lovely would the kingdom of love be.<-
<note>An Italian verse potentially referring to the "gates" of the senses or the intrusive nature of certain desires.</note>

That which is honorable and just seems to exist by civil law and not by nature; <margin>15</margin> but opinion has great power over our disposition, so that what is desired and binds the appetite seems almost natural, and vice versa.

It happens that the same thing may be bound or not bound depending on its disposition: as in love <term>Venus: the goddess of love, here used to denote sexual desire or the physical act</term> when the vessels are swollen or emptied; in a disturbed or a tranquil mind; likewise, the same food can taste bitter <margin>20</margin> or sweet to the same person, as they are affected in different ways. And I have seen pregnant women crave ashes.
