<meta>This page continues the philosophical investigation into the nature of "bonds" (vincula), shifting from the previous page's discussion on the subjectivity of judgment to a metaphysical hierarchy. The author is now categorizing how beauty acts as a binding force across different levels of existence—from the material world to the divine mind—and how various classical philosophers defined this captivating power.</meta>

<page-num>640</page-num>

It is obscure in the subject of <term>corruptible things</term> <note>Latin: *rebus corruptibilibus*. In Renaissance philosophy, this refers to the physical world where things are born, decay, and die, as opposed to the eternal celestial or divine realms.</note>, less obscure in nature, clear in the soul, and clearest in the mind.

Bonds are found in the harmony of character, the form of the body, the consonance of voices, and all other things that flow from buildings, statues, <margin>5</margin> poems, and speeches. These are: to Plato, "the beautiful"; to Socrates, "an excellent charm of the soul"; to Timaeus, "a tyranny of the soul"; to Plato, "a privilege of nature"; to Theophrastus, "a silent deception"; to Solomon, "a hidden fire" and "stolen waters" <note>A reference to Proverbs 9:17: "Stolen waters are sweet, and bread eaten in secret is pleasant."</note>; to Theocritus, "an ivory detriment"; to Carneades, <margin>10</margin> "an anxious kingdom"; and to others in other ways.

This bond is not the body itself, though it is occupied within the body; for the same body that is beautiful today may, by some accident, be foul tomorrow. Hence, the "beautiful" is one thing, the "body" is another, and the "bond" is yet another.

<margin>2r</margin> This bond serves both to harmonize the parts of the body by a certain incorporeal reason, and also to draw something to the body by that same <margin>15</margin> reason.

This bond is not a physical mass, nor does it consist of mass, although it is concerned with mass; for not only large things, but also small things may appear beautiful. Often large things are ugly and small things are beautiful, and vice versa. Frequently, while the size remains exactly the same, <margin>20</margin> beauty is removed by some accident; likewise, beauty may persist even when the size is changed.

This bond is a certain <term>species</term> <note>Latin: *species*. In this context, it means the "form" or "visible essence" of a thing that is perceived by the mind or soul, rather than its physical matter.</note> of a thing which travels from the object to the soul, yet it does not depart from the underlying object—just as fire, when emitting and communicating its own form, is not diminished; or like an <margin>25</margin> image that exists first in the subject, then in a mirror, then in the medium, and finally in the eyes.

The bond that proceeds from the body has no single, defined physical part; for although we are captivated by sweetness of speech, the eyes, the gait, the jaw, and so on, if these same features were assigned to different subjects, they would not bind us in the same way or to the same degree. <margin>30</margin> For another reason, it has no defined physical part because grace proceeds from every part: hence Plato considers the beauty of the soul to be incorporeal and spiritual, although once the soul is seized, it renders the entire body of the beloved graceful.

<summary>This page defines the "bond" of beauty as a metaphysical force that exists independently of physical matter or size. It compiles classical definitions of beauty—ranging from "stolen waters" to "an ivory detriment"—and explains how beauty acts as an incorporeal "image" that can captivate a lover without the object losing its own essence.</summary>

<keywords>Plato, Socrates, Solomon, beauty, bonds, incorporeal form, species, harmony, grace, metaphysics of love</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the investigation into the nature of the "bond" (vinculum), specifically challenging the classical definition of beauty as mere proportion. Bruni moves from the abstract definitions of the previous page to the psychological and physiological experience of being "bound" by attraction, noting how love can persist or vanish regardless of physical form.</meta>

<page-num>641</page-num>

It seems to be false that the bond arises from a certain proportion of all the limbs together with the sweetness of colors; if that were true, the Platonists say, only composite things would bind us. Yet, as it stands, pure colors, a single voice, the brightness of gold, and the whiteness of silver <note>original: "fulgor auri, argenti candor." The text trailing off suggests "and similar things."</note> [likewise bind us].

<margin>5</margin> Nothing fades and ages more quickly than beauty, and nothing more slowly than shape <note>Latin: *figura*. Bruni distinguishes between the underlying geometry of a body and the ephemeral quality of "beauty."</note>; therefore, beauty and the "bond" are not the same thing as shape. Indeed, even while the same beauty and shape remain, love can pass away, as happens to some after the enjoyment of the thing they loved. The bond, therefore, exists in a certain harmony, not only of the limbs with one another, but

<margin>10</margin> also in a certain "co-disposition" <note>Latin: *condispositione*. A technical term here implying a specific, almost chemical-like matching between the observer and the observed.</note>, so to speak, between the captor and the captured. For sometimes, even if we find nothing in one girl to criticize by reason, and in another girl we find many faults, the former nonetheless displeases us while the latter pleases. Likewise, color by itself does not bind; for a brighter color in an older person is looked down upon, while a softer color in a younger person binds.

<margin>15</margin> It is not pure color, such as entirely white or entirely black, but the mixed; it is not a simple voice, such as the high-pitched or the deep, but the middle; it is not one running note or tone, but several together.

This knot is difficult to find; therefore, it is not easy to untie.

The bond binds the spirit primarily through sight, hearing, and through the
<margin>20</margin> imagination.

There is a certain kind of bond that is pleasing to the one bound, and another that is unpleasing—such as that by which the owl draws the weasel, or the wolf detains [its prey], and so on; just as an <term>incubus</term> <note>A malevolent spirit believed to weigh down or haunt people during sleep.</note> occupies the rational spirit, a demon occupies the <term>energumen</term> <note>A person believed to be possessed by a demon.</note>, the cock [scares] the lion, or the mullet stops the ship <note>Latin: *mugil navim*. This refers to a common classical myth that a small fish (the remora or "stay-ship") could physically halt a massive vessel by clinging to it.</note>.

<margin>25</margin> The bond does not seize the soul unless it ties and binds it; it does not bind the soul unless it reaches it; it does not reach the soul unless it is carried by certain means. It reaches through knowledge in a general sense, binds through affection in a general sense, and draws through delight in a general sense. We say "knowledge in a general sense" because sometimes we do not know by which sense we are being seized.

<margin>30</margin> Likewise, I have experienced loving what I have only heard of; even when absent and regarding a physical appearance unknown to me, I was somehow pining away. I say "in a general sense" because through...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of the "bond" (vinculum) that connects a lover to the object of their affection. While the previous page focused on the physical limitations of beauty and proportion, this section shifts to the Platonic theory of how this bond is transmitted through the senses and categorized into different levels of spiritual and physical experience.</meta>

<page-num>642</page-num>

We are all conquered through several senses and through each individual sense, and sometimes by a sense that is indeterminate and not well-known.

Plato posits three vehicles for the bond: sight, hearing, and the mind. For grace conquers through the voice, form through sight, and character through the mind.

<margin>5</margin> Many things are bound by affection through these three vehicles, which consequently desire to be bound in action, through touch in general; hence, the visible thing does not conquer the eye, but conquers *through* the eye; the audible thing conquers through the ear; and reason conquers through the mind.

<margin>10</margin> There are four movements in the process of binding: first, "injection" or induction; second, the binding or the bond itself; third, attraction; and fourth, the coupling which is called <term>fruitio</term> <note>original: "fruitio." In Renaissance philosophy, this refers to the ultimate enjoyment or possession of a beloved object for its own sake.</note>. Unless this happens through all the senses by which the bond was conveyed, it will not be perfect. Therefore, the lover would wish to migrate entirely into the beloved—with tongue, mouth, eyes, etc.

<margin>15</margin> There is a triple love and a triple <term>raptus</term> <note>original: "raptus." This refers to a state of being "seized" or "carried away" by divine or overwhelming inspiration, a key concept in Platonic thought.</note> for the Platonists. For it carries one away toward either the contemplative, the active (or moral), or the voluptuous life. The first is raised from the sight of bodily form to the consideration of the spiritual and divine; the second perseveres in the mere delight of seeing and conversing; the third descends from sight to the lust for touch.

<margin>20</margin> Through the first, the ingenious are moved; through the last, the dull; and through the middle, those of average disposition. The first bond is called divine love, the second human love, and the third <term>beastly love</term> <note>original: "amor ferinus." This represents the lowest form of desire, driven by purely animal instincts rather than reason or spirit.</note>. They entice in three ways: intellectually, animally, and corporally. The first is the "splendor of the good."

The bond is not equal in every conqueror, nor is it the same in every person who is conquered.

Because this bond turns sight, hearing, and the mind toward the highest good, it is like a certain "circle of divine light" emanating from the good, residing in the good, spreading itself through the good, and eternally flowing back to the good. It is like the one principle of all things, or rather, the unifier of all principles.

Hence, first the mind is decorated by the order of ideas; second, the soul <note>original: "animus."</note> by a series of reasons and numerous discourses; third, natures...

<summary>This page outlines the Platonic hierarchy of love (divine, human, and beastly) and describes the sensory process by which a person is "bound" to beauty. It concludes by describing love as a divine circle of light that originates in and returns to the "Good."</summary>
<keywords>Plato, divine love, human love, beastly love, senses, fruitio, raptus, circle of light, Neoplatonism, beauty</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the technical breakdown of the "bond" (vinculum), specifically moving from the general movements of affection discussed on page 642 to the specific aesthetic requirements—order, measure, and appearance—needed for a body or voice to successfully "bind" a lover. It also introduces the paradoxical idea that God and the Universe are not "beautiful" in a human sense because they lack the composite parts required for aesthetic proportion.</meta>

<page-num>643</page-num>

...to the seeds, fourthly matter with forms. Giving life to all things, softening, soothing, arousing. | It orders, procreates, rules, and completes all things. It opens, purges, illuminates, and makes all things pleasing. It moves, inflames, and entices all things.
<margin>5</margin> Nothing is conquered unless it is most suitably prepared, because that splendor <note>original: "fulgor." This refers to the divine light or radiance that emanates from the source of beauty.</note> is not communicated to all things in the same way.
The preparation of bodies for binding consists of three things: order, measure, and appearance; 1. order signifies the spacing of the parts, 2. measure signifies quantity, 3. appearance signifies figure, outlines, and colors. Just as in the bond of the voice:
<margin>10</margin> 1. order consists in the ascent from the low to the high pitch and the descent; | 2. measure consists in the progression of appropriate thirds, fourths, fifths, sixths, tones, and semitones; | 3. appearance consists in being melodious, clear, and sweet. In all things, those proportional to these three dispose them for binding, whether in composite or simple things; for through these, color pleases, etc. | Thus the soul is adapted by disciplines,
<margin>15</margin> so that through them the image of the divine countenance may shine within it.
God, an angel, and the soul do not bind us as bodily things do, because they do not affect us, because they do not strike the senses by themselves; or rather [they bind] by another kind of bond, which [is grasped] by the metaphorical hand of affection and intellect <unclear>........</unclear>.
<margin>20</margin> Therefore, the preparation for binding is twofold, and it renders the bond equivocal in meaning.
Thus we desire through all senses, and through all senses we are conquered.
We are conquered not by simple and absolute things, but by composite and well-arranged ones. For the bond is a grace arising from <term>concinnity</term> <note>original: "concinnitate." A technical term in Renaissance aesthetics meaning the harmonious arrangement of different parts into a unified whole.</note>
<margin>25</margin> of many things, the opposite of which is the unpleasing or the base. | God does not have beauty in Himself, because He does not have an ordered composition; He does not have this because He does not have parts. He is, however, the source, author, and actor of beauty and the bond. | The gods, likewise, are not beautiful. The universe is not beautiful, as it might seem; | for it consists in a certain simple reason with its

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;Just as it is necessary for the one who seeks to bind <note>original: *vincire*; in Bruno’s magic and psychology, this refers to capturing the attention, will, or soul of another</note> to possess a somewhat universal understanding of things, so that he may be able to capture
<margin>5</margin> man (who is a kind of summary <note>original: *epilogus*; Bruno views man as a "microcosm" or a condensed version of the entire universe</note> of all things). Thus, some of them are related to fish, others to birds, to snakes, and others to reptiles, both according to their genus and their
<margin>10</margin> specific types. Just as is told in the myths of Proteus and Achelous <note>Both are Greek mythological figures famous for their ability to change shapes at will to avoid being caught</note>, the same underlying matter migrates into various forms and figures, so that for the purpose of binding, one must continually employ different and
<margin>15</margin> diverse types of knots. To this end, one must consider the character of men—now of the young, now of the old, now of those in their middle years, the noble, the wealthy, the powerful, the fortunate; to these, add the character of the envious, the ambitious, the mili- <note>The word is cut off and likely completes as *militum*, meaning "of soldiers" or "military men"</note>

<meta>This page transitions from the general justification of why one must study "bonds" (the psychological and magical links between things) to the specific characteristics of the "Binder"—the active agent or force that establishes these connections. ### ON THE BINDER IN GENERAL.

->Article I. The kinds of binders.<-

Binders <note>original: *Vincientia*; those entities or forces that perform the act of "binding" or capturing the interest and will of another</note> throughout the universe are God, the Demon <note>original: *Daemon*; in Bruno’s Neoplatonic context, this refers to intermediary spirits or supernatural intelligences, not necessarily "evil" beings</note>, the Soul, the Animal, Nature, Chance and Fortune, and finally Fate. This
<margin>5</margin> universal binder, which cannot be designated by a single name, does not bind by way of the appearance or the physical sense of the body; for the body by itself does not strike the senses, but does so through a certain power existing within the body and proceeding from it. Therefore, the "binding hand" is a name used metaphorically, which is turned and inclined toward the act of binding by a
<margin>10</margin> manifold preparation.

->The effects of the binder. Article II.<-

This binder is the one who, in the act of binding, the Platonists <note>referring to followers of Plato and later Neoplatonists who believed in a hierarchy of being and the power of "Ideas"</note> say decorates the mind with the order of Ideas; fills the soul with a series of reasons and numerous discourses; fertilizes nature with various seeds;
<margin>15</margin> informs matter with innumerable conditions; gives life to all things, soothes them, caresses them, and excites them; orders, procreates, rules, attracts, and inflames all things; moves, opens, illuminates, purges, pleases, and completes all things.

->How it binds by art. Article III.<-

<margin>20</margin> An artisan <term>artisan: *artifex*; anyone who creates or manipulates things through skill, whether a craftsman, a magician, or God</term> binds by art, since art is the beauty of the artisan. Surely someone will gaze upon the beauty of things artificial and natural as if astonished and dazed, if they do not at the same time contemplate the genius <note>original: *ingenium*; the creative power or innate talent</note> by which all things have been made.

<summary>Bruno identifies the various forces—from God to Fate—that act as "binders" in the universe, explaining that they influence others not through physical contact but through an internal power. He describes the binder's role in the Neoplatonic sense as the force that organizes the mind, nature, and matter through beauty and art.</summary>

<keywords>The Binder, hierarchy of being, Neoplatonism, Art and Beauty, universal forces, Giordano Bruno, psychological influence</keywords>

### That it binds man by many things. Article IV.

<margin>5</margin> Among those things that bind, far more surely bind humans than beasts; likewise, more things bind those of a lively intellect than those who are more dull. This is because those of higher intellect abound in more faculties and powers; they take more parts, circumstances, and goals into account, and are consequently driven by more desires <note>original: *appetitibus*; refers to the natural inclinations or "appetites" of the soul toward an object</note>.

<margin>10</margin> ### How the sense is a pander for the binder. Article V.

Lust <note>original: *libido*; in this context, any intense drive or attraction</note>, rare and excited only by natural impulse, conquers a dull man; his food is limited to a few coarse types. Eloquence does not soothe him, charms <note>original: *veneres*; literally "Venuses," referring to aesthetic or sexual attractions</note> do not entice him, nor does music, nor painting, nor the other allurements <note>original: *lenocinia*; refinements or "panderings" that seduce the senses</note> of nature.

<margin>15</margin> ### Why one is not satisfied by a single bond. Article VI.

I am therefore bound by many things, and I feel many binding agents, because the degrees of beauty are diverse and distinct. Hence, one thing burns and binds me for one reason, and another thing for another. But if every reason <note>original: *ratio*; the underlying logic, proportion, or cause of attraction</note> were gathered into one, perhaps one single thing <margin>20</margin> would please on behalf of all and from all. However, nature has by no means allowed this so far; instead, she has scattered the various bonds of beauty, joy, goodness, and the passions contrary or different to these, producing them distinctly and separately according to the manifold parts of matter. It happens, indeed, that someone is occasionally <margin>24</margin> held by only one object, either because of the senses...

<summary>Bruno argues that humans, especially those with high intelligence, are susceptible to a vast array of "bonds" or attractions because their minds can perceive many different forms of beauty and purpose. He explains that since beauty and goodness are fragmented throughout the material world, we are naturally drawn to many different objects rather than a single perfect one.</summary>

...stupidness, which is blind and sluggish toward the remaining orders <note>The "orders" refer to the different categories of bonds or attractions Bruno has been categorizing</note>, either because of the intensity of a single bond which so uniquely afflicts and torments the person that their perception of all other things becomes numbed, overwhelmed, or suppressed. By their contempt for the ignoble things of this life, which are but temporary, they testified that they had achieved a life similar to the Gods even within this mortal body. Thus, they believed they had attained, and demonstrated to others, the highest good and exceptional virtue.

### Who is most easily bound. Art. VIII.

<margin>10</margin> The person who is most truly "human" is bound most powerfully by the appearance of the most worthy things; such a person finds far more pleasure in hoping for the most noble things than in possessing those that are vile. Indeed, we are easily sickened by the possession of the latter; but whatever we do not easily possess, we die for <note>original: *deperimus*; to be desperately in love with or "dying for" something</note> more ardently.

<margin>15</margin> ### How the same thing binds by opposites. Art. IX.

Confused and in some way even contrary things seem to be the binding agents, even when they come from the same category of binder, particularly when the contrary effects and passions of the bonds are observed. For whoever (for example) has been invaded by the bonds of Cupid <note>The Roman god of desire; Bruno uses him as a symbol for the psychological force of attraction</note> <margin>20</margin> will be seen—by the sensation of one and the same fire and snare—to be driven to cry out and to be silent, to joy and sadness, to hope and despair, to fear and audacity, to anger and gentleness, to weeping and laughter; from which comes that poem:

> I who carry the high banner of Love <note>original Italian: *Io che porto d'amor l' alto vessillo*</note>

-> A binder does not bind diverse things with a single bond. Art. X. <-

<margin>5</margin> Nothing is absolutely beautiful so as to bind purely as a source of joy, nothing is absolutely good so as to entice purely as something useful, and nothing is absolutely great if it is finite. That which is absolutely beautiful and good and great and <margin>20</margin> true binds the affection, the intellect, and the whole being absolutely. Therefore, we strive to abound in many arts, for there is no thing that finds it loathsome to exist in a universal and simple state, <margin>25</margin> but rather to be "this" and "of this sort," or "that" and "of that sort." <meta>This page continues from page 659, where Bruno discussed the relativity of beauty and how different things appeal to different species. He now explores how beauty is not a single, absolute entity but is distributed across individuals and species, requiring a specific "fit" between the binder and the bound.</meta>

<page-num>660</page-num>
<header>GIORDANO BRUNO</header>

...a particular and absolute beautiful, good, or true thing, etc., does not exist; there is nothing—not only beyond any genus <note>A general category or class</note>, but not even within a specific genus or species—that can bind simply and through the same degrees. Nonetheless, the appetite <note>The innate drive or desire</note> for the beautiful, the good, and so on, is present in all things; for all things desire to be absolute and beautiful in every part, at least according to the condition of their own species and genus. For beauty and goodness are of one kind for one species, and another for another; in one species, one of the opposites dominates, while in another, the other prevails. Furthermore, the total beauty <margin>88^v</margin> and goodness of a single species must be sought only in the species as a whole, throughout all eternity, and across all individuals taken one by one. Zeuxis <note>A famous Greek painter from the 5th century BCE</note> testified to this regarding human beauty when he painted his portrait of Helen from several different maidens of Croton <note>A city in Southern Italy famous for the beauty of its inhabitants; the legend says Zeuxis selected the best features of five different girls to create a "perfect" image</note>. Indeed, even if there were a girl who was beautiful in every part or in her entirety, how could it be that she could provide beauty in every possible manner? For there are countless variations of physical beauty within the female species, of which only one kind can be found in any single individual. For beauty—whether it consists in a certain symmetry or in something else that is perceived as incorporeal <note>Meaning spiritual or non-physical</note> within a physical nature—is manifold and arises from countless arrangements. Therefore, just as the roughness of one stone does not fit, match, or cohere with the roughness of every other stone, but only where the curves and hollows correspond, in the same way, not every form <term>species|In Bruno's thought, the "species" is the mental image or form that enters the mind to trigger attraction or "binding"</term> will settle comfortably in every soul. Thus, different individuals are bound by different objects; and even if the thing that binds Socrates and Plato were the same, it would nevertheless bind this one differently...

->Various instruments of the binder. Art. XIII.<-

<margin>5</margin>Nature has dispersed, distinguished, and in a way sown abroad the objects of beauty, goodness, truth, and dignity; therefore, many things can bind many people for many reasons and for different ends. A good farmer <note>original: "agricola"</note> binds and becomes lovable for one reason, a cook for another, a soldier for another, a musician for another, a painter, a philosopher, <margin>10</margin>a boy, or a girl—this one because she walks well, that one because she speaks better. Among these, there is no one who alone possesses everything and in every way; but whoever is found skillful and successful in many things according to types <note>original: "species"</note> and modes, he will bind more people, rule over more, and through the many will triumph over all within his kind.

<margin>15</margin>->Favorable conditions for the binder. Art. XIV.<-

Just as there are different times, different occasions, and different feelings that arise, and not by one and the same measure; so also there is nothing single and simple, or of the same quantity and quality, that can please everyone equally, <margin>20</margin>nay, not even individuals, or one person at different times—just as the same food or the same measure and quality of food is not always pleasing. The same judgment applies to everything by which the appetite <term>Appetitus: The natural drive or desire toward an object, common to all living things in Bruno's philosophy</term> is bound.

->Differences between things that bind. Art. XV.<-

<margin>25</margin>And there are those things that bind by themselves, and those that bind through something belonging to them, which is either a part or a certain quantity,

and there are things that bind by the logic of another thing—which they assist, serve, or for which they prepare—just as a beautiful building arises from unformed parts.

->The various capacity of the binder. Art. XVI.<-

<margin>5</margin> There are many things which, while they are beautiful, bind us as "goods" <note>original: "bona"; here meaning useful or beneficial objects</note> nonetheless—such as a horse, a ship, a house, a statue, a dog, or a bird. However, a beautiful human is not bound <note>The "bond" here refers to the psychological or spiritual attachment formed between the observer and the object.</note> so as to be considered good, nor is a good human bound so as to be judged beautiful; for it happens by a certain accident <margin>10</margin> that crime and error may coexist with beauty. Indeed, consider a beautiful but poor woman: she is more easily troubled and more readily enticed by gifts. The logic of diverse things is diverse, of opposites it is opposite, and of likes it is similar.

->The seat of the binder. Art. XVII.<-

Some who make few distinctions, such as the Platonists, think <margin>15</margin> that what binds is the appearance <term>species: In Renaissance philosophy, this refers to the "sensible form" or image of an object that travels from the thing to the observer's mind.</term> of the thing, which proceeds from the object | to the soul, <margin>89</margin> yet does not depart from the underlying object—much like fire, which communicates its nature without being diminished, or like an image which exists first in the object, then in a mirror, in the intervening space, and in the eyes. Yet, considering more deeply, <margin>20</margin> we find that the consistency of the bond is indeed in the body and in something sensible; but, like the soul—whose condition the power of the soul follows—it has no defined part in the body. For even if the wound of love <note>original: "vulnus amoris"</note> comes from the eyes, the mouth, or the complexion, it will not seem to be found in them simply, nor to arise from them alone; <margin>25</margin> for the eyes, when viewed by themselves and separately, do not have the same power as they do when compared and combined with the rest of the facial features. A similar judgment applies to the mouth and the nose.

<margin>5</margin> a similar thing can be said of color, such as that which would not please even in a painter's box. Therefore, the logic of beauty is altogether indefinite and uncircumscribable, and similarly the logic of the pleasant and the good. Consequently, the logic of a bond is not to be perceived entirely in the subject matter <note>original: "re subiecta"; here referring to the object or person that exerts the attraction</note>, but also, according to another no less principal part, <margin>10</margin> in that which is being bound; for though the quality and substance of food have not changed at all, it is now rejected after a meal, though a moment ago it was greedily consumed. The bonds of Cupid <note>Bruno uses Cupid to represent erotic desire or the psychological drive toward an object</note>, which were intense before union, are released by a modest discharge of seed <note>original: "modico seminis iactu"; referring to the physiological release of tension</note> <margin>15</margin> and the fires are tempered, even though the beautiful object remains exactly the same. Thus, the entire logic of the bond is not to be attributed to the object alone.

### Preparations of the binder. Art. XVIII.

The binder is said to be prepared for binding by three things: order, mode, and species. Order of the parts provides the intervals, mode defines <margin>20</margin> the quantity, and species <term>species: In Renaissance philosophy, this refers to the visual "form" or "appearance" that projects from an object to the eye.</term> is signified by figures, outlines, and colors. Just as in the bond of the voice, order consists in the ascent and descent through deep, sharp, and middle tones; mode consists in the proper progression of thirds, fourths, fifths, sixths, etc., tones and semitones; <margin>25</margin> species consists in resonance, sweetness, and clarity. These three things are proportional in all matters, whether composite or simple, where there is a preparation for binding.

### Diversity of preparations. Art. XIX.

Regarding bonds, there is one kind of preparation derived from signs and traces that indicate only the harmony of the soul, and through this, the soul is moved to pursue only a living enjoyment <note>original: "animalem... fruitionem"; enjoyment pertaining to the "anima" or the vital, sensory experience of a living being</note>, so that it might cling to it and be united with it; but grace, having its preparation in the body and things of this sort, namely—

<summary>Bruno argues that the "bond" of attraction depends as much on the internal state of the observer as on the object itself, using hunger and sexual desire as examples. He identifies three components of attraction: Order, Mode, and Species (form).</summary>

...by the disposition of the limbs, or that which arises from the garments that surround the body, binds the soul to the pursuit of physical enjoyment. Where, however, the preparation exists in both [the soul and the body], it will drive more vehemently toward both types of enjoyment, or it will draw from both principles. Furthermore, there are those who are so bound by the soul of another that they even desire the body itself, which is its vessel. Likewise, a few apply themselves more to the soul, such that they look down upon any physical appearance <term>species: here, the visual form or outward appearance</term> lacking the preparation of the soul; as is told of Socrates, who used to command a handsome youth to speak first, before he would decide upon his love toward him. <note>This refers to the famous anecdote where Socrates says, "Speak, that I may see you," suggesting that the beauty of the soul is revealed through speech.</note>

->The condition of the binder. Art. XX.<-

Flatterers magnify modest virtues, diminish vices, excuse faults, and attribute crimes to virtues; they act so cautiously that they do not reveal their own art of flattery. Thus, they bind to themselves those who are not particularly astute, because it pleases and delights everyone to be loved and honored above all, and also because the ability to bind anyone is a sign of a certain predominant power <note>original: "virtutis"; here meaning capacity, effectiveness, or potency rather than moral virtue</note>.

->How the binder is bound. Art. XXI.<-

There is a certain joy and glory for the binder, and it is greatest and more vehement in proportion to how noble, praiseworthy, and excellent the thing being bound is. In that joy and in that glory is situated the force of the bond <note>original: "vinculi vis"</note>, by which the binder himself is bound in turn by the one who is bound. Victors, by praising those they have conquered, extol their own victory, and sometimes they deceive not only others but even themselves...

He also explains how flattery functions as a psychological bond and notes that the act of "binding" another person creates a reciprocal bond that affects the binder.</summary>

<page-num>665</page-num>
<header>OF BONDS IN GENERAL.</header>

...both in desire and in other social <note>original: "civilibus"; referring here to the interactions between people in a community</note> effects of bonds. A mind must be exceedingly base if it does not respond with a grateful heart to a lover who is distinguished and praises it, or who is otherwise bound to it from the soul.

<margin>5</margin> ### Distinction of the Binder. Art. XXII.

There is a type of binder through which we wish to become worthy, beautiful, and good, and there is a type through which we desire to possess what is good, beautiful, and worthy. The first kind of binding arises from an object we lack; the second from that which we possess in greater measure <note>Bruno suggests we are either drawn to things to complete ourselves or to things that reflect our own abundance</note>. From <margin>10</margin> these, it is not only the "good" itself that binds, but also the *opinion* of the good; yet a bond is always present everywhere with a certain proportion and suitability. Furthermore, imagination <term>phantasia: the faculty of forming mental images</term> and opinion bind more people than reason does; indeed, the former bind more intensely than the latter. For many people, because they love without reason—though not without a <margin>15</margin> driving cause—are indeed bound, yet they are ignorant of that by which they are bound.

### The Blindness of the Binder. Art. XXIII.

The logic of bonds is also, for the most part, hidden even from the wise. For what does it profit to cite the logic of analogy, similarity, kinship <term>congeneitatis: the state of being of the same kind or nature</term>, and such meaningless words <margin>20</margin> when we see that a human being hates nothing more than another human being—even a companion and one most similar—and yet sometimes loves nothing more, and this for an unknown reason? For any general reason offered is no reason at all, just as there is a certain dissolution <term>solutio: here meaning the breaking or loosening of a bond</term> and indifference <note>original: "apathia"</note> between those <margin>25</margin> of the same genus and species, such as between woman and woman, or man and woman; to which you may add the conditions of a man, an old man, or a boy.

What can you say about the love of those who love only what they have heard of, which is commonly described by the name of "devotion"? Is it not true that man is bound most powerfully to celestial and immaterial things—indeed, even to imaginary things and things never actually found? <margin>5</margin> Cease to categorize the power of these bonds by their external appearances, especially that power which works through incantation <term>incantationem: the use of spoken words, charms, or ritual songs to influence the mind or spirit</term>. Nor is there any reason for someone to claim that the force of a bond comes from the "good" itself more than the *opinion* of the good is able to bind; indeed, it comes from a hidden cause more than an obvious one. And as we have said <margin>10</margin> above, there are diverse differences and types of "goods" <note>Bruno argues that it is not what is objectively good that attracts us, but what we *perceive* to be good, even if it is invisible or imaginary</note>.

### The Skill of the Binder. Art. XXIV.

Just as we who are ignorant are bound more by a cautious flatterer than by a true friend, so the bonds and the effectiveness of the binder are skillfully formed and strengthened <margin>15</margin> if he forbids the fearful man from military service, or encourages the madly impious man to worship the gods, or the cruel man to serve his own interests. He blows upon the spark in the direction toward which things are already leaning—just as someone who wants to move a cylinder does not try to grab it by its flat ends or its corners, but turns it <margin>20</margin> by its round surface <note>This is a metaphor for psychological manipulation: a "binder" succeeds by working with a person's existing nature rather than trying to force them against it</note>.

### The Weapons of the Binder. Art. XXV.

The weapons of the binder are threefold. First are those within the binder himself, and these are of two types: essential or natural—namely, those which come from the nature of his species; and accidental or added—namely, those which follow the nature of the species, such as sagacity, <margin>25</margin> wisdom, and art <note>original: "ars"; referring to technical skill or "craft"</note>. Certain <margin>90</margin> factors are around him, such as lot, fortune, and chance, which create the meeting and the initial encounter; and certain things are above him, such as fate, nature, and the favor of the gods.

### The Binder’s Timing. Art. XXVI.

There is a sense of proportion in every act of <term>binding</term> <note>original: "vinciendi"; the act of exercising influence or psychological control over another</note>, which we continually experience in food and sex. For we are drawn and "bound" by a desire and love for these things, but not always for the same things, nor in the same way, nor in the same measure, nor with the same fluctuations of time. For a person's <term>complexion</term> <note>the specific physical and psychological temperament of an individual, often determined by the balance of their "humors"</note> flows and changes rapidly with time, as do all things that result from that temperament. Therefore, with foresight and deliberate planning, one must recognize the right time for binding in advance; the present opportunity must be seized by the one present with the utmost speed, so that the one capable of binding may bind and tighten the bond as soon as possible.

### The Binder's Perception. Art. XXVII.

Just as the bonds themselves are subtle, that which is bound is almost imperceptible and deep; it is not something that can be easily examined from the surface. Furthermore, it is transformable from moment to moment, behaving toward the binder no differently than <term>Thetis</term> did when avoiding the embraces of <term>Peleus</term> <note>In Greek mythology, the sea-nymph Thetis changed into various shapes—fire, water, and wild beasts—to escape Peleus; he could only "bind" her by holding on tight through every transformation</note>. The binder must respect the order of change and the power of the form that follows after the one currently present. For although matter is indefinite and open to innumerable forms, it is not equally distant from all of them at once. Instead, from the current state, there is only one form that is most likely to follow next; another might follow only after several intermediate steps, and some remain very distant indeed.

<margin>5</margin> ### The Binder’s Enticements. Art. XXVIII.

A binder does not secure a "bindable" subject easily, just as a general does not easily capture a heavily fortified citadel, unless an entrance is made through some domestic traitor, or by some other agreement of a consenting or yielding party, or through some manageable servant.
<margin>10</margin> In this specific way, <term>Venus</term> <note>referring here to erotic love or physical attraction</note> does not conquer nor easily storm the citadel where the vessels are empty, the spirit is disturbed, and there is burning anxiety; rather, the citadel is betrayed by swelling vessels <note>likely referring to the humors or physiological readiness</note>, a tranquil soul, a quiet mind, and a body at leisure. Once the turns of these guards and watchmen have been observed, one must suddenly dare, rush in with force, act with all one's strength, and
<margin>15</margin> never cease. The same must be observed in all other acts of binding.

### The Binder’s Ladder. Art. XXIX.

The binder does not unite a soul to himself unless it has been seized; he does not seize it unless it is bound; he does not bind it unless he has coupled himself to it;
<margin>20</margin> he is not coupled unless he has reached it; he does not reach it except through motion; he does not move except through an approach; he does not approach it except after he has inclined or turned toward it; he does not incline toward it unless he has desired and yearned for it; he does not yearn for it unless he has known it;
<margin>25</margin> and he has not known it unless the object has been present to his eyes and ears, or to the gaze of his internal senses, by way of its appearance or <term>image</term> <note>original: "simulachro"; a mental representation or likeness of the thing perceived</note>. Therefore, he causes the bonds to reach their target through knowledge in general, and he knits the bonds through <term>affection</term> <note>original: "affectum"; the emotional state or disposition of being moved toward something</note> in general: knowledge...

### The gates through which the binder attacks. Art. XXX.

<margin>5</margin> There are three gates through which the <term>hunter of souls</term> <note>original: "animarum venator"; Bruno's term for the practitioner who seeks to influence or control the minds of others</note> dares to bind: sight, hearing, and the mind or imagination. If it happens that he enters through all these gates, he binds most powerfully and ties most tightly. Through the gate of hearing, he enters armed with the voice and with speech—the "child of the voice"; <margin>10</margin> through the gate of sight, he enters armed with beauty, gesture, movement, and a fitting appearance; through the gate of the imagination, mind, and reason, he enters through character and the arts. From there, once the entry is first made, second comes the coupling, third the binding, and fourth the attraction. Through all the senses, the bound person meets the binder, until the <margin>15</margin> obligation is made so perfect that the former migrates into the latter, or desires to migrate, where the bond of desire is concerned. For there are also unpleasant bonds proportional to these, which we shall discuss in our writings on natural bonds—such as the way a toad draws a weasel by some hidden power of the spirit, or how the rooster's voice <margin>20</margin> breaks the lion, or how the suckerfish <note>original: "mugil"; while usually meaning a mullet, in this context Bruno refers to the "remora," a small fish legendary for its ability to stop large ships by attaching to them</note> stops a ship by touch, or how a <term>possessed person</term> <note>original: "energumenus"; one who is under the influence of an external spirit</note> drinks in a demon through the imagination, and how a melancholic or "windy" humor acts like a magnet toward a <term>nightmare</term> <note>original: "incubum"; here referring to a distressing spirit or a heavy, oppressive sensation during sleep</note>.

Therefore, this field of the binder contains thirty intentions, namely from:

# ON THINGS SUBJECT TO BINDING IN GENERAL.

->The species of the bindable. Article I.<-

Concerning God, or universal nature, or the universal good, or absolute beauty, which is the center of the great 
<margin>5</margin>world, there are four convertible things. These are such that they cannot withdraw from Him—unless they wish to be reduced to nothingness—nor can they leave Him any more than a circumference can leave its own center. These four (I say) are movable in a circle around their own 
<margin>10</margin>binder, so that they remain perpetually in the same order. According to the Platonists <note>Followers of Plato and the later Neo-Platonic tradition, such as Plotinus, who viewed the universe as a series of descending levels of reality.</note>, these are Mind, Soul, Nature, and Matter. Mind <note>original: "mens"</note> is stable by itself; Soul <note>original: "anima"</note> is mobile by itself; Nature is partly stable and partly mobile; and Matter is entirely mobile and entirely stable <note>Bruno suggests a paradox here: matter is constantly changing form (mobile) but remains the underlying substance of everything (stable).</note>.

->The condition of the bindable. Article II.<-

Nothing is bound unless it is most aptly prepared, because that 
<margin>15</margin>splendor is not communicated to all things in the same way.

->The form of the bindable. Article III.<-

All things that are bound sense it in some way. In the substance of this sense, one can observe a certain kind of knowledge and a certain kind of appetite <note>original: "appetitus"; in this context, it refers to a natural striving, desire, or gravitational pull toward an object.</note>; in no other way does a magnet <note>original: "magnes"</note> 
<margin>20</margin>attract and hinder according to its kind. Therefore, one who wishes to bind must in some way instill a sensation into that which is bindable; for indeed, the bond follows the sensation of the thing just as a shadow follows a body.

->A comparison of the bindable. Article IV.<-

Consider how men are bound more than beasts, and 
<margin>25</margin>how beastly and stupid men are bound least of all to heroic bonds <note>original: "heroica vincula"; refers to the "heroic" or noble passions that drive a person toward divine knowledge or great achievements, as opposed to base, physical desires.</note>.

---

...are [more] fit than those who have obtained a clearer soul. As for natural bonds, the common people are more subject to them than the philosopher; hence it is a proverb that "the wise man rules the stars." <note>original: "sapientes astris dominari"; a common Renaissance aphorism suggesting that while the stars/planets influence human impulses, a person of reason can overcome these celestial predispositions.</note> Regarding bonds of the middle 
<margin>5</margin>kind, the generation of gluttons boasts of restraint, while the generation of the lustful boasts of sobriety. <note>Bruno likely refers to how people focused on one vice often perform the virtue of another to mask their true nature, or how one strong passion can suppress others.</note>

### Distinction of things subject to binding. Article V.

From what was just said, one may consider how the intensity of one bond makes another kind of bond less 
<margin>10</margin>effective or weaker. For this reason, the German is less stirred by Venus <note>The Roman goddess of love, used here to represent sexual desire or romantic passion.</note>, and the Italian less by excessive drinking; the Spaniard is more prone to love, and the Gaul <note>original: "Gallus"; referring to the French.</note> to anger.

### The seed or fuel of the bindable. Article VI.

Something is bound most effectively when something of its own is within 
<margin>15</margin>the binder, or because the binder commands it through some part of the subject itself. Hence necromancers <term>Necromancers: here used in a broad sense for practitioners of "binding magic" who believe they can influence the living or the dead through physical relics.</term> (to demonstrate by one class of example) through the nails and hair of the living—indeed, even through pieces of clothing and footprints—trust that they can exercise command 
<margin>20</margin>over the entire body. Likewise, through bones and any parts of the deceased, they call forth the shades. For this reason, it was not without thought that the ancients took the greatest care with burials, preferred funeral pyres, and counted leaving a body unburied among the harshest punishments. Orators, too, capture goodwill <note>original: "benevolentiam captant"; a technical term in rhetoric (captatio benevolentiae) for the effort to win the favor of an audience at the start of a speech.</note> through their art, specifically so that the listeners and the judge might have something of themselves within the speaker.

### The time of the bindable. Article VII.

<margin>25</margin>According to the variety of age and time, the same thing becomes bindable in different ways, and various things serve as bonds for one and the same...

...[materials] are not arranged in a single way, nor are they composed of the same elements in equal measure. <note>The text begins mid-sentence, likely completing a thought about how the physical and spiritual makeup of a person dictates their character.</note> Observe from this that one who is younger and more flexible grows into a man who is more constant and prudent; an old man becomes more suspicious and morose; and one who is decrepit feels only contempt and disgust.

<margin>5</margin>
### Differentiation of things that can be bound. Article VIII.

For this reason, one who wishes to "bind" <note>In Bruno’s philosophy, "binding" (*vincire*) refers to the act of capturing someone's attention, love, or will through psychological, rhetorical, or magical means.</note> must take notice that among those subjects capable of being bound, some are moved more by nature, some more by judgment or <margin>91ᵛ</margin> prudence, and some more by use and habit. Thus, the skillful practitioner should secure and constrain the first group through bonds prepared from natural things; the second group through reasons, demonstrations, signs, and arguments; and the third group through things that are familiar and necessary.
<margin>10</margin>

### Aversion of the thing to be bound. Article IX.

Since the mind is bound more strongly to a single object the more it is distracted and relaxed from others, it is worth the effort for one wishing to fix a subject upon a single thing to render that subject sluggish in other affairs and matters, or even better, to lead them away from the worry of such things. Indeed, a more pleasant activity excludes another pleasant one: a mind intent on the ears <note>Focusing intently on listening.</note> lets the eyes relax; one looking too 
<margin>20</margin> attentively becomes deaf; and when we are vehemently rejoicing or grieving for one particular cause, we do not do much else. We are either idle, or we cease, or we are slowed down in our work; this is what it means to be distracted, drawn away, held, and bound. Hence the rhetorician <term>Rhetorician: a master of persuasive speech who uses emotional appeals to sway an audience.</term>, through laughter, through envy, and through other passions, dissolves the bond of love, or binds the subject to hatred, 
<margin>25</margin> contempt, or indignation.

### The number of those capable of being bound. Article X.

Those who are contemplative are bound to divine things by the sight of sensible forms <note>original: "sensibilium specierum aspectu." Bruno refers to the Neoplatonic idea that physical beauty can lead the mind toward divine truth.</note>; those who are pleasure-seekers descend through the sense of sight to the abundance of touch <note>The Latin "copiam" (abundance) appears here, though other manuscripts suggest "concupiscentiam" (lust/desire).</note>; and those who are ethical <note>In this context, "ethical" refers to the social or civic person who finds fulfillment in human interaction and community.</note> are drawn toward the delight of social interaction.
<margin>5</margin> The first are considered **heroic**, the second **natural**, and the third **rational**. The first are higher, the second lower, and the third are in the middle. The first are said to be worthy of the heavens <note>original: "aethere digni." The ether was considered the substance of the celestial spheres.</note>, the second of biological life, and the third of the senses. The first ascend toward God, the second cling to bodies, and the third move away from one extreme to approach the other.

<margin>10</margin> ### The motion of the bound. Article XI.

In things that are composite and variable, and indeed in all things that undergo a change in their nature and disposition—such as the soul and the spirit <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "spirit" (*spiritus*) was often viewed as a subtle material vapor that connected the immaterial soul to the physical body.</note>, which take on various roles through bodies and the motions of bodies (although both
<margin>15</margin> substances are most constant and eternal in their own simplicity)—desire arises from lack, drive arises from desire, motion arises from drive, and release arises from motion. From this, it follows that no bond is eternal; instead, there are cycles of imprisonment and liberty, of binding and release from a bond—or rather, a migration
<margin>20</margin> from one kind of bond to another. And just as this is natural and precedes, accompanies, and follows the eternal condition of things, so nature "binds" through variety and motion. Art, which imitates nature, multiplies, varies, diversifies, orders, and composes these bonds in a successive series. Furthermore, stasis
<margin>25</margin> is so abhorrent to things that we sometimes even strive more for what is forbidden and are more deeply affected by the desire for it. <note>Bruno is paraphrasing Ovid's *Amores* (3.4.17): "Nitimur in vetitum semper cupimusque negata"—"We always strive for the forbidden and desire what is denied."</note>

<summary>Bruno categorizes people into three spiritual classes (heroic, natural, and rational) based on what attracts them, and explains that all psychological bonds are temporary because the soul inherently seeks variety and motion.</summary>

For it is just as natural to desire to be released from bonds as it was, just a moment ago, for us to be able to be bound to them by a certain voluntary and spontaneous inclination.

->The indefiniteness of the bondable. Article XII.<-

<margin>5</margin> The more elements a bondable subject is composed of, the less it is restricted to specific bonds. Hence, human pleasure is less determined to one single time, individual, or sex than that of beasts; for just as perhaps all horses are equally able to bind a mare <note>original: "vincire." In this context, Bruno uses "binding" to describe the capture of attention, desire, or reproductive instinct.</note>, not all men are frequently <margin>10</margin> able to do so with a woman. This degree of variety and this indefiniteness exists between humans and beasts, just as it exists between a true man and a brutish one, or between a more sensitive person (who is also more deeply affected) and one who is more dull. And what is said regarding one kind of bond should be applied to all kinds and species of bonds.

<margin>15</margin> ->The foundation of bondability. Article XIII.<- <margin>92^r</margin>

The primary reason why anything is capable of being bound is partly because it desires to be preserved in the state of being that is currently present to it, and partly because it seeks to be perfected as much as possible according to that state and within it. This is <term>philautia</term> <note>original: "philautia." From the Greek *philautia*, meaning self-love. In Renaissance philosophy, this was seen as the basic instinct for self-preservation and self-interest.</note> in a general sense. Therefore, if someone were <margin>20</margin> able to extinguish self-love in a subject, they would be rendered extremely powerful in binding or releasing that subject in any way they chose. Likewise, once self-love is ignited, all things are more easily tethered by the various natural bonds that suit them.

->The relationship of the bondable. Article XIV.<-

<margin>25</margin> Observe the friendship and enmity of animals, their sympathy and antipathy, their kinship and diversity, and the cir... <note>The text breaks off mid-word, likely intended to be "circumstantias" or "circumstances."</note>

...circumstances of these things; and let there enter into the mind, within the human species, particulars and individuals one by one—first all the species of other animals, and then the species of all other things, in a certain order and analogy—so that <margin>5</margin> you may grasp how great a variety and suitability of bonds you require.

### The diversity of the matter of those who can be bound. Article XV.

Although every bondable thing is, in a way, a composite, one is called simple, another multiple or compact, <margin>10</margin> another simpler, and another more mixed. For this reason, some are bound purely and others impurely; some bonds are pure, others impure. In the same way, some pleasures and pains are pure, others impure, and others mixed. For instance, Epicurus judges the pleasure of Venus <note>original: "voluptas Veneris." This refers to sexual desire and the physical act of love.</note> to be impure because it is accompanied by pain and an unquenchable desire <margin>15</margin> (through which the whole body strives in vain to pass entirely into the other), and it is followed by a somber exhaustion. However, if there were things in which the principles never fail—as is perhaps the case with the stars and the great animals or spirits of the world <note>original: "magna mundi animalia seu numina." Bruno famously argued that stars and planets were living, sentient beings with their own souls.</note>, in whom weariness does not occur and in whom <margin>20</margin> the outflow and inflow of substance is equal and the same—these would be most happily bound to themselves within themselves.

Therefore, whoever wishes to bind in a civil or social sense <note>original: "civiliter vincire." This refers to "binding" people through rhetoric, politics, or social influence.</note> must examine the diversity of compositions or temperaments. He must deliberate, define, and establish one approach for heroic natures, another for ordinary ones, and another for more brutish minds. <margin>25</margin>

### Degrees of those who can be bound. Article XVI.

Just as with regard to natural impulses, children are less bound, for the reason that nature in them is preoccupied with growth...

Men in their stable age <note>The "consistent" or "stable" age refers to adulthood (prime of life), after the rapid growth of youth has ceased.</note>, as they have a greater power of the **genital seed**, seem therefore more capable of being bound. ->The Temperaments of Those Who Can Be Bound. Article XVII.<-

### Signs of the Bondable. Art. XVIII.

In this consideration, physiognomy <note>The historical practice of judging a person's character or fate from their physical features, especially the face.</note> also plays its part. ### The Duration of the Bondable. Art. XIX.

The elderly are both harder and more unsuited to being bound; the young are more unstable and more apt [to be bound]; but those in their middle years <margin>15</margin> are bound fittingly, stably, and with art.

### The Reaction of the Bondable. Art. XX.

Mutual favor produces mutual bonds. Bonds are also found in jests <note>original: "scommatibus," meaning biting or witty jokes.</note>, in acting, and in wit; through these, someone who is otherwise ugly and deformed can artistically bind those who are <margin>20</margin> susceptible to such things. ### The Heterogeneity of Bondable Subjects. Art. XXI.

Add to this that a species may have the quality of being bound by a different species—through love, hate, admiration, piety, 
<margin>10</margin>compassion, and other things of that sort. Thus, <term>Lesbia</term> is celebrated as being bound by her sparrow, <term>Corinna</term> by her little dog, <term>Cyparissus</term> by his doe, and the dolphin by <term>Arion</term>. <note>Bruno lists famous literary and mythological examples of bonds between humans and animals: Lesbia (from the poet Catullus), Corinna (from Ovid), Cyparissus (from Ovid's *Metamorphoses*), and Arion (the musician saved by a dolphin).</note> In short, in every species there are seeds of 
allurement toward the others. I say nothing of the sympathy between man and 
the lion, and I pass over the wonders I have known regarding the intimacy between a 
<margin>15</margin>dragon and a boy.

### The Mutation of Bondable Subjects. Art. XXII.

It is not difficult for a bondable subject to change from one type of bond to its opposite, just as the binder is also changeable; whether this occurs according to the reality of the thing or according to 
<margin>20</margin>opinion, it makes no difference. For instance, someone by whom I was once bound due to a reputation for learning—once that reputation was taken away by a greater light, bonds of contempt and indignation soon followed. Those bound by the appearance of a <term>blooming age</term> <note>original: "virentis aetatis," often used to describe the "green" or flourishing years of youth.</note> and beauty, which are not also reinforced by the bonds of 
character and intellect, are in time loosened and erased.

It is a hidden cause that binds one to love, hate, or contempt 
<margin>93^r</margin>beyond the act of reason; and it is a futile law of <term>Adrastia</term> <note>original: "Adrastiae." In Greek mythology and Platonic philosophy, Adrastia is a figure of inescapable destiny or Nemesis. Bruno suggests here that these sudden attractions are often attributed to fate when the rational cause is hidden.</note>...

...argument <note>original: "mentum," the conclusion of the word "argumentum" from the previous page.</note>, which claims that the reason for love—which arises from the sight of a presented beauty—is a certain recollection of divine beauty which the soul had perceived before it was received into the companionship of the body. ### Definition of the Bondable subjects. Art. XXIV.

<term>Theocritus</term> <note>A Greek pastoral poet from the 3rd century BCE, famous for poems about the lives and loves of shepherds.</note> attributed love and other passions, by which individuals are bound, to chance, fortune, and a certain "undefined" something; but he would have judged more correctly by considering and calling
<margin>15</margin>that thing "hidden and determined" which he called "undefined" simply because it was not apparent. Indeed, it arises from a determined principle of <term>complexion</term> <note>original: "complexionis." In Renaissance thought, this refers to the specific balance of "humors" or physical qualities in a person that dictates their temperament.</note>, which either nature has granted, or which use and habit have introduced.

### The Sense of the Bondable subjects. Art. XXV.

<margin>20</margin>The <term>Achaeans</term> <note>An ancient name for the Greeks.</note> referred the fact that something might be bound by love, hate, or other passions not to reason or a type of knowledge, but to fortune; hence they used to worship Love and Fortune at the same altar. Certain <term>Platonists</term> support this judgment, saying that
<margin>25</margin>mute animals are not always bound by love because they lack reason and <term>prudence</term> <note>original: "prudentia," meaning practical wisdom or the ability to judge a situation.</note>. But those people have too crude a perception of the nature of knowledge and intellect—which, along with the <term>spirit of the universe</term> <note>The "spiritus mundi" or "world soul," a central concept in Bruno's philosophy where a single vital force animates all matter.</note>, fills all things and from all things...

<summary>Bruno critiques the Platonic idea that love is merely a memory of divine beauty, arguing instead that attraction is determined by an individual's specific physical and habitual "complexion." He also challenges the idea that animals lack the "reason" required for love, suggesting that a universal intellect animates all beings.</summary>

### The Flight of the Bondable. Art. XXVI.

One person binds themselves with one kind of bond, and another with another, sometimes <unclear>......</unclear>, in order
<margin>10</margin> to escape from a single kind of bond. Hence, the one who wishes to bind must observe this: they should operate through the media of those things by which the bondable subject is already bound, specifically by complying with the bonds by which that subject is held. Thus, a Nymph lured a hunter—who was drawn away by love, anxiety, and occupation with wild beasts—
<margin>15</margin> toward Venus <note>The goddess of love, representing erotic desire and physical attraction.</note> using gifts of his own kind: specifically a horn by whose voice fleeing beasts were halted. A soldier might also be led away from other emotions by the virtue of arms and incantations. Therefore, hunting, fasting, drunkenness, gymnastic exercises, and generally various anxieties
<margin>20</margin> and leisure, as well as various abstinences and luxury, etc., all bind from the direction of Venus. Just as in this kind of bond, so must judgment be made in the others.

### The Substance of the Bondable. Art. XXVII.

There are two causes of bondability, and these same things belong to the essence of the bondable subject, insofar as it is bondable: knowledge according to the kind, and
<margin>25</margin> appetite according to the kind. If you grant something that in no way desires, you grant something that can in no way be spiritually bound.

### *Perfect Binding. Art. XXVIII.*
<margin>93</margin>

That which is tied through all its faculties and parts is bound perfectly. Therefore, the number of these parts must be investigated by the binder, so that if they wish to bind to the point of perfection, they may ensnare the bondable subject through many means, or even through all of them. To the binder, the various nourishments and enticements of the mind and spirit—corresponding to their diverse powers—must not be doubtful or inaccessible.

### *The Tying of Bondable Subjects. Art. XXIX.*

It is not possible for anyone to bind someone to themselves unless the binder is also bound to that person; for the bonds cling to and are inserted into the one bound. A binder who binds a subject to *another* <note>original: "vincibile alteri"; a third party, like a matchmaker or a politician acting for a sovereign.</note> is only bound by accident; however, a binder who binds a subject to *themselves* cannot help but be bound as well. Yet the binder holds this advantage over the one bound: they are the master of the bonds and sometimes are not affected or moved in equal measure. Proportional to this teaching is the fact that a pimp <note>original: "leno"; a procurer or someone who facilitates bonds for others.</note> binds and is not bound; but a female friend is not bound to a male friend in act unless the male friend is also bound to the female friend in act. Yet, from the spirit, the reason for the bond is sometimes hidden, whereby the loved object is bound to the lover, whom it sometimes does not know, let alone love. Within the same species and in the same order, Eros <note>The Greek god of love; here representing the impulse of desiring.</note> without Anteros <note>The god of reciprocal love; here representing the returned affection that completes the bond.</note> laments and is unfortunate. ### The Truth of the Bondable. Art. XXX.

<margin>5</margin> For a bondable subject <note>original: "vincibile"; the person or thing intended to be influenced or tied.</note> to be truly bound, it requires not so much "true" bonds—that is, those based on a factual or physical foundation—as it does apparent bonds, which arise from opinion. For the imagination can bind truly even without "truth" in the external sense, and through the imagination, the bondable subject is truly tied. For even if there were no Hell, the belief and imagination of Hell—despite having no basis in factual truth—creates a real and true Hell; <margin>10</margin> this is because the phantastic image <term>phantastic species: in Renaissance psychology, these were the mental images or sensory "forms" that populated the imagination and drove human behavior.</term> possesses its own kind of truth. From this it follows that it acts truly, and the bondable subject is truly and most powerfully constrained by it. So long as that belief and faith are eternal, the torment of Hell is eternal, <margin>15</margin> to such an extent that even the soul, once stripped of its body, still retains these same images. Nevertheless, or rather even more powerfully—sometimes due to a lack of discipline, or a certain perverse pleasure, or because the image has been so deeply absorbed—the soul persists in its misery for ages. We do not think much of the fact that common "philosophers" <note>original: "philosophantes"; likely referring to the Scholastic or Aristotelian academics of his time.</note> <margin>20</margin> do not grasp this and foolishly reject it with their most ignorant doctrines; since when we were children and inexperienced, we were just as full of their "logical" arguments as they, the "experts" and old men, are now. We forgive these "adults" for their views in this regard no less than we judge that we ourselves should have been forgiven <margin>25</margin> when we were children.

<summary>Bruno argues that psychological reality is as powerful as physical reality, suggesting that the "truth" of a bond depends more on the subject's imagination and beliefs—such as the fear of Hell—than on objective facts. He dismisses traditional philosophers who fail to recognize the objective power of subjective mental states.</summary>

# ON THE BOND OF CUPID
## AND IN A CERTAIN WAY IN GENERAL.

We stated in the work *On Natural Magic* <note>original: "De naturali magia"; this refers to one of Bruno's other foundational texts on the interconnectedness of the universe.</note> how all bonds are referred to the bond of love, <margin>5</margin> how they depend on the bond of love, and how they consist within the bond of love. Indeed, through thirty types of "knots" <term>knots (nodi): Bruno's term for the specific psychological or spiritual points of connection that allow one person or thing to influence another.</term> it will be easily demonstrated that love stands as the foundation of all emotions. For he who loves nothing has no reason to fear, hope, boast, be proud, dare, despise, accuse, excuse, <margin>10</margin> be humbled, feel envy, be angry, or be affected in other ways of this kind. The material is therefore wide-reaching and the consideration or speculation is broadly spread, to which we have given a handle under the title "The Bond of Cupid"; and this contemplation should not be thought to retreat too far from civil institutions <note>referring to social and political life</note>, <margin>15</margin> precisely because it is wonderfully more ample than any civil institution.

->Definition of the Bond. Article One.<-

Among the Pythagoreans and Platonists, the "bond of beauty" is called a splendor, a ray, and a certain act—or at least a shadow, a likeness, and a trace of it. First, it is diffused <margin>20</margin> into the **mind**, which it decorates with the order of things; second, into the **soul**, which it completes with a series of things <gloss>or "series of reasons"</gloss>; third, into **nature**, which it distinguishes and supports with seeds; fourth, into **matter**, which it adorns with forms. This ray is most clear in the mind, clear [in the soul...]

<summary>Bruno introduces the "Bond of Cupid" (Desire) as the fundamental basis for all human emotions and social structures. He explains the Neoplatonic concept of beauty as a "ray" that descends through four levels: Mind, Soul, Nature, and Matter.</summary>
<keywords>Cupid, Desire, Love, Passions, Neoplatonism, Beauty, Mind, Soul, Nature, Matter, Natural Magic</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the "Definition of the Bond" (Article I) from page 684, specifically discussing how the bond of beauty manifests in physical matter and social interaction before moving to Article II on the "Origin of the Bond."</meta>

<page-num>685</page-num>
<header>ON BONDS IN GENERAL.</header>

...in the soul, obscurely in nature, and most obscurely in the substance of natural things, so they say. This bond is not found in physical mass, <note>original: "mole"; referring to the physical bulk or weight of a body.</note> nor is it a persistent mass itself, although it is active around mass and throughout the magnitude of the universe. This is because not only large <margin>5</margin> things but also short ones appear beautiful; likewise, within the same species, large things may be deformed while small ones are beautiful, and vice versa. Often, while the same physical quantity remains, beauty is removed by some accident, and yet beauty can persist even when the quantity is changed. A most charming infant or young boy is pleasing, but the bond does not fully conquer <margin>10</margin> unless it is an adolescent of a certain age. Therefore, mass does play a part; for this remains true even when the form, figure, and complexion of the thing are not varied in the slightest. From this, one can lead into the civil types of binding, <note>referring to the ways people influence or "bind" one another in social and political life</note> through the measures of quantity in which the form and efficacy of the bond consist: you should refer these, I say, to gestures, words, clothing, customs, <margin>15</margin> laughter, and other signs of the emotions.

### The Origin of the Bond. Article II.

Certain of the Platonists define the bond as arising from a specific proportion of the limbs, occurring alongside a certain sweetness of colors. Yet, for those who look more closely—at least <margin>20</margin> at the fact that it is not only composite things made of a variety of limbs that bind, but sometimes a pure color or a pure voice; likewise, nothing fades or ages more quickly than beauty, while nothing is altered more slowly than the figure and form that shines outward from the composition of the limbs. <margin>25</margin> Therefore, the bond of beauty seems to reside in something other than the figure and proportion of the limbs; indeed, while the same beauty remains, as does the figure...

<summary>Bruno argues that beauty—the fundamental bond of attraction—is not a result of physical size or mathematical proportion alone, but exists in subtle signs like gestures and voice. He challenges the traditional Platonic view that beauty is merely the "proportion of parts," noting that beauty can vanish even when the physical structure remains unchanged.</summary>
