...sometimes after the enjoyment of the thing loved, love passes away. For this reason, the logic of a bond <note>original: "vinculi ratio"; the underlying principle or "reason" that makes a psychological or social tie effective.</note> consists especially in a certain mutual disposition between the captor and the captive. Indeed, sometimes <margin>94v</margin> in the beauty of a young girl, or socially in a person's conversation, <margin>5</margin> speech, dress, and actions as a whole—even though we have nothing that can be argued against by reason—they still do not please. Yet in another person, even though many or individual traits might be displeasing, that person will nonetheless please. It is quite foolish what they report concerning the bond of color, for they do not distinguish between color itself and <margin>10</margin> that which surrounds the color; for how does color by itself conquer, when a brighter color in an older person is displeasing and looked down upon, while a softer color in a younger person binds and seizes? Likewise, in social life, a serious and "consular" <note>original: "consularis"; referring to the dignity and authority associated with a Roman Consul, implying a speech that is overly formal or authoritative.</note> speech coming from a youth, however much it may shine with <margin>15</margin> skill, provokes more mature judgments to indignation by its appearance of arrogance; while a charming, flattering, and flowery speech from the mouth of an elder breeds contempt, and sometimes excites laughter and provides material for mockery. Thus, in the care of the body, in words, and in deeds, one thing is fitting for a matron, another for a <margin>20</margin> virgin, another for a girl, another for a boy, for a man, and for an elder; likewise, one thing for a soldier, and another for a civilian. <note>original: "togatum"; literally "one wearing a toga," the garment of Roman citizens in peace, used here to distinguish a civilian or statesman from a soldier.</note>

### The Indefiniteness of the Bond. Article III.

It is not so difficult (I believe) to bind and to loosen, as it is to find the bond—in those instances, I mean, in which <margin>25</margin> the bonds are attributed more to chance than to nature or art. Indeed, the bond that proceeds from the body has no defined part of the body; for there are eyes,

He then introduces the difficulty of identifying exactly where a bond resides when it arises from the body.</summary>

### *The Composition of the Bond. Article IV.*

The bond of the lower Cupid <note>original: "Cupidinis inferioris"; refers to earthly or physical desire as opposed to higher, spiritual love.</note> is such that we are bound by things that are composite and arranged; however, we are not <margin>10</margin> captured at all by things that are simple and absolute. There are even those who go so far as to despise such things; for them, God will not be thought to possess beauty in Himself, because, since His nature is a certain "simplicity" <note>In Renaissance philosophy, "simplicity" refers to being pure, undivided, and non-material, unlike the "composite" nature of physical bodies.</note>, it does not shine forth in the structured arrangement of a composition. <margin>15</margin> Yet it remains a matter of faith that He is the author and perfecter of all beauty and of every bond. Because of the weakness of their intellect, people do not distinguish between that which is *beautiful in itself* and that which is *beautiful to us*. Similarly, in social life, he lacks wisdom who does not distinguish between what is beautiful to all men and to <margin>20</margin> reason, and what is beautiful to *these* particular men according to custom, usage, and occasion; such a person desires to bind others incorrectly.

### *The Number of Bonds. Article V.*

Bonds consist—whether confusedly or consistently—of the form of the body, the condition of the body, the movement of the body, the <margin>25</margin> harmony of voices and speech, the elegance of manners, fortune, and the meeting of sympathies; by these things not only are humans bound to humans, and wild beasts...

<summary>Bruno explores the distinction between universal beauty and subjective attraction, arguing that while humans are often "bound" by complex physical arrangements, the ultimate source of all bonds is the "simple" beauty of God. He also begins a list of specific factors—such as speech, movement, and luck—that create these psychological ties.</summary>

...to wild beasts, but even wild beasts are bound to men. To this pertains the fact that, by natural character, a child upon seeing a snake, or a lamb upon seeing a <margin>95r</margin> wolf—even with no prior experience or knowledge—is mortally terrified; yet upon seeing an ox or a sheep, they play and rejoice together.

There are fumigations <note>original: "fumigia"; refers to incense, vapors, or medicinal scents used to influence the "spirits," which in Renaissance medicine were the subtle fluids connecting the soul to the body.</note> by which various men and various spirits are captivated. I have known people who remarkably abhorred the scent of musk and all those fragrances which are universally considered sweet, to the point that they would even collapse from the disturbance of their spirit; and among others, I knew one who took marvelous delight in holding bedbugs, crushed with his fingers, under his nose.

Thus, different things are bound by different things—not only contraries by contraries, but also by diverse things. And in civil matters <note>Referring to "civil bonds" (*vincula civilia*), or the social and political ties that hold human society together.</note>, the same style of speech, bodily adornment, and harmony or ease of manners is not approved of by a German as it is by an Italian, or even by one German and another; so much so that an Italian, departing from the norm, might possess a German temperament, or a German an Italian one. 

Hence there is difficulty, and greater prudence <term>prudentia; here meaning practical wisdom or the skill of a "binder" to navigate human nature</term> is required in "binding" civilly, especially when the bonds are cast not at a crowd, but at an individual. Indeed, it is easier to bind many than to bind one; just as a single arrow shot into a flock of birds can, even by chance, strike several more easily than a more precise aim can strike one specific bird out of many.

->The Gates of Bonds. Article VI.<-

The gates through which bonds are cast are the senses, and of all these, sight is the greatest and most noble; the others act more specifically according to the variety of their objects and powers. Thus, the sense of touch is bound by the smoothness of the flesh, hearing by the harmony <note>original: "symphonia"</note> of a voice, smell by sweet breath, and the soul by the elegance of manners...

<summary>Bruno explores how individual and national temperaments dictate what a person finds attractive or repulsive, concluding that the five senses—led by sight—are the primary "gates" through which psychological and social bonds are formed.</summary>

### The Kinds of Bonds. Article VII.

We understand there to be as many kinds and differences of bonds as there are kinds and differences of beauty; these differences, in fact, seem to be no fewer than there are primary things—namely, according to their species <note>original: "speciem"; in Bruno’s thought, this refers to the specific form or mental image that defines a thing.</note>. Add to this that in individual species, different particulars are bound in different ways and by different things. The hungry man is bound to food, the thirsty to drink, the man full of seed to Venus <note>Reference to sexual desire and procreation.</note>; this man is bound to a sensible form <note>An object perceived by the senses.</note>, that man to an intelligible one <note>An idea perceived by the intellect.</note>; one is bound to a natural form, another to an artificial one. The mathematician is bound by abstractions, the practical man by concrete things; the hermit is bound to masturbation by an absent form <note>original: "absente specie masturbans eremita"; Bruno is providing a blunt psychological observation on how the imagination can "bind" or stimulate a person even when the physical object of desire is not present.</note>, while the social man is bound by a present one. Different things according to every kind bind different people; indeed, bonds proceeding from different sources do not carry the same power within them. For the music of a boy or a youth binds, but that of a girl does not bind in the same way, nor does that of a man; strength binds by making a man highly esteemed, but in a woman, it binds very little; a young girl binds through her simplicity and honesty. However, if an adult is affected by such simplicity, it releases them from the bonds, and they become more and more displeased.

Thus, art is not detached from nature, and refinement does not depart from simplicity.

### Description of a Bond. Article IX.

<margin>20</margin> To **Plato**, a bond is a second kind of beauty or conformity; to **Socrates**, it is an excellent loveliness of the soul; to **Timaeus**, it is the tyranny of the soul; to **Plotinus**, it is a privilege of nature; to **Theophrastus**, a silent deception; to **Solomon**, it is hidden fire and stolen waters <note>A reference to Proverbs 9:17, often interpreted in the Renaissance as the allure of forbidden or secret desires.</note>; <margin>25</margin> to **Theocritus**, an ivory detriment <note>original: "eburneum detrimentum"; suggesting a beautiful but costly loss.</note>; to **Carneades**, a restless kingdom; and to **me**, it is a joyful sadness and a sad joy <note>original: "tristitia hilaris, hilaritas tristis." This paradox was Bruno's personal motto and appears on the title page of his play *Il Candelaio* (The Candlemaker).</note>. Other descriptions of the passions and types of bonds have an analogy to the present passion and bond, through those things which we have brought forward in the preface of this part.

<summary>Bruno argues that true attraction (binding) requires naturalness rather than over-refined affectation, famously defining the "bond" through a series of philosophical paradoxes ending with his own motto: "joyful in sadness, sad in joy."</summary>

### Distribution of Bonds. Article X.

For a perfect act, perfect things are bound; noble things are bound to the noble or to those who have been ennobled. To an imperfect act and to a defect, however, those things are bound in which there is some imperfection and <margin>5</margin> defect. Therefore, it was said in earlier sections <note>original: "in superioribus"; referring specifically to page 672 and 644 of the manuscript.</note> that something of the thing to be bound must already exist within the binder. A girl who is entirely chaste, in whom no seeds of <term>kindling</term><note>original: "fomitis"; a term used in theology and philosophy to describe the "tinder" or spark of desire or sin that remains in a person.</note> exist, cannot be bound to lust by any art or by any star, provided she is not touched, nor even reached—I say, without her participating in the hands of the binder, and <margin>10</margin> without some outpouring from the binder’s hand toward her. Of the immature, I shall say nothing; for in all acts there is a need for a certain "seed," and yet not all seeds proliferate everywhere. Who would not try in vain to ensnare <note>original: "irretire"; literally to catch in a net.</note> the sick, the elderly, the cold, or the mutilated? But who would not <margin>15</margin> be able to involve the person who is the opposite? In <term>civil bonds</term><note>original: "civilibus vinculis"; social or legal ties that govern human society, as opposed to natural or magical ones.</note>, a proportional judgment is entirely easy to make.

### Degrees of Bonds. Article XI.

Things in the universe are so ordered that they exist in a single coordination, such that by a certain continuous <margin>20</margin> flow <note>original: "fluxu"; a Neoplatonic concept where influence or "emanations" stream from the divine down through the layers of the world.</note>, a progression can be made from all things to all things. Some of these things cohere to others immediately, just as individuals of the same species do for natural propagation; among these, the bonds are kindred, familiar, and very easy. Other things, however, are subordinated through certain intermediaries, <margin>24</margin> and in these cases, it is necessary to pass through and penetrate all the intermediaries in some way, so that the bonds may be stretched out from the binder toward the thing to be bound. And so, the <term>divine powers</term><note>original: "numina"; spirits, gods, or divine influences that inhabit the natural world.</note>, through the nature of things...

<summary>Bruno argues that for a "bond" or attraction to work, there must be a shared quality or "seed" between the binder and the subject. He further explains that the universe is a continuous chain where bonds are easiest between similar things, but can be established between distant things through a series of intermediate steps.</summary>

<margin>10</margin> ->The Magnitude of the Bond. Article XII.<-

There is a certain divine power in all things; love itself is the father, the source, and the <term>Amphitrite</term><note>In Greek mythology, the goddess of the sea; here Bruno uses her name as a metaphor for the vast, all-encompassing "ocean" of bonds that contains everything.</note> of all bonds. By this bond, superior things provide for inferior ones, inferior things are turned toward the superior, and equals are associated with one another; ultimately, this is the perfection of <margin>20</margin> the universe according to the principle of form.

->The Effect of the Principal Bond. Article XIII.<-

A single love, a single bond, makes all things one; yet it shows different faces in different things, so that the same entity may bind different things in different ways. Hence, the same <term>Cupid</term><note>The god of desire, used here as a personification of the binding force of attraction that operates across all levels of reality.</note> is said to be both higher and lower, <margin>25</margin> the youngest and the most ancient, blind and yet most keen-sighted. ### Comparison of Bonds. Article XVI.

<margin>15</margin> The bond of all things is chiefly that of Venus <note>Here used as a metaphysical symbol for the force of attraction and unification.</note>, and the second kind is that of love, to whose equality and unity the bond of hatred is primarily and chiefly referred. For indeed, as much as we love one of a pair of opposites or contraries according to its kind, so much consequently do we hate and <margin>20</margin> despise the other. These two affects—and ultimately that single affect which is love—rule over all things (in whose substance hatred is included); love rules over all and elevates, directs, regulates, and moderates them. By this bond, all other bonds are loosened; thus animals bound by the bond of Venus <margin>25</margin> do not tolerate other females (in the case of females) or other male rivals (in the case of males). They neglect food, drink, and sometimes life itself; nor do they desist even when conquered, but having been crushed by the stronger, they [strive] all the more in...

### *The Time and Place of Bonds. Art. XVII.*

<margin>10</margin> Just as the propagation of things does not occur everywhere or always—even if the best seeds are sown—so too the ensnaring bonds do not conceive the power of their effect perpetually and everywhere, but only at the appropriate time and with a suitable disposition of the subjects.

<margin>15</margin> ### *The Distinction of the Bond. Art. XVIII.*

A bond that is purely natural or purely voluntary (according to the logic by which the common people distinguish between nature and will) does not exist. For the will, through its participation in the intellect and intelligence <note>Bruno argues that "will" is not a blind urge but is filled with a cosmic intelligence.</note>, flourishes everywhere <margin>20</margin> except where there is nothingness (as I have shown in other places); from which it follows that many people argue many things in vain. In us, according to reason, there are three distinct types of bonds (although they are all grounded in a single root of nature): the natural, the rational, and the voluntary. <margin>25</margin> Therefore, we cannot moderate one type of bond by means of another. For this reason, the laws of the wise do not forbid loving, but rather loving *beyond* reason; whereas the slanders of fools, without reason, prescribe the limits of reason to reason itself, [and to] the law of nature...

->The progression and ladder of the bond. Art. XVIII.<-

<margin>5</margin> The embrace of the bond and of Cupid <note>original: "Cupidinis"; Bruno uses the name of the god of love to represent the psychological force of desire and attraction.</note> is completed by the Platonists <note>The "Platonists" refers to the Neoplatonic tradition (like Marsilio Ficino) which analyzed the "ladder of love" as a sequence of mental states.</note> in this way. First, the form <term>species</term> <note>In Renaissance psychology, a "species" is the sensible image or likeness of an object that travels from the object to the eye.</note> of the beautiful or the good, and things of that kind, is carried into the external senses; second, it is drawn back into their center, which is the common sense <term>sensus communis</term> <note>The internal faculty where all five senses are unified and processed.</note>; third, into the imagination; fourth, into the memory. From there, the soul, through a certain natural inclination, <margin>97v</margin> <margin>10</margin> desires: first, to be moved, turned toward the object, and seized; second, having been turned and seized, it is enlightened by a ray of the beautiful, the good, or the true; third, enlightened and illuminated, it is set on fire by the sensitive appetite; fourth, being set on fire, it longs to cling to the beloved; fifth, clinging to it, it is even mixed and incorporated <margin>15</margin> into it; sixth, once incorporated, its former shape is lost, and it in a way abandons itself and is influenced by an external quality; seventh, it is transformed into the very subject of the quality into which it passed and by which it was so affected. They call the turning toward the movement the *preparation* of Cupid; the turning itself the *birth* <margin>20</margin> of Cupid; the enlightenment the *nourishment* <note>original: "pabulum"; literally "fodder" or "fuel."</note> of Cupid; the setting on fire the *growth* of Cupid; the clinging the *impulse* of Cupid; the incorporation the *mastery* of Cupid; and the transformation the *triumph* or *perfection* of Cupid.

->The condition of bonds. Article XX.<-

There are certain external things that bind, such as gifts, favors, honors, and duties; but they truly bind only when they do not bear that appearance by which they are offered <margin>20</margin> as if to "buy" love in return. For the appearance of trade <term>mercaturae</term> <note>Bruno warns that if a gift looks like a transaction, it loses its power to truly bond the soul.</note> is the appearance of utility and ignobility, and it leads to contempt.

->The property of bonds. Article XXI.<-

<header>GIORDANO BRUNO ON BONDS IN GENERAL.</header>

...humble and honorable; for the proud man loves those by whom he sees himself magnified <note>original: "magnifieri"; to be made great or held in high esteem.</note>, and all the more so the greater the person who does the magnifying. Indeed, it is a greater thing to be magnified by the great than by the small; in fact, we are even accustomed at times to despise being esteemed by the latter.
<margin>5</margin> The binder <note>original: "Vinciens"; the person establishing the psychological or magical bond.</note> watchfully protects the specific quality in which the proud man takes pride. For some—namely, soldiers—wish to hold the first rank in physical strength and vigor; therefore, if one does not grant them the first rank in worldly power or sagacity, they bear it easily.
Those philosophers, however, who glory in the knowledge of things, very <margin>10</margin> easily bear it if they are not magnified for their physical vigor. The same judgment applies to the casting of other bonds.

<margin>98<sup>r</sup></margin> ->The Grace of Bonds. Article 22.<-

Bonds cause one to desire the appearance of gratitude. For there arises (to introduce one kind of bond) a complaint among lovers, where they mutually presume that one owes something to the other. <margin>15</margin> The lover judges it the debt of the beloved to restore his soul which has been taken away—since he, having died in his own body, now lives in another’s. <note>This refers to the "transformation" mentioned on the previous page, where the lover's essence is transferred to the object of desire.</note> If the lover flatters the beloved less, she complains as if he cares for her less; the lover, in turn, complains against the beloved if <unclear>...</unclear>

<term>milites</term> (soldiers) — representing the active, physical life.
<term>philosophi</term> (philosophers) — representing the contemplative life centered on knowledge.
<term>amantes</term> (lovers) — those bound by the specific bond of erotic or spiritual desire.

<meta>This page transitions from the bibliographic concordance of the previous page into the actual philosophical text of Giordano Bruno. It explores his metaphysical arguments regarding the nature of the soul, specifically proving that the soul is an enduring substance rather than a temporary accidental property of the body. The text references his mnemonic system of "30 Statues."</meta>

<margin>on the part of receptivity?</margin>
It is called the sex and the receptacle. The material form <margin>the soul, that is, nature</margin> <margin>that the soul or divine souls are seen</margin> is such from the divine substance, yet not everything that enters there takes on that form and <unclear>becomes</unclear> an accident, because it is not capable of that same likeness. <margin>and various other things then said</margin> There is <unclear>a figure</unclear> both in negation or sending away, and in naming or repeating, and in prayer or petition; or see the section on the Atrium of Cupid.

<margin>
And it does not receive the condition of an accidental form <term>accidental form</term><note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a quality that can change or disappear without the thing itself ceasing to exist (like hair color), whereas a "substance" is the core essence</note> on the part of its formation. Every such accidental form vanishes through a certain dissolution or <unclear>loosening</unclear>, because once the material principles are consumed, the substantial form arising from their joining together ceases, just like more temporary accidents. The Soul, however, since it is a virtual Substance, persists in the truth of its essence no less than the material, elementary, and corporeal substance. Hence it is not even said separately: "The body is dissolved into dust and atoms; but the Spirit returns to its father." That is, it does not contain the form of something <unclear>vanishing</unclear> or going into nothingness, such as form and color, or any symmetry whatsoever.
</margin>

# From the Atrium of Cupid

On the part of judgment: Because judgment is provided through the soul—if it is not the soul itself which alone judges—but on the part of love: since the soul especially loves, and through that love it is seen to exist.

On the part of Choice: Because the soul itself <unclear>reveres</unclear> and through it the seeds of choice are picked.

The origin indeed of judgment, love, choice, speech, and the power to descend—if you choose all these—cannot be a mere accident.

# From the Hide of Amalthea <note>original: "Ex pelle Amaltheae" — referring to the goat-skin associated with the nursing of Zeus, here used as a mnemonic locus</note>, that is, From Difference

On the part of common difference, or difference according to genus: because the soul is a certain subject <note>A "subject" here means a foundational entity in which qualities reside</note>; however, no accident is a subject, whether in trees or in blackbirds.

On the part of alteration: Every accident is altered by the alteration of the subject, and it <unclear>acts</unclear> if it <unclear>is moved</unclear>. [...] it sees God: such things in all and concerning the world from above [...]

On the part of otherness or essential difference through which there is a holy possession, which is eternal; or through the markers of those contracting, those things which differ in genus. Therefore, the soul cannot be a material thing or a formal accident, because of the <unclear>vicissitude</unclear> and <unclear>change</unclear>.

# From the Field of Flowers <note>original: "Ex Campo Floris"</note>

On the part of eternity, which would not follow by reason: Every accident and corporeal form consists in a composition, preserved in a day or a whole period and a certain complexion. The Soul itself, however, creates its own character; it preserves itself, and not from changing principles, in which some things <unclear>decaying</unclear> and remaining consist. It is formed only as a substance. And life, preserving itself, acts so that it cannot depart from itself.

On the part of pure being: Because every accident flows into nothingness through corruption. Similarly, the form resulting from composition is <unclear>split</unclear> when dissolution arrives.

The Soul, however, is a substance which, as it is <unclear>indivisible</unclear> and impartible, does not suffer <unclear>extinction</unclear>.

On the part of transmutation: Everything that is corrupted is either converted as accidents are—and accidental forms are said to be corrupted—or it passes into something else.

The Soul, however, neither vanishes—because it is not an accident, which is the accident of a rational form—nor does it pass into something else, because it is a simple and single substance. It may perhaps pass elsewhere to operate, or to other mutations, but not into another subjective being, just as a <unclear>cause</unclear> might pass from one variety into another, or from the governance of nature to the building of a house.

In every way, it must be placed in the category of Substances and efficient causes, like bodies, yet not in the category of bodies or composites, or forms enslaved to bodies.

# From the Catapult <note>original: "Ex Catapa litis"</note>

From the greatest distance of contraries: in matter, opposites are more likely to be joined in the same time and the same subject, and they are perpetually distant by diameter.

Regarding contraries, however, the soul—or contrary forms—are unique in the soul, because they are understood from the same conception, so that the species and concept of one contrary <unclear>is derived</unclear> from the concept of the other. Therefore, it is not only material—as has been said—nor does it admit a material likeness in its subjective way of receiving. Far be it, then, that it could be an accident or a material form, <unclear>which</unclear> might seen to come upon it over a long stretch of time.

<column-break/>

Thus we have discussed, proving the soul to be a substance, not an accidental form, not an Entelechy <note>Aristotle’s term for the "actuality" of the body; Bruno argues here that the soul is more than just the body’s function</note>, not a harmony, nor any other similar thing.

Many more means can be drawn to prove the same thing, and whatever else can be taken by following the other members of the statues. Since we have selected only these prior ones as more convenient or weightier, the consequences will be seen everywhere, because we have grown accustomed to keeping this order: to proceed from the lighter means to the weightier and most powerful ones, so much so that the Last seems to include the union of all the others.

And so, giving thanks to GOD, we have completed the inventive Act through the 30 statues.

->The rest is so that each one, according to<-

what he believes, may be able to obtain from this light a good, better, or best fruit, and become accustomed to these things well, better, or best. For it contributes much not only to have encountered good discipline and light from good sources, but this seems to be the primary thing: That a person should strive to truly possess what they have, and cultivate the field according to their faith, and by watering the field with constant meditation on things, make the proper seeds of their own genius grow in those things, take increase, and let the fruit be offered in its own time. Unhappy and <unclear>deserting</unclear> are those whom even the divine powers testify they cannot cure; through leisure, torpor, and innate laziness, they bury their talent and leave the crop to be gnawed away by mice.

<meta>The previous page discussed the metaphysical nature of the soul as an enduring substance. This page shifts into the practical application of the "Lullian Art" to medicine, specifically the classification and timing of fevers (tertian, continuous, quotidian, and quartan) using the symbolic alphabet and geometric figures characteristic of Ramon Llull’s system.</meta>

## § v
And it is called a "tertian" fever <note>original: "tertiana"; a fever that recurs every third day by inclusive counting—meaning there is one day of fever, one day of rest, and then fever again</note> because the illness is discovered on the first day and is extended on the following day. And if B <note>In Lullian medicine, letters like A, B, C, and D represent specific elements or humors; B usually represents Air/Blood</note> abounds less in A <note>A usually represents Fire/Choleric humor</note>, the heat of the tertian fever consumes the natural heat in its usual way, and when extended, it becomes imperceptible as if dried out.

## § iij
And if the tertian fever is multiplied through the dimension <note>original: "dimm," likely abbreviation for "dimensionem" or "diametrum"</note> of BF, a double tertian fever follows. And since it is multiplied through the dimension of BF, a long-lasting state is maintained across all dimensions and regions. For on the 3rd day, it moves into the "house" of CG, and on the 5th day, it returns to the "house" of BF; therefore, on the 5th day, the patient is troubled more severely because it returns there, as happens on the 9th rather than the 7th, and on the 13th rather than the 11th, and so on for the others. And the tertian fever is multiplied so much through the dimension of BF that the double tertian is transformed into a continuous fever.

## § iiij. & v.
If a tertian fever is perceptible on the first day in the dimension of BF, it is very "wise" <note>likely meaning subtle or discerning in its progression</note> in B, and less strong than in D, and [less] than in H. ¶ And so, through these things we have said concerning tertian fever, the doctrine for the management of all other fevers is given. Nevertheless, we shall say something about the others individually and in order.

# Chapter iij. On continuous, slow, and very acute fever
## §. i.
A slow continuous fever differs from a very acute one in this: that the very acute fever is equal in all its regions born in the body. However, a slow continuous fever is [greater] in some regions and larger in others. Therefore, a very acute continuous fever stands out as greater than other fevers. For it troubles [the patient] so strongly and so frequently that it nearly conquers the man’s natural governance, which he cannot resist because the form of the body exists as a unity with life... <note>The text here becomes dense with Lullian jargon regarding the "ruling" of the soul over the body</note> therefore, the patient suffering such a fever is dissolved into something indigestible. Wherefore it is signified here that if any patient [moves] from a tertian or quotidian fever into a continuous one, it is so that they might be in a state of natural vigor.

# Chapter iiij On quotidian fever
## § I
A quotidian fever <note>original: "quottidiana"; a fever that occurs every day</note>... differs long from a double tertian; for the quotidian itself is caused by phlegm... because it caused digestion... and because the quotidian itself [is of] blood.

<column-break/>

<unclear>through a long diminution in which the humor... in which if the pulse and not unless the condition of which also the reason from the deep to the depth upon the perpendicular from here... which through the reason for also in its own way the discourse of governance</unclear> <note>This unclear passage appears to be using Lullian "perpendicular" logic—a method of connecting different concepts on a grid—to analyze the pulse and the depth of the illness</note>

# Chapter. v. on quartan fever
## §. i.
Quartana fever <note>original: "quartana"; a fever recurring every fourth day, typically associated with "black bile" or melancholy</note> is treated through the "house" of E-G. To have a perfect knowledge of this and other fevers, one must have recourse to the **Second Figure of the Art** <note>A key diagram in Ramon Llull's system consisting of three interlocking triangles</note>, namely to the **green, red, and saffron triangles**. For the beginning and cause of any disease are investigated through the "angle of the beginning," as will be seen in the chapter on the **grade of the elements** <term>gradus elementorum</term><note>A Lullian concept where qualities like heat or moisture are measured in four degrees of intensity</note>. For through such knowledge it is revealed how the fourth grade—which was the active agent through appetite and form—is corrupted and destroyed on account of the fever. Thus, it cannot hold the other grades ordered under itself toward a single end; because of this, each of the elements themselves seeks the end that suits it. Hence, one is not ruled or ordered by another, and thus the natural thing is destroyed, and the elements themselves are mixed together without any order. In this mixing and motivation, it is revealed that this is due to the destruction of the fourth grade, where the nobler <unclear>disposition</unclear> was, which potentially held the other four grades under it; and their operation, which was in the third, second, and first grade, would be reduced to the end of the aforementioned actual fourth grade without the formal [ordering]. However, since the cause of such a disease and [fever] are both the cause of death and thus coincide—as, for example, in **melancholy** <term>melancolia</term> <note>The humor associated with Earth, Cold, and Dryness</note> from predominance—therefore, a fever caused by melancholy requires a more dangerous cure than a [standard] quartan fever.

## § ij
For a quartan fever is to be treated in the region of E-G, because it invades the patient from the fourth day unto the fourth day.

## § iij
In the house of E-G, the fourth grade is disordered from its natural state on account of an overabundance... <unclear>for some reason</unclear>

<meta>This page continues the manuscript's exploration of natural philosophy, moving from the specific medical applications of the "Lullian Art" (seen on the previous page) back to the foundational principles of Aristotelian Physics. It specifically addresses the relationship between "Prime Matter" and "Form," referencing both Aristotle and Thomas Aquinas to define the basic "stuff" of the universe.</meta>

In matter and form, there are types of things composed of essential parts. Matter is spoken of, and form is called the "reason" <note>original: "ratio"; here meaning the defining principle or essence</note> of changeable things. Likewise, "prime matter" <term>materia prima: the most basic, formless substrate of all physical reality</term> is the first subject of a thing and the first ground of the changeable. <margin>Privation, which is matter [and] corruption <note>referring to the Aristotelian triad: matter, form, and privation (the lack of a form)</note></margin> This is according to the nature of how things are able to change and be generated.

To Thomas <note>likely Thomas Aquinas, the 13th-century philosopher who synthesized Aristotelian thought with Christian theology</note> it seems that changeability is found in prime matter because something else can be predicated of it. For prime matter would not exist unless, when all qualities are taken away from a thing, that same essence and its parts remained behind. Similarly, according to Aristotle, matter is subject to corruption only because change occurs within it—namely, by the arrival of a form and the departure of its opposite. Therefore, matter is incorruptible and ungeneratable; for if it were generatable, it would have to be made out of something else, and it would be necessary for another thing to underlie that generation, and thus prime matter would not be the "first" subject. Truly, the "appetite" of matter <note>the scholastic idea that matter "desires" or is inclined to receive a form</note> remains the same even when the matter itself is made ready to receive a form.

## Definition

Therefore, matter is defined as the "first subject" of each individual thing. This "first subject" does not refer to time <margin>it seems / within the part of the subject / to prepare in time / generally to flow by reason / that which is before the first / the greatest universal / in the front / as if the matter and matrix / of human things / and its own</margin> because it underlies no specific form in time; rather, it relates immediately to "substantial form" <term>substantial form: the essential nature that makes a thing what it is, such as "humanity" or "goldness"</term>. Through the mediation of substantial form, "accidental forms" <term>accidental forms: non-essential qualities like being tan, tall, or cold</term> then follow. These accidents belong to a different kind of subject, which is the "composite" thing—that which is already built from these parts: the first subject and the substantial form.

<keywords>prime matter, substantial form, accidental form, Aristotle, Thomas Aquinas, corruption, generation, scholastic philosophy, metaphysics</keywords>

<meta>This page marks a significant shift from the previous page's abstract philosophical inquiry into Leibniz’s "Prime Matter" and "Individual Forms." We move from the theoretical nature of the soul and substance to a grim historical record: the 1600 account of the execution of the philosopher Giordano Bruno, as recorded in the archives of the Confraternity of San Giovanni Decollato.</meta>

->Thursday, February 16:<-

<margin>
Justice <note>a contemporary euphemism for a state execution</note> of an impenitent heretic, his miserable life ended.
</margin>

At 12 o'clock at night, the Company <note>The Confraternity of San Giovanni Decollato, a lay organization dedicated to comforting those condemned to death</note> was notified that Justice was to be carried out on a heretic the following morning. For this reason, at 6 o'clock at night, the comforters gathered and went to Sant' Orsola. Having gone as far as the Large Tower <term>Torrone: the main prison of the Roman Inquisition</term>, they entered the secret cell. The sentence was read to him, and seeing that he remained as hard as a stone <note>original: "simile sasso"; implying he was unmoved by the legal warnings or the threat of death</note> despite the written charges and warnings, etc. —

Giordano, son of the late Giovanni Bruno, an apostate friar <term>apostate: one who has abandoned their religious vows or faith</term> from Nola in the Kingdom <note>The Kingdom of Naples</note>, the impenitent heretic. He was exhorted by the said fathers with all charity, and they called for two Fathers from San Domenico <note>Dominicans</note>, two from the Gesù <note>Jesuits</note>, two from the New Church, and one from San Girolamo. These men, with all affection and great learning, showed him his error; yet, in the end, he remained forever in his cursed obstinacy, his brain and intellect spinning with a thousand errors and vanities. He persevered in his obstinacy so that he was led by the ministers of Justice to the Campo de' Fiori, and there, stripped naked and tied to a stake, he was burned alive. He was accompanied throughout by our Confraternity singing the litanies, and we comforted him until the very last moment, but he never wished to hear of any devotion; with this, he finally ended his miserable and unhappy life. —

<summary>This harrowing eyewitness account records the final hours and execution of Giordano Bruno on February 17, 1600, detailing his refusal to recant his beliefs despite the efforts of various religious orders.</summary>
<keywords>Giordano Bruno, Inquisition, execution, Campo de' Fiori, heresy, Roman history, Confraternity of San Giovanni Decollato, apostasy</keywords>
